episodes.title: Surviving White Island and what happened next — Stephanie Browitt's story
episodes.description: At 23 years old, Stephanie Browitt willed herself to stay awake long enough to survive a volcano eruption on New Zealand's Whakaari / White Island. More than six years later, her resilience and sanity remains as strong as ever.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. In December 2019, Stephanie Brout, along with her mum, her dad and her sister, flew up from Melbourne to Sydney, where the four of them boarded one of those supermassive cruise ships called the Ovation of the Seas that was going to take the family around the South Pacific. One of the day trips the cruise was offering when they got to New Zealand was the chance to visit a live volcano on an island named Wakaari, or White Island. This is New Zealand's most active volcano. But the Brout family didn't know that. They weren't told. Nor did they know that the day before the ship had left Sydney Harbour, the New Zealand authorities had issued an alert that White Island was now entering a phase where an eruption was more likely than normal. . . .

For centuries there were these institutions in Italian cities set up by the church to receive foundlings, the children of unmarried mothers. shocks. So we keep hearing from our leaders. So in Australia, the government is preparing to hand
down the budget. And we've had both the Treasurer, Jim Chalmers, and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese
repeatedly say, look, even if this war ended tomorrow, the tail, the economic tail is still
going to be long. How long? And are we still just talking about oil at that point? Or are we talking
about all those other supplies that we've been trying to get through from the Middle East, such as helium
and some really important ingredients for things we don't even realise necessarily that we're using?
What is it that defines that, Talwin? And how long do you think it really is?
So right now, markets are suggesting the tensions could remain high for weeks or months, not years.
Now, by the way, we have a long history of underestimating the duration of wars. So don't take optimism
too seriously. But if you look at oil price futures, they seem to suggest that oil is going to be high
through 2027, 28 and 29. Not as high as it is right now, but higher than it was before the war,
substantially higher. So, you know, the shock that persists will be maybe a third as large as it was.
We're doing really rough arithmetic, but it'll be about a third of what we're suffering right now
for a couple of years. Now, some of that might be because there's been some literal destruction of
ports and drilling infrastructure and so on that literally takes time to rebuild. But I also
suspect part of what's going on there is, well, actually, if they just get together and they hug it
out, lots of things get back to normal, that would be good. But it's also possible they hug it out in
a year's time, they're back at it. And all of a sudden, the Middle East feels more dangerous.
And what markets are pricing is not this shock, but the possibility that the world has revealed itself
to be more dangerous and there'll be future shocks. So that's the lookout for the future
part of this. The defence spending that comes out of this, which, as we discussed, I think could be
very, very large. It would be realistic to think of that as being high for a decade.
The rewiring of global power and of global influence, if, for instance, the American security
umbrella becomes unreliable for the Australians, that's incredibly expensive, right? Do you really
want to go and set up a military for a country of our size? And do you want to try and do that quickly?
We're not there yet, but we've also seen things like the president sort of half walk away from NATO,
which does sit and train a lot of really important military spending. And then there are sort of harder
things, which is sometimes revealing a vulnerability is just as bad as creating one. And this exercise
has revealed the global economy is vulnerable to attacks on the Strait of Hormuz. And it is not the
only choke point on the globe. And so now that Iran understands its strength, how will it use it?
Now, my guess is one of my favourite things about being Australian is often the rest of the world
forgets about us. And that would be marvellous. I mean, it hurts our feelings, but it would be marvellous
because if they're in the business of extracting concessions and they come after the Americans and
they come after the Europeans and they simply forget that we exist, that would be great. It could be
they come after the developed world in a way that really has an effect on Australia.
Justin, what is your assessment of the US economy and its ability to withstand these shocks?
Issue for who wins a war is a function of how much you can damage the other side,
for which the United States is clearly overwhelmingly the world's greatest power
and how much damage you can withstand. And that, I think, is a very telling part that the administration
refuses to talk about. But the extent of suffering in the United States is A, real and B, substantially
less than anywhere else on earth almost. I mean, the Middle East countries that are all rich,
they think this is great. But we are roughly speaking, the United States is roughly speaking,
energy independent. And so it has hurt the US less than it's hurt Europe, less than it's hurt Asia.
Well, so no one likes the present anymore. And if his ability to withstand political heat is very low,
it doesn't matter how destructive his bombs are, because the Iranians can keep the strait closed
and exact political pain upon him that he seems quite unwilling to wear. And so it's not a question
of the state of the Ukraine. But I think this is important, which is what matters here is a function
of the willingness to withstand economic pain that translates into political pressure.
Because the president went to war without ever asking Americans for sacrifice, without ever explaining
why this is important, the commitment of the folks in the suburbs is zero. They just pissed that petrol's
more expensive. And as a result, they're willing to vote out Republicans at the next election
based on this. And as a result, the president has a very weak hand because the economic pain
translates into a degree of political pain that the president is unable and unwilling to withstand.
What are the policy options available to the US? And how would you compare those to the policy
options available to the Australian government? Institutionally, are there any differences that
make one stronger than the other or put one in a better hand than the other?
Yeah. The US started the war, the US can end it. Albo could sit around and decide war's a really bad
idea, but no one cares. And I mean that with all due effect and reverence for our prime minister.
What about inflation though? Isn't this something that policymakers will be preoccupied with if
energy costs are driving up prices? Absolutely preoccupied with, but things like a petrol tax
holiday, gimmicks and Band-Aids. Well, that's what we did in Australia.
There's a reason I said that. I read the Australian papers now. And even the populist Americans have
avoided it. It doesn't change the other one. So you don't think the government should have done
that to insulate from the shock? You actually think it's better to have people feel that pain?
No, I'm against pain. But if you gave me a bucket of money, $100 million, and you said,
Justin, you get to give $100 million to alleviate human suffering, I wouldn't give it to drivers
rather than non-drivers. And I wouldn't give it to people in proportion to how fuel inefficient their
cars are. That's what a gas tax holiday is. It is a terribly, terribly targeted social policy
that goes to rich more than poor, that goes to folks who drive big cars rather than small cars,
that has differential impacts by urban versus rural. It is hard to imagine a social problem
for which a petrol tax holiday is the efficient solution. Can we zoom out a bit from that?
You said in your Boyer lectures that Australians, the strength of Australia's institutions, I mean,
we've been hearing this right from the financial crisis through on, that the strength of our
institutions in Australia will insulate us from the global shocks. Is that still your view here in
2026? Having strong institutions means we will deal better with these shocks than if we had weak
institutions. Unquestionably, yes. So, a very simple one is the exchange rate helps us. Having a
floating exchange rate helps us a whole heck of a lot. Even better, Australian policymakers,
as much as you could and every day do, criticize, you know, what they do today versus tomorrow and when
they do it and how they do it. And I just played that game. Australian policymakers are still more likely
to make choices that are in the public interest than is the case in many, many other countries.
So, Latika, I love your question and I love it because what it forces one to do is zoom out.
So, so often in Australian economic policy debates, the question is, will the RBA rise off or not
tomorrow? What's going to happen to fuel prices next week? Fair enough, reasonable questions,
but they're actually fundamentally boring. The really important question is,
why is Australia one of the world's most prosperous nations? What led to that? How can we defend that?
And how can we even lean into it so that, you know, everything that makes life in Australia grand
is even grander? Justin Wolfers, thank you so much for joining us again on Global Roaming.
A pleasure.
Geraldine, if he is right about some of the things he was saying there,
it might be the second interview we've done together where we both leave feeling reassured because
he also wasn't entertaining any notion of a global recession really, was he?
Just a mild one, which I might add that if you look underneath the IMF, they do say there could be
a mild recession. But as he also makes it plain, and I thought he did that quite well,
mild recessions, you know, two words, can have huge impacts on daily lives for real people. So,
you know, don't let's be cool about mild recessions, but I don't know quite when though.
No, I think only Mr. Trump and the Iranians might know when, Geraldine, because as he rightly says,
the greatest policy option of all, to paraphrase Whitney Houston, is stopping the war. And really,
there's only two parties now who have a stake and interest in doing that. And
no progress there so far, Geraldine.
No. And I mean, and just that bit about institutions. I mean, one of the things that
I think is going to be very interesting to look at in Australia is just how the Reserve Bank
manages all of this. You know, they are determined that the inflation jockey, shall we say,
won't be let out of the cage the way it was in the 70s and early 80s when in the last gigantic sort
of oil price rise shock we had. And there's been very sort of sobering reminders of people giving
interviews sort of saying, look, this is the moment we must not yield, even though we'll have
to explain ourselves. And Australians will say, two more interest rate rises, you've got to be kidding.
But they say, you know, people with short memories don't realise what damage it did to expectations,
employer, labour relations in the 70s, when people just believed that prices were going to keep going
on up. So that's another very interesting aspect, I think, of what we're going to watch in the
aftermath. I agree. And I'm watching with interest the Australian budget. What is it? A couple of
weeks now. If I was in government right now, Geraldine, and I watch the UK with some
dismay and agog, I would not let this crisis go to waste. This is the time, if you're a government,
that's been toying with some difficult policy decisions or some difficult arguments to sell
that they might never have been able to do but secretly wanted to do.
Now, Latika, we've had some interesting feedback. And this is from Gail. I've never heard anybody
quite so certain of his own opinion as James Crabtree, who was our guest last week, Latika,
on the State of the UK. Nor did he come up for air. But I would have liked Latika to challenge him
within the interview on his optimism. And who are the big spenders she referred to who've left London
making it less vibrant? How does that work? In what way has it affected the city? The crime situation
is self-evident. Crabtree may be correct, but maybe put your concerns to him directly next time. Thank
you. Thank you, Gail. Now, Latika.
Gail wants a fight club, Geraldine.
He was optimistic. I think it was good to take stock of what James had to say because
maybe he's right. You know, he did speak about a lot of institutional strengths. And when he put
it the way he did about he'd rather be in Europe and having the club of all these countries around
him than Australia. He'd rather have the universities than our universities. I heard him say that.
No, I, I, that was a little snobbish, too. I, I don't disagree with him about the European club,
though. I, I do think Australia could be quite vulnerable very suddenly. Things like that,
I didn't totally disagree with him. But I think what I was trying to say in my commentary at the
end, Gail, was that a lot of these things are a vibe about where London's at at the moment. And I
think James was talking very much about some of the fundamental institutional strengths.
Don't forget to write to us. You can see that we do respond. We let you influence us. We love your
questions and feedback. Our email is global.roaming at abc.net.au. Thanks to our producer on this
episode, Aston Brown, and acting executive producer, Kylie Gray. Kylie Morris, and I'll be back tomorrow.
We're talking to American attorney, writer and former executive director of Human Rights Watch,
Kenneth Roth, about accountability in war and how the International Court of Justice case against
Israel and the International Criminal Court case against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is progressing.
See you, Geraldine. Bye-bye.
You've been listening to an ABC podcast. Discover more great ABC podcasts, live radio and exclusives on the

title: ABC Business Daily with Carrington Clarke and Alan Kohler - ABC listen
description: The podcast that helps you unpack the latest business and finance news. Analysing the stories moving share markets, shaping industries and affecting the Australian economy. Monday to Thursday, ABC Senior Business Correspondent, Carrington Clarke, examines the biggest business news with ABC's specialist reporters. From finance to AI technology and politics, the team will break down what happened, why it matters and what it might mean for you and your financial future. On Fridays, trusted Australian financial journalist Alan Kohler hosts an in-depth interview with the decisions-makers, innovators and strategists who are shaping the economy. 'That’s Business with Alan Kohler', invites well-known CEOs, entrepreneurs and politicians in for a deep dive into the tough lessons learned and unspoken rules driving Australian business. Host Carrington Clarke is a former economist, ABC North America correspondent from Washington DC and East Asia correspondent from Seoul, He previously worked as a Sky News Journalist and Fairfax Media editor. He has also reported for ABC Investigations’ flagship current affairs television program ‘7.30’ and ‘The Business.’ Host Alan Kohler AM is a former editor of The Age, The Australian Financial Review (AFR) and a columnist for The Sydney Morning Herald and Chanticleer in AFR. He was also the business editor for ABC Investigations’ flagship current affairs television program ‘7.30’ and the host of ‘Inside Business.’ For more sharp insights, clear explanations, and business news coverage you can trust, hit follow or favourite to add new episodes of ABC Business Daily and That's Business with Alan Kohler to your playlist, on ABC listen app, or wherever you get your podcasts.

episodes.title: The ACCC takes Woolies to Court
episodes.description: The cost of a family pack of Oreos became the centrepiece of the opening day of a court case pitting the consumer watchdog against supermarket giant Woolworths.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Why do humans hold on to stuff? Oddments we don't use and yet can't quite throw out. It's not just you and me. Australia's oldest library is crammed with stuff that isn't books. Terrible paintings, old menus, human hair. Is this history or hoarding? I'm Annabelle Crabb. Come and have a rummage through the story of us told by our stuff. Search for the History or Hoarding podcast on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts. The cost of a family pack of Oreos became the centrepiece of the opening day of a court case pitting the consumer watchdog against supermarket giant Woolworths. The ACCC says Woolies price drop marketing misled customers about what discounts were being applied to a range of items. And in the United States, the Senate gathered to grill Trump's nominee for Federal Reserve chair amidst the backdrop of a criminal investigation against the man currently holding that position. Welcome to ABC Business Daily. I'm Carrington Clark. And I'm ABC Business reporter Steph Chalmers. Steph, thanks so much for joining me. So let's maybe use these Oreo biscuits as a way into this story, because what is actually at stake in this case? What is Woolies accused of? Yeah, I mean, the Oreo biscuits really exemplify what we're hearing about over, it's over 260 items that Woolworths is alleged to have done this behaviour on. So essentially, they're saying that discounts Woolies offered were false because they artificially raised the price ahead of then dropping the price so that they were able to offer promotion. So if you look at the Oreos family pack, as you discussed, that was sold for several years for less than $4. Then the price was very briefly raised to $5. And then it was dropped to $4.50 and promoted as price dropped. So that's really the crux of this case that the ACCC has brought against both Woolies and its rival Coles. Those supermarkets are defending it separately. So we had the hearings into Coles earlier in the year, and now it's Woolworths' turn. We're talking about Oreos this time instead of dog food, which is a little bit more pleasant. I feel a bit more familiar with Oreos. I don't buy that brand of dog food that was being discussed in the Coles trial. But I think it's something every shopper can relate to is seeing those red or yellow stickers on the shelf and kind of intuitively knowing what they mean. And that's what the ACCC is arguing is that it really is consequential if these aren't genuine discounts, if the price was artificially raised and then lowered. They're saying, you know, the magic, the subtle magic, they called it, is that consumers know what these tickets mean. They have a very short period of time to kind of glance at them and know what the promotion is offering them that is supposedly a lower price. And then, you know, they're saying it isn't a lower price because it was raised very briefly. Yeah. I mean, it is such a fascinating case in that we obviously have a consumer watchdog and a competition watchdog for a reason, right? The ACCC is there to kind of protect the interest of consumers by making sure that any business isn't misleading them when it comes to pricing. And there are rules around how you can identify what is a discount and what isn't a discount. But it isn't as ironclad is it about exactly how long a product has to be at a certain price before you can reduce it. And one of the arguments from Woolies is that these price drops, as they call them, were happening at a time when prices were going up at a rapid rate, otherwise because of inflation. And so that's one thing that customers also recognize, right, which is that the price of milk today is not the same price it was 10 years ago. And so we have a natural kind of inflation happening or I should say an economy-wide inflation happening. And so Woolies is trying to argue that in, say, the example of the Oreos, yes, it might have only been a temporary window where this price went up. But it was a genuine discount because it would have stayed up if they weren't able to negotiate a better deal with the supplier. Yeah, exactly. So the ACCC is talking about this manufactured price spike, whereas Woolworths is saying, no, that wasn't just something we did for the purpose of this promotion. This was a genuine cost increase that our supplier came to us and negotiated. And what, you know, if you don't think about it that much, you might be surprised, but most people probably aren't surprised, that these price drop periods are pre-negotiated. And that's in the evidence as well that's being presented in this case is that when the supplier and Woolworths are talking about raising the price, they're also pre-planning dropping the price. So it's not, you know, they just decide willy-nilly to offer a discount because they feel sorry for people having to pay $5 now for Oreos. This is all planned. And that is part of what the ACCC is arguing as well is that it's not genuine because it is kind of planned and they've only offered it for a very short period of time. And that's misleading the customer into thinking they're getting a better price when in fact they were getting a better price for several years when Oreos were less than $4. I mean, I think a lot of people are obviously very attracted when you go shopping around a supermarket. They almost instinctively look for those yellow or red tags to indicate that something is a reduced price. People like to feel like they're getting a bargain. The businesses themselves know that this is a very effective tool. But yes, there's this kind of fundamental question of whether or not it's okay for the business to be negotiating with the manufacturer to discount kind of in advance for the price after the price is going up. So they're basically saying they've spoken to the manufacturer. The manufacturer says our costs have gone up. So this is what we need our new normal price to be. And then the supermarket says, well, let's work out a way of reducing the price for a set period because we want to ensure we're selling more of them. And perhaps we're looking at what our competitors are charging for that same product. And that seems to be fairly standard in Australian retail. That element of it doesn't seem to really be in contention here. You hear about price investment and it's really considered part of their marketing budgets for particular products are offering these discounts periodically. Or the price dropped tag is kind of a longer term signal that the price has been cut. So the argument here between the ACCC and Woolies is really around is this time reasonable? And as a result, it's really led to, you know, it's better me than you having to listen to this. It's really quite dry, quite legalistic. I thought you were enjoying the first day, Steph. For a few minutes I was. But yeah, it was quite, you know, quite technical around essentially the judge was saying, why are you bringing in all these other things about inflation and why you are raising the price? Aren't we really just arguing about whether you need to raise it for longer and otherwise it's misleading for customers? And whether there should be clear rules about how long it needs to be at a higher price before you can say that it is now a special or discounted price. Exactly. And there are rules in other jurisdictions about this. So I was just having a look in the UK. I think it's around 28 days. You have to have this price establishment period before you can then advertise a discount from a particular price. So we don't have that here. So the ACCC is prosecuting this on this misleading, you know, element of the pricing. So it could be quite consequential for how supermarkets have to price items depending on what the outcome is. And I think the other thing to mention is because we have such dominant and few supermarket chains here, you're talking about things like the Coles down, down promotion and price drop tickets are woolies. I think most Australians could just instantly picture that in their mind. It really is kind of part of the visual language of shopping. You know, it's not like some niche thing. episodes.title: Fuelcast: A shipment secured
episodes.description: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Energy Minister Chris Bowen have announced four additional cargoes of diesel have been secured for Australia. It’s an additional 200 million litres of diesel, coming from South Korea, Brunei and Malaysia.
episodes.transcript: This is an ABC podcast. Welcome to FuelCast. I'm Carrington Clark and this is your source to stay on top of the numbers behind the ongoing energy crisis. It's Wednesday, April the 22nd. We're recording mid-morning. Let's dig in. The price of Brent crude has risen to US$99 a barrel. And since we last checked in, the national average price of unleaded has dropped to $1.98 per litre. And the national average price of diesel has dropped to $2.88 per litre. Today I'm joined by Ian Verinder to dig into today's major energy headlines. Good morning, Ian. Good morning, Carrington. Ian, we've just been watching the Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Energy Minister Chris Bowen. Tell us about these four additional cargoes of diesel being secured for Australia through BP, Viva Energy and Export Finance Australia. They say it's an additional 200 million litres of diesel and the cargoes have come from South Korea, Brunei and Malaysia. Ian, does this fill you with any optimism? Well, it's better than not having it, let's face it. And, you know, we as a nation have the highest consumption of diesel per person than any other country on the planet. And the reason for that is we're, you know, a massive mining country and a huge agricultural country as well. So we require vast amounts of diesel to keep our industry going. And it's a big continent with a relatively small population, which requires a lot of transport, intercity transport, all run by diesel. There's a percentage of cars around about, I think, 10% of passenger vehicles run on diesel as well. And those vehicles, they're subject to what's known as what economists call elasticity of demand. You know, if the price gets too high, you don't drive your car. You catch the train, you walk, you ride a push bike. But when you're, you know, driving a Mack truck from one city to another, or you're running BHP's, you know, iron ore division up in the Pilbara, you have no option but to keep using the same amount of fuel regardless of the price. And so we need supply. And that's what we're concentrating on at the moment. Supply, not so much price. Yeah, that's right. So it's good to not be obviously caught short. The worst nightmare would be for the Bowsers to run dry or there not be enough supply of diesel, as you say, to fuel our mining industry or our agricultural industry. But we don't actually know how much is being paid for this diesel. And so we don't really know what that means for the price of diesel here at home, do we? Well, we don't know anything really. It's totally opaque and look at the moment and quite rightly, the government is focused on supply, just making sure we've got enough fuel to keep the country running. Bye, Ian. Thanks, Kerrickson. Thank you.
