episodes.title: Why hasn't the price of natural gas spiked?
episodes.description: When Russia launched its full scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, it sent the price of natural gas soaring - and Australian consumers faced steep hikes in their electricity bills.
episodes.transcript: This is an ABC podcast. What would you do if someone you loved vanished and you discover the person she's been living with isn't who they said they were? I'm Dominique Bayens, host of Expanse, The Nan Up 4. Is he, you know, a murderer? A self-styled cult leader. It's just not knowing the emptiness, really. That just kills you. This is the bizarre story of The Nan Up 4. Binge all episodes now. Search Expanse on ABC Listen and iView. When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine back in 2022, it sent the price of natural gas soaring and Australian consumers faced steep hikes in their electricity bills. But this time around, when once again war has sent the international price of gas skywards, Australia has remained relatively insulated. So what's the difference this time around? And a major tech announcement with long-serving Apple CEO Tim Cook stepping down and anointing his successor. Welcome to ABC Business Daily. I'm Carrington Clark. And I'm the ABC's Chief Business Correspondent, Ian Verinder. Ian, thank you so much for joining us. We've been very focused, obviously, on the soaring price of petrol and diesel. But here in Australia, we're not as focused on the soaring international price of gas. This is something that's obviously preoccupying people, both in East Asia and in Europe, where they have seen a real impact on the price that they're paying for their gas. Why aren't we paying increased prices here in Australia in the way that we did during that Russian invasion of Ukraine? Well, I think it gets down to the amount of power that the gas exporters actually have. And if you've cast your mind back to 2022, I mean, what everyone was focused on, the cost of living crisis. And what was really underpinning that cost of living crisis? I mean, everyone was just up in arms about electricity bills that were doubling each year. Extraordinary rises. I know. And what really drove that was the price of gas. And the reason for that is, even though a lot of our electricity is generated by coal, a lot of it by renewables, and only a smallish part by gas, gas is the swing factor. Gas is what economists would term the marginal cost producer, right? So essentially, when you can't generate anything more from coal, when your renewables are offline, you switch on the gas to generate that last little bit. And because it's the marginal cost producer, it actually sets the price. And so as a result of that, our electricity bills soar. Now, if you look to across the country, New South Wales and Queensland use a lot less gas than they do in, say, Victoria, right? So Victorians use a lot of gas for household heating, for cooking. And so they were getting the double whammy. They were getting huge electricity bills, plus these massive increases in price for their gas supply. Now, this time around, it's suddenly not happening. Not only are we not getting the price hikes that you would have expected if you use the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine as a base model, we're not getting those price hikes, we're actually getting cheaper gas than we had just a few months ago. So this does seem strange. Back in 2022, there was a lot of kind of political pressure and public pressure about gas companies extorting, it was some of the language used, the Australian consumer, because they were making huge profits by selling gas from Australia into this global market. And they were instead sending that gas offshore, even though there was huge demand for it here. Why hasn't that played at this point? Well, they were actually siphoning gas out of the domestic system, right, and then sending it offshore because the prices they could get offshore were just extraordinary. And so as a result of that, you've got massive price rises here. But even before the Russian invasion of Ukraine, I mean, we had, you know, there was uproar across the country because gas prices, you know, before on the East Coast we're talking about here, before the export market opened up and around about 2010, 2012, gas prices were about $3 a gigajoule. We're now just, you know, in heaven because they're $10, right? But during that war, they went up to above $20 a gigajoule. So just massive price hikes. And that had, you know, three successive prime ministers try to intervene to stop this. Now, you had Malcolm Turnbull with his ADGSM, I think it was, what is it, Australian Domestic Gas Supply Mechanism. You had Scotty Morrison with his big stick. Do you remember the big stick? And then you had Anthony Albanese with price controls. None of it worked. None of it worked. But suddenly it's all working now. Taking one step back, because I think this is a thing a lot of people struggle to understand, because we have a situation where prior to Australia becoming a major exporter of gas, we actually had less gas supply. We weren't getting as much gas out of the ground. But yet then when we started exporting gas, so there's more supply, people think, well, if you've got more supply, don't the fundamentals tell you that you should actually have lower prices? But the issue was by Australia becoming a gas exporter and having these facilities, we actually became a price taker for the international price. So whatever was kind of the international price, and when we saw a big spike, suddenly Australians' consumers were paying that price instead of just having whatever the domestic supply and demand curve gave you. That's part of the problem. And that's absolutely right. So we've gone from having an oversupply in the domestic market to we're now hooked into the global market and we're paying their prices. But there was a fundamental fault in the whole process. And that was we had three exporters out of the East Coast market. And the Santos-led consortium decided to double the size of their processing plant on Curtis Island, which is just off the coast of Gladstone in Queensland. They were going to have what's known as a one-train plant. And then they decided, nah, the other two have got two-train plants. We're pretty sure we've got enough gas in the ground to cover this. We'll do a two-train plant. And so they doubled the size of their plant. To justify that, they then sold export contracts to Asian buyers. And then when they started, actually after the plant was built, or while the plant was being built, they tried to source the extra supply of gas and they failed. So they didn't have the supply of gas to justify the size of their plant. And they'd sold far too much in the way of forward contracts to Asian buyers. So that left them with a shortfall. And how did they fill their export contracts? They went into the domestic market and bought gas out of the domestic market. So they essentially raided the domestic market, took gas out, and that forced the price of Australian domestic gas much higher. So let's cut to today. You would have expected, as you said, if you're following the playbook of how this worked last time around, last time we saw a war cause the price of gas to spike linked to the oil price spike that we've seen. This time it doesn't happen. And it doesn't appear to have been explicitly because of government telling them they couldn't do it. Why is it that we haven't seen a massive rise in the price of gas for Australians? Well, it's one of those extraordinary events, I guess, where a threat, right, that's overhanging everything, has more impact than the actual law that's about to be imposed. So after years of just, you know, outrage and uproar, particularly from domestic manufacturers here who use a lot of energy, but also from households across the country, the government last year threw caution to the wind and went, right, okay, East Coast, we're going to have a gas reservation policy. It works on the West Coast. Why can't it work here? And by that stage, the three exporters basically threw up their hands and went, oh, okay. So late last year, the government said, we're imposing this. We've gone through the whole consultation process, which of course was, I think the decision was made before the consultation process started. We're going to impose this tax. Now, here's the general model that we're going to impose, which will be that each of the three exporters will have to be providing gas into the domestic system. That's going to be very hard for Santos, which has got the shortfall. The other two, one's run by Origin, the other one's run by Shell. They have consistently provided gas into the domestic system. It's the Santos consortium that sucks it out. So they've said, this is going to be the general model, but we've got to work out how the whole thing works. Now, because that's probably not going to be worked out until later this year, each of the exporters is really just walking on eggshells at the moment because they don't want to be penalized or hit with some massive model that is going to really stop them from making money. And right now, you've got this shortage around the world because of what's happened in Iran and the Strait of Hormuz being closed. So they don't know what to do. Now, on top of that, there is also the Greens, which have forced a select Senate hearing into the tax arrangements around our big gas exports. The fact that, you know, this is a huge industry that exports multiple billions of dollars worth of gas each year and pays, well, what a lot of people would argue would be an insignificant amount of tax on that. So they've got this double whammy of here's the gas reservation policy, which is yet to be properly formulated, and the potential for windfall profits tax. So you mentioned the fact that there's already a reservation system in place for the West in Western Australia. There isn't on the East Coast. How did that come about? Why do we have two different systems operating within Australia? I think people always find that kind of confusing, the role of the state versus the federal government. And how is it working in Western Australia? And these concerns raised by people about a reservation policy and what that potentially means to the viability of these export projects, just give us how, what the experience in Western Australia has shown actually occurs if you reserve a certain amount of the gas. Well, firstly, I mean, everybody thinks that resources in the ground belong to the Commonwealth and belong to the people of Australia, which is kind of true, but it actually gets down to a state basis because Australia is a federation of states. And so it's the, not Australians per se, but the people who live within the states. Those resources belong to the states and shouldn't be governed for people who are just currently alive, but for future generations as well. Now, how does it work? Well, and how did that come about? Well, the East Coast gas exports come from gas that's supplied out of Bass Strait, out of New South Wales, out of Queensland. So the gas all gets, you know, comes from all the, each of those three states. So obviously there was difficulty in trying to come to some kind of arrangement between the three states. To get some kind of policy there. But it was actively explored and decided, this is the Gillard government. They were already under pressure from iron ore taxes and the resources rent tax on iron ore. We've seen how effective a campaign can be from resource companies when there's ever a suggestion that there might be a higher rate of tax imposed on their exports. And they very successfully managed to force the then Labor government to junk that resources rent tax, come up with a second best option, which was then completely thrown out when Tony Abbott became prime minister. So the Labor government at the time looked at it and said, no, we're not going to have a reservation policy here. Now, interestingly, over in the West, I have spoken to the then Premier, Alan Carpenter, who was the person who imposed that tax. And he told me this story about how he was sitting in a room with, you know, the chief executive, senior executives from the biggest resources companies around the world about, this is really around Northwest Shelf and all of the offshore gas projects that happen there. And apparently at one stage, you know, he said, look, we're going to have this gas reservation policy just to ensure that there's enough gas for Western Australians into the future. And so for every bit of gas you export, there's going to be 10% of that reserved for Western Australians. He said somebody thumped the table and said, there will not be one molecule of gas that will be reserved for domestic use. If that's the case, the deal's off. And he said, well, if that's the situation, ladies and gentlemen, I'm sorry to have wasted your time. Meeting's over. Next day, there's a knock at the door. We've gone through the numbers again. We can make it stack up. We can make it work, yeah. And so it's worked quite well for Western Australia. And you've only got to look at that Ukraine crisis a few years back and gas prices in the West, despite it exporting far more than we do here on the East Coast, gas prices in the West were substantially below what the East Coast gas prices were. And unfortunately, there's no pipeline between Western Australia and the East Coast, which would have equalized the prices somewhat. You point out in your article, this is a great kind of, I guess, microcosm of how this has played out within Australia, between the East and the West, where we used to have on the East Coast of Australia, a fertilizer production business fed by gas, urea, which is one of the things that we're now struggling to get enough of because of the interruption to global supply. And they weren't able to get the gas at a price that could make it still stack up on the East Coast, which is obviously a major, creates sovereign risk for Australia if we can't produce it here at home. How has that now played out with the different policies about gas reservation in the East Coast versus the West? Look, I think it's going to be a lot easier for businesses to source domestic gas supplies at a reasonable price. You know, during the period when I think it was when the Labor government had imposed that price cap of, say, $12 a gigajoule, and particularly through the Ukraine crisis, I think gas prices went to about $23 a gigajoule if you're a business trying to lock in long-term supplies. So it was just uneconomical for most big industrial users. And you're talking about smelters. You're talking about all sorts of, you know, massive uses of energy here. But, you know, the urea example is just a great example of where everything went wrong. I mean, here we are, one of the world's biggest agricultural exporters. So we have, there's a ready home market for fertilizer. And we've got the key ingredient to make it as well. So why wouldn't you be making it here for your own market and then exporting, you know, whatever is left over? But nothing. This is the whole idea of value adding on the kind of resource. You've got the gas on the ground. You're also trying to produce agricultural goods. Why would you be sending the gas overseas to a river? You've got the market and the ingredients. I mean, it's just a no-brainer, really, isn't it? And yet it went broke because they couldn't source the key material to make it. Because, you know, urea is essentially nitrogen and hydrogen combined. And you use nitrogen out of the air and hydrogen out of the gas. You combine that and, Bob's your uncle, you've got urea. And, you know, so there's all these other countries that can make it. But we surely should have been the country making more than anybody else and exporting it. And, I mean, you know, you think the Middle East is now a major producer of urea. And this is where we're getting most of ours from. There's not a lot of agriculture around that part of the world. It's a bit dry. And, you know, so it's just extraordinary that that plant in, what is it, Gibson Island in Brisbane, that it shut down at that point. What do you make of this current inquiry into the gas industry here in Australia? Coming ahead of the budget, is there any chance that the government, given the scar tissue involved from previous attempts, which we've spoken about, of taxing the resource industry? Do you think there's the political will for the Labor Party to actually impose a higher tax on the gas industry? Or do you think they would be scared off doing that because of the likely fierce opposition? Until now, there's always been a real problem with trying to increase tax on miners. And, you know, we saw that during the Gillard era when, you know, the tax on iron ore, which should have been, again, a no-brainer. And even in the past few years, we've seen attempts to modernise the resources rent tax on petroleum. Australia was a groundbreaker in doing that when Paul Keating, as Treasurer, introduced that. You know, what was that, 30 years ago or more? But our petroleum industry has changed from one of oil to one of gas. And the petroleum resources rent tax that's in place at the moment is well-suited to an oil-producing country, not a gas-producing country. And so there was an attempt to modernise it just a couple of years ago, but it has not resulted in any more income sort of flowing into Australia. Now, there does seem to have been a change in attitude amongst the general population and maybe the extortion of prices that the gas exporters were charging through to here, which led to that inflation. You know, maybe that has worked against them. But there doesn't seem to be, I think, the general appetite from ordinary Australians to prop up multinational corporations making huge amounts of money here. Yeah, and I think one of the reasons why the time might be ripe is because when Australians are paying more every time that they go to fill up a tank of fuel at the Bowser or they are looking at how inflation is starting to flow through. And at the same time, they know that there is gas that's leaving Australia's shores. As you say, it's owned by the Australian people. And they don't feel like they are getting a fair cut of that profit, that that might change the political environment enough or atmosphere for the government to be willing to take that step. But it would be interesting to see how quickly they think they could impose that. And the government is saying whatever they do will not affect the contracts that are already in place with exporters, particularly to places like the East Asia. And this is where it gets really complex. And you want to make sure that you come up with a model that doesn't increase the price here. So if you add, say, for argument's sake, 30% tax, you don't want to see a 30% price hike here as a result of that. So formulating a model, which would probably be best done by taxing exports over a certain price. But then you don't want to impact the price for your customers either. And our friends at Politics now are unpacking the political fight surrounding this inquiry on today's pod, if you want to hear more on this matter. Ian, we've also had big news out of the United States. Yes, Apple, one of the world's biggest, most influential companies, has had Tim Cook steering the ship for 15 years, an extraordinarily long time to be leading a company, particularly when you're not the founder. And he took over in the shadow of Steve Jobs, a tech icon, a man that really brought Apple back from the brink of bankruptcy and then put it firmly back on the map with the advent of the iPod and the iPhone. He's handing over to an engineer, which seems to have been very much welcomed by those Apple fanboys who wanted somebody who they think would be very focused on product, as opposed to what Tim Cook was seeing as really good at, which was making sure the supply chain works efficiently and that Apple's making lots of money. What did you make of the announcement? Very interesting timing because, you know, here we are. Are we in the midst of this AI revolution? Probably not yet. We're at the very start of it all. All of the big tech companies have invested huge amounts of money in artificial intelligence. It's a very crucial time right now for them to try to turn the amount of money that they've invested into some kind of returns. Now, you know, Apple has not gone down the same path as a lot of the others. When you compare it to the other Magnificent Seven, Apple is the lagger. They are not spending the hundreds of billions of dollars that you seem to hear about constantly from other companies going down the path of ever more money being thrown at artificial intelligence. Instead, they almost seem to be waiting to see how this plays out. Well, they haven't invested in AI infrastructure. They haven't invested in data centers and the like. They have invested in artificial intelligence, but they've been very specific in the investments that they've made. Whereas a lot of the other companies have just splashed huge amounts around on everything. Now, by doing that, they've actually returned quite a bit of money to shareholders. So the shareholders aren't particularly upset with the strategy so far. So that's what I'm saying. It is a very interesting time for Tim Cook to be leaving right now. But his replacement has a lot of experience within Apple. Yeah, John Ternus, 25 years in the company. The guy's only 50. So half his life has been spent at Apple. He's also kind of been the anointed one for a little while. There's been rumors that he had been positioned to take over, taking on increasing responsibilities when it comes to design within the company. This is not Tim Cook leaving because people are pushing him out. He has been, by most accounts, a very successful CEO. And he has now been seemingly able to hand the baton over. But it is a fraught time for Apple as it tries to navigate this next stage, isn't it? Yeah, but his replacement has been involved in every major product, you know, iPad, iPod, Macs, you know, everything. And look, this is really important for Australian shareholders as well, or just ordinary Australians, because our big super funds have something like $9 billion worth of Apple shares, right? And I think AusSuper, Australian super, has around about one third of that. So, you know, there's a major incentive here for, well, a big hope, I guess, from Australians that this actually does work out. Because Tim Cook, the profits that he generated while he was chief executive, rose tenfold during his reign. Yeah, and it's not often that a CEO, particularly one who's not a founder, kind of breaks through into public fame. But Tim Cook did do that, right? He's been there for such a sustained period. Apple is such an important company around the world. They obviously have these big flashy announcements around new product launches. But it's also a very public role. And particularly under the Trump administration, tech CEOs have become very big public figures and have to walk a very fine line when it comes to kind of public inquiries and about how the technology is being utilized. Apple hasn't been as controversial a company as, say, Meta or Google when it comes to privacy or advertisements. But particularly with artificial intelligence, I think he's going to be a public face of a big company at an important time. And he needs to be able to withstand that kind of public scrutiny, doesn't he? Yeah. And as you mentioned before, the supply chains. I mean, you know, Apple is a kind of a design company in many ways. And it outsources all its production, a lot of it to China. And, of course, Donald Trump's China approach and the tariffs and the trade wars with China really put Apple in the middle of that fight. And, you know, so there's been a lot of politics that they've had to try to, you know, delicately sidestep their way around there. I think Tim Cook has played a very deft diplomatic game, it appears. He has managed to say on the right side of Donald Trump, apparently there has been a lot of backroom dealing when it comes to the tariff war and about how what exemptions could be put in place. But also they have had to recalibrate the way that the products are manufactured, including by moving the distribution to different parts of Asia in particular. India is placing an increasing role in the manufacturing of those products. But we've still got a couple of years at least of Donald Trump. And this is going to be part of the challenge for the new CEO to make sure that you're not seeing product development interrupted by whatever tariffs might go up. And look, you know, if you think about the way Apple has conducted itself and the supply chains by having huge amounts of, you know, components and things manufactured all around the world, in many ways it's actually stopped the piracy that other companies would have experienced. Because if you've got a massive operation in China, there's a real incentive for them to keep, you know, generating an income from you rather than to go out there and just try and pick up an iPhone, pull it apart and, you know, reverse engineer it. So I think in some ways they've managed to maintain control over their processes. And if it, you know, shifting it all home, which is what Donald Trump would love to see happen, may not be, well, it's not really a realistic proposition anymore, is it? I mean, when you think of the size of these companies, we almost have lost sight about how massive they now are. I think Apple's now the third biggest company in the world. It's worth $4 trillion, around $4 trillion US dollars. I mean, this is, there are many, there are not many countries with that kind of GDP, right? This is such a massive operation. And now you've got this new 50-year-old taking the helm. It'll be fascinating to watch how it goes. Ian, thank you so much for joining us. Pleasure. That is it for today's episode of ABC Business Daily. We'll be back with both a Fuelcast episode with Ian Verinder, the man sitting with me right now, and another episode of ABC Business Daily tomorrow. To make sure you don't miss out, make sure you're following us on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts, and I will catch you later. See ya.

segments.text: This is an ABC podcast.
What would you do if someone you loved vanished
and you discover the person she's been living with
isn't who they said they were?
I'm Dominique Bayens, host of Expanse, The Nan Up 4.
Is he, you know, a murderer?
A self-styled cult leader.
It's just not knowing the emptiness, really.
That just kills you.
This is the bizarre story of The Nan Up 4.
Binge all episodes now.
Search Expanse on ABC Listen and iView.
When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine back in 2022,
it sent the price of natural gas soaring
and Australian consumers faced steep hikes in their electricity bills.
But this time around, when once again war has sent
the international price of gas skywards,
Australia has remained relatively insulated.
So what's the difference this time around?
And a major tech announcement with long-serving Apple CEO Tim Cook
stepping down and anointing his successor.
Welcome to ABC Business Daily.
I'm Carrington Clark.
And I'm the ABC's Chief Business Correspondent, Ian Verinder.
Ian, thank you so much for joining us.
We've been very focused, obviously, on the soaring price of petrol and diesel.
But here in Australia, we're not as focused on the soaring international price of gas.
This is something that's obviously preoccupying people, both in East Asia and in Europe,
where they have seen a real impact on the price that they're paying for their gas.
Why aren't we paying increased prices here in Australia in the way that we did during that Russian invasion of Ukraine?
Well, I think it gets down to the amount of power that the gas exporters actually have.
And if you've cast your mind back to 2022, I mean, what everyone was focused on,
the cost of living crisis.
And what was really underpinning that cost of living crisis?
I mean, everyone was just up in arms about electricity bills that were doubling each year.
Extraordinary rises.
I know.
And what really drove that was the price of gas.
And the reason for that is, even though a lot of our electricity is generated by coal,
a lot of it by renewables, and only a smallish part by gas, gas is the swing factor.
Gas is what economists would term the marginal cost producer, right?
So essentially, when you can't generate anything more from coal,
when your renewables are offline, you switch on the gas to generate that last little bit.
And because it's the marginal cost producer, it actually sets the price.
And so as a result of that, our electricity bills soar.
Now, if you look to across the country,
New South Wales and Queensland use a lot less gas than they do in, say, Victoria, right?
So Victorians use a lot of gas for household heating, for cooking.
And so they were getting the double whammy.
They were getting huge electricity bills,
plus these massive increases in price for their gas supply.
Now, this time around, it's suddenly not happening.
Not only are we not getting the price hikes that you would have expected
if you use the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine as a base model,
we're not getting those price hikes, we're actually getting cheaper gas
than we had just a few months ago.
So this does seem strange.
Back in 2022, there was a lot of kind of political pressure and public pressure
about gas companies extorting, it was some of the language used,
the Australian consumer, because they were making huge profits
by selling gas from Australia into this global market.
And they were instead sending that gas offshore,
even though there was huge demand for it here.
Why hasn't that played at this point?
Well, they were actually siphoning gas out of the domestic system, right,
and then sending it offshore because the prices they could get offshore
were just extraordinary.
And so as a result of that, you've got massive price rises here.
But even before the Russian invasion of Ukraine, I mean, we had, you know,
there was uproar across the country because gas prices, you know,
before on the East Coast we're talking about here, before the export market opened up
and around about 2010, 2012, gas prices were about $3 a gigajoule.
We're now just, you know, in heaven because they're $10, right?
But during that war, they went up to above $20 a gigajoule.
So just massive price hikes.
And that had, you know, three successive prime ministers try to intervene to stop this.
Now, you had Malcolm Turnbull with his ADGSM, I think it was,
what is it, Australian Domestic Gas Supply Mechanism.
You had Scotty Morrison with his big stick.
Do you remember the big stick?
And then you had Anthony Albanese with price controls.
None of it worked.
None of it worked.
But suddenly it's all working now.
Taking one step back, because I think this is a thing a lot of people struggle to understand,
because we have a situation where prior to Australia becoming a major exporter of gas,
we actually had less gas supply.
We weren't getting as much gas out of the ground.
But yet then when we started exporting gas, so there's more supply,
people think, well, if you've got more supply,
don't the fundamentals tell you that you should actually have lower prices?
But the issue was by Australia becoming a gas exporter and having these facilities,
we actually became a price taker for the international price.
So whatever was kind of the international price, and when we saw a big spike,
suddenly Australians' consumers were paying that price instead of just having whatever the domestic supply and demand curve gave you.
That's part of the problem.
And that's absolutely right.
So we've gone from having an oversupply in the domestic market to we're now hooked into the global market and we're paying their prices.
But there was a fundamental fault in the whole process.
And that was we had three exporters out of the East Coast market.
And the Santos-led consortium decided to double the size of their processing plant on Curtis Island,
which is just off the coast of Gladstone in Queensland.
They were going to have what's known as a one-train plant.
And then they decided, nah, the other two have got two-train plants.
We're pretty sure we've got enough gas in the ground to cover this.
We'll do a two-train plant.
And so they doubled the size of their plant.
To justify that, they then sold export contracts to Asian buyers.
And then when they started, actually after the plant was built, or while the plant was being built,
they tried to source the extra supply of gas and they failed.
So they didn't have the supply of gas to justify the size of their plant.
And they'd sold far too much in the way of forward contracts to Asian buyers.
So that left them with a shortfall.
And how did they fill their export contracts?
They went into the domestic market and bought gas out of the domestic market.
So they essentially raided the domestic market, took gas out,
and that forced the price of Australian domestic gas much higher.
So let's cut to today.
You would have expected, as you said, if you're following the playbook of how this worked last time around,
last time we saw a war cause the price of gas to spike linked to the oil price spike that we've seen.
This time it doesn't happen.
And it doesn't appear to have been explicitly because of government telling them they couldn't do it.
Why is it that we haven't seen a massive rise in the price of gas for Australians?
Well, it's one of those extraordinary events, I guess, where a threat, right, that's overhanging everything,
has more impact than the actual law that's about to be imposed.
So after years of just, you know, outrage and uproar,
particularly from domestic manufacturers here who use a lot of energy,
but also from households across the country,
the government last year threw caution to the wind and went,
right, okay, East Coast, we're going to have a gas reservation policy.
It works on the West Coast.
Why can't it work here?
And by that stage, the three exporters basically threw up their hands and went, oh, okay.
So late last year, the government said, we're imposing this.
We've gone through the whole consultation process,
which of course was,
I think the decision was made before the consultation process started.
We're going to impose this tax.
Now, here's the general model that we're going to impose,
which will be that each of the three exporters will have to be providing gas into the domestic system.
That's going to be very hard for Santos, which has got the shortfall.
The other two, one's run by Origin, the other one's run by Shell.
They have consistently provided gas into the domestic system.
It's the Santos consortium that sucks it out.
So they've said, this is going to be the general model,
but we've got to work out how the whole thing works.
Now, because that's probably not going to be worked out until later this year,
each of the exporters is really just walking on eggshells at the moment
because they don't want to be penalized or hit with some massive model
that is going to really stop them from making money.
And right now, you've got this shortage around the world
because of what's happened in Iran and the Strait of Hormuz being closed.
So they don't know what to do.
Now, on top of that, there is also the Greens,
which have forced a select Senate hearing into the tax arrangements around our big gas exports.
The fact that, you know, this is a huge industry that exports multiple billions of dollars worth of gas each year
and pays, well, what a lot of people would argue would be an insignificant amount of tax on that.
So they've got this double whammy of here's the gas reservation policy,
which is yet to be properly formulated,
and the potential for windfall profits tax.
So you mentioned the fact that there's already a reservation system in place for the West in Western Australia.
There isn't on the East Coast.
How did that come about?
Why do we have two different systems operating within Australia?
I think people always find that kind of confusing,
the role of the state versus the federal government.
And how is it working in Western Australia?
And these concerns raised by people about a reservation policy
and what that potentially means to the viability of these export projects,
just give us how, what the experience in Western Australia has shown actually occurs
if you reserve a certain amount of the gas.
Well, firstly, I mean, everybody thinks that resources in the ground belong to the Commonwealth
and belong to the people of Australia, which is kind of true,
but it actually gets down to a state basis because Australia is a federation of states.
And so it's the, not Australians per se, but the people who live within the states.
Those resources belong to the states and shouldn't be governed for people who are just currently alive,
but for future generations as well.
Now, how does it work?
Well, and how did that come about?
Well, the East Coast gas exports come from gas that's supplied out of Bass Strait,
out of New South Wales, out of Queensland.
So the gas all gets, you know, comes from all the, each of those three states.
So obviously there was difficulty in trying to come to some kind of arrangement between the three states.
To get some kind of policy there.
But it was actively explored and decided, this is the Gillard government.
They were already under pressure from iron ore taxes and the resources rent tax on iron ore.
We've seen how effective a campaign can be from resource companies when there's ever a suggestion
that there might be a higher rate of tax imposed on their exports.
And they very successfully managed to force the then Labor government to junk that resources rent tax,
come up with a second best option, which was then completely thrown out when Tony Abbott became prime minister.
So the Labor government at the time looked at it and said, no, we're not going to have a reservation policy here.
Now, interestingly, over in the West, I have spoken to the then Premier, Alan Carpenter,
who was the person who imposed that tax.
And he told me this story about how he was sitting in a room with, you know, the chief executive,
senior executives from the biggest resources companies around the world about,
this is really around Northwest Shelf and all of the offshore gas projects that happen there.
And apparently at one stage, you know, he said, look, we're going to have this gas reservation policy
just to ensure that there's enough gas for Western Australians into the future.
And so for every bit of gas you export, there's going to be 10% of that reserved for Western Australians.
He said somebody thumped the table and said, there will not be one molecule of gas that will be reserved for domestic use.
If that's the case, the deal's off.
And he said, well, if that's the situation, ladies and gentlemen, I'm sorry to have wasted your time.
Meeting's over.
Next day, there's a knock at the door.
We've gone through the numbers again.
We can make it stack up.
We can make it work, yeah.
And so it's worked quite well for Western Australia.
And you've only got to look at that Ukraine crisis a few years back and gas prices in the West,
despite it exporting far more than we do here on the East Coast, gas prices in the West were substantially below what the East Coast gas prices were.
And unfortunately, there's no pipeline between Western Australia and the East Coast, which would have equalized the prices somewhat.
You point out in your article, this is a great kind of, I guess, microcosm of how this has played out within Australia, between the East and the West,
where we used to have on the East Coast of Australia, a fertilizer production business fed by gas, urea,
which is one of the things that we're now struggling to get enough of because of the interruption to global supply.
And they weren't able to get the gas at a price that could make it still stack up on the East Coast,
which is obviously a major, creates sovereign risk for Australia if we can't produce it here at home.
How has that now played out with the different policies about gas reservation in the East Coast versus the West?
Look, I think it's going to be a lot easier for businesses to source domestic gas supplies at a reasonable price.
You know, during the period when I think it was when the Labor government had imposed that price cap of, say, $12 a gigajoule,
and particularly through the Ukraine crisis, I think gas prices went to about $23 a gigajoule if you're a business trying to lock in long-term supplies.
So it was just uneconomical for most big industrial users.
And you're talking about smelters.
You're talking about all sorts of, you know, massive uses of energy here.
But, you know, the urea example is just a great example of where everything went wrong.
I mean, here we are, one of the world's biggest agricultural exporters.
So we have, there's a ready home market for fertilizer.
And we've got the key ingredient to make it as well.
So why wouldn't you be making it here for your own market and then exporting, you know, whatever is left over?
But nothing.
This is the whole idea of value adding on the kind of resource.
You've got the gas on the ground.
You're also trying to produce agricultural goods.
Why would you be sending the gas overseas to a river?
You've got the market and the ingredients.
I mean, it's just a no-brainer, really, isn't it?
And yet it went broke because they couldn't source the key material to make it.
Because, you know, urea is essentially nitrogen and hydrogen combined.
And you use nitrogen out of the air and hydrogen out of the gas.
You combine that and, Bob's your uncle, you've got urea.
And, you know, so there's all these other countries that can make it.
But we surely should have been the country making more than anybody else and exporting it.
And, I mean, you know, you think the Middle East is now a major producer of urea.
And this is where we're getting most of ours from.
There's not a lot of agriculture around that part of the world.
It's a bit dry.
And, you know, so it's just extraordinary that that plant in, what is it, Gibson Island in Brisbane,
that it shut down at that point.
What do you make of this current inquiry into the gas industry here in Australia?
Coming ahead of the budget, is there any chance that the government,
given the scar tissue involved from previous attempts, which we've spoken about, of taxing the resource industry?
Do you think there's the political will for the Labor Party to actually impose a higher tax on the gas industry?
Or do you think they would be scared off doing that because of the likely fierce opposition?
Until now, there's always been a real problem with trying to increase tax on miners.
And, you know, we saw that during the Gillard era when, you know, the tax on iron ore, which should have been, again, a no-brainer.
And even in the past few years, we've seen attempts to modernise the resources rent tax on petroleum.
Australia was a groundbreaker in doing that when Paul Keating, as Treasurer, introduced that.
You know, what was that, 30 years ago or more?
But our petroleum industry has changed from one of oil to one of gas.
And the petroleum resources rent tax that's in place at the moment is well-suited to an oil-producing country, not a gas-producing country.
And so there was an attempt to modernise it just a couple of years ago, but it has not resulted in any more income sort of flowing into Australia.

Now, there does seem to have been a change in attitude amongst the general population and maybe the extortion of prices that the gas exporters were charging through to here, which led to that inflation.
You know, maybe that has worked against them.
But there doesn't seem to be, I think, the general appetite from ordinary Australians to prop up multinational corporations making huge amounts of money here.

Yeah, and I think one of the reasons why the time might be ripe is because when Australians are paying more every time that they go to fill up a tank of fuel at the Bowser or they are looking at how inflation is starting to flow through.
And at the same time, they know that there is gas that's leaving Australia's shores.
As you say, it's owned by the Australian people.
And they don't feel like they are getting a fair cut of that profit, that that might change the political environment enough or atmosphere for the government to be willing to take that step.
But it would be interesting to see how quickly they think they could impose that.
And the government is saying whatever they do will not affect the contracts that are already in place with exporters, particularly to places like the East Asia.
And this is where it gets really complex.
And you want to make sure that you come up with a model that doesn't increase the price here.
So if you add, say, for argument's sake, 30% tax, you don't want to see a 30% price hike here as a result of that.
So formulating a model, which would probably be best done by taxing exports over a certain price.
But then you don't want to impact the price for your customers either.
And our friends at Politics now are unpacking the political fight surrounding this inquiry on today's pod, if you want to hear more on this matter.
Ian, we've also had big news out of the United States.

Yes, Apple, one of the world's biggest, most influential companies, has had Tim Cook steering the ship for 15 years, an extraordinarily long time to be leading a company, particularly when you're not the founder.

And he took over in the shadow of Steve Jobs, a tech icon, a man that really brought Apple back from the brink of bankruptcy and then put it firmly back on the map with the advent of the iPod and the iPhone.

He's handing over to an engineer, which seems to have been very much welcomed by those Apple fanboys who wanted somebody who they think would be very focused on product, as opposed to what Tim Cook was seeing as really good at, which was making sure the supply chain works efficiently and that Apple's making lots of money.
What did you make of the announcement?
Very interesting timing because, you know, here we are.
Are we in the midst of this AI revolution?
Probably not yet.
We're at the very start of it all.
All of the big tech companies have invested huge amounts of money in artificial intelligence.
It's a very crucial time right now for them to try to turn the amount of money that they've invested into some kind of returns.
Now, you know, Apple has not gone down the same path as a lot of the others.
When you compare it to the other Magnificent Seven, Apple is the lagger.
They are not spending the hundreds of billions of dollars that you seem to hear about constantly from other companies going down the path of ever more money being thrown at artificial intelligence.
Instead, they almost seem to be waiting to see how this plays out.
Well, they haven't invested in AI infrastructure.
They haven't invested in data centers and the like.
They have invested in artificial intelligence, but they've been very specific in the investments that they've made.
Whereas a lot of the other companies have just splashed huge amounts around on everything.
Now, by doing that, they've actually returned quite a bit of money to shareholders.
So the shareholders aren't particularly upset with the strategy so far.
So that's what I'm saying.
It is a very interesting time for Tim Cook to be leaving right now.
But his replacement has a lot of experience within Apple.
Yeah, John Ternus, 25 years in the company.
The guy's only 50.
So half his life has been spent at Apple.
He's also kind of been the anointed one for a little while.
There's been rumors that he had been positioned to take over, taking on increasing responsibilities when it comes to design within the company.
This is not Tim Cook leaving because people are pushing him out.
He has been, by most accounts, a very successful CEO.
And he has now been seemingly able to hand the baton over.
But it is a fraught time for Apple as it tries to navigate this next stage, isn't it?
Yeah, but his replacement has been involved in every major product, you know, iPad, iPod, Macs, you know, everything.
And look, this is really important for Australian shareholders as well, or just ordinary Australians,
because our big super funds have something like $9 billion worth of Apple shares, right?
And I think AusSuper, Australian super, has around about one third of that.
So, you know, there's a major incentive here for, well, a big hope, I guess, from Australians that this actually does work out.
Because Tim Cook, the profits that he generated while he was chief executive, rose tenfold during his reign.
Yeah, and it's not often that a CEO, particularly one who's not a founder, kind of breaks through into public fame.
But Tim Cook did do that, right?
He's been there for such a sustained period.
Apple is such an important company around the world.
They obviously have these big flashy announcements around new product launches.
But it's also a very public role.
And particularly under the Trump administration, tech CEOs have become very big public figures
and have to walk a very fine line when it comes to kind of public inquiries and about how the technology is being utilized.
Apple hasn't been as controversial a company as, say, Meta or Google when it comes to privacy or advertisements.
But particularly with artificial intelligence, I think he's going to be a public face of a big company at an important time.
And he needs to be able to withstand that kind of public scrutiny, doesn't he?
Yeah.
And as you mentioned before, the supply chains.
I mean, you know, Apple is a kind of a design company in many ways.
And it outsources all its production, a lot of it to China.
And, of course, Donald Trump's China approach and the tariffs and the trade wars with China really put Apple in the middle of that fight.
And, you know, so there's been a lot of politics that they've had to try to, you know, delicately sidestep their way around there.
I think Tim Cook has played a very deft diplomatic game, it appears.
He has managed to say on the right side of Donald Trump, apparently there has been a lot of backroom dealing when it comes to the tariff war and about how what exemptions could be put in place.
But also they have had to recalibrate the way that the products are manufactured, including by moving the distribution to different parts of Asia in particular.
India is placing an increasing role in the manufacturing of those products.
But we've still got a couple of years at least of Donald Trump.
And this is going to be part of the challenge for the new CEO to make sure that you're not seeing product development interrupted by whatever tariffs might go up.
And look, you know, if you think about the way Apple has conducted itself and the supply chains by having huge amounts of, you know, components and things manufactured all around the world,
in many ways it's actually stopped the piracy that other companies would have experienced.
Because if you've got a massive operation in China, there's a real incentive for them to keep, you know, generating an income from you rather than to go out there and just try and pick up an iPhone,
pull it apart and, you know, reverse engineer it.
So I think in some ways they've managed to maintain control over their processes.
And if it, you know, shifting it all home, which is what Donald Trump would love to see happen, may not be, well, it's not really a realistic proposition anymore, is it?
I mean, when you think of the size of these companies, we almost have lost sight about how massive they now are.
I think Apple's now the third biggest company in the world.
It's worth $4 trillion, around $4 trillion US dollars.
I mean, this is, there are many, there are not many countries with that kind of GDP, right?
This is such a massive operation.
And now you've got this new 50-year-old taking the helm.
It'll be fascinating to watch how it goes.
Ian, thank you so much for joining us.
Pleasure.
That is it for today's episode of ABC Business Daily.
We'll be back with both a Fuelcast episode with Ian Verinder, the man sitting with me right now,
and another episode of ABC Business Daily tomorrow.
To make sure you don't miss out, make sure you're following us on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts,
and I will catch you later.
See ya.

episodes.title: Will the budget bring us 'back to the future?'
episodes.description: After a brief window of hope that traffic through the Strait of Hormuz would start to normalise, a harsher reality has kicked in. With both Iran and the US firing on vessels, the oil price is surging once again.
episodes.transcript: This is an ABC podcast. I really am. Join me for ABC News Daily. Find us on ABC Listen. After a brief window of hope that traffic through the Strait of Hormuz would start to normalise, a harsh reality has kicked in, with both Iran and the United States firing on vessels and causing the oil price to surge once again. Meanwhile, there's fevered speculation about what the government could unveil in this year's federal budget due to be released in early May. Could the capital gains discount be in for a major overhaul? Welcome to ABC Business Daily. I'm Carrington Clarke. And I'm the ABC's Business Editor, Michael Yander. Michael, we've seen another major shift in the energy markets. At the end of last week, we saw oil prices plunge because of declarations about the Strait of Hormuz from both the United States and Iran that it was open once again. And now the price has bounced back up because of multiple incidences around the Strait. That means it's basically closed off. What do you make of it? And what does it mean for the global economy? Well, the first thing I'd say, Carrington, is I was surprised how little the oil price bounced. I mean, it's up 6% as the time we're recording about 11 a.m. in Sydney. I would have thought the rise would be much bigger given that very few ships have still made it through the Strait of Hormuz. I mean, there is no oil and gas really coming out or certainly not much more than there was before this apparent ceasefire. Yeah. Does that indicate that actually people think this is once again a temporary blip and that we will see enough desire to actually get the Strait open up again, that this is only going to be closed for a temporary period? Yeah, it does seem like markets continue to bet on hope and faith, hope that the Strait will reopen soon in the next two or three weeks before the oil crunch gets really bad, and faith in, I don't know, President Trump and the Iranian regime to come to a settlement when they seem poles apart on certain key elements. See you, Carrington.

Some other estimates put that at up to 4%, but that's lower than the impact we're seeing on property prices from something like interest rates going up.
So there's a lot of experts for a long time who've said this is not that hard.
At the margins, it will help first home buyers compete against investors and discourage speculative
investment in property, and it won't do too much to discourage genuine long-term investment in rental properties.
It'll be very interesting to see exactly how fierce the opposition plan or opposition campaign against this will be.
Another one that could be a case of back to the future is the standard or instant tax deduction.
Now, Michael, you've got some history with this as well.
I don't know if it's scar tissue or how you would describe it, but explain to us what it is and what it could mean and how it might impact people out there when they do their tax returns.
So the reason we're talking about this today, Carrington, is that Jim Chalmers has released the draft legislation for a $1,000 standard or instant tax deduction for your personal income tax.
So we all know at tax time, you go and try and find your receipts of what are my work-related expenses, and you put in the number, and your taxable income gets reduced by that amount.
So what they're saying here, and it had already been announced, but it's now going to Parliament for debate, is if you want, you can just tick a box and say,
I'll have a $1,000 deduction for work-related expenses.
No receipts needed.
No calculations required.
No accountant involved.
So unsurprisingly, the certified practicing accountants have already come out very strongly against this proposal,
because it will put some of their members out of a lot of their bread and butter work.
But you can still claim charity and non-work deductions on top of the $1,000,
and if your work-related expenses are more than $1,000,
and I don't know about you, Carrington, but just my union fees alone are over $1,000,
so I won't be ticking that box myself,
but you can claim those deductions.
You just have to use the old system and have the receipts to back them up.
So you talked about the history of this, goes back to 2010,
which was one of the first budgets I covered at the ABC,
and then-treasurer Wayne Swan, who had a staffer at the time by the name of Jim Chalmers,
who is, of course, now our treasurer,
had proposed in the 2010 budget to bring in a $500 standard tax deduction,
which had been broadly recommended by the Henry Tax Review,
and that was going to go up to $1,000 in the next financial year.
So that was supposed to come in in 2012-13.
Never happened.
Announced, but not enacted.
And so much for inflation, Carrington.
I mean, it was supposed to be a $1,000 standard deduction back then,
and the government's still proposing a $1,000 deduction now,
and $1,000 buys you a lot less work-related expenses than it did back in 2013-2014.
Yeah, but a very round number, and people like round numbers often,
and maybe it won't be so onerous on the budget at a time when they are trying to look for extra revenue.
Yeah, and look, going back into more of the history of this proposal,
back in 2021, Stephen Hamilton, a tax economist who was then at the Blueprint Institute think tank,
proposed a $3,000 standard deduction.
That would have cost the budget back then about $5.1 billion,
but it would have resulted in about $4 billion in compliance savings,
both some to the tax office, but also a lot to individuals.
So their estimate-
So this is the argument, right?
This is one of the main reasons that we're even discussing this,
because people might say, well, why should you have an automatic deduction?
You should have to explain what your deductions are.
But it's about simplicity, and basically the government's saying it costs so much to actually
check to make sure that people are being compliant with the legislation.
It's actually going to be maybe net-net if you just allowed, or somewhere around there,
and just a fairer system for most people.
Yeah, well, back then, the estimate from the Blueprint Institute was that Australians spent
$2.3 billion a year on managing their tax affairs.
Now, some of that's high-wealth people who are going to keep spending that money,
because they will still keep claiming their deductions.
But a lot of that is people going to their local suburban accountant and getting them to
do their tax return to try and find the extra receipts and get them a few hundred dollars extra.
And if you just have a $1,000 blanket deduction, the government's estimate now is that that
would cover about 42% of taxpayers.
About 6.2 million people would be better off just ticking the $1,000 box,
not worrying about their receipts and claiming that back.
And it is actually a progressive tax cut for many of those people, because they tend to be
people on lower incomes who don't have as many work-related expenses.
So you're basically giving a backdoor tax cut to a lot of low-income people
at a relatively minimal cost to the budget and some savings in both individuals and the tax office
compliance.
What's the argument against this?
It seems to be in some ways a no-brainer.
Why did it not get brought in originally?
And why might people argue against it at this point?
Yeah.
So the basic reason it didn't get brought in originally is that Wayne Swan back then was
desperately trying to get the budget back into surplus or at least balance because he was
copying stick from the other side of politics about having persistent deficits after the global
financial crisis.
And as the blueprint modelling shows, and of course that's a much bigger deduction, but
there is a substantial cost associated with this kind of policy because you are giving some
people who are not entitled to this deduction a free ride.
Like they may have spent nothing on work-related expenses that they could claim, but they still
get to claim the $1,000.
So it's basically just a tax cut.
But if you're on the top marginal tax rate, that can be a tax cut of $470.
Most of those people claim their deductions anyway.
So the reality is for the average person, this could be a boost of about $205, the government's
estimating.
But $205 times more than 6 million workers covered, and you can see why there's a budget
cost associated that in the past they've decided not to pay.
Yeah, fascinating.
Well, we'll wait to see what other speculation we get over coming weeks about what's actually
in this budget and when the government actually settles on what potential changes might be
made to that capital gains discount as well.
Michael, thanks for joining us.
Thanks, Carrington.
That is it for today's episode of ABC Business Daily.
We'll be back with another episode tomorrow.
And if you haven't already listened to it, remember we have our latest Fuelcast episode
in your feed this morning, right before this one.
Make sure you're following us on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts.
And if you'd like to send in a question, email abcbusinessdaily at abc.net.au.
Catch you next time, Michael.
See you, Carrington.

episodes.title: Fuelcast: A Strait choked once again
episodes.description: Petrol and diesel prices have been falling in recent days - but the Strait of Hormuz is once again under pressure. Iran has fired on multiple ships attempting to pass through it, and the US has seized an Iranian-flagged container ship.
episodes.transcript: This is an ABC podcast. Welcome to Fuelcast. I'm Carrington Clark, and this is your source to stay on top of the numbers behind the ongoing energy crisis. It's Monday, April the 20th. We're recording mid-morning, so let's dig in. The price of Brent crude is currently around $96 a barrel after a significant rebound after a renewed confrontation in and around the Gulf of Hormuz. And since we last checked in, the national average price of unleaded has dropped to $2.04, and the national price of diesel has dropped as well down to $2.97 per litre. Today, I'm joined by Alan Kohler to dig into today's major energy headlines. Good morning, Alan. Good morning, Carrington. Alan, petrol and diesel prices had been falling in recent days, but the Strait of Hormuz is once again choked off. Iran has fired upon multiple ships that attempted to travel through it, and the US has seized an Iranian-flagged container ship. So what happens now? Well, as you say, the Strait of Hormuz is closed again. It was open for 24 hours after Iran said on Friday morning New York time, it was actually Friday evening our time, that the Strait was completely open, but it's closed again because America refused to remove its blockade of Iranian ships. So there you go, it's closed. And of course, Brent crude and the benchmarks, West Texas and Brent, having fallen sharply 10% on Friday, are now rising again because of that. The price of petrol has come down, but that seems mainly to be because of the normal petrol price cycles that we see in Australia, which last about 30 days. And, you know, price goes up and down, sort of random, not randomly, but certainly of its own accord. And that's the reason they fell. The Melbourne radio got very excited this morning about there were four petrol stations in Trugger Niner at less than $1.80 per litre, which was unleaded $91.95 is still all above $2, $2, $2.13, $2.20, that sort of price. And that's the national average is kind of on the rise again. And we'll probably keep going up as, unless the Strait of Hormuz opens again. Alan, are we approaching a major pinch point for global supply? There are still, it appears, maybe some ships that got through that strait before the beginning of the war that are arriving at refineries, but are refineries going to start running out of crude input? And is that going to mean a real crunch in supply in coming days or weeks or months? Yes, definitely. Of course. I mean, the Asian refineries that we import our diesel and petrol from rely on Middle Eastern crude, in particular to make diesel, and they aren't getting any. They've still got some on hand, and there are still some ships on the water, but already the Singapore refinery has reduced its output by 20%. As I understand it, other refineries in Korea and Malaysia and Brunei are doing the same. Anthony Albanese has done deals with these countries to sort of guarantee supplies of gas in return for guaranteed supplies of petrol and diesel and jet fuel, but there's a limit to how far that can go. I mean, that doesn't mean we'll necessarily be at the front of the queue. We'll be somewhere near the front of the queue, I think, as supplies dwindle. But even, obviously, if supplies go completely to zero, then there's none for anybody. And at some point that will happen unless they can keep it going. They are able to get some crude from somewhere else. I think they are getting some from America, and elsewhere, perhaps Venezuela, but that's not entirely suitable for making diesel. So, there's a bit of a problem with that. Yeah, I think we saw, even though the estimates were around 20% of the world's usual supply of crude came through that choke point, the Strait of Hormuz, in normal times, even though we've seen that completely choked off, that hasn't been a complete 20% reduction. Maybe some people have estimated maybe 5% because we have seen some offsetting by the ramping up of production in other parts of the world, including the United States, in part because the price has gone higher and some of those ones that were marginal at lower prices became economical. But there does seem, there is a limit on that, isn't there, about how much that production can be ramped up. And as you say, a lot of these refineries are set up to deal with a particular type of crude oil, and if that crude oil is not coming through, they just can't produce in the way that they were beforehand. Correct. So, you know, I'm not an expert on any of this stuff, but it does seem to be that there's a limit to how adaptable those refineries are to crude oil from other reservoirs around the world. I mean, it does seem to be that they're pretty particularly geared for that particular crude oil, has to do with the amount of sulfur in it and the amount of other impurities they're able to deal with. So as to exactly what happens if this, if Australia for Meuse stays closed for, you know, like a month or three months or something, exactly what happens to those Asian refineries that we rely on is a bit hard to know. I mean, whether they completely stop producing or whether they just produce less, I just don't know. Alan, as we start this next week, I'm concerned about asking you, but are you more or less optimistic about the outlook for this energy crisis? Well, I'm obviously less optimistic than I was on Friday night. I woke up on Saturday morning and, you know, everything was fine. So that was an optimistic moment. Return to normality. That was an optimistic moment. And now it's less so. I mean, what seems to be going on in the talks between America and Iran that are taking place in Islamabad, which is what it's all about now, is the same sort of discussion that was taking place between 2013 and 2015, which led to the joint comprehensive agreement that was between Iran and six other countries, including the United States, which ended up with this agreement that Donald Trump cancelled in 2018. But they did sign an agreement in 2015, which was a pause in Iran's uranium enrichment for 10 years in return for freeing up Iran's frozen assets abroad. So they seem to be negotiating the same thing again. It's worth noting that for that 2015 agreement, that took 20 months to negotiate. They started off in Geneva. They ended up in Vienna. They went for 20 months and eventually came up with a deal, which Trump cancelled in 2018. And now here we are negotiating again. I mean, Trump reckons that this time the negotiations will take, will be really quick. I don't know. Well, we know Donald Trump doesn't have a lot of patience for long-term negotiations. But as you say, this has proven to be a tricky problem to solve. And the first challenge will actually be getting them all into the same room again, because Iran at this point, at least, seems to be suggesting that they're not open to that possibility. Alan, thank you for joining me for Fuelcast. Not at all. Thanks, Carrington. And I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like,
