Welcome to Fuelcast. I'm Carrington Clark and this is your source to stay on top of the numbers behind the ongoing energy crisis.
It's Friday, April the 17th. We're recording mid-morning, so let's dig into the numbers.
The price of Brent crude has risen to $98 a barrel.
It's still under $100 a barrel, but it is creeping up ever so slowly.
The national average price of unleaded has dropped to $2.12 per litre.
And the national average price of diesel has also dropped down to $3.08 per litre.
Today I'm joined by Alan Kohler to dig into today's major energy headlines.
Welcome, Alan.
G'day, Carrington.
Now, the big news, of course, is this Viva fire down in Victoria where you are.
The fire is now out, but its occurrence has raised, again, questions about Australia's vulnerability to cuts in fuel supply.
The Prime Minister has visited.
He says the facility is now operating at 80% capacity for diesel and jet fuel production and 60% for petrol production.
How concerned should we be about the lasting impacts of this fire?
Obviously, apart from the specific shortfalls in both diesel and petrol and jet fuel, it's a wake-up call, obviously, about how vulnerable we are.
I mean, with two only oil refineries in the country, one catches fire and we're in trouble.
And then the Prime Minister has to go around Asia begging for more petrol and diesel, please.
The timing almost couldn't be worse.
At the moment, there is no seeming link to any sort of ramp-up production.
It seems to be an accident.
They're not treating it as suspicious.
Viva has suggested that they're not going to be passing on any costs of repair to customers.
But I found that a kind of interesting comment because surely in a competitive market, the price is being set by all the players and it shouldn't be about Viva alone setting what the price should be.
But does this potentially mean we're going to have an interruption of supply domestically?
If they're at 80% diesel and jet fuel and 60% petrol, then obviously it will have an impact on supplies.
It must.
You know, and it isn't possible really for imports to fully replace them because imports are in short supply as well.
And that's what's going on.
That's why Anthony Albanese is travelling around Asia because there clearly is a shortfall in imports which needs to be bolstered in some way by promising to secure the supplies of gas.
I mean, the thing is that he doesn't actually own the gas, right?
And the people he's talking to, which is the heads of state, prime ministers and so on, they don't own the petrol and other fuels.
So all they're doing really is promising not to cut it off.
Do you think there will be any lasting impact from this petrol diplomacy?
Do you see the agreements that are being struck, as you said, if it's – these are company to company, usually transactions that are occurring.
Is there anything that can be done at the political level or does it have to be some sort of declaration of emergency in order to actually change the status quo?

I think we can assume probably that the companies involved, the gas companies here and the fuel companies in Asian refineries, that they are selling as much of the product as they can because they want to make as much money as they can.
So I don't think it's within Anthony Albanese's power to increase those supplies.
What he's promising to do is to not reduce them if things get dire, you know, as a result of the closure of the Straits of Hormuz.

He's saying to the Sultan of Brunei and the Prime Minister of Singapore and so on that we will not cut off your gas or, you know, you'll be at the last – you'll be the last country we cut off or whatever.
I'm not sure exactly what he's saying, but that's kind of what's going on.
They're modifying the Singapore Free Trade Agreement, for example.
So there are actual – there's not just verbal assurances, there are actual changes taking place to documentation.
And the messaging does seem to be from most countries that what they're going to do is prioritise their own domestic consumption.
But if there's fuel left over, then that they will prioritise Australia in that queue.
But obviously, for all countries, domestic considerations will trump any sort of agreement that they're signing with other countries.
They're not going to allow their own supplies to be in question, are they?
Of course.
That's right.
And that goes for Australia as well.
I mean, what – I mean, what Anthony Albanese is talking about is the possibility of a domestic gas reservation kicking in,
which he's saying we won't allow that to affect those other countries that are buying our gas if they kind of keep the supply of fuel coming to the extent possible.
So, I mean, obviously, he's got to make sure that there's enough gas in Australia first.
Alan, we're finishing the first week of fuel cast.
This week we've had the double embargo put into place, a fire at one of Australia's two refineries.
Are you feeling more or less optimistic about the state of the energy market?
Well, the energy market is a mess, let's face it, particularly for Australia.
We've learnt this week how much successive Australian governments have messed it up.
You know, allowing eight refineries to close over several decades was a bad idea.
Allowing oil exploration to decline to be replaced by gas exploration.
I mean, that's what the companies did.
There was no kind of guidance, no kind of central decision making going on in Canberra.
Is that a good idea or not?
So here we are with almost no oil coming out of Australia and two refineries.

I think that, you know, I mean, I think it's very interesting that around about the time these refineries were closing and Australia was making these decisions to not pursue renewable energy and not to electrify the Australian economy.
China was making the opposite decisions 20 years ago to electrify its economy, to invest in EVs, high-speed rail and renewable energy.
And now we're seeing the difference.
Yeah.
And we'll see whether or not this proves to be an inflection point for the uptake of electric vehicles here in Australia.
Alan, that's all we have time for on this episode of FuelCast.
Thanks for joining us.
Good on, you, Carrington.
Thank you.
Alan, you'll have another episode of That's Business later today.
Who are you chatting with?
Daniel Wood, the Chair of the Productivity Commission.
So listen in.
We will be back in your feeds with all things fuel for FuelCast on Monday.
Thanks, Alan.
Thanks.

engagement.takeaway: Authenticity in queer country music is a defiant journey of self-discovery, resilience, and finding truth beyond societal expectations.
bestQuotes: Host: "Giddy up! We're celebrating the best music from the best queer country artists curated by ABC Country."
Artist: "Truth makes you grow and sets you free. Sorting out your friends from your enemies. And I'm happy, nobody thinks. And out these days, humanity wins. Kindness pays."
Artist: "Because legends never die."
Artist: "The less I seek my source for some definitive, closer I am to find."
Artist: "I'm not a mountain lion, I'm not a grizzly bear. I'm just a soft little man, and I don't care."
engagement.whyListen: In the shadowed honky-tonks of a world demanding conformity, this broadcast cuts through the haze. Witness the raw, unvarnished anthems of queer country artists who dared to ride against the tide. From the 'guilty little sin' of a hidden kiss to the defiant roar that 'legends never die,' this is the soundtrack of souls forging their own truth, one note at a time. Tune in, and let the grit and glory of authenticity burn through your speakers.
engagement.socialPost: Forget the stereotypes. Queer country isn't just a genre; it's a revolution. 🤠 This episode of 'Celebrating Queer Country Music' on ABC Country dives deep into the raw honesty of artists who've traded 'guilty little sins' for anthems of self-acceptance. From 'Rhinestone Cowboys' to 'soft little men,' discover the defiant spirit shaping modern country. #QueerCountry #LGBTQIA+ #CountryMusic #Authenticity #LegendsNeverDie #ABCCountry

audiogramCaptions.text: I used to want to kiss a cowgirl, felt like a guilty little sin.
I learned to live inside a dream world. I had to keep my feelings in.
Truth makes you grow and sets you free.

I still kissed more cows than cowgirls.

episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. ABC Cricket Podcast time with one of your boys, Corbin Middlemass with you today. There is no Ed Cowan. One more week. Now I promise Ed will be here next Monday to chop it up with us on the ABC Cricket Podcast. But never fear, I always have a suitable replacement. George Bailey last week joined me for a great chat. And I got a message during the week too, by the way, when I threw it out there basically saying, hey, get in contact with us. We do have an email address, which is abccricketpodcast at abc.net.au. That's abccricketpodcast at abc.net.au. And let us know who are a couple of the people that you would love to hear from during this period while the IPL was going on, Ed's getting refreshed in some random part of the world, wherever he may be today. And Liam got in touch with me. And one of the first things that Liam said was, Corb, would love for you to have a chat with Ryan Harris if you can bring him on. Well, Liam, I've done exactly that. The all-conquering coach of the South Australian cricket team, Ryan Harris, is my special guest today on the ABC Cricket Podcast. A man who took over 100 test wickets. He's got over 300 first-class wickets. He was an absolute warrior, sending them down for Australia for many years. And now he is taken to the coaching game. And boy, has he had success straight out of the gates. Won three of the last four major domestic titles in Australian domestic cricket with the team that I'll still call the Redbacks, the mighty South Australian cricket team. Twice winning the Sheffield Shield, the drought-breaking title, while then defending it, obviously in the season just gone. And then chucking a one-day title the year before as well to add to the list of accolades. His name is Ryan Harris. And I'm pleased to say he joins me as my guest on the ABC Cricket Podcast. Ryan, firstly, congratulations. Thanks, Torb. Yeah, it's a nice feeling to be obviously sitting here again with a Sheffield Shield sitting in the room next door. It's quite a good feeling. Well, that'd be set the Australian cricket fans thinking we would have just taken one. We had to wait like 30 years or whatever to get a drought-breaking title. And then you go out and you back it up away from home in a Shield final. I mean, what a 12, 13 months for SA cricket. Yeah, it has. It's been three years since I've been back at South Australian cricket. So, Saki here. So, it's been a huge couple of years. And, you know, the reason I moved back is I thought I could see some real growth in this group. Obviously, it's tough with the line-up that we've had for a while. But he had a tough year this year with a few little niggles. And, you know, just chuffing... You know, his eyes... He couldn't get his eyes level and stable. So what he's done this year has been quite phenomenal. Still be able to take a foot in the early 40 weeks, I think it was. And do it, you know... There were times where he probably wasn't at his best, but he just kept fighting and fighting. And he, you know, by the back end of the year, I think he found a way just to deal with it. And he started bowling probably, you know, to the way he can bowl. And, you know, he took a lot of wickets to the back end, obviously, in the final against Queensland. He took, you know, a good pile of wickets. And so he's had a really tough year. I think, you know, I think he's just a good cricketer. I would love to have seen him play a handful of test matches, you know, up to this date. But I don't know if it's going to happen. He might be past him now. But, I mean, if you talk to him, he's like, yeah, that'd be great. But I just want to keep winning here. So he's got great attitude towards Australia. Great segue. I was going to ask you about the importance of winning. So I know it used to drive the Victorian boys mad back in the day about, you know, they would have this great team, a lot of really good players, but often their guys were overlooked for national selection and they'd go somewhere else. And, you know, to be fair, Australian cricket's always been pretty successful over the last 25, 30 years. So it's hard to say necessarily they got it wrong or they should have picked this guy at any one time. But do you think we value winning enough when it comes to selection? And I look at, you know, in track and field, for example, there's a difference between being a really good runner and being a racer. And you look at someone like Lockie Kennedy at the moment who's, you know, dynamic on the track. And he thrives in competition when there's guys alongside him and it brings out the best in him. I wonder in Australian cricket where, you know, we often look at the next best player, but he might be playing in a struggling team, for example. Is there something to be said for guys that are actually winning and the importance of getting it done in games and that wins and losses matter? Does it mean as much in cricket compared to just, you know, individual performances? Oh, I understand. Absolutely. And I think if I talk from a team perspective, I mean, I played for South Australia for six years, I think it was, or seven years. And what you talk about there, like the Victoria guys, we had really good sides. We just didn't know how to win. Yeah. And one thing I learned, which I carry with me a lot, the way I coach as well, is when I moved to Queensland to play cricket, you walk into that environment, they just expect to win. They knew how to win. And I took a lot from that. You don't even think about it. You don't even talk about the result not going your way and losing. And if you do lose, then it's like, well, you know, why did we do it? And then we don't do it again. And so you've got to have that. No doubt. I think winning is a, I think it's a culture. And again, one of the things I've changed here a bit as well is, you know, when we play second-leven cricket, we're playing some young kids and given opportunity and that, we use it for that. Yeah, that's cool. But we've got to actually win. We've got to learn how to win games. Same as under-19s. I think it's a culture, to be honest. And so I learned that hugely moving from a team that we had a very good team with, you know, Greg Blewett, Darren Lehman. So I mean, we had a group of, a really good group of guys here in Adelaide to want to move to Brisbane. And it's just, you walk in and you walk into those four walls in Brisbane, it was Queensland cricket. It was like, well, we just don't expect to lose. We just, we're going to win everything. And they had been pretty successful in the years leading up to that. So I took a lot out of that. And on the stage here now, I say to the boys, I don't coach to lose. You know, we play to win and yet sometimes it doesn't go to plan. And if it doesn't go to plan, then we work out why pretty quick to get back on the other side of it. Yeah. Sometimes it feels like maybe the way we talk about it in the press as well, where it sort of feels like, oh, they're talent pathways and they're producing players to play for Australia or, you know, grade crickets, producing players to play for their state. And that's all well and good. But ultimately the aim of the game is to win. So keep the, keep the main thing, the main thing. Just on, on your own coaching journey. So if you were to look at what motivates you as a coach, what your philosophy is, like who has a couple of the things, I guess that, or what are a couple of the things that, that, that I guess you would base your philosophy as a, as a coach around? Oh, I mean, well, it's a good question as well. I mean, there's a few, I mean, having, having some fun, having fun is one of the big things is that, you know, when we come out and play here, we get all serious at times, but the bottom line is, I even, I write it up on the board every time in the change room is we have our three or four different points that I keep writing up. And the bottom line is we have fun and we do it together, you know, and, and that's, that's, that's one thing that I just, I just say, whether the boys look at it, I don't know, but I put it up every, every game and, and well, I mean, they do, they do have a lot of fun playing with each other, but the other, I think the other thing is just, yeah, it's hard. I always find this question hard to answer because I put putting into words, I've got a big philosophy written on my computer, but putting into a couple of words, but you know, the other one is passion. I'm very passionate about what I do. And I think I want them to know, I want the players to know again, like I said earlier, that whenever they go into, into battle that I'm on there with them and I ride it with them. I get disappointed with them. I get happy with them. I guess that, that's sort of, that shines through a fair bit because I do like, I do, I do the odd, you know, Rhino rev up. I think Dizzy used to call it. I do get them in a circle and give them a good, you know, have a good chat with them. But so passion is probably one, probably one that I've had to learn a lot more of is as a coach is, is learning the game of technicals. You know, I was never a captain. I was never great at being a tactical person. So, you know, I've been lucky enough to spend some time. I mean, when I finished, you know, obviously playing with some really good captains, but on the flip side, on the other side of the fence, you know, Darren Lehman got me, got me around a lot when I was sort of learning how to coach. I've been with Ricky Ponting. I've been with Mike Hessen. The guys that are, that I look at, look back on and who are pretty good, you know, ambassadors of the game and know the game pretty well. I mean, I played under Ricky, for instance, for example, and then I went and coached with him at Delhi in the, in the IPL. And I, you know, it's a great sort of example, I guess, of having to learn more. I would, I would try, I would do the bowling meetings and, you know, I'd sort of finish it and go, geez, I felt, I felt like I did that one pretty good. And then Ricky would stand up and say a few other different things. I'd be like, yeah, I probably should have mentioned that. Yeah. Probably should have said that. Probably should have done that. Probably should have said that to him. And it just made me think that, I mean, we know, we all know what Ricky's cricket brains like. It's phenomenal, but it made me think that, yeah, I've still got a fair bit to learn here about the tactical part of the game. So, yeah. So I look back on all those, those sort of examples. That's, that's sort of maybe the coach or making, not maybe making me the coach. I'm trying to be. My next question was going to be influences guys that you've sort of, yeah, helped you along the way. So, I mean, Ricky Ponting, Darren Lehman, a couple there that you both mentioned. Is there any others you, you want to give a little hat tip to? Oh, I mean, Wolf has been, Wolf has been great. You know, from the start, he gave me an option. Obviously my career came to an end abruptly, unfortunately, you know, with my knee. And I was able to travel with him a few times around and actually see, sit on the other side while the boys are playing, how it, how it actually worked. Troy, Troy Cooley is probably the other one. He's, he's one that, you know, I spent the whole time at Cricket Australia with. Obviously he was a coach of mine as well, but he, he got me really going in the art of coaching and he talked about the art of coaching and, you know, another, just another guy with so much knowledge around fast bowling, but also, you know, being a coach and, and, you know, what, what it actually takes. So, I guess those two. The other one was Pat Howard, actually, the other cricket high performance manager at Cricket Australia. Here's another one who I'm still in touch with, a very, very smart guy, you know, came in, got a lot of criticism around being from rugby wise, a rugby bloke doing cricket, but he was really smart guy that, and, and, and, you know, just, he, he, he knew cricket a lot more than what people think, but what he didn't do is he knew he wasn't the expert on cricket. So he'd speak to a lot of cricket people as well. So Greg Chappell was around that time, Darren Lamb and Troy Cooley. So, as well as some ex-great. So he was another guy that taught me, you know, about coaching, but also a lot about business, you know, just about how, how to be, how to be a person that relates to a lot of different other people when, you know, when you're working in an organisation like Cricket Australia. So he was another guy that I guess I'll look back on. And, you know, as I said, I still touch base with him now that it gives me some good, good advice. So I've had, well, that's some really good people along the way that, that, that have been, you know, absolutely, um, give me some great advice. And, and again, I'm still on the journey. I'm not anywhere near finished. Um, so I still have a bit to go. Uh, your passion's obvious and everyone that we run into in Australian cricket talks about that with you. We saw it as when you played and you were just such a warrior in the way that you went about it. And, you know, you don't seem like the modern cricketer in terms of our scans and stress fractures and everything else. It's just, you know, plow on, keep playing and everything else. How do you go with the, I guess the modern player or the younger guys coming through or whatever it turns out to be? Have you had to, have you had to sort of almost catch yourself at different times thinking, right, I've got to have a broader lens here than just, Hey, this is what I did. So this is what's going to work. How challenging has that been as a, you know, to, to, to deal with so many different personalities in the, in a dressing room that obviously coaching would, would, would throw at you. Yeah. Very challenging at times. It has been. There's, there is exactly that. Some of the minds, well, the mindset I've had to change is, you know, especially from a bowling point of view is, you know, some guys are sore. It's like, well, how sorry are you? Can you, can you bowl through it? Or is it actually an injury? You know, if it's an injury, then fine. But if it's not push on. And, and, you know, there's definitely times where I'm a lot better at now. Obviously I can, I've talked to the medical staff quite a lot. I do push, I still push them, the medical staff to push the players a fair bit. But again, it's, you've got to be very careful doing that because if it, if it is wrong, it can cause sort of, you know, longer term injury. So that's, again, I'm still learning how to do that, but, but I, I do, I do push the players quite a lot. And I know, well, when they know, and I think that's the relationship I think I have with a lot of the players, if not all of them, that if there is something that's not right, I will, I won't go through the medical staff. I'll go straight to them and talk to them. And, you know, you know, if, if there is something not right, then they look me in the eye and they, and I know, I know straight away that something's not right. So, yeah, I think we're really good here with, with the way we sort of, I think most Australian cricket, to be honest, the States, I can't, I can't talk for the other States, but, you know, we always talk about, and, and I probably got a little bit caught up in it when I was starting coaching in Cricket Australia around workloads and about this and that, and, you know, about two, bowling not enough or bowling too much or bowling the exact amount of balls that you, that the planner says, and that's it. you know, I did, but coming out of that, even now, I mean, we, we, we, you know, quick, quick, the season is quite a challenging season. So, you know, our bowlers, the, the issue obviously we have is our batters have to face bowlers. And sometimes, you know, we, we, we don't, we don't always do that here because we have to allow the bowls to bowl once a week rather than twice a week, or if they need to bowl, you know, not at all to be fresh for games. And, you know, so we're quite open to, to, to getting what the individual needs. And I think the other, part of that as well is, if, you know, we, we still use the same planner. We still say there's 42 balls to bowl this, this week, this day, or each day, but it's, it's, we, we go on time, you know, and for bowls, again, if a bowl is not bowling well enough, then he keeps bowling until he gets, until he gets the right feel. And, you know, you can't go into, you can't go into a game knowing you bowl the right amount of balls, but, you know, 70, 70% or 80% of those balls have been in the wrong spot. Yeah. You're not going to go into a game feeling good. Right. So, you know, so we're, we're really conscious of that here. And again, I've got a really good group, pretty experienced group now that know what they need and, and how much they need to do before, you know, going, leading into a game. So, um, definitely have changed my tune a bit on that. I was, I was a little bit, um, caught up in, I guess, in, yep, just exactly this, exactly that amount of, and then away you go. But I learned pretty quickly though, that, yeah, the skill level, the only way you get better at bowling is to bowl. And, um, you know, even, even at times we talk about being injured, you know, sometimes you saw, you've got to bowl when you saw, because you're never going to be a hundred percent feeling right. Um, and if you, if you do, if you are, then you're not trying hard enough. Yeah. Um, because you're always going to be sought when you bowl. Two more for you. Um, first of all, that coaching a state team. So, I mean, cricket coaches are relatively new thing in the history of the game, but, uh, obviously these jobs were incredibly popular for a long period of time. There's only six of them in the country. So, um, you know, that they're always highly competitive jobs to have in more recent times, though, it feels like, you know, cricket coaches, the appeal of the T20 franchise scene, for example, and, you know, you go away and essentially make, um, you can make a, yeah, an annual salary worth in basically doing two tournaments or whatever it turns out to be. And that's eight weeks worth of work. And you can jump around and do a bunch of those, but it's, it's in and out. It's not the sort of regular contact like it is to, to be a state coach, for example. What is it that appeals to you about this? Cause clearly you, this, this fulfills a passion for you that, uh, that obviously, you know, you like the idea of, of working with players and player development that goes into it that you don't necessarily get when you just roll up and get a collection of the best players in the world for a, for a two week T20 tournament or whatever it turns out to be. Yeah. I mean, firstly, uh, I, I'm, I look at the opportunity to be able to do that. I, I do, I do like the game of T20. I wouldn't say I love it. I love four day cricket. I love five day cricket. I love one day cricket. I'm still, I'm still growing the love for T20 cricket. I played a little bit of it, but, and I've coached a little bit of it. But, and the other part to that is I don't, and this is going to sound really, I don't know how it's actually going to sound, but I don't think a lot of that is proper coaching. I think you're, you're looking after a group of, a group of men for eight weeks, 10 weeks, you know, you're not, I mean, I've seen Ricky do it. Ricky is really good at it. He does coach a lot. Um, and I've seen snippets of Justin as well, Justin Lania, but I feel as though for me as the bowling coach, it was more, again, looking after what, you know, trying to preach what Ricky would say or, or the head coach. But I just, I didn't feel, and maybe because I haven't head coached in one of those leagues, I didn't feel it was proper coaching. Um, and that's probably, that might be another reason why I'm sitting here, not over there in the IPL as well. I might not have been very good at it, but I just find what I do here. Um, this is a program. You get to run your own program. Um, and I think for, again, for majority of the coaches, there's, again, there's a, there's a few guys that, that, that it just happens naturally. And that is the Pontings and Langers because there's such strong personalities and good leaders and amazing readers of the game that there's not too many that you can just walk out of it. Um, or I guess go to playing or doing what they, what they did into a big coaching role like that. And, and to be honest, my name's probably not big enough either to do that in the IPL, which, which is okay. I don't, I don't mind that. So for me, and the other part of that, as I've said to you before, is I, I had to go back and learn a lot, a lot of the games. I didn't see the game in a technical or a tactical way that, that was, was great. It was just bowl fast, hit the top of off and bowl the occasional bounce. Then when I had an opportunity with the bat, get as many as I could, um, hit the ball to the gaps. That was the way I sort of looked at the game. So I, I, I've had to learn a lot of that as I've been through, but yeah, I think the opportunity to run a program, it really excites me. As you say, and it's funny when you say there's only six of us around that. I hadn't actually thought of it like that. You know, and we, what we do, our jobs are, you know, pretty important in, in, in helping get cricket, you know, Australian cricket strong. And that's the detail of it. I haven't really probably thought of it in, in, in detail like that, but I just, I just love the opportunity to run a program. I'm with God, I work, you know, I work, I briefly did it with Queensland cricket as an assistant and doing different things up there. I've come down here in South Australia and give me opportunity to, to, I guess, fulfill another dream. You know, playing was a dream. Now coaching is a dream. And then they've given that opportunity. And I, and I work, I work at a great organization. I've got great people around me and coaches. I've got a great general manager. I've got a great CEO and I've got a great president and a great board. So I'm very happy with what I do. And they allow me to, um, do what I want to do and, and with the program and run the program. So, and, and from now on, it's, it's, you know, we, we, we set a standard now that yet we've won two, but, um, probably after four or five weeks, once I have a break, we're going to win three and four and five. See, that's what we want to do. And, um, that's, as I said before, I don't coach to lose and the players don't play to lose now. So, um, I think, yeah, long winded answer. Again, I just think having that, having that opportunity to, to work in a, to run your program or a program, uh, I think that's, that's what excites me. Last one for you. And you're going to get this question a whole lot, I'm sure. And it's, it's maybe it's the blessing in the curse of having success. It's, it's great to have success, but often what happens when, you know, people are in successful positions or that they, they achieve well, everyone basically says, you know, what's next? What are you going to do next? Where are you going to go next? It's, do you want to coach the national team one day? Is that the, the, I guess the, the end goal that you look at in terms of, of coaching? Yeah, you're right. I've, I've been asked that a lot in the last week again, or the two weeks. Um, I think ultimately, yes. Uh, I think it's like when, so the way I look at it, and I've said it a number of times publicly as well, is when you get into a job, like in this industry, playing or coaching is that, you know, you, you, you play well, you earn your role, earn your spot, you know, in state cricket, you play well, you earn your spot in the Australian team. You've got to keep earning your role, earning your spot and, and performing. I see that here now. I, I, I sit here and everyone's, oh, he's got to coach straight. Firstly, we've got a pretty good, pretty good coach at the moment. He's doing a bloody good job, Andrew McDonald, um, who I don't think will be going anywhere soon. We've also got another guy, I don't have voters who won three or four state titles. And how many, 15 bloody BBL titles. He's not going, he's going to ride as well. So I've got, I've still got a long way to go. Um, and there's a lot of good coaches around the country that, again, that are lining up for that job. Um, but I mean, ultimately, yeah, I will, I do want to do it, but I don't, I don't expect it to do it tomorrow. I'm still young in my coaching. As I've said to you, I'm still learning a lot about the game. Um, you know, if the opportunity comes up one day to put my name in the ring, then yeah, if it's the right time and right. And the other part of that, if it's the right time for my family, because once I get on that bus, it's, it's a long time away and I've got young kids. So, um, you know, a few factors there, but yeah, bottom line is I'd love to one day. Um, but again, I'll, I'll, I'll, I'll wait, earn my, earn my, earn my spot, earn my, um, the, you know, the, the right to do it. And if that's next year, great. If it's 10 years and that's what it is. So, um, but in the meantime, as I said, I'm working in a pretty good place. I love what I do here and I've got a bit of work to do yet. So. You're a popular man in Australian cricket. It's nice to see good things happen to, uh, to good people and your coaching journey is, uh, is certainly up and to the right. Have you got a holiday planned or anything exciting? What are you going to do in your, your little time, just small time you get before, uh, next season starts? Yeah, I'll, I'll get through this next two weeks of kids school holidays. I'm going to recreate myself from a golf clubs and try and get some nice scores. But just while we've been talking, my wife's been flicking through places for holidays next week. So that's my next part after, after I get off the phone here to go and try and organize it. That's a time with family. So yeah, I'm looking forward to that. We'll let you go and do it. Uh, Ryan, appreciate your time as always. Congratulations on all you've achieved so far and we'll, uh, we'll stay close. We'll chat to you soon on the, uh, on the ABC cricket podcast. Thank you. Nice chatting. Thanks, man. Thanks, man.

So from a South Australian point of view, I always look at the Shield team and

And yet in a way that no one else has been able to for the last 20 years,

episodes.description: Chief selector George Bailey is one of the most influential figures in Australian cricket and joins Corbin to talk through the life of a selector.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. ABC Cricket Podcast time with one of your boys, Corbin Middlemass in today. There is no Ed Cowan. He's taking a well-earned break, as we say, in the industry. There's no such thing as a cricket off-season. The IPL obviously ongoing at the moment. But Ed's going to just try and take a little bit of time off and recharge the batteries. During that time, when Ed isn't here, I'll be joined by some of the heavy hitters in Australian cricket. So if there's a special guest in particular that you want to hear from on this podcast, of course, your favourite cricket podcast, you can hit us up at abccricketpodcast at abc.net.au. That's abccricketpodcast at abc.net.au. And I haven't forgotten, by the way, about Ed and his all-time ODI team. So we'll hold him to that. First up today, the guests don't get too much bigger than this. A man who we talk about all the time here, along with his two selection buddies in Andrew McDonald and Tony Dottomater. My guest today is the chief selector of the Australian cricket team, George Bailey. We talk about the relationship between the team and the press, which we debate, obviously, ongoing here on the ABC Cricket Podcast. People might have different opinions on whether the documentaries being there or not being there is a good thing. I certainly feel like the access to players and the amount of press they do, and then individually with different podcasts and their own social media accounts, I think you're still getting a tremendous insight as to where players are at. The past player criticisms directed at him and at the team more broadly, how that impacts him. I don't perhaps always say it this way, but it's a strength. We don't get the benefit of hindsight. I guess everyone watching and critiquing, they do get that. Who might be the next cab off the rank for the Australian cricket team? And the contract list, which was released last Wednesday. Who got in, who missed out, and what the team is prioritising over the next 12 months? There's no doubt at times we're going to have to go deeper than that. I think always with those contract lists is trying to strike the balance of rewarding those that have performed well in that men's team, particularly across the test space and with what's coming up with the test schedule. And also trying to make sure that you've got all bases covered and a nice balance across that list. So here it is. My chat with the Chief Selector, George Bailey. Former three-format cricketer for Australia, a man who captained his country on many occasions in the white ball format. He is now the Chief Selector of the Australian cricket team. George Bailey joins me on the ABC Cricket Podcast. George, appreciate your time. Howdy, Cole. Squads out. So we learnt that when it came through on Wednesday. What are your key takeaways from the contract list that Cricket Australia released? I think looking forward and understanding that it's a really busy schedule and the contract list is a starting point. There's going to be no doubt at times we're going to have to go deeper than that. I think always with those contract lists is trying to strike the balance of rewarding those that have performed well in that men's team, particularly across the test space and with what's coming up with the test schedule and also trying to make sure that you've got all bases covered and a nice balance across that list. You mentioned as part of it that you have had a leniency towards a longer format of the game, putting this contract list together, given the fact that there's so many test matches in the next 12-month window. So the only three guys that I'm looking at here that are specifically white ball players at the moment, Mitch Marsh, who of course has played red ball cricket in the not-too-distant pass, Adam Zampa and Nathan Ellis. It means there's no Glenn Maxwell, there's no Tim David. Is that their choice? Is that your choice as to how that comes about? Obviously, with the advent of franchise cricket and so many other options, 12 months of the year, how did it come about to leave a couple of those sort of white ball specialists off the list? I think it's looking ahead with what the 12 months is and clearly, I think it's potentially 20, 21, but 20 tests in the next 12 months. Effectively, the red ball focus is going to be huge, but also understanding that at the back end of that, we launch into a 50-over World Cup and then 28 is a home T20 World Cup as well. No idea where the Olympics fit in that at the moment. I haven't got any information. You might have more on that than me. I'm still chasing up. I guess they're three of the key pillars around that white ball team. There's certainly other very important members of multi-format players in that list as well. Is there actually a cut-off date for the Olympic qualification? Are you guys aware of when that has to be, like when you need to be ranked in a certain position or to automatically qualify? No, no idea. No, no. I'd love to know. It's crazy, isn't it? The whole cricket world seemingly in the same boat with that. Jake Weatherald's part of it. Sam Constance isn't. Is that an indication as to what's going to happen the next time the team rolls out in the white clothing in Darwin, that Jake Weatherald will be the opener as he is the incumbent? He is the incumbent. Obviously, playing a part across the Ashes across the summer, also rewarding his consistent performance across a couple of years of domestic cricket as well. Yeah, not shying away from the fact that I think there were a couple of things technically that were targeted and potentially exposed across that Ashes period. But we think he can play. And I think he's got a good opportunity now. He's going to head across to Leicester and have a little stint over there. And in and around that, a good chunk of time where he can get really busy with the coaching staff and, you know, in particular, Michael DiVenuto in that batting space to focus on that. But, you know, as to I won't lock him into that Bangladesh series. I think we've been pretty consistent. You know, we'll pick a team when we need to pick a team. We've got a number of camps across the winter as well, again, which will, you know, encompass a range of players inside and outside that contract list. And, you know, he'll be a part of that and we'll work to that closer. What should we expect from, I guess, the makeup of those teams? Like people would say, yeah, hey, this is a top end series against Bangladesh. It's an opportunity to get a glimpse into the future. Do you look at it more as, you know, this will be not a development team because obviously when you wear the bag of green, it's never that. But is it likely to be a full strength, fully loaded Australian team for that first test in August? Yeah, well, we treat every test match as that. Now, within that, you know, how that shapes up balance wise. We haven't done a great deep dive into, you know, potential conditions up there. We had a little bit of A cricket in the top end last year, some red ball cricket. And we've obviously been up in that part of the world for some white ball cricket as well. So we know the grounds. But no, I think, you know, I would hate to toy with the idea of treating any test match as a development opportunity. And particularly, you know, I think that would be unfair to the players too who invest so much into, as you said, it's not easy to play test cricket and they need to be rewarded for that. Your coach was on radio in Melbourne a couple of days ago and spoke about Webster and Green and that he can see them both playing in the same team in the middle order. He did also preface that by saying, look, I haven't spoken to my fellow selectors yet. I get the opportunity here to speak to one of them. Is that how you see it, given Usman Khawaj's retirement and the fact that there is a spot at number five? Do you see the potential that, you know, that that middle order includes both Webster and Green? Yeah, absolutely. I think we've been on record of saying that those two can play on the same team in the past as well. Well, yeah, I don't see it as a hindrance, the fact that they both have a skill set across the bat and ball. Again, you know, hopefully they both are available to boot. The ball increase by that stage of the year, that'd be helpful. But again, it'll be striking the balance of what we need. I guess specifically, yes, you know, to Uzi or that number five spot opening up. But yeah, I mean, I think we've seen Cam back across a range of positions. I know he probably wasn't as, probably didn't quite get the output that he would have liked across the Aussie summer. But even thinking back to the tricky wickets in the West Indies and again, not massive scores, but in terms of contributions and percentage of runs in what were winning totals, he did really well. So he certainly got the skill set to do that. You know, Alex Carey is another one, I think, who, you know, he's gone up to six. He's got some flexibility there too. So, yeah, no, I mean, I guess the starting point is they can absolutely both play on the same team. Can he bat five, Alex Carey? I reckon he could, whether, you know, whether it suits the balance and understanding that he, you know, on the back of spending however long he may need to in the field. And most of it up to the stumps now, he seems to be loving that. Yeah, what an incredible summer he's had. Congratulations on the Ashes. I mean, a 4-1 series victory at any time is absolutely worthy of celebration. And certainly I think Australian cricket fans appreciated that. Andrew McDonald spoke about the review. And I think in the radio interview with Gerard Waitley, he even had it in front of him and spoke about the subcategories and the training and preparation, all the different areas. Can you give us a little insight as to how that review went? Yeah, I mean, we review every major series. So it's not like it was a special touch point or anything. So it was just, yeah, going through. And I certainly don't have it in front of me, Corb. Apologies for that, unprepared. But, yeah, going through the same sort of four, five, six sort of major headlines and just reviewing. And no two series are the same. So I think there's always little bits you take out of it. I think that, you know, certainly from my area in the selection management, one of the big thing that we try and look back on is just to make sure we, you know, was there anything we missed? Were there any sort of questions or challenge ourselves sort of moments that we didn't foresee? Yeah. And, you know, the ashes, it was the planning for that would have started 12 or 14 months before. You obviously tighten it up as you go. But even as close as probably a month out compared to how that series played out and the personnel that we ended up having available at different times. Some of the guys to step in, some of the late moving parts, even on the morning of games. So, you know, your best laid plans can often be thrown out. But I think what was most pleasing was, you know, how well guys were able to step in and step into some different roles, step in and perform and step in and help that team win. And, you know, it's probably two summers in a row where, you know, the Indian Test Series and the ashes, just the scrutiny and the interest in it's been phenomenal. And I think, you know, that's awesome. And so to see the players, whether that, absorb that with all the different changes that were happening and then come out the other side with a 4-1 victory was very satisfying. They did well. Obviously, we're part of that in what we do on this podcast and certainly in our analysis of the team. I mean, it feels like certainly coming out of Cape Town, there was this Amazon series and it was about showcasing the personalities of the Australian cricket team and who the guys are. And obviously, we've seen less of that in recent times. And it feels like there's been a conscious decision to try and keep the walls a little bit higher. Is that player driven? Is that led by you guys as a selection panel? What's the, I guess, what can you tell us about that? The fact that, and is that part of it, the way that what you're alluding to there, that the criticism or the scrutiny feels like it's as sharp as it has been? No, not at all. I mean, people might have different opinions on whether, yeah, the documentaries being there or not being there is a good thing. I mean, I certainly feel like the access to players and the amount of press they do. And then individually with some, you know, different podcasts and their own social media accounts, I think you're still getting a tremendous insight as to where players are at. But there's probably a focus at certain times within the team to try and, you know, when you do get a day or two in between tests to try and really protect around that. And understanding that you obviously see the physical output within a game, but then also that for players, it's a home summer. But, you know, you only get to potentially stay at your house once for the majority of players. So just understanding the little connection point there with family and friends is also critical. And just being able to freshen up, knowing that, you know, it's coming again and the opposition's hard. So there's been a conscious effort, I think, at different times to protect a day or two. But I think the access is really high. And I still think players are pretty good. I mean, a lot of that potentially comes down to the individual personalities of certain players and where they're at and what they're willing to share. Is this stuff we can do better, do you think, as the press? I don't know, mate. I hadn't really. I mean, I think internally I always, we always think that it's, you know, your good times, you're never going as well as you sometimes are built up to be externally. And vice versa, when things don't go well and you have a bad game or a bad series, things aren't as dire as they seem to be as well. So it's probably just a keeping of the balance and understanding that like anything, you know, particularly in sport, that there's natural ebbs and flows. And it's not certainly in a player's career or a player's series, it's not linear where there's just this constant performance. And they're always working on trying to perform better and trying to fit their role in the team like we are as staff in terms of constantly trying to evolve with the team as well. We've seen, I think there was an article by Tom Deason recently where he detailed his exchange with Cam Green following that Sheffield Shield game. Is that a concern in the, I guess, the relationship between the player and the press and then also Cam more specifically as how he's going as such an asset for Australian cricket as a guy who's about to embark on a pretty long and sometimes difficult IPL campaign? No, I mean, I haven't spoken to Cam directly about that. I imagine, and you know him, you would have spoken to him many times across his journey. I'm very comfortable in saying it's an out of character reaction from him. So that's something that he will potentially reflect and speak to, you know, at some point. But no, I think for the vast majority, using Tom as an example, we've had a number of away trips. I think generally the guy, the cricket writers, the tour, I think everyone gets along well with them. And, you know, everyone just understanding that players have a job to do, the press have a job to do. And, you know, if that works well in, you know, together, I think everyone benefits. You've copped your fair share of criticism too for, you know, again, I'm not trying to blow smoke here, but it's sort of you've had great results clearly in your time as a chief selector. And yet, you know, former players have been critical as, you know, whether you're able to make hard calls on players. We only obviously get a chance to judge on what the team looks like when it goes out there. How do you go with that as a former player? You know, often the criticism's coming from guys that either you played with or that are, you know, past members of the Australian cricket team. How do you go handling that while also trying to, you know, follow the vision and continue on the path that obviously you have for this team? I think fundamentally it's a, you know, I don't perhaps always say it this way, but it's a strength. You know, I don't, I can't recall ever being in a situation with this team where it feels like if we don't send this 11 out, we can't win the game. So again, it's probably just not so binary around black and white of this is the 11 that can win. I think the coaching staff and playing group have bought into the, and have built up a system where they like to think that there's different ways that they can win a game. And part of that will be the way your team's structured, part of that will be the opposition and clearly the surface at different times as well and being flexible and being flexible within that. So, you know, we don't get the benefit of hindsight. I guess everyone watching and critiquing, they do get that. And, but, you know, we never, I don't think we've ever been in a situation to say where, I don't want to use specific examples, but player X gets a tight selection call going his way. Now it's not to say that we, that we also don't believe that if we'd gone with player, player wide that we also wouldn't have got the same result. It might've been done differently, but we can still, we can still win the game that way. So I try and see it as a strength that, you know, it's great that there are other options and people are publicly backing other options. You know, I imagine in some cases there's some, there's some bias around why people are certain, you know, have certain fondness for players that aren't in the team. But it's, you know, it's a, it's a strength. Hopefully that continues. And hopefully the Australian cricket team continues to have options when it's picking, picking 11s or picking squads. Just on hindsight, if you had your time again, would you play a frontline spinner in Sydney? No, but you could. I mean, yeah, I mean, that's, that's, I think we can continue to debate that. We debated it right up and right up until the morning of the game. Our starting, our starting position is that we don't like not picking a spinner. We don't, we like picking a spinner. We don't, I think when we're putting a test 11 together, the starting premises, there will be a spinner in it, but not, not trying to fight, not trying to fight the conditions just to prove a point at different times. But again, that, I mean, that's, that's probably a good example of one where, yeah, I think we could have played a spinner and I would like to think that we will get the same result. The game might've played out differently, but, but hopefully you could still execute that. In recent times on the schedule, the, the test summer has been starting in Perth. I noticed as, as one of the subheadings in that Ashes review, it was sort of training and preparation. I think you're a fascinating watch in your team and how it's presented in Perth. So two years in a row, split results, one, one, lost one. I think clearly, if you look back on the, the India series, the team warmed into it and clearly, you know, with a better team by the time the, the five test series ended, ended against India, but it didn't start well and you copped a lot of criticism there. Have you refined that or have you reviewed, like, what's the best way to be able to, to start in Perth to make sure that the best version of the Australian cricket team is the one we get in the, in the first red ball test of the summer? So there's a, there's a number of factors. I think it depends what you've got in and around that test series, what guys have been coming up off. Have they, have they got enough body of work to be able to perform their role? You know, particularly the, around the fast bowlers and making sure they've got up to the intensity or, or miles in their legs, if you want to call it that. And yeah, as you said, we, we, we lost a couple in the lead up this year, which is never, never ideal. And then there's other years where on the back of a lot of cricket, you might be trying to, to massage them in. Yeah. I, I, I haven't sort of looked back on that and said that, you know, we won the game. So the preparation for this year was good. And last year's preparation was, wasn't good because we lost the game. I think there's, there's things that happen within a game that, that affect that anyway. And I think both, both games had some individual circumstances that, that blew the game in the directions that they went. But yeah, that, that is part of the review. It's part of the planning process when you go forward is to, well, you know, what, what does it look like? What's it, and we're already looking at, what does it look like for the start of this summer? I think we've got a reasonable block of white ball cricket against England leading into the four tests against New Zealand. So I guess from a selection philosophy point of view, do you see batting positions more specific in the T20 game than you do in the, in the test arena? No, not necessarily. And I think that's, you know, I don't think that'll, that'll necessarily happen overnight, but that's, that's a work in progress. Can we develop that as that can? And again, knowing that conditions, you know, we've seen Travis do it for a number of years in the subcontinent where we feel he's best suited at the top. And then when the opportunity was there, it looks like it works quite nicely in Australia as well. And also, I'm seeing, you know, that, that may not suit every player. It may not suit every player's personality as well. But again, it's, you know, how, how does it fit? How does it make the team function as a whole? Well, I think you're always, whenever you're putting a team together, you're trying to play to your strengths. There's always going to be a way, you know, the staff talk about a way that you are prepared to lose the game in a quest to try and win it and win it on your terms. Whose responsibility is it to, and I know this is a buzz term, sort of future-proof the team? I mean, I look at you guys as selectors and the next series always feels like the most important one. And so then naturally you've got an older team. But understandably, if I was picking the team, I would think I want to put the best players together that I possibly can at this particular point in time to make sure that we're going to win. So is it the responsibility of the States? Is it also you guys while sort of keeping one eye on the here and now? Whose responsibility is it to make sure that, that the team's not just good today, but also good in five or 10 years time? Yeah, I think that's always, always a focus. And you, you know, once you, once you go into the crystal ball, I think it's dangerous to assume that it will be perfectly future-proof. And I get the narrative because, you know, I think over the last few years, if you put Warner, Smith, Kawaja, Cummins, Hazelwood, Stark, Lyon, you've got guys that are going to come up in, in conversations for, you know, some of Australia's best ever players and in Australia's best ever team. So, so yeah, what does that look like when they aren't there for a game or a series or when they eventually move on from formats or altogether? I think managing expectations that you don't necessarily replace 100 test players with the next bloke who's going to play 100 tests that I think the vast majority of Australia's 400 and however many test cricketers, you know, if we find a group of players that play 20 to 40 tests, it might be 10, then that gets you through a year or two years. And that can be, you know, that can be particularly important at the right time as well, you know, depending on their skill set. So understanding that, yeah, understanding that it's not necessarily about unearthing generational talent every time it is someone who comes in to the Australian cricket team. And then I think we've also, you know, we've, and this is something, you know, we're looking into and the collaboration and working with the states is, it's going to be as critical as it ever has this year. There's no doubt about that with the scheduling that we have, but we're really, really excited around some. We've had a look at Marley Beardman at different times. Jack Edwards is someone who would have played probably more for Australia and, you know, is injured again now. There's a litany of those guys that I think have the capacity to build into it. Now, you know, they're fast bowling examples. They're young and injuries, you know, tend to happen. But trying to strike that balance of when they're getting their body physically right, not trying to lose too much time where they're also not being able to develop skill or game sense. So that's a critical bit, I think, around the fast bowling space. I also think the continued investment, you know, this is probably specifically around subcontinent, but, you know, the MRF program that we've sent players to for a number of years. We've had guys get repeat entries around that. We think that's important. Repeat subcontinent exposures. So, you know, an Aussie A series to India again. We had one last year. So some good consistent repeat entries there. MRF development. And again, you know, as you touched on around spin and at different times not seeing as much of that as perhaps we'd like in shield cricket, but continuing to explore ways that we can still have guys developing and being ready when that opportunity comes. So I think there's different mechanisms. You know, what does it look like in five years? I'm not going to sit here and say that, but I don't subscribe to the theory that it's going to be a drop off a cliff. Last one. Obviously, at the end of the Ashes, it feels like sort of an end point. Yeah, I hope so. I certainly hope they do. I mean, that's back, I guess, to that contract list and the guys that have been performing in Test Cricket. I hope that they're there until the end of that Ashes series. You know, throw in a 50 over World Cup, I think, at the end of that as well, which was similar to 2023. I think we had a pretty busy Test schedule leading into that as well. Yeah, there's certain players that have already jumped off certain formats and, you know, that's, you know, a decision by them to potentially elongate their careers in the Test space. So that's one way of doing it. I think you've seen and will continue to see, particularly the guys that are multi-format players. There will be times that, you know, you can't be everything to everyone at all times. So just making sure that at the right time, they do get the opportunity to invest back in. You're a lot closer to it and know a lot more about it than we certainly do here in the press and on the ABC Cricket Podcast. So, appreciate your insights as always, George, and thanks for spending the time to take me through it today. No problems. Cheers. Cheers. Cheers. Cheers. Cheers. Cheers.
