episodes.title: Shield final confirmed but the season batting numbers are grim reading
episodes.description: We know it will be Victoria vs South Australia in the Sheffield Shield final but the real question is, why have the runs been so hard to come by this season?
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. ABC Cricket Podcast time with your boys, Corbyn Middlemass and Ed Cowan for your Monday. My name's Corbyn Middlemass. I'm in my home port, as the Australian cricket team would refer it, here in the beautiful city of Melbourne. Ed Cowan is on the other side of the world, somewhere in a completely different time zone. Hello to you, Teddy. Corby, you're coming through loud and clear though. I might not be close, but I can hear you. Too loud. How are you? No, good. Loud enough. Beautiful. I'm well. I feel like I'm a little bit short on cricket. It's a bit of domestic cricket, sort of kicking around. Obviously, I'm just waiting for the IPL to start, I'm sure, like every cricket fan. Oh yeah, are we all? But not a whole lot of international cricket going on, obviously, for our lads, but no shortage of talking points, which is why we're here to chop it up on a Monday. Where are you? Are you going to tell us where you are in the world? I'm in Canada. Okay. I'll give you that. In Canada. Hopefully. Enjoying the winter, a bit of snow, a little time out. I was about to say. Time out for Teddy before work kicks in again next week. So, a little bit of work, a little bit of play, a little bit of play, a little bit of work. That's my trip. Yeah. More play for you, I think, is encouraged. No, never. I'm pleased that you're having a little bit of downtime and you're a very busy man. You still carved out a little bit of time to chat to me, so I appreciate that. I'll never miss it. I'll never miss it, Corb. We got a final in the Sheffield Shield, so South Australia is going to play Victoria. Bit of an anti-climax, must be said. A huge anti-climax. Yeah. I know the point system, you know, people are a fan of for various reasons, but... Hang on. Whoa. Who's a fan of the point system? I've never met anyone who is a fan of the most unfollowable point system in world sport. So, tell me who's a fan of that. Are you a fan of it? No. I just... I don't know. Oh, so you're not a fan. No. Not that we're 0% of this podcast, but I get what it's trying to do, but, gee, when you think we could have had this perfect end of the season where, you know, you need to win and you're in and everything else, and all of a sudden, after the first 100 overs, gone. Yeah, 10 overs into day two or whatever it is, or four overs into day two. It's... The whole thing's already decided. South Australia are through, and, you know, well done to them. Nothing against them, but it feels like the rest of the round now doesn't mean anything. Totally. Like, there was an opportunity for South Australia, you know, having to win the game if Queensland were pushing hard for a victory, or, conversely, if South Australia was struggling or there was a draw going on, Queensland could have set up a game, and instead, as you rightly called out, it's decided on one, you know, poor innings down at Bell Reve from Queensland not being able to get any bonus points that no one really understands. Anyway, and all of a sudden, after 10 rounds of the Shield and, well, you know, nine and a half rounds of the Shield and excitement building, it's just flat. It's muted. What's the answer? Do we go back to the old first innings points? There's some middle ground for sure. So what this is trying to encourage is positive attack in cricket. Yeah. And so there's a world where, yes, there's first innings points, but maybe you outsize an outright victory. So, you know, way back when you were in Nappies, it was six points for a win, two points for a first innings win, and not an outright win, and obviously not cumulative. So if you won outright and first innings, you only got six points. Yep. So what you, you know, there's ways and means that you could maybe manipulate those points. So it's much more on offer for an outright win to encourage teams to play for it, rather than, you know, this attacking cricket, which is trying to basically say anything after batting for 100 overs isn't really valuable, unless you feel like you can drive massive advantage in the game. Yeah. And incredibly, we haven't got any top order players in the country, and everyone averages in the mid-30s. So work that one out. And the rules are set up to obviously incentivize the, you know, being a glorified limited overs game. So, yeah, I think it needs an overhaul. It's a couple of years in a row that we've seen, you know, the points system obviously play a role in, you know, ladder positions and everything else. I think we had a very similar conversation this time last year. So South Australia were informed of the situation. So Ryan Harris decided to tell his team when they came off at T on the second day. So they had an advantage over Queensland, and as a result, they're going to go through and play in the final. The knock-on effect is interesting. So Brendan Doggett, who'd been ruled out for the year with a hamstring injury, is now in the mix to possibly return and play in the final. So he suffered that fielding against New South Wales last month. It also ends the first-class career of Usman Khawaja without him stepping on the park. So he has not played in this round due to the impending birth of his third child. So unfortunately, we've seen Uzi for the last time. He played round nine, and that's it for Usman Khawaja. So he won't go around again next year for Queensland. But we've got our finalists now. It starts 10 days from now, Victoria in South Australia at Junction Oval. Yeah, that's sad. I mean, it's the right call-out. It's sad about Usman, you know, not being able to... I'm sure he'd probably reconciled it emotionally himself. But, you know, many of his fans and the cricket fraternity would have loved to see one last game, for sure. But you're right. I think the two best teams are playing in the final. The two best bowling attacks are definitely playing in the final. And we know bowlers, you know, bowling attacks win Sheffield Shield. So it feels right the right two teams are playing. And I think it's setting itself up for an excellent contest. Day three of all these games. So this is the final round. We've got a little preview here. South Australia and Victoria. Both teams made almost identical scores in the first inning. So there was three runs between them with Victoria on top there. So Victoria got their 300 largely by committee. So 66 for Callaway, 59 for Peek. Two of their young star batsmen. And then Will Southerl and the skipper also with a half century. Earlier in the match, Henry Hunt topscored with 81. And Ben Menenti made a late little fight in 53. Four for Todd Murphy, which is good to see after he was obviously left hanging as the 12th man. The back end of that test series in the home summer, obviously, in the Ashes. And Scott Boland amongst the wickets again with three for 66. So this is well set up. I imagine both teams will be just trying to keep a few cards up their sleeve before the final at the same venue, obviously, taking place, as I said, in nine days from now. Anything jump out at you from that game? Not really. It's now, I mean, it's just sad that it's going to peter out, no doubt. Who has the better attack? Victoria or South Australia? Victoria. Yeah, I think so. Who has the better batting line-up? Yeah. Victoria have a better spread. South Australia, probably if we're picking in the schoolyard, you might take Sanger and McSweeney pretty high or whatever. Yeah, obviously Carey. Alex Carey. That's part of it. He goes okay. So, yeah, it'll be a fun final. And, yeah, hopefully there's a reasonably good wicket, as there has been most of the season at Junction Oval for that matter. A couple of these other games, just on some individual performances. The 100 for Cam Green obviously stands out. So, it feels like the storyline around Cam Green gets reinforced again. That, yeah, he's struggling at international level, but every single time he drops back and plays domestic level, he proves that he's too good for the grade. And so, he has, again, here with 135. He can't do much more than that. So, it feels like, you know, that's in the absence of anyone else really knocking down the door for his place in the test team. You'd feel like if there was a test starting tomorrow, he'd be hard to leave out again. So, you're right. Either one of two things happen from here. Either he has a breakout series that puts at least to bed the conversation for a moment, or he gets dropped. And until one of those two things happen, we're going to keep muddling around, wondering whether he's the guy or not. And anyone that saw the game or highlights, you know, you watch him bat against New South Wales. Yes, so, and you think he's just too good for this standard of cricket. So, you know, is it technical? Is it emotional? Is it psychological? As to why he's not at his best when he's playing test cricket? Which one of those is holding him back from test cricket? And it's probably a little bit of all three. You know, personally, I still think he has a lot to deliver for this test team, and he will. It's more a question of role. And so, at the moment, you know, trying to perform the role of a top order batsman, it's bloody hard. And so, you just get the sense that he's a number six who bowls a bit. I know he had a little bit of that opportunity during the Ashes, but he's been, you know, all over the place, really. And so, to bed that down, he needs a series. But at the same time, it's pretty hard to look past what he keeps delivering in the level below. So, it is. And then you look at the rest of the field. So, I sort of went through, given the fact we're nearing the end of the Sheffield Shield season. So, the guys that have scored over 600 runs for the year, and by the way, the top end of this is Pete Hanscom, 688 at 36, and then it's in Takam Bancroft, 665 at 35. And then the guy who comes in as the third leading run scorer in the tournament this year, feels like the forgotten man of Australian cricket, who was the spruit player 12 months ago, Sam Constance. So, he got scores of 38 and 31. He's the third leading run scorer. He's got 660 at 33. So, it hasn't been a year where he's had, you know, big gaudy hundreds or anything like that. In fact, it's been a lot of what he delivered in this match. It's been starts, and then hasn't really gone on with it. So, for a guy that's averaged 33, he's made 38 and 31 in this match. And that's about what the summer has amounted to for Sam Constance. So, how are we meant to feel about him? I mean, he's still such a young player. It feels like his name's certainly not as close to the top end of the conversation as it was this time last year or last winter. And yet, he's in and around his peers. It's not as if they've completely, you know, lapped him. He's right there with them. But at the same time, it doesn't feel overly convincing from what we've seen from him. This is an interesting case study because for someone who's a speculative buy, he's been a model of consistency. So, I think he got out for 31 today in the second innings. But, you know, since Christmas, 44, 28, 27, 35, 37, 28, 38. So, no 50s, no real failures. And, you know, to be honest, as an opening batsman, that's kind of criminal. To get yourself in and to get yourself out, that's emotional and mental, not technical. And so, you know, to be able to grind out a 70 or an 80 or 150, you know, that turns your season around. But as you say, he hasn't been lapped by the pack. So, I don't know whether that says more about Sam or less about those around him. But on the upside, this is a kid. This is a kid learning the game. There's a full shield season in his kit bag that he can draw on and his experiences. And he's got better for it. So, again, we're looking for opening batters. No one is screaming out saying, pick me, pick me, pick me. And he's probably only a couple of scores away. So, I think it's a good news story. I just don't feel great about it. Yeah. They're fascinating reading. And this is the problem the selectors are going to have. So, say we next play a test match in August against Bangladesh. You look through the lineup and the incumbents at the moment. You think, well, Head plays. Smith's going to play. Carey's going to play. I think Green plays. I think he comes back and scores 100 here. They're going to stick with him. I think Webster plays. Khawaja drops out. So, there's five of your seven immediately. You need two more players. You need top order positions. The question is, do you stay with Wetherald? And do you stay with Marnas? So, I mean, Marnas scored good runs when he played domestic cricket, particularly against the white ball. But if you look at the top run scorers in domestic cricket, so, as I said, the top end is north of 660 but averages in the 30s. And then you have to go all the way down to 560 runs for a season to get to someone that averages 40. And that's Wetherald. So, 562 at 40. Jake Lehman averages 40 as well, but now he's not eligible to play for Australia, nor is he in the conversation to play as a top order player. And then even if you talk to the data a little bit further, you go, well, who are the 100 makers? Who are the guys that are going to put up big runs or whatever it turns out to be? Matt Renshaw's got 300, so that leads the way. But then two each for Marnas, for Lehman, for Curtis Patterson, for Harper, and for Hanscom. So, they've got 200s, and then everybody else is one or fewer. So, that's what the batting ranks look like in domestic cricket for those that are next up. And I feel like we don't even have the Jake Wetherwood case like we had last summer where we felt like, you know, whoever you want to go with, you can always resort back to, you know, there's a standout in domestic cricket. There's no name there that really jumps off the page to me, Teddy, that says, hey, I should knock out the incumbent, even though the guy in the seat hasn't absolutely batted down his position yet. Yeah. In this case, the incumbent keeps his spot, even despite the question marks. And you're right. You know, like someone like Curtis Patterson, who we've talked a lot about, and I'm sure we will when we come to the one-day tournament, 200s but averaging 34. So, you know, as a high-quality top-order player, that's a middling season. But across the board, kind of scratching my head, is it the player quality? Is it their ability to translate their technique across formats? Or simply is it that the wickets are spicier than they've ever been? I don't know. I've watched enough shield cricket to think, yeah, there's some life in the wickets, but it hasn't at any stage looked horrific or unplayable. It does build up, though. I do have a lot of empathy for the top-order players when consistently every wicket has a little bit in it. You know, historically, maybe the Gabba was a bit of a seeming wicket or Belle Reve, and then you got back to the Adelaide Oval and you just knew that that was a run fest and you could get your confidence back. Like, every single ground around Australia now seems. Every single one. And so, you know, you can get in these little moments of five, six, seven innings where you don't do much wrong. You feel like you're playing well, but you look at the score sheet and you've gone, you know, 10 or 20 or, you know, balls had your name on it. So I do have empathy for that. That's hard work. And that is probably the difference. It's not that there are wickets with life in them. It's the quality of wickets with a bit of juice in them is probably higher, or the quality of wickets on average is lower. And then the balls, obviously, with the prouder seam. And I know the players talk a lot about that. This is where it's sort of, you talk about the sympathy for the top order players. Brings me to one guy who's certainly a forgotten player in test cricket. And I'm not suggesting, you know, for a second that they're going to pick him because when he was scoring big, huge runs, they didn't pick him. So they're probably not going to do it now. But underrated season, all things considered for Cam Bancroft. So 665 at 35, which again, you know, is north of his average when he's at his best, but plays half his games at the WACA. He's batted nine times. He's the only player in the competition, other than Jordan Silk, to have not scored over 56 times. So six of his nine hits, he's gone 50 plus. Yeah. In the end, in a season where runs are hard to come by, it's the second leading run scorer in the competition. On the back of a horrendous summer last year, it's not a bad follow-up. Plus he'll get to play in England as well. So he'll keep his red ball form going, but got a little half century in this fixture while Cam Green went large. That's the sand grabber coming out on you. Yeah. I mean, it's going to be an ongoing conversation though, isn't it? In terms of, you know, where are our batters? Who are the next guys? Who are the top order players? What's it going to look like if not now in the, you know, in the medium term? Just on the last of those games, Tasmania, 198 and then six for 264 batting the second time. They took a 21 lead on the first inning. So effectively 284 ahead. The last time I checked that score, Queensland all out 178. And as a result, their hopes of making the final went with it. Wetherald 39 and 62. So again, sort of same kind of thing as what we're talking about with Constance, with Bancroft, now with Wetherald, sort of getting out at difficult times. 82 for Jordan Silk in this game as well. And in terms of the bowlers, Mick Nisa, who certainly had a fine summer, obviously playing test cricket for Australia, 5 for 37. And Xavier Bartlett had 3 last time I checked that score as well. Teddy, the one-day cup came to its conclusion on Wednesday on a cold night down in Tasmania. And New South Wales have a bit more silverware in the cabinet. There is a whole lot to pull apart from this game. But Curtis Patterson saw New South Wales home with an unbeaten 50. So that gives him 300s and three half centuries, averaging over 100 for the tournament. And appropriately, he led New South Wales to a victory here. They had to beat the number one team in consecutive games on their home patch to get it done. And I think that makes you a pretty worthy champion. Yeah, it does for sure. I mean, in both games, Tasmania batted first. And we know the advantage of chasing runs at Belle Reve. So they didn't do any justice to their season in either of those innings. And in both of them, really, New South Wales kind of chased it down easily. There were a few little moments in the final. A few hiccups, you could say. I mean, it wasn't an easy target on a wicket that was offering plenty, more like a four-day wicket and, you know, 120 in 20-odd overs. But Curtis Patterson looked really like he was playing a different game. He was playing a different sport at times. Everyone couldn't put bat on ball and he didn't miss the middle. So it was a sensational innings. It capped off a fantastic season for him and a great season for New South Wales. And, you know, a great way to send Greg Shippard off as the coach. Well, that's the unmissable talking point, isn't it? So 39 days after he was sacked for essentially not... I thought I'd get it in. I knew you were going to talk about it. So I thought I'd get it in. For not winning titles, which was part of the J-Day. All of a sudden, he wins a title, but he's already lost his gig. I think there were reports coming through that he was in the karaoke singing, I'm still standing. Well, he was for a minute, but obviously this round of Shield cricket will be his last as the coach of New South Wales. On retrospect, does it change anything as to what it means for New South Wales, whether they got the decision right or wrong? Well, I don't think anyone's denying the quality of Greg Shippard as a coach. You know, probably Australia's most successful domestic coach. A fantastic mentor to many great players. I think the question that probably arose was, aside from the titles, is he the coach to bring this next generation of New South Wales players to play Test cricket? I don't know the answer to that. But, you know, there are a few times in the last couple of weeks that you've probably thought, you know, you can see how that decision was made by the CEO because, you know, when they pulled out against Tasmania, three down or four down with 20 overs to go and shut up shop and didn't actually play for the win. They dominated the game but didn't play for the win in the end. And then again last week against Queensland, you know, very much the same. There was obviously rain affected. But, you know, that mentality of playing for win rather than first case is not to lose, then a draw and then a win. I think these young players need instilled in them. It's a win-at-all-cost attitude. They need to learn to win. And, you know, I'm sure that was probably top of mind for the last couple of weeks as well. Yeah. I think I said this at the time when we spoke about it. It was an error one way or the other. It was either an error to re-sign him at the stage that they did or it was an error to sack him at this particular point. I mean, the fact that he'd had a two-year deal and he was essentially 25% of the way into it. He was halfway through his first summer of that new deal. So you don't even give him a chance to prove that he can do the job. And then you decide that actually we've got the wrong guy. So you either got it wrong originally or you got it wrong in retrospect. It sort of – and it only feels like he was able to prove that on the way out with a title in the way that it ended. But it's not going to change anything. I think that's a fair view to have for the record. Yeah. It's, you know, the task force to win titles. He did it. So new coach, it feels like you put your finger in the wind. Everyone's reporting that Brad Haddon's going to be the guy to coach New South Wales. Is that over the line? Can you give me any insight as to am I waiting for the other shoe to drop? Is this about to be announced or anything like that? I have no insight here. I'm sorry, Corb. Okay. So it's not like I'm going to wake up tomorrow morning and it's going to – then we're going to press release and say Brad Haddon's a new coach. Not that I'm aware of, no. Okay. Johan Boiter's future will be determined on the success of the season was a quote that I read in a News Corp column. So pressure on at the Bulls. Chris Rogers off contract in Victoria but has had a near perfect season. So if he wants to coach again, I imagine that that will be the case. Unless maybe another state comes calling. Maybe someone picks up the phone and rings Chris Rogers. He's proven he's been able to develop a whole lot of young talent and turn that program around. And then there's Bo Casson. Of course, former leg spinner who represented Australia and played test cricket in 53 first-class matches for WA and New South Wales. He's the new coach of the team I call the Western Warriors. So he will lead them. Well done to Bo Casson. Yeah, that's a great reminder I need to text Bo because that's a great appointment. Great person and excellent coach. Someone who actually behind the scenes had a big influence on my career in the last couple of years when he was the assistant coach in New South Wales. Just a duck to water when he took on coaching having had to retire early from cricket with his heart condition. Has the right temperament. Has the right technical and tactical knowledge. I think that's an astute appointment. I was very sad when he left New South Wales. But he's obviously a native WA boy and the allure of family and bringing up kids. With his Western Australian wife was too great. So he'll do an excellent job. He's got a great squad. I thought that was an excellent appointment. I saw Tyler Lewis's article in the News Corp paper say that Tim McDonald was among the leading candidates also in the frame. Another former teammate of yours. One of Voges' assistants. And it was quoted as saying, industry sources say he did not apply in support of Casson. What did you make of that? I know they've been a unit together for a period of time. But basically said, I'll sit this one out. And yeah, there might be a senior job for me down the track. I mean, interesting. I mean, Tim's been a fast bowling coach. You know, made his career as an excellent swing bowler. Both, you know, mainly for Tasmania really. And, you know, you've got to be a head coach. It's very hard to translate the two. But sometimes you just need a bit more time to develop. I think if I was, I don't know what happened. But I'm sure he probably stuck his finger in the wind. And that was probably a thoughtful stand down. Just one more before we move on from domestic cricket. I've got a list of a question during the week, which basically referred to the New South Wales captaincy. Jack Edwards has given it up during the year to Nathan Lyon, to Steve Smith. And then Curtis Patterson obviously leads them in the final and ultimately goes on to become the title winning captain there. Is this a little sign of what's to come? Will Jack Edwards be the captain of New South Wales next year? As far as I know. I mean, he didn't captain. He's injured at the moment. So, you know, all those moments of giving up were for a specific reason. Yeah, there's no doubt being an all-rounder, opening the bowling, batting at six and being captain takes its toll. And when you're a young captain still learning that and you're still trying to play for Australia as Jack is, you can imagine the emotion that goes into these fixtures. So there's no doubt that New South Wales will have to manage that probably a little bit better than they did. But you saw the back half of the season, you know, that toll started to play out in the injury. So I expect him to be the captain, no doubt. But how that plays out might be slightly different. Maybe does the four-day, not the one-day. I don't know. It hasn't been a discussion yet. Sounds like me on this podcast, the way you're running through it. I've got to host the show. I've got to give the sharp opinions and lean on all my cricketing experience and everything else to be able to pull us along on the ABC Cricket Podcast. By the way, one thing we have done, Declan Burns got on board and he's keeping us all in order here. And after many years of doing it and sort of leaning on our Instagram and our LinkedIn to be able to field questions from our family here on the ABC Cricket Podcast, we have an email address. How about that as a break? Tell me. I'm going to send one in. The email address is abccricketpodcast, that's us. It's abccricketpodcast at abc.net.au. It's line of length. It's like Josh Hazelwood. Sometimes vanilla ice creams taste great. The sprinkles are what... I mean, that is as vanilla as it gets. The sprinkles are what you put in the email. So abccricketpodcast at abc.net.au. So abccricketpodcast at abc.net.au. And we can field your questions on a weekly basis here on our little pod that could. All right. From Hayden from Richmond in Victoria. Sends me a message saying, Hi Corbyn, love the ABC Cricket Podcast with Teddy. Ends. Full stop. Idea for the one-day cup going forward. Requires 11 days per summer. First five matches to be played prior or after a shield match, which is how we love it back in the day. You play a shield match, then you play the one-day game. Then the next five matches played after the big bash, three days apart, and then you have a Sunday final. So I don't mind it. So basically, first part of the summer, play a shield game, then you play your one-day off the back of it. And then essentially, you have a mini lightning carnival. So 10 matches per team plus a final. Total of 31 matches. Tournament done. So BBL ends. And then as a way to transition back into sort of red ball shield cricket, we have our 50-over little lightning carnival. We crown a champion. We get it done. We're out of there. What do you reckon? Love it. Get that on the socials deck and, you know, send it into Cricket Australia's inbox. Excellent idea. I like it. You've done well, Hayden. From Trent. Can you please discuss this on the pod? Nathan McAndrew. He's been high on the wicket takers list for years, and he's usually fit. Where is he in the pecking order of fast bowlers for the test team? Thanks. Love the pod from Trent. Well, he's fit. So that's a starting point. Puts you in the top 10 fast bowlers. I mean, this is someone who's absolutely impeccable about their preparation, their fitness levels, always has been. An excellent bowler and, you know, a Trojan-style fast bowler. Would that translate to test cricket? I think in certain conditions. He'd have a decent day out occasionally. I don't think, you know, I think his test career may, if ever given the opportunity, is confined to very much the fill-in here and there, and he ends up playing two or three tests. He's not the answer, I don't think, to solve the next generation. She's obviously ageing, but what a custodian of Shield cricket that he's been. It's proven a great story. This is someone who took a truckload of wickets in club cricket in Sydney, a truckload of second-leven wickets, never really got the recognition, probably wrongly in that state, and then proved that taking wickets is a skill, and he moved that skill to South Australia where he's really led an attack. But he stays on the park. Excellent competitor. Excellent fielder. Great person. It's hard to really argue against. You know, hopefully he does get the recognition he deserves and that would come in a baggy green at some stage. I think when you were away a couple of weeks ago, Xavier Doherty was certainly pushing his claim, saying, look, he'd be right there. Wouldn't be surprised that his name's been chucked around and spoken about in selection. So he feels like he's high on the list as a man, obviously, that watches a lot of domestic cricket, as we know. Our man Xavier from Hobart. Did you watch the 100 auction, the very first auction? Previously they had a draft, but four IPL owners obviously now involved in the 100. Did you sit in front of the TV and watch the all go under the hammer? No. Yeah, that doesn't surprise me. Tell me what happened. What I saw was the headlines of Beth Mooney, who's now definitely looking for a new house, that was big money. Nearly $400,000. Yeah. Amazing. Yeah. episodes.title: Reckoning with the depth of India's T20 dominance
episodes.description: India thumped NZ to make T20 World Cup history and Corbin and Ed can't see anyone competing with them in the near future.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. ABC Cricket Podcast. I'm with your boys Corbyn Middlemass and Ed Cowan for your Monday. India, the champions of the world again at the T20 World Cup. We have one round left in the Sheffield Shield. We're down to three teams in contention for the title. Speaking of titles, the one-day cup is coming up. But this Wednesday, the final at Bellwave Oval. Plus, Women's Series comes to a close. Curtain comes down on Elisa Healy's career. We've got a whole lot to chop up. My name's Corbyn Middlemass. Ed Cowan is in Sydney. Hello, Teddy. Corby. Here we are. Big Monday pod. Oh, yeah. I mean, world champions. India. First team ever to go back-to-back, which you weren't big on that stat leading into the tournament. But, hey, it's... First host country to ever win it. First host country to ever win. Oh, didn't you? And the first three-time champions that we've ever seen. So, they've now won the T20 World Cup more than any other team. They were obviously coming off a high after posting 253 in the final. They beat the second-best team in the tournament, England, there. And then took on New Zealand in the final. And what an interesting game we saw last night. A 96-run win. So, 96-run win in front of 100,000 at the Modi Stadium in Ahmedabad. Abhishek Sharma, Sandru Sampson got them off to a great start. The opener's put on 92 in the power play alone. And Sandru Sampson, when this tournament was on the line, boy, did he bring his best cricket. So, 97-not in the Super 8s in that must-win game against the Windies. 89 in the semi, 89 in the final. He was named player of the tournament. Ishan Kishin scored a neat little half-century. 255 India posted. So, they actually beat their semi-final score of 253. And then New Zealand, in reply, they lost Finnell and Early. Lost Ravindra to the first ball that Boomerah bowled. Boomerah finished with four for 15. He struck twice. In the 16th over in consecutive balls. Picked up another one in his 18th. 18th and really apart from a half-century for Tim Seifert. They never got going. The Black Caps, in the end, they were all out for 159 with an over to go. So, all out in the 19th over. Big win for India at the World Cup. This is what you call a real fizzer. A fizzer. As it's not across the Dutch. Yes. But in terms of, you know, the script playing out, it was almost to a tee, wasn't it? You know, New Zealand push hard throughout the tournament. The underdog scrapped their way to another final in a World Cup or Champions Trophy and then can't get over the line. I mean, realistically, this game was done after six overs. I mean, 90 in the power play. Everything's against you at that point in time. You just can't wrestle back momentum for the rest of the game as much as you try. And so, you know, they tried to take the pace off the ball consistently and it kept being taken over the fence. So, the Indian T20 cricket is only accelerating. They have the strongest T20 league in the world. They, you know, their younger players are exposed to the pressure of the IPL, which is probably now far greater than most international T20 games. They have this talent funnel and pipeline for this format of the game like no other nation. And so, it's kind of hard to see how other countries are going to compete with them, really. And that's a bit of a bare case. But these World Cups roll around every two years. And you'd be hard-pressed to suggest India, even though it's in Australia, aren't going to start favourites for that one as well. Yep. I think that's a pretty good breakdown. When you think about they've got the best T20 batsman in the world in Abhishek Sharma, he didn't have a great tournament. So, he was off. Surikuma Yardav gets a golden duck in the final. Wasn't really a huge factor throughout. And in the end, Sandro Sampson was great when he needed to be. Jasper Boomer is phenomenal. I mean, it's nothing that hasn't been said before. But, you know, whatever format of the game it is, he's a cut above the rest. And we saw that, obviously, on display again. You know, key moments in this tournament. Yeah. And we talked about it before the tournament started. But what they have been able to do is identify key white ball players. And so, a lot of these names aren't household names to a lot of the Australian audience, aside from if you follow the IPL or the T20 team. They, the modern way is ingrained into them. And they walk out to bat and they try and hit six from the first ball. They've got change-ups. They bowl, you know, it's great spin. You know, T20 spin. And realistically, they could probably field three teams. And those three teams would all make, you know, close to the semifinals. There is so much depth in this format of the game coming out of India. And, you know, it's very hard to compete with because their up-and-coming players, as I said, are exposed to this and ours, you know, muddling along. I mean, they did lose in the group stage, didn't they? South Africa got them. They had to... That was an aberration, though. That was a real aberration. Yeah. They had to pull it out against the West Indies. And England probably pushed them more than, you know, most teams. I think it's clear to say that England were the second-best team, though, Teddy, in the tournament, given they beat New Zealand in the final by 96 runs and they beat England by only seven runs. episodes.title: T20 World Cups every two years just don't resonate
episodes.description: The T20 World Cup final awaits but the real question is - should this tournament continue to be staged every two years?!
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. ABC Cricket Podcast time with your boys, Corbin Middlemass and Ed Cowan for your Friday. We've got our finalists at the T20 World Cup. It will be New Zealand and India for all the marbles. The penultimate round of the Sheffield Shields underway. There's a women's test match which starts today at the WACA ground. And it also doubles up as the last time we'll see Elisa Healy in international cricket. My name's Corbin Middlemass. I am in Sydney. Ed Cowan is also in Sydney and yet we're not in the same room, which I know my podcast co-host is a little snaky about. But good morning to you, Teddy. Corbin, why don't you just call me and say I'm calling the football, the big game that was on last night, whatever, whoever played, whoever. We've got a Friday podcast. Why don't you come into Ultima? It's just down the road, across City Tunnel. I'd be there and you and I could have hugged it out and done this face-to-face because our chemistry is so much better when we're in person. I apologise. I must admit I'm the sort of guy, I don't like disappointing people as you know. So I'm sort of like late night the night before doing my teams for Friday night. I've got to go to the Gold Coast next. Rush in here, do a footy pod. Then I've got a cricket pod. Then I'm on a plane. So I was like, I didn't want you to come all the way in and then we're, you know, I feel like the only time I get with you is on air and then I'm leaving again. So that was sort of my thinking behind it. I didn't want to give people false hope that I had time, which unfortunately I don't have a lot of that. At the moment I'm here for work. It's a business trip. I could have done with a hug, but anyway. Apologies. Apologies. It's lovely to see you though through the screen as we usually do in the universe online. Have you got something for me off the top? I know you've been keen to spit this out. I mean, not that keen, but I did note that New Zealand have qualified for the World Cup final. And I can't remember, it was so long ago when we were making our predictions about which team, aside from India, could really make a charge of this. And I said New Zealand and you kind of had that little glint in your eye like, that's stupid. And now I'm thinking maybe not so stupid. But Finn Allen, let me buy you a beer. I can't believe how let down I've been here. So I feel like my prediction was more bold on England. And yet England were a better team than New Zealand in the tournament. They beat them in the tournament. They almost pulled off the greatest run chase in just about World Cup history. And yet they fell seven runs short. And somehow the team that you picked is the team that's there waiting for them in the final. And so the team that I picked, who were on this unbelievable Cinderella run, somehow fell a stage short. And now I'm an Indian dinner down as a result of it. I'm going to have to cough up there. I couldn't believe it. Couldn't believe it. And I love it. Honestly, no one remembers who gets knocked down in the semifinals. You might as well get knocked down in the group stages. England, Australia, South Africa. They all get lumped in together of that World Cup of 2026 that no one will probably remember a single ball. You're on the scrap heap of history, aren't you? When you go out in the semifinal stage. So Mumbai last night. Let's break it down. Yeah. Mumbai last night. So 253 beat 246. I mean, this was what we thought the tournament was going to be leading in. And it delivered last night. So India clinched a seven run semifinal thriller. Jacob Bethel almost led England to a record T20 chase. Will Jacks got Abhishek Sharma in the first over. Samson was then dropped by Harry Brook in the second over. He went on to make 50 off 26 and made 89. And in the end, that felt like the game. Do you reckon that drop catch cost them the game? Had to have, didn't it? Guy gets dropped in the second over. He makes 89. If he makes 50, they win. Then the Indians took two. Like if you actually weigh it up. The old adage, catchers win matches. India took two great catches. England dropped a dolly. And, you know, seven runs was the difference. Anyway, keep going. You can give me a great little description. Same guy involved twice. So Akshar Patel took a blinder running back from the infield to deep cover, looking over his shoulder, somehow took it, sliding, you know, face down, head first towards the boundary rope. And then his second one was even better where he stayed on his feet, but he's running at speed, about to head out of, outside the boundary. Takes the catch. And in the same motion as we've seen multiple times in, you know, the modern game, but at full pace, takes it, never breaks stride, whips the ball back to his teammate and able to complete a superb outfield catch to get rid of Will Jacks. The partnership forming there. And then in the end, yeah, that were the two catches which made the difference. They couldn't stop Jacob Bethel. He was run out in the final over for 105, 50 off 19, 100 off 45 balls. It's the first T20 international century in a semifinal lost, which is hardly surprising, but one of the quickest ever off just 43 balls and really underlines his status as the future star batsman of global cricket. We saw him do it, obviously, in Sydney at the SCG test match. And what a knock from Jacob Bethel, albeit in a losing cause. What jumps out to you, Teddy, on what we saw last night? I mean, before we talk more broadly, Corb, I mean, Bethel, he has really announced himself in the last, you know, three and a bit months. This was someone, you know, we knew who could play. He scored a fantastic 90 in New Zealand, you know, a full 12 months ago. He had one ODI 100 only, so no four-day professional 100s under his belt. I mean, here we are in an Ashes 100 of the SCG, a World Cup semifinal 100. And so, you know, this momentum of the next superstar of world cricket is certainly building. And between, you know, Bethel and Harry Brook, the future looks bright for England. There's no doubt about that, particularly in the short forms. But they both look fantastic players. But how many three-format players are there nowadays? The proper elite batsmen across formats? Well, very, very few. Like, less than a handful. But I think, you know, we've talked about this a little bit. I think test cricket is converging pretty quickly with the shorter formats in terms of how the skills are being applied. For many years, they were kind of segregated. And so, you know, your Warners and your Coley's were real standouts. You know, they were technicians in all three formats. And, you know, T20 and test cricket require different techniques. Now the one technique's being applied essentially to all three formats. And we're getting a different type of three-format player. And you see a Travis Head, you know, a Jacob Bethel. They're going about their business almost in exactly the same fashion. So it is a little different and, you know, something to keep an eye on as that trend continues. So a few things come to mind. It was the same in the other semifinal. This was played on an absolute postage stamp. You know, so the two semifinals were made for television really to have these 250 scores. And this was the game that delivered it. I think you pinpointed the key moments. I guess the only other thing that stood out was, was it the 18th over that Boomerah bowled? You know, you give the ball to your world-class, you know, superstar and they delivered. And that's what England probably lacked at the back end of their innings. So it was a great game of cricket. Excellent. India were pushed by, you know, an England team that was peaking at the right time. And, you know, from write-offs at the start, it would have been a fairy tale. But at every time, India have been challenged here, aside from that one little hiccup. They've had some fixtures to win here and they showed their class. So they'll go in as absolute firm favourites. But who knows, in a T20 game, in a final, you just never know what's going to happen. One player can go off. Finn Allen did in that other semifinal. And, you know, you've got a different shape of game on your hands. Well, this is what New Zealand do, though, isn't it? This is their role to roll up and be the other team in the World Cup final and sort of pointy ends of tournaments. It's not so much collecting silverware that's been the thing for the Kiwis over the years. But, yeah, you mentioned Boomer last night. I mean, in a game where, what, 12 and over plays 12 and over. And in the end, he goes for six and, you know, with three overs to go and a team trying to hunt down 250 and looking like they're good things. You can't buy that. That's amazing. That is world-class. Pay every dollar for that. So back to Kolkata. The other night, you alluded to Finn Allen. Fastest T20 World Cup 100 ever. So the previous one, by the way, was Chris Gale, who did it off 47 balls. That was the record. He's done it off 33 in the semifinal stage of the tournament. New Zealand securing a place in the final, a dominant nine-wicket win. We were lucky enough to see him, obviously, in the big bash. We talked about how New Zealand went without him in the lead-up tournament, the bilateral series against India, and then to have him slot into that lineup and what he's capable of. I mean, what a knock. And you saw it in the latter stages of the big bash. This is a guy that knows how to win games off his own bat. And, you know, he did that single-handedly. It felt South Africa were probably 50 short. You know, like there were balls that were flicking the outside edge of the bat and no one was running to chase the ball to the boundary. It was like it's North Sydney Oval, but with an outfield that's concrete. Yeah. So South Africa were restricted with the spinners. They lost wickets early and they kind of – they got their way to, you know, 160, but it needed a two-handle in front of it. And particularly when, you know, Allen and Seiforth went absolutely berserko in the first three or four hours. And they were just playing good cricket shots. It wasn't risk-taking chaos. And you looked up and they were none for 50 or four. You thought, well, this game's done. And then Finn Allen just iced it totally. You know, there were a couple of overs there that went for 20. You know, the thing that came to mind watching extended highlights were it didn't really feel like a 33-ball hundred. There were no massive sixes. He wasn't taking dramatic risks. He just kind of hit the ball in the gap. You know, there were some great T20 shots for sure, but he didn't try and hit the ball too hard. They served up some length that he just kind of got a hold of. But it was a hell of an innings and he paced it nicely. You know, he was – I think the 50 was up 19 balls. And so, you know, the last 20 came pretty quickly when the game was iced. But they fielded well. There was only, you know, one Glenn Phillips of all people dropped at catching the outfield. But aside from that, they fielded well. I thought tactically New Zealand were excellent the way they set their matchups up. You know, the way they bowled, particularly with the very, very short boundary on one side. And South Africa were pretty average, having not lost a game the whole tournament. They played without the freedom. You know, and I absolutely hate the word chokers. I don't think it's fair. But they played the game slightly constricted. And so, you know, you can join the dots on that. You can call it whatever you want. But, yeah, unfortunately for South Africa, there it is. I mentioned the record. So, fastest World Cup 100. I know that the World Cups do roll around every two years. And the game has changed for a period of time. I'm stunned that the fastest 100 previously at a World Cup until two nights ago was 47 balls. I mean, I would have thought someone in that time would have scored one quicker with, you know, the amount of associate nations that are involved. And, you know, we've had World Cups in India in the not-too-different past and on good wickets with smaller boundaries. So, it was Gale 47 balls, Gale 50 balls, the two fastest leading into the tournament. And really all the way up until the last two nights. So, now we've had Bethel off 45 and Finn Allen off 33. That's the fastest hundreds we've ever seen. So, I was a little surprised that we hadn't had quicker ones in World Cup history. Not to downplay the achievement. Better than two of all over 100 and representing your country. But did that surprise you a little bit? I think it did. But what surprised me was how far the boundaries were in. I mean, you know, honestly, that New Zealand-South Africa fixture, it felt like some of those boundaries were 45 metres. I think the minimum's 50. It felt like it was 50 all the way around at one point. They were tiny. Armadabad is the location, the Modi Stadiums on, what, Sunday night our time or when you go to bed Sunday night, early Monday morning. So, start... Are they going to pack it out? I hope so. What is it? 130? Something like that. 130 large? Yeah. All I can think about is Donald Trump, Virat Koldai. That's right. And Sachin Denduka. I hope they do. I hope they do. Remember the test match that they played there, that they tried to fill it as much as they could, I think, for the first day. But let's see. Who are they playing? New Zealand. So, India and New Zealand. See, I've given up on the tournament now that England has been eliminated. All right. Let's leave the World T20 there. It feels like the Australians have been done for like four months, hasn't it? Like, this tournament's still going and yet the Aussies were eliminated so early in the piece as it reaches its conclusion. Who do you like? Are you tipping the upset? No. No, neither am I. Yeah. I would love to say, I mean, that would be... It'd be something. Imagine, just think about this. So, New Zealand, not so long ago, went to India in test cricket and clean swept them in. Yeah. You know, and we talked about it at the time, but it was probably maybe their greatest cricket achievement. It would have to come close. Clean sweeping India in a test match series in India. Yeah. Better than World Test Championship? Yeah. Probably, I think. Yeah. I don't know. Anyway, it's all up there. And so, imagine... Felt like the biggest upset since, like, Lake Placid when it happened. Like, I remember thinking, like, no one would possibly think that that would get it. That's right. And then won the one-day series from memory. Don't quote me on that. They then, you know, in the lead-up to this tournament, were pretty poor, but didn't have their full-strength team in India. And here we are. We've got a showdown. So, I mean, there are chance. I would say it's 65-35. Like, I'm not full-tilt India. So, if things go their way, and they could well go their way, they're a shake. I mentioned this line about the Sydney Swans last night. It reminds me a little bit about New Zealand cricket, too, that they're like the other team in your favourite sports movie. So, if you remember the movie and, you know, whatever team the lead character is competing on or whatever it turns out to be, they're the other team. That often find themselves there. So, we'll see if they get their storybook ending in India, perhaps, this time around New Zealand. A couple of feedback questions from our listeners. The Tarelgan Tiger was pretty quick to message me after he heard the news that the Pakistan players had been fined approximately $25,000 Australian dollars by the PCB for their T20 World Cup performance. So, they weren't fined for their behaviour or anything like that. It was simply due to their performance and their exit at the Super 8 stage of the tournament that they have been docked a portion of their pay. Oh, man. I hate it. It makes no sense to me. So, each to their own. You know, no judgement. But imagine, you know, this is a group of players that probably feel far more pressure than any Australian cricketer has ever felt in their life. They have the weight of a nation, both in a sporting sense, in a political sense. You know, so much of the identity of Pakistan is wrapped into their cricket team. And they would feel that. And I don't think the way selectors or the PCB or, you know, how they rotate coaches, I don't think that helps the players feel settled and stable and be able to play with the freedom that they probably like. And, you know, so I just don't know what this achieved. It feels like it's almost, you know, like getting a parking ticket. And it feels like capital revenue raising. Like, for what purpose would you find the players for poor performance? I don't get it. You wouldn't think it's going to help them perform better going into the future, would it? Like, to think that your pay is going to get docked for that. It's, yeah, it's all a bit whiffy. I'm not so sure about that. episodes.description: As potential Pakistan player bans for Indian owned teams in The Hundred get debated in the UK, Corbin and Ed ponder the domino effect here in the BBL if the league is privatised.

episodes.title: Will Trump 'blink first' and end the war?
episodes.description: Donald Trump went into the war with Iran thinking it would be over quickly. More than seven weeks later there’s still no obvious off ramp, with uncertainty surrounding a second round of peace talks in Pakistan.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Hi News Daily listeners. Just stopping by quickly to let you know about my new pod. One of Australia's most baffling missing persons cases. In 2007, four people vanished. The family lived a bizarre alternative lifestyle. It was dubbed a death cult. But after months of investigation, I don't think this story can be condensed into that simple headline. I'm Dominique Bayans, host of Expanse, the Nanup Four. Binge all episodes now. Search for Expanse on ABC Listen and iView. Donald Trump went into the war with Iran thinking it would be over quickly. Now, more than seven weeks later, with a ceasefire about to end, there's still no obvious off-ramp, with uncertainty surrounding a second round of peace talks in Pakistan. Today, a former Iran negotiator in the Trump administration, Nate Swanson, on what the US president needs to do to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hamus. I'm Sam Hawley on Gadigal land in Sydney. This is ABC News Daily. Nate, we first spoke to you at the start of the war in Iran on day one. That was more than 50 days ago now. So has it been going as you would have predicted? In some respects, yes. But in most respects, no. I mean, I think it was not totally surprising that Iran escalated so quickly based on the scope and size of the initial US and Israeli attack. But never, I think, would I ever have guessed that it would go this long and that it would be still so messy 50 days in without a clear idea of how exactly this ends and really still even at this point what the objective is. Now, up until July last year, you were on Trump's Iran negotiating team. So just tell me, back then, were you articulating what the risks of going into this war would be? And was he listening? Well, I'm a career civil servant across multiple administrations and, as you noted, with the Iran team at the end. I do not have a personal relationship with President Trump by any measure. Never briefed him, unlike other presidents. But to his team, when I was still there, I think they were genuinely interested in diplomacy. But obviously there was a willingness to use force that was kind of unique from other administrations. I think in his first term, he did the strike that killed Gossam Soleimani. And then before I left, there was the midnight hammer operation that we did in connection with the Israelis. So, I mean, Trump was clearly more comfortable using force than other U.S. presidents. And I think, yeah, he didn't really fully understand the risks associated and how a conflict could go bad so quickly. So that is kind of unique to the president. And I think, you know, he has a very, very small inner circle. And I think they're all fairly confident this would be easy, which was a mistake. Yeah, all right, well, a two-week ceasefire has been in place. But the Strait of Hamuz has been an ongoing problem. And, I mean, events have hardly been peaceful, have they, with the U.S. attacking an Iranian cargo ship. A nighttime mission in the Arabian Sea. U.S. Marines boarding an Iranian-flagged cargo ship after its engine room was fired upon. Vacate your engine room. We're prepared to subject you to an enabling fire. Did you predict any of this in relation to the Strait of Hamuz that has become such a massive problem for the entire world? Yes and no. I mean, I thought Iran would lash out the Gulf and try to shut down the Strait. I think what surprised me was really at the first outset is that Iran was able to get, you know, their own exports out for really up until the last two weeks. You know, so for the first six weeks of the war, they basically kept, you know, traffic from the Gulf out. But, you know, their own exports oil to China were still basically happening. So to me, that was quite shocking and was quite significant. And I think also, you know, the Strait has always been this theoretical threat that, you know, the U.S. and others have been worried about. But it was never a practical reality. And Iran made it a reality, you know, almost instantly in the first, you know, 24 to 48 hours. And I think it's really proven to be, in many ways, much more effective than any of the other means of deterrence. It's quite a bit more effective than the proxies. It's quite a bit more effective than their nuclear program. And really even their missile program to some extent. So, I mean, it's really been a, you know, a huge boon for Iran to be able to utilize this power, this new power, in ways that are really quite unforeseen and quite effective. So, I mean, things can have long-lasting implications, unfortunately. And because of that Strait of Hamuz and Iran's seemingly upper hand in it, it considers that it's winning this war. Yeah, I think there are certainly quite a few within the Iranian administration who believe they're winning the war. And I think there's definitely some merit to it, right? I mean, it's different than the U.S. or a Western definition of winning, right? They don't need to defeat the U.S. or defeat Israel militarily. They just need to survive. And they're fighting an asymmetric war. So every day that goes on that the Iranian regime holds, that the, you know, the Islamic Republic is still the face of the country, you know, that's victory. And so they've done that. And they've shown that, you know, that there's no immediate fall coming. And in some ways, they're stronger than they were. So, yeah, I think that defines them in a victory. And I think they also are, you know, emboldened by the Strait as this new security guarantee that they really have lacked since Hezbollah was, you know, so thoroughly defeated in 2024. So it's a new thing. And you can understand why Iran feels that way. But at the same time, they have been pummeled militarily. I don't think there's any point in denying that. You know, I mean, I can't remember what the total number of strikes between U.S. and Israel were. But, you know, it's like well over, I think, 15 or 25,000 strikes. I mean, so it is, you know, this long-lasting damage that Iran has suffered. But, you know, kind of paradoxically, they've been hit so hard militarily, been pummeled militarily, but they've like reestablished deterrence. So you can understand why some in Iran feel like they've won so far. All right, well, Donald Trump, of course, Nate, has been acting erratically. He keeps switching from saying a deal is possible, negotiations are underway, to then saying he's going to blow up every bridge and power plant in Iran. And now, of course, again, there's these conflicting messages about this latest round of peace talks in Pakistan. What do you make of all of that? Well, the president is unique. I can't say that this is typical U.S. president behavior in terms of how they act. You know, the implications of it on Iran are unclear. I think they don't know how to react to this. I think they ultimately feel, though, that it's a sign of weakness on the U.S. side. You know, if you take the day that he threatened to wipe out, you know, civilization, that very same day then, you know, Iran basically didn't change their position and the president announced a peace deal by the end of the day. So from their perspective, you know, they did nothing. Trump basically folded and basically agreed to Iran's framework for talks. It reinforces their own strategy. And so, you know, and that's to their advantage, I think. Yeah, and Iran says it doesn't trust Trump. It sees these peace talks. It's reported as a way to make it surrender. And the two sides, they're so far apart, right, when it comes to a lasting peace deal and the conditions of that. Yeah, no, absolutely. I think Iran's not going to surrender or capitulate. I mean, that much has been made clear through the history of U.S.-Iran relations, but really even just this, you know, 18 months or so of Trump's administration. You know, the entire premise has been that, you know, the U.S. is the dominant military power, has all the leverage Iran should capitulate, and they haven't. And they didn't before the war, they haven't during the war, and they're not going to at the peace talks now. And so I don't think you're going to ever see in the near future Iran, you know, negotiating away the Islamic Republic. But I don't think that's what these talks in Islamabad are about. I mean, I think it's a much, much narrower scope. And I do think it is in the interest of both parties to end the war, to de-escalate, and maybe find some, you know, mutual ground here. So I think that is possible. But, you know, it's not going to change who Iran is. Just on a side note, Nate, and interestingly, Trump had said that J.D. Vance wouldn't be attending these talks in Pakistan, but then Iran seemed to demand that he had to be there or they wouldn't be there. What do you make of this role that J.D. Vance is playing at the moment? Well, two things on that. So the first is just there's a lot of posturing going on on both sides. Will they be there? Won't they be there? And I think that's mostly noise. For the most part, it's just trying to get the strongest position going into talks. For J.D. Vance's role, I think Iran doesn't trust, you know, Wyckoff in particular, but Wyckoff and Kushner in tandem. episodes.title: When will the Iran war hit your grocery bill?
episodes.description: Shoppers have been dismayed by grocery price rises for years, now there are warnings that food will cost even more as the effects of the Iran war reach consumers.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Do you ever look at your kids and think, they've got it easy, life was so much harder back in my day? Well, have I got the podcast for you. It's called Wait, They Did What? We take a trip back in time to when kids could buy fireworks, cars didn't have seatbelts and we all had to sing God Save the Queen. They did what? They did what? I can't believe that. Check it out with your kids. Wait, they did what? It's on ABC Listen and ABC iView. COVID, Ukraine, now Iran. For years, the food supply chain has faced severe pressure and the cost has been passed on at the supermarket checkout. So, how bad is it this time? And when will another round of price hikes really kick in? Today, we speak to an expert in the costs around our food supply and to South Australian grain grower Louise Flohr about the increasing pressure on farmers. I'm Sam Hawley on Gadigal Land in Sydney. This is ABC News Daily. Louise, as a farmer, you're very used to uncertainty, but my gosh, this must feel like next level at the moment. It is, Sam. And it's a lot of decision fatigue at the moment in the grain growing community. We're trying to manage the things that we can and, yeah, just trying to keep an eye on all of the different things that are sort of getting thrown our way at the moment. We're managing high fur prices, high fuel, and we're probably looking at higher interest rates coming at us soon. So, it's a lot to be dealing with at the moment. Yeah, I bet. And for farmers like yourself, you're having to make decisions without knowing, I guess, what is around the corner, not knowing how long this war is going to last for. So, just explain that for me because I know there are farmers who are sort of deciding not to plant crops this year, maybe halving their crops. So, what position are you in right at the moment? Look, it's business as usual here, Sam. We aren't in a position where we can cut down our area. We need to be putting in our whole program. So, there's a few tweaks around the edges with some different crop types. But, yes, it's business as usual and keep calm and carry on because, yeah, we can't afford to halve the input. What's happened with this war, which is really different to what happened in the Ukraine war, was we saw prices go up relatively to the price of wheat. And so, prices were all relative. But this war has been different in that at the moment, we sort of experience high input costs, but the price of wheat's not really changed. So, it's really, you're right, we are going in really blind. We are going to wear these high costs, but we're not seeing the same relative increase in the price of grain at the end of the year. So, we expect it will go up, but, yeah, we can't see it yet. Now, you obviously rely heavily on your farm on diesel. Just explain for me that the machinery you use and how much diesel it requires. So, say per month, what does it cost you and how much of an increase have you seen at this point? So, we've seen diesel go up about 40% and we're lucky we had a bulk 30,000 litre diesel tank on farm. So, we are able to purchase it in bulk. But we are at our absolutely highest peak of fuel usage at the moment. We're seeding, so the tractor's sort of going around the clock. We're trying to ameliorate our soils where we can, which is really high diesel intensive use. So, yeah, we're at peak diesel use at the moment and, yeah, we're using thousands of litres of diesel a week at the moment. I mean, a tank of diesel into a tractor might be 200 litres. So, two by, what are we paying now, $3 a litre? Yes, it's enormously expensive. But also, hay production is a big part of our program. So, we're also, you know, driving trucks on the road. We can't pass those costs on. So, we've had contracts in place and we can't pass those costs on, unlike, say, a Qantas. Yeah, we just simply can't pass those costs on. So, it's, you know, absorb, baby, absorb. We have to absorb these costs. That comes off your bottom line. 100%. Basically. On the back of our patch has had two quite severe droughts. It's tiring. There's a fair bit of grower burnout in our patch. So, it's a really tricky time. Farming is always tricky, but this adds a lot of complexity. And as you said, fertiliser too, right? That's a real problem as well. Are you experiencing any shortfall or is it just that it's costing you more at this point? At this point, we are experiencing price increases only. We are sorting out a fertiliser in January. We are just experiencing those higher prices. Yeah, look, urea, which is what we use to put on our crops after they're emerged and growing. There may be some shortages with that. I'm not too sure, but we've got urea locked in. So, we're feeling okay. We will be putting a bit less out just simply due to the cost. And I suspect that will be happening around the place a fair bit too. Yeah. All right. And in your view, how does this compare to, I guess, the last war that you had to deal with, the Ukraine war? Is this worse to that? Yeah, so far it's worse. Absolutely. Ukraine is a major competitor for growing wheat. They're really good at growing wheat in that Black Sea region. So, when their production is disrupted, price tends to go up. And I'm not saying people benefited out of the Ukraine war, but we saw price of fuel go up, but we also saw the price of grain go up. So, it's a really, it is a pretty awful situation at the moment with those input costs, yet no changes to that grain price. So, yeah, it's, look, it's precarious. We're keeping calm. We're controlling what we can control and just take a day at a time. I'm Stefan Vogel. I'm the general manager of Rabobank's research team in Australia and New Zealand. And it's great to talk today about fuel, fertilizer, and everything that the Strait of Hormuz might mean for our farmers and consumers. Absolutely. All right. Because, of course, the uncertainty over the Strait of Hormuz, Stefan, just continues. And that will have, won't it, an effect on the food supply chain. Just explain that for me. Absolutely. And it already does have an impact for sure. Right now, a lot of what is happening is more based on fear than real shortage of supply. But if you look at the Strait of Hormuz, it is a real important bottleneck for many, many goods that we need in Australia. 80% of our beef, sheep, grain move to the world market, but we're actually extremely reliant on imports. So diesel imports, about 80% of the diesel we're using is coming from abroad. But clearly, we are also very heavily importing fertilizers from the world market. So more than 90% of the nitrogen fertilizer that we use in the country is coming from abroad. So the whole supply chain is feeling the impact right now. And the concern clearly for farmers is I need to put a crop in the ground and we're in the planting period right now. Do I have the fertilizer? Do I have the fuel to actually make that crop happen, to harvest? Because prices have gone up massively for both fertilizer and fuel on farm. Okay, why don't we consider how much more we will be paying for things when we do go to the supermarket? Now, Stefan, fresh vegetables and fruit, they're really vulnerable, aren't they? Yes, the fresh produce sector is definitely a more vulnerable one. Clearly, if you think about the timing, you need to get them off the farm at the time when they're ripe. Fresh produce is maybe more vulnerable in terms of prices and seeing those price changes maybe a bit quicker in the supermarkets. And it is, first of all, the transport and the fuel costs that are adding in it from a supply chain perspective and from a food perspective, not so much the fertilizer cost. Yeah, I have seen some reports it's potentially between 15 to 30%. For growers, the damage is already done. The National Farmers Federation warning your groceries could cost up to 20% more. What about meat and chicken? What about dairy products? The meat prices of beef and sheep meat were relatively strong already on farm, given of a local supply shortage of sheep meat, for example. The world market is still in good demand for our meat. So with that, we don't expect that the prices for those products on farm will rise as much as the cost these farmers are facing. While on the supermarket side, the transport side will be part of it. The processing side of it will be part of it.
