episodes.title: What’s driving soaring rates of adult ADHD?
episodes.description: Over the past eight years ADHD diagnoses among Australian adults have surged, especially among women. You might be surprised to hear where the ADHD capitals are.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. For years, our buyers have been told the same thing. He was an internationally acclaimed artist. Whose work is available in Australia through only one gallery. His works were selling really well. But workers start to notice something unusual. He's not contactable by any means. They couldn't find any presence of him online. In Search of the Missing Artist, a new three-part series that investigates the strange business of making art. Search Background Briefing wherever you get your podcasts. Over the past eight years, the diagnosis of ADHD among Australian adults has surged, especially among women. And you might be surprised to find out where the ADHD capitals are in Australia. Today, Norman Swan, on his Four Corners investigation into data that's never been collated before and whether it shows ADHD is being over-diagnosed. I'm Sam Hawley on Gadigal Land in Sydney. This is ABC News Daily. Norman, Frio or Fremantle in Perth. It's this old port area, although it's pretty ritzy nowadays. But you have found something really unique about the suburb, haven't you? Because it has a much higher rate of people diagnosed with ADHD than anywhere else in the country. Yep. It's the hottest hotspot. So Four Corners has been looking at ADHD in adults in Australia. And it's very hard to get data. So we commissioned a group at the University of New South Wales, the Medicines Intelligence Research Program, who worked with the Australian Bureau of Statistics, to look at ADHD diagnoses. Now, there's no record of who gets diagnosed with ADHD in Australia. So you've got to infer it from who fills out prescriptions for ADHD drugs. So it doesn't matter how many scripts you fill in a year. You've just got to have filled it at least once. And so we can see for the first time ever, actually, in Australia, the geographic spread and variation of what we infer to be ADHD diagnosis rates. It's a dramatic map. And Western Australia stands out. So to June 2024, 4.4% of adults in Fremantle fill the script for an ADHD drug. This is an extraordinary rise, by the way, over the last few years. And you look at women under the age of 44, it comes up roughly around 6%. But since then, the rate of prescriptions for ADHD drugs have gone up by another 30%, in fact, more than that. So then you're up around 8%. Wow. When you ask the experts what actually is the rate of ADHD in the community, it's between 2.5% and 3%. So something's going on because you've just got these sky-high diagnosis rates. Right. Yeah. So in a suburb like Fremantle, experts would expect a rate of around 2.5% as everywhere else, but it's at 4.4%. On average. On average. So the question is, of course, why, which we will get to. But before we go on, I guess, why don't we just reflect on what the symptoms of ADHD are so we can get a better understanding of exactly what it is. It is a neurodevelopmental disorder, meaning that it's been there probably since birth. In other words, you've got a genetic predisposition. And you cannot diagnose ADHD accurately without evidence of it being there in childhood in some shape or form. School reports, teacher reports, there needs to be correlation because there really isn't any such thing as ADHD which suddenly appears in adulthood. So it's a neurodevelopmental disorder and involves impulsivity. It involves problems with emotional regulation. It involves hyperactivity, which includes this inner restlessness. There are other features of it as well. And the key here with ADHD is that it's not a simple condition. There's no test for it. It's a matter of clinician judgment, which is why this variation may arise. Two clinicians may not agree on whether or not somebody has ADHD. And if you get it wrong, it can be serious because these symptoms could be symptoms of another mental health issue, which if it goes undiagnosed and untreated, means the person could come to harm. OK, well, Norman, let's return to Fremantle because, as you said, experts would expect about 2.5% on average of the population to have ADHD there. But it's far, far higher. But what about other places? Now, you spoke to Dr Michael Folster from UNSW. And he has really been analysing this data, I suppose, to find the hotspots across the country. So what has he found? Yes, he was one of the team that did this analysis for us at the University of New South Wales. Wow, Michael, this looks amazing. What have we here? So this is a map that shows the proportion of adults aged 20 to 65 who filled at least one prescription for ADHD medicine. So this is numbers of people? Absolutely. It's effectively the number of people being treated for ADHD. So one of the first places we went to was Sydney. He asked me to guess what I thought we were going to find in Sydney in terms of the high prevalence areas for filled prescriptions. Well, I would have thought the higher income areas, North Shore, Eastern suburbs. Let's take a look. It's not. No, we actually see a really different pattern. So here in Sydney, we see the highest rates of ADHD medicine use and adults are in the inner West and around Marrickville and around the Blue Mountains. And that's at about 3.4%. And then if you go to Melbourne, it's not the eastern suburbs of Melbourne, Toorak, Armadale and so on. It's the inner northern suburbs. It's like Brunswick and Darabin South by a long way. OK, well, let's unpack that a bit more then and try and figure out with you what is going on. Now, there is much more awareness, first of all, isn't there, of this condition? Yeah. You know, people sometimes show up to a doctor already knowing that they have this or thinking they do. I hesitate to recommend this. In fact, I don't. But you just got hashtag ADHD in TikTok or Instagram. People with ADHD always feel like they have so much to do. They have such a huge to-do list. When they achieve something, they won't feel any sense of accomplishment, only a mild sense of relief that it's done. You know, the algorithm will start delivering you short videos. Here are the typical features. And filling your head with stuff that is, while not inaccurate, it misleads you into thinking this is the only possibility that it's ADHD and convincing you that your symptoms are the symptoms of ADHD. We live in an economy where attention is the currency. So, you know, mobile phone, social media. We're on Instagram the whole time. We have kids to look after. We've got high cognitive load. We've got aging parents. We're the sandwich generation. And therefore, we just feel overwhelmed by the stuff that's hitting us. We feel that we can't cope with all this. We can't pay attention to one thing. I'm not completing tasks. And some of that will be people, particularly women with ADHD who have not been diagnosed. And some will be misleading yourself into thinking that the cognitive load of life is, in fact, ADHD. And you point out in your story that there are actually clinics that are set up just to diagnose ADHD. You go and do some sort of questionnaire. It costs you a lot of money, thousands and thousands of dollars. And then you go and have a telehealth appointment so you can get the medication. Just explain that because there's concern about that, isn't there? So there's been the growth of large telehealth clinics who do a broad range of psychiatry. But in fact, their core offering is ADHD and autism spectrum disorder diagnosis. So there are questionnaires which are well validated, which you can do yourself, which some people are misled into thinking are diagnostic. And there really are only just a bit of help for the psychiatrist. People like Professor David Cockhill at the University of Melbourne, who's one of Australia's leading experts, in fact, an international expert in ADHD, are worried about the quality of assessment. Questionnaires are not accurate enough. And they do lead to what we call a lot of false positive recognition of ADHD. A psychiatrist should not rely on these questionnaires for diagnosis. They are not diagnostic tools. Yet anecdotally, we hear of clinics where the psychiatrist accepts the findings of the questionnaire, gives you a short consultation, and you go away with a script for a psychostimulant. And we don't know the rate at which they say no. We hear a lot of feedback from people living with ADHD and those who suspect they have ADHD that their assessment has been very quick. But it's really consisted of just filling in those questionnaires, having the doctor look at them, and then having a rubber stamp. That's not acceptable. Telehealth is turning out to be a bit of a problem in a few different areas, and it may well be an issue here with ADHD. All right. The other question you had, Norman, was about the influence of the big pharmaceutical companies and the impact, I suppose, they have on doctors and the panel of experts that come up with the guidelines on how these drugs should be prescribed. Now, just to note, you as a doctor, you have received yourself a payment from one of these big companies before. Yes, I gave a speech at a conference sponsored by a pharmaceutical company that produces ADHD medications. So I'm well aware of the issues here. And one of the people we spoke to was Professor Lisa Cosgrove of the University of Massachusetts, Boston, who studied conflict of interest and what can happen when you take the pharmaceutical industry's shilling. People get defensive because the implication is, I've done something wrong. And that's not the case. Identifying conflicts of interest is in no way suggesting that someone has engaged in research fraud or done anything wrong. Rather, the real crux of the issue is that those ties engender inevitably implicit bias. We're all vulnerable to implicit bias and we're blissfully ignorant of the way in which that implicit bias can be manifest. And when you look at the references used to back up what's called the National Guideline for Clinical Practice in ADHD, which is like the Bible for people to use to make the diagnosis, which is not a bad guideline, by the way, but a third of the references that they use to back it up have people on the authorship line who've received pharmaceutical funding. And then when you look at the prescribing guide in Australia, which is advising doctors on the selection of drugs and how they should be used. Again, not a bad prescribing guide, but nonetheless, several of the members of that committee had received pharmaceutical industry funding. And so it just creates a problem of trust. Where does the bias arise? And people could actually argue that with me. You know, my bias in my reporting of the issue, people make that judgment when they see the four corners. All right. Well, Norman, you've had a really good look at this very insightful data. The first we've ever had, as you say, in Australia. I guess the question people are really asking now is why is it then that there are these pockets across Australia in Fremantle, for instance, that have this higher rate? Did you get to the bottom of that? It's complicated, isn't it? It is very complicated and you can only speculate. For those of you who know Australia and they know Fremantle, they know Brunswick, they know Marrickville and Sydney. Very similar populations. So it's a younger population, well-educated. They do have money, but not a lot of money, but they do have money. They are probably more accepting of neurodivergence and there's less stigma around it in those suburbs. And they're more aware and more concerned about their health and well-being. What's hard to explain is why women dominate. That's partly catch-up, but we've probably gone beyond catch-up. And I think it's just the general problem that women have as they reach midlife. They are unfairly squeezed by life. And some of those women do have ADHD and some women probably don't, but they have other issues that need to be dealt with. Yeah. And on the other hand, of course, Norman, so costly to get a diagnosis. There must be people within society that can't actually afford a consultation at this point. That's the other side of our data. There are ADHD deserts and there's huge ADHD deserts in Australia where the rate of diagnosis is far below where it should be. So Fairfield in southwest Sydney is the second lowest area for filled prescriptions in the country. And if you look at where they sit in terms of the prevalence of filled prescriptions compared to the actual prevalence of ADHD, 90% of adults with ADHD in Fairfield are likely to be missed. Right. Well, Norman, of course, people should always speak to their own doctor for specific advice. But what's your message to those who are hearing this and thinking maybe I or someone I know has ADHD? How careful do they need to be to make sure they get the right diagnosis? Everybody should have a GP that they know and they trust. And sometimes that's a bit of a journey. People can get so locked in to the belief that they have ADHD. This is something which you really want to be sure about with your doctor and be open to that there are other possibilities here. And you want to find a psychiatrist or a clinical psychologist who doesn't conduct what they call ADHD assessments. They conduct a proper psychological assessment of your mental health and well-being and come to a diagnosis, one of which might be ADHD, but another might be others. So it's just being careful and slow and not jumping to conclusions and not seeing a clinician who jumps to conclusions. The producer is David Cody. I'm Sam Hawley. ABC News Daily will be back again tomorrow. Thanks for listening.

In Search of the Missing Artist, a new three-part series
that investigates the strange business of making art.

Over the past eight years, the diagnosis of ADHD among Australian adults
has surged, especially among women.
And you might be surprised to find out where the ADHD capitals are in Australia.
Today, Norman Swan, on his Four Corners investigation
into data that's never been collated before
and whether it shows ADHD is being over-diagnosed.
I'm Sam Hawley on Gadigal Land in Sydney.
This is ABC News Daily.
Norman, Frio or Fremantle in Perth.
It's this old port area, although it's pretty ritzy nowadays.
But you have found something really unique about the suburb, haven't you?
Because it has a much higher rate of people diagnosed with ADHD
than anywhere else in the country.
Yep.
It's the hottest hotspot.
So Four Corners has been looking at ADHD in adults in Australia.
And it's very hard to get data.
So we commissioned a group at the University of New South Wales,
the Medicines Intelligence Research Program,
who worked with the Australian Bureau of Statistics,
to look at ADHD diagnoses.
Now, there's no record of who gets diagnosed with ADHD in Australia.
So you've got to infer it from who fills out prescriptions for ADHD drugs.
So it doesn't matter how many scripts you fill in a year.
You've just got to have filled it at least once.
And so we can see for the first time ever, actually, in Australia,
the geographic spread and variation of what we infer to be ADHD diagnosis rates.
It's a dramatic map.
And Western Australia stands out.
So to June 2024, 4.4% of adults in Fremantle fill the script for an ADHD drug.
This is an extraordinary rise, by the way, over the last few years.
And you look at women under the age of 44, it comes up roughly around 6%.
But since then, the rate of prescriptions for ADHD drugs have gone up by another 30%,
in fact, more than that.
So then you're up around 8%.
Wow.
When you ask the experts what actually is the rate of ADHD in the community,
it's between 2.5% and 3%.
So something's going on because you've just got these sky-high diagnosis rates.
Right.
Yeah.
So in a suburb like Fremantle, experts would expect a rate of around 2.5% as everywhere else,
but it's at 4.4%.
On average.
On average.
So the question is, of course, why, which we will get to.
But before we go on, I guess, why don't we just reflect on what the symptoms of ADHD are
so we can get a better understanding of exactly what it is.
It is a neurodevelopmental disorder, meaning that it's been there probably since birth.
In other words, you've got a genetic predisposition.
And you cannot diagnose ADHD accurately without evidence of it being there in childhood in some
shape or form.
School reports, teacher reports, there needs to be correlation because there really isn't
any such thing as ADHD which suddenly appears in adulthood.
So it's a neurodevelopmental disorder and involves impulsivity.
It involves problems with emotional regulation.
It involves hyperactivity, which includes this inner restlessness.
There are other features of it as well.
And the key here with ADHD is that it's not a simple condition.
There's no test for it.
It's a matter of clinician judgment, which is why this variation may arise.
Two clinicians may not agree on whether or not somebody has ADHD.
And if you get it wrong, it can be serious because these symptoms could be symptoms of another
mental health issue, which if it goes undiagnosed and untreated, means the person could come
to harm.
OK, well, Norman, let's return to Fremantle because, as you said, experts would expect about
2.5% on average of the population to have ADHD there.
But it's far, far higher.
But what about other places?
Now, you spoke to Dr Michael Folster from UNSW.
And he has really been analysing this data, I suppose, to find the hotspots across the country.
So what has he found?
Yes, he was one of the team that did this analysis for us at the University of New South
Wales.
Wow, Michael, this looks amazing.
What have we here?
So this is a map that shows the proportion of adults aged 20 to 65 who filled at least
one prescription for ADHD medicine.
So this is numbers of people?
Absolutely.
It's effectively the number of people being treated for ADHD.
So one of the first places we went to was Sydney.
He asked me to guess what I thought we were going to find in Sydney in terms of the high
prevalence areas for filled prescriptions.
Well, I would have thought the higher income areas, North Shore, Eastern suburbs.
Let's take a look.
It's not.
No, we actually see a really different pattern.
So here in Sydney, we see the highest rates of ADHD medicine use and adults are in the inner
West and around Marrickville and around the Blue Mountains.
And that's at about 3.4%.
And then if you go to Melbourne, it's not the eastern suburbs of Melbourne, Toorak, Armadale
and so on.
It's the inner northern suburbs.
It's like Brunswick and Darabin South by a long way.
OK, well, let's unpack that a bit more then and try and figure out with you what is going
on.
Now, there is much more awareness, first of all, isn't there, of this condition?
Yeah.
You know, people sometimes show up to a doctor already knowing that they have this or thinking
they do.
I hesitate to recommend this.
In fact, I don't.
But you just got hashtag ADHD in TikTok or Instagram.
People with ADHD always feel like they have so much to do.
They have such a huge to-do list.
When they achieve something, they won't feel any sense of accomplishment, only a mild sense
of relief that it's done.
You know, the algorithm will start delivering you short videos.
Here are the typical features.
And filling your head with stuff that is, while not inaccurate, it misleads you into thinking
this is the only possibility that it's ADHD and convincing you that your symptoms are the
symptoms of ADHD.
We live in an economy where attention is the currency.
So, you know, mobile phone, social media.
We're on Instagram the whole time.
We have kids to look after.
We've got high cognitive load.
We've got aging parents.
We're the sandwich generation.
And therefore, we just feel overwhelmed by the stuff that's hitting us.
We feel that we can't cope with all this.
We can't pay attention to one thing.
I'm not completing tasks.
And some of that will be people, particularly women with ADHD who have not been diagnosed.
And some will be misleading yourself into thinking that the cognitive load of life is,
in fact, ADHD.
And you point out in your story that there are actually clinics that are set up just to
diagnose ADHD.
You go and do some sort of questionnaire.
It costs you a lot of money, thousands and thousands of dollars.
And then you go and have a telehealth appointment so you can get the medication.
Just explain that because there's concern about that, isn't there?
So there's been the growth of large telehealth clinics who do a broad range of psychiatry.
But in fact, their core offering is ADHD and autism spectrum disorder diagnosis.
So there are questionnaires which are well validated, which you can do yourself,
which some people are misled into thinking are diagnostic.
And there really are only just a bit of help for the psychiatrist.
People like Professor David Cockhill at the University of Melbourne, who's one of Australia's
leading experts, in fact, an international expert in ADHD, are worried about the quality
of assessment.
Questionnaires are not accurate enough.
And they do lead to what we call a lot of false positive recognition of ADHD.
A psychiatrist should not rely on these questionnaires for diagnosis.
They are not diagnostic tools.
Yet anecdotally, we hear of clinics where the psychiatrist accepts the findings of the questionnaire,
gives you a short consultation, and you go away with a script for a psychostimulant.
And we don't know the rate at which they say no.
We hear a lot of feedback from people living with ADHD and those who suspect they have ADHD
that their assessment has been very quick.
But it's really consisted of just filling in those questionnaires, having the doctor look at them,
and then having a rubber stamp.
That's not acceptable.
Telehealth is turning out to be a bit of a problem in a few different areas,
and it may well be an issue here with ADHD.
All right.
The other question you had, Norman, was about the influence of the big pharmaceutical companies
and the impact, I suppose, they have on doctors and the panel of experts that come up with the guidelines
on how these drugs should be prescribed.
Now, just to note, you as a doctor, you have received yourself a payment from one of these big companies before.
Yes, I gave a speech at a conference sponsored by a pharmaceutical company that produces ADHD medications.
So I'm well aware of the issues here.
And one of the people we spoke to was Professor Lisa Cosgrove of the University of Massachusetts, Boston,
who studied conflict of interest and what can happen when you take the pharmaceutical industry's shilling.
People get defensive because the implication is, I've done something wrong.
And that's not the case.
Identifying conflicts of interest is in no way suggesting that someone has engaged in research fraud or done anything wrong.
Rather, the real crux of the issue is that those ties engender inevitably implicit bias.
We're all vulnerable to implicit bias and we're blissfully ignorant of the way in which that implicit bias can be manifest.
And when you look at the references used to back up what's called the National Guideline for Clinical Practice in ADHD,

which is like the Bible for people to use to make the diagnosis, which is not a bad guideline, by the way, but a third of the references that they use to back it up have people on the authorship line who've received pharmaceutical funding.
And then when you look at the prescribing guide in Australia, which is advising doctors on the selection of drugs and how they should be used.
Again, not a bad prescribing guide, but nonetheless, several of the members of that committee had received pharmaceutical industry funding.
And so it just creates a problem of trust.
Where does the bias arise?
And people could actually argue that with me.
You know, my bias in my reporting of the issue, people make that judgment when they see the four corners.
All right.
Well, Norman, you've had a really good look at this very insightful data.
The first we've ever had, as you say, in Australia.
I guess the question people are really asking now is why is it then that there are these pockets across Australia in Fremantle, for instance, that have this higher rate?
Did you get to the bottom of that?
It's complicated, isn't it?
It is very complicated and you can only speculate.
For those of you who know Australia and they know Fremantle, they know Brunswick, they know Marrickville and Sydney.
Very similar populations.
So it's a younger population, well-educated.
They do have money, but not a lot of money, but they do have money.
They are probably more accepting of neurodivergence and there's less stigma around it in those suburbs.
And they're more aware and more concerned about their health and well-being.
What's hard to explain is why women dominate.
That's partly catch-up, but we've probably gone beyond catch-up.
And I think it's just the general problem that women have as they reach midlife.
They are unfairly squeezed by life.
And some of those women do have ADHD and some women probably don't, but they have other issues that need to be dealt with.
Yeah. And on the other hand, of course, Norman, so costly to get a diagnosis.
There must be people within society that can't actually afford a consultation at this point.
That's the other side of our data.
There are ADHD deserts and there's huge ADHD deserts in Australia where the rate of diagnosis is far below where it should be.
So Fairfield in southwest Sydney is the second lowest area for filled prescriptions in the country.
And if you look at where they sit in terms of the prevalence of filled prescriptions compared to the actual prevalence of ADHD, 90% of adults with ADHD in Fairfield are likely to be missed.
Right. Well, Norman, of course, people should always speak to their own doctor for specific advice.
But what's your message to those who are hearing this and thinking maybe I or someone I know has ADHD?
How careful do they need to be to make sure they get the right diagnosis?
Everybody should have a GP that they know and they trust.
And sometimes that's a bit of a journey.
People can get so locked in to the belief that they have ADHD.
This is something which you really want to be sure about with your doctor and be open to that there are other possibilities here.
And you want to find a psychiatrist or a clinical psychologist who doesn't conduct what they call ADHD assessments.
They conduct a proper psychological assessment of your mental health and well-being and come to a diagnosis, one of which might be ADHD, but another might be others.
So it's just being careful and slow and not jumping to conclusions and not seeing a clinician who jumps to conclusions.
The producer is David Cody.
I'm Sam Hawley.
ABC News Daily will be back again tomorrow.
Thanks for listening.

episodes.title: What Putin gains from the Iran war
episodes.description: What does Russia’s Vladimir Putin make of the Iran war? He’s one of the few beneficiaries, making vast sums of money as the oil price spiked and Donald Trump temporarily eased sanctions.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. For years, our buyers have been told the same thing. He was an internationally acclaimed artist. Whose work is available in Australia through only one gallery. His works were selling really well. But workers start to notice something unusual. He's not contactable by any means. They couldn't find any presence of him online. In Search of the Missing Artist, a new three-part series that investigates the strange business of making art. Search Background Briefing wherever you get your podcasts. What's Vladimir Putin been up to since the start of the Iran war? Well, he's one of its only beneficiaries. He's made billions as the oil prices spiked and Donald Trump eased sanctions temporarily. The world's attention has been diverted from his war in Ukraine. And the thorn in his side, the NATO alliance, is crumbling. Today, international relations expert Rajen Menon on Trump's threats to withdraw the US from NATO. And whether Europe can defend itself against its hostile neighbour. I'm Sam Hawley on Gadigal land in Sydney. This is ABC News Daily. Music Rajen, it's often been said since the start of the war in Iran that Vladimir Putin is one of the only winners, that Russia has gained and not lost anything. What's your assessment? Well, that is largely correct because oil is an extraordinarily important part of the Russian budget. I think it's about 40% of all budget revenue. So two things have happened. One is that President Trump, to ease oil flows into the global economy, to bring the prices down, temporarily suspended sanctions on Russia. And of course, the price of oil has gone up by about, I don't know, 45% since the beginning of the war. So yes, he certainly has been a beneficiary of this war in that respect. All right. Well, let's Rajen look a bit more deeply at how Russia is actually gaining from this war. Now, one problem for Donald Trump and perhaps a win for Russia is that the military powerhouses in Europe have not come to his aid. Even though, of course, Donald Trump has asked repeatedly for help, they have said no. And he's really angry about that, isn't he, with nations like the UK and Spain and many others. I call up France, Macron. Would love to have some help. If you could, could you please send ships immediately? No, no, no. We cannot do that, don't we? We can do that after the war is won. And so I learned about NATO. NATO won't be there if we ever have the big one. You know what I mean by the big one. We ever have the big one, hopefully we won't. Relationships are very good with the big one. Better than with NATO. It's extraordinary. Now, one should know, and you probably know this, but just to set the stage, if you look at the NATO Treaty of 1949, it says that the collective security provision, Article 5, is operative when any of the members of NATO is attacked. The only time Article 5 has been invoked is 9-11, and it was invoked to defend the United States. But in this instance, no NATO member was attacked. A NATO member, namely the United States, attacked another country. What's extraordinary about this is there's been a sweeping kind of rebellion. I mean, it varies from intensity to country to country, but even Keir Starmer, who kind of looks like a mild-mannered banker, and, you know, like all British prime ministers' values, the so-called special relationship with the U.S., has had it with Trump and said, I'm not going to be bullied into doing this. Whatever the pressure on me and others, whatever the noise, I'm going to act in the British national interest in all the decisions that I make. And that's why I've been absolutely clear that this is not our war, or we're not going to get dragged into it. Incidentally, it's not just Trump, where even people who have been seen to have become quasi-Trump whisperers, or people who've gotten Trump's confidence, like Giorgia Maloney in Italy, for example, have turned against him, most recently because of his attack on the Pope. But even before that, she also took the position that this is not our war, this is not a war we were consulted on. So I think Putin is happy looking at NATO, gripped by crises, that works to his advantage in many ways. Yes, because as you say, NATO members do not have to join a war that they weren't consulted about in the first place. Correct. Now, of course, they've again said no thanks to Donald Trump when he requested they help with this blockade of the Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz. So again, they're at loggerheads with Donald Trump. Yes, and there's a reason for that, because a blockade under international law is an act of war. So if you're enforcing the blockade, you have joined the war against Iran. Trump may not realise this, but anyone with even a cursory knowledge of international law understands it, and certainly people like Starmer and others recognise it. All right. Well, it seems like Mark Rutter, the NATO chief, he's really the only one at this point, Rajan, that is sticking by Trump. You know, he once called him daddy, of course. He says NATO members have been a bit slow to act in helping America. What do you make of how he's handling all of this? You know, to be honest, Sam, he looks really pathetic because he's completely out of step with the alliance that he's leading. And the more he gets behind Trump and tries to take NATO into wars that his members don't want to get into, the less credibility he has, I think, among the members of the alliance. So trying to ingratiate himself with Trump, it's a kind of form of self-abasement. But beyond that, it doesn't lead anywhere because it's not as if Trump is going to look at you next week and say, oh, Mark, you did such a great job. You supported me. Now I'm going to do this, that or the other for you. Friendship's been nothing. I mean, look, for example, what happened after Orban lost the election in Hungary. Trump just completely stopped speaking about Orban. Well, Mark Rutter was asked about this daddy comment quite recently at a Ronald Reagan Institute address. And yes, it appears like he will never, ever, ever live that down, Rajan. I was not calling him my daddy, but saying. But of course, daddy has also a special connotation. And I now have to live as this the rest of my life. And I own it. And the president owns it because he brought out T-shirts. He made a movie. Daddy is home. And he returned to the United States. This is all so funny. And this is why I like him so much. He will not. And he's not going to get any big Christmas present from Trump. But more importantly, even if he didn't directly call him daddy, as he tried to explain, well, in Dutch, it means this, that, and the other, just the use of the word was really politically tone deaf. Yes, indeed. All right. Well, Rajan, Donald Trump has, on numerous occasions, now threatened to pull the United States out of NATO. In recent days and weeks, he's called European allies cowards and NATO a paper tiger. And he has said that Putin knows that too. Now, the Wall Street Journal has reported that these European nations are planning for this US exit. What do we know about that? They're obviously quite concerned that this is a real possibility at this point. Yes. So I'll put my cards on the table and say that I've long been a proponent of European strategic autonomy. I made this argument first in the book I wrote in 2007, and most recently, in an article that I wrote for an outfit called the Institute for Arts and Ideas in London. Having said that, this has been a catalyst, because I think NATO has fundamentally had to realize that the day will come when it cannot rely on American protections. Here are a couple of things that have happened. In 2024 and 2025, in the aggregate, each year, defense spending in NATO went up by 20%. So defense budgets are increasing. The German Bundeswehr, the German army, which was shambolic, they are now putting large amounts of money into it. There is a kind of joint defense production document that's been drawn up to reduce duplication and invest in defense industries. There is talk about, more than talk actually, serious negotiations, about whether it is possible to make the Anglo-French nuclear deterrent an umbrella for all of Europe to replace the American umbrella. There are attempts to base forward many more NATO troops on the eastern flank. And so for the first time, I think NATO is taking steps to prepare for the day when it might not be able to rely on the United States. And there's no case to be made that Europe lacks, whether population or wealth or technology or defense industries, the wherewithal to defend itself, because it has only one significant threat. Russia. It doesn't have to be a global power like the United States with a galaxy of bases all over the world. All right. But let's look then at the ramifications of the US actually pulling out of NATO. First, of course, Ukraine, because, of course, Ukraine has been heavily dependent on arms and intelligence from the United States during the war with Russia. Yes, there has been this dependence. But bear in mind that under Trump 2, the most recent iteration of Donald Trump's presidency, the United States ceased direct military support for Ukraine. An alternative was set up called PURL. I won't take the time to spell it out for you. But under this arrangement, the Europeans could request equipment from the United States that they then had to pay for and transfer to Ukraine. But what was delivered and at what pace and when the deliveries were made were entirely up to the United States. And the Ukrainians have long felt that Trump was kind of slow walking it. So the military dependence on the United States has long ceased and the Europeans have stepped up. So the Europeans may not be entirely able to fill the American gap, but they are stepping up for one simple reason. Donald Trump likes to say this is not our war, that is the Russia-Ukraine war, because we have this, quote, big, beautiful ocean separating us. Well, the Europeans cannot say that. They're joined at the hip to Ukraine in the sense that if Ukraine falls, their security future looks much more vulnerable. And what about beyond Ukraine, though? Should these European nations be concerned that Putin could invade other nations? Estonia, Rajan is worried. Poland, Finland. Right. So let me say this. It's very easy for me as an American sitting in New York City to say what I'm about to say. And I completely understand that a Estonian or a Latvian or a Finn, for example, would feel entirely differently. But here's the way I look at it. The Russians have fought Ukraine, a manifestly weaker adversary, for longer than it fought Hitler's armies. It has sustained 1.1 million casualties, that is dead and wounded. Maybe about 300,000 of those are deaths. This is a country that has a very, very low birth rate and is barely reproducing itself, and maybe even there's a net reduction in population. And then the economic consequences have been enormous, just not to mention that all these destroyed areas that Russia now claims have to be rebuilt. So my view is, given the poor showing of Russian army, given the bad experience of the war, and given the economic cost, Russia will be licking its wounds for some time to come. The Russia that will emerge from the Ukraine war is a Russia that can be handled by a robust European defense posture much more easily than the Russia that was before the Ukraine war. Russia might be depleted, but the threat is still real, isn't it? Because, as we saw, the UK's Defence Secretary, John Healy, he recently revealed Russia had sent submarines to spy on British cables and pipelines in waters north of the UK. And to President Putin, I say, we see you, we see your activity over our cables and our pipelines, and you should know that any attempt to damage them will not be tolerated and will have serious consequences. So, I mean, that would be a worry for NATO nations. Yes. Yeah, you raise a very good point because it's not just tanks crossing the border. Russian activity against NATO can be manifested in many, many different ways. Cyber warfare, for example, trying to cut undersea cables, espionage and so on. And that will continue. I had in mind at the moment just the question of, can Russia make a sustained assault against the combined resources of non-US NATO? And I'm skeptical that it can. Now, there are experts here who would disagree with me. And I'm sure, again, I want to emphasize this. I understand that people in East Central Europe will have a different idea, but I think it is a problem that Europe can manage on its own. If it puts its mind to it. What's your view? Do you think Donald Trump will jump? Do you think he will remove the United States from NATO after all of these years, all of these decades? You know, I'd rather bet on seeing a unicorn on Central Park and walk tomorrow than on whether Donald Trump will do X or Y. The behavior has been so erratic that it's becoming increasingly difficult to know what he will do or what he won't do. So, you know, anything is feasible. Nothing would surprise me anymore. Thank you. And Anna John. Audio production by Sam Dunn. Our supervising producer is David Cody. I'm Sam Hawley. ABC News Daily will be back again on Monday. Thanks for listening.

episodes.title: The President vs the Pope
episodes.description: What’s behind US President Donald Trump’s attack on Pope Leo? After the leader of the Catholic Church criticised Trump’s threats to destroy Iranian civilisation, the president unleashed.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. When energy costs jump, everyone feels it. At the Bowser, on the Power Bill and across the economy. I'm Alan Kohler. And I'm Carrington Clark. On ABC Business Daily's Fuelcast, we break down the latest in fuel, energy and the forces driving prices. It's a quick, clear update on what's moving, why it matters and what it can mean for your wallet and the wider economy. Find Fuelcast in the ABC Business Daily feed on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts. Is Donald Trump sane enough to be commanding a war? Debate over the US leader's mental health has reignited since he began verbally attacking the Pope and posted an AI image depicting himself as Jesus. Today, David A. Graham from The Atlantic magazine on what Trump's behaviour says about his ability to govern. I'm Sam Hawley on Gadigal land in Sydney. This is ABC News Daily. David, you have noted that Donald Trump has a so-called media crash out, which begins on a Sunday and it ends in the early hours of the next morning. So I gather you've been tracking this for some time, have you? Yeah, we've always sort of been tracking Trump's social media since 2015. Yes. But he does seem to have gotten into this new pattern in the last few weeks. What seems to be happening is every Sunday as he kind of tunes back into the news and prepares for the week ahead, he gets on Truth Social, his social network, and starts posting up a storm. And there will be tirades about whatever he's angry about, you know, targeting the Pope in the latest example, but also Democrats and other Republicans who he's upset with in other instances. And then mixed in with memes and campaign endorsements and whatever else might be on his mind on into the early hours of the morning. Yeah, and very early hours by the look of it. I mean, sometimes it's really, really early, like 4 a.m. It's not clear to me when Trump sleeps because he is often posting very late and will be posting again early in the morning too. Yeah, wow. Okay, well, on Sunday, last Sunday, the president was having a particular moment, wasn't he? Things weren't as he wanted them to be and this is when he launched into Pope Leo. Right, Trump had had kind of a rough weekend, I think it's fair to say. We had seen Viktor Orban, his ally and kind of role model in Hungary lose, and negotiations with Iran had gotten nowhere. And he's been taking some criticism from the Pope over the war in Iran. And he decided it was time to say something about that. And he uncorked his long post, starting with Pope Leo was weak on crime, and then criticizing the Pope for making statements about foreign affairs, saying he needed to mind the Catholic Church, complaining that he met with a democratic strategist, and really just venting whatever frustrations he had. Yeah, wow. And he doubled down on that Truth Social post when he was actually asked about it by reporters later. Do you apologize? No, I don't, because Pope Leo said things that are wrong. He was very much against what I'm doing with regard to Iran. And you cannot have a nuclear Iran. Pope Leo would not be happy with the end result. You'll have hundreds of millions of people dead. And it's not going to happen. So I can't. I think he's very weak on crime. But just remind me, David, what was it that Pope Leo had actually done to offend Donald Trump? What was his crime in Donald Trump's eyes? It seems like the thing that really got Trump is that Leo was out saying that people in positions of power should seek peace rather than war. On this day of celebration, let us abandon every desire for conflict, domination, and power, and implore the Lord to grant his peace to a world ravaged by wars and marked by a hatred and indifference that makes us feel powerless in the face of evil. He also said that, you know, people should not make war in God's name with many people. Took as a swipe at Pete Hegseth, the U.S. Secretary of Defense, who's used a lot of really strong Christian rhetoric to justify and to talk about the war. Yeah, he sure has. Well, it did get worse, though, didn't it, David? Because not long after these truth social posts condemning the Pope, Trump then posts this bizarre image of himself, an AI image, where he appears as a Jesus-like figure. I mean, try and explain that image for me, just in case there are some people that haven't seen it by now. Explaining it is so hard. So it's got Trump with a sort of glowing orb in his hand, putting his hand on and appearing to heal an elderly man, and there's people looking up. Up at him in a sort of prayerful way, and there's all this patriotic imagery of a flag and fighter jets and bald eagles and what seem like maybe angels or maybe gargoyles or something in the sky above him. Very much Jesus-like sort of glow about him. Absolutely. And not surprisingly, it causes this huge stir. And in the end, he does take it down. But then, I mean, unbelievably, he then tells reporters that actually the post was meant to portray him as a doctor. What did you make of that? He did say this. He did? Well, it wasn't a picture. It was me. I did post it, and I thought it was me as a doctor and had to do with Red Cross as a Red Cross worker there, which we support. And only the fake news could come up with that one. So I had just heard about it, and I said, how did they come up with that? It's supposed to be me as a doctor making people better. And I do make people better. I make people a lot better. It seems like the sort of thing that he was really reaching for some kind of spin. I mean, this is an image. I don't know where Trump came across it in this instance, but it has been floating around in some version for a couple months now by fans of his who are very clear that he is meant to be looking Christ-like. And I don't think there's really any denying what was going on. But Trump was also clearly feeling a lot of heat, including from his own supporters. You know, you've got these people on the hard right who are very religious, and we're talking about, you know, this post being blasphemous or, you know, suggesting that he was possessed by demons. And I think the heat just got too much for him, and he had to take it down and come up with some kind of excuse. Yeah, sure. And I don't think you ever need to be Catholic to consider that post pretty offensive. I think the Pope is making very pointed statements about the war, but also doesn't seem to be seeking a confrontation with Trump exactly. Now, David, in a moment, why don't we talk about this really intensifying debate over whether Donald Trump is sane and fit to be commanding a war. Vance, the vice president, Marco Rubio. So why on earth would he attack the Pope? I think for Trump, there are really two kinds of people. There are people who are his supporters and there are people who are against him. And I don't think it really does make a lot of sense. And I think what you see is him lashing out more than taking any kind of considered strategy by attacking Leo. It's very ironic. You know, he complained that Leo is, you know, sticking his nose in politics where it doesn't belong, which is something that J.D. Vance has also said. It would be best for the Vatican to stick to matters of morality, to stick to matters of, you know, what's going on in the Catholic Church and let the president of the United States stick to dictating American public policy. You know, what the Pope says is we're talking about issues of war and peace and poverty and, you know, kindness to strangers. These are Christian values. And as you say, you know, Trump has called on Christian imagery very often. Pete Hegseth has been doing this frequently. It seems like Trump is perfectly happy to mix religion and politics where it suits him. He's just very upset when that kind of rhetoric is used to critique him. Right. Yeah. And Trump's vision of Christianity, it doesn't stack up with what's written in the Gospels, that's for sure. He's referred to communion as drinking a little wine and eating some little crackers. That's right. You know, he's been asked what his favorite Bible verse is and been unable to answer. He has misnamed books of the Bible in public appearances. You know, he doesn't attend church regularly. He skipped church on Easter this year. So even as he, you know, has many followers who are very religious, he doesn't seem to be engaged in it at all. I think for him it's just an instrument. It's not a personal system of belief. Well, David, as we discussed, Donald Trump has many rants on social media. But one of the most shocking posts, of course, was this threat to the whole civilization of Iran. Now, that was criticized, wasn't it, by a number of high profile MAGA figures. Yeah, it really was an amazing and shocking post. And although we have seen a lot of outrageous statements from Trump, I think this was one of the lows, even by those standards of his time. And it got poor reactions across the board. I mean, you had some of the people who are in his coalition but have been a little bit more anti-war. People like the conservative pundit Tucker Carlson objected to it and said that if he attempted to do anything to carry that out, the U.S. military should refuse to do it. And then outside of Trump supporters, I'd say it was met with shock and dismay and horror. And the former Trump supporter Marjorie Taylor Greene, she was on CNN and she was incredibly scathing. I think we have to truly question the mental stability of any president that threatens to wipe out an entire civilization of people. As was Candace Owens, who is a far right podcaster. I mean, you guys obviously know my perspective. Trump is very clearly under demonic influence. I think Paula White probably put a spell on him of some sort. These really disjointed, extreme posts, including, of course, the attack on the Pope, they have, haven't they, David, led to concern about his mental health? And I think it's fair to say that concern is growing. And it's not just now his political opponents who are talking about that, is it? No. I mean, we're seeing even in the most, you know, down-the-middle news sources, people raising questions about this. You know, the New York Times asking whether he is sane and fit. We see Democrats requesting that he have some sort of mental evaluation to see if he is fit and raising the possibility of the 25th Amendment to the Constitution, which allows for the removal of a president who's unfit. And you see a lot of people also comparing this to Joe Biden, saying, you know, we had a president in the last term who seemed not always entirely with it. And now we seem to be repeating the same thing with Donald Trump, who also is very old. Yeah. But the 25th Amendment, just to explain that a bit further, that allows the removal of a president, but the bar is really high, right? Exactly. This is something that we've never seen actually used. And the intent was if a president was incapacitated by illness or, you know, in a coma or had a heart attack or what have you, that there would be a way for removing them and putting somebody in place. But it requires the president's own cabinet to act to invoke this and to make it happen, which is, I think, why it seems like such a long shot, because what we see from Trump's closest advisors and cabinet members, rather than any move away from him, is fawning praise. You know, talking about his brilliant leadership of the war in Iran and how no other president could have done this. So for now, and certainly publicly, they seem to be rallying around him. All right. So it's a really high bar and unlikely to happen. The White House has defended David Trump's behavior, saying he's sharp and he's keeping his opponents on edge. I think you really need to look no further than these social media things we're talking about. You know, you can talk about the bizarre Christlike image. You can talk about the threat of genocide. These are not signs of a president who is thinking particularly clearly or acting with any kind of deliberation. He doesn't seem to have a clear strategy for the war in Iran. He's spinning his wheels on that. And I think, you know, although there are reasons to be particularly concerned based on his behavior and statements in the last couple of weeks, this is also part of a longer pattern. Trump's temperament has always been questionable for the presidency. You know, when we talk about his sort of norm breaking or about the unprecedented things he does, what we're talking about is doing things that would have been considered unthinkable for any other president previously. We don't see a lot of careful judgment. And I think that's one reason he's been in so much legal trouble. And one reason why, with the exception of the 2024 election, he has been unable to win popular votes. David A. Graham is a staff writer at The Atlantic. This episode was produced by Sydney Peed and Anna John. Audio production by Sam Dunn. Our supervising producer is David Cody. I'm Sam Hawley. To get in touch with the team, email us on ABC News Daily at abc.net.au. Thanks for listening.

episodes.title: The 'doomsday' scenario for fuel supply
episodes.description: The US blockade of Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz could make the fuel crunch in Australia even worse. The government’s urging Australians to do what they can to use less fuel, but when will more severe restrictions kick in?
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Everybody's talking about fuel. Whether you're in need of filling up the tank for the week and you're watching the dollars tick over at the Bowser or you're watching weekend plans, holiday plans, business plans change. To help get your head around the latest, you can find Fuelcast in the ABC Business Daily feed on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts. What does Donald Trump's blockade in the Strait of Hormuz mean for our fuel supply? Well, it's not great. Today, Sol Kavanek, energy expert at MST Financial, on why we're facing a doomsday scenario that's been war-gamed for decades. I'm Sam Hawley on Gadigal Land in Sydney. This is ABC News Daily. Donald Trump says the US military's blockade of ships entering or departing Iranian ports has begun. The Prime Minister is returning to Southeast Asia this week, travelling to Brunei and Malaysia in an effort to secure ongoing fuel and fertiliser supplies amid the global energy crisis. In a fiery social media post, Donald Trump threatening to blow to hell any Iranian vessel who fires at us or at peaceful vessels and warning that no country who pays a toll to Iran will get safe passage. We can't let a country blackmail or extort the world because that's what they're doing. They're really blackmailing the world. We're not going to let that happen. So, the blockade threatened by Donald Trump is now in place. So, we're going to consider what that means for us and our fuel supply. This will make the oil crisis worse, won't it? At least in the short term. Well, that's right. So, basically, the oil market is now rewound to before the ceasefire and Trump's bombastic ultimatum was made. So, we're back on an escalatory pathway for the conflict and for oil markets. Except this time, with Trump's blockade of Iran, the remaining one to two million barrels of oil that was still coming out of the restraint, which was the Iranian barrels, that's now going to be stopped as well via the blockade. So, it's taken an extra one to two percent off the global oil markets. Right now, there's no live fire or war on. We're still within this tentative ceasefire period. And so, there's lower risk of direct attacks on oil infrastructure right now. But that could change at any moment. All right. So, the US is now stopping ships from leaving and entering ports in Iran. Now, this will be, won't it, a huge hit to Iran's economy because more than 50 percent of its exports and actually most of its revenue comes from oil. Oil is simply everything to Iran, isn't it? It's the vast majority of the government revenue and the foreign revenue for the country. The one caveat with that is, given the lag times involved in shipments of oil and payments, Iran's likely to still be receiving money from its oil customers for several weeks or even a few months before that actually dries up. But once it does dry up, it's going to be a massive impact on the regime's revenue and the Iranian economy. All right. So, it's going to hurt Iran's economy, but it's also going to harm everyone else's as well, right? This has implications that are not just one way. Well, with the blockade, essentially what Trump is doing is making sure Iran feels the financial pain in addition to the rest of the world, which is suffering economically from the weaponisation of energy and the blocking of the Strait of Homoos. So, before the blockade, we had about 11 to 13 percent of the world's oil offline. That increases to 13 to 15 percent with the blockade in place. So, look, it's still a massive supply disruption. And on the demand side, it's equivalent to the demand drop we saw in 2020 in the wake of COVID. So, that's the implied drop in economic activity around the world that would be needed to address this shortfall in oil supply. The difference in 2026 is the way that drop in activity is distributed around the world will be very different. Yeah. Because we weren't really driving around as much or flying anywhere during COVID. We're still going about our daily lives, aren't we, today? It's a very different time. That's right. And I think back during COVID, it was the more developed economies like Australia which did the harshest lockdowns. Whereas now, more developed economies like Australia, we actually have a greater ability to pay for fuel. So, we'll actually fare relatively better compared to more developing economies you can't pay. And they're actually going to go without even more. All right. Well, Seoul, Iran has promised to retaliate. It says, No port in the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman will be safe. Now, these are all big oil producing areas, aren't they? So, it's a pretty serious and rather scary threat. So, what's most worrying now for oil markets is if this blockade develops into the conflict restarting and Iran directly attacking oil infrastructure and oil export infrastructure like ports, which they've threatened to do. And the reason for that is if you start to see more successful attacks on oil export infrastructure, what it means is even after the war ends and the Strait of the Woods opens up, that will take months or even years to repair. So, we end up with a shortage of oil that will last much, much longer than the end of the war. And that is actually a much scarier scenario for oil markets than just a short-term temporary disruption to the Strait of the Woods, which could open up readily again once the conflict is resolved one way or another. OK, so, Sol, the world's supply of oil is under great threat. So, let's have a look now at what that means for supply here. The Prime Minister, Anthony Albanese, he's in Asia trying to shore up supply in Brunei and Malaysia this week, Singapore last week. Australia, of course, is at the front of the queue because of the strong relationship that we've built up with Singapore. But we live in very uncertain times. And just noting that supply from Singapore for us is particularly vital, isn't it? It is. Singapore is a major refining hub. They refine much more oil than they need domestically. And so, what the government needs to do here is to make sure that that fuel is available for us to buy because we are approaching crunch point now where, up until today, we're still living off the oil that left the Strait of the Woods before the war began. That's about to dry up. And what you're going to start to see is countries all over the region and around the world are going to start leaning on their political relationships, offering political favours and incentives to try and divert fuel away from Australia and to their countries. And that's why our government is engaging diplomatically now to try and fend that off and make sure that we can still compete and buy fuel on market and it's not taken away from us due to political reasons. But that can't be guaranteed, can it? Because, I mean, I know Singapore relies on our LNG, of course, so we're in a good negotiating position, if you like. But the supply just can't be guaranteed, can it, from Singapore? And by the way, the Singaporean Prime Minister did not guarantee that. He just said he hoped that the supply would continue and he would work towards doing that. But that's not a guarantee, exactly. That is correct. So Australia has leverage because right now, as difficult as the oil market is, the LNG market is an even more difficult situation and many of these countries need our LNG even more than we need their fuel. And so that gives the Australian government leverage in these discussions. But to the extent that the government is not fully successful in its diplomatic approach here, then we are going to be potentially left short. And that's why you're starting to see already some signals from the government about demand management measures being taken place in Australia. You've seen the release of the advertising campaign. The global fuel shortage is affecting us all. To keep us moving, the government has been working to secure Australia's fuel supply and has... Essentially encouraging people to be more conservation conscious and use less fuel with their cars. You know, make sure your tyres are pumped up, etc. Every little bit helps. For fuel-saving tips, visit fuelplan.gov.au. Authorised by the Australian Government, Canberra. We're also going to see measures where government employees are asked to be working from home where they can, you know, more restrictive on government travel. This is the beginning on the path towards rationing. I hope and expect we won't get to the drastic stage of having to ration fuel and forcing people in cities to go without, etc. But we're at the beginning of the steps towards that end result. The fact that the government is starting these demand management approaches and strategies is a sign that behind the scenes, despite their calm words, there is some panic in the government. They realise a shortage could come and they realise their diplomatic efforts are not being fully successful. And so they do have to prepare for the contingencies that we might end up short of fuel, particularly next month. Yeah, well, it's just spent $20 million on an ad campaign, so I guess that's not a sign of calmness. Absolutely. Well, so just lay it out for me. Chris Bowen, the Energy Minister, he says we're looking pretty good for the short term. Since this war began, not a single cargo that we have expected to arrive in Australia has failed to arrive. Any cancellations of forward orders have been replaced and more. For now, Australia's supply of liquid fuels is unimpeded, with 57 shipments en route. But overnight developments could risk supply in the near future. Does it mean ongoing concerns, you know, in June and July? Sure. But we'll continue to manage those and I'll continue to give updates. But in your view, in what month and when is crunch time? So the beginning of crunch time is in the next week or so. So the very last tankers of crude from the Middle East that left before the war are due to arrive, including in Australia, I think, in the next week. And then that's the last of them. So that's when the real shortage begins. So the real crunch is going to come later this month and particularly in May. And right now, the government has, you know, according to their reporting, we have contracted for fuel to get us through most of May. The problem is that in a time of crisis, contracting for fuel does not necessarily mean the fuel is going to arrive. So the proof is going to be when the fuel actually arrives in Australia. And in a time of crisis, we will see governments all over the world pulling strings to try and divert that contracted fuel away from us. We do need a plan for the contingency that that fuel doesn't arrive. And the stock levels that we have, they're not readily available everywhere they need to be. So the truth is you'll start to see structural shortages well before our stock levels actually reach zero. What about jet fuel? Because, of course, we are a nation of travellers. That's right. So right now, the most acute fuel shortage is in jet fuel, followed by diesel. And you're already starting to see some airports around the world. I think I've seen most recently in Italy restricting flights. This is going to be a problem for Australia. So flights is probably one of the most critical areas that should be hit first. Qantas is cutting back on some services as it reveals an expected $800 million increase to its fuel bill. The next most important or the next most critical fuel will be diesel. And this has, I think, wider ramifications for the economy because so much of Australia's rural economy, particularly in agriculture and mining, relies on diesel to operate. I don't know if you're a vegetarian or not, but if you're not, if you have a chicken burger for lunch, the chicken patty in your chicken burger, it takes a cup of diesel through the supply chain to get that chicken patty on your burger. And if you have a beef burger, it's two cups of diesel, right? That just gives you an indication fuel is required for absolutely everything in our day-to-day lives. And when it's suddenly not available, the availability of everything, including a chicken burger for lunch, and the cost of everything goes up. Now, just tell me then, Sol, before the war started, in Australia's big population centres, we were paying something like $160, $170 per litre for unleaded petrol, maybe $180 per litre for diesel. I guess what everyone wants to know is, will it return to that level at some point, or will we be stuck with these very high prices for a very long time? There's simply no unscrambling of this egg, and the market is not going to go back to the way it was prior to the war. Oil prices are not going to return back to where they were in January. Now, they can come down from their current pricing levels, but I don't think we can go back to what prices were before the war for at least a year or two, even after the war ends. People forget that this is the doomsday scenario for oil that's been war game since the 1970s, and it's now playing out. Sol Kavanick is an energy expert at MST Financial. This episode was produced by Sydney Peed and Cinnamon Nippard. Audio production by Sam Dunn. Our supervising producer is David Cody. I'm Sam Hawley. ABC News Daily. We'll be back again tomorrow. Thanks for listening.

episodes.title: How Iran is becoming Trump’s forever war
episodes.description: The peace talks failed, so now US President Donald Trump wants to further disrupt the vital oil shipping route, the Strait of Hormuz.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Fuel prices can jump overnight, energy policy can shift fast and the flow and effects reach everything from households to the wider economy. I'm Carrington Clark and on ABC Business Daily's Fuelcast, we bring you a quick update on what's happening in fuel, energy and why it matters. Every Monday, Wednesday and Friday, the ABC Business Daily team will bring you the latest in under 10 minutes. Find Fuelcast in the ABC Business Daily feed on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts. The peace talks failed. So now Donald Trump wants to disrupt the vital oil shipping route, the Strait of Hormuz, even further. A US blockade will stop ships entering or departing Iranian ports, but will it really work to bring an end to the conflict? Today, Husayna Bish from the Arab Gulf States Institute on what to expect and why this is becoming very much like a forever war. I'm Sam Hawley on Gadigal Land in Sydney. This is ABC News Daily. Music Music Music Music Music Music Marathon peace talks between the US and Iran have failed to reach a breakthrough, raising fears of a reignited war. The historic face-to-face meeting ran more than 20 hours but ended in a deadlock. J.D. Vance says he was in contact with President Donald Trump multiple times through the negotiations. We've had a number of substantive discussions with the Iranians. That's the good news. The bad news is that we have not reached the agreement. And I think that's bad news for Iran much more than it's bad news for the United States of America. Husayn, J.D. Vance, the Vice President, he has largely been missing from this war. episodes.title: Alan Kohler’s case to nationalise childcare
episodes.description: The ABC’s Alan Kohler thinks the treasurer should nationalise the childcare system and take centres out of the hands of for-profit businesses.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. When energy costs jump, everyone feels it. At the Bowser, on the Power Bill and across the economy. I'm Alan Kohler. And I'm Carrington-Clark. On ABC Business Daily's Fuelcast, we break down the latest in fuel, energy and the forces driving prices. It's a quick, clear update on what's moving, why it matters and what it can mean for your wallet and the wider economy. Find Fuelcast in the ABC Business Daily feed on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts. The ABC's Alan Kohler thinks the Treasurer should nationalise the childcare system. That is, taking it out of the hands of for-profit businesses. With lingering concerns about the quality and safety of some centres and families struggling to afford the bills, is now the time for a radical shake-up. Today, Alan on the case for change. And a childcare policy expert on whether it could really work. I'm Sydney Peed on Gadigal Land, Sydney. This is ABC News Daily. Uncertainty in cost of living pressures. The government claims it'll be its most ambitious budget to date. And Alan Kohler has one late suggestion for the Treasurer. I've got an idea for next month's federal budget, although it's probably a bit too late. Alan, you went on ABC News recently and dropped a bombshell of an idea for the federal budget to nationalise childcare and kindergarten. And make them free. I imagine you had a bit of reaction to that. Did you have any missed calls from the Treasurer? No. No. Jim Chalmers didn't ring me, but certainly got a big reaction. It was certainly... A lot of people called me a communist. But it was pretty positive. I think a lot of people believe there's a problem. And the problem isn't simply that childcare is, in my view, too expensive. Also, the private school sector, both primary and secondary, is subsidised by the government, but the subsidy is only available to not-for-profit organisations, whereas with childcare, three-quarters of them are profit-making businesses, and yet they're subsidised as well. So I think that's an inconsistency that also needs to be looked at. Okay. Well, Alan, we're going to step through this idea with you. Childcare is a huge issue for families. Just getting your kid a spot is hard, and even if you can get in, it's just so expensive. So how big a change would this be? Oh, well, I think it would be massive. And I do think it's connected to housing affordability, too, because the fact that house prices are now more than twice the relationship to incomes that they were 25 years ago, that's changed the whole dynamics of running a household, so that the mortgage is now much more, and quite often, whether or not both partners in a family want to work, they have to work because they need to pay the mortgage. So suddenly, there's been a massive change in the way households operate. And of course, if you both work, then you've got to get childcare if you've got kids under five. There is a subsidy, obviously, and it can be 80% of the cost for low-income families, but the means test tapers off pretty quickly. And so if you're a middle-class family earning a reasonable salary, you're not getting much subsidy, if any, and because you've probably got a million-dollar mortgage, you're in strife. The two costs together are really crippling. Well, let's step through exactly how this scheme would work in your mind. You've done some of the numbers. Let's talk about the big one. The government would have to buy out these operators to get this idea over the line. It would cost tens of billions of dollars, wouldn't it? It would. I sort of had a stab at 50 or 60 billion. That was a pretty wild guess. I took one of the operators, looked at their market share and looked at their market value. I think it's roughly correct. Then the question is, well, how do you finance the acquisition of the childcare operators in the wild and crazy event that it was actually nationalised? And I thought, well, they could issue childcare bonds to super funds. Just explain a bit, how does the childcare bonds that super funds could invest in work? Just explain that a bit more. Oh, well, the government issues bonds now to finance its deficit. They're IOUs, effectively, that pay interest. And the interest rate on those bonds at the moment, the 10-year maturity bonds, is about 5%. That would cover the cost of buying them. And then you've got to run them. You know, at the moment, if you subtract the profits that they're making, there's probably 15 to 20 billion in actual cost of running them. And I'm saying, well, you know, if it was free, a lot more people would use it. So the cost would probably increase to, I don't know, 30 billion. The cost of running them and paying the interest on the bonds would be in the order of 30 to $35 billion a year, half of which is covered by the cost of the subsidy now. And, well, the other half, I'm saying, consider that to be an investment. So the government would run the childcare centres that employ the staff as public servants, I presume. It sounds a bit expensive, but as you say, you think it could be viewed as an investment. So just explain that a bit more. What's the case for that? Well, the case simply is, at the moment, what they're doing is subsidising private companies' shareholders. You know, I don't think that's a very good way to go, but there we go. That's just the way it's grown up. So owning the centres themselves would make it more of a state system. I mean, just simply extending the provision of public education to kids under five. I don't think it's particularly radical to do that. You know, we currently have a state education system for people, you know, between five and 18. I'm just trying to get people's minds a bit focused on this problem. Well, just on that issue of nationalising, you know, what does history tell us about the quality of services that taxpayers receive when something is privatised? Because, I mean, we haven't seen many examples of services that have been nationalised or re-nationalised, really. No, in fact, what we've seen is lots of things being privatised. Obviously, Qantas, Commonwealth Bank, Telstra, are they better now than they were? I don't know. I'll leave that up to their customers to decide. It is generally felt as a truism among economists that private sector does things better than the government. And, you know, that's possibly true. Competition certainly works to improve things. And, you know, there is competition between childcare centres at the moment. But, look, there are problems with safety, child safety in these centres. You know, I think that there are question marks around the quality of the childcare centres as they are. And I think it's patchy. Let's face it. I don't know whether you or people you know have got experience with childcare centres, but my experience with grandchildren is that some of them aren't that great and some of them are fantastic. Right. Well, we know the Prime Minister does want to do more on expanding access to childcare. These are the building blocks of a world-class, universal early education system. Getting fees down for families, getting wages up for workers, getting more places for children, more centres... So what do you think, Alan, what are the chances of Anthony Albanese hearing this idea of yours and getting to work on implementing it? Oh, zero, I'd say. Right. I don't want anyone to get the idea that I think it's going to happen. I think the days of nationalising things are well and truly over. I mean, I suppose I was just trying to draw attention to what clearly is a problem. There has been a Productivity Commission report on it, and they've recommended lifting the subsidy to ease the cost of living problems for people. In a way, that just further entrenches the problem to some extent. I think they're a bit stuck, really. I don't think there is the prospect of a big change. So I do think that probably what will happen is they'll just sort of fiddle with the subsidy a bit and help people out. But there's a limit to what they can do because they're trying to reduce the budget deficit. Well, Alan, we're going to see what a childcare policy expert thinks about this idea. So thanks very much. They'll hate it. They'll hate it. Ah, well, let's see. Thanks so much for stepping us through. Righto. My name's Elizabeth Hill. I'm Professor of Political Economy and Deputy Director of the Australian Centre for Gender Equality and Inclusion at Work at the University of Sydney.
