episodes.title: Former South Korean president sentenced to jail
episodes.description: Former South Korean president Yoon Suk Yeol is sentenced to five years in jail over crimes relating to his failed attempt at imposing martial law in the country.
episodes.transcript: Former South Korean President Yoon Song-yeol has been sentenced to five years in jail over crimes relating to his failed attempt at imposing martial law in the country. Kyung Moon-hwang is a professor with the Korea Foundation at the Australian National University. What do you make of the five-year sentence? This is the first of four charges against him. Well, I personally think that the seriousness of all of his crimes, of course, they were all centered on his botched attempt to impose martial law and to essentially install himself as a petty little dictator. The verdict was correct, but the sentence was much too light. It was half of what was requested by the prosecution. And given the seriousness and the terrible severity and outcomes and consequences of what he did, it seems to be a very light sentence. Although it is just the beginning, he has many, many trials coming up for countless charges, including the most severe one in about a month, which is his leading the insurrection. And so I doubt that he is going to ever leave jail the rest of his life. But this first verdict, I think it was a bit disappointing in that it was not as large of a sentence as it should have been. Professor, can you take me through what actually happened when he announced this martial law? I recall it happening and it was just, it was so chaotic. I don't think anyone knew what was going on at the time. Well, it was just such a shock that this country that had achieved democratization even more than 45 years earlier, anyway, that it all of a sudden had this man declaring martial law, taking the country back to the battle days of the dictatorship. And so I think it was the shock more than anything else that was the prevailing sentiment at the time. And then, of course, the legislator quickly moved to reject and overturn that martial law declaration within a couple of hours. And that night then was just an extraordinary evening. And everything that has come about afterwards has been really a reflection of the polarization of the country in so many ways. Although it has, of course, also driven that polarization even further. But what has come out in the meantime has been just as concerning as what started the whole thing. And that is this extraordinary, crazy declaration of martial law by Jung. And as you mentioned, four trials all in all, and prosecutors will be seeking the death penalty ultimately. How likely is that? Well, I think that's much more of a symbolic gesture. South Korea, even though it has not formally or legally abolished the death penalty, has not implemented an execution in many, many years. And so it's really not a possibility. But as the prosecutor said a few days ago, the point is that this request for the death penalty is a reflection of the severity, the utmost severity of the crime itself. And so even if he is found guilty and sentenced to death, there's almost no chance that it will be carried out. But most likely he will, of course, spend the rest of his life in jail unless somehow he is pardoned later on. But they're working on ways to prevent that from happening legally. That is Kyung Moon Hwang, who is a professor with the Korea Foundation at the Australian National University. And of course, of course, of course, of course.

episodes.title: How the US seized Russian oil tanker fits into Trump's plan for Venezuela
episodes.description: The US military has boarded and seized a Russian-flagged oil tanker in the North Atlantic Ocean that has been trying to evade a US blockade for weeks.
episodes.transcript: The US military has boarded and seized a Russian flagged oil tanker in the North Atlantic Ocean that has been trying to evade a US blockade for weeks. It's one of two Venezuelan linked oil tankers intercepted by the US within a few hours as the Trump administration pledges to tightly control the country's oil industry and use its blockade to pressure its government to cooperate. To help us get to the bottom of this very fast-moving and complex story, I'm joined by energy analyst Clayton Segal, who's a senior fellow for energy security at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies. Now, when it comes to Venezuela's oil, we know that they have some of the biggest oil reserves in the world, but they don't export much because they mainly deal with crude oil. What's your reaction to Marco Rubio's comments on the US plan to essentially take over Venezuela's oil, which the US had said before, but now we're hearing that term indefinitely being thrown around? Well, I think we've reached an important milestone with the new information coming from the Trump administration. After four weeks of this pretty unprecedented naval quarantine that, as the Secretary said, has been blocking Venezuela's exports, and now, of course, with the dramatic events of last weekend, we now have the outlines of a plan, of an approach from the administration on what to do with Venezuela's oil in the short term. And as Secretary Rubio said, the idea is for the United States to basically administer those oil exports and to market Venezuela's oil production to the international market at higher prices than they have sold for during the sanctions program, in which the major buyer of Venezuelan oil, which is China, has enjoyed some very steep discounts. So now the United States apparently is going to be taking Venezuelan oil and on its own volition, marketing it to the international seaborne market. We'll see what kind of demand there is in the marketplace for that Venezuelan crude. What happens to current contracts in place? I know we're talking about the future and how the US will manage this, but Venezuela already has contracts to export oil to a number of countries, I understand, including China, Iran and Russia. What's the status of those contracts now? China has a stake, a footprint in Venezuela's oil sector, and was expecting in the coming years to develop it and to reap the benefits of that position in the Venezuelan oil industry. Now it seems pretty clear that the Trump administration is determined to shut China out of that positioning and the potential benefits from it in the coming years, not only to squeeze the volumes of Venezuelan oil that were added to China, again, at those discounted prices, but also to maybe make them exit their positions on the upstream side in Venezuela in favor of maybe more involvement from American and Western companies. So I think it's a pretty big shakeup that will capture attention in Beijing, first of all, about the volumes that are going to change from Venezuela, and then longer term, looking at the geopolitical balance of power. We're also rattling the saber. We hear that rattling from Washington against other oil producers, Iran, Colombia, maybe even Mexico. So China, which has to import 11 million barrels per day, might be concerned about what's next. Yeah, having a look at what's next indeed. Now, when it comes to these two ships that have been seized, the US is accusing them of breaking US sanctions. Could you explain what those sanctions are and their function for the United States? The United States has sanctioned Venezuelan oil generally. Venezuela, like Iran and like Russia, has had to rely on this so-called shadow fleet to move its oil, to transport its oil to market, and get around those sanctions and get around the enforcement authorities. But in the most part, it has succeeded in choking off those oil exports. segments.text: The US military has boarded and seized a Russian flagged oil tanker in the North Atlantic Ocean
that has been trying to evade a US blockade for weeks.
It's one of two Venezuelan linked oil tankers intercepted by the US within a few hours
as the Trump administration pledges to tightly control the country's oil industry
and use its blockade to pressure its government to cooperate.
To help us get to the bottom of this very fast-moving and complex story,
I'm joined by energy analyst Clayton Segal,
who's a senior fellow for energy security at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies.
Now, when it comes to Venezuela's oil,
we know that they have some of the biggest oil reserves in the world,
but they don't export much because they mainly deal with crude oil.
What's your reaction to Marco Rubio's comments on the US plan to essentially take over Venezuela's oil,
which the US had said before, but now we're hearing that term indefinitely being thrown around?
Well, I think we've reached an important milestone with the new information coming from the Trump administration.
After four weeks of this pretty unprecedented naval quarantine that, as the Secretary said,
has been blocking Venezuela's exports, and now, of course, with the dramatic events of last weekend,
we now have the outlines of a plan, of an approach from the administration
on what to do with Venezuela's oil in the short term.
And as Secretary Rubio said, the idea is for the United States to basically administer those oil exports
and to market Venezuela's oil production to the international market at higher prices
than they have sold for during the sanctions program,
in which the major buyer of Venezuelan oil, which is China, has enjoyed some very steep discounts.
So now the United States apparently is going to be taking Venezuelan oil and on its own volition,
marketing it to the international seaborne market.
We'll see what kind of demand there is in the marketplace for that Venezuelan crude.
What happens to current contracts in place?
I know we're talking about the future and how the US will manage this,
but Venezuela already has contracts to export oil to a number of countries,
I understand, including China, Iran and Russia.
What's the status of those contracts now?
China has a stake, a footprint in Venezuela's oil sector,
and was expecting in the coming years to develop it
and to reap the benefits of that position in the Venezuelan oil industry.
Now it seems pretty clear that the Trump administration is determined to shut China out
of that positioning and the potential benefits from it in the coming years,
not only to squeeze the volumes of Venezuelan oil that were added to China,
again, at those discounted prices,
but also to maybe make them exit their positions on the upstream side in Venezuela
in favor of maybe more involvement from American and Western companies.
So I think it's a pretty big shakeup that will capture attention in Beijing,
first of all, about the volumes that are going to change from Venezuela,
and then longer term, looking at the geopolitical balance of power.
We're also rattling the saber.
We hear that rattling from Washington against other oil producers,
Iran, Colombia, maybe even Mexico.
So China, which has to import 11 million barrels per day,
might be concerned about what's next.
Yeah, having a look at what's next indeed.
Now, when it comes to these two ships that have been seized,
the US is accusing them of breaking US sanctions.
Could you explain what those sanctions are and their function for the United States?
The United States has sanctioned Venezuelan oil generally.
Venezuela, like Iran and like Russia, has had to rely on this so-called shadow fleet
to move its oil, to transport its oil to market,
and get around those sanctions and get around the enforcement authorities.
But in the most part, it has succeeded in choking off those oil exports.
And so importing countries, particularly China,
which, by the way, was taking a full 80% of those Venezuelan oil shipments
before the quarantine, are going to have to make adjustments
and probably have to find substitute oil supplies.
Clayton Segal, who is an energy analyst and a senior fellow for energy security
at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies.

episodes.title: NRL Monday: Dragons drama and what's next
episodes.description: What is doing at the Dragons? On NRL Monday, Andrew Moore runs through a day of high drama at St George Illawarra including the sacking of Shane Flanagan, the club’s handling of the situation, and the appointment of Dean Young as interim coach.
episodes.transcript: It's time for kick-off. Welcome to NRL Monday with Andrew Moore. Insights, analysis and all you need to know in the NRL on ABC Radio and ABC Sport Digital. Yes, hello, thanks for being with us on NRL Monday. I'm Andrew Moore and very much looking forward to the next hour where your calls are welcome on 1300 361 700 or text 0467 92022. The big focus tonight is what's happening. It's in George Illawarra sacking coach Shane Flanagan. I'll have my say on all of that shortly and certainly welcome your thoughts. But as you heard in the news, Dean Young has been appointed interim coach and that's in the last, what, 45 minutes or so. Only hours after we're all told that that wouldn't be confirmed until tomorrow and we're hearing that training sessions for players have been cancelled tomorrow because of this board meeting. So I don't know. It seems like it's all a bit of a mess. But Dean Young, who did coach them on an interim basis six years ago, former player, as Adam told you in the news, he won a comp with them in 2010. He is in the hot seat for the remains of the year at least. I'm going to speak shortly with my colleague here, Matthew Elliott, to get the personal side of things when a coach is sacked, when there's constant outside speculation about your job. What's it like immediately after being fired from such a full-on and public position? Matt's lived through it all, so looking forward to that. Ruan Sims will co-host the second half of the show and the Sims family household must be a buzz of Dragons conversation. Three of them played for the club. Ashton, Corbin and Tarek will be buying and selling with Ruan, getting her thoughts on the weekend's footy. And also before the end of the show, our producer, Ralph Tucker, with his director's cut. That is, as he is our producer on the weekend's end of this show, his highlight of our weekend broadcasting. Boy, there are some good games on the weekend. Canberra holding on to beat Melbourne at Canberra Stadium in a sensational game. Melbourne has now lost five games in a row. Nathan Cleary did it again. An extra-time field goal to steer Penrith home over the Dolphins at a hot and steamy Darwin. Latrell Mitchell ran a muck as South Sydney inflicted the 11th straight loss for St George Illawarra, effectively ending the tenure of Shane Flanagan as coach. Brisbane skipper Adam Reynolds did it again. A late field goal to give his Belega team a one-point win over the West Tigers at Campbelltown. I have no idea how the Broncos are going to field a team this week against Canterbury. Michael Maguire might have to play. Prop Payne Haas suffered a medial ligament injury to his knee. That will keep him out for between six and eight weeks. He'll miss at least the start of the State of Origin series for New South Wales. Siddharth Ketani Staggs. He has a foot injury. Jesse Arthur's a high ankle tear. No idea at this stage how long they'll be missing. And then what about front rower Corey Jensen? He's in hospital having suffered a pulmonary embolism, which is a blood clot in the lungs, which sounds horrible. And he'll be out at the very least for a few weeks, probably more than that. How did they beat the West Tigers? The Sydney Roosters came from 24-12 down to beat Newcastle and a stunning effort from a very inexperienced and injury-ravaged Parramatta Eels team yesterday. What an effort to knock over Canterbury, Bankstown and very convincingly at Western Sydney Stadium. So the top eight sees Penrith on top. They lead the Warriors, West Tigers, South Sydney, Sydney Roosters, Manly Warringah. Yes, three wins in a row for Kieran Foran. They made short work of North Queensland in Townsville, Cronulla Sutherland and Newcastle. And outside the eight, we have Brisbane, Canterbury, North Queensland, Canberra, Parramatta. Melbourne is 15th, only ahead of Gold Coast and winless St George Illawarra. All right, let's get into it. Be part of NRL Monday. Call 1300 361 700. You're with Andrew Moore on ABC Radio and ABC Sport Digital. Yeah, dramatic 24 hours for St George Illawarra supporters. And if you do follow the Dragons, I would love to hear your take on it all tonight. You can text me on 0467 920 222 or call on 1300 361 700. Shane Flanagan gone as coach after the club's 11th straight defeat, losing on Saturday night to South Sydney at Stadium Australia. The club made this announcement this morning, but a number of things confuse me. So here is first of all St George Illawarra Chief Executive Tim Watsford and then Chairman Andrew Lancaster. I want to begin by confirming that Head Coach Shane Flanagan and General Manager of Football Ben Harron have departed the St George Illawarra Dragons by way of mutual agreement. The decision followed discussions between Shane, Ben and club leadership and all parties agree that time was right for a new direction in the club's football program. Changes have been made and we'll continue to evaluate changes that we need to make. We got here, we got to this position as a club and we will get out of this position as a club. Whoever takes control of this club understands that there will be a significant amount of pressure and expectation and rightly so. Our job is to get to the right solution, ensure that we've got the right person and people in charge of this organisation and we've taken great steps. The guy to my left's done a great job since we've put him into the gig. So it's about making sure you're making the right decisions for the right reasons and working on the club's success. Our fans expect success. We expect success. Now here's what I don't understand. This is what confuses me. You call a media conference this morning but without naming a new coach or an interim coach. Again, it was only in the last hour that Dean Young has been appointed after a pretty confusing afternoon. Now remember when Manly Ringer sacked Anthony Seabold, the news came out on a Friday night that he was gone. Then Jason King and the Manly side held a media conference on the Saturday morning and that's when they announced Kieran Foran was the coach. They seem to have all their ducks in a row and Dragon's not so much the case. And next, this was a mutual decision. I'm not sure anyone would believe that. Someone had to speak first. Either Andrew Lancaster said to Shane, sorry mate, we're letting you go. Or Flano said to Andrew Lancaster, sorry mate, I'm out. Now if that was the case, Shane Flanagan simply resigned. Otherwise he was sacked. Now should he have been sacked? Probably. This team has lost 11 games in a row and like I said a number of times over the past week or so, Shane Flanagan knows how to coach. He's won an historic premiership with Cronulla Sutherland in 2016. The Sharks won an only title. But it seems where he missed up big time is the construction of the roster. In my view, it is a wooden spoon roster. It just is. There is no speed in that team other than Tyrell Sloan and he's only there at fullback because Clint Gutherson is injured. Val Holmes, who I loved watching play, an outstanding player. He's become a liability. He can't defend, offers nothing in attack and they can't keep picking him. Gutherson himself, a heart and soul player. And honestly, I thought Parramatta was dumb letting him go but he hasn't had any impact on the team's goal of actually winning games. They're looking at re-signing veteran hooker Damien Cook even though Jacob Little is the best hooker at the club. A major signing this year was Daniel Atkinson from Cronulla Sutherland. Terrific player but he has not been very good. And Kyle Flanagan. Look, I feel for Kyle because the criticism of him is way over the top and wrong because despite what some may tell you, it is not all his fault. But the absolute fact is the Dragons cannot and will not win any games with Atkinson and Flanagan in the halves. There are players in the forward pack who just shouldn't be in first grade every week. How are they getting picked week after week when they cannot win a game and if the answer is we just don't have the depth? Well, that's another strike against the roster construction. Nowhere near good enough. And I do feel for you Saints fans. The board cannot escape criticism and that includes the chairman. They're ultimately the people to sign off on player contracts. History shows coaches should not have too much power when it comes to all of this. I mean, look at Des Hasler going back. Brian Smith, not a good idea. But again, it is the board who signs off on all of these decisions. And Andrew Lancaster, the chairman of a team in total disrepair and who has just sacked the coach. Now listen to this. Is he blaming the media? There's been a lot of media coverage over the Dragons these past few weeks. A lot of it absolutely deserved. Some of it poor and some of it about personal agendas. I've been in media longer than most. Our coverage of this great game, of this great club, should be better. Readers, viewers and listeners do deserve better. Yeah, he's been involved in the media for over 30 years and very successfully, mind you, running the Wynn Corporation. But I've got to say, having been around in this game for 40 years, the Dragons normally get good publicity. Shane Flanagan has many mates in the media who have done right by him as much as they can. None of this situation is the fault of the media. It's the fault of the coach, the playing group and the board. All right, that's my rant. I'm keen to hear from you. Text 0467 92022. Especially you Dragons fans, what are your thoughts on how this has played out? Do you agree with the decision to replace Shane Flanagan as coach? Who do you want as the replacement full-time? We know it's Dean Young in the interim. The last two Dragons coaches have been very experienced but have not worked out. I'm talking about Anthony Griffin and now Flano. Prior to that, it was club legend Paul McGregor with no first grade coaching experience. So what are you looking for in your next coach? In the names I've heard and read and there's been a million of them, some particularly far-fetched, Ben Hornby would do for me. And remember, the club has a massive game to prepare for. The Anzac Day clash against the Roosters on Saturday at the Sydney Football Stadium. The last win for the Saints was in round 23 last year. Ironically, against Shane Flanagan's premiership winning team, Cronulla. And here we are up to round eight in 2026. What a mess. Got something on your mind? Call Andrew now on 1300 361 700. This is NRL Monday with Andrew Moore on ABC Radio and ABC Sport Digital. Well, look, a person within our ranks with plenty of coaching experience is someone who played for the Dragons. He loves the club, but he coached Canberra, Penrith and the Warriors in the NRL. He's seen it all. He was dumped from the Warriors in kind of weird circumstances. Remember Penrith when he was about to get the sack, we all were told, after a night game at Penrith and then he entered the press conference. No one wanted to ask him a question, so he made that choking signal with the tie, faced a board meeting the next day, but did emerge still as coach of the Panthers. He's been with our rugby league coverage on the ABC since 2015 and can offer a great perspective on all that's happened with his beloved St. George Illawarra Dragons. Matthew Elliott, how are you going? Oh, Andrew, I've got a few tears in my eyes, but nothing like a tumultuous day in rugby league. I know. Andrew, just I want to dig inside, you know, how the sausage is made for a sec. How is life as a coach when your team can't win for love nor money? The outside noise gets really loud about the coach's future. Does it become loud internally? What are those days or weeks like when you can almost see the writing on the wall or don't you? Well, you tend to just focus on your job, I must admit with that. And I think the only time I really experienced that was at Penrith when you sort of mentioned that timeframe there, Andrew, the interesting timeframe that I went through. And yeah, not the amount of games that Paul Flannoy had to endure either, but you really focus on the young athletes that you've got in front of you on a daily basis because if you don't genuinely care for them, you shouldn't be there anyway. So, yeah, I didn't find that too big a distraction. It was more the distraction on the players and yourself that you were concerned about. So, what's it like when the day after that game at Penrith, you had to front the board? I remember interviewing you after you emerged as coach to the surprise of so many outsiders looking in. What is that like when you have to face the board? Are you in there defending your job and why you should stay? Is it that simple? I'd like to say no, but it is that simple, yes. And I guess what you're doing is rather than defending yourself, it's the approach that you're taking with the club and the trajectory that you're taking the club on that you're talking to the board about. And again, it just depends on what the conversations you've had prior because I told them that prior to that, at the beginning of that year, that this was going to be a difficult year because there was a big transition going on and stuff like that. So, it wasn't as though this came out of the blue. I don't know what conversations Flano had prior, but they said there were ongoing conversations apparently. So, a decision is made, you're gone, the coach is gone. What's the next few days or weeks like? It's really hard, Andrew. It genuinely is really hard because you go to work every day with a bunch of young people that want to get better every day. And even though some probably haven't looked like they're doing that, you're really invested in the relationships. It's such a special environment. So, I found that really tough. And the next tough thing is, in all of it, the only thing that you can do is take responsibility for what you need to do better. And I must admit, I went through a fair bit of denial prior to that, blaming other people, walking around like a victim. So, I guess we all respond to those things in an individual way. But it's not until you actually sit down and go, OK, what is it that I can take responsibility for out of this circumstance so I can actually do something about it? I've said this often. This roster at the Dragons is not good. To me, it's a wooden spoon roster. But the player retention hasn't been good. The development of young players has not been very successful. How much say or power should a head coach have in terms of rosters, whether that's retaining players or bringing some in? Oh, the fundamental say, you know, Andrew. And also, you know, the pathway system that I heard about getting a little bit of a rap is certainly another thing that you just have to look. Look at Penrith, young players come in from their team or if you want to look at Melbourne or other clubs that have had continual success. The quality of young players, it's not about the amount. There's some great young players, you know, in the area from, you know, St. George all the way down into the Illawarra that I don't believe that that has been done in the way that, you know, represents the club the way it needs to be. That's for sure. But there's a lot of things in play. There's no doubt about that. I'm speaking with three-time NRL coach and our colleague here on ABC Sport, Matthew Elliott, former Dragons player. Has this joint venture just been a dismal failure over the last 26, 27 years? I think, you know what? Can I, I'll take the club's stance on this. Let's not call it a joint venture, but also let's look at the amount of success over the last decade because like a decade's a fair time in rugby league, isn't it? There hasn't been a great deal. All right. And then what's the common denominator? Of course, it's not coaches. So there's, there's got to be a common denominator. And at some point, you know, the board, you know, I use the word responsibility at, you know, earlier in our conversation, the board needs to look at what are the decisions we're making and how do we need to make them better? Because there's a bit of evidence, you know, that they haven't been doing the, you know, the right thing around the decisions they've been making at a board level because that's where primarily the decisions are coming from. So Matthew, you love this club. What, what is, I mean, you just hear gibbering with me on the radio, but what advice would you give to the club in general about how to, how to write this really deeply sunken ship? Well, I got the opportunity to work there a couple of years ago as well, Andrew. And the first thing, yeah. And the fact that they're all in one venue, it's not a split because a lot of the time the administrative staff working in Coggera, the footy staff were working in Wollongong. That's no longer the case, but you've got to create a foundation of an organisation. All the great organisations. If you work at the Melbourne Storm or you work at Penrith or, you know, the club, everyone feels involved in that organisation. You don't work there. You get to go to that club every day and contribute. And I think that's the first thing is creating a culture that, you know, where success isn't optional. That's the first thing I think needs to happen. And the decision makers around that need to work out how to do that in a way that works, you know, particularly for that organisation. And at the moment, you know, and this might sound like I'm being a bit harsh, but at the moment, there's a fair bit of evidence that that's not been happening. And if all that rests on the head coach, just get used to failing. Because if you're expecting the culture of the organisation to be created just by the head coach and not by the whole organisation, that's a major issue for the club. And I think that's a really key area that needs to be developed, along with, as I've already said, about the young talent that's coming into the organisation organisation also needs to be nurtured in a way that, you know, people are stealing kids off you rather than kids leaving you and going, you know, I learnt something that I never learnt when I was at the Dragons. All right, Matt Elliott, I appreciate your insights for a tough time for your club. But I look forward to chatting to you about this again when we're at the footy on Thursday night at Leichhardt for West Tigers Canberra. See you then, mate. Can't wait, buddy. All right. And actually, Matty's coming in here next Monday night as my co-host. 0467 920 222. Evening, Andrew. I don't believe the Dragons can blame depth with their New South Wales Cup team coming second. I'm just glad focus is off my tiger pies from Filthy Phil. Now, they're going all right, you almighty West Tigers. episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. ABC Sports coverage of the NRL Premiership. NRL Saturday. On your radio, ABC Sport Digital Radio. And ABC Listen. Can our panel of ABC Rugby League experts handle six questions in three minutes? Can they avoid getting stuck on the fence? And can the referee, Andrew Moore, avoid going into the bunker? It's time for Six Again. Now I'm going to ask you boys two separate questions about the same issue. Luke Lewis, Shane Flanagan will lose his job coaching the Dragons on Tuesday. Why should that happen? Oh, he definitely will lose his job. I think it will happen purely because there's no runs on the board. But it has to happen, I think, because he's probably built the side that aren't delivering. He's probably pulled those leadership guys that he wanted in there. And they're probably the worst players in their team at this particular point in time. So I reckon that's what it's going to come down to. They're going to look at it. John Gibbs, Shane Flanagan will keep his job coaching the Dragons on Tuesday. Why should he? Well, he should because I don't know whether much is going to be gained by getting rid of someone in the short term. I'd like to be in and around the team to know exactly what is going on in there because it's not good. If you look at results specifically, then he wouldn't. But there's got to be other things at play. And everything needs to be taken into account. So that's why he should. Luke Lewis, what's the bigger injury issue for the Broncos in your view? Payne Haas or Rhys Walsh? Oh, gee, that's a big one. I think Payne Haas is a massive one. But I'm going to go Rhys Walsh for X Factor. And just try scoring ability and the way that he played in the grand final. If he can pull out a couple of those games while Payne Haas isn't on the field, I think Rhys Walsh could change the game and win your game. episodes.title: The Raiders are their own worst enemies
episodes.description: Back to back wins for Canberra Raiders have given great entertainment to the neutral but gun centre Simi Sasagi reckons they're making life harder for themselves than it needs to be.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. ABC Sports coverage of the NRL Premiership. NRL Saturday. On your radio, ABC Sport Digital Radio. And ABC Listen. Luke Lewis, Michael Kariannis, I'm Andrew Moore here on NRL Saturday on ABC Sport. We raved about Simi Sasangi in Perth last week. We raved about Simi Sasangi last night. We've raved about him in games. Canberra has lost. He's been outstanding playing in the centres for Canberra. And he's on the line. Simi, how are you going? Hey, guys. How are you? Mate, we're well. And part of the reason why we're having so much fun at the footy is watching you play. It is incredible, the turnaround from sort of Mr Utility, what do you need, Ricky? Okay, I'll fill in there, to becoming the form centre in the competition. How have you found it? No, good, bro. I'm just enjoying my footy at the moment. And it's kind of a, it's pretty, it's a fuzzy feeling, man. You know, did a lot of training in different positions and I found myself in centre. Well, it didn't take long for you to have an impact last night. You scored this try in just the sixth minute of the game. Sanders to Strange. Then away through hands it goes. Making half a break with a one-handed pass. Away to Simi Sasangi for the try. That was brilliantly done by Ethan Strange. And it's a try to Simi Sasangi. Billy Walker blows that horn and Canberra is in front. They did that pretty easily. Great set up by Strange and the finish from Simi Sasangi. Yeah, you guys are off to a great start, Simi. 12-0 in no time. And then I think it's played you guys this year. You play so well for patches and then make mistake after mistake for a little while to allow the opposition back in. Is that one of the main areas you guys need to improve upon? Yeah, we were pretty much our worst enemy in the last couple of weeks. You know, they've scored at the back of our errors. But, you know, it's definitely something we want to work on. Yeah, Simi. First of all, mate, congratulations on your form. You've been amazing to watch, especially on that right edge. But the combination with you and Strange, it looks like it's just building nicely. How's that coming along at training? You know, have you been putting a lot of work into that? Or is it just something that's just clicked? No, I think it's something we really worked on in the preseason. You know, Strange is a good player. And I'm kind of just reacting off him. And we kind of just bounce off each other. What's your best position, mate? Do you love playing in the centres? Or is it in the back row? Or do you like that utility role? Well, at the moment, I'm kind of enjoying centre at the moment. I've definitely played a lot of back row and middle. But I think at the moment, centre is probably something I'm enjoying at the moment. Well, you should be enjoying it because you're killing it out there. Now, do you have any thoughts about, obviously, rep football, the way that you're playing? Because I tell you what, you are the informed centre at the moment. And there'll be a lot of talks about playing State of Origin. Is that something that you're interested in? I don't even know if I'm manageable with Origin. I don't think so. That's what I was going to ask you that. Because, obviously, you were signed by the Knights at a young age. When did you come across to Australia? I came over too late. I came over when I was 16. Okay. So you just missed the cutoff by a few years. Yeah, he goes. Just change the date of birth. Look, you've got him all excited about playing Origin now. It's something he can't do. Well, I got a bit excited too watching him play. So, sorry, mate. No. Take us inside the sheds at a half-time. We saw Corey, obviously, give away that penalty in possession. And Melbourne hurt you after that. And it looked quite animated in the sheds between Ricky and Corey. What was that like? I was all right, bro. Our talk was pretty calm, actually. You know, we just needed to get back to playing our style of footy. And I thought we did that in patches in the first half. And, you know, like I said, we're our worst enemy. You know, they scored two tries at the back of our areas. But that was something we can control. And that was, you know, it was something we can fix. You're talking about being your own worst enemy. You're like that in Perth as well, where you look like you're going to run away with the game. And then South came back. Like, how do you guys address those sort of moments within games at the moment where you're sort of allowing teams to come back? Yeah, I think just in those patches, we get a little bit frustrated. I think we just need to stay calm. We get a bit frantic. And that's something we need to work on going forward, eh? It is fun to watch from a distance. I'm sure it's not as fun when you're on the field or in the coach's shoes. But Hudson Young, he's actually copped a two-game suspension for a high tackle late last night. I've seen that. Yeah, which is a shame. His form is incredible. As someone who's played, you know, plenty of back row, what have you seen from Hudson Young over the last, say, 18 months that have even driven him further than where he was as a player? Yeah, his form is unreal. He's a freak, man. The stuff he can do. I think he just plays a lot of confidence here. You know, the stuff he does with the ball, man, everyone just kind of just – I feel like I'm in the grandstand just watching too. But, no, he's a freak, man. I spoke to you after the game, mate, last week in Perth and just a choir week's try. And, you know, you threw him the pass out of dummy half. How many times did you guys watch that during the week in video? Oh, no, he'll be loving it too. He'll be watching it too. No. It was pretty crazy, right? Like you said – Yeah, it's crazy. There's nothing to do with the ball, man. It's just – like I said, man, I feel like, you know, when Hudson does their stuff and when Kyle runs the field, man, he feels like he's just a little kid in the stands just watching. Well, I had that feeling last night watching him up against Sufa Longo. He's an exciting machine for Melbourne. Yeah, no, he's a freak, man. He's another freak too, man. There's nothing to do with the ball. I think you're getting close to that description, Simi. The way you're playing is unreal at right centre. It really is. And I'm not saying it to embarrass you. We've all been talking about it. And it just seems that you're a natural, perfect centre. And probably you and Herbie Farnworth might be the form centres in the game. Is there a centre that you based how you played that position on? Someone that you admired in the centres? Not really. I kind of just want to play my own footy. You're just going out and doing it. Yeah, I think so. I'm just enjoying my footy at the moment. I play a lot of confidence and probably a fan at the moment, I guess. Well, you're playing a little bit differently to how chilled you sound on the phone, Simi. Congratulations on the form and a couple of wins. I tell you what, a good challenge coming up through the week. Is it Thursday night, I think, at Leichhardt against the West Tigers? As you'd be well aware, they're playing great footy. Yeah, yeah. Tigers in good form, but we need to be on the A game. It should be a good game, man. Yeah, can't wait. All right, Simi, thanks so much for joining us. Well done. No, thanks for having me, guys. Awesome. Good fun. Simi Sasangi, Canberra Raiders right centre, who's been just braining them. And just sounds like the most calm, relaxed dude of all time. He reminds me, his voice reminds me exactly of Britton Nickerar. Yeah, right. When I was sitting there going, geez, he sounds like a Britto. But he is playing outstanding football. He seems like a very humble kind of guy. Didn't know really how to sort of take his raps that he was getting, but he deserves it. He's been amazing on that right edge. And I thought he was brilliant in the semi. He played a semi-final game last year, I think he filled in at 5'8". And he was outstanding in that position as well. So for me, watching him and looking at what he can do on a footy field, he's just a natural footballer. He just gets out there, plays, happy to have the ball in his hand. He's got good footwork. He's strong. He's willing to put his head anywhere out there to make tackles for his team. So, you know, he's probably thriving out there on that right edge. He's got a great little footballer inside him in Ethan Strange. And that combination, I feel like that combination is getting super strong. And it's only, what, round seven. I feel like as that combination goes, the more footy they play at the back end of this year, it's going to be lethal sight. Let's talk about the footy last night. And first of all, at Canberra Stadium, terrific crowd on a cool night. 17,321, a topsy-turvy first half. Canberra led 12-0 after nine minutes and looked like Melbourne weren't in the game at all. And then Corey Horsburgh gave away a dumb penalty for having a crack at the referee whilst in possession. And that turned things around. Melbourne went to halftime with a 16-12 lead. And then a really entertaining second half. Canberra held on to win 26 points to 22. And among the try scorers for Canberra in the second half, their outstanding 5-8, Ethan Strange. Pass away Hudson Young. He gets a two-handed ball away to Starling. And then back to the right it goes. Heavy defence now. And off the way back to Hudson Young. He dummies his way into the defence. McDonald holds him up there with Grant eight metres away. Starling sends the ball right smithies to Sanders. Then he got the pass away to Sasangi. Passed one and two. Oh, what about that? Then he throws the pass. What an incredible try for Strange. Semmy Sasangi. Simply the best. Great effort by Sasangi. Strange finishes it off. Amazing skills by Canberra's new right setter. He is an absolute gun in the setters. Alan Tung gave three points though in the ABC Player of the Year to Hudson Young who was brilliant again. But he has copped a two-game suspension for that late high tackle on Suha Falongo in the 78th minute. Two points. Semmy Sasangi in one point to Melbourne's brilliant fullback Suha Falongo. It was a really entertaining second half, Michael Cariannis. Canberra though now have won a couple in a row. They're imperfect. But they are fun to watch when it clicks. Yeah. And a big win against Melbourne Stormside has a lot of struggling. But yeah, Canberra have just... They still have that touch of class, don't they? That we saw it at times last year. We saw it last week with Kaya Week scoring arguably the try, the individual try of the season with that runaway, what, 98-metre effort. And then you mentioned it last week in the call as well, Semmy Sasangi, that he was the form centre of the competition. And it's hard to argue with you at the moment, Andrew. The way he's just, you know, he's probably played a lot of halves, a lot of back row since making his debut for Newcastle a few years ago. But he's been so lethal on an edge and his timing with his passing has been first rate. So he's added an extra dimension to their attack that probably wasn't there last year. And we'll talk to Semmy Sasangi very shortly. So, Louis, I'll ask you about Melbourne. And I think we're all in lockstep with you. It is almost impossible to see this current team making the finals. And that's now five losses in a row for them. Yeah, it's very hard to watch. I had the red button. I had the cough. But sorry about that. What are you laughing at, Andrew? I'm not going to interrupt you anymore. The Melbourne Storm, it's hard to watch. You expect them to bounce back. But for me, they're lacking so much confidence at the moment. The best player in their team is Suofalongo at fullback. And it's obviously really his first rule season. He's playing busted at the moment as well. But for me, Kim Munster, he just looks so under the weather at the moment. I don't know what it is or if he's playing injured. But he's just doing the little things I've never seen him do. Like miss simple tackles, one-on-one tackles. He's not in sync with his group on the same edge. He's trying to do everything by himself. And I reckon that just comes down to the confidence. When you get your confidence down, you're not working in the team. You're just trying to come out and solve the problem on your own. There's a fair bit going on there. But they're just off with everything. I feel like their skill levels are off. Their fitness looks not superior to most sides. Or something that we're so used to seeing from the Melbourne Storm. So I just can't see where their next win's coming from. Obviously, every game's going to get closer to a win. And you know they're going to win again. But the way that they're playing, I don't know what to say. Like I'm in shock. Like this is the first time I've ever seen Melbourne since I've been playing be anything like this. Well, Canberra did make mistakes after the lead. Some of the things they do are inexplicably bad compared to when they're playing great passages of play where they look unbeatable. But then they make such silly mistakes. And I thought, MC, that was playing Melbourne into form. Because when they strung those three tries together over a 14-minute period, they looked like Melbourne. They did. They did. But I'm with Louis. I've got major concerns around Cam Munster's form at the moment. And as Louis said, like, Sulphur Longo is the most likely option. Harry Grant's still dangerous out of dummy half. And when you've got someone like that, that's, like you said, been in the game, you're just going to do everything you can. And it's a fresh start as well for us. Obviously, there's a lot of external pressure with Sieves at the start from the media. So since Sieves has left and Foz has taken over, there hasn't really been much chat about how should we go over the last couple of weeks. And I think it's just been mentally refreshing for the whole group. Yeah, I could imagine. The other thing is to, how does it feel, I suppose, being coached by someone that you played against last year? Is that a bit weird? Because I know I never experienced anything like that. I thought, you know, last year you've probably been doing video on how to target Kieran Foran's, you know, flaws in the game. So has that been weird? Yeah, it has been, mate. We've actually watched a couple video clips throughout the week on the teams that we've played. And there has been clips from the Titans up against that team. And Foz has been in the picture for a couple of days. So I've had a couple of moments in the video room when I was like, oh, that's weird. Like Foz is in these clips that he's presenting to our team now as the head coach. So, yeah, it has been a little bit different, a little change up, which is, you know, very different to having someone that hasn't played the game as a coach with Sieves. So a little bit different there. What about the banner? Is the banner real there? We've obviously, you know, because he's still so fresh and he's like a player. And, you know, when the boys come in, you always, you know, you take the mickey out a little bit and have a bit of fun. You got that sort of going there with Foran at the coaching realm there? Yeah, I've probably got to build a better relationship with Foz at the minute. I'm not too sure if I can get into him and be cheeky. Like, obviously, it took me a little while with Stick to be able to rip into him when I'm in a good mood, but then also he'll dish it backwards. Whereas I think Foz is just too nice of a person. He's not going to dish you out a whole lot. So I might have to keep probing a little bit to see what I can find or play some pranks in his little office upstairs or something. You mentioned the couple of changes that he made compared to where you guys are at under Anthony Seab. But what are one or two subtle changes that Foz sort of wanted you guys to focus on? Yeah, he just wanted us to be physical and compete. He said, you know, we've got a good side here. We know what we've got. If you're being physical and going after the contest with your defence, but then also when you've got the ball, if you're running to be genuine to try and find a line break, that's going to do our team wonders. And it was just more of a defensive focus about just being connected. And if we can do those things for longer periods of time, we're going to win more games than we're going to lose. So it's only been a very simple focus. And it probably sounds stupid to the people that watch football, but they're like, what do you mean by being physical when you defend and run? And that's the whole part of the game. But it's about being able to do that in longer periods of time and being able to concentrate and just getting off to a fast start. Obviously, the last couple of weeks, we've been able to start the games pretty well physically. And then that set us up for a good platform throughout the rest of the games. Obviously, terrible news regarding Tom Trvojevic and his hamstring. But you guys seem to regroup pretty well. What was that feeling like when he went off? And I know how vocal he is on the field. Does that mean someone like you needs to step up in that case? Yeah, well, when he actually got tackled, I just thought he got like a mad cork in his quad because it was pretty heavy contact. And obviously, Tom's a big body and he demands that. So my first thought was, oh, you know, he's just got a mad little cork in his quad. He'll be all right. And then he got up and I kind of seen him drag his foot across the grass. And I was like, oh, no, he's done his hemi, which is very unfortunate because he's someone that's so diligent. He works on his body every single day. I've never seen anything like it. It's unbelievable. And obviously, it's very sad news for Tommy. But, you know, we've got senior players in the team like me, Brooksy, Jakey Trvojevic, Hamale and Siwa that can, you know, we're the senior leaders of the team. And we just got to put the team first and make sure we're doing all those little things. And then we've got a pretty handy replacement. When you lose someone like Turbo, he's irreplaceable. But the next best in our team is obviously Tolu. And Tolu can come up with some special plays in games. And he did that on the weekend. You know, he usually is an attacking weapon. But on the weekend, I think the best part of his game was all his defensive efforts. He saved a couple of tries. And it's a lot different going from sitting out in the centres, trying to cruise into all the hard work that you have to do as a fullback. Like when teams are on your try line, you go on sideline to sideline. And with Tolu, he's an explosive power athlete. He's not someone that's built for endurance. But I thought he was our best player the other night. Yeah, he's done some incredible things so far this year. And the first test without Turbo comes next Sunday. The game will be calling at Brookie when you play Parramatta, a big rivalry matchup. But I'd imagine everyone's going to see the importance of this. Stamping your authority back at Brookvale Oval. Yeah, that's one thing that we've already spoken about. Like I said, we've had three games at home. I've been very disappointed with three losses to start the year. That's not what any team wants. We want to try and make it a fortress for the rest of the year. And our fans probably deserve a good performance. So we'll be doing everything we can this week, like we have been the last couple of weeks, to put the team first, to make sure that we're doing everything we can properly, at training, with video sessions, working on your body, and whatever Foz wants to do game plan-wise, so we can give our fans a good game of football and hopefully get our first win at home. And we've caught Canberra the last couple of weeks. We were in Perth last week, the three of us, and I was in Canberra last night, and they've had a couple of high-scoring, narrow, you know, heart-wrenching victories. Have you been keeping much of an eye on your old team? Yeah, I have been, mate. I've obviously got heaps of close friends down there, especially Zach Hosking. I talk to him every single week, mate. So a little bit different, obviously, sitting at the couch, you know, cheering him on. And my missus gets up to me all the time, because a little fella, obviously, born down there, and he's got a little Raiders jersey. So every time they play, I put the Raiders jersey on him, to watch Uncle Zach and a couple of the boys. And she's like, get that crap off. So, yeah, obviously, you know, the things that the club down there done for me, obviously, given me the opportunity to come up here. And, you know, my games obviously evolved under stick. So, you know, there's no sourness or bitterness towards the club. I still love all the guys down there, and even talk to stick often. So hopefully they can keep winning games, but not go too good. Well, the only sad news is you're now going to have to tackle Hudson Young at some point rather than offload to him. He's on fire, even though he's just got to suspension. Jamal, always good to chat to you, mate. We look forward to calling this renewed Manly Warringah team on Sunday against Parramatta. Well done on the last few weeks. Thanks for joining us. No worries, fellas. Appreciate it. Discover more great ABC podcasts, live radio and exclusives on the ABC Listen app.

you scraped past the Dragons in a bit of a scrappy game in Wollongong,
and then you were far too good for the Cowboys in Townsville.
So things have gone beautifully.
Was there a time either at training or on the field where you thought,
OK, this is the team I've joined.
We're starting to click.
Yeah, well, there was probably moments in the first three games that I thought,
you know, we got a bit of resilience, a bit of grit amongst the team,
but it just wasn't in long enough periods.
Like I felt as though round one when we played the Raiders,
they're a good team with a good forward pack,
and we got out to a handy lead early and then we let it go
and then we're able to fight back.
So there was little moments throughout those first three games.
And then I think just the Dolphins game into the Dragons,
we just did that for longer periods of time.
And we only needed one win because football, you know,
if you're winning, it's a habit.
And then you just find a ways to win.
And then when you lose, then it's a habit as well.
So we kind of flipped those habits.
And just the one win gave the team confidence
because we know we've got a great team.
We've got so many X-factor players in our squad.
We just had to find a way to make it work.
And narrowing our focus onto those little effort areas,
we've been able to do that the last three weeks.
And when you're winning, football's fun, Ryan.
That's the main reason we play.
Well, Jamal, you've been amazing to watch.
Even last year, you were outstanding.
But I think now, the last couple of weeks,
you've been up in the 3-2-1s pretty much every week.
But the difference with Kieran Foran as a coach,
is it the way that he comes to training?
And do you think it helps because he played the game last year
and been so recent in understanding the way the game's played,
that helps with you guys the way that I suppose
he gets his messages across to you?
Yeah, definitely.
I think the best part about Foz is how he speaks.
You know, his very first speech to the team when he did take over,
it was early in the week.
And I was ready to play football then, sit in the video room.
He's just got this presence about him, the way he speaks.
He doesn't try to overcomplicate things.
And he challenges you in areas that he knows that you can deliver in.
But then also, he's got manly DNA in him.
He's been at the club for good times and bad times,
so he knows what it takes.
And when you've got someone like that, that's, like you said,
been in the game, you're just going to do everything you can.
And it's a fresh start as well for us.
Obviously, there's a lot of external pressure with Sieves at the start
from the media.
So since Sieves has left and Foz has taken over,
there hasn't really been much chat about how should we go
over the last couple of weeks.
And I think it's just been mentally refreshing for the whole group.
Yeah, I could imagine.
The other thing is to, how does it feel, I suppose,
being coached by someone that you played against last year?
Is that a bit weird?
Because I know I never experienced anything like that.
I thought, you know, last year you've probably been doing video
on how to target Kieran Foran's, you know, flaws in the game.
So has that been weird?
Yeah, it has been, mate.
We've actually watched a couple video clips throughout the week
on the teams that we've played.
And there has been clips from the Titans up against that team.
And Foz has been in the picture for a couple of days.
So I've had a couple of moments in the video room when I was like,
oh, that's weird.
Like Foz is in these clips that he's presenting to our team now
as the head coach.
So, yeah, it has been a little bit different, a little change up,
which is, you know, very different to having someone
that hasn't played the game as a coach with Sieves.
So a little bit different there.
What about the banner?
Is the banner real there?
We've obviously, you know, because he's still so fresh
and he's like a player.
And, you know, when the boys come in, you always, you know,
you take the mickey out a little bit and have a bit of fun.
You got that sort of going there with Foran at the coaching realm there?
Yeah, I've probably got to build a better relationship
with Foz at the minute.
I'm not too sure if I can get into him and be cheeky.
Like, obviously, it took me a little while with Stick
to be able to rip into him when I'm in a good mood,
but then also he'll dish it backwards.
Whereas I think Foz is just too nice of a person.
He's not going to dish you out a whole lot.
So I might have to keep probing a little bit to see what I can find
or play some pranks in his little office upstairs or something.
You mentioned the couple of changes that he made compared
to where you guys are at under Anthony Seab.
But what are one or two subtle changes that Foz sort of wanted you guys to focus on?
Yeah, he just wanted us to be physical and compete.
He said, you know, we've got a good side here.
We know what we've got.
If you're being physical and going after the contest with your defence,
but then also when you've got the ball,
if you're running to be genuine to try and find a line break,
that's going to do our team wonders.
And it was just more of a defensive focus about just being connected.
And if we can do those things for longer periods of time,
we're going to win more games than we're going to lose.
So it's only been a very simple focus.
And it probably sounds stupid to the people that watch football,
but they're like, what do you mean by being physical when you defend and run?
And that's the whole part of the game.
But it's about being able to do that in longer periods of time
and being able to concentrate and just getting off to a fast start.
Obviously, the last couple of weeks,
we've been able to start the games pretty well physically.
And then that set us up for a good platform throughout the rest of the games.
Obviously, terrible news regarding Tom Trvojevic and his hamstring.
But you guys seem to regroup pretty well.
What was that feeling like when he went off?
And I know how vocal he is on the field.
Does that mean someone like you needs to step up in that case?
Yeah, well, when he actually got tackled,
I just thought he got like a mad cork in his quad
because it was pretty heavy contact.
And obviously, Tom's a big body and he demands that.
So my first thought was, oh, you know,
he's just got a mad little cork in his quad.
He'll be all right.
And then he got up and I kind of seen him drag his foot across the grass.
And I was like, oh, no, he's done his hemi,
which is very unfortunate because he's someone that's so diligent.
He works on his body every single day.
I've never seen anything like it.
It's unbelievable.
And obviously, it's very sad news for Tommy.
But, you know, we've got senior players in the team like me,
Brooksy, Jakey Trvojevic, Hamale and Siwa that can, you know,
we're the senior leaders of the team.
And we just got to put the team first
and make sure we're doing all those little things.
And then we've got a pretty handy replacement.
When you lose someone like Turbo, he's irreplaceable.
But the next best in our team is obviously Tolu.
And Tolu can come up with some special plays in games.
And he did that on the weekend.
You know, he usually is an attacking weapon.
But on the weekend, I think the best part of his game
was all his defensive efforts.
He saved a couple of tries.
And it's a lot different going from sitting out in the centres,
trying to cruise into all the hard work that you have to do as a fullback.
Like when teams are on your try line, you go on sideline to sideline.
And with Tolu, he's an explosive power athlete.
He's not someone that's built for endurance.
But I thought he was our best player the other night.
Yeah, he's done some incredible things so far this year.
And the first test without Turbo comes next Sunday.
The game will be calling at Brookie when you play Parramatta,
a big rivalry matchup.
But I'd imagine everyone's going to see the importance of this.
Stamping your authority back at Brookvale Oval.
Yeah, that's one thing that we've already spoken about.
Like I said, we've had three games at home.
I've been very disappointed with three losses to start the year.
That's not what any team wants.
We want to try and make it a fortress for the rest of the year.
And our fans probably deserve a good performance.
So we'll be doing everything we can this week,
like we have been the last couple of weeks,
to put the team first,
to make sure that we're doing everything we can properly,
at training, with video sessions, working on your body,
and whatever Foz wants to do game plan-wise,
so we can give our fans a good game of football
and hopefully get our first win at home.
And we've caught Canberra the last couple of weeks.
We were in Perth last week, the three of us,
and I was in Canberra last night,
and they've had a couple of high-scoring, narrow,
you know, heart-wrenching victories.
Have you been keeping much of an eye on your old team?
Yeah, I have been, mate.
I've obviously got heaps of close friends down there,
especially Zach Hosking.
I talk to him every single week, mate.
So a little bit different, obviously, sitting at the couch,
you know, cheering him on.
And my missus gets up to me all the time,
because a little fella, obviously, born down there,
and he's got a little Raiders jersey.
So every time they play, I put the Raiders jersey on him,
to watch Uncle Zach and a couple of the boys.
And she's like, get that crap off.
So, yeah, obviously, you know,
the things that the club down there done for me,
obviously, given me the opportunity to come up here.
And, you know, my games obviously evolved under stick.
So, you know, there's no sourness or bitterness towards the club.
I still love all the guys down there,
and even talk to stick often.
So hopefully they can keep winning games,
but not go too good.
Well, the only sad news is you're now going to have to tackle Hudson Young
at some point rather than offload to him.
He's on fire, even though he's just got to suspension.
Jamal, always good to chat to you, mate.
We look forward to calling this renewed Manly Warringah team
on Sunday against Parramatta.
Well done on the last few weeks.
Thanks for joining us.
No worries, fellas. Appreciate it.
