episodes.title: NRL Monday: The death of the disruptor
episodes.description: NRL head of football Graham Annesley joins Andrew Moore to break down the controversial disruptor rule plus could Melbourne Storm seriously miss the finals and why are teams performing so well without their stars?
episodes.transcript: This is an ABC podcast. It's time for kickoff. Welcome to NRL Monday with Andrew Moore. Insights, analysis and all you need to know in the NRL on ABC Radio and ABC Sport Digital. Yes, hello and welcome to NRL Monday. I'm Andrew Moore. Great to be with you for the next hour talking rugby league. And there are some amazing games to talk about from round six. And how about this table? Penrith on top despite losing. They're on 10 points. And the team's rounding out the top four. You've got Wes on 10. The Warriors are North Queensland on eight. What a great and different looking top four that is. Then at South Sydney, Newcastle, Canterbury, Bankstown and the Sydney Roosters. They're all on eight points. And on the outside looking in, we've got Manly Warringah, Cronulla Sutherland, Brisbane, the Dolphins, Melbourne, Gold Coast, Parramatta and St. George, Illawarra. So from last year's finalists, the Sharks, Broncos and Storm aren't in the top eight. And while the Dragons win the start of the season has their fan base up in arms, what about the Eels? Second last on the table. And I know they have plenty of injuries, but who doesn't? Not a good enough excuse for pathetic performances like yesterday. Surely that's unacceptable for Parramatta fans. Your calls are welcome tonight on 1300 361700. And yes, Queensland listeners, you're with us live from now on 1300 361700. And you can text me on 0467 920 222. Plenty to talk about. Luke Lewis will join me in the studio for the second half of the show. Lou and I flew back from Perth late last night thanks to some wonderful delays, but had a great time at the doubleheader on Saturday. And out to dinner on Saturday night. It was a little bit like magic round in Brisbane. Different NRL jerseys were everywhere, especially Warriors and Bulldogs jerseys, curiously, because they didn't play. NRL football manager, Graeme Anersley will join me shortly to talk about this ridiculous disruptor plague in the game at the moment. Not really from the players, but the decisions around it. And Graeme Anersley says the bunker got at least two of those calls wrong on the weekend. We'll tell you who's hot and who's not. Who or what will Louie be buying and selling? And the director's cut, which is our producer, Ralph Tucker's main highlight from our NRL coverage. NRL Monday, it's 22 minutes to seven. Be part of NRL Monday. Call 1300 222 702. You're with Andrew Moore on ABC Radio and ABC Sport Digital. Boy, we so often talk about coaches under fire, don't we? Like Shane Flanagan currently. It's in George Illawarra on the back of 10 straight losses. My understanding is the Dragons don't want to sack Shane Flanagan if they can help it. But at what point does the losing streak become too much to bear? But on the other end of the scale, one month ago, Todd Payton couldn't coach. It was a bad performance or two away from looking for another job. Well, his North Queensland Cowboys have won four in a row, including Friday night's thriller over Brisbane. It's the first time, by the way, we've ever had a 35-31 scoreline. They're now in fourth place, North Queensland. Look, they should be a good team. With the likes of Jason Tamalolo, who's playing really well again. Tom Dearden, Scott Drinkwater. Young Gun, Jackson Perdue. Ruben Cotter, Reid Marnie. There's a lot of talent in that Cowboys team. They should be good. And at the moment, they are. And plenty of credit must go to Todd Payton. And people have always questioned Benji Marshall's ability to coach since he started and replaced Tim Sheens. He's had a rough couple of years. But this Tigers team is different. Still playing an exciting brand. Still imperfect. But some of their talented young players are really stepping up so far in 2026. And a couple of the veterans like Adam Dewey and Alex Twole, who looks a completely rejuvenated player, have stood up. Benji Marshall, like Todd Payton, deserves a stack of credit, don't you think? If it happens in Rugby League, you'll hear it first on NRL Monday with Andrew Moore on ABC Radio and ABC Sport Digital. By the way, the Match Review Committee has today announced charges against two players from yesterday's games. Parramatta centre Will Bensany has been fined for a high tackle on Bove for Moore. While west second rower Samuel Afainu has been fined for dangerous contact on Phoenix Crossland. Two players have been suspended from the weekend games. Penrith centre Casey McLean for one game. And Brisbane lock Patrick Carrigan for two weeks. They're going to miss him on top of the injuries they already have. Why are so many teams shining with star players on the sidelines? It's a really strange phenomenon this season. And Matt Elliott started talking about this on Thursday. Canterbury went up against unbeaten Penrith without its best player in Captain Stephen Crichton. And they won comfortably in the end out playing the Panthers for most of the game. Bronson Sherry returned from his exile and was sensational for the Bulldogs. The West Tigers yesterday thrashed Newcastle at Campbelltown without their best player arguably in Jerome Lewi. I'll tell you what, as I mentioned, Adam Dewey. Hasn't he been outstanding the last couple of weeks? The Knights were well beaten yesterday. They've been playing great footy, though, for coach Justin Holbrook without their two most expensive stars in Caelan Ponga and Dylan Brown. Brisbane almost knocked over North Queensland, even though they didn't have Rhys Walsh, Adam Reynolds or Ben Hunt. Did you see the game that half Tommy Duffy had, Thomas Duffy had for the Broncos? Almost won it against his former club. The Warriors were again without key five-eighth Luke Metcalf on Saturday night. And their season went horribly wrong when he was injured last season. He was so great for the Warriors. But since coming back, halfback Tanner Boyd has gone into his shell. On the weekend, the Warriors, they were brilliant again. Luke Metcalf wasn't there again. It's not Luke's fault. But the way these players are standing up when the stars are out is really impressive. And the point is, don't write off teams based on who's out. As Matt Elliott always tells me, focus on who's in. And it also tells me that there is so much talent in the sport not getting a regular opportunity that next year when the Perth Bears come in and in 2028 with the PNG Chiefs, the NRL is going to be just fine, I reckon. 1-300-361-700 is the number to ring. Doing the hard yards to bring you the latest in NRL. This is NRL Monday with Andrew Moore. On ABC Radio and ABC Sport Digital. On the text line 0467 920 222. As a long-suffering Tigers fan, whilst it's great to see us at the top end of the ladder, what's even better is the depth of the squad and the buy-in towards Benji Marshall. Rich, I'd take a bow. Thank you, Paul. Hi, Andrew. Which game are you calling on Saturday and Sunday? Well, Paul, you've got me on the hop here. Next Saturday, we're at St. George-O-Lewarra against South Sydney at Stadium Australia. And on Sunday, we're doing the 4 o'clock game at Western Sydney Stadium, Parramatta and Canberra. I'll run through the whole weekend a little later on, Paul. Andrew, nice to hear you every Monday. We enjoy the evening with Luke. Thank you, Dion. Good to hear from you. And Ants as well. Welcome back from Perth. Maury, hope Louie or MC didn't play tricks like hiding your phone or laptop in transit from WA to Sydney. I'm really happy my green machine won over South. You should be too, Ants. They were terrific, apart from a very nervous 10 minutes or so. And we're at the airport with the Raiders for a little bit yesterday. And every player or official we spoke to was like, oh, we thought it was gone. But Canberra won a thrilling game in the end, 36 to 34. Graham Anersley coming up shortly. The Melbourne Storm, they can't make the finals this year, can they? Can they? They look really ordinary on the weekend and they have done for a number of weeks. They're on a four-game losing streak, which is difficult to even imagine with Craig Billamere's coach. He said that he may as well have been at the pub having a few beers after that game against the Warriors. It's currently not a great roster. And while I mentioned that some teams have really lifted without star players, it seems that the Storm has lost maybe one too many players this year and others have been struggling. For example, you know, Cameron Munster. He's been struggling big time for the past couple of seasons, other than when he's captain of Queensland, of course. But when was the last time Munster had a massive influence on a game? It's been a while. And that's most definitely not because of a lack of effort. There is always that with Cam. He's ultra competitive, but I would imagine it's the cumulative effect of injuries. No Ryan Pappenhausen. What's he doing now? Did I read or see that he's caddying on the golf course? Ryan Pappenhausen just didn't want to play footy anymore. I miss watching him. I love watching the pap and not to mention that mullet. Elias Akatoa out for the year. Xavier Coates out for about another month. Nelson Aceves-Solomona no longer at the club. Jerome Hughes and Harry Grant not having their usual influence. And while it's impossible not to have enormous faith in Craig Bellamy, and if anyone can turn them around, he can, but as the late great Jack Gibson used to say, you need the cattle. And for the first time in an age, I don't think the Melbourne Storm has the cattle. Tell me if I'm wrong on 1300 361700 or text 0467 920 222. Well, the disruptor is a word I probably would prefer never to hear again, let alone have to refer to it. Now, one thing I'll say about the NRL's head of football, I think that's his current title, Graeme Anersley, when he talks, you can tell he's telling you the truth. He used to be an outstanding referee. And Graeme said yesterday that two of the decisions to penalise for the dreaded disruptor were wrong on Friday night in Brisbane and in game two of the game we called in Perth when Robert Toyer was denied a try. And as I said on the weekend, I like how the NRL evolves with the rules and interpretations. Don't mind the six agains. I don't mind the NRL trying things. But this disruptor seems absolutely stupid to me. So to correct me on that attitude, Graeme Anersley is on the line. How are you, Graeme? Good, Andrew. How are you doing? I'm very well. And before we go on, I just want to publicly thank you for words you said about me and to me during my little hiatus last year, mate. It was very much appreciated. Thank you. We're all very happy to see you back. Yes, thank you. And I miss your Monday briefings. Do you? Well, my week is a little bit easier, but at times like this, you know, maybe we could make things a little clearer if we were doing them. But, you know, I think it's got to get the balance right. I guess so. Well, it's good to hear you on a Monday here. So please explain. I get why we can't have players knocked off the ball when they're, you know, their eyes up. They're in a precarious position. But why are players penalised when legitimately contesting the footy? Well, they shouldn't be, Andrew. And that's the whole point. And I guess, you know, that's why yesterday we came out and said that the two instances that have created the most controversy, the Toya and the Drinkwater incidents, in our view, were the bunker exercise incorrect judgment on both of those, because in our view, they were genuine contests. And that's all this is about. I mean, you know, you talked about the dreaded disruptor word. And sometimes these things get titles these days that, you know, we don't necessarily give them. But at the end of the day, when you're talking about disruptors, what you're really talking about is obstruction. And obstruction's been a rule in the game for over 100 years. And it's the role of the referees, and in this case, the bunker, to ensure that players have an equal opportunity to contest the ball and that no one's unnecessarily interfered with. I was going to say, when did you stop refereeing? 1990 what? 1908. Oh, no, now. Come on. But I'm going to say the rules, then, as you're describing it, aren't any different. If you're contesting the footy, you should be all right, if you get there on time. 100% Andrew. But unfortunately, you know, coaching methods evolve. And what we, you know, and I'm not being critical of coaches here. Their job's to win football games and their job's to be as, I guess, as on the ball with the rules as they can be and looking to exploit the rules where they can. But what we've seen over more recent years is an increasing trend of kick chases coming through at a great rate of knots. In some cases, having no intent to genuinely contest the ball and taking out a catcher who is standing there literally defenseless, waiting for the ball to drop out of the sky. That's the sort of thing that we're trying to stop. Sometimes they disguise it well and sometimes they don't. But when two players go up at roughly the same time, they're both trying to catch the ball. That's a genuine contest. And that's the thing that we don't want to see ruled out of the game. I do worry. And again, I quite like the fact that things get tinkered with. It doesn't worry me. I love the speed of the game. I love the fact that we don't have to have detailed explanations about every set restart, even though that drives many people nuts. But I worry we are making the game too complicated. And you'll be there now on both sides of it, on the field, even if it was back in 1908. And now in your current role, are we making it too complicated? Well, I don't think we're making it too complicated. I mean, there are a lot of rules in the game. And those rules are there to ensure that two teams in any particular game get an equal opportunity to try and win. And it's up to the players. And, of course, any game has to have rules. So what's happened, of course, in the modern era, Andrew, is that, you know, we've got high-definition televisions and we've got instant replays and bunkers. And we look at things, you know, 100 times in slow motion. And if we weren't doing that, people would still be complaining because we were getting decisions wrong. The number of decisions that we get wrong now with the incredible technology we've got are very small compared to the number of decisions that are made during a game and across the course of a round of football. But there will always be tight calls that will be subject to conjecture and disagreement. We just don't think in these two cases that there was much doubt that these were genuine contests and should have been ruled as such. How do you rate, Graeme, how the set restarts are being interpreted? Well, I think, Andrew, the thing about set restarts is that they're about trying to keep the game flowing and get a reasonable level of compliance with the laws of the game in the ruck and the 10 metres without stopping the game, without the referee becoming the centre of attention. And I think, Andrew, that, you know, you will recall, as well as I do, that it's not too long ago that in decades gone by, you know, it wasn't uncommon for referees to be blowing 30 penalties in a game. That's 30 stoppages. And, you know, some of it was very difficult to watch. We've basically taken two-thirds of the penalties out of a game now. It's not often we get more than about 10 penalties in a game. It can happen, but rarely. And some of that has been replaced with set restarts because we still have to have some kind of defence against teams exploiting the rules and putting the opposition at a disadvantage. And if we don't have that, then we've got pretty much mayhem on the field. So it's a good initiative to keep the game moving, to try and ensure that we get compliance with the rules and to ensure that the referees aren't the centre of attention. I have said this often. I go back and watch a lot of old games on YouTube from, you know, even the 1980s. And you have to remind people, penalty counts were 18-13 and 17-10. And it was, and also scrum penalties back in the day. I congratulated Liam Kennedy when I saw him after the first game of the doubleheader in Perth. That South Canberra game, there was five penalties and three restarts by my count. And we had a stunning game. The next game wasn't anywhere near as good, Cronulla and Roosters. And we had 10 restarts and 10 penalties. Why so different? Or is that just the way it's always been, individual interpretation? Well, it's not only individual interpretations, Andrew. And of course, there will be some differences. I mean, you know, no two people are the same. So they will look at things slightly differently. But, you know, we can't discount the fact that teams are different as well. And there are some games that are much more difficult to control than others. There are some games that are played in a very different way than others. So, you know, there are games that are much more aggressively played. And I don't necessarily mean foul play, but just the nature of the way the game unfolds. There are some games that are very much open and the referee can literally stay out of the game. So some of it depends on the players and how difficult the game is. And a referee can't just abandon their responsibilities because they want to keep the game flowing. So, you know, there's a bit of that as well. So I'm not saying that the referees don't have some influence over that. But the players play a role in it as well. All right, Graeme, just finally, do I officially have your imprimatur to brush the word disruptor and just use the term obstruction? 100% Edward. I don't know where it came from, but it's kind of written into folklore now and probably forevermore. But if you want to be the first one to try and turn back the tide, I'm very happy to do that. Hey, I'm always turning back the clock in one way or another. So from this moment on disruptor, you're out of here. Graeme Annesley, great to hear you back on a Monday. We'll talk soon. Thanks, Andrew. Head of football at the NRL, Graeme Annesley. I'm really happy about that, the term I find awful, let alone the rulings of it. And hopefully all of that means that we are going to see some common sense with this rule. And you heard, Graeme, it's not officially called by that dumb title and we won't be calling it that anymore. It's an obstruction penalty. And it does make you think other league terms that have gone away in recent years, ones that you miss. Remember when an obstruction of player running behind a teammate was called a shepherd? A dangerous throw used to be known as a spear tackle. Do you remember the terms that we used to describe scrum penalties? And I think there were 19 or 20 infringements you could have in a scrum. But some of the titles for the penalties were screwing the scrum, not retiring, feet across, loose arm, and on it went. I don't miss scrums, but I do miss some of those descriptions. How about you? Is there a rugby league term that you miss? Or a current one that you dislike immensely? 1-300-361-700. Is the number to ring or text? 0467-920-222. On the text line, a question for Louie. Oh, I'll have to remember this one. Paul from Wagga when he joins me after the news. Read Bellamy tearing strips off young Joey Chan. Does this happen often or is it done behind closed doors? A lot different now than back in the day in regards to cameras in dressing sheds. If Joey Chan is a gentle soul, he may think twice before signing up again. I'll ask Louie about that, Paul, after the news. Also on the text line, Andrew, do you think the set restarts would be better refereed with two referees? I don't know. I don't think anything's better with two referees. But that's just my opinion. I didn't like them when they were there. I much prefer one referee. But let me say this. I think referees would be better if they were left more to their own devices. I think the good referees, and we've got some really good refs out there, Grant Atkins and Ash Kline and Adam Gee and Liam Kennedy, and I think Spigniew Tuklas Radamski is the one on the rise, and Wyatt Raymond is a very good referee. If these guys were allowed to follow their instinct, I reckon they would be so much better because really the way they're set up is now they are not allowed. episodes.description: Another round, another loss for St George Illawarra. Some were encourage by their performance in the defeat by Manly - but not Luke Lewis. He thought talk of an improved effort was a cop out.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. ABC Sports coverage of the NRL Premiership. NRL Saturday. On your radio, ABC Sport Digital Radio. And ABC Listen. Let's get to last night's game. And MC, you and I were having a very intimate viewing of the St George Illawarra Manly Ringer game in your hotel room, watching it off your laptop. Yes. We couldn't get it on the TV. But we saw enough to know that Manly did enough to beat St George Illawarra despite a good effort by the Dragons. That final score in favour of the Seagulls after they trailed at one point, 28 points to 18. They led 16-0, then the Dragons led 18-16. Reuben Garrick scored this his second try. We get back and away from the kickoff of Manly here. Garrick receives a pass on the outside. Dummies. He burns Val Holmes for speed. Over halfway, Garrick. They're all chasing him. Overcomes Sloan. Won't catch him. And they score from the kickoff. Oh, dearie me. Dearie, dearie me, Dragons fans. Garrick scores his second try. And that was dearie, dearie me at that point. Reuben Garrick, three points in the ABC Player of the Year from Matthew Elliott. Two to second rower, Homoli Olukowatu, who has been charged with a high tackle on Jacob Little and been fined. One point to Dragons front rower, Toby Couchman. And, look, there was some easy try scored in the game, actually, for both sides, MC. That Luciano Lelewitt try was ridiculous from a tap. Effort there from the Dragons, but the fact is they've lost 10 in a row. What did you make of it? Yeah, I think you summed it up perfectly. A better effort this week compared to that game that we were at last week where they were just so poor and off the pace against North Queensland. But, again, it was lapses in concentration. Some poor defensive re-tom to Voivich over Kyle Flanagan for one of the first try, I think it might have been. And then from the kickoff, they shift wide and take advantage of some lazy switched-off defense from the Dragons and score again. So that's probably been it. Well, it's definitely a concern for the Dragons, but they were more spirited this week than they have been in the past couple. It wasn't always the best game of footy, to be fair, down there in the gong last night. But for Manly, Louis, that's two out of two for Kieran Foran. Yeah, a big smile on Kieran Foran's face after the game in the press conference. And he knew that it wasn't all going to be the same as the way the week before sort of flowed. But they got the job done and they didn't play their best football. But at the end of the day, it's all about winning and coming up with the right plays at the right time. And they did that. And attention to detail, that play off the kickoff where Ruben Garrick scores that try. That's a play that they had planned. So good research, I reckon, from Kieran Foran during the week where he's seen an opportunity that if we do get a kickoff, just keep an eye up on the defense. They come up and in a lot. Let's play back down the sideline. And it was Saab who comes up with that catch and comes up with a beautiful little play. So really good, smart play there from the Seagulls. I thought they played well. But gee, we talk about effort for the Dragons. I reckon it's a cop-out. I'll be honest with you. Talking about, oh, it's a better effort. It's not a better effort. It's 10 weeks, 10 losses. Horrible football. And the least, I say this all the time, the least a rugby league supporter expects out of his team is effort. Effort. That's the least. I don't reckon there was effort. All right. I've seen bits and pieces of it. Some of the plays, effort's getting thrown in your head into tackles where you know you've got to make them. And sometimes some of the attempts were horrible. I sit and I go, there's no effort in that. I don't know what everyone's talking about. Oh, the effort was better. I find that bizarre. But anyway, so that's my opinion on it and take on it. But I just feel like the Dragons are so, so far behind. Their confidence levels are absolutely shot. episodes.title: Michael Maguire says the Broncos are "always looking to the future"
episodes.description: Andrew Moore, Matt Elliott and Ruan Sims chat to Brisbane Broncos coach Michael Maguire as Brisbane prepare to blood some new players after injuries to some of their playmakers.
episodes.transcript: This is an ABC podcast. NRL Thursday on ABC Sport. Rugby League is on your radio. ABC Sport Digital Radio and ABC Listen. The Brisbane Broncos, as we mentioned, battling some injury concerns. Albeit their form has certainly returned after a sluggish start to the season. They've won a few in a row, but so have their opponents tomorrow night. The North Queensland Cowboys and the Broncos coach Michael Maguire. He joins us online. G'day, Michael. How are you? Good, Andrew. Thanks for having me on. I remember talking to Justin Holbrook a few weeks ago after Dylan Brown and Kalen Ponga were injured. And I asked him, how do you cope without them looking ahead? He said, well, we don't have a choice. We have to. We've got to get on with it. And I guess you're in the same boat. Yeah, we are. It is. We've had a bit of practice of this over my journey in the last 12 months where we've lost halfbacks and five eights with Adam Reynolds and Benny Hunt. But we've managed to find the right people to come in and do the job for us. So I think it's just another one of those cases where we get to blood a few of our younger guys coming through. And I'm really looking forward to it, to be honest. You know, they work really hard together. And we've had them in plenty of times with the first grade boys. So it's about now going out and playing. Yeah, that was the question I had. How much time have they spent training with first grade? And young Tom Duffy must be that pumped against his old team. Yeah, as I said, I'm really looking forward. Tommy's come in and he's had an absolute ripper of a preseason. He's had plenty of reps with all our sort of senior boys. So I'm looking forward to seeing how he can just roll in and just do his job. I think that's the one thing that he has come to the club doing. He just plays his part. And, you know, he doesn't need to go outside of what he's capable of. And if he does that for us, well, we'll all be happy for him. Mate, I thought Jesse Arthurs did a really good job at fullback. What do you see him bringing to the team over the next couple of weeks? Yeah, Matty, he did do a great job for us. He's really composed, yes. I think, you know, nothing really bothers you. So wherever you put him, he just plays and plays his role. So, look, you know, he's got a different style than obviously what Ressie has. But also, too, he's got a fair bit of speed. So we've just altered a little bit around what it might look like. But Jesse can slot in anywhere. So he'll come in and just perform the way Jesse does. Mate, I know that you're more than a team coach. You're a club coach. And, you know, when we look at you've got players out injured. But you've got a bit of turnover coming up in the future just related to birth certificates. What's the pathways like going into your team? Yeah, we've got some good kids coming through, Matty. But also, too, you're always looking at how you can bolster your squad. And, you know, internally, like, you know, we've got Billy Walters still there. And, you know, Benny Hunt will come back. Obviously, that's the ageing group that I suppose you're talking about. So we've got options. And it's a matter of just working our way through it. And, you know, each time we go through a game, we're looking at different capabilities. Like Tommy's coming in. We've got Pezzik coming next year. So we're always looking to the future, I guess, through recruitment. But also, too, internally, we've got some good young ones coming through. And what about the opposition, mate? They've got a little bit of confidence coming into this game. What do you see of their key threats? And, you know, what have you got the team really focusing on? Yeah, Matty, their spine's up and about at the moment. But they're just jumping off the back of their forwards. You know, big Jason Tomololo and Cowan Esa, they're sort of rolling forward. And then their spine come to life. So, you know, we're going to have to be really strong defensively. You know, I think they've shown that over the last couple of weeks where they can shift and move together very quickly. So, you know, adjusting your line, you need to be aware of that. But also, too, you know, when it gets a bit quicker, you've got to be able to control them through the middle. So it's going to be a real good test for us defensively. But, you know, the boys have really worked hard over the last month to be able to improve that area. So, you know, they're getting a few results off the back of the work they're putting in. So we're going to have to be at our best tomorrow. Well, Mad, you actually already touched on what I was going to ask you about. Unsurprisingly, the forward pack really interests me. It's unsurprising. But what I really love with your forward pack is the amount, just the work rate they have is absolutely phenomenal. And their ability to be able to switch transition really, really quickly. It's so important as this game speeds up, isn't it? It is, Rowan. I mean, they've worked really hard at that. And, you know, we work hard at that at training. And they're getting the benefits of how hard they want to work for each other. And it's something there that I'm, you know, really proud of them of how hard they want to work in and around their training to be able to make sure they put that in the game because it has sped up. You know, it's – and, you know, you've got to be able to handle those speeds and through Paddy Carrigan and Payne. And then we've got our bench coming on in Xavier and Tolts. You know, they're doing a great job for us up the front there. So it then allows our back rowers to play their part. But, you know, we've got Brendy back now, you know, on our left edge. So we sort of missed him a bit earlier. He was – he did a great job for us at the back end of last year. And he's come in firing. So they were all just working well together. And I think that's, you know, why – you know, the way the game's going with the momentum. You have to. You've got no choice. And to be able to achieve at our level and what we're trying to achieve is a group together. Yeah, and not every day do our listeners get to hear from a head coach. I'd love for you to explain to them briefly on what – you've seen this evolution of this six-player bench and what that's brought in as a coach when it comes to your selections and, you know, how you can utilise tactics throughout the game. Yeah, it is really interesting, Ron. I'm still sort of trying to discover it. I mean, you know, tomorrow, you know, it'll come out in time that we're going to have Hayes, Berriman, and Josh Rogers on our bench. So you can have specific players now as you're 18, 19 to be able to cover certain positions when you want to have the cover around the team. So it does add a little bit of a different dynamic of how you're looking at your bench. And so, look, if all of a sudden you do have an injury to your outside backs, you can move someone into a specific role that can play a specific position. So it does sort of give a bit more of a luxury to a coach, not thinking that you've got to have a back rower that can cover the centres and then who can cover your fullback position because you can have one of those on your bench as well. So that's the sort of evolution of how this man bench is coming around in my eyes. Can I ask you, Madge, if you don't mind about Penrith? You played them in round one. You knocked them over in the prelim last year. And they whitewashed you in game one of the season up in Brisbane. And they're playing footy that I don't think we've seen for a long, long time, if at all, for five weeks straight. And they're going in as obviously a hot favourite tonight against Canterbury. Have you seen something in Penrith from your casual observations, Michael, that you haven't noticed of them even when they went on that run of four straight premierships this year? Not so much, Andrew. The thing I'm seeing is that they've got a lot of players that have played together. I think when you've played a lot of footy together, the cohesion of your team, and everyone talks about time spent together, you understand the habits of each other. I think at the moment they've just really nailed it. They're being able to play a brand of footy. They've got a couple of young guys that came in last year. They've now spent another 12 months with those more senior players. Nathan's on fire at the moment with the way he's playing. And, you know, that's the leadership part that goes on in any team. I think that's just really gelled for them. And, look, you know, there's plenty of twists and turns throughout the season. So they're up and about at the moment, and each team will have their moment in time where it might turn a little bit. But at this present moment, they're playing some good footy, aren't they? Right, mate. It's time for me to cut to the chase. He's standing up for this one. We're getting around to it now. So, mate, you'd be really proud of your team, I reckon, because there was some early season controversy, and that really galvanised them and got them to play well. And I'm just wondering whether you need a little bit more controversy. And I can talk about you not buying a coffee for three years. All right. Just sponging off me the whole time. Would you think that'll get the team? So if they win, can I just take credit for that? Oh, mate, I don't mind who takes the credit for winning that extra, to be honest. Look, it was a challenging period for us, but our group's been through a fair bit of that, Matty, over time. And I appreciate the support that I get out wide. But the one thing I do know about the group and what's going on internally, there's a lot of great things. And when you see that, the external stuff, you sort of just wonder where on earth that does come from. But internally, that's the stuff that really matters. And, you know, I see that as why the team has turned a little bit of a corner, if you call it. But, you know, we've got a long way to go and we've got to keep improving and all the rest of it. But to see some of our younger guys coming in this week, I'm actually really excited for tomorrow. You know, another great challenge for us. But also, too, it gives, you know, Jesse Arthur's playing his 100th game. You know, just different little things like that happen within a team. And we applaud that. And that's the special part of what goes on. And the external stuff will just play its path. It's just great to see. Look, I don't, don't, we're not going to get into the whole Ben Teo thing and what happened there. But all I want to know in relation to that is, did you learn how to deal with friction between a head coach and an assistant coach when you were working with Matthew Elliott? Well, Matty taught me a lot. That's it. A lot of good stuff, Matty. But, you know, I did learn a lot as a younger coach back then. And, you know, and I applaud all the people that I've worked with. And Matty's one of them that's helped me get to where I am right now. He taught me a lot about the game, how to watch the game. You know, I was a naive young coach back then. And I never forget him saying, Matty, you've got to watch more football. And I can now go, I get why he says that. Because you understand, you know, the more you watch, the better you're going to see things. And that's just the art of becoming a coach. Yeah, that took a turn I wasn't really hoping for. But anyway, Michael McGuire always... He knows how to buy coffee now, too. Yeah, yeah. For all your assistants. I'm sure. Matty, so good to have you on, mate, as usual. Good luck tomorrow night against the Cowboys, and we'll chat soon. Nah, good on you guys. Thanks for having us on. Good luck, Matty. Thanks, Matty. Good luck. See you, man. See you. Let's get to Michael Kariannis with MC's Hammer Time. You can't touch this. Time to find out all the latest rugby league news. And speculation. Here's Michael Kariannis with MC's Hammer Time. Michael, of course, rugby league's number one journalist with the Daily and Sunday Telegraph and works with us as well. Hello, MC. Good evening, team. How are we? Very well, mate. Have you finished packing for the Perth trip? I've squeezed all my stuff in. Very much looking forward to seeing you bright and early tomorrow. Not too early, but we've got a few days to spend together. Nah, it was some very, very quality time. But I know you were very stressed about packing your bag, so I'm glad Clara did it for you in the end. So it is going to be interesting, MC, to head over to Perth, bearing in mind the Bears are not far away. Mal Meninga will join us in the box, the inaugural Perth Bears coach on Saturday in the pregame show between 2 and 3 Australian Eastern time. So it will be interesting to get a vibe actually being there and at the massive Perth Stadium to see what the interest level is like compared to previous years. Yeah, no doubt. And see what sort of, you know, are fans walking around in Bears gear or are they walking around in South Sydney gear or Roosters gear, that sort of stuff as well. It's going to be interesting to see what sort of get up the fans are wearing. But you're right, this is, there's another game later in the year, but this is the biggest event in terms of NRL games in Perth this year. So, yeah, it's going to be interesting to see what sort of vibe there is there. Tell you what, injuries have been a massive story since last weekend and all through the week, haven't they? Oh, no doubt. A few long-term ones, you know, Parramatta, you have Bailey Simonson gone for the season. That's a big one, no doubt about that. A couple of returning players as well. Cole Flanagan returns for the Dragons. There'll be much intrigue around that inclusion from the concussion playing him at half-back as well. So, yeah, lots around in terms of, you know, guys in and out of line-ups. I'll bring Matthew into this, and Drew, if you want to, about Daniel Atkinson, because he's obviously a terrific rugby league player, but he has not seemed well adjusted to be playing in the half-back role and sort of that dominant position. Should it make that much difference whether you wear number seven or number six, or does it depend on individual game plans? It also depends on the teams and the structures and the systems of play that they have, Andrew. So, a lot of... I'm just having your... Watermelon. Wow. So, a lot of teams will split their halves left and right side. Daniel Atkinson hasn't done a bad job as a half, but what you haven't seen from him is his dynamic running game that he gets to do and play ad-lib footy when he gets at six, in the old style of six. So, when we watch the Bulldogs tonight, they'll have a left and right half. So, that's... Again, that structure changes from team to team, whereas Penrith don't do that. Cleary drifts from one side to the other, and the 5'8", and the fullback play left and right. So, it's a little bit of a different dynamic from one team to another. So, yeah, it's an interesting one. Daniel Atkinson is a great ball carrier, can really light a game up. Have we seen that from him in five rounds of footy yet? No. No. We have learnt that he can kick a ball okay, but kicking a ball okay doesn't win you a game of footy. And I think it was you on Monday, MC, that let us know and wrote that the Dragons were putting on hold contract negotiation talks with Damien Cook, and in fact, all contract talks were being on hold. What's the week been like at Dragons headquarters? Yeah, it's been busy. It's obviously been in the headlines following that loss. I guess from the moment the fans boot him off the ground, there was lots of phone calls laid on Saturday night into Sunday morning just regarding the future of Shane Flanagan, and not just Shane Flanagan alone, but the makeup of the footballing staff. And then later on Sunday, Monday was the news around the fact that they'd put on hold all extension talks for all those players, headlined by Damien Cook, who they were in advanced discussions for a one-year deal. So look, there's no doubt there's pressure on everyone in the organisation, not just Shane Flanagan alone. It's all his coaching staff. It's his support staff there. And some of these players, you know, a lot of them are going to be on show tomorrow. We're talking about Tyrell Sloan, Blake Laurie, Christian Tupolosu, obviously Damien Cook, Harme Felle. There's a stack of them, Jadon Seward, a stack of guys who don't have their long-term future sorted. And they all have played first grade at some stage this year. So it's an interesting time for the Dragons at the moment. I am happy for them to pick Tyrell Sloan because he's got speed. That team we watched MC on Saturday against the Cowboys might be the slowest NRL team I've ever seen. Yeah, and as the game's getting faster, the Dragons are getting slower. That's probably the best way to describe it. All right. What else have you got, Michael? Yeah, bits and pieces around the Eels. You mentioned the injuries. Well, you know, their chief executive, Jim Sarantinos, reached out to Andrew Abdo during the week to try and see if there's any sort of potential for salary cap dispensation for acts of foul play, committed on players that they're going to lose long-term. The NRL said no very, very quickly because they're not going to change salary cap rules mid-season, but it's definitely something that clubs will explore in the post-season to see if there is an appetite for that or if you pick up a... In the Super League, if you pick up a player, an injury, a season-long injury for a player within the first three rounds, you're able to replace them. So that might be something that comes to light. And our man, Connor Watson, Andrew, has formally been told by the Roosters that he's free to negotiate with rival clubs. Look, this has been simmering in the background for the past few weeks, but now formally been told he can move on from the Roosters at the end of the season. So where do you think would be a good fit for him? Would the Dragons be looking for someone like a Connor Watson getting a bit of speed? It's interesting, Rue, because I feel like Connor's potential destination might be PNG. So if he gets that sorted, then he's got to work backwards for 12 months. Yeah. And then it becomes open. You know, a player like Connor Watson would, you know, for a 12-month period maybe doesn't help the Dragons, but you look at some of the other sides in the competition, you know, Melbourne, they're losing Tyron Wishart. Does he go parachute there for 12 months? You know, like there's all these parameters at play if it's only going to be a 12-month deal. yeah, that's one of the What about Manley? Manley, well, Manley would want him long-term, I suggest, Andrew, no doubt. But they might be interested in him for a 12-month deal as well because they desperately need another hooker on their books. But for mine, Connor's best position is 13. As a number two hooker on your books, but, you know, primarily playing in that 13 role. MC, give me a hand here. I agree with all the potential destinations for it. Why are the Roosters letting him go? Can someone, well, I'm sitting here looking at the contribution he makes to that team and I'm going, oh, okay, makes sense to let him go. Not. Yeah, I think there's probably some confusion amongst Connor and the Roosters at the back end of last year and potentially for his old management stable as well. So, Connor had indicated to the Roosters that he was keen on joining R360 at the end of this year and the Roosters granted him permission to go explore that. And in the interim, as the weeks and months pass, they essentially, Matty spent his money. That's what they told him. So, he indicated to them that he wanted to get out of his contract a year early potentially and the Roosters said no worries and the R360 situation didn't get off the ground but by then the Roosters had moved on. You're on fire, MC. You're making sense again. I love it. Twice. Thanks, Matty. That's a rare praise from you. Thank you. He was due. All right, MC, I'll let you go back to packing. I'll see you at the airport tomorrow and can't wait for our Perth experience over the next few days. Yeah. Thank you, Andrew. See you, team. Have a good night. See you. Michael Carriana. He didn't say boys once then. I'm so proud of him. Yeah, well, again, he was due. He did so well. He was due. And you know what? I should have praised him to his ears. And at home... Not while he was off the air. Oh, he'll be listening. Yeah. Well done, MC. That was awesome. Because at home, he's got his wife, Clara. He's got two daughters but the one he always refers to is Max the dog. It's a little bit of a worry. Discover more great ABC podcasts, live radio and exclusives on the ABC Listen app.

episodes.title: The Cowboys defence is their best offence
episodes.description: North Queensland's Jaxon Purdue continues to impress on and off the field. He scored a double as the Cowboys smashed the Dragons BUT reckoned their win was all based on hard work in defence.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Well, Louie and I were at Jubilee yesterday where North Queensland absolutely crushed St. George Illawarra with 16 points in each half to win 32 points to nil. And Louie gave three points in the ABC Player of the Year to Tom Dearden. Two points to thrilling centre Jackson Perdue and one point to 5'8", Jake Clifford. Again, the Cowboys dominated and now they've won three in a row. Let's find out how they're feeling about things. Jackson Perdue is on the line. Jackson, how are you doing? Hey, good. Thanks, guys. Thanks for having me. Mate, it's always a pleasure. You were good enough to come on on your 20th birthday last July, I think it was, as you're in the middle of a festive look around town. So we appreciate you very much. And the way things have changed from a probably less than ideal start to the season, the way it's built up over the last three weeks must give you guys an enormous amount of confidence and hope. Yeah, it was a rough start to the season, you know, going down our first two games. And, you know, especially at Leichhardt when we got dusted by the Tigers, you know, that one hurt us. And we sort of had to have a look in the mirror and have a look at ourselves and seeing what we wanted to be as a footy team. And we sort of really come together and connected really well. And then, as you can see, the past three games, yeah, we've been really connected and we've fought our way to good wins. I asked Toby Rudolph this on NRL Monday after the Sharks had lost a couple and then they rebounded with a great win last Sunday over Canberra. Is there a moment where you guys as a team unit, this may not even involve the coaching staff, where you do have a bit of an honesty session when, again, you've lost the first couple of games of the season that you need to really rectify this straight away? Is there that moment where you guys have a team meeting or a few of you get together and talk about how you can fix things? Yeah, definitely. There definitely is. But also, you know, it was only the first two rounds of the season. So we also knew that we had plenty to work on and plenty to build on. But I guess there's units like, as I say, like our left edge, you know, Murray Tualagi calls a meeting and really taking the leadership role with our left edge and sort of come up with some clips and what we want to be known as a left edge defensively mainly. So I guess all the units, you know, the middles, the spine, left edge, right edge sort of come together and talk about what we can do better and what we can improve on each week. Well, Scott Drinkwater set up the first points of the game with a magnificent 40-20 and then an individual try beating a couple close to the line. But then you, Jackson Perdue, scored these tries just before half time. Sends the ball away left through hands and it's Clifford. Getting the pass back to Perdue over halfway. He's over the 40, the 30 beats two. Valhans won't catch him. He's special this young boy. Jackson Perdue scores. A long range try. It was too good for the Dragons. Jackson Perdue, a brilliant individual try. He'll play it right in that far corner to Chester. Comes left to Deirdre. Then away through hands. Drinkwater to Clifford. Left foot kick for Jackson Perdue. Oh, that's in his purview to score brilliant tries. What about the lovely sweet kiss off the left boot? It was a great... I am a gibber, fair to you. That was a great kick from Jake Clifford off his left boot. But that first try, especially, Jackson, a long range job, as we heard, it came after you guys had to defend your own line for set after set after set. And that... Talk about setting or turning defence into attack. You guys pulled it off beautifully. Yeah, I think that try just really showed the hard work that we did, you know. It was, like you said, we defended our own line. And that's what we've sort of been practising in the pre-season. And at training each week. So, yeah, it was good to score a try off the back of our hard work. And sort of give the middles a rest. Because they're working their bums off in the middle tackling. So, yeah, I guess it was good to score a meat pie. And give the middles a bit of a break. Jackson, that left side that you talk about. Yourself and Murray Tulangi, you know, defensively. But also attacking-wise. Jake Clifford. His last couple of weeks have been what we know Jake Clifford can do. But he just seems to have taken it to another level. Yeah, he's been really awesome. I think at training, you know, he's really been a leader with our group. And he's got a run-first mentality. And when he's got that, he's always on. You know, he's such a strong runner of the ball. And he's setting up our outside boys. And really connecting with the spine. So, yeah, I think when he's, like I said, when he's got a run-first mentality, that's when he plays his best. And he's been killing it for us. I think it's important too, Jackson, because I'm, you know, I'm talking with you previously. You were brought up as a half when you're coming through the paths while you were in the halves. And now you're settled there. Jake's settled there too. Because sometimes when the size not going well, there's, you know, a bit of chopping and changing. But it seems to be a very stable line-up now, which gives your younger blokes in particular a lot of confidence. Yeah, it does. And I think, you know, playing with the same team and the same edge week in, week out gives you a bit of comfortability and a bit of confidence. Because you know what everyone's going to be doing. You're on the same page. So, yeah, I guess it's only round five. So we're still connecting and still learning what each other's doing. But I think for the past three weeks we've been, like I said, really connected. And we've been, you know, doing hard work behind the scenes, that training, doing extras together, watching extra videos. So, yeah, it's a long season ahead of us. And hopefully we can keep doing the same thing. And obviously your coach, who was under pressure, but now he's not under pressure. Three wins. It's amazing how winning takes care of everything. But I think Todd Payton, I think it's pretty obvious for all to see that he's sort of, all subtly, all bit subtly, he's changed his demeanour. He's a lot more, he's calmer. Yeah, definitely. Yeah, he's definitely been calm. And, you know, he's took accountability of him last year, where he was a bit frantic, he thinks. And he sort of said that to his group, that he doesn't want to be a version of himself last year. So he's really took accountability. And coming this year with a really good attitude, and, you know, our new coaching staff have been awesome. Blake Green and Weller, they've been, you know, outstanding towards our group. So, yeah, Todd, he's been awesome so far. And he's been, yeah, really chill and really, I guess, helping our players out and taking the time to, you know, do the extra video. Yeah, he's been really good. Jackson, I just want to ask you a general question about captain's challenges. And we asked this of Scott Drinkwater a week ago, and he laughed that Reid Marnie's been barred for life. Is Reuben Cotter, I appreciate he's one of your captains, has he been barred for life after yesterday? Yeah, he's banned for life. But I can't really talk because I think I'm banned for life with my kicking license. Oh, you're gone too? I'm going to make a break. I only have my kicking license. And if I'm making a break, I'm doing no more grubbers. Yeah, well, you wanted a third try, didn't you? That's what that was about. And the game was in the bag. Yeah, I was kicking side and it was being greedy. Wasn't that supposed to come off the outside of the foot and not the inside? Yeah, I don't even know what happened. Everything just happened too fast. I've never seen a player react like that when you've got the game wrapped in the bag. I thought you were going to rip your own head off. Yeah, I was spewing. I wasn't happy. So 32-0, three wins in a row. Titans, Melbourne Storm and Dragons. And if you guys go on to play finals footy and have a great year, do you think it will be that comeback against Melbourne, the thing that you guys will be referring to and we in the media will be referring to as the turning point? Yeah, I reckon so. You know, that was a good comeback. And I think we really fought hard for that win and we stuck to our game plan and our framework, which obviously suits us the best. And I think it's a big credit to our spine. You know, when our spine's moving and playing on the front foot, all of our teams playing well. And as you can see, when we come back in the storm, all of our spine had their hand from the ball and had a really good comeback. So, yeah, I think we took a lot of confidence away from that. But saying that, it's still a long season ahead. And, yeah, we're ready to go for the rest of the year now. Well, it's going to be a big test also on Friday night at Lang Park. The big brother, the Brisbane Broncos, albeit they'll be without players. I don't know whether you've heard the news, but Rhys Walsh won't be there. Not that you like to see players get injured, but that is going to make the task a little bit easier. Someone you don't have to look out for. Oh, yeah, definitely. You know, when there's a player like Rhys Walsh that's injured, it does hurt the Broncos. But I guess, yeah, it is a good thing for us. And we know how damaging and dangerous he is. But saying that, you know, they've got good depth in the Broncos and the next man up mentality, I'm sure, will be a big thing there. So, yeah, we'll ID and get to homework on who's going to be playing that position and get to work just the same as we would with Rhys Walsh, I guess. Well, Jackson, it was thrilling to watch you play yesterday. And unfortunately for North Queensland, so many of the headlines, I get it, are about St. George, Lawara and their woes. But if you take your eyes off the Cowboys at your own peril, three straight wins. Well played, mate. And good luck, Ian, to the Broncos. Thank you, guys. Thanks for having me. Appreciate it. Our pleasure. Love talking to Jackson Perdue. Love watching him play. And he was thrilling yesterday. And after that, seemed like quite a ridiculous experiment at the time, even of him playing 5-8 last year. He just seems a dead set. I don't know, as you mentioned, he played a lot of... Yeah, he played all his football. He looks such a natural centre. And the other position you could see him in, I reckon, is full-back. Do you love Rugby League? NRL Sunday. On ABC Sport. On your radio. ABC Sport Digital Radio. And ABC Listen. Can our panel of ABC Rugby League experts handle six questions in three minutes? Can they avoid getting stuck on the fence? And can the referee, Andrew Moore, avoid going into the bunker? Yeah. It's time for six again. Righto, John Gibbs. How many more weeks does Shane Flanagan have left us in Georgia Lawora, coach? Well, I would say he's maybe got a couple at the most because if they have two more losses, they won't be able to continue going along, you know, the trajectory they are. That's now five in a row, four last year. That's nine in a row, which is a record. And the other games you could excuse, yesterday's game, albeit less concentrated also on Cowboys, was hopeless. Perfect timing. Louie, how many Panthers will play in game one of the State of Origin series? Now, I'm going to set the bar at six and a half. Over or under? I say over. I'd nearly say, I'm going to say ten. Well, who are those ten? Because I was looking, I don't know that there is ten. I'm going to go Dylan Edwards, probably. One. And then you're going to go Milky Jenkins. And you're going to go Nathan Cleary, Brian Tottle, Isaiah Yeo, Liam Martin. That's six. Okay. We'll get back to it. Gibbsy, which top four team from last year should fans be more concerned about? Melbourne or Canterbury? Melbourne. Because Melbourne have just been an institution, particularly under Craig Bellamy, and they're just not playing. We had this discussion on Good Friday, but they're not playing well. There's a few blokes, and I think finally Craig Bellamy is getting really frustrated with some of the things that are happening. Canterbury are a battling side in terms of attack. Louie, three wins in a row for North Queensland. Are the Cowboys ready to return to finals footy this year? Oh, I can't say yes at the moment. I feel like their game's definitely gotten better. They're getting better as a team. They've travelled well. But I want to see another two or three good consistent weeks from them before I say yes. So I'm sitting on the fence on that one. I think they'll make the eight now. I think they've got confidence. They've got belief. And also some of the other sides aren't going that well. So there's a real opening there, and they're on an upward trajectory, which is good. Gibbsy, the Dolphins are off to a less than stellar start, especially with the expectation of them this year. What's going wrong with them? I'm not quite sure because I know that Louie, like me, had high hopes for them this year. But it's an attitude thing, you know. And some of the things that happened last week against Manly were terrible. I mean, Morgan Noles, for instance, he will be, he'll look at his game and say, what was I doing? I think they'll get their mojo, but they want to get it quickly. But they've got an attitude shift. Louie, finally, we're seeing regular throwing away of captain's challenges. They've been awful, some of them. But we're seeing a lot of really bad ones. Why do you think that is? I think some of the ones are just, they're throwing it, trying to have a free throw at the stumps, to be fair. I think they're just hoping. They're not really sort of thinking about it. The other thing is, too, they put too much trust in players that they probably shouldn't. So I think that's what it is. I don't think there's any particular reason why that's happened. It's just dumb decisions. It depends on the game situation, obviously. If it's late, you need to breathe. That doesn't matter. Nothing going on. There are weird ones like the Reuben Cotter one yesterday. But we've seen several already this week that are blatantly not challengeable. Blatantly knock-ons and they go challenge it. They generally, in their head, don't know the rule, maybe. Or is it that clubs aren't valuing them enough? Because if you have one up your sleeve late in the close game, we've seen time after time how valuable that can be. They can be so important. But there may well be one where you haven't raked, where you've just had your hands on your ball, on the ball, and you get penalised. And you don't have that ability to come up with a captain's challenge, which in a tight game can be absolutely critical. The Reuben Cotter one yesterday was just a bonehead. You're talking about an experienced player, one of their leaders, a state of origin player, Australian player. What was he thinking? He just went over and grabbed the bloke. Yeah, it was the most blatant foul ever. But there's been several of them already this year. NRL Sunday on ABC Sport. Rugby League is on your radio. ABC Sport Digital Radio. And ABC Listen. Getting to know you. Getting to know all about you. Well, so far, it's been royalty, really. We've had Josh King from Melbourne and now Max King from the Canterbury Bankstown Bulldogs, New South Wales State of Origin front rower and one of our favourite guests on our weekend coverage. engagement.takeaway: Artistic freedom often clashes with political solidarity, forcing tough choices that define legacies and impact global movements.

engagement.whyListen: In the shadow of apartheid's brutal twilight, artists faced a stark choice: amplify the struggle or profit from its cracks. This episode unearths the raw, high-stakes decisions that forged legends and sparked fury, revealing music's true power as both a weapon and a compromise.
engagement.socialPost: Paul Simon broke the apartheid boycott for 'Graceland.' Was it artistic genius or a moral failure? This episode dives into the raw controversy, the stars who played Sun City, and how music became the soundtrack to a burning nation. #Apartheid #Graceland #Boycott #MusicHistory #PaulSimon #NelsonMandela
