episodes.title: 04 | Boycott! | The Grapefruit Ladies
episodes.description: It's 1984, and in Dublin, Ireland, 21 year old shop assistant Mary Manning refuses to sell a South African grapefruit. Her action draws world attention to the campaign to hit Apartheid where it hurts, by crippling the South African economy.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. It's July the 19th, 1984. A fresh summer's morning in downtown Dublin. And 21-year-old Mary Manning is on her way to work. I was working in Dunn's Stars and Henry Street, which is an art supermarket in Ireland. Everyone in Ireland knows Dunn's supermarkets. They're as Irish as Bunnings is Australian. So Mary's on the bus, travelling into work, thinking about, well, what most young people are thinking about. My main goal was getting money to go out the following weekend or buy clothes or do something. And travelling to work as normal, not knowing that this was going to be a day that would completely change my life. Oh boy, will it ever. Mary's in a union. And the union's asked its members not to handle any fresh produce that's been imported from South Africa. No unpacking it. No ringing it up at the cash register. And today's the first day of the action. Mary knows what a boycott is. It's when you stop dealing with a company or a country to protest this cruelty or exploitation. But she doesn't know much about what's going on in South Africa. We'd heard the word apart that we couldn't even pronounce it properly. We'd heard a Nelson Mandela and maybe Steve Biko. We didn't know anything about really what was happening in South Africa. Still, she's a loyal unionist. So when organisers call for a boycott, she jumps right in. That first morning, Mary stands at the till. Her manager's watching her super closely. And it's making Mary very, very nervous. When a customer brings a South African grapefruit to her register, Mary makes a decision that will change not only her life, it will change the course of a movement. I could see she had two grapefruit. And I was thinking to myself, don't come to my register. But she came to my register anyway. And I said to her that I couldn't handle them. We had a union policy in support of the Black people of South Africa. We were refusing to handle South African goods. And she was fired to boycott the goods. I was told I was suspended indefinitely. Suspended indefinitely. Ten other DUNS workers are suspended that day too. They all go on strike. The union's anticipating this. And it sets up a picket line right out at the front of the main store. One of its first supporters is legendary Black South African unionist Nimrod Sejake. He'd been a member of the African National Congress, the ANC, back home in the 1950s. And had been arrested and detained at one point with Nelson Mandela. He'd managed to leave the country. And eventually made his way to Ireland to live in exile as a political refugee. On those long days on the picket, Nimrod tells Mary about life under apartheid. About the violence and the racism and the injustice. But he explains it in a very Irish way. He told us that South Africa was like a pint of Guinness. I think at the time there were about 33 million Black people were ruled by about 2 million white people. And the white people sat on top of the Black people like a pint of Guinness. So they kept the Black down. So I suppose that was kind of something that we could visualize. Once we started to learn what was happening over there, you couldn't unsee it. Trust a South African and an Irish woman to bond over beer. Little does Mary Manning know that refusing to sell a single grapefruit will change the course of history. I'm Sisonkem Semang. And on ABC Rewind, this is Boycott. The fight to end apartheid. Episode 4. The Grapefruit Ladies. That same July in 1984, as Mary Manning's refusing to scan grapefruit in Dublin, I am sleepless in Canada. Until now, I've grown up in the ANC community in exile. First in Lusaka and then in Nairobi, Kenya. But we're citizens of nowhere. And my mom desperately wants us kids to be citizens of somewhere. And so we've settled in Canada. But because South Africa's in the news all the time, 10-year-old me worries a lot. I see police tankers, tear gas and bullets shooting at Black people. South Africa is starting to go up in flames. It's turning into a holocaust. Crossroads dawn. The wreckage from yesterday's fighting still smoulders. So does the anger. So will the war. These people of Crossroads, they were coming out of the police vehicles. We were looking at them, straight at them. And that keeps me wide awake at night. I have zero idea that all around the world, an army of ordinary people, like Mary Manning, is taking action to help kids like me be free from the shackles of apartheid. While I'm in bed worrying, the anti-apartheid movement has honed in on a clear tactic. To end apartheid, the flow of money has to stop. No money for sport, no money for culture or for South African businesses. Governments are going to have to make hard decisions. Question is, will they have the courage to do so? Unless the major Western countries impose sanctions against South Africa as a means of prodding further reforms, the black population will turn to violence. We in the West have to try and understand that the desire for political freedom, the desire for political rights, burns just as fiercely in the mind and the heart of a black as it does in our own. Until now, the most prolific boycotts have been on the sporting field. The Australian government banned white-only South African teams after the controversial Springbok rugby tour in 1971. But behind the headlines, it's trade unions leading the fight against apartheid, both inside and outside South Africa. And why are unions so involved? Well, sorry to go all Karl Marx on you, but that saying, workers of the world unite, it's been with us a long time, since the 1850s at least. And solidarity has been a core principle of union organizing ever since. No matter where workers happen to live, they support each other. So unions everywhere have been agitating for economic boycotts ever since the South African Communist Party and the ANC first asked them to in the late 1950s. It's been a slow burn, but it's now, in the 1980s, that things really kick off internationally. A few years before Mary's grapefruit moment, a young Australian merchant seaman called Joe Deacon flies into Cape Town to join a cargo ship. He jumps in a taxi at the airport with his mate Wally Pritchard. They head for the dock, and it doesn't take long before they're confronted by the reality of apartheid. On one side of the road, on the left-hand side of the road as we're driving, we see shantytowns with a barbed wire fence. Yet on the other side of the road, we've got these palatial homes. Joe and Wally are stunned. They've been hearing about apartheid through their union, the Seamans Union of Australia. But seeing it for themselves is something else. We said to the driver, what does this mean? And the driver said it very, very sharp and very short in two words. Pointing to the left-hand side where the shantytowns were, blacked. Pointing to the other side where the palatial homes were, white. And I thought, well, we... And when we bedded down in our hotel waiting for our vessel to bring it back to Australia, all through the night, you hear screaming, you hear gunshots. And that was my introduction to apartheid. And I was very determined from then on that I am going to play some sort of part in its downfall. If you're a seaman who works on cargo ships loaded with the oil that the apartheid regime needs to fuel its economy, obviously, it's only natural to use your voice to spark an oil embargo. When they get back to Australia, Wally and Joe take their plan to stop the supply of oil to South Africa to the head of the Australian Maritime Unions, Pat Garrity. And Pat said, yes, yes, but you need to do your homework, son. It needs to be a worldwide movement. Of course it does. Why go for anything less? So Wally gets in touch with the Danish seaman's union. Because the Danes, even though we had ships going to South Africa, the Danes had many tankers going there. It turns out that oil is apartheid's Achilles heel. Because South Africa has no commercial oil reserves. None. It relies entirely on oil imports. So, if you can stop oil getting into the country, then you just might be able to stop the army and the police from using its tanks, planes and helicopters to terrorise the black population. And of course, slow down the entire economy while you're at it. Soon enough, Australia's three maritime unions have convinced workers on ships and docks in Australia, Denmark and Britain to stop working on all vessels taking oil to South Africa. It got off the ground like a rocket. Through the firemen and deckheads, the union members who manned the tugs, they played a massive part in delaying ships, in stopping ships. Port workers refused to handle the lines of some vessels that they knew were trading with racist South Africa. And that had a massive effect. There are times when South Africa only has enough oil to last a week. The cost of oil imports doubles, and that hits the apartheid economy hard. But shipping companies don't like this. It hurts their bottom line. So they fight back against the boycott. They were threatening the union. Never stopped me from doing what I had to do. People were getting slaughtered by the colonialist machine. And we're going to sit there and twiddle our thumbs? No, we're not. And we said, in no uncertain terms, you could shove 45D of the Trade Practices Act where the sun doesn't shine. Shove those writs where the sun don't shine. I love it. All this resistance just makes the maritime workers even more radical. Australian unions are in close contact with unions in South Africa. In fact, their actions are almost always inspired by what's happening there. And boy, is there a lot happening. When government cracks down hard on black South Africans in the mid-80s, Australian unions expand their boycott, refusing to offload, pack up, or sell anything to do with South Africa, not just oil. A black ban on all things South African starts from midnight to night. It's aimed at bringing about what's described as progressive change in South Africa and the payment of proper award provisions to South African unionists. Australian postal workers refuse to process mail to South Africa. If you've got family or friends in South Africa, tough titties. And telecom workers refuse to connect international phone calls to and from the South African embassy in Canberra. Let them figure out how to communicate with their racist prime minister in Pretoria. It's a move which opposition leader John Howard has likened to shooting oneself in the foot. It's a futile exercise in terms of helping the blacks in South Africa. And it will probably backfire on a lot of Australians. And I think that's regrettable. I'm going to stick my neck out here and say that John Howard was on the wrong side of history on this one. There was nothing futile about helping black people in South Africa. In 1980 South Africa, life for black people is as bad as it's ever been. There is repression. There is death. There is detention of even children. There is torture. There is killings of activists inside prisons. There is hanging. But there is resistance. Matches. Defiance. Defiance. Zwellin Zimavavi is the General Secretary of the South African Federation of Trade Unions. He's also a bit of a hero of mine. Zwellin Zimavavi was born into a very poor family. One of 15 kids. And he grew up in a small rural village in the Northern Cape. His father, an itinerant farm worker. I know the life of evictions. Of dismissal of the parents of my father sitting on the middle of nowhere in the roadside. In the coldest Northern Cape winter. All of us cramping under the donkey cart. And all of us waiting for him to return. And he will walk all day having dismissed from this farm. Looking for opportunities in the next farms. And they will return empty handed. Zwellin Zimavavi doesn't go to school. Like so many little ones, he works. Putting up fences. Feeding animals. And in his part of the country, the farms produce nuts and citrus fruits. Yup. Including those grapefruits at the heart of Mary's strike. He grows up listening to stories about the treatment his parents and older siblings have had to endure. What really developed my political consciousness was the stories at home. In the fireplace. The stories will start almost every evening. The dismissals. The beating up of a certain so-and-so. Vavi stores all this away. Until he's working his first job as a young man in the 1980s. Now, I need you to picture this. Young Vavi is recruited to work in a mine. He's got no real choice. There are no other jobs. And he's poor. The mining company puts him on a train with thousands of other black workers. And he's sent to the colossal Anglo-American gold mine on the reef. Just outside Johannesburg. His identity pass is stamped. Vavi's only allowed to be in Johannesburg for work. When he gets to the mine, he's taken to the worker hostel, where he'll live. We were 15,000 workers in the hostel system. In their segregation. Zulus, Corsas, Pondos, Batas, Swatis, Mozambicans, Shangans, Lesotho, this side. The apartheid was being reinforced right into the single-sex hostel line. The single-sex hostel was like living inside a barricaded prison. It was like a concentration camp. Vavi and the 15,000 men he works with are only allowed to visit home once a year, at Christmas. That's the only time they can see their wives, their kids, their family and friends. This whole arrangement, the mine recruiter in rural areas, the train, the pass, the hostel and the once-a-year visit, it's the crucible of apartheid. It makes the companies very rich. It keeps the workers very poor and controls the movement of the black population. It's the primary reason apartheid exists. It's also the reason mine workers are at the forefront of pushing for change. By the 1980s, these horrendous conditions have led to the formation of a powerful new black union, the National Union of Mine Workers, the NUM. One of its founders is Cyril Ramaphosa, the current president of South Africa. And Vavi is a very active member. There is a conscious effort to make apartheid unworkable. There's defiance campaign after defiance campaign. And the funerals? The slogan then was, every time they kill one, they conscientize 10 more black people to fight. Every time they kill 10, they conscientize a thousand more. And every time they kill 100, they conscientize millions of people to join the struggle. So every funeral was a rally. As the unions mobilize inside South Africa, the temperature is getting high. This weekend, after a year of almost continuous violence, in which 500 people have died, the South African government has imposed a state of emergency in an attempt to extinguish protest against the country's apartheid laws. In 1985, the South African government declares a total state of emergency as it tries to control the deepening unrest. It gives security forces shoot-to-kill powers. And they are mass detentions. According to the Daily Police Bulletin, 792 people have now been arrested. But despite the arrest, violent deaths in the townships are continuing. Four people were killed in the township of Davidson in the last 24 hours, when police say army and riot units opened fire on a crowd that was stoning police vehicles. It's incredibly violent. The apartheid government has a taste for blood, and it cracks down hard. But the repression is met with a rising tide of defiance. Black political parties, like the ANC and the PAC, were banned back in the 1960s. But in 1979, under international pressure, the apartheid government legalizes black unions. And by the 1980s, they are mushrooming. They form the Congress of South African Trade Unions, COSATU. And around the world, unions take their cue from what COSATU is saying and doing. COSATU is talking with Australian unions, mailing them videos with intel about what's happening on the ground. Kim Sattler's a unionist and an anti-apartheid activist here in Australia, and she's watching those tapes. And we'd all sit in a room and watch these really dark, poorly filmed, terrible sound videos. But we got it from the horse's mouth. And when the boycott campaigns began and the messing with that message here in Australia was, you can't do boycott because it will stop people from being able to work and they will lose their jobs. COSATU actually had the workers who were directly affected that, telling us how important it was for them that we did boycott. And we tried to follow their guide around what to boycott. Saying that boycotts will only hurt black people in South Africa is an argument regularly thrown at by supporters of apartheid and by businesses and governments that don't want to lose money under trade sanctions with South Africa. Kim knows it's absolute BS. If the news wasn't enough, the tapes make it very clear. South African workers want boycotts and sanctions. So, at a moment of levity here, she decides to create a bit of mischief in the freezer aisle of a well-known supermarket that stocks South African goods. We imported a lot of fish from South Africa in that period. And one of the first things I remember doing was taking all the fish out of the frozen fish cabinets in the supermarkets and just leaving it out to thaw while I did my shopping. Oof! The stench of apartheid making its way through the aisles of the supermarket. Other activists, like Paul Kaplan in Perth, are also madly targeting companies doing business with South Africa. For months, we went weekly, on a Saturday morning, to a different store. Two, three, four, don't shop at coal stores! One, two, three, seven, eight, coal sales apartheid! Picketed it, put up our signs and banners, distributed leaflets telling people not to buy South African products and going to various Shell petrol stations and picketing them and telling people not to not to fill up with Shell. But here's the problem. A heap of individuals are taking extraordinary action against apartheid all around the world. They are trade unions doing what they can, sporting bodies banning South Africa from competing. But the movement needs economic sanctions. It needs governments to put their money where their mouth is and stop trading with South Africa. This is the next big fight. Historian Peter Lim has done the sums. During apartheid, Australia is making more money off trade with South Africa than ever before. From 1965 to 1992, Australian exports actually rose from 22 million to 334 million with companies such as BHP, IXL, profiting from trade with apartheid, even sometimes at the expense of Australian jobs. I mean, the Labour government in WA in the 80s imported railway bogies or suspension from South Africa even at a time when they were opposing apartheid. Rio Tinto Zinc made massive profits from mines in South Africa. In other words, the dollar spoke louder than morality. The dollar spoke louder than morality. Ain't that the truth? Given the lack of action from political leaders, the movement focuses on isolating South Africa, not just economically, but like, literally. The movement wants to make it hard for white South Africans to fly around the world as if nothing is wrong with their lifestyles. So, South African Airways becomes a big target. One of our big focuses was South African Airways shopfront. We would pick at it regularly, but in the end, South African Airways had to abandon that shopfront altogether and go up onto the second floor with security and everything. It's only a small win, but it contributes to a bigger payoff a few years later, when in 1987, the Australian government banned South African Airways from flying into Australia. one step closer to isolation. We went into the airport and sang and danced and chanted in joy as one of our main targets had been subject to the boycott at last. Back in Dublin, Mary Manning and her colleagues are eight months into picketing Dunn's supermarkets. There's some pretty miserable Irish weather, but the picketers are there regardless. This is the young Mary speaking with the Irish broadcaster RTE back in 1985. I have quite an awful lot of ground support out there for us. It's a surprise just to see how much support there was. But then again, you're always going to get downright racist. Are there racist around? There are. Which is, we never thought at the beginning of the strike that there was actually racist living in this country, but it's amazing how many people there are. We've been called n*** lovers and it shocked us to think that people thought that way about a person that the only difference is the colour of their skin. Like we were told all the blacks are forests, the jungle, they're only out of the trees, you know. And it really shocked us, you know. As Mary spends her days on the picket line, our family is living in Canada and Baba's working for a big international charity which runs humanitarian projects in different African countries. He's gone for long stretches and my mum carries the load on her own. We have zero contact with friends and family in South Africa. Baba's still not allowed back into the country. But we see enough on the news to know what's happening there. Another four people have been killed in the last 24 hours. But how did they die? Kerry Wheel put that question to the police public relations officer in Pretoria, Major Van Royen. The mob was dispersed with shotgun and rifle fire so I take it they were shot. By your security forces? Yes, oh yes. Does that give you concern at all? Oh yes, most definitely. We don't like to shoot people. But revolution is in the air and another new organization is in town. The United Democratic Front. Now, unlike the unions, the UDF is a little harder for the government to dismiss because the UDF is an alliance. It includes unions but it's also got neighborhood associations, young people's organizations and crucially, church groups. These other groups give the UDF cover because it's one thing to fight a union, it's another to fight the church. Now, let me tell you something. South Africans are deeply religious and so, it's no surprise that a priest emerges as a key leader of the UDF. And he's not just any priest. His name is Bishop Desmond Tutu, a black bishop and he's a remarkable man. The day anybody can show me that the Bible supports a partake, that day I will take my Bible and tear it into little strips and I will stop being a Christian. Desmond Tutu wears the Anglican church's purple cassock with a tasseled belt around his waist like what medieval monks wore and he's slight with a twinkle in his eye and a laugh that fills the room. But his stature is deceiving. Desmond Tutu is a force. His words have power. Bishop Tutu regularly puts his body on the line, standing with his arms outstretched to protect protesters from the police. And his message is consistent. He doesn't preach moderation. We do not want apartheid reformed. We don't, I mean, who wants Frankenstein reformed? We want apartheid destroyed. Bishop Desmond Tutu's efforts gain global recognition. And in October 1984, he's awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. On his way to Sweden to pick up his prize, Tutu makes an important stopover. He's heard about the Dunn's shop workers in Dublin who refuse to scan South African produce. And so, Bishop Tutu visits Mary Manning and her fellow protesters. That was one of the big turning points because we had the priests and nuns putting up an argument that you're hurting the black people of South Africa. Well, here was a black bishop of South Africa who was saying, you know what, we should be commended for what we're doing. So people started to kind of say, well, you know, maybe they're not wrong. Maybe there is something in this because he was a religious man that made a lot of people who were using the religious aspect of it, you know, they couldn't use that argument anymore. It's been a really hard few months for Mary and the other strikers. They're being slammed in the media, labelled troublemakers. But now, a man of the cloth, a Nobel laureate is on their side and Ireland starts to see that the Dunn store workers may be more than just fringe radicals. While the striking grapefruit ladies are getting a boost, in Australia, on the other side of the world, the anti-apartheid movement has a major setback. Ever since the controversial Springbok rugby tour in 1971, Australia's ban on playing South African sporting teams has held strong. South Africa's also been kicked out of the Olympics. It's in Sporting Siberia. But then, an Australian cricket tour of South Africa is announced. It's a shocking development. And a flagrant thumbing of the nose to the anti-apartheid movement that thought it had won this fight, but apparently not. The proposed tour of South Africa by Australian cricketers has struck a raw nerve with the Hawke government. The Prime Minister has opposed the trip and threatened that the players involved can expect close scrutiny of their financial affairs by the tax office. I respect the right of people to have a different point of view, but on the issue of race and colour, this government is immovable. I and this government will not change our view about that obnoxious system of apartheid. Graham Yellops, one of the cricketers, offered a chance to go. And for him, well, the decision's pretty cut and dried. We're over there purely and simply to play cricket and we're not concerned with the politics of the country. These days, you can earn millions playing cricket overseas. But in the 80s, if you play cricket for Australia, you also need a day job. Players only make about 12 grand a year. The Rebel players are being offered $200,000 to go on the tour. It's a huge amount of money at the time. So for many of them, it's a no-brainer. Australian pace bowler Carl Rackerman also says yes to the tour. Obviously, there was going to be some criticism, but it wasn't something that was unexpected and it wasn't something that really bothered us that much. There was polls taken that showed we had something like 70% support from the Australian public. So that was probably more important to us than the few critics. Most people, and certainly myself, we went for financial considerations. That was the bottom line and this was a lot of insurance for my future. The Hawk government calls the players mercenaries. But the public's thinking, if the government's not prepared to take a stand and stop trading with South Africa, why should cricketers take the fall? Lots of players, including Australian captain Alan Border, refuse to join the Rebels. But star West Australian player Kim Hughes does sign up and protesters make him pay. They travel from one suburban cricket pitch to another, disrupting his Perth club games until one day someone gets hurt. An ABC reporter called Debbie Bishop, who was a fearless reporter, she went to Kim Hughes' home ground, Floriat. She was confronted by the manager of Floriat Club and thrown down the stairs and had her arm broken. The night before, someone, not part of our group, had damaged the cricket pitch at Stephen's Obel. So when we arrived on the Saturday with our batters and placards, the police were there in large numbers and then suddenly the TRG, the tactical response group, swooped on us and arrested five of us, including me, chucked us in the paddy wagons. Once again, police violence is used against sports protesters. At backyard barbecues, school pickups, around the proverbial water cooler, everyone in Perth is talking about the rebel cricket tour. One of them is a socially conscious young man who's part of a church youth group. We had a regular group meeting that we called the Third World Group and we'd actually talk about Third World and social justice issues. His name is Simon White. Simon and his mates are trying to work out what playing cricket has to do with supporting apartheid. How do sports boycotts help anything? They want to write about this for the church newsletter, The Gnat. And they're trying to work out who to talk to about this when old maid Derek pipes up. And our friend Derek said, well, before I left work I looked it up and I've got Desmond Tutu's phone number. Why don't we give him a call? What? I have so many questions about this. They seriously think they can call up the Nobel Prize winning Bishop Desmond Tutu who spends his days mediating conflict in apartheid South Africa? Bless. And we were just like, you can't do that. You can't just call up the guy. And he said, why not? We've got his number. Let's give it a go. So we called up the phone. Somebody answered and we said, can we speak to Bishop Tutu? This is ridiculous. And the person who answered the phone said, hold on a minute. And then we were talking to Bishop Tutu and we just said to him, oh, hi, you know, we're kind of a bit starstruck here that we we just explained who we were. We're a group of people in a small group attached to a church and we wanted to ask him. So he proceeded to spend the next half an hour talking to us what the rebel cricket tour meant for people in South Africa. Do you remember what he said specifically? Obviously, he was totally against it. He saw these people as sort of mercenaries. He, of course, talked about sports and politics and said how you can't distinguish between the two and how this is hitting a regime where it hurts. It was just a lovely connection with a guy who I think was such a charismatic figure in that period. And such a hero. I'll end up marrying this man, Simon White. Clearly, we were always meant to find our way to each other. the cricket tour and the cricket tour was going to be in the future. Anyhow, despite all the protests, the cricket tour goes ahead. Despite international condemnation of their lucrative two-season tour, he said the rebels were proud of their actions and Hughes answered criticisms that his team was made up of cricketing has-beens. We've got a new name for the team and it's called the A-Team. The players' performances on the field will be just the same as if they were in the official cricket side. For the record, white South Africa wins most of the games. But it's not just cricket. Pretty soon, a rebel Australian rugby team also tours. And it's equally controversial. But that's enough about sport. I'm getting a headache. A year after Mary Manning refused to scan that South African grapefruit, the Dunn store workers are still out of work, still on the picket line outside the main shopfront in central Dublin. Mary and her colleagues are surviving on a small stipend from the union, 21 pounds a week. They're still considered troublemakers, even if their support is growing slightly. But when Bishop Desmond Tutu visits them on his way to pick up the Nobel Peace Prize, he invites them to South Africa so they can see apartheid for themselves. They spend months fundraising for their affairs. And finally, Mary and her eight colleagues board a flight to Johannesburg. They are so excited. For most of them, it's their first time overseas. I've estimated it right about quarter to the hour and we made it a few minutes on the leg. But when they land... We noticed there was a load of soldiers on the tarmac and kind of didn't think anything about it because we just told us we didn't know what it was like over there. And we were brought into the airport and we were approached by someone in the airport and they said, follow us. So there was 32 armed guards, some in front for some behind us, going up three or four flights of stairs. Are a few shop assistants from Ireland really that much of a threat to the security of South Africa that they need 32 armed men? The women are terrified by the presence of so many men with guns. After all... The only news we heard of coming from South Africa was people falling out windows and falling downstairs. They've heard the stories about the special branch police throwing activists out of windows and pushing them down stairwells. So we were terrified. I mean, literally, nobody knew where we were at this stage. Mary and her friends spend eight hours in an airless room at the airport, confused, tired, and anxious. Then finally, they're told they can't enter the country. They won't get to see apartheid and segregation for themselves, won't get to talk to black South Africans to hear firsthand about the violence and the repression. Through my father, really, he was there during the war. And I remember him saying to me, he said, you won't like what you see there in terms of the people, exploitation of people. episodes.title: Why David Pocock thinks the new gambling reforms are "infuriating"
episodes.description: The Australian Government has introduced new reforms around gambling advertising in an attempt to shield young sports fans from the negative impacts of problem gambling.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. What's gambling really costing you? For free and confidential support, call the number on the screen or visit the website. If you're a sports fan, I can imagine you've heard that disclaimer before. The Australian government has announced a raft of gambling reforms that come into effect in January next year. The reforms include restricting gambling advertising on broadcast TV between 6am and 8.30pm, ban it completely during live sport and on radio at school drop-off and pick-up times, and a ban of online ads where it can't be verified that the users are over 18. The government says the aim is to reduce the exposure that children have to gambling companies, but many are calling for more action. Given the amount of income that sports betting brings into the major sporting codes in Australia, finding a balance will need more than just taking a punt. I'm Poppy Penny and this is ABC Sport Daily. David Pocock is a former Wallaby and is now an independent senator in the ACT, who has long been vocal about the need for gambling reform in Australia. David, earlier this month, the government introduced stricter regulations around gambling advertising to limit children's exposure to gambling harm. What kind of harm does gambling do in this country? Well, per capita, we're the biggest losers in the world. Gambling has been normalised by gambling advertising to the point where three out of four young Australians now think that gambling and betting on sport is just a normal part of enjoying sport. And this is something that the parliament has been grappling with for a number of years now. We're not doing something radical here in Australia. We're playing catch-up. What's radical in Australia is that we have the greatest gambling losses of anywhere in the world, 40% higher than the nation that comes second. What do you do in a society where you have something that can become a real issue for people in our community, so normalised by the gambling industry, and then raking in massive, massive profits? And so the parliament had an inquiry, and there were 31 recommendations saying, this is a public health issue. This is how we can actually turn this around. And one of the central recommendations was to actually have a phased-in ban on all gambling advertising, saying, if you just make some tweaks, history shows us that this is an industry that finds loopholes. And so we just need to go with a full gambling ad ban in recognition that no one's saying you can't have a bet, but we've got to stop the normalisation of gambling in our community. We are getting the balance right. Letting adults have a punt if they want to. But making sure that our children don't see betting ads everywhere they look. You've been on record in saying that these reforms are hugely disappointing. Why is that? For a number of reasons. The big one being that history shows us that partial bans don't work, and that's why this landmark Murphy report, which was backed by every party in the parliament, and every independent in the parliament, said a three-year phased-in ban on all gambling advertising is the only way that we can actually deal with this. The government, when they announced they were going with a partial ban, then delivered the analysis underlying that. And if you actually read the government's own analysis, it shows that a full ban would be cheaper to implement because there's less regulation involved. It's just a blanket ban that comes in over three years. And it would actually provide more benefits to Australians. So we've got a government that has gone for the option that doesn't actually put Australians first. It's an option that the gambling industry will be happy to live with. Between 6am and 8.30pm, we will cap the number of TV ads for betting agencies at a maximum of three per hour. We will ban all gambling ads on radio during school pickup and drop off. Beyond that, there are huge issues with things like inducements, where people get bonus bets, free bets. And if you talk to researchers in this space, they are the most harmful part of the whole sort of gambling advertising and the way that they hook people. Because we know that it's actually a smaller number of Australians that are losing the most money. And often that is off the back of free bets, bonus bets, where people feel like it's risk-free. And that's where we see a lot of people, particularly young men, getting into a lot of trouble. And the government has just not even gone with that recommendation. And that was the most urgent recommendation that was given three years ago. They said that inducements should be banned immediately. Government's not doing that. So wide sweeping reform would have significant impact on the bottom line of a number of sporting codes and broadcast partners and that sort of thing. If you could pick just one thing to change from these government's reforms, what's the top of the tree for you? Well, the gambling ads is the big one. It's what's normalising gambling. It's what's setting up young people for failure. And if we're going to turn this around as a country, you have to look at gambling advertising. We believe that Australians wanted in particular, and the terms of reference to the Win Sum You Lose Sum report, wanted in particular the reduction of exposure of children to gambling advertising. So the reforms that we have landed, and you would have seen Free TV, who is the peak for broadcast television, come out and say this will have a really significant impact to their bottom line. So this has been difficult. And nonetheless, we have made meaningful reform. Yeah, there is the reality that free-to-air television sports broadcasters are deriving income from this. A couple of our major sports now actually get a kickback, a percentage of each bet placed on, say, NRL, AFL. The report from Peter Murphy and her colleagues actually raised concerns and said, listen, we're losing sight of what sport is actually about in this country, and it's no longer just about the enjoyment, the community, the challenge. It's now just it's becoming the sort of avenue to market gambling. So I would go there as to the impacts, you know, we could put a one and a half, two percent levy on bets in this country and more than compensate free-to-air television and probably invest a lot, lot more money into things like community sport, grassroots sport than is currently being invested. So, you know, this is just about political will. And yet again, we're seeing vested interests being put ahead of the interests of the Australian people. Kids are still going to be seeing gambling ads. So that's what Murphy said to stop. Have you canvassed the Greens and or the Coalition for their support on some of these reforms or what you're proposing? Working on it, I'm concerned that the Coalition will wave these through. I think that's really disappointing given what I hear from a lot of people in the Coalition is the talk of family values and focusing on the family. And I don't see what is more squarely about family values than actually protecting young people from a predatory industry. So I would love to see some pushback from the Coalition to actually say at a bare minimum, we've got to fix some of the loopholes in what's been proposed. And, you know, a big one for me is the PM announced that there'll be no gambling ads on sport before 8.30pm. We all know that a whole heap of games kick off at 7.55, 8pm. And so the second half of these games, there are no rules. And so for the Coalition, I'd say at least go with what your former leader, Peter Dutton, said where at least an hour before and an hour after we're not going to have any gambling advertising if they're not willing to actually go with the full ad van. You mentioned the fact that we know that money from gambling is deeply tied to broadcast deals, which is tied to the game and the promotion and the growth of some of our major sporting codes. Both Andrew Abdo and Gillian McLaughlin are both on the record as saying that it contributes heavily to funding grassroots and the women's game for both of those codes. The fans like the fact that child prices are $5, adults are $27. We like that we're investing $55 million in game development every year. How realistic is it to implement further reform without massively compromising some of those things? I mean, I think you've got to start. You know, I'm a former freshman athlete, so I get what this means for sports. But I think we've all got to step back and say, well, what is sport actually for? And I think at its core, sport is about so much that is good in our society, a place where communities can come together, get to know people that you otherwise wouldn't hang out with, challenge yourself physically, mentally, and be part of something bigger than yourself. We cannot lose sight of that. As to the raw dollars and cents, again, something like a levy could actually ensure that there is more money for things like grassroots sport, for women's sports. So I think it's a real cop-out. So, yeah, I'm a little bit cynical about some of the lines that we get, but I do get the financial side of things. And the thing I say to my parliamentary colleagues is, well, let's solve that. But we've seen the real-life cases come forward in that Murphy report and since, and these are people who have felt the real adverse effects of problem gambling. Have you heard from any of those people in response to these reforms? I have. So many people. It is devastating to hear people talk about either their experience or, in the most tragic cases, talking about a loved one that has taken their life due to gambling addiction. And the thing that often comes up in that is that people who know they have a problem and are trying to deal with it, they say, you cannot escape it. Everywhere you turn, there are ads. When you're on a losing streak, you're getting inducements. It is not working. And so I find it not just disappointing, but actually really infuriating that we have political leaders, well, in some instances won't even meet with those people, but must know that that harm is happening and still puts vested interests ahead of protecting Australians, doing the right thing. And no one is saying that we should make gambling illegal. There's a ridiculous argument that gets rolled out by the Prime Minister and others. All we're saying is let's actually protect young Australians. Let's not put people in a situation where it is so hard to find help. And in the last year or so, Poppy, I've noticed such a big increase in the number of young men who've pulled me aside at events saying, hey, could we just talk privately? And then they say, thanks so much for what you're doing on gambling. I'm struggling with it. And it is so hard because you're just getting smashed with ads. And all the ads portray it as something that is so much fun. You know, you're hanging out with your mates. You're having wins. You're betting on the footy. The reality is, is that I'm staring at my screen in bed by myself at 3am chasing losses. People really wanted that saturation and targeting of gambling advertising reduced. And they wanted the exposure of children to gambling advertising reduced. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Minister for Communications, Annika Wells, are both adamant that these reforms have struck the right balance between allowing Australians the freedom to have a bed, as you say, it's not about making gambling illegal, but protecting children from the harm that it can cause, particularly with some of the advertising. Do you think that there's a possibility that these reforms are, at the very least, a step in the right direction to potentially stronger reforms like the ones that you're proposing? Well, they're clearly better than nothing. I don't think we should settle for better than nothing as Australians. They can clearly be strengthened. But, you know, in terms of striking the right balance, again, this is something that the Parliament grappled with through the Murphy inquiry. And they said, you know, a phased in ban over three years would allow sports to make some adjustments. I think something like a levy could plug that gap. My concern with this is everything I've seen from the Albanese Labour government is that if they make a small tweak to an issue, they then just say, OK, we've done that. And every time you ask a question about, hey, you made that reform, it's not really working or didn't go far enough. They'll just say, listen, we did it. It's working great. Let's move on. And so I really do think this is an opportunity for the Parliament to at least make these reforms a lot better. And I think that that's the test for MPs and senators. Who are you here to represent? And I really hope that, you know, the coalition work with the crossbench in the Senate to ensure that we at least have reforms that don't have ridiculous things like no ads in the first half, but second half there'll be a deluge of gambling ads. That just doesn't cut it. David Pocock, it's an ongoing conversation and we're looking forward to seeing how it plays out. Thanks so much for your time. Thanks a lot, Poppy. Headlines. New South Wales and Queensland have today announced their women's state of origin squads ahead of Game 1 next week. New South Wales will bring back 14 players from the team that won the Series 2-1 last year. Plus, welcome back Millie Elliott, who will make her return after giving birth in September. The Maroons are facing the enormous challenge of replacing Ali Brigginshaw and Taryn Aitken, who are both unavailable for selection and have named five potential debutantes. Soccer and former Premier League champions Leicester City have been relegated to the third tier of English football next season, just 10 years after winning the title. A decade ago, they were champions of England. They lifted the Premier League trophy here, but tonight they are relegated to League One, the fifth club in the Premier League era to suffer back-to-back relegations. This will be the second time in their 142-year existence that they have played in the third tier comp. Netball Australia CEO Stacey West has announced her resignation after less than three years in the role. West was appointed back in December 2023 and guided the organisation through a time where the sport was struggling financially and was in a dispute with players about pay. Mark Falvo will serve as interim CEO. And Rugby Australia have announced that they're back in the black after a successful British and Irish Lions tour, turning $36.8 million in losses last year into a tick over $70 million in profit this year. I'm Poppy Penny and this is ABC Sport Daily produced by Declan Byrne. Thanks to Sky Channel 9 and BN Sports for the extra audio used in this episode. We'll see you next time.

Soccer and former Premier League champions Leicester City have been relegated to the third tier of English football next season,
just 10 years after winning the title.

the fifth club in the Premier League era to suffer back-to-back relegations.

I'm Poppy Penny and this is ABC Sport Daily produced by Declan Byrne.
Thanks to Sky Channel 9 and BN Sports for the extra audio used in this episode.
We'll see you next time.

episodes.title: Tom Boyd on the ‘suffocating nature’ of footy in wake of Elijah Hollands’ episode
episodes.description: Elijah Hollands’ mental health episode against Collingwood on Thursday night has raised many questions, particularly of the Carlton Football Club. How did this happen? Why was he allowed to stay on the ground?
episodes.transcript: Just a heads up before we get into today's episode, it is discussing mental health. ABC Listen, podcasts, radio, news, music and more. We are determined to ensure a considered process, not just an understanding of what happened, but to ensure the key learnings come from this, not just for us, but the broader football community and industry. That's Carlton CEO Graham Wright speaking about the ongoing investigation into Elijah Holland's mental health episode on field against Collingwood last Thursday night. Vision of Holland's in-game has spread like wildfire and the questions of Carlton and their handling of this have come thick and fast. How could this have happened? Why was he allowed to play? And how can we stop this from happening again? I'm Poppy Penny and this is ABC Sport Daily. Tom Boyd is a premiership player for the Western Bulldogs and since retiring, in 2019 has been an advocate for mental health and wellbeing. Tom, I know your experience and what Elijah Holland's has experienced are different things, but I'm hoping to talk about how this has and might continue to play out through your eyes. How did you feel about what you were seeing on Thursday night in the match between Carlton and Collingwood? Yeah, thanks for having me for starters. I think one of the things that's critically important to understand is that regardless of what's actually happened during these moments when really significant attention grabbing issues pop up within the footy world in particular, these things tend to be extremely polarising and it obviously creates an enormous amount of speculation. And I'm probably one of the few people, I suppose, who's experienced a combination of things, a huge amount of attention and mental health being at the core component of that. And so for me, I think really around the responsibility that we all have and the lifelong impacts that these types of moments can have. And I think there's this naivety in many ways that people have to say, hey, it's just a 48 hour news cycle. It'll go away in two days or a week. That's not really how it works. What happens, and I've experienced this firsthand for the better and the worse, is that your entire life can be shaped by these moments. And it infects every part of your life into the future. And so for me, you know, as a father of two young kids, I put myself in the position of really just looking at it to say, if this was my kid, how would I want them to be treated? And what would I want them to feel from the support of the football public and his friends, family members, and of course, the footy club as well? Carlton have since come out and said that this was a mental health episode for him on the field and that they were aware he was struggling during the game. We were aware that he was struggling in the game and he's had, potentially had anxiety previously and panic attacks. And our guys were dealing with him in the game that obviously he was having some problems. You've been inside the four walls of a footy club and as you say, are really uniquely placed to speak about this. How is it possible that he played three and a bit quarters of footy? Yeah, I've thought about this from both angles, frankly. To look at it through the lens of the actual pragmatic preparation for a game of footy, I can see both arguments, right? I can see the fact that really building momentum for a game of footy is like a wave. You start, you enter the ground, you build up, build up, build up. And everyone's job is one, as a player, to get themselves to the position where they can play their best footy. But for the support staff, the coaching staff, the medical staff, their job is to get their players to the point where they can play the best game. And that really is the number one, two, three, four and five priority. And whilst I can see the concept that people would say, with all of those touch points, did they not notice something throughout the warm-up and the lead-up? And I don't know the answer to that. And again, to your point off the top, I don't really feel the need to speculate. But what I can say is that that heightened pressure as you lead into not just any game of footy, but the game of footy of Collingwood and Carlton at the MCG with 80,000 people is incredibly difficult to pick out moments in time and then go, yeah, there's a trend of an issue here rather than people seeing erratic moments over any course of time. And that's regardless of the issue. And the second thing I would say is that as you do build up to these games of footy, there is a great hesitation from staff and support, staff in particular, to knock people off their game. And the concept that someone would go in and say, hey, you don't see me yourself today as this player goes to put themselves out in front of 80,000 people, I think is a pretty questionable concept. At the risk that they were wrong and then they throw this player off and the player has a bad game. This is quite a severe set of consequences that could exist. And so for me, I think through the lens of the fact that one, as we talk about this topic, I think it's critically important that we don't talk about Elijah, but we talk about the issue as a whole and how in any moment within a game of football, if this injury of sorts was considered to be an Achilles or a knee, they would have been brought off the ground. And the question from my point of view is rather than focusing on the club or the player, if you focus on the issue, how can this be better served and supported into the future? So we use this as a learning moment and a point of improvement rather than something that we continue to regret into the future. Since the game, we have been working through a thorough process surrounding the circumstances both leading into and throughout the match and remain in close consultation with the AFL and the AFL-PA. So as you say, the AFL has strict injury and concussion protocols. If a player hurts their hamstring, they're out for the rest of the game. If they get a head knock and is concussed, they miss the following week. Do we need some kind of similar framework to check in with players around their mental health, both pre-game, post-game and also in-game? Yeah, it's an interesting concept. I think it is a challenging framework to implement. I'm probably not the academic person to talk through around what that could look like. And to be fair, there is a lot of connection, in particular with the assistant coaches, the medicos and those types of things as you progress players to get ready, right? And I think this is one of the interesting parts is you sort of arrive at the ground, you deal with the medicos first. We understand that Elijah's got some mental health issues and he's been very open and honest with that. But I feel like he's got great medical people. We've got fantastic medical staff here who have a long history with Elijah as well and understanding his issues. Then you move to the assistant coaches, then the senior coach, and then you go out with the trainers and you start the game. And I think that broadly speaking, the perspective of all of those people, I mean this as genuinely as I can, is they want the best for everyone there. And that is a really important thing to keep at the forefront of our minds. Whether there was mistakes made or issues that could have been prevented, that's another conversation. The intention of these people is incredibly pure and that's why they're in the jobs that they're in. And so for me, I'm not sure on the practical solution in terms of putting a framework in place to actually vet players. And I'm not sure how that would practically work, whether it's feasible academically or not. But I do think that this sort of overall concept, and this was something, by the way, that came up when I actually took time off the game. My message to the public was, just like any other injury, I need to rehabilitate myself to get back out and do my job. And if we look at it through the lens of that and the safety of our players and our people and our staff and the players that obviously make the game possible, I think that's going to serve us well in how we treat these things moving forward. Elijah himself has spoken about his own mental health battles and he's spoken publicly about a game last season against Sydney where he came off and he felt like he's like he couldn't breathe, he wasn't contributing. He described it himself as a mini panic attack. Have you ever experienced anything like that? What would that be like for him in game? Yeah, and I think it's important to remember that these games are not just one moment in time, right? It's not like the game itself is the episode. And I'm talking from my own personal point of view now, rather than what happened last Thursday night. From my perspective, it was a cumulative effect over a number of years as I continue to have worse and worse issues, particularly around sleep. And by the way, particularly around sleep leading into games. And so the concept of turning up to a game of footy where, and I often say, you know, it'd be great to play in front of 60,000, but I used to play in front of about 25 as a Bulldogs player. Turning up in front of 25,000 people, completely underdone from a rest and recovery point of view, unable to concentrate. And then really trying to use whatever means are necessary to get myself to concentrate and focus and prepare so that I don't end up on the back page of the paper as the person who failed. It's an extraordinary amount of stress to add on to what already is an incredibly stressful environment being an AFL footballer. And so for me, I know a lot of players who have dealt with the challenges of preparation for games. And obviously, this is an example where it spills down into something that's more visual rather than what I would say a lot of players are dealing with under the surface as they prepare for these high pressure environments. Yeah, he sort of feels like he's let people down, but we've just got to keep supporting people through those situations. In your experience, when you did come in feeling maybe like you weren't well enough rested or you weren't entirely 100% mentally or physically ready for a match, did you feel as though you had opportunities to say to someone, I don't feel right, I'm not right to play mentally? Yeah, probably all week up until game day. And this is one of the great challenges of professional sport. It's really the defining factor that says to me, we need to learn how to manage these things rather than hoping. It seems unreasonable to me that we're going to massively prevent every issue. It's a really competitive environment. It's incredibly stress inducing and high pressure. And so for me, like anyone, whether it's mental or physical, most of the players that you see running around on the screen every single week have some significant health issue of some kind, right? Whether they have got an ankle that's hurt or a hamstring that's sore or a back that needs surgery or a shoulder for that matter, as I played with for a long time. The challenge with the mental side of things is that these can be incredibly long lasting issues. They don't get the same treatment because they're not as obvious in terms of how to deal with it. And the rehabilitation, by the way, it doesn't have as clear a milestones, right? When a finger is broken, you can see when it's healed. And this is where I think one of the great challenges for the game is how do we think about the sustainable and long looking approach to our players who are making the game possible? Because often is the case that we look at these things very short term and it is the next game that's the most important. The conversation is getting louder around the competition for some kind of mental health round to shine a bigger light on this issue. Bailey Smith added his voice to that chorus as well. I just want to shout out the Dawson family this week and Elijah Hollins last night. I don't know if I'm out of pocket saying it, but I think it's about time the AFL get a men's mental health round. It just makes me feel sick during the week and hopefully the AFL community wraps their arms around them and we can do something. Is it something you'd like to see? Do you think this is something that could have an impact? Look, my perspective is this. I think that there is a value to bringing attention to an issue in an incredibly specific and heightened way and we do it with every issue. But really what I see is the greatest opportunity for the game of the AFL circles is that they can be the greatest force for improving overall health, not just mental health, in our society today. And the clear goals from the game that they've laid out in their strategy is to grow participation by a huge amount over the course of the next six, seven or eight years as they approach 2030. And by and large, if they just execute on that in an effective way, they're going to make a positive impact in this space. If you layer onto that, that if a concerted effort was made to prioritize the mental health of those communities that they're engaging with anyway, in some way, shape or form through partners, awareness, education, support, funding, you name it, they're going to make an enormous impact. And this is why I see the opportunity for a mental health round, not to be a review of everything that's gone wrong, but actually a great way to celebrate the incredible impact that our game does has as of this day, but equally to encourage that concerted effort over an extended period of time and use that, I suppose, it's a review and celebration point for the progress that we've made in the last 12 months. So I certainly would be behind it. Just finally on Elijah and his family, his dad put up a heartfelt post about his quote, beautiful boy on Instagram today after the news that he's been admitted to hospital. His brother, Ollie, plays in that same team and is potentially in the team for this weekend's game against Fremantle. We saw what Jordan Dawson has been through with his brother in the last week or so. How would you like to see the AFL community, be it fans or footy clubs, wrap its arms around players in times like this? Yeah, I think it's important to remember just the magnitude, as I mentioned earlier, of the suffocating nature of what's going on at the moment. I mean, this is a position I personally have been in where you don't feel like you can leave the house. You don't feel like you can have a conversation with anyone. You have a very, very small circle of trusted people who feel like you actually can rely on and feel like who they support you. And as with this conversation has evolved, obviously, since Thursday night, I think it's critically important to remember the sheer magnitude of what this conversation actually means, not only for Elijah's life, but also for the people who are close to him, the broader footy club and the community as a whole. And if nothing else, if we can put ourselves in the shoes of that person being someone that we care about and realising that the game's ability to impact mental health in a positive way is incredibly important. Tom Boyd, thank you so much for sharing your experience with us. We really appreciate it. Thanks for having me. And if you or anyone you know is struggling, you can always contact Lifeline on 13 11 14. Headlines. The NRL have moved to bring in new safety guidelines for the men's and women's competitions to limit contact training. In season, men's players are to engage in no more than 100 minutes of contact training on a regular seven day turnaround. And for NRLW athletes, that drops to 85 minutes. For both men and women on five and six day turnarounds, that drops to 40 and 50 minutes respectively. During the NRL preseason, the limit is no more than 200 minutes per week. And for NRLW, it's 115 minutes. The changes come in a bid to reduce injuries, including concussion. Staying with NRL and the Dragons have named Dean Young as their interim coach for at least the rest of 2026. The changes continue at St. George Illawarra with assistant coach Michael Ennis parting ways with the club just 24 hours after head coach Shane Flanagan. AFL and Zach Butters has had his $1,500 fine for abusive or offensive language toward an umpire overturned after the tribunal deemed there had been a miscarriage of justice. What was that miscarriage? Tribunal member Jason Johnson was driving his car during final submissions and Port Adelaide successfully argued that he could not have properly considered the deliberations if he was also focused on driving. Long story short, Zach Butters is no longer out of pocket $1,500. I'm Poppy Penny and this is ABC Sport Daily produced by Declan Byrne.

episodes.title: Shane Flanagan is gone, but do the Dragons’ problems run deeper?
episodes.description: In round 23 of last year the St George Illawarra Dragons were celebrating a win over the Sharks and a contract extension for coach Shane Flanagan.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. This is clearly a significant moment for the club. We understand the disappointment and frustrations from our members and our fans feel and we know that results and performances have not met expectations from this proud club. Dragons CEO Tim Watsford announcing that the club and coach Shane Flanagan have mutually agreed to part ways after a 0-7 start to the year. The Dragons have lost 11 straight matches, their last win over the Sharks in 2025, right after Flanagan signed a contract extension. He didn't make it to that extension. We've only made it through seven rounds this season and we've seen two coaches moved on already. Can the Dragons follow in Manly's footsteps and change their 2026 fortunes with a change at the top or do their problems run much deeper? I'm Poppy Penny and this is ABC Sport Daily. Michael Kariannis writes about Rugby League for News Corp. And MC, the Dragons have come out today and said they have mutually agreed to part ways with coach Shane Flanagan after just 54 games at the helm, along with the general manager of football, Ben Harren. Can you walk us through this decision from management? Yeah, obviously big news out of the Dragons this morning and I don't think anyone's shocked by it. It had been coming because the Dragons just kept losing matches and 11 straight losses now dating back to last year. So it's been a bit of a horror show for St. George of the War over the past few months and culminated in two big scalps, the head of football, Ben Harren and coach Shane Flanagan. I want to begin by confirming that head coach Shane Flanagan and general manager of football, Ben Harren, have departed the St. George of the War over the Dragons by way of mutual agreement. Flanagan was re-signed the week after they beat the Raiders and before they beat the Sharks in round 23 last season, which actually just happened to be the last two wins he coached them to. Party time at Coggera. What a celebration for the first time in 11 starts after 10 straight losses. It's a drought-breaking derby win in most impressive circumstances for the Dragons. In the week they re-signed their coach Shane Flanagan, this is the players saying, and Flano we trust. It's a big win for them. He didn't actually even make it to that extension. How did we get from those results to today? It's unbelievable. It really is. Who would have thought that he would have been sacked before or parted ways with the club before he won another game after inking that contract extension? It was just unheard of that that was the case. So, yeah, it's a surprise, no doubt about it, back then. But given the way the season transpired, they just can't find a way to win games. Gold Coast 22, St George, Illawarra 14. The Dragons remain winless. That's the issue. The roster's not great. And as a result, their coach is no more. The CEO and chairman were at pains to stress today in the press conference that this was a mutual agreement. Can I make the point, we've already made this statement, you say moving on, that's not what we just said. We talked about a mutual agreement. And as I said, we've been speaking with Shane and the football staff along the way. This is not something that you just do because you choose to on a Monday morning. How mutual do you think it really was? Or is that just a big saving face exercise for everybody? Oh, a little bit of, I think Shane knew his time was up. There's no doubt about that. I think he felt, you know, he'd got the best out of the playing group. And those days, like, of trying to fight his way out because he was, you know, a month ago, he was quite steadfast in his belief that he could turn the tide. All I know is I can just do my best. And that's what I do every day when I go to work. Making sure that we prepare the team the best we can. It hasn't worked so far this year. But, you know, I'm not going to give up. I think he came to the realisation that perhaps this was a task a little bit too hard for him now. He did say a week ago, you know, he thought he hadn't lost the dressing room. Players have taken ownership. We haven't lost the dressing room. We had a good training session today. We're in good meetings. I've got a good relationship with all my players. Do you think that that is the case, that he genuinely felt like that? Or was that a line trotted out by a coach who knew he was in trouble? No, I think he felt like that. I think he felt like that. Whether or not that was the reality is different, right? But, no, he definitely felt like he still had the support of the players and was pretty adamant about that. But the issue has been the players just aren't responding. Tackle made. Over the touchline. Well, here's the answer to your question. Full-time Dragons get flopped. Well, I can't remember the last time I heard that for a home team. It's not the greatest roster in the NRL. It is probably the worst roster in the NRL. And these are the phone effects of it. He said recently as well that if someone better was out of the side, I would put them in. Trust me. What was he dealing with talent-wise on the park? You mentioned their roster is probably the worst in the comp. So, was their problem his coaching? Or was him moving on just sort of a circuit breaker for what is a bigger problem with their talent and depth? Yeah, there's no doubt. Like I was sort of intimated, I don't think it's a very strong roster. I think the roster's quite poor and not balanced properly. And the fact that, you know, he's got his high-end recruitment wrong. And he's much to blame for that Shane Flanagan. No doubt about that. So, was it coaching? Was it the roster? It's definitely the roster. And maybe it's a combination of coaching as well. We keep turning up on Monday, mate. And we just keep working hard. And that's what I'm so lucky as a senior player here that we have such a great bunch of guys that have got a great attitude. These young boys, great head on their shoulders. And we just keep working hard. Keep doing what the coach is doing. Keep learning. And just keep pushing harder. And things will turn, mate. Because he's going to have to front up on the weekend with this club? No doubt. No doubt. Kyle was one of the first players in through the doors this morning, though. The players were unaware when they came to Wollongong for training this morning. By then, the reports had already broken that he was no longer going to be the coach. But, yeah, it's tough for Kyle. They're a close family. Kyle's a contracted player through to the end of 2027. And, yes, we will provide every means possible to support Kyle. And as we have, we'll continue to support Shane. Kyle's been the brunt of lots of criticism of late. He's a good kid. I know him well. I like him. He's very respectful. So, hopefully, this is a bit of a break for him as well, away from that scrutiny surrounding his dad and selection and these sorts of things. Why do you think the club chose now? They've got the Anzac Day match this weekend and then they have the bye. Do you think that they could have waited the extra week and gone into the bye and dealt with this? Or why do you think now is the time? I think in an ideal world, that would have been the play. But I think it's just too far gone. I think the situation is just too far gone. I think Shane had come to the realisation that he wasn't the best man to coach the club anymore. And once you come to that conclusion, well, there's no other option. When things are going bad, they're going bad. You know, some of the young boys got a chance tonight. You know, they tried hard as well. But we're just not getting it done, you know. We can try hard. NRL's not about trying hard. I think every team, every person in the competition tries hard. And you don't get points for trying hard. They said this morning that they haven't made a decision yet on their interim coach. Do you think they'd be hoping they have a similar result? What's the bar for them this season? I guess to win a game would be a start for them. Whilst the Dragons have underperformed, I don't think anyone had them as, you know, top eight hopes at all. So that's the way this has played out. Now where Manly have got some really elite talent that can win a game for them, the Dragons don't have that. So, yeah, there's no interim coach yet. We will communicate our interim coaching arrangements following discussions with our coaching staff today. There's a board meeting tomorrow. Hopefully they can work it out before then, because it is a little bit embarrassing to not have anyone in charge of your footy site, even if it is for 24 hours. One's Dean Young, who's the assistant coach at the moment. And, you know, if they do give him the job, he'll be catapulted into the interim capacity in the short term. The other one is Ben Hornby, the 2010 Premiership winning captain, who's now Wayne Bennett's right-hand man at South Sydney. I think whoever takes control of this club understands that there will be a significant amount of pressure and expectation, and rightly so. Our job is to get to the right solution, ensure that we've got the right person and people in charge of this organisation. They're probably the two leading candidates. I wouldn't assume that there would be anyone else really in the mix. So, yeah, they're the two.
