I think the benefit around it is that there's not a lot of players contracted long term, so it's probably only a little bit of pain. Usually when a coach comes in, a new coach comes in, he's got to wear two or three years of pain because of legacy contracts. That's not going to be the case here. The guys that I was probably critical of in terms of their deals, they expire at the end of next year. So it's actually not the worst spot or the worst club to be at. If you're someone like Keon Kolamatangi, who is heading to the Dragons next year, what are you thinking? Well, I spoke to him on the field for ABC after the game on Saturday, and I asked him that question, are you still committed to going to the Dragons? Yeah, I signed a contract. Yeah, I'm going to be there. So I've just got one more year here and no five years there. So obviously a lot can change in a year, but yeah, I've got it. I'm not doing anything. But no doubt he'd be having some thoughts going, oh, would I really be making that same choice again? Where does it leave the club more broadly? They won their last premiership, as you say, in 2010. Do you think that this move has moved them forward closer to competing, or do you think it has set them back? They're no closer to competing this week, without Shane there. So as I said, they need to rejigger the roster. They need to rejigger that roster desperately. And without that, there's no chance of competing anytime soon. I'm going to speak to three groups, to our fans, our supporters and our members, our results on the field, and our performance is not to your expectation. It is not to our expectation, and we are clearly taking steps to address this. What do they need, apart from an upgraded roster, but what do you think that this club does need, on-field or off-field, to be back competing in the pointy end of the season? On-field, it's definitely like I've been banging on is their roster, right? Like they just need to rejigger it, get some top-end talent in, like Calumatangi. Off the back of that, they need a bit more stability. The board is legacy issues with the board from either side of it, which is continued. But I'd say the number one factor would be, or is, some top-end talent. Michael Kariannis, two coaches in seven rounds. The NRL really is a rollercoaster. Thanks so much for picking us through this one. No worries. Anytime. Headlines. Staying with NRL, and we are at the point of the season where injuries draw origin availability into question, and Payne Haas has been ruled out of the opener with an MCL injury that will keep him out for six to eight weeks. Add to that Tom Dravojevic's hamstring injury, and the New South Wales team might have some fresh faces this year. Speaking of injuries, the AFL was no better, with the big news being the Western Bulldogs confirming that Sam Darcy has indeed ruptured his ACL and will miss the rest of the season. Carlton have ruled Elijah Hollands out of their clash this weekend with Fremantle after he experienced what the club are calling an unprecedented mental health episode during their match against Collingwood on Thursday night. The AFL has asked the club to investigate and share their findings with the league. Former NRL star Zach Lomax, who actually once played for the Dragons, had his first start in Super Rugby for the Western Force after coming off the bench last week. It would seem he's adapted well to the code switch, scoring a try in their thrilling comeback over the Crusaders. Here's Donaldson, flips it across, here's the moment, Lomax in the corner, welcome to the West. There has been a lot of chat about sprinting on this podcast recently, and you know what? It's not going to stop. As long as we have Australians running super fast, and Eddie Nkia has added his name to that list. He broke the Australian all-conditions record over 100 metres, covering the distance in 9.84 seconds. But an illegal tailwind means it won't count as a national record. Patrick Johnson's days as the national champion appear numbered. In the Premier League, Man City continue to catch Arsenal, beating them 2-1 over the weekend. It's arriving. Holland! Manchester City have trailed Arsenal in the table for so long this season. Is this resurrection day? Is this when City come back to life? The Gunners are clinging to a three-point lead at the top of the table with a little over a month to go in the season. One to watch with interest. Golf and Australian Hannah Green is on a hot streak in the LPGA, winning the LA Championship, her fourth win in five starts. She came from six shots behind in the final round to push it to a playoff, and birdied the first hole to take the title. I'm Poppy Penny, and this is ABC Sport Daily, produced by Declan Byrne. Thanks to Stan Sport for the extra audio used in this episode.

episodes.title: Peter Bol on winning, parenthood and the joy of running
episodes.description: Peter Bol is a five-time 800m national champion and after winning that title last weekend, next on his list is trying to win gold at the Commonwealth Games later this year.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Pete gets away in the stretch. Can he make it to fifth? Boys won't come away. And April Rahman's coming home hard. Boll stretching away. It's not a big margin, but it's enough. And he celebrated just before the line. To win one national title is impressive, but five is downright incredible. Peter Boll is the 800 metre champion again, and it means he's heading to his second Commonwealth Games, hoping to go one better than his silver medal back in 2022. Since his last appearance at that event, he's spent time out of the sport, become a father and worked a heck of a lot on the mental side of competition. After disappointing results at the Paris Olympics and recent World Championships, Boll is shaping up to return to the global stage. How is he feeling about that challenge? We ask him. I'm Pobby Penny, and this is ABC Sport Daily. Peter Boll is the national 800 metre champion for a fifth time and has qualified for his second Commonwealth Games. Peter, you've held on to your national title. What does that mean to you? Oh, it means, I guess, a lot. I've always wanted to win the national championship multiple times. So to be able to do it five times is quite special. To do it once, it's like anyone can do it twice, you might fluke it. But five times, you're kind of like, yeah, I'm that guy. I can do it multiple times. Yep, Pete, we can count as well. It's a handful. It's five of the best Australian championships. What kind of confidence does it give you? Yeah, I think track and field is all that confidence. So winning at home gives you the confidence to be able to go overseas. And obviously taking that confidence over there, it's a big advantage. So in terms of international, it's a huge confidence boost. And also personally, just to know that you can continue to perform at the track at the highest level consistently is great. We know that your best is among the best in the world. Where do you feel you're at at the moment? I mean, I just came, great question. I just came back from world indoors and I was fourth. I would say probably around the world at the moment, I'd be within that top 10, which is a good place to be. But we always, you know, track is a brutal sport. No one really knows beyond top three. So you got to be in that top three position. So we've got a little bit more work to do. But yeah, definitely, I think around that top 10 in the world at the moment. What does that work look like for you heading into the Comm Games? A lot of physical training, obviously. The physical demand is there, but also a lot of mental training and just making sure that confidence is always there. Mentally sharp, making sure that you're resilient, handling pressure, all those things. As I say, that result on the weekend does mean you're heading to the Commonwealth Games. You didn't have the Olympics you probably hoped for in Paris. You missed the final at the World Athletics Championships last year. How are you feeling about pulling on the green and gold again on an international stage like this one? It's always a privilege to be able to put on the green and gold and represent yourself and your family and everything you can understand for. So despite whatever result that previously happened, you know, that pride is always there, which is just kind of consistent, which is cool. Yeah, maybe the drive is a little bit different sometimes with more disappointments. But no, I'm pretty resilient and I'm happy for the challenge and always looking forward to the challenge. So I'm really excited to be able to go to my second Commonwealth Games. And I was second last time at Birmingham. And to be able to do one better would be incredible. Do you use those performances where you didn't perhaps get the results you were after as fuel? Yeah, use it as fuel and as like just mental prep. You've got to watch those tape. You've got to be able to sit down and watch those bad races and like why did it go that way? What could I have done better? What do we need to work on? And all that. And that's something with your whole team. So that's not just something for me to do alone. I've got my coaches. I've got my manager, you know, because most performances, bad performances happen off the track. You know, the bad decisions you kind of made, the races you didn't do and or maybe training a little bit too hard or the lifestyle was a bit too hectic, whatever it is. So everything kind of has to come in one. The physical part generally is pretty good. It's getting everything else together. How hard do you work on the mental side of what you do? It's really hard. And I think that's why I've been able to be consistent, you know, getting a fifth championship, but also being able to run at a high quality as such for so many different years. Peter Boll and Josh Ralph. And here comes Mason Cohen. So Ralph and Boll finding it out. Boll is holding. Ralph trying to come in. Cohen flashing late. Boll still holding. Ralph's coming. It's going to be a dip. So I've been running for years now and still have the highest quality. And that's credible, but more so the mental side of things. We know you had time out of the sport in 2023 with the anti-doping investigation, which obviously you were eventually cleared of. Are you running with a point to prove? No, I'm never running with no point to prove. I'm just running for the joy of it. And that's what makes it, I guess, inspiring. But that's what gives me purpose. You know, I'm not running to prove anyone or do anything. I'm just running for my own joy and to present myself, my country. And that's what I run for. Do you still get joy out of running? Yeah. I mean, yeah, like when you win your fifth national title, that's pretty exciting. If you don't, I think it's time to hang up the spikes and you will know when that is because I won't be on the track. Well, we hope that's still a little while off anyway. You've become a father in the last couple of years as well. Has that changed your approach to training or competing or what your motivations are at all? Yeah, in a sense, it's like, well, I think it just made it more purposeful. Like, because time is everything. And, you know, literally in our sport, time is everything. But also time away is everything. So if I'm spending time away in training, so it better be something that I enjoy doing and love to do. And that's going to inspire my family and my daughter. So I take it quite seriously. I guess probably more seriously than before. I think before we kind of take it for granted. But now it's like, oh, well, yeah, I really want to do this. Athletes in their 30s, I think it's only natural to start looking at what the future looks like. And we start asking these questions. You mentioned you still get joy out of running. So you're not hanging the spikes up just yet. But what does it look like for you post Commonwealth Games? Is it all eyes on LA in 2028? Yeah, we take it one year at a time. And, you know, Comm Games is the major focus this year. Nationals was just a major focus. And now we shift to Comm Games. And after Comm Games, we shift to the World Championship next year. And then there's LA. So it's always, you know, we take it step by step. Because, you know, to be able to do something great as the Olympics, everything kind of got to work out well. You know, the training at home, the championships at home. There's no point in dreaming for LA without having everything else planned. You know, we don't want to just rock up to LA and say, oh, wow, it's the fourth Olympic Games. Want to be able to be there and be competitive to do that. You've got to focus on smaller projects leading up to that. Have you thought at all about a Brisbane Olympic appearance? When is that? It's the one after LA. No, I haven't gave too much thought about it. I mean, I've seen everything that's going around and how much excitement is around Brisbane and, you know, how much athletics in Australia has picked up. So I'm sure that will be a fantastic Olympics. But I haven't thought too much about it in terms of competition-wise. But, yeah, definitely been seeing everything around the campaign. As you mentioned, it is an exciting time for athletics fans. And in particular, I know everyone is excited about an athlete that you're close to. And that's Gout Gout. You've said previously he's like a little brother to you. How did you feel watching him run that blistering 200 on the weekend? I mean, it's always incredible to share the same track with such elite, elite, elite performance. You know, that's the fastest junior that we're seeing. And he performed on that track like just an hour after I performed. So it's nice to be able to be there to perform and share that track with him. Gout's in front. He's coming away now for Murphy. Can he be as quick as this morning? Incredible. Oh, 19.68. Where's the win? The win's legal. He has absolutely done what everybody thought he might. But he's done it at 18 years of age. You know, just watching him grow physically, mentally, and it's been awesome because obviously we've got a little bit more of a personal relationship. So it's been great to watch that and super pumped and super excited to see what he is able to produce. I think we've still got so much more to go. He's just getting started, really. Have you spoken to him? What advice have you given to him? I actually try not to give him much advice because I think he's just doing his thing and he's got his support team that are wonderful and everything's working. If he needs something, you know, Gout is super sharp. If he needs anything, he'll reach out. And so far, he's got it all under control. The best I can do is just be there. Just be a friend and brother to him. And that sometimes doesn't require any advice. It just requires being there. Peter Boll, congratulations on your fifth national title. We can't wait to see you at the Commonwealth Games. Thanks so much for your time. No, thank you. Thank you for having me. I hope you enjoyed that little Saturday special. I'm Poppy Penny and this is ABC Sport Daily produced by Declan Byrne. We'll be back in your feeds on Monday. Catch you then. Thanks to Australian Athletics for the extra audio used in this episode.

episodes.title: Fri Fix: LIV Golf's murky future and Netball Australia chooses eyeballs over money
episodes.description: LIV Golf has had a rollercoaster 24-hours. Rumours started to swirl that the league would have to fold due to funding cuts then the CEO poured cold water on that then their broadcast went off air for two hours.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. You know, it was a lot of reaching and grabbing for headlines and clickbait and stories. For us, it's like we're business as usual, but if you want to ask me if this business is tough, I would say absolutely. That was Live Golf CEO Scott O'Neill at the top of their broadcast from Mexico City before it actually went off air for a couple of hours due to power outages. Bad timing for the Rebel Golf League, with rumours swirling that the Saudi-backed public investment fund was going to pull their funding, putting the future of the league in doubt. Is golf's big disruptor about to be disrupted? And Netball Australia has signed a new TV rights deal, putting the sport back on free-to-air. It's an organisation that has been plagued by financial problems in recent times. So how might this help? I'm Poppy Penny and this is ABC Sport Daily. Dean Bilton is a journalist with the ABC and he's been following this story as it unfolded over the last couple of days. Dean, all the talk yesterday morning was that Live was set to fold. Then there was an email from the CEO essentially saying nothing to see here. And then the event in Mexico City got underway, albeit with a couple of hours off air due to power outages. Can you fill in the blanks for us? I feel like everyone's still catching up on the blanks because it changed hour to hour. It basically started from a couple of like Twitter accounts effectively saying there's some big news coming for Live, hinting at, you know, potential trouble ahead. That kind of spiralled and eventually came through reports from the Financial Times and the New York Times, The Athletic, Golf Digest, like proper reporting from journalists both inside and outside the golf world that, without putting any strict timeframes on it, suggested that the Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund, which has been bankrolling Live from the start, are effectively going to pull their financial support. You know, having been in private equity now for over a dozen years, this is the process you go through. And sometimes it's not smooth and sometimes it's not easy. But I can tell you, given the momentum of this business, we're really excited about where we are and the position where we are. The reports didn't specify if that was going to happen today, if that was going to happen at the end of this 2026 season. But all the reports were pretty consistent in saying that the PIF is changing direction, moving away from the very heavy investment they've been making in global sport. And that is going to effectively see Live without a financial backer. As you say, Scott O'Neill, the CEO of Live Golf, who took over from Greg Norman about 18 months ago now, sent out a company-wide memo to everybody in Live, which conveniently made its way into the media, into the wider public, basically saying, full throttle, full steam ahead for the rest of this season, nothing to see here. We're changing the game. We're pioneers. Kept referring to Live Golf as a startup, which is very cute. Don't worry about it. We're teeing off in Mexico tomorrow. Everything is going fine. Live has always been very public and open and proud of the long-term backing that the PIF has offered. And they've spoken about, you know, we're totally funded through to 2030 to 2032. They've bragged about this and they've used that as a selling point to sponsors and investors. And now this email comes out in the wake of this reporting and suddenly nine more events in 2026 is the most that they can promise. Scott O'Neill has since spoken after the power came back on in Mexico today on the Live Golf broadcast. And without saying it particularly out loud, kind of admitted that a little bit himself. You know, this notion of, do you have to raise money? Probably. Like, this is business. From my vantage point, it doesn't look like it's going to have a happy ending for Live Golf. So if Live Golf does go under beyond 2026, what does it mean for the players who left the PGA Tour to join Live Golf? Do you think that the PGA would welcome them back or is there going to be a lot more to it than that? It's so hard to tell. And I think it's going to vary player to player. The PGA Tour earlier this year, around about conveniently the exact same time that Brooks Koepka came out and said he wanted to leave Live and return to the PGA Tour, opened up this very brief window, this amnesty period for a select handful of players via this arbitrary list of criteria that the Tour just created themselves. Effectively saying Bryson DeChambeau, John Rahm, Cameron Smith, a couple of others. If you would like to come back, you tell us in the next week and we'll have you back with some financial restrictions placed, but no suspension. In that period, Koepka did return to the PGA Tour, but the others all stayed where they were. Now, if Live Golf is not an entity at all going forward, or if it's not an entity with the same sort of financial backing that drew the players there in the first place, it's hard to imagine, you know, the likes of Rahm and DeChambeau, who's been trying to negotiate an insanely lucrative contract with Live over the last few months. Cameron Smith as well and others are going to want to stick around on this Tour for much, much less money than what they were initially promised. So at that point, the cards, you know, it kind of falls to the PGA Tour. Do they open this amnesty period again and say, all is forgiven, don't worry about it, you guys come on back? It would be great for them to have these sort of players back, but then you definitely risk peeving off the entire rest of the PGA Tour field, who stayed true to the Tour and didn't leave when they were presented with the money in the first place. So that's going to be a delicate balance. It's a bit of an unknown because the PGA Tour has kind of been making it up as it goes along as well. The other interesting thing, Dean, is that Live has made commitments to hosting events around the world, including in Adelaide, which we know is a really successful event, both for the competition and for South Australia. What happens there with those commitments? Yeah, that's a big question. I mean, Live Adelaide is probably the event on the Live calendar. It's by far the most successful. We had 5.5 million people turn into our event in Australia with the great Anthony Kim win, the Rocky Balboa story of today. It was the largest golf event in the history of the country. The question then becomes, does Live still exist next year, either as the same version, if they manage to find the exact same amount of money that the Saudi PIF has put into them, which is highly unlikely, or if it is continued backed by some other investor, which seems the only way that Live will continue beyond this year. Live Adelaide probably does still exist at that stage, but then does Bryson come? Is John Rahm still on the tour to come? Does the event still exist, but with a version of, you know, the bottom rung of Live players, plus whoever else they managed to get in to fill the field? Does Live Adelaide draw the same crowds if Cameron Smith, John Rahm, Bryson DeChambeau aren't there? We know how to put on a show. We know how to grow the game. I've seen the kids on the first tee. It's hard to imagine a world where Live Adelaide next year looks the same as it did this year, which is such a shame for Aussie golf. The biggest losers out of all of this are potentially Aussie golf fans. Dean Bilton, it feels like there is still plenty to play out here. Thanks so much for your time. Thanks, Bobby. Brittany Carter is a netball writer for the ABC, and Britt, broadcast right deals aren't often sexy for sports fans. But for netball, it could be really significant. It will return to Frida Air TV with this new deal. Why is this so important? This is really important, Poppy, because netball has been behind the paywall with Fox for the past five years. The average audience per match isn't that great. So in 2024, netball Australia revealed that audience was at 57,000 on average per game, which, as we know, isn't a lot. And so some of its bargaining power has been lost because of that and its ability to grab commercial deals and go out to tender for this broadcast deal. So the cost of the deal is less than what they would have got with Fox in 2021. So they're getting less cash injection at the time of this deal for 2027 and beyond. But they have to almost take a step backwards, get more eyeballs on the sport from a Frida Air audience and more of a casual fan. episodes.title: The emotional toll of Alexa Leary's traumatic brain injury
episodes.description: You might have seen Paralympian Alexa Leary winning gold medals, dancing on the pool deck and giving the most bubbly and joyous interviews.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Love it. I'm so proud of myself. I'll really tell you that. I am so proud of myself. You might have seen one of Alexa Leary's incredible poolside interviews. She's bubbly, fun, the life of the party and at the Paris Paralympics she won two gold medals and broke two world records. Before all that though, Leary had a serious cycling accident at age 19. Her parents were told to say their goodbyes multiple times. Well, Leary's just released a book called Sink or Swim, which documents her second life. And she joins us today to bring us into her reality of living with a traumatic brain injury for the rest of her life. I'm Declan Byrne. This is ABC Sport Daily. Alexa, firstly, congrats on the book release. How are you feeling about it? Yeah, I'm feeling really good. I'm really happy that the book is finally out. Like it's been a year or so now and I'm like, yes, it's out. It's out. I always imagine the coolest bit is when you get it, you get to see it. It's in your hands. You can smell the pages. What was it like when you got that first hard copy? Oh, I couldn't believe it. I had like a little tear in my eye because I was like, I'm so happy this is finally out. Like it just made me so happy and proud for how much it's taken and time like that. It's amazing. And what about the hardest part? Because I kind of think that's the cool bit, but the hardest part is the actual writing. What was the toughest bit? So like to get it out all on the paper, like to get it all out, to say the truth, to just put out the truth of my accident and even before and after. It was just so much to say that. And also the biggest thing is like bringing in about a traumatic brain injury. There was just a lot of factors in there that it was hard for me to talk about, but I wanted to share it in the book. So it was really incredible putting it on there. Did you have to make a commitment to write something down or to someone to be like, I'm going to be, you know, an open book, all the good bits and all the bad bits are going in. Yeah. So like, I didn't want to put some bits in it, but then I got to terms of going, you know, Lex, it's a good thing to do that because it's going to help a lot of other people. So that's how I felt upon doing it. Was that the goal? Did you have something from the start that it was about helping other people? Yeah, of course. And also bringing awareness of traumatic brain injuries because it's something that I suffer with for the rest of my life. And, you know, it's going to bring out so much awareness. You wrote it with Ali Pascoe. The book features not only your voice, but lots of people close to you. So your parents, your brothers and sisters, doctors. For people who don't know, you had that cycling accident, age 19, resulted in your traumatic brain injury, which is, you know, a lot of what the book is about. But reading those early parts, parts that you don't remember, you say you don't remember anything about it, anything before it, really tiny snippets, but now it's down on paper. What was it like to, I guess you would have heard bits and pieces and you were taken back to the scene, but what was it like to see it written down by these people who experienced it, you know, firsthand? Yeah, no, it was a lot because, you know, after the accident happened, my parents had to like fully sit me down and talk to me and tell me because I wiped all my memory and everything from the day of the accident. Like the neuro doctor said, I won't have four to five year prior, like any memory. So it was really hard for me to process the accident. And yeah, that was just like a hard factor to actually even see the photos and things on paper. It was, it's really hard even reading, reading it in the book. It got me like, I did cry because it was like hard to read my brain. I was so bad in the accident, like in the hospital, I couldn't walk and talk. So I was gone. My brain was out, but in rehab, I had to come to terms with it. I'm living a second life flex. Like you've got to, you've got to realize this. And that's why my parents had to sit me down and tell me exactly the story. Reading it and knowing you from like an outsider's perspective, someone who's seen the videos of you as this like bubbly, fun person, this who's full of life, you know, the way you talk about music and living your life. I just can't hold back. I've just got to let go. I've got to get the, got to get the guns out and go for it. I can't stop myself. And then reading the book, it was really eyeopening. Do you think that's what you want people's reaction to be is to, to see the entire spectrum of what you live with? Yeah. Because like people just think, oh, she fell off a bike. Oh, that's, that's it. It's like, oh no, no, I'm living a full second life. Like I have severe traumatic brain injury, like damage in my brain. It's changed my whole life. And so that's like, it's, it's difficult. It's really hard living with the TBI. I have to be honest with you right now. It's so hard. The heightened emotions is one thing that you hear about. Tell us day to day where that shows up. Yeah. So my emotions go insane. I get sad, happy, angry, depressed in a day, in a second. It's like insane. And my emotions is just, oh my goodness. Like I can't even explain to you. That's why I have a behavior coach to help me guide me into the right direction of my behavior. But honestly, oh, when I wake up, I don't even know who I am sometimes from the memory. It's just, it's really hard. I have to be honest with you right now. It's so hard. How are you doing today? Well, this is a stressful day, you know, telling people about your book and about these hard parts of your life. Yeah. It's actually been a very busy day. And sometimes I don't remember, but it's okay. My brain's like 50 first dates, but it's fine. So when you say you wake up, does it take a second to work out what mood am I in? Like, what is my brain giving me in this moment? Yeah. And like mostly every night before I go to bed, I do write out my notes of what I'm doing the next day. So I'm on board with what I'm doing. So I know that my, to try tame my emotions, to not make them so heightened. So that's a big thing that I have to do, which is it's hard. So after the accident, how long was it before you were again swimming? Because doctors said to your parents, they said a few times, be prepared to say goodbye. They said you mightn't walk or talk again. Yet it wasn't that long before you were swimming again and competitively. Yeah. So like when I got out of the hospital, the neuro doctors literally said to my mom and dad, like we want to get Lex's right side because I'm physically damaged from the brain. So I destroyed my left side, which made my right physically damaged. And so now I'm left-handed. Weirdly. I was always right, but now I'm lefty. Yeah. I'm left-handed now. My right is really hard. I'm always a physio and things like that, but it's hard. Anyway, so the neuro doctors were like, get in, swim, and we want to get her to try work the right side. And that's where it all started. And literally it was just, I had passion and I was like, I want more than just, you know, rehab. I've had a massive accident. I've got to go out there and do something good for myself. So that was the biggest goal. And I don't know, look where it's got me. I'm like, yes, Lex, you did it. Hey. She is on fire. She is not holding anything back for Singapore. Stand by for the world record line to be within touching distance. There it is. Can Alexa Leary hunt it down. Your dad talked about in the book, like channeling that anger that you had. So that emotion into swimming, was that how you saw it? When you got in the pool, you were able to harness all this energy. Yeah. A hundred percent. Like, you know, cause I was frustrated. Like I'm living a whole second life. I was just always like, I want, I want this, I want my old life. But if I think about it, I go, no, I don't. I love who I am now where I'm learning to accept her and understand her. But yeah, no, it's just, I don't know. Life is just hard. It can be like, honestly, it is difficult. And making the Paralympics is extremely hard. It's, it's beyond just living a hard life. So how does your, your TBI affect training that those tough sessions in the pool, which you have to do if you want to be a gold medalist like you are? Yeah. Like, honestly, it's tough because like, especially with like my behavior, like every morning at training and I'm training my little heart out and stuff like that, but it's really debatable on my emotions and behavior. To be honest with you, it's, it's, it's difficult, but like I get through it and it's like, I don't know. I'm very, I'm very determined and passionate person. When I want something, I'm not, I'm going to fight for it. And that's what I've done since getting out of the hospital, even in the hospital. episodes.title: Does the Lance Collard hearing raise more questions than answers?
episodes.description: St Kilda’s Lance Collard has been handed a nine-week suspension from the AFL tribunal for a homophobic slur during a VFL match last month.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. You could argue that the word has been in his vocabulary at some point in the past. You could equally argue that he more than most should deeply know the impact of it, given what he's gone through. That's the CEO of the AFL Players Association, James Gallagher, on some of the intricate considerations surrounding the handing down of St Kilda's Lance Collard's nine-week suspension for using a homophobic slur in a VFL match. The fact this incident went to a disciplinary hearing was unusual in the first place. There was extensive questioning of witnesses and between the hearing and deliberations, it went for three days. It feels now that we might have more questions than answers. What's the balance between punishment and prevention? Could the way this played out be a deterrent for others in reporting things they hear on field? And given how many parties were involved and impacted, were there any winners out of this? Yes. I'm Poppy Penny and this is ABC Sport Daily. Marnie Vinyl is a multi-award winning journalist with the ABC and has been following this tribunal hearing since it started way back on Thursday last week. Marnie, firstly, can you explain to us the penalty that Collard has been handed and the reasoning that the tribunal gave? Yeah. So Lance Collard, 21-year-old player at St Kilda, he has been handed a nine-week suspension with two of those weeks suspended. So basically looking at a seven-week suspension, and this is following his 2024 suspension for using the exact same slur in which he received six weeks. So it was debated a lot what this sanction should look like with the AFL going pretty hard that it has to be more than six weeks, given that was his original sanction. And Jeff Gleeson, the tribunal chair, he did really acknowledge the impact that this kind of homophobic language can have on the community. As he handed down his sanction, he really did stress that Hayley Conway, the CEO of Pride Cup, who gave evidence in that initial hearing, her words where she said that this can have really lasting impacts on the queer community within the AFL. And we know that, you know, there's no openly gay men currently playing within the AFL and a lot of players feel like they have to hide their sexuality through all levels of football. And so homophobic language can be really harmful and also a deterrence to keep those players within the system. So noting that they thought that the slur had to have a pretty big consequence. One thing that was interesting to me in the disciplinary hearing was Jeff Gleeson asking whether a lengthy suspension would serve to simply punish or if it would act as an actual preventative measure or a deterrent to discourage not only Collard, but other players from using this kind of language. Where do you think they landed on that point? It's an interesting point that the AFL and the tribunal are kind of wrestling with because we're seeing these really hefty sanctions handed down in the AFL's crackdown on homophobic language that has spanned the last three years. But then they're wrestling with, well, okay, how do we get the balance right? Preventing the language from being used in the first place. Sanctioning and penalty can't be the only response. You know, it has a role to play, but at the moment it's kind of being seen as the solution and it's not. The solution has to start much earlier. Because Collard was suspended back in 2024 for six weeks for using a homophobic slur. And then two years later, he's back and he's now facing the tribunal for the exact same slur. So how do we make sure that these penalties are actually working? The fact that this even made it to the tribunal, I think is interesting in itself, because if we think back to other instances of homophobic language being used on the footy field, like the Isaac Rankin or the Jack Graham instance, which we saw last year, the AFL made their decision on suspensions and penalties behind closed doors. So the fact that it played out in a tribunal was very interesting. Why was that the case? Yeah, the first disciplinary hearing in AFL history, which made it pretty significant. And like you mentioned, there's been so many cases of homophobic language being sanctioned. Isaac has received a format sanction for using a homophobic slur towards a Collingwood opponent. The language used was offensive, hurtful and highly inappropriate. But in those cases, all those players pled guilty. And one of the reasons that Collards was so hefty this time is the tribunal said, well, he showed no remorse. So in him pleading not guilty, they decided that there should be no discount to that penalty where previously, well, the only kind of statements that players say, or we hear from players around these cases is usually just an apology that feels very put together with the club, where in this particular case, we got to hear from Collard himself. We got to hear from the players who reported the slur in the first place. We got to hear about Collard's background. There were so many elements that were really uncovered during this process that we've just never seen before. When you've got two versions of events, it's not a great place to start from when dealing with really challenging issues that the game is facing. On the first day of these hearings, you mentioned the Frankston players who reported the slur in the first place. They gave evidence to the disciplinary hearing and they were examined extensively. They've also received unsavoury attention on social media in the wake of all of this. Is there a risk that the way that this has played out for them might discourage others from coming forward at any level of footy? I found it very interesting when those two Frankston players were giving evidence in that first hearing because it kind of became very apparent that they did not want to be there. I mean, the second player who gave evidence said that they were told they would just have to make an initial statement on game day and that would be it. And rather it snowballed into, as he put it, this whole thing. He said that he was quite hesitant to give evidence, but when he said that, he was told that he might be compelled to do so, so legally required to attend the tribunal. And as you mentioned, they were cross-examined extensively. There were reports that the cross-examination was quite gruelling and they were really questioned and had their integrity in a way questioned. And because the players had to be publicly named when they gave evidence, it meant that social media could weigh in on the evidence, but also on them as people. And so these two players have now been named across social media in a lot of commentary that is, as you say, unsavoury, but I would argue weighs into abuse. What we've seen again is a process that ultimately has caused harm all over the place. The AFL Players Association have also released a statement today criticising the process. What is their argument about how cases like this one can maybe be better handled in the future? So the AFLPA did come out with a pretty lengthy statement and they really did lament the process. I think we've got a lot of work to do to set up, you know, really bespoke processes that should lead us to the outcome. I think having some clarity about what those outcomes might look like is helpful for the game. I think we saw that through COVID. I think that was really helpful for the game. It meant that we were able to get through issues and incidents quickly with clarity for everyone involved. They want a lot more of a nuanced and I guess compassionate look when it comes to this kind of process. They want things like diverse backgrounds to be taken into account, the harm that these kind of hearings that play out publicly can have on the queer community, but also the First Nations community. We know that Lance Collard is a First Nations man, as is Isaac Rankin. And so all of these communities that are really harmed through such a public case as this, to be taken into account on how these matters are handled. Collard's background and upbringing was actually raised as part of the evidence for this. What were they asking to be considered? And I guess how might the AFLPA want that to be more inclusive in the future? Yeah, it was raised a lot. I mean, this is a 21-year-old Indigenous player who's come into the AFL system. And we know that some Indigenous players can struggle when they're moved away from community and, you know, putting these clubs in the city. And it was mentioned quite a lot during the hearing. I mean, Lance Collard now lives with Nazaya Wanganin-Millera. That's a fact I'm not sure the public knew before this because together they're trying to assert themselves as positive role models on other young Indigenous men. And the Saints lawyer really stressed just how much work Collard had been doing in this particular area. You know, I spoke to people this morning who said, that it is not excusing Collard's use of that language at all. It is unacceptable. And it's a word that he knows is unacceptable because he's been sanctioned before. He's done the training. He's been explicitly told how unacceptable it is. But he's a young Indigenous man who grew up in a community where words like this were said quite a lot. And that is a generational consequences of Indigenous communities across Australia. And I'm no expert at all to talk about that. But it is a factor that played so heavily into this particular hearing. I mean, the Saints lawyer said that when he was arguing for a fine or a lesser sanction, that this could be a sliding doors moment where you've got a kid from a hard background who could slide back on the wrong path and potentially have this sanction ruined his life. My understanding is he's, whether devastated is too strong a word, but like he's deeply impacted obviously by this outcome. He's gone, gone back to WA to spend some time with family. They've got the five days to assess any appeal options. It'll be interesting to see whether they go down that path. I think if it was a fine or a lesser sanction, they might have accepted it. But nine weeks with those two suspended is a long time. And the Saints lawyer was pretty gung-ho during the hearing about just the toll that that could take on Collard. So I wouldn't be surprised if they decided to appeal. And whether this is the right way to really tackle the issues that are affecting so many Australians. When it's a case like this that is so public, the queer community are further battered and bruised because, of course, you have social media who have an increase in homophobia. I mean, I personally feel like a few years ago, I never saw the F slur anywhere. And now I'm seeing it everywhere because every single time these cases come up, it emboldens corners of the internet to feel like they can use it and debate whether it's OK or not to be saying across social, well, to be saying anywhere. You have a lot of people across social media that are attacking the queer community and saying that they're too soft in all of this. And, you know, it's the queer community's fault that players are going to be sanctioned this particular way and have their careers ruined. And then you have the Indigenous community having a lot of people weighing in on the intersection of race in all of this. And then, of course, the players involved, they're impacted. So it does really feel like there are absolutely no winners when these really high profile cases play out. Is there a better way to handle it? It's a really good question. So I would love to see prevention over punishment. I would love to see all clubs do more training. I would love to see people take this a lot more seriously. I would love to get to a stage where we have openly queer players in the AFL and we can talk about them without having to assess all the risk that them being open does. So it's a very big question, but I kind of just hope that the AFL are really taking all of this on board and listening to all of the voices that have so much to say about this because we're not seeing these sanctions going away, it seems. Marnie, it's been a big story. Thanks so much for stepping us through it. Thanks, Poppy. Port Adelaide's Zach Butters was also in front of the AFL tribunal last night for an incident between him and umpire Nick Foote on Sunday night. Butters was accused of having asked Foote, how much are they paying you? Which he strongly denied. The tribunal agreed with umpire Foote's recollection of events and Butters is set to pay a $1,500 fine. He spoke after the hearing. Incredibly disappointed with the result tonight. I stand by knowing what I said and what I didn't say, especially what I didn't say. Port Adelaide will have the option to appeal the decision. He received tutoring from Adam Treloar on handballing and appeared to be quite the natural. He was actually there for a charity partnership, but it would bring a few more international eyeballs to the game. And in Super Rugby, Moana Pacifica are looking for new owners or they risk having to leave the competition entirely. The financially challenged club are currently sitting on the bottom of the table, having won just one game this season. It would make them the second club in two years to dissolve due to financial hardship after the Melbourne Rebels in 2024. I'm Poppy Penny and this is ABC Sport Daily produced by Declan Byrne. Thanks to SEN for the extra audio used in this episode.

episodes.title: Patrick Johnson on the Australian sprinters coming for his record
episodes.description: Gout Gout and Lachie Kennedy were the headline acts at the 2026 Australian Athletics Championships and they didn’t disappoint.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Gout's in front. He's coming away now for Murphy. Can he be as quick as this morning? Oh, incredible. Oh, 19.68. Where's the wind? The wind's legal. He has absolutely done what everybody thought he might, but he's done it at 18 years of age. The world will be shaking. That's 18-year-old Gout Gout becoming the national champion in the 200 metres, running sub-20 seconds. Add to that result, Lockie Kennedy becoming the first Australian to run 100 metres under 10 seconds on Australian soil. We've been talking about the sprinting boom that's coming in Australia, and I think it's officially here. For over 20 years, Patrick Johnson has held the 100 metre record, but is it only a matter of time until it's broken? We ask him. I'm Poppy Penny, and this is ABC Sport Daily. Patrick Johnson is the fastest Australian over 100 metres for now. Patrick, you set a time of 9.93 back in 2003, but Lockie Kennedy is closing the gap. How did you feel over the weekend watching Kennedy run 9.96 twice? Oh, it was great to see you. I think it was something that I knew that we've got the talent in this country. I've always said that, and I sent a message out to Lockie and just said, congratulations and welcome to the sub-10 club again. And how's that feel? But I think like anything, this is the standard that we wanted to see in this country. And I'm happy to be the first, but I'd never want it to be the last. And I think there's proof in the pudding now with so many incredible athletes now coming out and running fast and not only in our sprints and our long distance, but our field events as well. So it's great to see track and field particularly getting that opportunity to really be on the world stage, which has always been a world sport. Kennedy clearly in front. Browning's having a really good run. How quick is it for Lockie? It's very, very quick again. It's 9.97. It may come down. It may come down to 9.96. It is spectacular. He's first Australian championship. He's a star. Is there a small part of you that wants to hang on to the record? Oh, not really. I think I was very honored to do it in 2003. And I've always been really clear that records are meant to be broken. And I did that a while ago. And I was really, really want the next generation to take over, take ownership of that. And now leading into Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games, it's an incredible time. You've got LA coming up as well, Commonwealth Games. So there's incredible opportunities where the athletes now have something to look forward to and a home Olympics. Of course, I was able to go to Sydney Olympic Games in 2000, but a home Olympics is really different. I think there's a real sense of this country where the athletes see a future where they're all looking at, I want to be in the Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games. And it's only five years away. Lachie's been pretty clear that he has your record in his sights. The sky's the limit. Like I said, I want to try and go 9-8 this year. I definitely want to break the Aussie record. Do you get the feeling that it is only a matter of time before he gets there? How fast do you think he can go? I think the sky's the limit for Lachie and even some of the other sprinters, you know, Gout Gout and a few others coming through. I think you've got to have the standard. So you've got a standard to look for. Now you set the standard, your own standard, and what you look forward to. So I think there's a reality check here, what we run in Australia, what runs overseas. So there's a real opportunity to level that up, which I think, you know, as Australians, we've always been such a great country competing against the rest of the world. I think now in spritting and some of the other long distance events, we're just elevating where we should be. And it's timely, I think, for us to be a country that not only has a talent ability, but we have the opportunity to showcase it as well. What does it feel like to run sub 10 seconds? What would Lachie have been feeling on the weekend? Well, I think he put it very instinctively where it's very easy. Yeah, it just felt easy, you know, so I think I got a bit more in the tank, but I mean, it's good to see I'm in good form. And I think running fast, I mean, again, you forget the six hours a day of training and the mental strain and the commitment and the pressure, but running is pure connection. I mean, I say it's pure spirituality where you're connected to mind, body and soul. But I think Lachie sort of felt that it was so easy to run fast. The thing is now to duplicate that and be consistent, which is always going to be the reality where consistent, not only in Australia, but also against the international rivalry. You've got a lot of international athletes who can run fast. So the test will come is keep backing that up consistently. And then of course, leading it to Commonwealth Games or major championships or into Olympics, which is where you want to do your best. I want to make a bit of pattern of it. You know, I want to make it routine. I want to make it up to standard. You mentioned the other result that got a lot of sprinting fans talking across the weekend, and that's of course, Gout running 19.67 in the 200 meters. It's the new under 20s world record. It's a new national record by some distance, breaking the previous record, which he also held. What did you think as he came flying towards the finish? To me, it was about, it was great to see him enjoying his running. I think, you know, the expectation, the hype, the pressure on him, his coach and his family and everyone, I wanted him to get back to just running free for himself. And I think it was great to see him enjoying that because again, I think Melbourne showed he, he, he's still in great shape, but he had to work on a couple of technical things. Oh no, that definitely fired me up for sure. Knowing that 200 is my baby and I just had, I didn't put together a race I wanted to. So coming out here, I just want to prove to myself and the rest of the world that I'm here to stay. The best thing an athlete can do is work on himself or herself. And I think that just shows the opportunity where he went out and said, look, I've had that thinking in my head, I'm going to run fast. He's probably already done it in training, but he wanted to do it in a competition. And I think for him, I was more relieved that he was actually going back to him himself, run free, run free from pressure. Honestly, it's, it's good when people, you know, compare you to the best in the world. And then at the end of the day, I know I'm me, I'm doing my own thing. And I mean, there's no pressure for me because as soon as I go down and track, it's just me, the track, my spikes, and I go by myself. Run for who you are. And he came out and exceptionally not only himself, but a lot of the athletes behind him were able to go with him, which is probably the first time that you get the confidence that Aiden Murphy and a few other, Calum Law, that actually went with him and said, look, he's not unbeatable. He's just setting the standard for us. So we want to be able to go to that level as well. And I think that's what happens when you have a few great athletes coming out and performing well, you actually lift up the standard of all the other athletes because they believe they can win or they can be close to you. We have such incredible athletes in Australia and me being able to race these athletes and they've raced me, we push each other to the limits. And as you can see in our race, two Australians run sub 20. I mean, this is amazing. He's chosen the under 20s World Championships over the Commonwealth Games later this year. What did you make of that decision? Did you feel like it's the right one for him? Yeah, he's still young. And I think, you know, again, he's showing exceptional talent as a young age, but I feel there's an element here where you've got to let him be a young person, let him have fun, let him enjoy running. So I think we've got to remember that we put all this pressure on our young people to perform and be the best in the world, but we forget they're just kids as well. And they've got to have fun. And again, I'm really conscious that we do the sport because we have fun and we love it. So never forget that. Yes, there's pressure of yourself and your family and what you think and your sponsors. But when you get out there and run fast, I think you just want to do it for yourself and to your family and everyone else involved. But World Juniors is probably a really just a great stepping stone for him. We're not trying to, you know, it's a smart reality from his coach and his manager to say, look, there's five years. He's already shown exceptional talent leading into these couple of these major championships. Get his confidence up, get his training. He'll have his own growth spurts. He'll have his own technical areas or work on, but let him, let him do that. Tweaked a couple of little things, worked his hands a bit better, you know, just try to get his turnover better. And it worked. And I think this is a great decision by his manager and his coach and his family to say, look, let him just do the succession plan that he wants to do. And that's these races. And then he'll lead into those major, because he's got plenty of time. He's young. Let's let him make sure he enjoys what he does. And that's running fast. He is young and so is Lockie Kennedy. Gout's 18. Kennedy's only 22. Have you had much to do with either of them across the journey? And what advice would you be giving them? Oh, I send a message now and then to them just to, you know, wish him well, but also give them that sort of sense of empowerment and confidence. So I think to me, it's about succession planning or passing on knowledge or advice. And they can take it or leave it, of course. But I think I've proven, you know, even I wasn't young when I did it. I did it when I was 30 years old. So you could say I was totally different spectrums where you've got young people coming out running really super quick. I was a lot older when I did it. Good start by Matt Shervington on the outside. Kristen Malcolm got a fair start as well. Also going okay is Saudi Arabia and further out to Great Britain. Look to be well in front. Good bat in exchange to Dwayne Chambers. The Australians right there. Patrick Johnson trying to move up on the Italians. But it just proves it doesn't matter the age. It matters on who the support you've got around you and what's your plan ahead and your attack ahead around major championships training and whatnot. So for me, I just always send them a quick message usually to them and also their coaches. But yeah, I try to make sure that I have a low key approach to it because again, it's their glory. It's their opportunity. It's their time. I'm really keen to make sure the records I've set, they break it and go beyond and be the next superstars, which they already are. Kristen Malcolm They've both spoken about their friendship and the rivalry and the fact that it pushes each of them to be better and faster. And even though we didn't see them race against each other on the weekend, we know that that's the case. When you were racing, it was you and Matt Shervington sort of duking it out. What was that relationship like? And do you see a bit of that in these two? Matt Shervington Yeah, definitely. And I think, you know, Gowgow told what Lockie Kennedy did in the 100 metres and said, okay, he set the benchmark. And I think that's what we need. Matt Shervington This is what I've been waiting for. You know, right before this final, I went on my notes. Matt Shervington I set up running 1975 and 1967. Matt Shervington I think we've always loved rivalry, but we also love to see Australians winning. episodes.title: Will land sales future-proof Tassie's only uni?
episodes.description: Tasmania has a long tradition of young people growing up, spreading their wings, and leaving for the mainland - before for some, returning to the island.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Everybody's talking about fuel. Whether you're in need of filling up the tank for the week and you're watching the dollars tick over at the Bowser or you're watching weekend plans, holiday plans, business plans change. To help get your head around the latest, you can find Fuelcast in the ABC Business Daily feed on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts. Is Tasmania's only university facing its toughest test yet? There's a lot of hard-working Tasmanians out there. My boss is the boss of Tasmania. Tasmanians want us to get on with the job. North, south, east, west. I don't care where you live in the state. They've spent hundreds of millions of dollars on a misguided plan and they would not let go of that misguided plan no matter what facts were put in front of them and no matter how expensive it was becoming. I was barely on campus and when I was on campus, people weren't hanging around. Yeah, it was just, you'd go, do your thing, duck off again. Sandy Bay needs to change. The current layout and the condition of existing buildings does not allow the university to deliver for its students or drive the innovation Tasmania needs. Hello and welcome to TassieCast. I'm Ailey Ward coming to you from Nipaluna, Hobart. Did you or your kids go to the University of Tasmania? Maybe you've got fond memories of the now defunct uni bar or O-week shenanigans on top of what you learned, of course. Or maybe you or someone you know is considering ditching Tasmania's only university to go interstate. There is a long history of spreading your wings, becoming independent and finding your feet in the big smoke before maybe returning to the island. But the number of young Tasmanians bailing on UTAS has increased markedly. Local students choosing a uni interstate have increased from around 18% to nearly 30% in the past decade, adding to concerns about a brain drain. We know a growing number of jobs require some sort of tertiary education. But is our university equipped to keep pace and attract the students and staff it needs? After a controversial plan to move from its main Sandy Bay campus to the Hobart CBD was met with massive community opposition, UTAS is now hoping legislation, allowing it to sell some of its land, will help see the Institute realise a vision for a world-class STEM centre to support the next generation of Tasmanian scientists get their skills and stay here. But will it be enough? Following the ongoing debate is our investigative reporter Adam Holmes. Adam, it'd be fair to say between interstate and online competition, low staff morale and a challenging financial situation, UTAS is now at a real crossroads? Yeah, it has been facing this confluence of pressures like you just mentioned. It doesn't paint a particularly easy picture. Some of them are the result of external factors, but others could be described as self-inflicted. For example, the requirement to pay back $21 million in staff underpayment. There's been major changes to its arts and humanities courses, partly due to Commonwealth priorities. There's also the aftermath of COVID and how to manage international student enrolments. There's been a steady decline in international students since 2021, which UTAS has been trying to address through its dealings with the Commonwealth. But at the same time, domestic student numbers have actually deadly increased. This does include students from interstate. UTAS actually has lower entry requirements than many mainland universities, so that could be a factor there. And while all of this is going on, UTAS has been mired in this attempted relocation from Sandy Bay to Hobart CBD and associated property dealings. So a very quick potted recent history. UTAS had planned to move into the CBD and completely out of Sandy Bay. It brought up huge chunks of Hobart CBD. Now they've partly backtracked on that, although a substantial amount of the university is now spread around Hobart CBD. Their initial plan to sell all of Sandy Bay for housing was kiboshed, Adam. Yeah, and that was in the aftermath of the council elector poll that UTAS decided to change its plans. So this idea to relocate from Sandy Bay started in about 2015 under former Vice-Chancellor Peter Rathjen and continued under current Vice-Chancellor Rufus Black. And in 2021, they had a master plan to turn all of the Sandy Bay campus into 2,500 dwellings and neighbourhood amenity and had undertaken hundreds of millions of dollars in property transactions to facilitate this, including buying the old Forestry Building and Freedom Furniture site, the Webster site on Argyle Street in Hobart, the K&D site, or what most people know as the Swishers Basketball Centre, and others. There's also been sales from the purchases, like the Fountainside Hotel, Mid-City Hotel, the K&D as well. A lot of property dealings for a university. But having backtracked on much of these plans now, they've landed on this idea of four campus UTAS in Hobart. So four separate campuses. That's the city campus, a historic campus alongside Glebe, a waterfront campus and a retained Sandy Bay campus. And the Sandy Bay campus essentially has been neglected during this period of wheeling and dealing. And now it requires improvement to get it up to modern standards. Now, it needed the government for this to all kind of come together. Adam, after initially saying no way, the state government has now okayed some of UTAS's plans to sell some of the Sandy Bay estate. And legislation enabling that has just passed Parliament. Yeah, during the 2024 state election, the Liberals promised to introduce laws that require UTAS to get the support of Parliament by vote to sell any of its Sandy Bay campus as an oversight measure, as a result of all of these things that have been going on. This is land, of course, that was originally gifted to UTAS. But then there was the unusual spectacle of the government amending its own bill to slice out two pieces of land above Churchill Avenue and not just like slice them out from that, but also rezone them to inner residential. And this change came about after quite extensive lobbying by UTAS, who engaged the services of former Premier Will Hodgman to help get it done at a cost of $25,000. So, you know, small change for the UTAS. How the bill was amended is still quite unclear. And that wasn't discoverable under right to information. During this period, UTAS was also briefing another former Premier, Paul Lennon, for reasons unknown. Labor has been a vigorous supporter of UTAS's master plan for Sandy Bay and the housing component and all that. So with their support, this amended bill was able to pass the lower house and then the upper house with the support of several independents. People could be forgiven for being a bit confused about all of this, but can you tell us what is it that the uni can do now? Yes, everything about UTAS is a bit confusing and convoluted. In terms of the main Sandy Bay campus below Churchill Avenue, where most of the buildings are, UTAS would need the vote of both houses of parliament to sell any of that. But the bill enables them to sell two parcels of land on the upper side of Churchill Avenue, and that's about 27 hectares. That includes the Student Union building and former UniBar, which you would imagine is probably going to be demolished at some point. The inner residential zoning for this land allows for higher density housing, and having it rezoned already takes away one obstacle for UTAS. Any development on that land would still need to pass Hobart City Council. And as we've seen elsewhere in Hobart, housing development takes a long time to come to fruition, if at all. You have things like land banking going on with developers. There's never a guarantee that master plans and glossy pictures actually come to life. There's a remaining 56 hectares further up towards Mount Nelson that wasn't rezoned, but it also wasn't provided the same parliamentary protection of the main campus. It was somewhat forgotten during this debate, really. It wasn't mentioned in second reading speeches. UTAS is in discussions with the Aboriginal Land Council to hand this land back to the Aboriginal community. I contacted the Land Council, and those talks are ongoing, and there is interest. But the very top of that land was actually slated for housing in UTAS's master plan. So who knows if UTAS might try to at least use some of it in its land sale plans further down the track as well. In the meantime, what's been happening to course delivery? I mean, isn't that the core of the university? Yes, that's right. We're teaching people, the next generation of Tasmanians. So in addition to having, you know, academic staff questioning all these property dealings, there's also been reductions in some courses, largely in arts and humanities. There's a reduction in the languages that have been offered. You can't learn German here anymore. The National Tertiary Education Union estimates there could be up to 150 reduction in staff since 2023. Staff morale has been an ongoing issue. But UTAS did open its new forest building in the Hobart CBD this year, which could be a way of, I guess, improving morale. I've been in there. It's quite modern. But how that transition is managed is part of how UTAS, I guess, manages and addresses some of its staff morale problems. Challenges in the tertiary sector, though, they're not unique to Tasmania, Adam. No. And UTAS does regularly point this out in its annual reports that it's constantly having to adapt to policy reforms by the Commonwealth. This includes impacts on its international student quotas, but also the 2021 reforms by the Morrison government that essentially saw student fees soar, particularly for arts and humanities courses. And that resulted in major changes to student behaviour. This was pointed out by UTAS pro-Vice-Chancellor, Professor Nicholas Farrelly, in relation to humanities and social sciences, or HASS. If I had 15 seconds with the Prime Minister, yes, I'd indicate that the former Morrison government's Job Ready Graduates program has profoundly disadvantaged our Tasmanian HASS students, and it would be great to see some reconfiguration of the pricing. Adam, are lectures delivered in person at all anymore? I've been told there are significantly fewer in-person lectures, which may be a lingering after-effect of the COVID period. We all remember the Zoom meetings. Economist John Lawrence attempted to quantify this data by showing that in 2013, 33% of courses were fully online. That has risen to 73%. And I think the main change is that not all students have a choice as to whether they attend online or in-person, whereas in the past, that choice existed. And that does have an effect on campus life. But UTAS said this year that they have seen a 10% increase in on-campus attendees across its four Tasmanian campuses. Given that move to more online, is it understandable then that UTAS wants to change its physical infrastructure? I mean, are they outdated buildings meant for a different era? In some ways, yes. I mean, I mentioned the Forest Building earlier, and that certainly has those modernist elements, very open plan. It's essentially a large library, really. There's not the usual office-type layout that academics were used to. And I'm studying at UTAS at the moment, and my direct teaching staff are in the forest. They don't have their own offices. It's very small spaces for them, and that can cause some frustration. It's something that they're not used to. But it's this idea that open plan fosters collaboration, I suppose. You see that in other developments UTAS has undertaken. There was also the idea that having centrally located, like the forest, right in the middle of the Hobart CBD, really, that improves access from all of the suburbs of Hobart. But that argument was certainly not bought by the community, as we saw in the elector poll. episodes.title: Do we care enough about our pollies' mental health?
episodes.description: In what's believed to be the biggest study of its kind, a staggering 70 percent of almost 300 of our federal, state and local politicians who took part say the job has adversely affected their mental health.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Everybody's talking about fuel. Whether you're in need of filling up the tank for the week and you're watching the dollars tick over at the Bowser or you're watching weekend plans, holiday plans, business plans change. To help get your head around the latest, you can find Fuelcast in the ABC Business Daily feed on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts. Are you OK? Seems a lot of our politicians aren't. There's a lot of hard-working Tasmanians out there. My boss is the boss of Tasmania. Tasmanians want us to get on with the job. North, south, east, west. I don't care where you live in the state. Social media aggression, which can be deeply personal. I ignore it. My family see it. I've told them to ignore it. The notion that you can only be successful in politics if you're willing to be a head kicker is frankly complete bullshit. Social media is one thing, but also some of the behaviour you see within our council chambers, within our parliament, where in many other workplaces, or most other workplaces, you would not accept that sort of behaviour. The mental wear and tear is a real factor in me deciding whether or not I'd nominate later this year. Often when I talk to school groups who are in to watch question time beforehand, I'll say what you're about to see is not a very healthy display of adult behaviour. This is not a way that would be acceptable for your parents to talk to their colleagues at work or for your teachers to talk to each other at work. Hello and welcome to Tassiecast. I'm Ailey Ward coming to you from Nipaluna, Hobart. Have you ever listened to question time in state or federal parliament or checked out a local council meeting that's streamed online? To say it can be brutal is an understatement, and that must take a toll. We know it has and does because federal, state and local members have quit because it's caused or contributed to mental ill health. Former Premier Peter Gutwin cited burnout for his departure. Ministers have quit cabinet and gone to the back bench. And local councillors have thrown in the towel because of the toll the job was taking. Now, none of us make good decisions when we're not well. You know, sometimes my life can be perfectly fine.

that's at times debilitating.
And then other times I'm too happy.
I'm too impulsive.
I'm making the wrong decisions.
And look, you know, for a long time, only a few people knew sort of like knew about this.
And I think I was generally pretty good at masking at least the sadness.
Like I could, you know, go to work.
I'm pretty outgoing and bubbly.

Or I could sort of, you know, I'd be just crushed by the weight of depression.

I was nervous about speaking out because I guess I felt like a bit of a freak.
But look, I wanted to do the run anyway, because I'm a runner and I wanted to run a marathon
on the Great Ocean Road.
Often those runs come where you can sort of sponsor money for a charity.
It made sense to me to sort of raise money for mental health.
And then I kind of started thinking about, well, do I suddenly, you know, do I speak about it?
And I remember speaking to you about this and I drafted a long message.

And then, yeah, I did.
I chose to sort of share that on a public Instagram post.
And there was just this outpouring of support.
Like I was flooded with comments.
People messaged me, people I didn't know well.
People in person said something.
It was just, I was sort of wrapped in love.
It was pretty incredible.
And I'm so glad I did it.
And I guess it taught me that people are better than we think they are, except for maybe
internet trolls and that you don't know what anyone else is going through.
So choose kindness.
Thank you, Lucy.

seek help.
Until next time.
Cheers.

engagement.takeaway: The brutal, often toxic, political environment is not just a personal burden for politicians but a public crisis, eroding democracy and decision-making.
keyStatistics: 70% of Australian politicians say the job adversely affected their mental health.
A 2022 report found two-thirds of Tasmanian Parliament staff witnessed discrimination, sexual harassment, and bullying.
International study found politicians have worse mental wellbeing than emergency service employees.
40% of Australian politicians felt prevented from speaking out due to mental wellbeing concerns.
20% (one in five) of Australian politicians have considered self-harm due to job pressure.
73% of Australian politicians say gender influenced their experience.
71% of Australian politicians say their parliament workplace is the worst they've experienced.
bestQuotes: Ella Haddad: 'To misuse and to weaponise a word like misogynistic actually does a disservice not only to all women, but to men as well. For a word, the word misogynistic to be weaponised devalues the word. Better Politics Foundation: 'When leaders are exhausted, threatened or unsupported, decision-making suffers, polarisation deepens and our democracy weakens.'
engagement.whyListen: In the shadowed halls of power, where ambition clashes with vitriol, a silent crisis festers.
