episodes.title: The manosphere creeping into Tassie classrooms
episodes.description: The manosphere - the online world considered responsible for the rise in anti-social behaviour and fuelling misogyny is reaching Tassie classrooms. So how and why are men, particular young men getting caught up in this manosphere web?
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. I'm Carrington Clark. And I'm Alan Kohler. In 2026, business big and small is moving at a rapid pace. And ABC Business Daily is here to help you cut through the noise and spin. Monday to Thursday. And on Friday, I sit down with business leaders, founders, creators, changemakers and those in the know to ask them how they see the world because that's business. All in the ABC Business Daily feed on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts. Heard of the Manosphere? There's a lot of hardworking Tasmanians out there. My boss is the boss of Tasmania. Tasmanians want us to get on with the job. North, south, east, west. I don't care where you live in the state. We have allowed to settle an impression that more for women always means less for men, that this is a zero-sum game. Whereas actually, the research clearly shows, my own life experiences show, that when we rise, we rise together. A gender equal world would be a better world for men too. There's things that I think all of us can do, both as individuals and as a society and as a government, to make sure that our boys have access to the kind of information that balances out the negativity and the destructive and incredibly misogynistic content that they're getting fed online. As a mum of two teenage daughters, to hear that our sons are on average showing more conservative attitudes to relationships and to women than our father's generation does, it's really scary. And it tells us that the great strides that have been made by decades of the women's movement and movements for equality are being undone and being undone really quickly. Hello and welcome to TassieCast. I'm Ailey Ward, coming to you from Nipaluna, Hobart. This week's pod is slightly shorter than normal as a result of industrial action taken by union members at the ABC in the quest for better wages and conditions. OK, Manosphere. It sounds like it should be pretty innocuous, right? Like maybe just blokes connecting with blokes like men's sheds or something. But it's much darker than that. It's an online world considered responsible for a rise in anti-social behaviour, fuelling misogyny. And we've heard from Tassie teachers about the increasing threats and violence in schools. The bus service is cancelled. I mean, bus company Metro's reported massive increases in reports of abuse, violence and vandalism. That's not to say it's all perpetrated by males, but they are, according to the figures, the main offenders. Maybe you've seen Manosphere by renowned documentarian Louis Theroux, where manfluences promote harmful views in opposition to feminism and gender equality, which it blames for disenfranchising men and in severe cases can lead to violence. So how and why are men, particularly young men, caught up in the ugly Manosphere web? This isn't about shrinking away from the digital world. That's here to stay. But how do we handle the darker side? The ABC's Families reporter, Fiona Blackwood,'s been taking a look at what's being done to combat it. Vee, can you outline at the start, though, what do we mean when we say Manosphere? It's funny, isn't it? Because if you're not in it, you're not in it. And lots of people I spoke to when I was starting to do this story had never heard of it. Even some of the young people I spoke to who might actually be consuming some of the content had no idea about what the Manosphere was. But I think it's becoming more well known, particularly after the release of Louis Theroux's documentary. So basically, the Manosphere describes a community of online influencers and content creators who see men and boys as victims of gender equality and aim to reassert traditional gender roles. If you've been watching the latest series of Married at First Sight, Ellie, you might have heard one of the contestants saying that he wanted a submissive wife. Now, this has sparked debate with commentators talking about how that sort of language is coming directly from the Manosphere. So to go back, these are influencers, podcasters that promote traditional masculinity, male supremacy, misogyny, and in extreme cases, violence. At its most basic, it's a type of thinking that includes negative attitudes towards gender equality and feminism. So blaming women and girls for social and personal problems, dehumanising women, and believing that men should be self-reliant and show no emotion. Indigenous rights activist Thomas Mayo said at a recent No to Violence conference that he's worried that the attitude of boys and men towards women is going backwards. He said the social media algorithms are pretty good at saturating the feeds of boys and young men with this kind of stuff. We mentioned the online and you mentioned Married at First Sight. I'm not sure how that relates to the real world, but is it spilling over into the real world? Yeah, well, this is no longer just a fringe internet issue. These are harmful ideas and they're impacting directly, particularly on Australian classrooms. A recent report by Monash University heard from teachers who are saying that things are getting worse for them. And that process sort of started post the COVID era. I guess more people being online. Female teachers have reported being taunted by students with messages like, make me a sandwich, to imply that a woman's place is in the kitchen. There have also been reports of boys in classroom using hand signals made popular in the manosphere to symbolise male supremacy. And some teachers might not even know what these are or what they mean. She said teachers are also being baited by students to enter into debates about equality. And in serious cases, some female teachers have described in this report being circled by boys in the schoolyard, as well as reports of direct physical and sexual assault. It also found that the rise in the manosphere is impacting on the education of girls, with the guide reporting that one in four girls felt unsafe at school due to boys' behaviours. I think it's important to raise a point here that not all boys are attuned to the manosphere content and not all of them support it, of course. So those boys are sitting in the classroom and they're seeing their teachers being severely disrespected or the girls around them being belittled. And that can have an impact on those boys as well. A lot of what you mentioned there, Fee, is incredibly intimidating. But you mentioned some physical threats there as well. Yeah. I mean, for some teachers, the situation can become intolerable and they might consider moving schools or leaving the teaching profession altogether. And we all know there's a shortage of teachers. So Monash University and the Australian National Research Organisation for Women's Safety have put together a handbook and that's designed to help teachers identify the influence of the manosphere and how to manage it in the classroom. It's about trying to understand the pathways into the manosphere and its appeal to young men. It's also about helping young people develop critical digital literacy. It talks about whole school, consistent response to incidents of sexism and misogyny, making sure that teachers and students who have experienced these behaviours feel supported and that boys who have caused harm are held accountable. We heard at the top, Fee, from former Prime Minister Julia Gillard in a recent interview with the BBC, let's face it, moving through adolescence is often a really difficult time. You know, you're trying to find your tribe, as it were. But this rise in harmful attitudes being seen in classrooms is also being seen in the political sphere. I mean, Julia Gillard's misogyny speech, it's gone down in the annals of history. But we've got the current President of the United States calling female journalists derogatory things based on their looks. Julia Gillard is Chair of the Global Institute for Women's Leadership at King's College in London. And that recent research to mark International Women's Day was so eye-opening. More than 20,000 people across 29 countries, including Australia, were surveyed and 31% of Gen Z men agreed that a wife should always obey her husband. And one third said a husband should have the final word on important decisions. I mean, they're pretty staggering figures. But it's not just girls and women who are impacted by this toxic behaviour perpetrated by the so-called manosphere. That's right. And for some influencers, key beliefs of the manosphere overlap with other far-right groups. So there are links to homophobia, transphobia, white supremacy and racism and anti-immigration views. As Thomas Mayo said in his speech, it's not just about misogyny, but it's about division. What is the advice then to not just teachers, you know, there's a handbook for teachers on how best to try to tackle this. What about parents and carers like at home? Yeah, well, I mean, this guidebook could be handy for parents too, particularly if you have no idea about the manosphere. It sort of gives a bit of an overview of what it is. Parenting experts also say it's important for parents to understand why some boys might be attracted to the manosphere and talking to them about it. It's crucial to help them identify harmful content. Experts say parents need to emphasise that it's normal to be curious, but also to provide other perspectives. They say it might be a good idea to explore a specific piece of content with your child, trying to understand the world they're engaging with, what resonates with them, what doesn't. And also really key is exposing boys to different versions of masculinity than what they're seeing online. So real role models, dads, uncles, brothers, coaches, friends, people in their lives who are healthy male role models and finding ways to connect with them. Well, the non-healthy role models, that's certainly something that our politicians in Tassie have also been raising. Here's what Labor's Ella Haddad and the Greens' Vicar Bailey told TassieCast. Part of the danger of how these algorithms work and they push this content into the feeds of young men is that it's completely pervasive and it can take over so much of the content that they are seeing. And these types of views, I think, were always there, but they used to lurk in the shadows a bit. But now they are on tens of millions of screens of tens of millions of young men every day. We need to accept that Tasmania is no exception. Just because we're an island at the bottom of the world doesn't mean we're immune from these kind of influences because the internet, you know, straddles all people, basically. Fee, Man Cave, a mental health charity that works with young men, have weighed into this. What have they got to say? Yeah, I spoke to Ben Vassilou, who runs the Man Cave. They hold workshops for young men right across Australia. Here he is unpacking a bit more in depth about what the Manosphere looks like. The Manosphere is promoting content that's about getting jacked, getting ripped, getting rich quick. It's very anti-women. It's anti-gender equity. It's anti-gay and queer community. And what it's doing is sucking this vacuum and this opportunity where boys feel either lost, disconnected, or simply just need to be heard and feel belonging into this conversation and this content that's actually quite damaging. It's not all bad news, though, Fee. Ben Vassilou says things might be changing. That's right. The Man Cave has worked with over 100,000 boys over the last decade. He says it can't just be on teachers and parents to deal with this issue and that sometimes schools need to bring the experts in, like his organisation. He says they hold workshops without screens, without PowerPoint presentations, and they talk to boys. And he says the key is being able to have messy conversations that might not be politically correct, that go to the undercurrent of the language and hopefully shift and change behaviour. It's about getting boys to open up, talk about what's going on in their lives, what's happening in the world around them, and bringing up some hairy topics that teachers and parents might struggle with, and then showing them a different way. Here's a bit more of what he had to say. And we're seeing pretty significant impact across those workshops, and we're actually seeing boys reverse behaviours, reverse feelings of hopelessness, reverse misogynistic or homophobic behaviours. We're seeing that in real time, and also longitudinally, we're seeing thousands of boys actually change their view from what they've seen online. Fee, you've got young men in your life. What conversations have you had with them? I mean, I just spend a lot of time asking my son to clean his room, which doesn't really apply to this. But I would say for me, the best time to have these sort of conversations is in the car. So when they're kind of trapped, they don't have to have direct eye contact with you. I mean, I'm no parenting expert, but I guess it's all about trying to keep communication open, which can be really hard when they're teenagers. Let us know what you do with the young men in your life. Is it a chat around the dinner table or with that captive audience in the car like Fee does? Thanks very much, Fee. And thanks to you too for joining us on this truncated version of TassieCast. Until next time, cheers. You've been listening to an ABC podcast. Discover more great ABC podcasts, live radio and exclusives on the ABC Listen app.

episodes.title: Kunanyi/Mt Wellington: A mountain of a debate
episodes.description: Kunanyi/Mt Wellington is Tasmania's most visited natural asset but is a cable car the answer to getting more people on the mountain?
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Hi, it's Sam Hawley from ABC News Daily. The podcast that brings you one big story affecting your world each weekday in just 15 minutes. AI is changing not just how we work, but it's also changing how we fight war. And we see that on our screens. We see what's happening in Iran. We see what's happening in Gaza. We see what's happening in Ukraine. Join me for ABC News Daily. Find us on ABC Listen. It's a mountain of a debate. There's a lot of hard-working Tasmanians out there. My boss is the boss of Tasmania. Tasmanians want us to get on with the job. North, south, east, west. I don't care where you live in the state. I just love the rocks, the flora, the fauna, the whole aesthetic of the place. It's just such an amazing park just on our doorstep. I'm committed not only to the Cradle Valley cableway, but also a cableway on Kunani, Mount Wellington, and I've sought advice on developing a pathway to support this to happen. The pipe dream of a cable car, it stymies a proper conversation and real progress on credible solutions to the challenges that faces the mountain. A road that was built in 1930s that has been designed to accommodate traffic in 2030. We'd like to see Kunani return to Aboriginal ownership, but at least it's important that Aboriginal people are given the opportunity to have a say in its protection. Hello and welcome to TassieCast. I'm Ailey Ward coming to you from Nipaluna, Hobart. When was the last time you went up Hobart's Kunani, Mount Wellington? Is it one of the first places you'd take visitors? Or maybe you just look out the window of a morning to have a look to help you decide what to wear by gauging what the weather's going to do that day. Depending on where you are in Tassie South, chances are you have a view of some sort. Home to a vast array of native plants and animals, it's also of major cultural significance for many of the state's First Nations people. Although by no measure Tassie's tallest mountain, Kunani does dominate the Hobart skyline, providing an imposing backdrop to the city. And views from the summit are without doubt spectacular. In good weather, that is. It's already Tassie's most visited natural asset at around half a million people a year. But the government reckons it's still too hard for many to access it. And as we heard at the beginning, Premier Jeremy Rockliffe wants to see a cable car on it. Reporter Adam Holmes has been looking into the various reviews around its future management and access and whether those reviews might make that development easier. Adam, a government review of how the mountain and the surrounding park is managed began around about two years ago. Now, the final report is due soon and access is expected to feature heavily. Yes, due soon. And the report is actually overdue. And it's being delivered by the Department of State Growth, which is soon to be building Tasmania, apparently. But when this review started in 2024, access was just one of a broad range of matters to be looked into. So there were things like governance issues, values management like flora and fauna and Aboriginal cultural values. There's been concern about this not being core to what the government is doing here. And then there was a category user experience. And that's where access came into it. But as the review has progressed, this access question has become one of the main focuses. And that might be because that's what like dominates the public debate. What people seem to get most worked up about is this idea that access to the top of the mountain is restricted when there's adverse weather conditions and so on. And this focus on access has now created a few differences of opinion, it's fair to say. Well, before we get to the potential outcomes of the reviews, and there are a number of reviews underway, can we look at the current management? It's under the auspices of the Wellington Park Management Trust. Yes, the trust is the overarching authority for the park. It has representatives from government agencies like Parks and Wildlife, Tazwater. Also Hobart and Glenorchy Councils, they kind of all jointly fund it. Essentially, their role is to make sure that whatever happens in the broader Wellington Park is in line with an agreed Wellington Park Management Plan. And that's an incredibly important document that we'll probably return to later. But there is a fair bit of overlapping interest when you think of all the different bodies that have ownership there. So Hobart Council owns and manages the summit and the eastern slopes of the mountain. So that's what you see from Hobart, essentially. And that's where the vast majority of the visitor infrastructure is. And the council is spending close to $5 million a year to maintain that. And that's quite a lot more than any of the other bodies are spending on the park, including the state government. Glenorchy Council owns and funds a smaller part, Tazwater as well, Parks and Wildlife and so on. In the Tasmanian context, having so many different landowners and management interests happening. And it probably adds to a lot of the challenges that you see with the mountain. There are already a hell of a lot of people that use the mountain. And that's forecast to increase significantly, Adam. Has something got to give? I mean, you talked about all those different bodies involved. And also, is it sustainable to continue, you know, in this way? I mean, the road to the Pinnacle was finished being built, what, almost 100 years ago. And it is narrow and pretty hairy at times. Yeah. So on that demand question, the most recent forecast was that visitor numbers could increase from 500,000 to 700,000 by 2030. So all these different bodies are in agreement that changes are needed. Because as you say, Pinnacle Road, it was built in a completely different era. The government's review is taking a look at the options there, whether it actually is feasible to widen the road. Even if any of the fire trails leading up to the summit could somehow be developed into new road access as well. I feel like that's probably not going to happen. But interestingly, in the last 12 months to July, there was a 25% increase in the amount of people who enter the shelter at the Pinnacle. But in the same period, there was actually a slight reduction in the overall vehicle traffic. So that suggests that there might be some change in visitor behaviour that's happening. More people might be using buses. Fewer people are feeling the need to drive up there. And that sort of data could be used to assess all of these different options at the moment. Because there's actually four different reviews going on at the moment. The government's review that the trust is reviewing its management plan. The trust is doing a business case into various options. And Hobart Council is also looking into some proposals as well. So lots happening. So you can hit play and get updated while brushing your teeth or making your lunch. And it's always up to date, ready whenever you're ready to get across the day's news. Just search ABC News Top Stories podcast on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts. The race is on, but maybe not for much longer. There's a lot of hardworking Tasmanians out there. My boss is the boss of Tasmania. Tasmanians want us to get on with the job. North, south, east, west. I don't care where you live in the state. Green light now on Kingsley Jarman Fencing. Grade 5, 278 metres. Racing, Riviera Akira fairly had off in. Side starts to master to be joint leaders now with Dusty Rico burnt desires. It's just such a cruel industry and it is irredeemably so. Tasmania's got very good welfare standards. So, you know, we're told all these terrible things happen. It's not actually the truth. Hello and welcome to TassieCast. I'm Ailey Ward coming to you from Nipaluna, Hobart. When was the last time you went to a race meet? Greyhounds, pacing or thoroughbreds? Maybe you're a once a year race goer for, you know, that one that supposedly stops the nation. Or maybe you've never been and have no desire to. Legislation to ban one of the codes in Tassie, greyhound racing, passed the lower house late last year and will soon be voted on in the upper house. So is the end nigh for the industry? And if it is, what will it mean for the dogs and people currently involved? 7.30 reporter Adam Langenberg is weighing the odds of the ban. Adam, hello. Hi, Ellie. Adam, is it fair to say the industry was blindsided by the announcement from Premier Jeremy Rockliffe late last year that he would legislate to ban greyhound racing? It's absolutely fair, Ellie. Now, after the state election last year, the government found itself short of a majority. It needed to convince the Greens and, you know, mostly progressive crossbenches to keep them in power. It offered up a range of policy compromises to be able to do that, a review of the salmon industry. They previously scrapped a plan in terms of logging native forests and then banned the greyhound racing industry from mid-2029. It was offered as a way to get those progressive crossbenches and the Greens on board who had all said that this industry was a cruel one for a long time. Now, it passed the lower house very fast last year. It's currently before the upper house. They voted to delay that legislation when it came before them for a vote. But it is fair to say that the speed of all of this has caught the racing industry and the greyhound industry by surprise. They got a letter from Premier Jeremy Rockliffe in July last year that said the government was committed to the long-term sustainability and viability of the greyhound racing industry. And then to have this foisted upon them all of a sudden and the legislation rushed through Parliament definitely caught them by surprise and has rocked that industry. There's a lot of angry people out there. There has been growing public concern, though, Adam, about the industry, particularly animal welfare concerns, high injury rates and also the amount of public money that goes into it. Yeah, I think it's fair to say that public sentiment about the greyhound racing industry has been drifting the wrong side for the industry for quite a while now. That momentum started about a decade ago with that shocking Four Corners expose of live animal baiting, of poor conditions, of animal cruelty. Lots of that was in New South Wales. That led the New South Wales government at the time to announce a ban on greyhound racing. That was overturned after significant pressure from the industry, but also some colourful radio personalities. But it prompted action in other jurisdictions as well. In Tasmania, there was a parliamentary inquiry that looked into allegations of all different kinds of things. It found no evidence of live animal baiting in Tasmania, but also didn't rule it out. But it did find a whole range of things for the industry to improve on. Can we talk about some of those Tassie specifics, Adam? How many racing greyhounds are there in the state? And what do we know in terms of injuries or deaths? According to figures released just last week, there's about just over a thousand registered racing greyhounds in Tasmania. That number has increased slightly since the legislation came before the Upper House, which had been a concern raised by Racing Integrity Commissioner Sean Carroll, that if this legislation didn't take place immediately, that those numbers would rise. And that's what's happened. It has. It's only a slight increase, about 25 since the end of last year, but it is an increase nonetheless. In terms of injuries and deaths, you have to comb through stewards' reports to be able to find those figures. A group called the Coalition for the Protection of Greyhounds, they're an anti-racing group, they've done exactly that. According to that group, there were two deaths in Tasmania in 2025 of racing greyhounds and 267 injuries. Now, the greyhound racing industry says lots of those injuries are minor. The trainer that you heard at the beginning there of the podcast, Sharon Marshall, says if a greyhound breaks a toenail, that that injury is reported as an injury on a steward's report. So that's the claim of the industry. But yeah, 267 injuries among a thousand greyhounds. Has the industry lost its social licence? That's been the claim from opponents for a long time. They say it's a cruel industry, only there for the profit of gambling companies, basically. Now, the industry pushes pretty hard back against those claims. But from the public sentiment that we've been able to look at, it seems that those arguments of the anti-racing campaigners are starting to flow through and have an impact. EMRS, a polling company here in Tasmania, conducted its own polling after Tasmania announced the ban. It found 74% of Tasmanians supported the ban. There's not a whole lot of national polling about sentiments that comes from reputable polling agencies. It's lots of pro and anti organisations that put out their own polling. But that's what we've been able to glean from the EMRS data. And then if you look overseas, lots of jurisdictions are pulling out of greyhound racing. Certainly the momentum is away from the industry and not for it. Well, Australia is one of the few countries in the world that still has commercial greyhound racing. In fact, we have more than half the tracks, Adam. Yeah, that's right, Ellie. According to the organisation Grey 2K USA, there are about 95 tracks in the world. They're across the US, the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand. Now, that's going to drop to about 80 when New Zealand faces out their industry in the middle of this year. 49 of those tracks, according to that organisation, are in Australia. That has dropped recently. It was 65 only a couple of years ago. But yeah, so a huge proportion of those tracks are in Australia. Well, you mentioned across the ditch there, Adam. The ban in New Zealand does come into effect from July this year. It's had a 20-month wind-down period. If legislative councillors vote in favour, how is it going to work here? Yeah, so it's a much slower implementation period here in Tasmania than what you see in New Zealand, Ellie. 20 months in New Zealand, depending on when this bill passes, if it does at all. In the upper house, it will be longer than that, maybe on the three-year side. But there are some transitionary things in place as well. And we've missed one of those transitions, haven't we? We have, absolutely. So the first is a ban on the breeding of racing greyhounds. That was supposed to be from the beginning of this year. Obviously, that hasn't taken effect according to those timeframes. The other is that greyhounds over six or that haven't raced in more than 12 months unless they're injured would be required to be retired and deregistered. That will take place as soon as that ban passes the upper house, if indeed it does. And then the third is TAS Racing will have to provide consent before trainers can transfer a greyhound to another trainer. What's the racing lifespan of a greyhound, Adam? I mean, you mentioned six there. I mean, we know a greyhound lives longer than that. There must already be a lot of dogs that have finished their so-called career. What happens to them? The racing lifespan of a greyhound is actually pretty short. Some of them only race for a couple of races and are too slow or too injured and don't actually see many more than two or three races to begin with. But for the ones that have longer racing careers, they still only race for three years. And normally retire at about five. So there's, you know, a lifespan of another five years or nine. The average lifespan of a greyhound is 10 to 14 years. That's a long time that a greyhound has to live in another non-racing environment. What happens after a greyhound is retired has been a key concern for a long time. We don't really have stats about how many greyhounds are put down. The industry calls it wastage. We just don't understand what happens. And it's only now that the Integrity Commission in the racing space is actually putting in place a traceability officer to be able to keep track of exactly where those greyhounds go after their racing career happens. And it's certainly one of those arguments around winding up the industry that comes from those animal activists. There are greyhound adoption programs in Tassie. I mean, there's the one known as GAP. It hasn't always run according to expectations. And there are other animal welfare organisations, Adam, that also have taken on surrenders to find new homes. But, I mean, the numbers, I mean, you're mentioning there there's the, you know, the officers now looking at this. But there must be a lot of dogs that are going to need to find homes if this ban goes through. That's right, Ellie. There are quite a few providers out there on top of the greyhound adoption program, which you're right, has been criticised for not adopting out enough dogs and a lot of dogs being put down. The Dogs Home of Tasmania, for example, they're all preparing for a huge influx of dogs. Here's what the CEO of the Dogs Home, Mark Wilde, says about the preparations for what are normally a pretty complex set of behaviours in former racing greyhounds. The thing we wanted to get across was, I guess, the urgency around starting this transition because 30 June 2029 is coming around really quickly. There's a lot of dogs in the industry and they all need to find new homes. And so that generally takes time. If this ban gets through the upper house, what's the process? How will it work? So obviously in the first place, all those bans that were part of the transitionary process we talked about before in terms of the ban on breeding, they all come into effect immediately as soon as the bill passes. And then there's a transitionary plan that will be worked on by Racing Integrity Commissioner Sean Carroll. That's still under development. Animal welfare organisations, they're ramping up for an anticipated increase in adoptions required. What though is the industry doing? The industry is working as hard as it can to overturn the ban, to quash it. Everything that you can expect from an industry fighting to save for itself, it's been engaged in. Full page ads and so on, yeah. Exactly. So newspaper ads, TV ads, there's been a song. Everything that we can expect from the industry. They've refused to talk compensation because that's an admission of defeat. Lots of the campaign has been around maximising and amplifying the voices of local greyhound trainers and owners who have been doing this for a long time and face losing their livelihoods. They've suffered a range of blows, both in terms of the ban being announced, but then also an outbreak of kennel cough recently, which stopped the industry in its tracks for a little while. It's only just restarting. There are a number of deaths at about the same time as well that are not linked to kennel cough, but it has been a really big period of upheaval for the industry. Here's trainer Sharon Marshall, who we heard from before, talking about the impact. People are stressing and it's been very, very hard. That and the kennel cough and everything else. It's been a really, really hard few months. But, you know, people are trying to do the right thing, trying to keep going. Adam, independent economist Saul Eslake, he did a report into the financing of greyhound racing in Tasmania. And to say that it was scathing would be an understatement. Yeah, Saul definitely didn't hold back. He said the industry is almost totally reliant on government funding and he positioned it as throwing good money after bad. So what are we talking about here? How much money? Over 15 years, greyhound racing has received about $75 million of taxpayer funding. The amount each year has steadily increased. It's indexed under the agreement. Saul says by 5.6% each year, which outstrips education spending, which he highlights has increased by about 4% per year over the same period. Ellie, the funding deed for all three racing codes, including greyhound racing, expires in 2029, which is the same time that this proposed ban would take place. And Saul goes on to make the point that that money could be used elsewhere, given the state of Tasmania's finances. And we've just recently heard about major cuts and concerns at TASTAFE. Yeah, he sure does. People have listened to TassieCast over a while, especially me banging on about the state of the finances, will not be surprised to hear that Saul Eslake has been ringing the alarm about Tasmania's budget situation for a long time. Certainly his view is that money should be spent somewhere else. Okay, out of all of the codes combined, Adam, how much taxpayer money goes in? Ellie, so the deed was signed in 2009 for a 20-year period. Initially it was $27 million a year, but it's indexed. As of this year, we're expecting it to be just under $40 million. And then there's infrastructure spending, like track upgrades and facility improvements and those kind of things that are on top of that. Is there a balance sheet? I mean, like, is it ultimately cost neutral? Does it make money? Or are we, the taxpayer, forking out? This is where it gets a little bit contentious. The industry's commissioned its own economic modelling about its economic value and the jobs it created. A couple of years ago, it estimated the wider greyhound racing industry added an economic value of about $60 million a year to the Tasmanian economy, plus added 486 full-time equivalent jobs. Now, Saul Eslake doesn't like those figures at all. He says the job figures are overestimated. And then when he talks about the economic value, he points out that the method used has been criticised by official inquiries, the Australian Bureau of Statistics and the Productivity Commission. He just says they can't be accepted at face value. So we don't really know. We have no idea. It's always like had a go at doing his own, but we just don't know. Okay, in the coming days, how's the dice going to fall in the upper house? It's a really good question. I think it will be really tight. There's 14 votes on the floor of the upper house, and we only know how seven people are going to vote at this stage. On the banning side, there are five votes. Three Liberal members of Parliament, Meg Webb, the Independent, and Cassie O'Connor, the Greens member. We know that the two Labor MPs, Sarah Lovell and Luke Edmonds, are on the other side. So then there's seven swing votes, and you need three of them on side for greyhound racing to be banned. I think it's fair to say that the government and anti-greyhound racing campaigners are targeting five key independents. They're Ruth Forrest, Mike Gaffney, Rosemary Armitage, Beck Thomas, and Dean Harris. What are those five telling you? A lot of things. I think they're legitimately trying to work out how this is going to work. Lots of the upper house members would like to see compensation included in this bill, and they expect that the government might meet them halfway on there. So we're going to see some key independents meet with Jeremy Rockliffe next week with their concerns. I don't think that this can pass without compensation amounts being part of the legislation. So it'll end up having to go back to the lower house. There will be some amendments you anticipate if it gets through at all. Absolutely. And the pressure's on pretty hard here. The MPs that I've spoken to have all received lots of emails and texts, but nothing of the scale like the stadium debate that we've talked about before. It's much more muted than that, but there is pressure, and they are receiving messages from members of the greyhound industry locally who are all telling personal stories about how long they've worked for. What about the greyhound industry interstate? I mean, what's the sort of the feeling, and is there pressure as well from interstate not wanting to see a state have a ban? There 100% is pressure from the industry. I think they've largely left it to the local industry to lobby politicians and tell their stories as the way of doing that. I think that that's the coordinated campaign here. But 100%, we've talked about Australia being one of those big last bastions of greyhound racing. If one domino falls and says, right, we're out of greyhound racing, does that set a national precedent? That's the fear of the national greyhound industry. They're going to fight this as hard as they can. We've talked about some of the tactics they're employing. I think that amplification of local voices is part of it, whereas some of the upper house MPs that I was speaking to say they're getting lots of pro forma default templates from people who are against the industry. Not as many personal stories. So I think that that's a tactic that's maybe having some sort of impact. And I spoke to MPs who are concerned about the impact on lower paid people from regional Tasmania who've been doing this for the love of animals and racing for a long time and are concerned about the impacts that it's going to have on them. They feel like the Premier is targeting vulnerable working class Tasmanians. So it'll be really interesting to see how the government addresses some of those concerns. And I don't think that case got made any easier when the Premier talked about cashed up mainland thugs in the greyhound industry lobbying against this bill. I know a few people with adopted greyhounds, Adam. They're big sloths apart from the occasional Zoomy. What about you? Oh, they're much too energetic for me, Ellie. Although I have been really surprised at press conferences with large packs of greyhounds over the years. They're pretty docile. They've managed to perform better than lots of children I interview. So it's been good. I'm certainly an admirer from afar. A shocking pun, I know, Adam. But there is a lot riding on this vote. Thanks very much for joining us. And thanks to you too for joining us on TassieCast. Until next time, cheers.

Or are we, the taxpayer, forking out?
This is where it gets a little bit contentious.
The industry's commissioned its own economic modelling about its economic value and the jobs it created.
A couple of years ago, it estimated the wider greyhound racing industry added an economic value of about $60 million a year to the Tasmanian economy,
plus added 486 full-time equivalent jobs.
Now, Saul Eslake doesn't like those figures at all.
He says the job figures are overestimated.
And then when he talks about the economic value, he points out that the method used has been criticised by official inquiries,
the Australian Bureau of Statistics and the Productivity Commission.
He just says they can't be accepted at face value.
So we don't really know.
We have no idea.
It's always like had a go at doing his own, but we just don't know.
Okay, in the coming days, how's the dice going to fall in the upper house?
It's a really good question.
I think it will be really tight.
There's 14 votes on the floor of the upper house, and we only know how seven people are going to vote at this stage.
On the banning side, there are five votes.
Three Liberal members of Parliament, Meg Webb, the Independent, and Cassie O'Connor, the Greens member.
We know that the two Labor MPs, Sarah Lovell and Luke Edmonds, are on the other side.
So then there's seven swing votes, and you need three of them on side for greyhound racing to be banned.
I think it's fair to say that the government and anti-greyhound racing campaigners are targeting five key independents.
They're Ruth Forrest, Mike Gaffney, Rosemary Armitage, Beck Thomas, and Dean Harris.
What are those five telling you?
A lot of things.
I think they're legitimately trying to work out how this is going to work.
Lots of the upper house members would like to see compensation included in this bill, and they expect that the government might meet them halfway on there.
So we're going to see some key independents meet with Jeremy Rockliffe next week with their concerns.
I don't think that this can pass without compensation amounts being part of the legislation.
So it'll end up having to go back to the lower house.
There will be some amendments you anticipate if it gets through at all.
Absolutely.
And the pressure's on pretty hard here.
The MPs that I've spoken to have all received lots of emails and texts, but nothing of the scale like the stadium debate that we've talked about before.

It's much more muted than that, but there is pressure, and they are receiving messages from members of the greyhound industry locally who are all telling personal stories about how long they've worked for.
What about the greyhound industry interstate?
I mean, what's the sort of the feeling, and is there pressure as well from interstate not wanting to see a state have a ban?
There 100% is pressure from the industry.
I think they've largely left it to the local industry to lobby politicians and tell their stories as the way of doing that.
I think that that's the coordinated campaign here.
But 100%, we've talked about Australia being one of those big last bastions of greyhound racing.
If one domino falls and says, right, we're out of greyhound racing, does that set a national precedent?
That's the fear of the national greyhound industry.
They're going to fight this as hard as they can.
We've talked about some of the tactics they're employing.

I think that amplification of local voices is part of it, whereas some of the upper house MPs that I was speaking to say they're getting lots of pro forma default templates from people who are against the industry.
Not as many personal stories.
So I think that that's a tactic that's maybe having some sort of impact.

And I spoke to MPs who are concerned about the impact on lower paid people from regional Tasmania who've been doing this for the love of animals and racing for a long time and are concerned about the impacts that it's going to have on them.
They feel like the Premier is targeting vulnerable working class Tasmanians.
So it'll be really interesting to see how the government addresses some of those concerns.
And I don't think that case got made any easier when the Premier talked about cashed up mainland thugs in the greyhound industry lobbying against this bill.
I know a few people with adopted greyhounds, Adam.
They're big sloths apart from the occasional Zoomy.
What about you?
Oh, they're much too energetic for me, Ellie.
Although I have been really surprised at press conferences with large packs of greyhounds over the years.
They're pretty docile.
They've managed to perform better than lots of children I interview.
So it's been good.
I'm certainly an admirer from afar.
A shocking pun, I know, Adam.
But there is a lot riding on this vote.
Thanks very much for joining us.
And thanks to you too for joining us on TassieCast.
Until next time, cheers.

episodes.title: Inside a Hobart community needle exchange program
episodes.description: When you imagine someone using a needle exchange program, who do you picture? Chances are, it’s not always who you’d expect.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Hi, it's Sam Hawley from ABC News Daily. The podcast that brings you one big story affecting your world each weekday in just 15 minutes. The idea of regime change being affected from the air, it's got no precedent. Netanyahu and Trump's theory that Iranians will see the weakness of the regime and rush to replace it. I'm sceptical of all of that. I really am. Join me for ABC News Daily. Find us on ABC Listen. When you think of someone using a needle exchange, who comes to mind? Odds are it's not always who you'd expect. There's a lot of hardworking Tasmanians out there. My boss is the boss of Tasmania. Tasmanians want us to get on with the job. North, south, east, west. I don't care where you live in the state. What happens in this room stays in this room. I see a lot of people in the wider community and they're just regular people. I say g'day and I say g'day and we go on our way until I see them next in here again. Hello and welcome to ABC Tassiecast. I'm Selina Bryan, filling in for Airlie Ward for this episode, where I'm taking you out to Bridgewater Community House, where a state-funded needle and syringe exchange program runs out of the Jordan River Service. A recent study found that hundreds of former Queensland prisoners may have been exposed to hepatitis C and HIV after an inmate shared injecting equipment behind bars, sparking debate over harm minimisation and drug use in Australian prisons. And while Senior Harm Minimisation Officer Shane O'Sullivan does see local prisoners who've recently been released, this program here in Tassie is used far more broadly than you might expect. Thanks for joining us, Shane. So can you tell us what happens here? Well, it's basically an outlet to provide clean injecting equipment for people who use drugs. And what's the benefit of that kind of service of having a needle exchange? The benefit for the wider community is that we're minimising harm to everybody else and plus for the person who's actually using drugs. So by providing all the clean equipment, we can ensure that they're practising safe injecting methods. So what are the services that you have here? Can you talk us through that? We have basically a good range of injecting equipment that they could use for any type of opioid, methamphetamine, steroids. We also have naloxone and pranoxad, which are overdose medications, which have actually saved a few lives. So we do get feedback and it saves some people from overdosing. And we have a disposal, a 24-hour disposal method that safe bins that they can put their used equipment into. When you say it also helps harm minimisation in the broader community, how does that benefit come? Well, I suppose it's by not spreading things like Hep C, Hep B and HIV. So by ensuring that they're using clean equipment and they're disposing of it here in a safe manner, the wider community is much safer. And who do you see coming through this centre? A broad range of people. I must admit I was preconceived at what a drug user would be. They're ordinary people and sometimes have just had extraordinary things happen in their life, usually traumatic. And there's always a background story. It takes a very long time for them to trust you and tell you what the background is. So what happens in this room stays in this room. I see a lot of people in the wider community and shopping and that sort of thing. And they're just regular people. I say g'day and I say g'day and we go on our way until I see them next in here again. What addictions are people most commonly struggling with here? Methamphetamine. Methamphetamine. It's the drug of choice by probably 90%. A little bit of morphine use, the occasional heroin and cocaine. But yeah, methamphetamines are the big, big drug that's used in this area. Have you seen that change over your time here or has it stayed pretty steady? No, it stayed pretty static. I think it's easy to produce, it's cheap and it's readily available. So yeah, that's the drug of choice, unfortunately. And has pretty serious side effects for those who are addicted to it. Yeah, it's definitely hard to get off once they start. It's sort of hard to judge. Some people have got an addictive nature, I guess. Some come in here and they say, that's it, I'm not using anymore. And they quit that day and you don't see them again. But others try and they continually come back. So yeah, it must be very hard. Can you talk us through the numbers that you see coming in here each year? In 2025, we saw 1,054 people. 778 were male and 276 were female. So it's usually the same group of people, so it's the same cohort. They'll come in sometimes daily, sometimes weekly. Often you don't see them for quite a period of time and you wonder what's happened to them. Have they overdosed? Have they moved? Have they not used anymore, which is the best case scenario? Yeah, so we saw a broad range of people and most of them are working, functioning people in the community. You wouldn't know unless you actually dealt with them. And so there is quite a high percentage of men there. There are couples who come through as well, is that right? Yeah, there's definitely couples. Not a great deal of couples. There's usually a domineering one of the two. So I think sometimes one of the partners may not want to use, but they're pressured by the other person to use drugs. So yeah, that's always a bit of a difficult one to handle. And there are times where you almost form an unofficial counsellor role then as well? You do. Yeah. Sometimes I come in and shut the door, just cry on your shoulder. Just need somebody to talk to. You deal with a lot of people who have come out of prison as well, is that right? How soon do people come to you once they've been released? Sometimes it's straight out that morning. This is their safe place to come to. Some are homeless, some don't have family. So they know that they can come here, they can get something to eat, they can have a coffee, they can have a chat. And if they really need injecting equipment, yeah, we can provide that too. We saw news that more than 80 prisoners used a single needle to inject illicit drugs in one day inside a Queensland jail. That was according to a study published in the International Journal of Drug Policy. No Australian prison has a needle or syringe exchange program. Do you think that needs to change based on what you see? From what I see, yeah, it would definitely benefit. I read that same thing, sharpening needles on the concrete to use it again and again. Yeah, scary stuff. The damage that they would do to their veins plus the risk of spreading viruses between sharing that same noodle. Yeah, it's something, just personal opinion, yeah, I think it needs something to happen. How do you think that could benefit people who are incarcerated? I guess by testing them and helping them whilst they're incarcerated. Maybe when they come out, they've got a clean slate to start with again. We do see some here. We run regular Hep C clinics here the first Thursday of every month. So I encourage any of them that I know have just been released to come along. There is an incentive, a voucher that we give them for groceries to go and get some food at least. And that incentivizes them to come and get tested. We haven't had a huge amount of positive comeback. So that's been really good. Most of them test negative. But yeah, it's a very good way to do it. And do you see most people do follow through on that then? Like that you encourage people to come to that clinic. Do you see that they do? Yeah, well, it's an eight-week program or 12-week program on a pill. So basically all they've got to do is get tested if it's positive. They take the pill for 12 weeks and, yeah, they're cured again. And they can keep doing that. If they happen to get Hep C again, it's a repetitive thing. You can just take the pill and become cured again. There are other, as you mentioned, risks of needle use like that that they have seen in that study in prisons. Have you seen other people suffer other types of injuries or problems from needle use? I have seen a few. Some people come in and they'll show you their wounds where they're injecting in strange places. Sometimes their abscesses form. Other times some really bad scarring. So, yeah, it is a bit of an issue. But we are fortunate that we also have a medical group that comes here every second Wednesday. So if we happen to spot that at the same time, we can take them straight out and get them some medical attention. What prompted you personally to get involved in this work? Well, I came here as a volunteer teaching driving, of all things. And then all of a sudden they needed somebody to run the needle exchange. And it was sort of something I'd never even contemplated. I've never touched a drop of alcohol in my life. I don't smoke. And I thought ice was what formed in fridges. So to come here and do something like this was totally out of left field. And I wasn't sure what to expect, to be honest, with the people I was going to deal with. But I have, in the seven or eight years I've been here now, I've not had any disrespectful people. They're all extremely polite. They're all very thankful for what you do for them. And is the work here well supported by the community or are there still stigmas around it? No, most people that come in here, we have the regulars that come into the community every day, into the community house every day. I've never heard a bad word spoken about any of the people that come into the NSP. Yeah. I think it's accepted. They realise they're just ordinary people and have been put in bad situations. And unfortunately, some of these drugs, some of these opioids, the synthetic opioids, they're 500 times stronger than heroin. So the tiniest little drop and they're hooked. Yeah. So that addiction does become so hard to keep. Definitely. Thanks for coming out to Bridgewater with me. I'm Selina Bryan. Airlie Ward will be back with you next episode. And if you want to get in touch, you can email us at tassiecast at abc.net.au. Until next time. Cheers. You've been listening to an ABC podcast. Discover more great ABC podcasts, live radio and exclusives on the ABC Listen app.

episodes.title: Is that a side of antibiotics with your seafood?
episodes.description: After its public image took a dive last summer when millions of fish died ... the salmon industry sought regulatory approval to use an antibiotic in a bid to prevent more mass deaths.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Hi, it's Sam Hawley from ABC News Daily. The podcast that brings you one big story affecting your world each weekday in just 15 minutes. If wealth inequality gets bigger and bigger and bigger, and the super rich, the very rich take a bigger and bigger, bigger share of the wealth, the biggest consequence of that is unaffordable housing. Living standards will fall for ordinary Australians. Join me for ABC News Daily. Find us on ABC Listen. Food is medicine, right? Or is medicine in your food? There's a lot of hard-working Tasmanians out there. My boss is the boss of Tasmania. Tasmanians want us to get on with the job. North, south, east, west, I don't care where you live in the state. Well, I just think Tassel's taking the piss, quite frankly. Like, seriously, there's significant concerns around the use of this antibiotic. And public health advice remains that the fish are safe to eat. So I'm not concerned from an environmental health or from a public health perspective about the use of flifenacol. The federal regulator is seeking information because what we don't want to see is an impact on trade relationships and the ability for other really important aquaculture sectors in Tasmania to have access to those markets. Hello and welcome to TassieCast. I'm Ely Ward coming to you from Nipaluna, Hobart. Maybe it's your go-to for a healthy family dinner. It's a great source of protein, good fats and other nutrients which can help keep your heart healthy. I'm talking about fish, particularly oily fish such as salmon. It's also a massive shot in the arm to Tasmania's economy. The state's farmed salmon industry is valued at more than $1 billion a year and it employs a lot of people. There are plenty of people championing the salmon industry. But as it's grown, so too have the questions around its social licence, mass fish deaths, other animal cruelty issues, the impact on threatened species, waterways and more recently, particularly over the use of antibiotics. Federal approval to use one antibiotic to treat a bacterial disease in farmed salmon, flifenacol, is probably about to be revoked after traces of it were found in other marine life more than 10 kilometres from the closest farmed salmon pens. ABC Mornings presenter Leon Compton's been following the industry and its impacts on a regular basis. Leon, hello. We have indeed, Ely. We've been doing it over years and this flifenacol aspect of the story really has our audience talking right now. Well, Leon, the industry was left reeling after millions of fish died in their farms last summer. We all know there were chunks of fish washed up on southern beaches and live fish were filmed being put into a bin that was then sealed. I mean, to say it's not been pretty is an understatement, Leon. Absolutely. And we were talking about unprecedented levels of fish death last year. So we're talking literally thousands of tonnes of mortalities or morts as they're known, hoovered up out of the bottom of pens and then the question of where to dispose of them. Ely, we learnt that the industry and the government didn't even have a plan that could cope with the scope and the scale of what they were dealing with at the time. And a lot of where we find ourselves right now is the industry a season on trying to deal with that and make sure it doesn't happen again. Well, after that event, the Premier Jeremy Rockcliffe said in Parliament that the salmon companies were on notice and that the fish deaths were completely unacceptable. He also said he expected the highest degree of accountability and transparency. But in recent days, there have been government briefings and people were told to keep what they were told confidential. And it wasn't just leaders in politics that were told to keep what they heard confidential. We had the Leader of the Greens, Dr Rosalie Woodruff, start our program. And I said, have you been told to keep quiet? And she looked at me and she said yes. Off the back of a briefing in which she was asked not to repeat what was being discussed. And of course, in response to that request, she said no. But the issue about silence goes more widely than that. So as you know, Ely, we work really closely with the newsroom. We were making calls all weekend. You were making calls all weekend. And the level of silence that was coming back was, as they say, deafening. So what have you managed to glean? That there has been a widespread campaign and approach not to talk. But Leon, surely given that these farms are in public waterways and getting back to Premier Rockcliffe's call for transparency, surely there's a public right to know. There is a public right to know. And to give credit to the EPA and to NRE, I think it's fair to say there is more information that is publicly available now in real time in places where people like you and I and our listener can find it. It's better than it was. We're coming, of course, talking about an industry, though, where commercial incompetence can be really important. The industry might not want its competitors to know what it is doing. Some of the declaration rates when it comes to mortality death, for example, Ely, unless 0.25% of a lease dies in a particular period of time over a consecutive number of days, there's no need to declare that. And there are still real issues about whether or not regulations are keeping up with what the Tasmanian public want to know. For example, in that recent time, Meadow Bank, Huon wanted to use an antibiotic and did in a flow-through hatchery. And they decided to tell the EPA that they were doing it, but they didn't actually have to do it, even though that water is part of Hobart's catchment. And that was oxytetracycline. Can we go back to Florphenicol? With the emergency approval permit that was granted in November last year looking increasingly likely that it will be revoked, are the companies trying to get as much treatment into fish as possible? I wonder about that. So this announcement came out at, what was it, four or five o'clock on a Friday afternoon? The APVMA said the use of Florphenicol was under review. And then it was Sunday that the EPA website showed that Tassel, at five sites in the D'Entre Casto Channel, were going to start using the antibiotic. Now, five is quite a lot relative to how much of it has been used since November when it was first approved. And there was a feeling, perhaps, that they were rushing to get this antibiotic into the salmon in case the APVMA revoked the license to use it. Well, there are so many issues to dive into here, Leon. Any potential impacts on human health, the environment and other industries, including the abalone and rock lobster fishes. Now, the rock lobster industry was blindsided late last year because two of its fishing zones were closed just hours after the commercial season had opened because they're within three kilometres of salmon farms that had just started using this Florphenicol. Yeah. Imagine the shock. So Florphenicol can be used in the salmon industry. And then the cray industry was told, hang on a second, you cannot fish in these lease areas. And what we learnt was this was designed to protect the industry in case there was Florphenicol detected in international markets. And particularly China. And here's what James Lawrenson had to say. episodes.description: Imagine what you could do with 200 million dollars. That's how much money Tasmanians lost on pokies last financial year,
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. In late 2022, a torso was found in a wheelie bin on a vacant lot in Adelaide's north. Police discovered that it was 55-year-old Geoffrey McLean who'd been reported missing by his partner Cherie Glastonbury a couple of months earlier. Now, Cherie is on trial for his murder. Prosecutors allege that she and her new partner, Mark Murphy, killed Geoffrey with a drug overdose. On the case of the wheelie bin murder, we take you inside the courtroom for this trial. Search for the KSOP podcast on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts. What could you do with $200 million? That's what Tasmanians lost on Poki's last financial year. There's a lot of hard-working Tasmanians out there. My boss is the boss of Tasmania. Tasmanians want us to get on with the job. North, south, east, west. I don't care where you live in the state. I think the government should be really ashamed of what they've put in place. They've bent over to the industry and it's quite clear they've done deals with the industry to not put the absolute gold standard, which is the mandatory pre-commitment card, in place. We're about freedom of choice. We're about supporting people with gambling addiction. We support facial recognition technology. We support gaming care officers. That is a human touch in venues. I refuse to give up. The Poki Barons would love me to give up. Guess what, guys? Not going away. Hello and welcome to TassieCast. I'm Ailey Ward, coming to you from Nipaluna, Hobart. The amount of money Tasmanians lose on gambling is, by any measure, eye-watering. We're a nation of bettors and Tassies no different. I bet. Yeah, you heard that right. Many of us wager in some way, shape or form. Whether that's about if it's going to rain, the traffic lights turning red, or if the bus will be late and so on. And most of it is harmless fun. But for some of us, gambling becomes all-encompassing. Relationships, jobs, and in some cases, lives lost. According to Tasmanian social and economic impact studies, around 2% of the adult population has a serious issue with gambling. And in lower socioeconomic communities, it's almost twice that, around 4%. Now, this doesn't take into account the flow-on effect on partners, families or colleagues. It's bad and been getting worse. In the 2016-17 financial year, Tasmanians lost around $110 million on pokies. Last financial year, that figure had almost doubled. In recognition of the mounting problem, in 2022, the state government announced massive reforms, a mandatory pre-commitment card which would limit losses, among other measures. It was hailed as nation-leading by reform advocates. But that's now been ditched. The government scaled back its plan and recently announced different harm minimisation measures. But some say they've squibbed. When is a reform not a reform? Reporter Adam Holmes is going to help us work that out. Adam, what happened to that nation-leading reform? Yeah, hey Ellie. So, it might be best to start just by describing what the card was actually going to be. So, this is a mandatory pre-commitment card, which would have required all pokies players to register to get the card, then set maximum daily, monthly and annual loss limits. The idea being that players would have greater control over their losses and data on their losses, specifically targeting that cohort of people who are addicted to the pokies. And in Tasmania, 12% of pokies users are classified as moderate to problem gamblers. And these people who are losing a disproportionate amount on the pokies, usually life-altering amounts with little to no ability to be able to control their addiction. So, the card was announced by then-treasurer Michael Ferguson. It triggered a really interesting and, I guess, predictable response from the gaming industry. And then the government, over the coming years, we saw the Premier soften the language. The card was then effectively ditched. Now, we have a new suite of policies, including a ticket-in, ticket-out system. So, players would have to transfer their cash into tickets at up to $200 a time or $100 per machine. We also have opening hours for venues reducing from 21 hours a day to 17. And that, in itself, could be a major improvement, for example, if the hours were set exactly. For example, if it was midnight to 7am or something like that, they couldn't open. But we don't have that. They could just stagger the opening hours if you own more than one venue. And also, we have something called Gaming Care Offices. And there's currently planned to be three for the whole state. What are they? So, they are people employed by the Tasmanian Hospitality Association to head around to the about 100 or so venues. And to see if everything's going okay for everyone, to make sure that things are operating well, that people who appear to have gambling addictions are being, I guess, noted and cared for in a way. If they're aware of the exclusion scheme and things like that. Adam, didn't a government-commissioned report, though, find that the original proposal would actually have a net benefit to the economy? Yeah, this report by Deloitte was commissioned by the Premier. It was seen as a way to try to set an argument to get rid of the card. But it's actually ended up being the best argument for the pre-commitment card, ironically. And it was only released last month, which was well after the Premier had already made his decision to ditch the card effectively. And it showed that the card would be a net benefit to the Tasmanian economy of $230 million over just six years. And that's through reduced demand on mental health services, homelessness programs, the justice system, improved productivity in workplaces, enhanced disposable income for families. There was also an effect on the hospitality sector that was likely to lose hundreds of millions of dollars in economic activity. But that broadly depends on the business's profiles, those that rely the most on poker machine profit. They would face the biggest impacts, of course. But there were other venues that have a more broader income base, would be able to ride out a change much easier. And the broader hospitality sector could also benefit through having customers with more disposable income and being able to spend more on food and beverage. But it appears that advice was broadly ignored by the government. Isn't that a bit like the doctor telling you you need to take this medication in order to get better, but then you choose to ignore the advice? I mean, sort of, yes. Especially when you consider that the government also appears to be ignoring advice from its own gaming commission. That being that the facial recognition technology in venues, that policy doesn't work to actually prevent pokies harms. Which I guess makes sense because this is people who are on the exclusion scheme. They already have a significant problem with pokies. It hasn't been prevented. It's already happening. But that's a policy we're adopting. The Gaming Commission said that doesn't work to prevent harm. So yeah, that's two doses of medicine, I suppose, that we're not taking. So is mandatory pre-commitment, is it dead, buried and cremated? Well, we did have it confirmed by Treasurer Erica Betts that the ministerial direction for the pokies card is no longer active. And that's the mechanism by which the Gaming Commission was pursuing this policy. It's a technical term. But the Liberal Party does still have the policy of mandatory pre-commitment in Tasmania. There's just a caveat subject to a national approach. So it is still there. So not quite dead, buried and cremated. So will the government's new suite of measures then work to reduce harm? I guess overall, the Premier is saying that freedom of choice appears to be guiding their principles now. And that was kind of laid bare a bit by this exchange between Treasurer Erica Betts and the Greens' Cassie O'Connor. Some people do like it and it is a day out and they do decide to spend their $20, $30 with a meal or whatever. Is it worth it? No, no, no. A lot of people are actually disciplined and set themselves limits. Who is considered most at risk of gambling addiction, Adam? Yeah, we've had a range of studies now showing that people who are most at risk are males, normally aged 25 to 34, usually unemployed and educated to a diploma level. That age range is trending down as well to the people in their early 20s. Also, the pokies and sports betting are the forms of gambling that are most associated with moderate to problem gambling. In terms of the pokies, 2.3% of gamers in Tasmania are classified as problem gamblers. And that rate is three times higher than the rate for all other forms of gambling. Mark Kempster from the Alliance for Gambling Reform says this is because of the design of the poker machines. They provide players with that dopamine rush for success. They entice more gaming and they lock players into what psychologically is referred to as the zone. And that's a form of a loss of executive control, really. People will no longer have control over what they're doing. If you ever go into a pokies lounge and look around, you'll be able to identify people who are in the zone, particularly late at night and early hours of the morning. And you can also see that there isn't really anyone actually doing anything about that. Now, Mark Kempster is a gambling addict himself. Yes, he had an addiction to online gambling rather than the pokies. But in his role with the Alliance for Gambling Reform, he speaks with those experiencing pokies harm as well as their families. And he says just the broad range of effects is something that a lot of community just doesn't really realise. I'm getting four to five to six people a week whose families in that reach out to me. They've lost their life savings. There's young people who have lost all the money they've earned so far in their lives. They've stolen money. I know that people I work with, the Alliance, have spoken to people who are going through courts at the moment because of money they've stolen to fund their addictions. They've lost their family because of it. They possibly might never go to jail because of it. Like, it is so – it doesn't just affect the person who's going through the addiction. It pulls in the family and the community. People around them get affected by it. The stats show that for every person that's addicted to gambling, there's several other people around them will also be affected by that person's gambling addictions. Adam, we've got a long history with gambling in Tassie. We were the first state in Australia to have a legal casino. And the owners of that casino are still the biggest players in the industry. Yes, Federal Group, of course, then had two casinos soon after the first one, along with a dozen or so pokies venues through its Vantage Group. And they've been the beneficiaries of government policy for quite some time. Even when it lost its monopoly model on all pokies licenses in Tasmania, the government slashed its tax rate in response as a sort of an offset for them. And I guess this power is why Federal Group felt so empowered to directly challenge Michael Ferguson when he was trying to get the mandatory pre-commitment card up. And we had letters released under right to information that showed the exchanges and the barbs between them. And just the frankness with which Federal Managing Director Greg Farrell spoke to Mr. Ferguson was quite revealing. This was triggered by a Federal Group sending out fact sheets to all MPs, which Mr. Ferguson took exception with. And then, of course, they were having disputes over various facts. And soon after the 2024 election, Mr. Ferguson was no longer in the relevant portfolio. And after that, we did see this softening of the language. And I guess you also see some MPs and also Labor MPs arguing things that sound eerily similar to things that the industry, the THA and Federal Group also argue around pokies harm. Well, as you mentioned, Michael Ferguson, who you referred to there, resigned from the front bench for other reasons. That was the TT Line Ferry replacement saga, which we've talked about here on this podcast previously. Now, he remains on the back bench, but he's continuing to champion the cause, as we heard at the start. Yeah, the mandatory pre-commitment card was really his kind of legacy item, I feel. Because I recall debates a long time ago where he promised meaningful harm reduction when he was in the role. And everyone's like, oh, yeah, sure. All right, Michael. But then he really did come through with this mandatory pre-commitment card. And it really seems to be this moral cause for him, as he described in a speech to Parliament in 2024. He powered down all of the other machines, came to hers, and she blasted him. You can't. You can't turn this off. My Christmas presents are in this machine. I've got to get them back. And it taught me so much that not only do people have the right to play these games, they also have the right to a government and an opposition that will turn up, that will show up, defend their interests and defend them against their weaknesses, which we all occasionally have. Well, Adam, Labor, after a brief dalliance with ditching pokies from pubs and clubs, is now largely on a unity ticket with the Liberal government. Yeah, essentially. Of course, Labor's policy at the 2018 election to remove them from pubs and clubs faced this vigorous political backlash well-resourced from the industry. And they lost that election and dropped the policy. Labor did voice support for pre-commitment in 2021. And I recall asking one of their MPs, Ella Haddad, in 2023, if they still had that policy. And she said they did. But then there seemed to be this shift at that time. There's confusion about if they did or if they didn't. And then I recall former leader Dean Winter saying when he was leader, he didn't think the pokies were in the top 20 most important issues facing Tasmania. And then when the government announced its most recent policies, the ticketing, ticketing out, all those other things, Labor instantly was on board in principle saying, oh, they sound good. Leader Josh Willey also using language that sounded similar to the hospitality industry, particularly with the gaming care officer thing, that offers a human touch in venues. Well, as we mentioned, there were changes in 2023. Federal lost its monopoly. What sort of an impact did that have? So, yeah, venues in Tasmania now have their own pokies licenses. And that's a trend that just seems to be increasingly going up now. And how do we compare with other states? These are somewhat incomparable to the 30 or so machines that our venues have. These ones have many, many more. So for example, we want to bring in this facial recognition technology because South Australia are doing it, the ticketing system from New South Wales. And then we wait for the national approach to mandatory pre-commitment cards. New South Wales, Victoria and now Tasmania have all backed away because the industry knows that it will have a negative impact on their revenue because they won't be getting the money from the people who are their biggest spenders, who happen to be the people with the biggest problems.
