But as a long time observer of Tasmanian politics, major political parties are always extremely reluctant to adopt policies that affect what are perceived to be the largest employers in the state. Even if they have evidence that says it will help other parts of the economy, more so for this particular part. There's always this fear of the political backlash, especially now when you take into account that the Tasmanian Hospitality Association donated $217,000 to the Tasmanian Liberals last year and $31,000 to Labor. Now, we didn't find out about that straight away, did we? No, because those donations were made just before our new policies came into effect. So there was this significant lag before we found out about those donations. And now you have the government, it has its own internal and external advice saying mandatory pre-commitment cards are the way to go. But then it seems to choose the opposite, including policies that are based on no advice that we can determine, but seem to align with what the industry is requesting. So now we just have, I guess, rooms full of machines in Tasmania that are designed to get people addicted. We have minimal guardrails for people. And then the ones that we do have are the ones that the industry itself seem to really want. Thanks, Adam. I reckon it's a sure thing we'll be talking about this for some time to come. Thanks to you too for joining us on TassieCast. Until next time, cheers.

episodes.title: Is it time Tassie declared wild deer a pest?
episodes.description: They might look like Bambi but they're making a big mess. There are tens of thousands of fallow deer trampling across the landscape and they now outnumber some of our most iconic species. Featuring reporter Meg Whitfield.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Hi, it's Sam Hawley from ABC News Daily. The podcast that brings you one big story affecting your world each weekday in just 15 minutes. So it's basically raw sewage that flushes into the harbour that attracts baitfish. The bull sharks, they're drawn to the baitfish. It makes it very dangerous to be in the harbour immediately after big storms. Join me for ABC News Daily. Find it on the ABC Listen app. Oh dear, they're cute but incredibly destructive. There's a lot of hard-working Tasmanians out there. My boss is the boss of Tasmania. Tasmanians want us to get on with the job. North, south, east, west, I don't care where you live in the state. They are moving into the suburbs now. So they're getting closer and closer. So therein lies, you know, the urgency of the whole thing. With exploding numbers, we have to do something. I mean, to do nothing is not an option. The reality is deer are not the top of the hierarchy as far as damage done to farmland. Wallaby definitely are. Possum, cockatoos, ducks. There's a whole raft of other animals that present challenges to farmers. So I think deer are unfairly being maligned in this instance. We're prioritising a species that's been introduced over all of our native species, many of which are highly threatened and endangered and exist nowhere else on Earth. Hello and welcome to TassieCast. I'm Ailey Ward, coming to you from Nipaluna, Hobart. They might conjure up images of Bambi. And on any objective measure, they are stunning looking animals. But there are real concerns about the extent of damage deer are causing in Tassie, to the environment, to culturally sensitive sites and for farmers. In recent decades, their population has exploded. They've bred like, well, like another introduced species, rabbits. According to a government survey released last year over central and northeastern Tasmania, there was an estimated population of more than 70,000, up from around 8,000 in the 1970s. Now to put these numbers in context, it's estimated there are fewer than 25,000 Tasmanian devils in the wild in our state, the spotted-tailed quoll, fewer than 10,000, and the eastern quoll, around 12,000. So wild deer approximately double their combined number. Did you know, though, that they're not treated as an invasive pest across the state? They're actually partially protected. Now some argue that's a weird colonial hangover. They were brought here in the 1830s into the Midlands region as a game animal for recreational hunting, a piece of home, if you like. But their recent population explosion has led to calls from some to have that partially protected status removed. Now what does all this mean? Reporter Meg Whitfield has been looking into who has the deer in the crosshairs. Meg, deer were initially only in a discrete area of the state. How widespread are they now? Yeah, that's right. So around the 1970s, they were really centred around the Northern Midlands, Central Highlands kind of area. So Interlaken, Campbelltown, Ross, that kind of area. But the aerial survey that was done in 2024 has shown they've really spread westward and towards high conservation areas. There've even been satellite populations that have been reported on the Tasman and Freysenae peninsulas, Bruny Island, King Island, even around the peripheries of Hobart and Launceston. And what sort of an impact are they having? Well, if you ask TasFarmers, which is the peak body for farmers in Tasmania, it's really significant. They eat everything in their way, essentially. They do damage on farm property. So TasFarmers estimates it's in the tens of millions of dollars annually in terms of product that's lost, damage to farms and the cost of trying to get on top of these populations. So really significant. And here's Ian Saw from TasFarmers. The problem is that the deer are wrecking our environment and costing the farmers a lot of money. We've got farmers that have filmed mobs of 400 deer running across their paddock. So this isn't something isolated or small. It's widespread across Tasmania and the area is growing. And so widespread, in fact, Meg, they've made it into the World Heritage Area. Yeah, that's right. So there was a population around the central plateau and the walls of Jerusalem. Now, that's home to a really important ecological system there. There's lots of incredibly sensitive plant species, animal species and adult deer. They're really significant animals. They're big. They cause a lot of damage. They've got hard hooves. So they eat their way through the vegetation. They do something called ring barking where they rub their antlers on the trees to try and get rid of the velvet on those. And that causes damage then. They can impact on the regeneration of trees, which then brings bushfire risk. So it's a pretty significant impact they're having. And it's not an area where we want to see deer. And I remember hearing Bob Brown, who is not someone you would normally expect to hear advocating mass shooting. He actually called four shooters in choppers. And that has happened in an effort to get them out of the World Heritage Area. Yeah, that's right. There have been three aerial culls. So that's shooting that's happened from helicopters with very trained shooters using thermal cameras. That's resulted in about 1,300 deer being killed, removed from that area as they really try and eradicate that population. So that's been considered quite successful, those operations. And that will be monitored as well by the Environment Department as it goes on and figure out what happens next, see how much, if any population remains there. But yet people who you wouldn't expect to be on board with that have been supportive of it. The Invasive Species Council has said that that was a good move. They want to see efforts like that continue. But they do say other measures in other areas where we find deer haven't been so successful. This is a little bit of what Tiana Pirtle from the Species Council had to say. Government's main management tool to date has continued to be recreational hunting. And we know we've tried it. There's a lot of science to show that recreational hunting just doesn't really remove enough deer from a population to see those population declines happen. Something needs to be done. The issue we've found is that there's this continued reliance on people doing a hobby to take care of a problem that really needs a strategic and targeted and coordinated approach. Now, Meg, the government does want to increase the amount that can be taken through hunting. Yeah, that's right. So they're working on trying to open up more areas of private and public land for recreational hunting. They think that hunting can have a bigger role to play here in managing these deer populations. So in Tasmania, deer are kind of categorised into three zones in Tasmania. Zone one is that more restricted area and that's where deer typically were. So that Midlands kind of area and that's quite restricted. There's a hunting season opening soon there for adult male stags. That's the sort of the protected for hunting, that sort of traditional... Yeah, it's kind of viewed as an area that is for hunting more than the other zones. And then we've got zone two, which is kind of an intermediary zone. So that's a bit where they started spreading out. And then you've got zone three, which is an area where they really want to get rid of that spread even further. So that's less restricted. But of course, all of this hunting still takes place with permits and regulations on what you can do. It's very regulated. It might be helping farmers get rid of deer on their properties and they need to have the appropriate licences for that or recreational hunters. So all still regulated, but different restrictions in each area. Now, the recreational season opens this month. Yeah, that's right. So at the end of February, that's that two-month window where there's the open season for adult male stags. And so there's still bag limits. There's restrictions there, but that season does open soon. How do we compare with other states? So Tasmania is one of three places where we have that partly protected status for deer. Now, that applies to Zone 1, which is that Northern Midlands kind of area. But a lot of places do consider these pests. So we're kind of in the minority for how we actually classify deer at the moment in Tasmania. The Invasive Species Council of Tasmania say they really want that status to change. They say we're at a tipping point right now and the system we have isn't working. Now, deer have been seen, as you mentioned, in suburban areas. I mean, Mount Nelson near the Southern Outlet, for example, Riverside in the north. They're a concern for motorists too. I mean, I've spoken to someone who had a horrible experience hitting a deer at Canara in the Northern Midlands. Now, their car was a mess, not to mention the deer. And they're always nervous now approaching that section of road. Yeah, that's right. So it has been raised as an area of concern, both by the Environment Department about the potential for increasing incidents. And we also spoke to RACT, the insurer, about this. And they said that incidents involving deer and cars, they were 60% higher last year than the year prior to that. So that's a pretty big jump. And that was double the number of claims that they saw in 2019. So they say it is still a limited number. It's not one of the major influences in crashes, but it is growing. And incidents that involve deer typically inflict twice the amount of damages interacting with other wildlife. So it's a pretty significant issue. Because they're big. Exactly. There are others, though, who say, you know, you mentioned the Invasive Species Council. They're saying we're at a tipping point. You know, this is ridiculous. Their partially protected status has got to go. But there are others who say there's no need. Yeah, that's right. So I spoke to Carlo De Falco, who's from the Shooters, Fishers, Farmers Party. He represents the electorate of lions. And he's also a recreational hunter himself. And he thinks that classification should stay as it is. He thinks there are mechanisms that are already in place for farmers who are finding deer coming onto their property. And he also thinks that recreational hunting should have a bigger role. So he wants to see more areas of land opened up and for hunters to actually play a bigger role here. He thinks that deer are copping unjustified flack, basically, and that there are other animals that he says do more damage on farms. And so he wants to see more land opened up, less restrictions in that place. But he doesn't think the partially protected status is the issue here. So rather than wasting the deer, you know, like shooting them out of helicopters and leaving them to rot on the ground, we've got strategies in place to donate that deer to food charities. So we've fashioned that off the back of our conversations with New Zealand group Hunters for Hope, who have just donated this year 1,500 protein portions for disadvantaged families. So that's a win-win situation. Meg, the deer shot here in Tassie, it can't be sold. Yeah, that's right. So with the aerial culling, all the deer that were killed through that, they were left there to decompose. And for deer that's hunted recreationally, that has to be for personal consumption. That can't be sold. There are deer farms where there is deer meat, but that's a different situation entirely. And so Carly De Falco says he thinks there's actually appetite for more deer meat to be consumed. And maybe that is an avenue that we need to explore further. And there are some chefs who also want to see deer on menus more, and they want to see those restrictions change to make it easier and show people, look, here's an animal, we've got plenty of it, why can't we consume it? And where's the government at on this? I mean, there were quite a few recommendations out of the recent parliamentary inquiry, a call for increased population surveillance and a new invasive species action plan. Where's that all at? Yeah, that's right. So the state government does say this is an issue and they're trying to streamline processes. As I said earlier, they're trying to cut that red tape, make permitting easier, more streamlined, open up more private and public land to actually increase the amount of recreational hunting. In terms of that invasive species, that report, that was meant to be delivered in the first 100 days of government. You mean the action plan? Yeah, that's right, the action plan. That was meant to be delivered in the first 100 days of government. That hasn't happened yet, but we do know that that is actually underway. We've been told that there is progress being made on that. So hopefully we'll see that sometime soon. So they're saying they are really taking this seriously and they're trying to find those solutions and work with stakeholders to make it easier to get more recreational hunting happen and bring those numbers down. What about the removal of the partially protected status? We did ask the state government about that, but we didn't get a direct response about whether they would be open to changing that or not. Okay, thank you, Meg. Let us know your thoughts. Have you had a close encounter with a wild deer while driving or have you seen one over the back fence even? What do you think Tassie's strategy should be? Until next time, cheers. Cheers. You've been listening to an ABC podcast. Discover more great ABC podcasts, live radio and exclusives on the ABC Listen app.

I'm David Claughton and it's lovely to have your company as we join our reporters exploring regional Australia. This week we're getting a history lesson into how a summer fruit became a local favourite when we hear the story of how mangoes came to be grown down under. We'll meet a long-time listener to Australia's longest-running radio program as The Country Hour celebrates eight decades of broadcasting. And we're heading into the classroom to meet the young preschoolers learning about the dairy industry. Their lessons cover everything from tractors and cows to making butter in the hope that it might lead to a career in dairy well into the future. Some people might think it's really young to be speaking about careers with three, four, five-year-olds. But we know that young people know what career they don't want to do very early. And if we don't introduce them to a range of careers in the dairy industry at this young age, it's likely that they won't consider that when they are getting to their career-making decision time in their life. First today we start with a remarkable story from far north-western Australia. In 1967, a girl was standing barefoot on the hot sand of the Great Sandy Desert, amidst the low scrub and spinifex grass, surrounded by her family. Her photograph is taken, and her life changes forever. Bougarawoya and her family were removed from their traditional desert life and taken into a Kimberley mission. Now aged 70, she's never stopped wondering about that photo, and never forgotten her connection to her traditional land. Erin Park has the story. It's wet season in the central Kimberley. I'm driving about 300 kilometres inland from Broome, trying to get to a small community called Looma, where there's a woman with a very special, unusual life story that, as far as I know, has never been recorded before. Within minutes of arriving, I'm directed to her house. My name is Bougarawoya. I come from the bush. I've been coming in 1967. Bougarawoya grew up in the desert. The Dowling woman is one of only a handful of surviving elders in Australia who remembers life before contact with white people. Now around 70 years old, her life is one of quiet routines, walking daily to the aged care centre. She's really bossy at times, like most of the time, so yeah. But she's good. I've come from the great sandy desert. I was born in Widdity. What I call Widdity. I've been growing up all my life in the bush. Bougarawoya's ancestors had lived uninterrupted for thousands of years in the vast desert plains. We walk around everywhere. We collect everything. We took it everywhere. What a hole. But the 1960s were a time of great change in northern Australia. Suddenly there were new people moving across the landscape. White people. It was 1967 when Bougarawoya first heard the truck approaching. Do you remember the first time you saw a white person? Yeah, I was seeing a white person walking with shirt and trousers. And my sister, Sally, what was it? She went and ate in the bush. And I told my mummy, mummy, you look like us. Same. Bougarawoya's just told me something pretty crazy, which is that the moment that her life changed forever was actually captured on camera. Apparently that moment in the desert when she first saw white people, there was a woman there taking photographs. And she's got an album with the originals here at her house. So we're just going to have a dig around and try to find them. This is my mum. This is my grandmother. This is my mum. Shall we go outside and have a look? This is my mum. The single photograph shows her family's first interaction with the white fella world. The missionaries and welfare officers handing them clothes and guiding them into the back of the truck. But Bougarawoya says she used to have a whole set of photos that were taken on that life-changing day, including one showing her posing for the camera. But the photo album cannot be found. Maybe lost. Maybe stolen. I've been looking for the photos, but I couldn't find it. I don't know where he was. I promised to try to find the photos. They're irreplaceable. Showing the moment that two wildly different cultures intersected in that hot desert sand. So I'm back in Broome and I think I've had a breakthrough after several months of digging. There's a local historian and author who's passed me on this CD. She's had it in her possession for many years. It's got 23 images on it and she reckons one of them is that missing photograph showing Bougarawoya as a child. Before long, I'm back on the road to Luma. I find Bougarawoya in her usual spot. Hi, look at you. Hanging out with her best friend and next-door neighbour, Polly, who came out of the desert the same year. It's been six months since I came and visited you. You've been well? I've been well. And I look happy. It's time to show Bougaraw the photograph. Is this the photo you were telling me about? How do you feel to see it? See? This is me, Bougaraw. I came with the name of Bougaraw. I had the name because my dad called me the name. The photo was taken as the last of the desert families were moving on to cattle stations and church-run missions along the coast. Some voluntarily, exhausted by drought. Others rounded up reluctantly. The photographer was a nurse who was volunteering at the LaGrange Catholic Mission, where Bougaraw and her family were soon taken. Oh, they've probably been through a lot. A lot of changes. My mother. Bougaraw's cousin is visiting from Perth and seeing the photos for the first time. For her, a young girl, it would have been confusing. That picture says it all right there. Leaving home. You know? And wherever this mob is taking them. It would have been sad at that moment. But it would have been scary. Bougaraw went on to marry a man named Jimmy. And they had three children, two of whom have since died. Bougaraw visits the desert less now. She's getting frail and can no longer drive. But when she closes her eyes, she's back there. I'm sorry for that country. I've been sorry too. I've been crying everywhere I hold for a while. Because I get the memories in that place. They've come far, very far. A long way. And they're still here, you know. Managing both worlds, I guess. At this kindergarten in Victoria's South Gippsland region, the next generation of dairy experts and advocates are being nurtured from a young age. Hi there. I'm Faith Tabaloo-Yan, and I'm visiting the Lee and Gatha Community Preschool here in one of the state's largest dairy farming regions. It's the first time this preschool has run this Dairy in Kinder program, which aims to teach little learners about farming, sustainability and healthy eating. And it seems they're taking the lessons to heart. I've learnt that the milk gets processed. How does it get processed? A big factory. Big factory. And where does the milk come from in the first place? The cows. That's Campbell Wooding from Lee and Gatha. At just five years old, he's already an advocate for the local dairy industry. I was just eating cheese. Mmm. Some good cheese? Yeah. Campbell is among a handful of Lee and Gatha Community Preschool students, participating in a new Dairy in Kinder program, which is running for the next 12 months, funded by a $10,000 grant from the Gardner Foundation. Amy Cosby is a parent and dairy farmer from Lee and Gatha South. She says when it comes to ag education, starting early is key. Some people might think it's really young to be speaking about careers with, you know, three, four, five-year-olds. But we know that young people know what career they don't want to do very early. And if we don't introduce them to a range of careers in the dairy industry at this young age, it's likely that they won't consider that when they are getting to their career-making decision time in their life. So we will take kids out on excursions to dairy farms, probably ours, and also we'll bring some calves into the kinders next year during calving to show them how calves are fed. And, you know, perhaps for some of them, even though they live in a dairy region, if you are not connected with a dairy farmer personally through friends or family, you might never have been on a dairy farm, and you might never have interacted with a cow, you might not know anything about them. So by introducing it to young kids like this, they'll go home and tell their families, which is really important. And when they're hopefully they're in the supermarket, they're choosing to buy Australian dairy products. Ms Cosby's taken that approach with her own three boys, starting with five-year-old Oscar and four-year-old Zave. Oscar, why do you love being a dairy farmer? Milk the cows. What cow do you milk? My cow. Zavey, what do you like about being a dairy farmer? Cow. What do you like about the cows, though? Milk. And what do you like doing in the tractor? Coding filings. Bessa Wooding is the mum of Campbell, our other five-year-old dairy expert. She and her family moved to Leangatha in 2021, keen to leave city life behind. Despite having no farming background, Ms Wooding says she's all for more dairy education. Yeah, really excited. I think it's great for the kids to have this opportunity, especially kids that probably don't get a lot of experience or first-hand. And if we're going to have time on farms, I think that it's going to be great for the kids to get involved. Emily Duncan is a local parent who also sits on the Kinder's fundraising committee. We thought, why not jump on it? We have so many farms around Leangatha. What a perfect opportunity for us to capitalise on that. Despite not working the land herself, Ms Duncan says farming is a favourite topic in her family. I did not grow up on a farm, but I have a close family connection with my in-laws being dairy farmers, and my sister and her husband, dairy farming close by in Fish Creek as well. We talk a lot about where our food comes from. We talk a lot about Parr's Farm. We talk a lot about the farms around town and what they're growing and things like that. A lot of interest comes in the tractors. I have a two-and-a-half-year-old daughter that is really interested in tractors at the moment. And at the moment, it's silage season, so there's a lot of interest in the silage, whether we're baling or making a pit silage. So, yeah, a lot of the time we are talking about farms. So how do you bring the world of dairy into the classroom? Here's teacher Belinda Elliott to explain. All the basics of where their food comes from and simple things like farm animals. We relate it back to art projects and we incorporate it into even cooking experiences. This year we created our own butter by churning our own cream and cooking with that. We spread it onto some beautiful scones that we'd made and it was a really good way for children to get a good visual in how things are made in the dairy industry. And did the kids have a lot of questions about the butter? Yeah, they did. Well, they were more interested in the taste testing side of things too. They enjoyed the buttermilk, which we weren't sure if we were going to like that taste of that. But, yeah, they enjoyed that. They just, even the process of them being able to spread it onto their own food that they'd made and enjoyed the taste. So, yeah, it was a really good learning experience. Belinda Elliott, a teacher at the Leangatha Community Preschool in Victoria's South Gippsland region, ending that story from Faith Tabaloo Yun. Before that, Erin Park brought us the story of Boogger Awoya, who walked out of the great sandy desert in 1967, encountering white people for the first time. I'm David Claughton and you're listening to A Big Country. Still to come, mangoes are synonymous with summertime in Australia. We'll learn some of the history of how the sweet, juicy fruit came to be a staple of the Australian summer. And the country's longest-running radio program is celebrating 80 years on air this month. Among many long-time loyal listeners to ABC Radio's Country Hour program is an 87-year-old buffalo dairy farmer from south-east Queensland. Margaret Thompson has been listening in for as long as the Country Hour has been sharing rural and regional stories. Well, I love the girl. You have a pat. So gorgeous. And we've come into the dairy where the buffalo cows are all being very patient, waiting for their turn to be milked. I don't know if you can hear the chug of the machines behind us powering the suction cups, and I can see the milk going up into the pipes and coming out into this big tank here. How many cows are you milking in the moment? I've got about 40 on me. Recapping the top story in this bulletin, temperatures are expected to soar across south-east Queensland today. Now, as you can hear, the ABC is the soundtrack of this farm that I'm visiting today. And I am here with one of the most devoted Country Hour listeners that there could be. Her name is Margaret Thompson from Mullaney Buffalo. We've got the buffalo having a feed behind us as her son Michael is milking the cows in the dairy. You never like to talk about your age, but you are 87 years young. Margaret, what are your first memories of the Country Hour? It was always on at lunchtime. Everybody would come in for lunch, radio would be on, and that's it. And you'd listen to it, and then you'd listen to the Lawson. You're out in the country, you didn't have a daily pay fee. So if you didn't have the Country Hour, you didn't know what else was going on around you. And Queensland's a big place. Australia's even bigger. But my father and mother were always forward-thinking, so that they would pick up stuff on the Country Hour. That dam down there is one of the first red-soil dams, or dam that's been put in a red soil that was successful. They had the courage to do something different. And I guess the next generation aren't much different. I think sometimes it does run in families like that. Now, you are a person who has a deep love of learning. You're a Churchill Fellow who travelled overseas to learn about buffalo dairies before you and your husband, your late husband, started the dairy on this farm after deregulation. And you got rid of your traditional cows and switched to buffalo. Traditional dairy, yes. He badly wanted to do something that was different from the opportunity. So you've got to put your heart into it. And when he passed away, we really needed to keep that dream going. It was Mal, wasn't it? Yeah, it was Mal. Yeah, yeah. So the idea is always more important. You learn about different pasture grasses and that kind of thing. You know, people did things early, and Mal was the same. I don't call them dreamers, I call them visionaries. Sometimes it works and sometimes it doesn't. And you are still the treasurer after gosh knows how many decades of... No, I was secretary before. You were secretary before for the Merry River Catchment Coordinating Committee, which also cares for the land and this magnificent river that we've got that discharges into the ocean so that everything that happens on the land is very significant for the bottom part of the Great Barrier Reef. How much does land care mean to you? We were one of the original ones starting off Barung. Land care has always been important. And then gradually I moved through the ranks of land care, sitting on various committees in Queensland and actually was on the board of Land Care Australia at one time. So I've had a lot of chances to bring different ideas back. And what does it feel like to see the result? And I love doing stories about the work that's being done to repair some of the unintentional mistakes of the past with clearing trees along rivers and increasing erosion and that sort of thing. Sometimes they weren't unintentional. Sometimes they were what we were told was a good idea to do. You were told to destag the river and everything else, so you didn't have any place for the cod to nest. We're talking about the endangered Mary River cod. Yeah, departments and that have different ideas. Sometimes they're not always proven to be correct. But that's where sometimes the country comes in very good because you hear what they're doing in other regions. And believe it or not, I think as a group, we're talking about Emmett Tripple C there as a group, with our participants in our projects, they also become part of the family. And where does your buffalo dairy milk go? We go through Melanie Cheese down to what they call Cheese Time down to the Gold Coast. A lot that goes to Sydney generally makes into Indian sweets. You're also producing buffalo for meat for a whole range of projects, a real nose-to-tail approach. We try to do everything that way, Jennifer, that you don't waste anything. But we have so many different nationalities now. And buffalo were their prime food. You're always looking for something else. I find buffalo just to be mesmerising animals. They're so beautiful to look at and remarkably gentle, probably because of the handling that they get here. So you get rid of anything that's not true. You don't want to breed from anything that's not. What do you like about the animals? I've always liked animals, so that's it. But they're very family-oriented, and if you get one that likes you, then they like you. And that seems to go through the family. And what keeps you farming? I mean, lots of other people would have retired. What am I going to do? A long time ago, when dairy deregulation came in, somebody asked me, and I said, well, I can't ever imagine not having an animal to pat. It's special. I couldn't go line dancing. I've got nothing like that. And there's a challenge in farming. They're the taste of summer. And each year, Australians eat their way through as much as 75,000 tonnes of the King of Fruits. And while most mangoes are grown in the Northern Territory, the fruit owes its taste to the North Queensland town of Bowen, where two popular varieties were created. Some say there was a tree in Sydney's Royal Botanic Garden as early as 1823 that never fruited, and by the 1860s, a tree was growing in Rockhampton. What's not in dispute is mangoes were first commercially produced in Bowen. Queensland DPI Senior Principal Horticulturalist Ian Bally says they arrived from Asia, where mangoes have been eaten for thousands of years. In the late 1800s, boats coming to and fro from Bowen used to bring mangoes from Southeast Asia. Those boats would be travelling from Bowen, taking horses to India for the remount trade for the British Army. And as they sort of travelled that India to Australia route, they would pick up local fruit at local markets and ports along the way. Quite often those fruit and seed from those fruit were given to local farmers in the Bowen area. They were often grown on the farm of the harbour master there. And the better ones of those were then passed on again. And Kensington Pride was one of those ones that was passed on to a guy. Harry Lott had a farm at Adelaide Point. I think the farm was named Kensington. And from various selections and over time, the Kensington Pride sort of stood out as being something that was bigger, better and tastier than all the other selections. And it began to be grown around the Bowen area. The Kensington Pride is still the most popular mango in Australia, and all other varieties developed in Australia have some level of Kensington Pride genetics. Professor Heather Smyth is a flavour expert and the Deputy Director of Research at the University of Queensland's Alliance for Agriculture and Food. She's helped with breeding programs for most major modern Australian mango varieties. She said Kensington Pride's sweet, tangy flavour is unique due to a compound called alpha-terpinaline. So I've been tasting mangoes for a very long time. That strong terpini flavour, which we have come to know is the Australian unique mango flavour that consumers expect. Mangoes don't taste like that anywhere else in the world. They taste like that terpini flavour only here in Australia. And that's because of Kensington Pride or this Bowen style of mango. A hundred years after the rise of the Kensington Pride, a second popular mango variety came from Bowen, the R2E2. It's a large, round fruit with firm flesh and a sweet, fresh flavour. The original 40-year-old tree still stands at a research centre in Bowen. Mr Bally worked on its breeding program. He says research began in the 60s to combat shortcomings with the Kensington Pride. It was recognised that some of the international overseas varieties were much better producers, especially some of those from Florida that were in the 1940s sort of were selected over there. So this is when it was decided that, yeah, some crossbreeding needed to happen. The introduced varieties seeds were planted in the ground in Bowen. And as they began to crop, they were assessed for their suitability as commercial varieties for the Bowen area. And one of those trees was a Kent seedling, which became R2E2. It was selected because it was quite large, had a very good flesh-to-seed ratio, and had this great shelf life, much better for travelling than the Kensington Pride. Today, the Kensington Pride makes up about 40% of mango production, while the R2E2 makes up about 20% and is the number one export variety. Other popular Queensland varieties commercialised in the 2000s include the Calypso and Honeygold. Professor Smyth said they each have their own benefits. Yeah, Honeygold's got a beautiful, rich, sweet flavour and all that alpha-depinoline. It's certainly a premium version of mango. It's a beautiful mango. It's really golden in colour. The Calypso can be absolutely gorgeous when it's looking really good. It is a much, I would say, more delicate flavour compared to the other fruit. I would say a very clean version of that terpeni, piney flavour that you have from the KP, you also get in the Calypso mango. What's the best way to eat a mango? Under clinical conditions, Professor Smyth tastes mangoes at about 20 degrees to bring out the most flavour. Just before you want to eat it, put it in the fridge for a couple of hours just to cool it down, but not to cause the chill injury and make it sort of soft and glassy inside. And then cut it with your knife, prepare it, pop those cheeks out. Whether you want to cut off the cubes or whether you want to slice it up and use it in some other way, it's lovely to have cool mango, but just don't keep it in the fridge for long periods of time. However, as a child in Darwin, Professor Smyth developed her own favourite style. I was probably about seven years old and my friend had a swimming pool. The un-mango season, you could pluck off the tree, climb the tree, plot them into the swimming pool and then just tear the skin off with your teeth and then just tuck into the mango, just as it is, no knife, nothing else. And you saw dripping down your chin, dripping down your arms and then just wash it off in the swimming pool. So it's just the best. That's story from Liam McNally in Mackay in tropical North Queensland. Before that, we heard from a long-time Country Hour listener and buffalo farmer, Margaret Thompson. That's the show for today. I'm David Clawton. Thanks for listening and bye for now.

I think that it's going to be great for the kids to get involved.
Emily Duncan is a local parent who also sits on the Kinder's fundraising committee.
We thought, why not jump on it?
We have so many farms around Leangatha.
What a perfect opportunity for us to capitalise on that.
Despite not working the land herself,
Ms Duncan says farming is a favourite topic in her family.
I did not grow up on a farm,
but I have a close family connection with my in-laws being dairy farmers,
and my sister and her husband,
dairy farming close by in Fish Creek as well.
We talk a lot about where our food comes from.
We talk a lot about Parr's Farm.
We talk a lot about the farms around town and what they're growing and things like that.
A lot of interest comes in the tractors.
I have a two-and-a-half-year-old daughter
that is really interested in tractors at the moment.
And at the moment, it's silage season,
so there's a lot of interest in the silage,
whether we're baling or making a pit silage.
So, yeah, a lot of the time we are talking about farms.
So how do you bring the world of dairy into the classroom?
Here's teacher Belinda Elliott to explain.
All the basics of where their food comes from
and simple things like farm animals.
We relate it back to art projects
and we incorporate it into even cooking experiences.
This year we created our own butter by churning our own cream
and cooking with that.
We spread it onto some beautiful scones that we'd made
and it was a really good way for children to get a good visual
in how things are made in the dairy industry.
And did the kids have a lot of questions about the butter?
Yeah, they did.
Well, they were more interested in the taste testing side of things too.
They enjoyed the buttermilk,
which we weren't sure if we were going to like that taste of that.
But, yeah, they enjoyed that.
They just, even the process of them being able to spread it onto their own food
that they'd made and enjoyed the taste.
So, yeah, it was a really good learning experience.
Belinda Elliott, a teacher at the Leangatha Community Preschool
in Victoria's South Gippsland region, ending that story from Faith Tabaloo Yun.
Before that, Erin Park brought us the story of Boogger Awoya,
who walked out of the great sandy desert in 1967,
encountering white people for the first time.
I'm David Claughton and you're listening to A Big Country.
Still to come, mangoes are synonymous with summertime in Australia.
We'll learn some of the history of how the sweet, juicy fruit
came to be a staple of the Australian summer.
And the country's longest-running radio program
is celebrating 80 years on air this month.
Among many long-time loyal listeners to ABC Radio's Country Hour program
is an 87-year-old buffalo dairy farmer from south-east Queensland.
Margaret Thompson has been listening in for as long as the Country Hour
has been sharing rural and regional stories.
Well, I love the girl. You have a pat. So gorgeous.
And we've come into the dairy where the buffalo cows are all being very patient,
waiting for their turn to be milked.
I don't know if you can hear the chug of the machines behind us
powering the suction cups,
and I can see the milk going up into the pipes
and coming out into this big tank here.
How many cows are you milking in the moment?
I've got about 40 on me.
Recapping the top story in this bulletin,
temperatures are expected to soar across south-east Queensland today.
Now, as you can hear, the ABC is the soundtrack of this farm that I'm visiting today.
And I am here with one of the most devoted Country Hour listeners that there could be.
Her name is Margaret Thompson from Mullaney Buffalo.
We've got the buffalo having a feed behind us as her son Michael is milking the cows in the dairy.
You never like to talk about your age, but you are 87 years young.
Margaret, what are your first memories of the Country Hour?
It was always on at lunchtime.
Everybody would come in for lunch, radio would be on, and that's it.
And you'd listen to it, and then you'd listen to the Lawson.
You're out in the country, you didn't have a daily pay fee.
So if you didn't have the Country Hour, you didn't know what else was going on around you.
And Queensland's a big place.
Australia's even bigger.
But my father and mother were always forward-thinking, so that they would pick up stuff on the Country Hour.
That dam down there is one of the first red-soil dams, or dam that's been put in a red soil that was successful.
They had the courage to do something different.
And I guess the next generation aren't much different.
I think sometimes it does run in families like that.
Now, you are a person who has a deep love of learning.
You're a Churchill Fellow who travelled overseas to learn about buffalo dairies before you and your husband, your late husband, started the dairy on this farm after deregulation.
And you got rid of your traditional cows and switched to buffalo.
Traditional dairy, yes.
He badly wanted to do something that was different from the opportunity.
So you've got to put your heart into it.
And when he passed away, we really needed to keep that dream going.
It was Mal, wasn't it?
Yeah, it was Mal.
Yeah, yeah.
So the idea is always more important.
You learn about different pasture grasses and that kind of thing.
You know, people did things early, and Mal was the same.
I don't call them dreamers, I call them visionaries.
Sometimes it works and sometimes it doesn't.
And you are still the treasurer after gosh knows how many decades of...
No, I was secretary before.
You were secretary before for the Merry River Catchment Coordinating Committee,

which also cares for the land and this magnificent river that we've got that discharges into the ocean so that everything that happens on the land is very significant for the bottom part of the Great Barrier Reef.
How much does land care mean to you?
We were one of the original ones starting off Barung.
Land care has always been important.
And then gradually I moved through the ranks of land care, sitting on various committees in Queensland and actually was on the board of Land Care Australia at one time.
So I've had a lot of chances to bring different ideas back.
And what does it feel like to see the result?
And I love doing stories about the work that's being done to repair some of the unintentional mistakes of the past with clearing trees along rivers and increasing erosion and that sort of thing.
Sometimes they weren't unintentional.
Sometimes they were what we were told was a good idea to do.
You were told to destag the river and everything else, so you didn't have any place for the cod to nest.
We're talking about the endangered Mary River cod.
Yeah, departments and that have different ideas.
Sometimes they're not always proven to be correct.
But that's where sometimes the country comes in very good because you hear what they're doing in other regions.
And believe it or not, I think as a group, we're talking about Emmett Tripple C there as a group, with our participants in our projects, they also become part of the family.
And where does your buffalo dairy milk go?
We go through Melanie Cheese down to what they call Cheese Time down to the Gold Coast.
A lot that goes to Sydney generally makes into Indian sweets.
You're also producing buffalo for meat for a whole range of projects, a real nose-to-tail approach.
We try to do everything that way, Jennifer, that you don't waste anything.
But we have so many different nationalities now.
And buffalo were their prime food.
You're always looking for something else.
I find buffalo just to be mesmerising animals.
They're so beautiful to look at and remarkably gentle, probably because of the handling that they get here.
So you get rid of anything that's not true.
You don't want to breed from anything that's not.
What do you like about the animals?
I've always liked animals, so that's it.
But they're very family-oriented, and if you get one that likes you, then they like you.
And that seems to go through the family.
And what keeps you farming?
I mean, lots of other people would have retired.
What am I going to do?
A long time ago, when dairy deregulation came in, somebody asked me, and I said,
well, I can't ever imagine not having an animal to pat.
It's special.
I couldn't go line dancing.
I've got nothing like that.
And there's a challenge in farming.
They're the taste of summer.
And each year, Australians eat their way through as much as 75,000 tonnes of the King of Fruits.
And while most mangoes are grown in the Northern Territory,
the fruit owes its taste to the North Queensland town of Bowen,
where two popular varieties were created.
Some say there was a tree in Sydney's Royal Botanic Garden as early as 1823 that never fruited,
and by the 1860s, a tree was growing in Rockhampton.
What's not in dispute is mangoes were first commercially produced in Bowen.
Queensland DPI Senior Principal Horticulturalist Ian Bally says they arrived from Asia,
where mangoes have been eaten for thousands of years.
In the late 1800s, boats coming to and fro from Bowen used to bring mangoes from Southeast Asia.
Those boats would be travelling from Bowen,
taking horses to India for the remount trade for the British Army.
And as they sort of travelled that India to Australia route,
they would pick up local fruit at local markets and ports along the way.
Quite often those fruit and seed from those fruit were given to local farmers in the Bowen area.
They were often grown on the farm of the harbour master there.
And the better ones of those were then passed on again.
And Kensington Pride was one of those ones that was passed on to a guy.
Harry Lott had a farm at Adelaide Point.
I think the farm was named Kensington.
And from various selections and over time,
the Kensington Pride sort of stood out as being something that was bigger,
better and tastier than all the other selections.
And it began to be grown around the Bowen area.
The Kensington Pride is still the most popular mango in Australia,
and all other varieties developed in Australia have some level of Kensington Pride genetics.
Professor Heather Smyth is a flavour expert
and the Deputy Director of Research at the University of Queensland's
Alliance for Agriculture and Food.
She's helped with breeding programs for most major modern Australian mango varieties.
She said Kensington Pride's sweet, tangy flavour is unique due to a compound called alpha-terpinaline.
So I've been tasting mangoes for a very long time.
That strong terpini flavour,
which we have come to know is the Australian unique mango flavour that consumers expect.
Mangoes don't taste like that anywhere else in the world.
They taste like that terpini flavour only here in Australia.
And that's because of Kensington Pride or this Bowen style of mango.
A hundred years after the rise of the Kensington Pride,
a second popular mango variety came from Bowen, the R2E2.
It's a large, round fruit with firm flesh and a sweet, fresh flavour.
The original 40-year-old tree still stands at a research centre in Bowen.
Mr Bally worked on its breeding program.
He says research began in the 60s to combat shortcomings with the Kensington Pride.
It was recognised that some of the international overseas varieties were much better producers,
especially some of those from Florida that were in the 1940s sort of were selected over there.
So this is when it was decided that, yeah, some crossbreeding needed to happen.
The introduced varieties seeds were planted in the ground in Bowen.
And as they began to crop, they were assessed for their suitability as commercial varieties for the Bowen area.
And one of those trees was a Kent seedling, which became R2E2.
It was selected because it was quite large, had a very good flesh-to-seed ratio,
and had this great shelf life, much better for travelling than the Kensington Pride.
Today, the Kensington Pride makes up about 40% of mango production,
while the R2E2 makes up about 20% and is the number one export variety.
Other popular Queensland varieties commercialised in the 2000s include the Calypso and Honeygold.
Professor Smyth said they each have their own benefits.
Yeah, Honeygold's got a beautiful, rich, sweet flavour and all that alpha-depinoline.
It's certainly a premium version of mango.
It's a beautiful mango.
It's really golden in colour.
The Calypso can be absolutely gorgeous when it's looking really good.
It is a much, I would say, more delicate flavour compared to the other fruit.
I would say a very clean version of that terpeni, piney flavour that you have from the KP,
you also get in the Calypso mango.
What's the best way to eat a mango?
Under clinical conditions, Professor Smyth tastes mangoes at about 20 degrees to bring out the most flavour.
Just before you want to eat it, put it in the fridge for a couple of hours just to cool it down,
but not to cause the chill injury and make it sort of soft and glassy inside.
And then cut it with your knife, prepare it, pop those cheeks out.
Whether you want to cut off the cubes or whether you want to slice it up and use it in some other way,
it's lovely to have cool mango, but just don't keep it in the fridge for long periods of time.
However, as a child in Darwin, Professor Smyth developed her own favourite style.
I was probably about seven years old and my friend had a swimming pool.
The un-mango season, you could pluck off the tree, climb the tree, plot them into the swimming pool
and then just tear the skin off with your teeth and then just tuck into the mango,
just as it is, no knife, nothing else.
And you saw dripping down your chin, dripping down your arms and then just wash it off in the swimming pool.
So it's just the best.
That's story from Liam McNally in Mackay in tropical North Queensland.
Before that, we heard from a long-time Country Hour listener and buffalo farmer, Margaret Thompson.
That's the show for today.
I'm David Clawton.
Thanks for listening and bye for now.

episodes.title: Career change to pub owner and new priest turns heads in rural parish
episodes.description: Meet the pint-sized publican granny; motorcycle riding priest shares passion for social justice with rural parish; farming camels for milk and meat; agriculture students get out of the laboratory to taste life on the land.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. I'm David Claughton with you for A Big Country. Let's catch up with our reporters on the road in regional Australia. This week, putting theory into practice, we'll meet university agriculture students who are getting out of the lab and onto the land. They're visiting farms to see how their study plays out in practice. We'll visit a church congregation where the new priest is turning heads. Her tattoos, pink hair and motorbike may not be what the parishioners were expecting, but she's using her varied life experience to help others in the community. And we'll meet a pint-sized publican who's proving a drawcard and a social media star. At just 142 centimetres tall, grandmother Barb Parkinson is helping her daughter run a small-town pub on the Queensland coast. And she's posing for photos with passing tourists who come from all over Australia for a selfie. I actually feel like a grommet. Especially when I only, some of them, I only come up to like their waist. I'm getting used to it now, but do have people come out of their way just so they can get their photo taken with a really short grin. We'll meet Barb, the tiny publican. That's coming up. First today, across remote Australia, hundreds of thousands of wild camels are considered feral pests, with many shot and left to rot. But on a farm in south-east Queensland's Scenic Rim, camels are being milked to make cheese, skin care products and vodka, while their meat is being used in a range of cuts, including salamis. And the humped mammals are attracting thousands of tourists to the farm every year. Reporter Jennifer Nichols spoke with Paul Martin of Summerland Camels to hear how the venture came about. Around 2010, we were doing a big camel cull in Australia. The government was throwing a lot of money at it and people were asking, why can't we do something with these amazing animals? And we put a project together and here we are. This was a fully start from scratch project where we go, well, how can we domesticate feral camels for a start? So before we could go and raise capital, we sort of really needed to tick that box. So we brought in about 20 camels out at Lowood where we leased a property, started to domesticate them and then milk them and the yields were reasonable. So we thought, well, OK, we can now expand from here and sort of tap into that dairy intolerant market and that health market for camels. The idea was to sort of try and set something up close to a capital city. So we had the milk and the products that we could make from it. We used some seed capital to start. One of our investors funded a farm that we're at now. We had a crowd behind us, so we raised about $9 million to get to that point where we made our skincare products and cheese and got that into the marketplace. Then we raised probably another $2 million through crowdfunding. And that's sort of a mechanism where you're harnessing your crowd that are following you and like what you do and all the rest of it. And then they'll invest in your company. So it's not floated on the stock exchange. It's still a private company, but they can invest and get shares like you do normally, but then also get discounts for products and stuff like that. What's the good thing about camel milk? It's the only mammal milk that people with dairy allergies can have for a start. So from an environmental point of view, there's this movement sort of looks at a lot of the environmental impacts of nut milks and things like that with their heavy use of water and stuff. So going back to an adaptable animal, which is a camel is the most adaptable animal on the planet, that it can produce a milk for people that is of a health benefit as opposed to just a carrier for a cereal. So that's how we sort of started. Okay. And since then, gosh, I was just listening to your speech, staggered at the products that you can make from a camel. The vodka, for example. Yeah, yeah. It's amazing when you look back at the products we've made, but, you know, all our heads around trying to, okay, what can we make with camel milk that gives it shelf life? So the skincare products and then shelf stability with cheeses. You know, a lot of people say, oh, camel milk, I don't like it. But cheese, you know, you can half rot in a cheese and people still eat it. You know, so, you know, having a cheese. Stinky cheese. Yeah, that's right. Good stinky cheese. So, you know, cheese is an amazing way to get people just interested to go, oh, is that camel really? And then it was like, well, we've got whey left over. What do we do here? What can we do with it? That's where the vodka idea came up. You know, around 800 litres of whey will produce about 110 litres of alcohol. And then that's about 200 litres of vodka. And are you doing that all on site? So we do the brewing side of it, which takes about 14 to 20 days, depending on the time of year. Then we send that 800 litres in to get distilled. How many camels do you have? And how are you running them? And where are you running them? Our farm at Parrisville. So we've got 400 camels there. There's probably 50-odd in our tourism riding team. And then the rest are dairy camels and progeny coming through. So young females that we're keeping. So we're milking probably 70 camels. We've got another 30 that are about to give birth. So, you know, that'll get us up to about 100 by the end of the year. And it's a bit different to cows too, because you allow the calves to stay with the mums. Yes. So the calves need to be at this stage with the mums. Like the camels can hang on to their milk. They've got to express it. So you've got to look after them pretty well. And we take the calves off in the afternoon and we milk them. So we're milking once a day. And then the calf gets the rest of the milk for that day. Your cost of production's higher. How much does it cost at the shops? It ranges anywhere between $16 and $20 a litre. You know, that's a challenging thing for people, especially with the low-cost milk that has been ate for the last few years. But then a lot of your gut health supplements and yogurts, people will pay way more than that per litre for something that actually, that's what traditional people use camel milk for. So it's about a little bit of a branding story that we've got to try and educate people on. Meat and meat products. When did you start venturing down that front? Yeah, probably about three years ago. And our camels go generally because they're so quiet. Once they've spent 14 months in the dairy, they generally go out as pets. But we're also harvesting more females and we get all these other camels. So we really wanted to try and engage other farmers to run these camels. So they'll run them out in Western Queensland to control prickly acacia and Parkinsonia and all that sort of thing if they've got a way to sell them at some point. Overseas camel meat is eaten a lot. What sorts of products are you doing? We're marketing premium cuts to restaurants and supplying what they need. But then what do we do with the rest? So we've got all this trim and all the rest of it left over. So we've got charcuterie products. We've won a gold medal in Sydney with our pepper salami. Congratulations. Yeah, and I think a silver for our beer sticks down there. So we're using Schultz's at Plainlands. Again, another local guys that specialise in preserved meat. And agritourism is a big part of your model too to try to introduce more people to the camel. How's that going? We get 60,000 people a year now through the farm. So it's amazing. And it's a great way to introduce people to a domesticated camel. You know, most people, even if they've had anything to do with the camels, they've probably done it over in Dubai. And some cranky camel that they've had to ride in this desert that's sick of tourists. You know, the camels we've got are just amazing, like grass-eating Labradors. So people come, they feed them over the fence and they can go for a camel ride or go and see some baby camels. And then the view out where we are is quite amazing as well. Pauline Harley takes off her motorbike helmet and walks into church. She swaps her leather jacket for white robes and prepares for the service. I have been stopped once when I've been riding with my collar on. There was a double take from the police officer who was doing the breath test. Reverend Harley's arrival was a bit of a surprise to the more conservative churchgoers at Toowoomba West Parish. Phoebe Mitchell has been attending St Albans for 20 years. We hadn't had a minister for some considerable time. Pauline's arrival was a shock to some people. One, because she was female. And two, because of her hair. And she wasn't as orthodox as everybody else is. So unfortunately one of the upshots of it was that we did lose some of our people who didn't believe in having women as ordained ministers. I think originally in their minds they were getting a man, a male priest, because that's all they've ever had and known. And realised that I was tattooed and pink here. That first service here was a little bit of a shock to some people. I'm not worried about your lifestyle, who you are, young, old, disabled, not disabled. I think a church needs to look like it's community. Welcome Lee to our service. Welcome to St Albans. Reverend Harley didn't grow up in the church. Far from it in fact. I grew up with not a very good family life. So my mum, what I believe now, probably had what's recognised as severe mental illness. Because of past trauma in her life, and she didn't make her a very good parent. She was addicted to all sorts of things. Starting off from cigarettes, to caffeine, to codeine. Because of those obsessions, she neglected us. And she went from boyfriend to boyfriend. And because she swam in those circles, I was abused every which way. So one of her boyfriends, the then boyfriend at the time, decided he didn't want kids around. And I came home one day, and there was a box on the sidewalk of my stuff with a note, don't come back. Pauline spent six months living homeless. Eventually, she ended up moving to Australia with her then husband. And we thought by coming to Australia, we could leave all our problems behind as well. Unfortunately, gambling came with him. And there was casinos here. So as a Kiwi, I couldn't receive any government benefits. So I had to find a way to work. She worked a variety of jobs. In a fish and chip shop, Danish bakery, muffin shop, and then in IT, literally building computers. While studying in TAFE, her teacher mentioned there was work at a local church office. I thought, I've been in hospitality for so long, I'll give it a go. It was there she met Reverend David Cox, a man who became a friend, a mentor, and the person she calls her Aussie dad. So nervous, because I've not been around that sort of person before. And he was just this gentle, kind man. And he saw a broken person, and he was willing to give me a go. Yeah, and next thing you know, I'm at church every Sunday. For the first time, Pauline felt a purpose. A higher calling. There was this little thing in me that voice, I believe to be the voice of God, saying, I want you to look at ordained ministry. And I was going, no way. And tried to run away from that. Tried to get into doing border security for some stupid reason. But every corner I took, God slammed that back, my belief. And I was like, no, you're doing this. At the age of 40, having never graduated high school, she decided to become an ordained Anglican priest. One of my things I say to people is that you can't change your past. You can then make a choice, though, for yourself. And through the healing workshops and through the counselling that I did, my choice was, A, let my past forever dictate me in a negative way, or to use it in a positive way going forward in the future. So in my ministry now, I do have a passion for homelessness and those who are less fortunate. Since Reverend Harley became the priest in charge for the Toowoomba West Parish, there's been some changes. Phoebe Mitchell says they're now more involved than ever in volunteering and social justice. It wasn't an area this parish had ever touched. We're really fortunate to have someone like Pauline, who introduces and challenges us to step outside our comfort zones as well. Pauline's real. Pauline doesn't put herself above anybody else. She's one of us. She's one of everybody. Preaches and teachers through her life experience, which hasn't been easy. The purple bike parked outside St Albans is unique and distinctive, just like its owner, who's happy her married name is so appropriate. I've always loved bikes and I've always, always wanted a motorbike. I've always wanted a Harley, even before I became a Harley. Beyond being known as the motorbike riding priest, Reverend Harley wants her legacy to be one of service to the less fortunate. For me, it's important that I show parishioners actions are just as important in our faith journey. We just pray for our city that more and more people would step out of their comfort zones and help in our community. Thank you. And I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I guess, or out of their university classrooms, out into the space. And this is such, I suppose, a diverse region as well. How important is it for that to experience? Yeah, I mean, we get fantastic feedback at the end of this excursion, which we run every year by the way, and we go to a different region in New South Wales every year. Yeah, so a lot of them, as you hinted there, they're stuck in the lab, I shouldn't say stuck, they're in the lab enjoying their biochemistry or their plant pathology for example, or they're doing modelling on a computer. Some of them are doing quite a lot of field work already, but there's no way that they would otherwise be able to access a sheep farm and two beef farms and a research institute, all in the space of a few days. It would be very hard for them to organise that themselves in any way. My name is Damdola Karim, or you can call me Dami. Okay. Yeah, so I'm working with chicken, chicken nutrition, trying to find sustainable ways to produce chickens and also reducing the negative impact of reduced protein diets in chicken nutrition. My name is Kai Sin. I'm from Singapore. And I'm currently doing research on a novel horticultural production system. And I'm very, very happy to be on this trip. Let's just start with this trip. The last two or three days, what you've seen? Oh, it's been a lot. Yeah. And wonderful. For this year, we've been to a cattle farm. First today, across remote Australia, hundreds of thousands of wild camels are considered feral pests, with many shot and left to rot.

why can't we do something with these amazing animals?

Hundreds of people attended the pub's 125th birthday celebrations, which included a best-dressed granny competition in honour of the star publican.
For daughter Alicia, who had no idea that a retirement plan to buy a country pub in Queensland would end up making her mum semi-famous, she's really proud.
She's a little firecracker, that's for sure.
Yeah, and hard worker.
Like, there's nothing for her on a Tuesday when the delivery of alcohol comes through and she's thrown around cartons.
She's a real goer.
Like, and you can't stop her.
You can't stop her.
That's Alicia Smith, new owner of the Yandaran Hotel near Bundaberg in Queensland.
She was talking about her mum, Barb Parkinson, who's taken a career change from nursing to help her run the pub.
And you can see more on that story, including photos of Barb posing next to some of the pub's taller patrons who tower above her.
You'll find that story on the ABC homepage.
Head to abc.net.au and search for The Granny Publican.
That's the show for today.
I'm David Clawton and I'll be back next week with more great stories from beyond the cities.
I'll chat to you then.
