episodes.title: Turning crops into spirits and rare orchids thriving in old cemeteries
episodes.description: Turning red wheat and sugar beet into unique spirits, historic cemeteries offer protected habitat for rare orchids, learning from the best at bull-riding camp, country cafe building community.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. I'm David Claughton with you for A Big Country. Let's catch up with our reporters on the road in regional Australia. This week, not just a resting place for the long departed. We'll hear how historic cemeteries are providing undisturbed habitat for rare and endangered plants and animals. We'll meet a farmer who's adding value to his crops by turning them into spirits and hear how he's using some less common crops like red wheat and sugar beet to make unconventional alcohol. And we're visiting a tiny border town that suffered a series of setbacks but is now on the road to recovery with the help of a little coffee shop run by local women who see the value in building their community. We live here ourselves. We want a great town. We want a town to be proud of and that doesn't happen by everyone sitting on their bottoms. Like, you've got to get in and do the hard work. That story coming up. But first today, bull riding has a reputation as one of the most dangerous sports you can take up. But it's not proving a turn-off for aspiring bull riders lured by the action and adrenaline of the rodeo scene. Almost 60 up-and-coming riders had the chance to learn from the best at a dedicated bull riding camp in central Queensland recently. And reporter Claudia Sullivan went along to meet some of the talented young riders. There's an art to the popular, if not divisive, sport of bull riding. And the skill set is one that event organisers were concerned could be eroded if not fostered. That's why the organisation Youth of the Nation Rodeo Co organised a bull riding camp in Grace Mears' CQLX Sail Yards. The training day attracted some of Australia's biggest bull riding names, including world number three Brady Fielder. I'm ranked second in the MVP in the PBR Team Series and finished third in the world title race this year for 2025 in PBR and the best bull ride in the world. It's a great feeling. Yeah, incredible. Congratulations. Thank you very much. You know, it's a heck of a journey. I'm just grateful to achieve what I have so far. Yeah, did you ever expect to achieve it? You know, to be honest, I always had a big picture out there far away, but sometimes for sure I didn't know if I could ever do it. But never, ever gave up and just never let up one bit. And I'm grateful for where I'm at now. Are you hoping to keep competing as well? What's the goal? Absolutely, yeah. I plan on riding for the next few years at least and I'd like to become a world champion for sure. It's the main goal, whether I'm in team or individuals. So it's what I'm shooting for each and every time and I know if I do everything right, I'll be all right. Can you paint a bit of the scene for me about what it was like? Where were you competing? Over in America, in the United States. Just I've competed all over the world, really. Just especially in the States, you know, it's the biggest bull riding in the world, from Vegas, all around. It's New York. There's so many cool opportunities to go and visit these places, doing what I truly love. It's really cool. With eager students travelling from as far as the Northern Territory and Victoria, Harrison Prow was just one local future champion in the making, keen to learn the ropes. The best of the best here to coach, so I came here to learn some stuff. What's it like to see some of the best of the best? Oh, pretty cool. I could be just like them one day. So what's something that you've been learning today? Can you walk me through it? So for starters, we went on the drop barrel, which is just like a biking bull, but with a barrel. And then we went and do a shoot procedure, which is what you all do in the shoot, like what you do with your bull rope and that. Is that when you're slowly sitting on the bull? Yeah, it is in the shoot. And then put your hand in the bull rope, just like you do when you're riding one. Do you think you can tell how the bull feels beneath you, if it's like a happy or an angry bull? Not too sure. All the adrenaline rush makes you just like feel nothing really. Sometimes if they're just like running, galloping across the arena, you do sometimes, and it just feels cool and fun. Is it ever scary? Oh, not really. Only when one's chasing you. The sport is also notoriously dangerous. Attending the camp was Sam O'Connor. It was his first time back in the stadium since he broke his back bull riding in 2018. While he was left with a paraplegic disability from the accident, he still loves the sport and was there to help nurture other young riders. Instructing bull riding is, you know, you're starting with a lot of kids that have not learnt anything, so you've got to teach them the basic skills and the fundamentals of riding bulls. So teaching them how to get on them properly, to do the right movements. It's not just crack the gate and hang on for dear life. There's actual skill to it of following the beast, learning how to ride the momentum out of it, and yeah. Can you give me maybe step one, when you're hopping on a bull, like some hot tips? Getting on, just you want to be nice and calm. You don't want to be brain flustered or anything like that. The calmer you are, you're going to keep the beast calm as well. The less energy you use inside the chute, the more energy you've got to get out of the chute with. And can you tell me what makes you experience to do this bull riding training? Can you give me your catalogue? Well, yeah, I rode bulls professionally for about seven years. Sort of rode all over the world, America, Canada, Brazil. It's a sport that took me everywhere, which is what I loved about it. I got to see the world, see all of Australia, meet a lot of great contacts, and in my books it's the best fun you can have with your clothes on, I guess. And you were speaking a bit in past tense there about your bull riding days. Do you mind telling me a bit about how it came to an end? Yeah, so first of the first, so it happened on New Year's Eve. I broke my back at a PBR professional event. It's not ping pong, it is what it is. The true thing about the sport is it is dangerous. You can get killed. There has been people that have been killed. I broke my back and became a complete paraplegic. But the sport of bull riding is what's getting me mind strong, because you have to have a strong mind to ride bulls, and that is dangerous. So if you can get past that, I believe you can get past anything in life. And is there something that, I guess, maybe people don't know so much about your life now that you are paraplegic? What's changed for you? Lots of things have changed. Well, I mean, always run off my feet. It's a bit of a pun there, but yeah. So we had to relearn how to use your body. Once you break your back, you lose certain parts that don't work anymore. Your bowels, your insides and that sort of stuff. So you had to relearn how to use all that sort of stuff again and to get back out there in the world, you know. That's the biggest thing I can say to everybody is the more you can get out there in life, the better you can be. Well, today's your first day back training, isn't it? How does it feel being in the arena? Yeah, no, this is my first bull riding skill since being in a wheelchair. I broke me back here in Rocky. What was that back? Yeah, first of the first, 2018. So seven years ago, I broke me back, and now it's back doing the bull riding skill, helping the younger generation, which is something that I hope I can give them the same life I got they live, you know, getting to travel all over the world and do something you love doing. You're not at work any day. Every day is a great day because you're doing something you love doing, you know, and to hand that back on to young kids and hopefully they can get out there and live the life I got to live. Is there anything that you think people don't know, something you'd like to tell people listening, that they don't know about bull riding? Yeah, so a lot of people think it's cruel, you know. The biggest thing is it's cruelty to animals. A lot of people don't understand, but these bulls are looked after. They're like everybody's pets. The contractors that own the bulls and everything like that, they're their pets. So those bulls, you know, if they get hurt, that's their livelihood gone. So they're not going to put their bulls in any position that's going to hurt them, you know what I mean? And we all love that without bulls, we don't have a sport. No one wants to get out there and hurt the bulls in any kind of way. You know, there's rules against it. The bull gets cut. There's, you know, upper fines up to $1,700 per centimetre. Everything is designed. Our spurs, yes, we ride with spurs, but they're blunt. They're RSPCA approved. To a lot of people out there that looks at it as if it's, you know, cruelty to animals, it's, you know, you've got a bull that weighs up to 900 kilos to a cowboy that weighs up to about 50 kilos, you know. So no way we can hurt them, but, you know, they love to do it as well. A lot of bulls, if they don't want to buck, they'll just gallop down the pen, you know. So they've got to want to buck as well. So they love the sport just as much as the bull riders do, yeah. And there's a bit of action happening behind us. Can you tell me what's happening right now? Yeah, so we just bucked our first one. So one of the young fellas just got on a little potty. Well, it's a steer. I think they rode time too, so that's a good bonus for the young fella. So you've got the bull fighters there parted up with thigh pads, chest pads. You can hear when that young fella just fell off then. You can hear the thump. You will get winded. And that's the part where you find out whether you want to be a bull rider or not. If it's the first time, once you get winded a few times, it's either a full person or it's not full person. The camaraderie behind the chutes, you know, like, yes, it's a one-person sport. No one can help you once that gate's open. But then you've got the boys on the back of the chute. Everyone's out there to help each other to succeed, you know what I mean? Like, yes, we're versing each other in an actual bull ride together, but you'll see everybody on the back of the chutes cheering and trying to get you across the other side. On the outskirts of a small town on the New South Wales mid-north coast, life is blooming in an historic cemetery. Tucked among bushland, the graveyard, more than 150 years old, is home to a critically endangered ground orchid, the pale yellow double tail. It was first discovered at the site in the mid-1990s and since then, the Midcoast Council has carefully managed the area to ensure the orchid species is protected. There's only three or four sites where we know this species occurs, so it's really limited, extremely restricted in its range. I'm here at the graveyard site with the council's senior ecologist, Matt Bell, who regularly monitors the orchids. The orchid does occur in areas that are mown, if they're mown at the right time of the year, when the species isn't flowering. So it really relies on areas that have a native grassy ground cover. So it only appears when it's flowering, so you can only detect it in September or October when the flower spikes emerge. The flower spikes are very small. They're only about 20 centimetres high, but they've got a showy yellow flower on them, a beautiful, delicate, complex flower. But yeah, it's incredibly difficult to find because it's only obvious when it's flowering and it flowers for such a short period of time. So what sort of things do you do to preserve it? So it's essentially protect the flower spikes when they emerge. So it's to safeguard them from trampling or mowing or disturbance. We also look after the habitat. So we treat weeds. And what happens if there is a burial happening at that certain time when it's flowering? Yeah, so it's just the spikes are identified. They're flagged so that the operation can take place respectfully and appropriately, but the orchids are protected from any trampling or inadvertent harm. And so we have a long history of where the orchid spikes do occur, and they do occur in and amongst some of the gravestones. So it is a bit of a, there's a balance there. It's a very difficult tightrope that we have to walk in order to allow people to utilise the cemetery for its purpose, but also to preserve the orchids at the site. It's one of many places across Australia where historic cemeteries are providing relatively undisturbed habitat for rare and endangered plants and animals. In a rural area of Canberra, the 1883 Hall Cemetery also provides critical habitat for an endangered orchid. It's the only ACT site where the Tarango Leak Orchid is found. Matt Bell says cemeteries are far more than just a place of gravestones and burials. Well, cemeteries, they're set out so long ago. These cemeteries could be 150 years old. They were set aside for the purposes of a cemetery, but they also preserve nature. And the nature has been, it hasn't been harmed in being a part of the cemetery. So the native ground cover, the grassy layers are all intact, which means that orchids and a variety of species that have been impacted in other landscapes for development and other reasons, they're preserved in cemeteries. So we come to cemeteries to connect to our families and to our lineages and to our society, but we can also come to cemeteries and connect with lineages of nature and biodiversity, which is really special. Matt Bell says sightings of the rare ground orchid on the mid-north coast have been few and far between this spring, but overall its numbers seem to be holding steady. It's erratically flowering, definitely. And that presents challenges for us to understand the population because it's naturally erratic. If there's a declining trend in the number of flowering individuals, it's hard to detect when there's variability, and that variability might be a result of rainfall patterns or other seasonal factors. We're still working out a lot of knowledge about this cryptic and very rare plant. That story from Emma Siossian, who visited a graveyard in the Wingham area on the New South Wales mid-north coast, which is home to a critically endangered ground orchid. You can read more on that story and see photos of the orchid. You'll find it by searching Cemetery Orchid on the ABC homepage at abc.net.au. I'm David Claughton with you for A Big Country. Still to come, we're meeting a sixth-generation farmer who's adding value to his homegrown crops, using them in his on-farm distillery to make some unusual spirits like red wheat vodka. And we're visiting a tiny border town between Queensland and New South Wales where a group of local women have stepped up to help their community after a series of devastating blows. After drought, COVID closures and then fire, it was more than just bricks and mortar that needed rebuilding in Mungandai, as landline's Courtney Wilson discovered. Mungandai is like many small country towns. But there is a big point of difference here. As well as being the only town in Australia situated on both sides of a state border, there is a special spirit here that makes Mungandai stand out. And at the centre of it is a little green coffee shop called Flock. For Mungandai, Flock came about just when it was needed most. A few years ago, Mungandai suffered a series of setbacks in relatively quick succession that had long-time locals like Anna Harrison really worried about the town's future. People were having to let go of staff and families were leaving and that's really hard because we just know in small communities you just can't get that retention back and it's hard to build a community back after that. After three long years of drought came the COVID pandemic and border closures, which quite literally split this town in two. In 2019, the coffee shop closed. And then in 2020, a devastating fire wiped out several other shops in the main street, including the local supermarket. And that's our livelihood in Mungandai gone. Very sad to see. It proved too much for some and there were people and families who packed up and left. In a small community like this, that can be devastating. You know, it's one less person on the canteen roster. It's a family short swim club. Yeah, it impacts everyone. And I think the menu in the end was perfect for that. We pretty much now... For Anna Harrison, the bad luck that had befallen Mungandai was really concerning. She didn't want to see the town falter and she wasn't alone with those worries. She didn't want to see the town falter. So Anna rallied the troops. Five women, all from Mungandai or near enough, came together to find a way to bring a bit of spark back to the main drag. We live here ourselves. We want a great town. We want a town to be proud of. And that doesn't happen by everyone sitting on their bottoms. Like, you've got to get in and do the hard work. They decided their particular flavour of hard work would come in the form of a little coffee shop with a big goal, to help bring Mungandai back from the brink. I think there's lots of opportunities in a town like Mungandai. Despite each having busy lives, with 13 children between them, as well as farms and other jobs, the women were fuelled by a shared desire to give something back to their community. The five women played to their individual strengths, whether that was designing the menu, doing the logistical legwork, managing supplies or dealing with staffing. In a border town 750 kilometres south-east of Brisbane with no local grocery shop, none of that was easy. But boy, was it appreciated. Everyone comes here in the mornings, the ambassadors, the local police, everyone comes here sort of for a catch-up in the morning. It's great. It wasn't just the customers that benefited either. The ladies behind Flock were also finding unexpected fulfilment. Annette Hegney explains. Filled my cup in so many ways. Being able to see the community and have somewhere to call in for a cuppa that wasn't a pub. There are limited sporting facilities available for anyone who isn't in primary school. So it was great to have a place that they could come to and enjoy the community and just make the most of being in town. Pitching in when times are tough is something people in the bush are known for. And these five women are all quick to point out they're certainly not unique. Late last year, the time came for the original Flock 5 to pass on the baton. Luckily, another long-time local, Nikki Smith, stepped up. It's been a bit of a challenge, a lot more involved than really probably what I thought it was going to be. Probably 80 to 100 coffees a day. That's sort of average normally, yeah. It's going through about 15 kilos of coffee beans a week. It's not just people from Mungandai who've embraced the Little Green Cafe either. Plenty of passers-by are also lured by the promise of a barista-made coffee to stop and spend a little extra time in town. Best coffee ever! For the creators of Flock, it's a joy to see another local at the helm of their pride and joy and a real sense of accomplishment for what they helped create. The five of us are community-minded people and I think you need that drive to do what we did. I love the town of Mungandai. There's some really cool, interesting, fun people and to get the opportunity to get to know them in a closer way is really... I feel really fortunate, all the people we got to know better through that. So we spring sow our barley here but after the recent rain it's definitely helping it out quite a lot. Ross Shaw is pretty comfortable talking crops. That's because he's a sixth-generation farmer and agronomist from Victoria's Gippsland region. We're like a traditional sort of mixed farming operation. We run Aussie white sheep and we have cattle and we do hay and cropping as well. But two years ago, Mr Shaw decided to go against the grain. Yeah, returning to the farm I wanted to be able to value-add to our sort of commodities and have a little bit of extra income off farms so I've opened a distillery. In Gippsland, most grain just goes for feed. There's not really a receival for malt or flower grades or anything like that. Yeah. And we're standing here in the distillery, Ross, so can you describe what we're looking at? Yeah, so we've got the 1200-litre pot still in the corner and it's just going through a wash run at the moment, doing the first stage in making a single malt whiskey, basically. That'll run for most of the day and we collect the low wines and then once we've collected enough it'll go back again for a second distillation and make pot distilled single malt. And so you've been distilling for about two years now? Yeah, so for about two years we've been filling barrels with whiskey, mostly single malt, some wheat whiskey, a few other little experimental lines. Yeah, and we've just recently brought out a couple of clear spirits. So we did a wheat vodka, red wheat vodka and a sugar beet spirit. You heard that right. A sugar beet spirit and red wheat vodka. This year, the distillery pumped out about 400 bottles of both spirits. So where did the idea for them come from? I'll let Mr Shaw explain. Unlike whiskey, the clear spirits, you can get them to market a lot quicker. They don't have to sit in a barrel or age or anything. So we had the red wheat and we thought let's see how this goes with the vodka. Did a few trials and landed on a recipe that we like and it's quite a nice vodka. It's got a little bit of like a honeycomb sweetness, a little bit of graininess and it comes across quite well. And then the sugar beet spirit, the local town of Mafra was founded on sugar beets. So we thought surely we could make alcohol out of this. Anything with sugar or a starch sauce, you can ferment and make alcohol. So we took that historic crop. We had to, it was hard to find seed. We had to import some seed from Europe, grew the beets and took quite a while to figure out how to process these beets and get the sugar out of them. But we've come, we've sort of landed on a bit of a process that works quite well now. And yeah, making the sugar beet spirit. Now those recipes will remain a secret. But when it comes to whiskey, Mr. Shaw says the distilling process starts with an old dairy vat. Yeah, so this is an old 3000 litre stainless steel dairy vat. We crush our grain into here. So we'll crush about 600 kilos of barley if we're doing a single malt. And then about 2000 litres of water. And you've got to hold it at about 65 degrees for an hour basically. And the natural enzymes inside the barley turn the starch into sugar so that you have a fermentable sugar source for the yeast to eat and make the alcohol. So after it leaves the vat, it goes through a separator that separates the grain and all the husk away from our sugary water or sugary wash. And then that goes into the fermenter. And you pitch the yeast when it's at the correct temperature and that'll ferment for sort of a week, sometimes two weeks. And once that's finished, it goes into the still for the next part of the process. Right. And all up, including it staying in the barrels, takes about two years at least. Yeah, two years is the minimum ageing time for whisky in Australia. But we have, the way that we do it, we have to grow our grain as well. So we have that full grain growing season. So three years basically before we can have a bottle on the market. But quite often it will be longer than that because the whisky might need three to four years ageing time. So it's a very long process and you've got to have a lot of patience. And Russ is a sixth generation farmer. What is the rest of your family and your team thought of this kind of little side hustle that you've created? Probably was a little bit sort of apprehensive to begin with. But as we've sort of built it and gotten into it, it seems to be starting out quite well and everyone's involved. So dad helps me with the malting. So we malt our own barley here as well. So he loves doing the malting. And yeah, everyone sort of is pitching in a little bit here and there wherever it's needed. That was Ross Shaw, an agronomist, farmer and now distiller. He was speaking to reporter Faith Tabalugan from his on-farm distillery in Victoria's Gippsland region. To read more on that story and all the stories on today's program, head to the ABC website at abc.net.au. That's the show for today. I'm David Claughton and I'll be back next week with more great stories from our reporters in regional Australia. I'll talk to you then. You've been listening to an ABC podcast. And then we went and do a shoot procedure,
which is what you all do in the shoot,
like what you do with your bull rope and that.
Is that when you're slowly sitting on the bull?
Yeah, it is in the shoot.
And then put your hand in the bull rope,
just like you do when you're riding one.
Do you think you can tell how the bull feels beneath you,
if it's like a happy or an angry bull?
Not too sure.
All the adrenaline rush makes you just like feel nothing really.
Sometimes if they're just like running,
galloping across the arena, you do sometimes,
and it just feels cool and fun.
Is it ever scary?
Oh, not really.
Only when one's chasing you.
The sport is also notoriously dangerous.
Attending the camp was Sam O'Connor.
It was his first time back in the stadium
since he broke his back bull riding in 2018.
While he was left with a paraplegic disability from the accident,
he still loves the sport
and was there to help nurture other young riders.
Instructing bull riding is, you know,
you're starting with a lot of kids that have not learnt anything,
so you've got to teach them the basic skills
and the fundamentals of riding bulls.
So teaching them how to get on them properly,
to do the right movements.
It's not just crack the gate and hang on for dear life.
There's actual skill to it of following the beast,
learning how to ride the momentum out of it, and yeah.
Can you give me maybe step one,
when you're hopping on a bull, like some hot tips?
Getting on, just you want to be nice and calm.
You don't want to be brain flustered or anything like that.
The calmer you are, you're going to keep the beast calm as well.
The less energy you use inside the chute,
the more energy you've got to get out of the chute with.
And can you tell me what makes you experience
to do this bull riding training?
Can you give me your catalogue?
Well, yeah, I rode bulls professionally for about seven years.
Sort of rode all over the world, America, Canada, Brazil.
It's a sport that took me everywhere,
which is what I loved about it.
I got to see the world, see all of Australia,
meet a lot of great contacts,
and in my books it's the best fun you can have with your clothes on, I guess.
And you were speaking a bit in past tense there about your bull riding days.
Do you mind telling me a bit about how it came to an end?
Yeah, so first of the first, so it happened on New Year's Eve.
I broke my back at a PBR professional event.
It's not ping pong, it is what it is.
The true thing about the sport is it is dangerous.
You can get killed.
There has been people that have been killed.
I broke my back and became a complete paraplegic.
But the sport of bull riding is what's getting me mind strong,
because you have to have a strong mind to ride bulls,
and that is dangerous.
So if you can get past that, I believe you can get past anything in life.
And is there something that, I guess,
maybe people don't know so much about your life now that you are paraplegic?
What's changed for you?
Lots of things have changed.
Well, I mean, always run off my feet.
It's a bit of a pun there, but yeah.
So we had to relearn how to use your body.
Once you break your back, you lose certain parts that don't work anymore.
Your bowels, your insides and that sort of stuff.
So you had to relearn how to use all that sort of stuff again
and to get back out there in the world, you know.
That's the biggest thing I can say to everybody is
the more you can get out there in life, the better you can be.
Well, today's your first day back training, isn't it?
How does it feel being in the arena?
Yeah, no, this is my first bull riding skill since being in a wheelchair.
I broke me back here in Rocky.
What was that back?
Yeah, first of the first, 2018.
So seven years ago, I broke me back,
and now it's back doing the bull riding skill,
helping the younger generation,
which is something that I hope I can give them the same life I got they live,
you know, getting to travel all over the world
and do something you love doing.
You're not at work any day.
Every day is a great day because you're doing something you love doing,
you know, and to hand that back on to young kids
and hopefully they can get out there and live the life I got to live.
Is there anything that you think people don't know,
something you'd like to tell people listening,
that they don't know about bull riding?
Yeah, so a lot of people think it's cruel, you know.
The biggest thing is it's cruelty to animals.
A lot of people don't understand,
but these bulls are looked after.
They're like everybody's pets.
The contractors that own the bulls and everything like that,
they're their pets.
So those bulls, you know, if they get hurt,
that's their livelihood gone.
So they're not going to put their bulls in any position
that's going to hurt them, you know what I mean?
And we all love that without bulls, we don't have a sport.
No one wants to get out there and hurt the bulls in any kind of way.
You know, there's rules against it.
The bull gets cut.
There's, you know, upper fines up to $1,700 per centimetre.
Everything is designed.
Our spurs, yes, we ride with spurs, but they're blunt.
They're RSPCA approved.
To a lot of people out there that looks at it
as if it's, you know, cruelty to animals,
it's, you know, you've got a bull that weighs up to 900 kilos
to a cowboy that weighs up to about 50 kilos, you know.
So no way we can hurt them, but, you know,
they love to do it as well.
A lot of bulls, if they don't want to buck,
they'll just gallop down the pen, you know.
So they've got to want to buck as well.
So they love the sport just as much as the bull riders do, yeah.
And there's a bit of action happening behind us.
Can you tell me what's happening right now?
Yeah, so we just bucked our first one.
So one of the young fellas just got on a little potty.
Well, it's a steer.
I think they rode time too, so that's a good bonus for the young fella.
So you've got the bull fighters there parted up
with thigh pads, chest pads.
You can hear when that young fella just fell off then.
You can hear the thump.
You will get winded.
And that's the part where you find out
whether you want to be a bull rider or not.
If it's the first time, once you get winded a few times,
it's either a full person or it's not full person.
The camaraderie behind the chutes, you know,
like, yes, it's a one-person sport.
No one can help you once that gate's open.
But then you've got the boys on the back of the chute.
Everyone's out there to help each other to succeed,
you know what I mean?
Like, yes, we're versing each other in an actual bull ride together,
but you'll see everybody on the back of the chutes cheering
and trying to get you across the other side.
On the outskirts of a small town on the New South Wales mid-north coast,
life is blooming in an historic cemetery.
Tucked among bushland, the graveyard, more than 150 years old,
is home to a critically endangered ground orchid,
the pale yellow double tail.
It was first discovered at the site in the mid-1990s
and since then, the Midcoast Council has carefully managed the area
to ensure the orchid species is protected.
There's only three or four sites where we know this species occurs,
so it's really limited, extremely restricted in its range.
I'm here at the graveyard site
with the council's senior ecologist, Matt Bell,
who regularly monitors the orchids.
The orchid does occur in areas that are mown,
if they're mown at the right time of the year,
when the species isn't flowering.
So it really relies on areas that have a native grassy ground cover.
So it only appears when it's flowering,
so you can only detect it in September or October
when the flower spikes emerge.
The flower spikes are very small.
They're only about 20 centimetres high,
but they've got a showy yellow flower on them,
a beautiful, delicate, complex flower.
But yeah, it's incredibly difficult to find
because it's only obvious when it's flowering
and it flowers for such a short period of time.
So what sort of things do you do to preserve it?
So it's essentially protect the flower spikes when they emerge.
So it's to safeguard them from trampling or mowing or disturbance.
We also look after the habitat.
So we treat weeds.
And what happens if there is a burial happening
at that certain time when it's flowering?
Yeah, so it's just the spikes are identified.
They're flagged so that the operation can take place respectfully
and appropriately, but the orchids are protected
from any trampling or inadvertent harm.
And so we have a long history of where the orchid spikes do occur,
and they do occur in and amongst some of the gravestones.
So it is a bit of a, there's a balance there.
It's a very difficult tightrope that we have to walk
in order to allow people to utilise the cemetery for its purpose,
but also to preserve the orchids at the site.
It's one of many places across Australia
where historic cemeteries are providing relatively undisturbed habitat
for rare and endangered plants and animals.
In a rural area of Canberra, the 1883 Hall Cemetery
also provides critical habitat for an endangered orchid.
It's the only ACT site where the Tarango Leak Orchid is found.
Matt Bell says cemeteries are far more than just a place
of gravestones and burials.
Well, cemeteries, they're set out so long ago.
These cemeteries could be 150 years old.
They were set aside for the purposes of a cemetery,
but they also preserve nature.
And the nature has been, it hasn't been harmed
in being a part of the cemetery.
So the native ground cover, the grassy layers are all intact,
which means that orchids and a variety of species
that have been impacted in other landscapes
for development and other reasons,
they're preserved in cemeteries.
So we come to cemeteries to connect to our families
and to our lineages and to our society,
but we can also come to cemeteries
and connect with lineages of nature and biodiversity,
which is really special.
Matt Bell says sightings of the rare ground orchid
on the mid-north coast have been few and far between this spring,
but overall its numbers seem to be holding steady.
It's erratically flowering, definitely.
And that presents challenges for us to understand the population
because it's naturally erratic.
If there's a declining trend in the number of flowering individuals,
it's hard to detect when there's variability,
and that variability might be a result of rainfall patterns
or other seasonal factors.
We're still working out a lot of knowledge
about this cryptic and very rare plant.
That story from Emma Siossian,
who visited a graveyard in the Wingham area
on the New South Wales mid-north coast,
which is home to a critically endangered ground orchid.
You can read more on that story and see photos of the orchid.
You'll find it by searching Cemetery Orchid
on the ABC homepage at abc.net.au.
I'm David Claughton with you for A Big Country.
Still to come, we're meeting a sixth-generation farmer
who's adding value to his homegrown crops,
using them in his on-farm distillery
to make some unusual spirits like red wheat vodka.
And we're visiting a tiny border town
between Queensland and New South Wales
where a group of local women have stepped up
to help their community after a series of devastating blows.
After drought, COVID closures and then fire,
it was more than just bricks and mortar
that needed rebuilding in Mungandai,
as landline's Courtney Wilson discovered.
Mungandai is like many small country towns.
But there is a big point of difference here.
As well as being the only town in Australia
situated on both sides of a state border,
there is a special spirit here that makes Mungandai stand out.
And at the centre of it is a little green coffee shop called Flock.
For Mungandai, Flock came about just when it was needed most.
A few years ago, Mungandai suffered a series of setbacks
in relatively quick succession
that had long-time locals like Anna Harrison
really worried about the town's future.
People were having to let go of staff and families were leaving
and that's really hard because we just know in small communities
you just can't get that retention back
and it's hard to build a community back after that.
After three long years of drought
came the COVID pandemic and border closures,
which quite literally split this town in two.
In 2019, the coffee shop closed.
And then in 2020, a devastating fire
wiped out several other shops in the main street,
including the local supermarket.
And that's our livelihood in Mungandai gone.
Very sad to see.
It proved too much for some
and there were people and families who packed up and left.
In a small community like this, that can be devastating.
You know, it's one less person on the canteen roster.
It's a family short swim club.
Yeah, it impacts everyone.
And I think the menu in the end was perfect for that.
We pretty much now...
For Anna Harrison,
the bad luck that had befallen Mungandai was really concerning.
She didn't want to see the town falter
and she wasn't alone with those worries.
She didn't want to see the town falter.
So Anna rallied the troops.
Five women, all from Mungandai or near enough,
came together to find a way to bring a bit of spark
back to the main drag.
We live here ourselves.
We want a great town.
We want a town to be proud of.
And that doesn't happen by everyone sitting on their bottoms.
Like, you've got to get in and do the hard work.
They decided their particular flavour of hard work
would come in the form of a little coffee shop
with a big goal,
to help bring Mungandai back from the brink.
I think there's lots of opportunities in a town like Mungandai.
Despite each having busy lives,
with 13 children between them,
as well as farms and other jobs,
the women were fuelled by a shared desire
to give something back to their community.
The five women played to their individual strengths,
whether that was designing the menu,
doing the logistical legwork,
managing supplies or dealing with staffing.
In a border town 750 kilometres south-east of Brisbane
with no local grocery shop,
none of that was easy.
But boy, was it appreciated.
Everyone comes here in the mornings,
the ambassadors, the local police,
everyone comes here sort of for a catch-up in the morning.
It's great.
It wasn't just the customers that benefited either.
The ladies behind Flock were also finding unexpected fulfilment.
Annette Hegney explains.
Filled my cup in so many ways.
Being able to see the community
and have somewhere to call in for a cuppa
that wasn't a pub.
There are limited sporting facilities available
for anyone who isn't in primary school.
So it was great to have a place that they could come to
and enjoy the community
and just make the most of being in town.
Pitching in when times are tough
is something people in the bush are known for.
And these five women are all quick to point out
they're certainly not unique.
Late last year, the time came for the original Flock 5
to pass on the baton.
Luckily, another long-time local, Nikki Smith, stepped up.
It's been a bit of a challenge,
a lot more involved than really probably what I thought it was going to be.
Probably 80 to 100 coffees a day.
That's sort of average normally, yeah.
It's going through about 15 kilos of coffee beans a week.
It's not just people from Mungandai
who've embraced the Little Green Cafe either.
Plenty of passers-by are also lured
by the promise of a barista-made coffee
to stop and spend a little extra time in town.
Best coffee ever!
For the creators of Flock,
it's a joy to see another local
at the helm of their pride and joy
and a real sense of accomplishment
for what they helped create.
The five of us are community-minded people
and I think you need that drive to do what we did.
I love the town of Mungandai.
There's some really cool, interesting, fun people
and to get the opportunity to get to know them
in a closer way is really...
I feel really fortunate,
all the people we got to know better through that.
So we spring sow our barley here
but after the recent rain
it's definitely helping it out quite a lot.
Ross Shaw is pretty comfortable talking crops.
That's because he's a sixth-generation farmer
and agronomist from Victoria's Gippsland region.
We're like a traditional sort of mixed farming operation.
We run Aussie white sheep
and we have cattle
and we do hay and cropping as well.
But two years ago,
Mr Shaw decided to go against the grain.
Yeah, returning to the farm
I wanted to be able to value-add
to our sort of commodities
and have a little bit of extra income off farms
so I've opened a distillery.
In Gippsland, most grain just goes for feed.
There's not really a receival for malt
or flower grades or anything like that.
Yeah.
And we're standing here in the distillery, Ross,
so can you describe what we're looking at?
Yeah, so we've got the 1200-litre pot still in the corner
and it's just going through a wash run at the moment,
doing the first stage in making a single malt whiskey, basically.
That'll run for most of the day
and we collect the low wines
and then once we've collected enough
it'll go back again for a second distillation
and make pot distilled single malt.
And so you've been distilling for about two years now?
Yeah, so for about two years
we've been filling barrels with whiskey,
mostly single malt, some wheat whiskey,
a few other little experimental lines.
Yeah, and we've just recently brought out
a couple of clear spirits.
So we did a wheat vodka, red wheat vodka
and a sugar beet spirit.
You heard that right.
A sugar beet spirit and red wheat vodka.
This year, the distillery pumped out
about 400 bottles of both spirits.
So where did the idea for them come from?
I'll let Mr Shaw explain.
Unlike whiskey, the clear spirits,
you can get them to market a lot quicker.
They don't have to sit in a barrel or age or anything.
So we had the red wheat
and we thought let's see how this goes with the vodka.
Did a few trials
and landed on a recipe that we like
and it's quite a nice vodka.
It's got a little bit of like a honeycomb sweetness,
a little bit of graininess
and it comes across quite well.
And then the sugar beet spirit,
the local town of Mafra was founded on sugar beets.
So we thought surely we could make alcohol out of this.
Anything with sugar or a starch sauce,
you can ferment and make alcohol.
So we took that historic crop.
We had to, it was hard to find seed.
We had to import some seed from Europe,
grew the beets
and took quite a while to figure out
how to process these beets and get the sugar out of them.
But we've come,
we've sort of landed on a bit of a process
that works quite well now.
And yeah, making the sugar beet spirit.
Now those recipes will remain a secret.
But when it comes to whiskey,
Mr. Shaw says the distilling process starts
with an old dairy vat.
Yeah, so this is an old 3000 litre stainless steel dairy vat.
We crush our grain into here.
So we'll crush about 600 kilos of barley
if we're doing a single malt.
And then about 2000 litres of water.
And you've got to hold it at about 65 degrees
for an hour basically.
And the natural enzymes inside the barley
turn the starch into sugar
so that you have a fermentable sugar source
for the yeast to eat and make the alcohol.
So after it leaves the vat,
it goes through a separator
that separates the grain and all the husk
away from our sugary water or sugary wash.
And then that goes into the fermenter.
And you pitch the yeast
when it's at the correct temperature
and that'll ferment for sort of a week,
sometimes two weeks.
And once that's finished,
it goes into the still
for the next part of the process.
Right.
And all up, including it staying in the barrels,
takes about two years at least.
Yeah, two years is the minimum ageing time
for whisky in Australia.
But we have, the way that we do it,
we have to grow our grain as well.
So we have that full grain growing season.
So three years basically
before we can have a bottle on the market.
But quite often it will be longer than that
because the whisky might need
three to four years ageing time.
So it's a very long process
and you've got to have a lot of patience.
And Russ is a sixth generation farmer.
What is the rest of your family
and your team thought
of this kind of little side hustle
that you've created?
Probably was a little bit
sort of apprehensive to begin with.
But as we've sort of built it
and gotten into it,
it seems to be starting out quite well
and everyone's involved.
So dad helps me with the malting.
So we malt our own barley here as well.
So he loves doing the malting.
And yeah, everyone sort of is pitching in
a little bit here and there
wherever it's needed.
That was Ross Shaw,
an agronomist, farmer and now distiller.
He was speaking to reporter Faith Tabalugan
from his on-farm distillery
in Victoria's Gippsland region.
To read more on that story
and all the stories on today's program,
head to the ABC website at abc.net.au.
That's the show for today.
I'm David Claughton
and I'll be back next week
with more great stories
from our reporters in regional Australia.
I'll talk to you then.
You've been listening to an ABC podcast.
Discover more great ABC podcasts,
live radio and exclusives
on the ABC Listen app.

episodes.title: Island community doing golf differently and blossoms turn coffee plantation white
episodes.description: For two days a year, coffee tree blossoms turn plantation white; golf in a stunning setting brings community together on a remote island; lavender grower marks 35 years of labour of love; how conservation dogs are helping with turtle conservation.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Hi, I'm David Claughton and this is A Big Country. Thanks for tuning in for a trip around regional Australia. This week it's harvest time for many Aussie farmers and we'll check in on a pretty special harvest with a lavender grower who's picking the fragrant purple flowers by hand. We'll visit a quirky golf course in a spectacular setting on a remote island that's bringing the community together in camaraderie. And we'll learn about some very clever conservation dogs and hear how they're being used to sniff out freshwater turtle nests to help preserve the native species. They work in short bursts with well-earned rests in between. That sniffing that they're doing takes up a lot of energy. It's not just the physical, as in the legwork of it. It takes a lot of brain power for them to do it as well. They're really focused and on the job. So, yeah, and us handlers probably need a bit of a break as well. Tiring work for dogs and their handlers. We'll hear more about that conservation project coming up. Forget the selfies with pretty purple jacarandas or brilliant yellow sunflowers. White coffee tree blossoms are arguably even more spectacular. But to capture the site, you've got to get in quick as they only last for two days. Reporter Kim Honan was lucky to drop into a coffee plantation at Newry Bar near Barham Bay on the New South Wales north coast, just in time to see the blossom. She spoke to grower Rebecca Senfeldt. It is a beautiful and very special two days. The blossoms are on. You've got to come visit. And why does it only happen like one or two days of the year? The blossoms come in spring after a significant dry spell, which we've had eight weeks or so. And then the rains come, which they did last week. And on the 10th day, the flowers come out. So it has pretty much been on the 9th or 10th day today. And the blossoms on the coffee trees do only last two days. Then they drop. And then that tiny little bud of the next fruit starts to grow for the next 11 months into. It's got to last all the way till next October. The blossoms are white, but can you give a better description of what they look like and maybe what they smell like? Yes, Kim, their coffee blossom is really like a little star jasmine or orange or citrus blossom. And they smell extraordinarily sweet like a jasmine. That's the best description, citrus or jasmine blossom. And as I say, only two days. So it's very special. So you can just go right up to a tree. In fact, we've had people drive by a couple of years ago and have their windows down and come in on the day that the blossoms are out because they could smell the blossom in the air. It is a beautiful, sweet fragrance. So I hope those who visit will come and smell the blossom at least. And the bees are absolutely loving the blossoms. They're everywhere. Yep, they're going crazy. Often what we do is hear the bees first, the hum. They will be out in force. I mean, they're not interested in us, so I'm not worried about being stung. They're just focused in on getting that nectar out of the middle of that gorgeous little blossom. The bees love it. It's a very bee-friendly farm or bee-friendly industry. So I love that for the Australian coffee industry. So a very limited time to come and see the blossoms on the coffee trees. Do you get a lot of people here at the plantation wanting to take selfies with the coffee trees? I think they should. I think it's just marvellous. It is extraordinary. We think this has been the 38th lot of flowering. No, I exaggerate. The trees are 38 years old, so we probably had 34 years of coffee blossoms. And we think this is the best in at least six years. Remember, 2019 was so dry. It was really a drought season for the northern rivers or the north coast of New South Wales, and that's when we had a serious lot of flowers after that dry, and that's what we've got again after only eight weeks. So this amount of blossoming, do you reckon it's going to be a bumper crop next year? Oh, we deserve it to be. We really would hope so. I mean, every flower won't turn into a little fruit. We will allow some to drop and accept that, but it's a really good start. You've got to start with the blossom before you get the fruit. So, yes, it makes sense that we should see a good crop come through next year. Let's hope we can keep the crop on and get a super harvest in 2026. Well, I was hoping to get here for harvest. Turn up, the harvest is just done. Blossoms are out. How was harvest? Harvest was smaller than we wanted. A little bit of sad face here. With that, eight weeks of the dry, it was longer than we thought, and John really likes to let the trees relax with a bit of rain before we harvest. We do use our harvesting machine. If you're handpicking, you could handpick every day for about three months. Well, we're not going to do that. We really can't make money as a professional farm to do that handpicking for the size of our, you know, sort of 40 acres, 16 hectares or so of coffee trees. So, we just had to wait for the rain to come. But meanwhile, you know, some fruits dropping on the ground and then you get a bit of a storm through and more fruit drops on the ground.
