He says this place is about more than golf.
A lot of camaraderie.
And it's one of the strongest things I've seen in this community, actually pull the community together,
has been this golf club.
In a way, I've seen it get a lot of people out of the houses in the community.
Well, it's actually got them out of the house and out walking on country.
And for John, he's pretty pleased when he sees people enjoying his course.
And he gets a lot of joy from being out here too.
Especially the day after I've mowed.
Because there's a certain smell out here then when you've got fresh cut grass.
And especially you come out in the morning and the sun's shining and all the mountains are on.
You know, it's beautiful.
You can do it!
Oh, not all!
That's Dory from Louise Moylan on Truana.
And there's a great video on that golf course.
Search ABC Cape Barron Island and you'll find it.
I'm David Claughton with you for A Big Country.
Still to come, we're meeting a former nurse who stumbled into growing lavender
and now runs a flower farm alongside a thriving agrotourism business.
And we're heading to the Lower Murray River in South Australia's Riverland region.
Where conservation dogs are being deployed to sniff out freshwater turtle nests.
The native freshwater turtle population has declined significantly in recent years.
And it's hoped by detecting nests, baby turtles can be saved from predators.
Conservation dog handler Fiona Jackson told Anita Ward what's involved in training the dogs.
It takes a bit of work.
But what we're doing with our three dogs here is we're getting substrate from the natural environment
and adding some colloquial fluid, some turtle fluid to the substrate
and training with the dogs that any time they sniff out that odour, they get rewarded.
So any time they sniff out, they get rewarded with either a little bit of food
or their absolute favourite thing, which is a ball.
Why are they such a good tool in the detection process?
Dogs in general as a methodology, because of their sense of smell, it's just so incredible.
People say it's, researchers say it's anywhere between 10,000 and 100,000 times better than our sense of smell.
So anything that we're struggling to find in the natural environment, like turtle nests,
you can deploy a dog.
That technology of their sense of smell can be a real aid in finding those nests
or anything that's really difficult for us as humans, either as spotters or other methodologies that struggles.
How effective are they in finding the nests?
I know it's a relatively new process.
Yeah, so we are still training.
We've just started this week.
Actually, in fact, last week we just introduced the dogs to the odour.
So the training wheels are very much still on for our three.
But that being said, there's other groups around Australia and across the world who have done this successfully.
So it can be done.
People up in New South Wales, over in Western Australia, and even in Victoria, actually,
who have all successfully worked with conservation detection dogs to find turtle nests.
So we're confident that once our lot are trained up, they'll be able to do the same and help out here.
How long is that training process?
In terms of scent imprinting the dog on the odour, it takes a couple of weeks.
Then you've got to get the dog out, which is what we're doing this week,
is get the dog out in the natural environment, get them used to this environment.
And it then becomes very much a process of calibrating the dog across all the different odour possibilities
and complexities that there are in the natural environment.
So it's hard to say, but in terms of if you have a brand new dog, if you have a dog from PUP,
it can take anywhere to 12 months to 18 months to get a dog up and running.
But thankfully, the dogs that we've put on this project are already experienced.
So they have all their safety and welfare instructions in place.
So they're very safe in the natural environment, which is super important to us.
So we're hoping after a month or two of training on this odour specifically,
that they'll be ready and really calibrated to the odour to help and do searches in the natural environment here.
And tell us about the dogs involved.
Who are they and how successful have they been so far in getting that imprint?
So the dogs, we've got three dogs on this project.
Two very experienced dogs who are called Oakley and Rex,
who are actually out with us in South Australia at the minute
because they're also on the Murray Darling Carpet Python project,
which is what we've been doing this morning.
And they're super experienced dogs and have quite a few different threatened species odours that they're already on.
And they are scent imprinting now to three different turtle species.
So the broadshell, the eastern longneck and the Murray shortneck.
And then we've got a slightly younger dog, Aaron, who's three years old.
This is his first threatened species project, but he's still very experienced
and helps us out in our renewable energy projects.
And he is also just absolutely nailing his scent imprinting.
So we're really excited to take these trading odours that we have
and start putting them out here where we are at the minute down by the lake
and having him and the other two go out and start searching around here.
It's amazing work that you're doing and the dogs are doing.
Once they're fully trained for the turtles,
what does a day of turtle detection or nest sniffing out look like for them?
Yeah, there's definitely, they can go.
What we tend to do is we get up at very early.
We were actually up at 3.30 this morning to get up, to drive, to sight,
to be ready at first light and to do our Murray-Darn carpet python searches.
And it will be the same for turtles.
It will be up as soon as possible.
And they can usually go, dogs can tend to work.
It really depends on the terrain and the temperature.
But two to three hours is a good time.
And then they can have a nice rest and maybe do the same again
in the afternoon or evening.
And they can probably do that for two, three days.
And then they'll require a little rest and then do it again.
Because it's a lot of work.
That sniffing that they're doing takes up a lot of energy.
It's not just the physical, as in the legwork of it.
It takes a lot of brainpower for them to do it as well.
They're really focused on the job.
So yeah, us handlers probably need a bit of a break after three days as well.
I can imagine.
Once they're ready to go on this turtle project,
how confident are you they can help out with the conservation efforts
here in the river and along the Murray?
I am probably quietly confident.
Only because the folk that have done this already in Australia,
there's people that have done this and proven it.
It's not like we're doing a proof of concept here.
So those detection dog handlers that have done this already
and we're good friends with them have given us the confidence as well.
And they've really helped us in knowing exactly how to train the dogs,
how to get the best outcome.
So yeah, let's say quietly confident.
It's a pristine spring morning when I visit Anne-Marie Manders,
a lavender grower from Wandin in Victoria's Yarra Valley.
We're going for a stroll through her rows of purple lavender plants.
The two main lavenders that we do grow on a commercial basis is an intermediate lavender,
which has a gorgeous camphoraceous fragrance and is wonderful for keeping
moths and silverfish out of your wardrobe.
And it flowers and is ready for picking at the end of December into January.
The other lavender that we grow is an angustifolia lavender.
And that is a lavender that you can use in food products, drinks, teas, ice cream, scones,
biscuits, cakes, herb breads, all those sorts of things.
Now with the edible lavender, it is ready for picking at the end of November.
So there is a month between when we pick the edible lavender and when we pick the non-edible
lavender.
Now that was more a matter of good luck rather than good management in my case, because I
knew nothing about what I was doing.
That's because Anne-Marie never dreamed of becoming a farmer.
In fact, she had a whole other career as an operating theatre nurse before she and her
late husband decided to buy an old cherry orchard.
35 years later, the property now stands as a thriving lavender farm, attracting flower
lovers from across Australia and beyond.
And here's what Anne-Marie tells them about the harvest process.
Now when we pick the lavender, it's all picked by hand with a sickle, a small sickle, which
is what the strawberry growers use.
And it's a curved knife with a very sharp serrated edge.
We start very early in the morning at the latest at 6am.
If it's going to be a really, really hot day, we'll start at 5.30.
And that's when the lavender has got its strongest fragrance.
Having picked it in the bunches, the bunches are picked by hand, a rubber band is put on the
bunch. We then stack all those bunches into big picking bins and then we transport those
bins up into the drying shed where they are hung upside down to dry.
And in amongst all that lavender, you've got a bit of stick and a bit of leaf and there's
also some flower dust.
Now you don't want that in your lavender if you're going to be putting it into food or
if you're going to be, if it's craft work, you're going to be putting it into little
sachets or sleep pillows.
So we sift it and we have a series of three sieves and we pour the lavender through and
it sits in a big bin, like a rubbish bin and we shake it around.
It's all done by hand and people say, oh, this could be much, you could automate this
and have it on a shaker table.
But it doesn't, it's not hands on and I'm doing it more like the cottage industry, wanting
people to see how it was done in the olden days.
And I'm a bit olden day sort of in my approach and it gives people a wow factor and then
they can put their hands into that stripped lavender, rub it between their hands and smell
it.
And it is gorgeous.
And so now, Emery, you've got about 12,000 plants on the farm?
Yes.
And you started with how many?
Did you expect the farm to get so big?
No, I had no idea.
I didn't know anything about running a business.
I didn't have a tractor.
I had no knowledge.
And as far as making product, I didn't have a clue.
And then I had to learn about how to price it.
How was I going to talk to people?
Yeah, it started off absolutely at the bottom of the ladder.
And so coming back to harvesting and processing the lavender, so the fragrance and the oils,
they're actually contained in the flowers themselves?
Yes.
The actual oil is in the base of every little tiny weenie little flower head.
So if you look at the formation of a flower head, it's got a whole lot of little heads
within that big head.
And every one of those little heads has got a microscopic sack at the bottom.
And that's where the oil is.
Anne-Marie says most of her customers don't know much about lavender, but she's set on changing
that.
Some of them want to buy some plants to put in the houses in an indoor plant.
That's a definite no-no.
So that's where I actually teach them that lavender is an outdoor plant.
Secondly, it needs full sun, must have full sun.
Thirdly, you do not water it.
So you treat it almost with neglect.
However, you do need to cut it back once a year and cut off those flower stems and trim
it down into a neat, tidy bush.
And then it goes into a dormancy.
Unfortunately, lavender will not grow in the tropics.
It's too humid.
And people that come from Singapore or Asia, these countries, and want to grow lavender,
I say, no, if you want to grow lavender, sell up and come and live in Victoria.
Anne-Marie Manders.
She's a lavender grower in Victoria's Yarra Valley, where she spoke to reporter Faith Tabaluyan.
And you can read more about that story.
You'll find a feature article on the ABC website at abc.net.au.
Just search for ABC Lavender.
That's the show for today.
I'm David Claughton.
And I'll catch up with you again next week with more great stories from regional Australia.
I'll chat to you then.
You've been listening to an ABC podcast.
You can discover more ABC podcasts, live radio and exclusives on the ABC Listener.

episodes.title: Rare shrub thriving and moving fresh milk in kegs
episodes.description: Introduced bumble bees are thriving in Tasmania, researchers are tracking them to find out why; kegs replace plastic bottles to get fresh milk from farm to cup; endangered shrub with a yellow flower showing signs of resurgence; finding the next…
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. You're listening to A Big Country. I'm David Claughton. And it's lovely to have your company as we join our reporters exploring regional Australia. This week we're learning about a study of bumblebees on Tasmanian farms where the pollinators are being fitted with tiny backpacks holding radio transmitters to track their movements. We'll hear about a new way of getting fresh milk from the farm to the cafe or shop without the use of plastic bottles. And we'll meet researchers who are passionate about finding the next variety of one of Australia's favourite summer fruits. At the end of the day I love passion fruit. It's my favourite thing to work with. It tastes good and I eat far too much of it so I feel sick sometimes. I'll be out in the field, every fruit that I say I have to try. It's all good. I love it. A passion for passion fruit. We'll hear why new varieties of the fruit are desperately needed. That's coming up. First today we're heading to the New South Wales Northern Tablelands where a small property is believed to be the only place in the world where a unique and critically endangered yellow shrub grows. Reporter Bridget Murphy ventured into the bush to learn more about the rare plant. After about an hour of walking, ducking and manoeuvring through bushland on Stephen Walkden Brown's property Lomalangi, a bright yellow cluster appears in the distance. We've spotted the critically endangered Astrolasia ripestris, specifically this flower's subspecies, recurva. Here, near Armadale in the state's northern Tablelands, is the only place in the world where this plant grows. Stephen and his wife Yvonne bought the 200 hectare property in 2017. Unbeknownst to them, alongside its almost untouched bushland, it housed the critically endangered species. Ben Vincent is a senior regional conservation officer with the Biodiversity Conservation Trust. He says very little is known about the shrub. There's really little known about its life history, so there's plenty still to learn. It's critically endangered, that's its listing in New South Wales, and to get that listing, you have to be a plant with a very, very restricted geographic location, of which this one has. It's probably about 600 metres in length along a creek line and restricted to the parallel mountains there. And it also has to have very few mature individuals. Although it's a small and relatively simple-looking plant from afar, Mr Vincent says for those with a trained eye, it's striking. The heart-shaped green leaves full of these little star-shaped hairs, which make it kind of a fluffy, light green appearance. And then there's, you know, beautiful, really obvious yellow flower. They really do stand out. Stephen agrees. He says he is proud to consider himself a custodian to the plant. I think it does help that they are quite an attractive plant, a little bit bushy in the wild, but they have a very bright yellow, very distinctive and nice flower. There's a number of conservation efforts in hand. And yes, the fact that it's a lovely plant and where it grows is also nice along the creek banks in amongst some leptospermum over cover in amongst grass and things. So yeah, just walking through it and seeing these bright splashes of yellow when it's flowering. But even the non-flowering plant, it's got a sort of a furry, grey-green leaf that maybe it's an acquired taste, but knowing it's so rare, we think they look quite nice as well. Mr Vincent says despite its critical situation, there could be a prosperous future for the plant with a survey this year showing good signs. We were able to get out and resurvey the existing population and find the mature adults are about the same. So that's great. It means they're persisting well. But the exciting news was to see, I think we counted about over 600. So that's a great outcome. And these guys are, you know, they're probably 20 or 30 centimetres tall. So the point there is that they've been in the landscape now for probably four or five years and persisting well. So it's a good news story for this critically endangered species. It was believed, like so many other Australian natives, fire was needed to break sea dormancy. But it appears in this case, drought was the catalyst. It was thought prior to this resurvey that this plant species, like many astrolasian, needed fire in the landscape to break sea dormancy. And that may be the case. But as it turns out, severe drought like that, which we experienced in 2018 and into the end of 19, appears to also break dormancy. So, you know, the Australian floor is adapted to boom and bust drought situations like we had. Mr Vincent says private landholders like Mr Walkden Brown play a pivotal role in biodiversity and conservation. Private landholders are becoming more aware of what the Biodiversity Conservation Trust does in New South Wales, which is partner with private landholders to achieve conservation outcomes on their property. And yeah, look, I think it is becoming more popular. As part of his work with the state's Biodiversity Conservation Trust, Stephen receives funding to do his part caring for the plants. We do notice that some of them are being nibbled and we do have deer up on this block and there's feral goats as well. And so we're under our contract with BCT. We are obliged to try and control those species, which pose some kind of threat. The population's fairly healthy. We keep a watching brief on it and we're just so pleased that there are so many little seedlings. Because we've had, what, this is probably the fourth, at least the fourth, maybe going on for the fifth year of above average rainfall or pretty good season. So after the 2019 drought, it was terrible up here. But the plant seems to have responded to that run of good seasons. Just like Stephen and Yvonne inherited the beautiful endangered species, they also hope to pass it on, ensuring the plant is cared for in the future. We've got one of our children lives in Armidale and has a number of kids. So, you know, we would like this to pass on through the family after we've gone. That'll be their decision. But we love it. We come up here often. The kids and grandkids come up as well. And it's a very favourite spot. Like many cafes, this busy outlet in the coastal Tasmanian town of Penguin powers through milk on a daily basis. The milk is delivered weekly, in bulk, ready to supply caffeine-starved customers with their daily dose. But unlike other cafes, this milk comes in a keg and it's pulled out of a tap. This pub-like set-up is a deliberate choice. So it's something we've been looking at for a couple of years now. Cafe co-owner Rob Arvia speaking here. He had some misgivings about the system. The main hurdle had been cost at the start. So when we first went to market looking, when we first acquired the shop, the cost was around $12,000 to install a tap, which for a small business was completely unattainable. But fast forward to, I'm trying to think when this went in now, but it's been for longer than a year. The way he describes it is a bit like a vending machine. The cafe is responsible for the daily cleaning and refilling, but the supplier owns the infrastructure and is in charge of all the maintenance and milk deliveries. So that made it accessible for us, which was great. It's more expensive than mass-produced plastic bottles from a large dairy factory, and that's hard to pass on to a consumer. But cafe manager Grace Primrose reckons the benefits outweigh the costs. So we're looking at a fridge, which is hooked up with our kegs inside, and then we've got a milk tap where people can come and bring in their litre refills and refill every day fresh. And you also use this in the coffees? Yeah, definitely. So we fill up separate kegs that are two litres each and go and put them in the coffees, and it just makes the creamiest coffee. What's it like to use, I don't know if you've used a system where you've got milk bottles instead. What's the comparison? It's just fresher, and since we're topping it up every couple of minutes when we go through the litres, you're just getting fresher milk in your coffee. People definitely notice the milk and then come in and want to get the refills, they want to hear the story, they want to hear who's behind it. People really value knowing where the milk comes from. To Grace's point about the story, knowing that it comes from a single farm, people are willing to pay for that privilege. Something we're really proud about is the waste. So over a year, it's about 8,000 plastic bottles that don't come through our store anymore, which is incredible. I've worked in cafes my whole life that have the plastic bottles, and it's quite frustrating. You have to try and get them down small enough to go in the bin, and then you are using so much waste. So it's nice that we can return the kegs washed to him, and then he can refill them for us. And the farmer that does that refilling? Well, about 100 kilometres down the road, Gennaro Velazquez makes boutique Venezuelan-style cheese on what he reckons is one of the smallest dairy farms in Tasmania. We milk our own cows, so we milk 100 cows, and at the moment we produce more milk than what we put towards cheese. The solution? A couple of years ago, he started selling off his fresh milk both directly to customers and to a large nearby milk factory. And so by having milk, like in cakes or pre-filled bottles and plastic bottles, and then we also have skin milk and cream and things like that, it just brings security to our business. So it allows us to value up. Dairy farmers generally sell their milk to these giant, often global, processors, meaning they have little to no say over what price they get. And while Gennaro still sells some milk to a processor, he's been able to cut out the middleman for the rest, processing it on farm, choosing his own prices, and directly receiving profits from sales. Any milk that we are able to process through the factory and sell it as a value-added product, it is milk that we are not relying on what the commodity price or the industry in general wants to say our milk is worth. In a small business scenario like us, like milking 100k hours, to make it viable and to make it profitable and to make it sustainable in the long run, we have to look at ways of, you know, value-adding and doing all the things that are pretty much thinking out of the box. Each week, Gennaro's farm sends out milk to about 20 customers, including popular cafes. Some of it's in glass bottles, some's in plastic bottles, and since introducing it last year, about half is in these reusable milk kegs. It's sort of like a contribution to, you know, looking after the environment, reducing that use of single-use plastic. We started using this system back in April 2024. Not everyone loves them, but his share of customers is increasing. I guess for some people and for some operations, it's easier just to stick to plastic. You just get the plastic, fill up the bottles, they go and you don't have to know about them. As I said, people that care about the environment, that don't want to be using plastic bottles and don't want to be generating more rubbish than what we need to, you know, so we have a number of cafes that are now moving towards that because same thing, like you have the environmental contribution, but you also make it a lot easier for them. Once they're up, like set up and ready to go, it makes it a lot easier for them. And for customers like Rob Arvia at the cafe, there's something charming about having a local farmer come and drop their milk right at the door. Yeah, it's incredible. And obviously we are farmers first and foremost. So to have those connections and also for those people to be directly interacting with the team here, it's just invaluable. So yeah, wouldn't have it any other way. Farmer and cafe owner, Rob Arvia, ending that report from Meg Ferguson. Before that, Brigitte Murphy took us into the bush in the New South Wales Northern Tablelands, where a rare plant is thriving. And you can see more on that story, including pictures of the native shrub with a pretty yellow flower on the ABC homepage at abc.net.au. I'm David Claughton with you for A Big Country. Still to come, the researchers tracking bumblebees in Tasmania with the help of some high-tech equipment. And if you love passion fruit on top of your summer pav, you'll be pleased to know work is underway to develop new varieties to keep the fruit growing in Australia. Jennifer Nichols has this story from the Passion Fruit Research Patch on Queensland's Sunshine Coast. It's a beautiful flower that we're looking at. Yeah. You can see the blue colour here and it is beautiful. And yeah, we use this one. One of the reasons is if we can identify this is tolerant to different stresses like high temperature. Yeah. Hello. I'm Mubashir Alam. So you can call me Mo. I'm leading National Passion Fruit Breeding Program. You're doing some very important work because the plants that growers have been using, there's some problems with them. Yes. For the varieties, yield decline is happening. The size of the fruits are getting reduced. Growers are not making much profit. We want to release new varieties that are profitable for the industry, that can produce optimum fruit size, that have good flavour. What's involved in breeding passion fruit? The first thing is really important. We should have good germplasm. So that's the collection of these different varieties that have different good traits. We call it germplasm and you can call it genetic resource. Unfortunately, we didn't have when we started the breeding program, but our team did a fantastic job and we collected a lot of germplasm within Australia and from abroad as well. So that's the way we expanded our genetic resources and that also helped us to develop new varieties quickly. And then we have selected nearly 20 new accessions for the industry at this moment. We'll see how do they grow in growers plot in next year. So the accessions are the different genetic results of different seeds? Yes, results of different seeds. Even if we have collected from the same plant, these seeds are different. And so that one we have selected is the next session. So when did this project start? Started in April 2023, but we believe we made a good progress because at Genetic Resources we expanded over the last two years and we selected some new promising accessions for the industry. Usually within one year, we select one plant only. So then from one plant, we are multiplying. We have multi-location trials. So that gives us more opportunity to multiply them to apply in commercial orchard. So in the plant world, this is pretty speedy. It is much better than macadamia. I have been working with macadamia as well. It took 24 years to release a variety. But here, hopefully within three years, we'll be able to select a good one and within five years, we'll be able to give it to the growers. So it's very fast. Dr Mo Alam from the University of Queensland. Patrick Mason is another researcher from the University of Queensland. You've been involved in this work too? Yes. I actually moved from more of a fundamental genetics background to Mo's lab, which is very much involved in breeding, macadamia, and more recently, passion fruit. So I've actually only been here for a year and a half. But at the end of the day, I love passion fruit. It's my favourite thing to work with. It tastes good and I eat far too much of it. So I feel sick sometimes. I'll be out in the field. Every fruit that I say I have to try, it's all good. I love it. Well, I guess the passion for passion fruit is a good thing to have when you're researching them. Absolutely. Yeah, I just hope that trying all the fruits that I've been doing, hopefully it ends up with a good result for the farmers and good quality fruit for the consumer. It's challenging to be a farmer with all of the impacts of extreme weather, rising costs of production. How crucial is this work to passion fruit still being grown in Australia? Oh, it's very crucial. The industry is very much over-reliant on a small set of varieties. And so there has been a little bit of work by some other breeders who are farmers, but they've done a bit of breeding work like Keith Paxton, for example. He's produced a couple of good varieties, but at a fundamental level, we can't be reliant on just a couple of varieties for the entire industry because there's a lot of different areas. They've all got different disease pressures and different climactic zones. And so you need to have, I'd say a large number of recessions that farmers can pull from so they can really cater production to their farm and use varieties that work best in their farm. So it's very crucial. And moving forward, they're going to need a constant stream of varieties available. So one of the other issues that we have in the passion fruit industry is that it's a clone. So when you've got your good variety, you're basically taking cuttings from that and you're producing something that is exactly the same, it's genetically similar. But over time, kind of like humans develop cancer and other things, you get little mutations in your genome. Sort of a similar thing happens with plants as well, they'll develop these mutations and over time, that'll affect productivity. So if you continue to do lots and lots of cloning, cloning, cloning, you'll produce these somaclonal mutations and that affects production. And that's actually happened two of the most popular varieties which have been fantastic back in the 90s, Sweetheart and Misty Gem. Everyone was using them. Everybody loved them. Nowadays, they're basically unusable. The fruit size is too small and the productivity is poor as well. So we've had to move away from those. And so that just shows how important it is to have new varieties constantly coming through. To keep that productivity up. And again, that will ensure that the farmer's bottom line will be maintained. We're lucky to have two varieties at the moment that are in their advanced stages. And with a congregation of passion fruit farmers, we've put out calls for them to trial these varieties on their property. And so once we see interest and they're happy with these particular varieties, if that is the case, then we can go through the process of getting it protected with plant beater's rights. And then we can release it to the broader passion fruit industry and they can start growing. And so we're hoping to do that by the end of 2027. usually they use the leaves. Oh, here she is. Here is the receiver. That is the radio transmitter. The backpack is... It's looking great. It's secured. It hasn't moved at all. It hasn't moved at all. That's good. So, yeah, we need to wait her to completely wake up and eventually she will go back to foraging so that she can restock energy. Usually what we need to see is that queens have pollen on their bodies. And when they start looking for pollen, they are looking for lipids and proteins, which means that they are... they already have a nest. And they will eventually get new workers and the colony will grow during the summer. Well, my name is Eduardo Calderon and I am working with my colleague Maria Escobedo. I am a PhD student and Maria is a master's student. We are studying at Western Sydney University and we are doing our research on bumblebee ecology in Tasmania, which is an introduced species here in the island. They were introduced here in 1992. It is estimated that they were only introduced to queens and it was those two queens which actually populated the whole island, which is impressive. They are really successful here. We are trying to see what are the impacts of these new species, the good ones and also the bad ones maybe, to see how they are doing in different ecosystems and different habitats. Basically, we are focusing on the nesting side of these beasts to see how successful they are, how many workers are born in different nesting sites. How productive they are. Yeah, exactly. Our project is funded by Heart Innovation and we are also collaborating with the Tasmanian government and University of Tasmania to cover different factors and different elements of this species. So we are on a pepperberry farm today at Underwood. Yeah, exactly. We are working on pepperberry farms and also in some raspberry farms. We are trying to see how they interact not only with introduced species but also with native species such as mountain pepperberry. Have a bit of quiet, please, everyone. Just got one hour left of the Lions raffles. Three tickets, $5, 10 prizes to 90.
Rowan can head over to the corner at the Lions table at the bar. Your tickets, that'd be great.
Thank you. Join at 7 o'clock. 10 prizes.
It's pretty busy. It's quite a busy night. I think it's only about quarter to seven. So
this is probably as busy as I've seen it in about 30 years, I reckon.
Meet Rowan Alcock. He and his wife Karen have bought the Bimboka pub. It's the only pub in the
town of about 600 people, with the next closest one in Bega 35 kilometres away. Locals
feared their pub wouldn't reopen after spending six months on the market without a buyer,
until Karen and Rowan stepped up to the plate. Well, generally, Karen runs down to the pub and
tries to get the hotel going, managing the hotel. And I'll kick start my day off here and get a few
jobs done and then try and go outside and work, which hasn't been much outside work lately because
of the hotel. As well as being publicans, Karen and Rowan run a 526 hectare cattle farm. It's
certainly been a juggle. We do as much as we can here, do a fair bit here and head torches.
There's a lot of catching up to do. Over the last three months. Yeah.
And we've spent very little time here on the property. Yeah. Really. Absolute essential things only.
How's it going? Need a hand? Their daughters decided to come home to help.
27 year old agronomist Tash Alcock and her fiance Sam are lending a hand. We always joked about it.
Mum always came up with the crazy idea that we'd buy a cafe or something or other in town. We all had the
skids on. We're like, no, we're not doing that. We're not doing that. It's a terrible idea.
But when it all came down to it, we're like, yeah, no, we, I think we really should do this.
Their other daughter, 29 year old Jacinta, flew home from Darwin to help with opening night.
I thought they were like joking to start with, but they had discussed it and we talked about it back
and forth. And then, yeah, one day they're just like, yeah, we're going to buy the pub. And I was like,
okay, right. Looks like we're all in all hands on deck. So yeah.
Why do you think they did decide to go ahead with this?
They know that the pub is such an integral part of the town. We're 40 minutes from Bega,
but it can feel a lot further away than that. And it's a lot of little farms and people living out
of town. So you can very easily get isolated very easily, especially over COVID and during the bushfires,
especially after the bushfires, places like the pub were just integral.
The Yankees Gap bushfire swept through the region in 2018, burning along the Alcox boundary,
and then came Black Summer the next year.
There was about 10 acres left out of 1300 that wasn't burnt. We only lost one horse,
didn't lose any stock. We were lucky in the regards that we didn't lose our houses,
because there's three houses on this property. We didn't lose anything. We lost quite a few sheds,
a lot of machinery, all the irrigation. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
There's about $1.3 million worth of damage that no insurance for.
Even before the fires, Bamboka's economy was suffering. Many businesses had closed. In the
main street, you've got the pie shop and a post office, and that's about it. Karen and Rowan
hope the pub will bring the town back to life.
The town used to be really booming. It had a lot of shops, had service stations, had a grocery store,
all that sort of thing. But over time…
Two or three cafes at one stage.
Yeah. Over time, things have just gone backwards, and it's all got centralised,
all the shopping back into Bega. Yeah, the little place is sort of struggling. So,
Karen's tried to approach me a couple of times regarding buying a takeaway in town. One of the
shops, taken one over when it was shutting down, and I thought, no way.
I got howled down every time.
And I thought, no bloody way. We're not doing that. Like, that's… You might as well go milking
cows again. Is that… Is that the middle?
Yeah. Yeah, go off a little bit.
That's it?
Yeah.
Back at the pub, the Alcocks are putting out their new signs and welcoming their first patrons.
How are you? Thanks, mate.
Great. Wonderful.
It's got to work.
It will work. It's wonderful.
The pub has stood in town for decades, but the Alcocks decided to renovate and make it a cafe as well.
We're going to go and have a coffee now.
Here you go. You've got your first victims coming in.
Oh, coming in tomorrow.
Oh, it's great. It's great.
It'll work, mate. It'll work.
Local Bambuca residents, like Jenny Anderson, are loving it.
Communities like this have to have somewhere to gather.
You don't need to be a drinker. You might enjoy a good meal. You might enjoy a cup of coffee.
And to be able to have that choice is really important in a community like this.
So just wonderful to have locals by the pub, to have a local farming community come in and rescue us all.
Yeah, really, really great.
Another local, Julie Ringland, agrees.

We're so excited. We need something like this in a small town. We've always had the bakery, which is great. We're so lucky to have them. But to have the pub open again, it's just great. It's just got a beautiful vibe. If you walk into it, it's just, it's home.
Even the town's oldest resident, 91-year-old Madeline Filmer, approves.
Oh yes, I'd love to come and have a cup of tea or something. I'll have a beer as well, you know what I mean. I'm not ashamed to say it.
As challenging as it's going to be, running a pub and a farm at the same time, Karen and Rowan know they've done the right thing.
We probably should have done it 10 years ago when we were a bit younger.
Yeah, I wouldn't recommend doing it now.
But anyway, the aches and pains are, yeah, well, things are improving.
You're fairly urged to get into hospitality and do it bloody 20 years earlier than we do.
Do it earlier than we have, yeah.
This community needs this. Do we need it? Probably not.
But let's give it a crack and see how it goes.
Yeah, that's it.
Yeah. What's a town without a pub?
And so this bit of rootstock, because it got damaged, that rootstock's taken off and grown now.
Alan Edwards could talk about lemons all day long. That's because he grew up on his family's citrus orchard in Victoria's Yarra Valley region.
My dad bought this property. He changed the variety of lemons over. And then so they've been in since about 1950.
And you have a lot of memories of picking, growing up, spending a lot of time in the orchard?
Oh, hours and hours. And days and days and months and months.
Today, Alan runs the farm with the help of his son, Michael. When not working on his PhD research, Michael dabbles in growing quirky crops.
But his latest project involves an unusual flower.
On the side, I grow some things for chefs and distillers.
And in talking to distillers and getting to know them, they were interested in getting citrus blossoms.
Initially, it was grapefruit and now it's more lemons.
So we're running a project this year to see how we can, if we can get what they need.
And also basically to reduce the amount of fruit we have by picking the blossom before it becomes fruit.
So that's the idea.
And so this trial involves one block of lemon trees.
And so just talk me through what your plan is. And it involves renting out that block.
Yeah, exactly. So the distillers will rent that for a year.
They will do the more manual work on this, which is cutting back the trees.
And then we'll apply some fertilizer as a bit of an experiment in certain trees.
And then we can see if that can induce more blossom per tree.
But basically, we want to get the most amount of blossom from that field as possible.
And we've got 300 trees, so I think they'll get what they need.
They've got a year to do it.
So I think it'll be OK.
Michael says it takes a gentle touch to harvest the blossoms.
The actual product is super delicate and, you know, it can be bruised.
You have to pick it fresh because you're picking for aroma.
So it's much like how the fragrance industry would think about growing something.
Yeah, so it's a bit different.
And there's quite a short harvest window as well for these blossoms?
Depending on the variety.
So we have two or three varieties of lemons here.
The main variety we grow is Eureka.
So that will keep just producing blossoms throughout the year.
With some of the other lemon trees that we tested, which was Meyer lemon,
they have a much shorter window, but lots of blossom.
So there's always that as a backup.
But the client really liked the Eureka.
So that's what we'll go for.
Lauren Bonkowski is a co-founder of Marionette,
a Victorian distillery specialising in produce-driven liqueurs.
There was a bit of a gap in the market.
Everyone was making gin and whisky.
And we saw this big hole in the slightly less sexy category,
which was fruit and nuts and these essential cocktail ingredients
that we were using every day.
But Australians weren't making them.
Ms Bonkowski says they work with farmers across regional Victoria.
The most recent product we've made, elderflower.
That one we've really ran around the state trying to find the right blossoms.
It was quite an adventure because it's not a big industry.
So that led us to the streets of Trantham with a forager.
Usually it's a bit simpler.
We've gone out to Mildura.
It's one of our main supplying areas where our oranges and our almonds are grown.
We like to work directly with farmers.
We don't buy it through co-ops so that we can work with the farmers on the season in their schedules.
And we do a lot of work to make sure that we can buy their seconds fruit on farmers' timelines,
which has worked out really, really well for everyone.
Ms Bonkowski says after discovering citrus blossoms, they were hooked.
And they're at the heart of their latest experiment, an elderflower liqueur.

So we went out to the farm and we were lucky enough for them to let us pick a whole lot of different citrus blossoms and decided that the landland blossom is much more gentle and sort of supports the flavour profile of the elderflower putting in the liqueur.
And is this the first time that you're using these blossoms?
Absolutely.
Yeah. Blossoms are much harder to work with than fruit.

In different levels of distillation and maceration, the hardier fruits, so the citrus itself, has the most oil and they can really withstand maceration and really high-proof alcohol to draw out flavour.
Whereas blossoms are the complete opposite end of the spectrum, so you have to be really careful.
For Ellen and Michael, this citrus blossom project hasn't always been straightforward.
I think it's a learning curve for both of us.
In what way?
Well, we have probably little different ways of looking at things, so it's a bit of compromise between the two.
And Michael, what have you had to compromise on since working with your dad?
I do agree.
We do do things a little differently, but I think we understand the logic behind both.
Maybe there's an age thing as well to do with that because I'm willing to experiment more, obviously.
Dad, a little bit less, but it's probably because he has the experience which I really admire and absorb.
And Alan says he's glad to be farming as father and son.
As far as Michael experimenting is concerned, that's exactly what I was like.
When my father was doing this and I was doing it, there was that different way of looking at things.
And so I think it is good to experiment and use a little bit of NEOCE and work it out for yourself what works best.
Yeah, you need to know what fails as well.
Yeah, every experiment has got a failure, but you've got to learn by your failures.
Alan Edwards, a lemon grower from Victoria's Yarra Valley.
He was speaking with Faith Tabuluyan.
Before that, we met the new owners of the Bamboka Pub on the New South Wales far south coast.
You can read more on both those stories.
You'll find articles and pictures on the ABC homepage at abc.net.au.
That's the show for today.
I'm David Claughton.
I'll be back next week with more great stories from the regions.
Check to you then.
You've been listening to an ABC podcast.
Discover more great ABC podcasts, live radio and exclusives on the ABC Listen app.

episodes.title: Shearing record falls and international chefs getting a taste for Australian lamb
episodes.description: Team take out world record in shearing marathon; international chefs learning to love Aussie lamb; promoting flowers that are grown here, over those flown here; farmers transform land with tree-planting over four decades.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. You're listening to A Big Country. I'm David Claughton and it's lovely to have your company as we join reporters exploring regional Australia. This week we're meeting a delegation of international chefs who've gathered in a small town in rural Western Australia. They're visiting the country to learn more about our lamb and how to use it in culinary dishes. It's all part of efforts to get Aussie grown lamb on more plates around the world. We'll meet a couple who've spent more than four decades on the land, not only farming but also transforming the landscape through an extensive tree planting program. And we'll hear about one family's mission to educate consumers about where their flowers come from. With her brother and sister growing flowers on the family farm in Tasmania, when Bec Thomas decided on a career change from her corporate job, she joined the flower industry to promote locally grown blooms. That's coming up. First today to a record-breaking effort. A team of five shearers in southern New South Wales have set a new record for the most Merino lambs shorn over eight hours with five stands. Reporter Emily Doak was in the shed watching the record attempt. It's no ordinary day in the shearing shed at Morvern, south of Wagga Wagga. The five shearers, Lockie Robertson, Benjamin Duncan, Cameron Hicks, Toby Walker and Nick Lehman, are working at a frantic pace, aiming to set a world record. Toby says he's been training for months. It's been about six, seven months of long days of shearing, drive home, smash the gym for an hour and a half, diet, gear preparation. It's been a really long build-up. It's glad to be over, to be honest. People might have seen shearing in a shed during the day. Just how different is it in a world record attempt conditions? As intense as it gets. Today, that's my first experience. It's so mentally straining. I didn't realise how focused I had to be, and that was just all day. It's so dialled in and focused on what we're doing. Good to be shearing with these other blokes alongside you. Great bunch of guys. They were awesome. Everybody pulled through with a mammoth effort today, and it gave me a lot of strength to look around and see the other guys just not backing down an inch all day. It's not just the shearers that need to prepare. We'll grow a James Finlay supplying the Merino lambs, and says making sure there's a nice, even run has been a challenge in the drought conditions. We went through about 5,000, 5,500, and we've drafted that down to 2,650 ready for today for the five boys. And that's because they've got to be a fairly even lot, and they've all got to meet certain criteria in terms of size, weight, wall cut, that sort of thing. Huge logistical challenge. Yeah, it's always a bit stressful when you've got to make sure they average a kilo over everything. That's only about three months old. So when Lockie approached us a few months ago and asked us if we could do the record here, I was a little bit apprehensive with the way the season was going. It was pretty tough fed. We had everything in containment here until sort of July. So yeah, they were well fed. And then, yeah, it started to rain, and we let them out on the grass, and we've had a really good lambing. And we've been pretty fortunate this year. The lambs have actually been really quite even. The World Sheep Shearing Record Society governs attempts like this across Australia, New Zealand, the UK and South Africa. Eight judges are on hand today, and convener Johnny Fraser says this makes sure everyone is on a level playing field. So the lambs had to be one kilo of wool. We had to cut one kilo of wool each. So these did 1.4, which is well over the mark, which is good. So that was a start. And then after that, we're looking mainly out the back. The sheep go down the porthole, and we count out every half an hour. And we have four judges down there, two on each stand. And we are looking at any cuts or any roughness, stitch jobs that they've done and all that. And if there's any more than six sheep that are badly cut, after seventh one, the record will stop. So you've obviously seen a lot of records set, challenged, beaten over the time. How does this one rate here in the Riverina of New South Wales? To be honest, with this merino record, we've never really had a five-stand record before. And these guys aren't your show shearers. These guys are just good old shed shearers that I rate this as probably one of the better ones I've been to. In this high-pressure environment, there's no time for error, and each wriggling sheep can cost valuable seconds. After the first two-hour run, the shearers look exhausted. Smoko, though, is a time to look after the body, as Toby's mum, Sunny Awoko, explains. The ice bath is a rapid reduction of skin temperature, which also reduces the lactic acid build-up, especially in the legs. We've got no fancy plunge pools here. We've got a good old-fashioned bush ice bath. How's it work? Yes, we have an esky out the back. And we did have to shop long and hard because a couple of these boys have got pretty long legs. It's the final run. Hundreds of people are in the crowd cheering the shearers on. The final tally, 2,301. Cameron Hicks has been eyeing off a world record for years, so he's happy to have his name in the books. Glad to see the end of it, but I'm still pretty stoked in my efforts today. Big drain on your body. What do you do to recover? We'll stay hydrated, a lot of stretching and stuff, and just, yeah, monitor things. Can't get too crazy and go out and have too many beers, otherwise, yeah, you end up in a bit of trouble. And I'll tell you what, you Kiwis set a cracking pace, tracking this record as a team of five, but is there much competition between the stands for this special record attempt? Funny enough, there was two Kiwis in the team and they both led the charge, so yeah. We just won't mention that to the Aussies? Yeah, no, we've been living over here long enough that we've been adopted by you lots. Also from New Zealand, Benjamin Duncan was a late call-up, so he didn't have as much time to prepare, but he had the highest tally of 502. I'm probably a bit old to be doing this sort of stuff. You're obviously match fit, though. I think you might have been close to the top. I think I got lucky today. It must have been the pressure. Your first run, pretty good, but then you just built on that throughout the day. Was that something mentally that happened, or did you just get in your groove? Yeah, I sort of wanted to play possum for the first half of the day. Let Cam think he had a win? Yeah, yeah. And then just dragged him back. Nick Lehmans from Dimboola in Victoria. So you've just finished the eight hours. You're clearly exhausted. Did you have a figure in your head that you wanted this year? Not really. I was just trying to get a flow and stick with it. Try and push through the pain. And it's hard, obviously. What's hurting at the moment? Pretty well everything. The event also raised tens of thousands of dollars for charity, and Riverina shearing contractor Lockie Robertson says it's been tough, but worth it. Pretty sore standing near my back's on fire, and I reckon I'm torn my hamstring or something, to be honest. Tough day in the shed or a good day in the shed? I didn't quite hit the 400, which I wanted to, but I was pretty close. So I'm happy with the overall team effort, to be honest, in some sheep that probably weren't what we thought they were going to be. Just not getting a cut. The sheep, yeah, had a bit more dirt in them, and we were changing a cutter every, I don't even know, eight or nine minutes. So that was slowing us down, and took a bit more pushing than we thought, and yeah. I reckon it'll be easier to recruit a few Riverina young blokes to be shearers after putting on this spectacle for them today. Yeah, I reckon there's a few young fellas running around just wanting to have a chat, little kids and stuff, thinking it's all pretty cool, so that's good. This is Freshwater Creek, which doesn't really flow anymore, but the whole length of Freshwater Creek has been vegetated right down to the 90-mile beach where it ends, so we started it, but it's been taken up, which is really good. That's Fergus Irving, a wool producer from Woodside on Victoria's southeastern coast. We've jumped in the ute to check out the property where Fergus and his wife Rosemary have farmed since 1980. Ms Irving says after moving to the farm, they soon realised something was missing. Well, there weren't any trees, and we were running sheep, and sheep need shelter, so we started planting windbreaks, and we've belonged to a local land care group. They had a day on farm planning, and we employed a... Oh, I suppose he was a... A landscape architect. He was a landscape architect, and he came and helped us draw up a plan so as we could do it aesthetically as well as being useful. So that was the start. The start, specifically, of a multi-decade mission to fill their farm with native trees. Step one was to collect seeds. That was Mr Irving's job, and he had a pretty unconventional approach. I had a veterinary practice at the time, so I drove around the district, and I'd be aware of what trees were fruiting and flowering, and we had bags to put dead animals in, so I'd stop the car and pick seeds along the roadside from fruiting trees, and we'd tried to get a good variety, but the backbone of our windbreaks were Melaleuca ericofolia, the local tea tree, Coast Managum, Viminalis. Basically, that was probably... Oh, we'd have apple box and a smattering of all the other local trees, and most of it came from the roadside, although I knew where every patch of remnant vegetation was in the district, the Port Albert Racecourse, the Gifford Rifle Range Reserve, and various other little spots where there were good stands of indigenous trees. To plant these trees, Mr Irving turned to direct seeding. There was a local group, the Gippsland Tree Seeders, who built a direct seeder before they were really commercially available, and we used to mix the tree seed with chicken crumbles. The tree seeder had a disc on the front and a seed box like an ordinary pasture-sowing seeder, and we'd just go along, and we could plant kilometres and kilometres in a day. First of all, we'd use herbicide to flatten the pasture and then just direct seeding. I remember one day with one of my boys, we spent half a day and probably planted 15 linear kilometres of tree seeds, and they grew very well that particular day or that particular sowing period. Mr Irving says planting indigenous trees just makes sense. I want to recreate up to a point the landscape that was here, and also I presume that the local fauna probably prefers to be on local flora. So you're coming up to 40 years of this regeneration project. So how has the farm changed and transformed over those decades? When we bought the farm, there were very few trees on any farms in Woodside, and now most of the farms have got trees, but it's made a huge difference to this place. We have, I think we've just about sown enough trees, but all along our gullies, we have colossal numbers of birds. We've got some species we're not so keen on, like rabbits. We do have the kangaroos, wombats, echidnas, koalas. So we're looking after the local fauna, which gives us a lot of pleasure. Rosemary and Fergus Irving, wool producers from Woodside on Victoria's southeast coast, ending that report from Faith Tabuluyan. Before that, Emily Doak took us to the wool shed for a record-breaking shearing effort, and you can see more of Emily's story on the ABC website at abc.net.au. I'm David Clawton with you for A Big Country. Still to come, we'll meet the chefs who've travelled from around the globe to learn about cooking with lamb, and we're meeting a family working in the flour industry. With more than half the cut flowers sold in Australia imported and no country of origin labelling required, it's tricky for consumers to know where their flowers come from. A Brisbane woman decided something needed to be done so consumers could make informed decisions about what blooms they buy, and she had just the right connections to do it. Pip Courtney has the story. Three years ago, Bec Thomas called time on her 20-year corporate career, bought a van, leased a shop, and became a flour seller. Her mates were baffled, but Bec was on a mission. When buying cut flowers, she wants us to ask, were they flown or grown? I wanted to educate people. I wanted people to be aware of where their flowers are coming from, and I wanted them to get to know their farmer. I wanted them to know Rob grew these. The issue is personal. The reason is on her wall. Bec's brother Rob grows flowers. Rob and sister Pip, she's also on the wall, run one of the biggest oriental lily growing businesses in Australia. Several days a week, flowers from the family farm at Flowerdale, where Bec grew up in northwest Tasmania, arrive in Brisbane. They're pretty much picked, they're cooled, they're packed, put on the boat overnight, and a cool truck meets the boat the next morning, and then zooms up the coast, and then I go and grab the flowers, and then we bring them to market. As well as lilies, Rob and Pip send tulips, delphiniums, stocks, snapdragons, sweet william, and status. There are also flowers grown by several other Tasmanian growers. She wants to start conversations about the downsides of imported flowers, starting with how long they last. Sister Pip says growers want the same transparency for country of origin labelling, like we have for food. You don't know how that's been treated prior to us getting it, who's picked the product, how old is that person, where have they come from, how it's chemically been treated, the residues on the plants, you know, all that sort of stuff. Do you think many people have bought flowers, thinking they're Australian, and they're actually from overseas? Absolutely. Bec's career change came after learning about the impact rising flower imports were having here, especially on rose growers. There's a lot of imported roses that come all the way from, you know, Colombia, Ecuador, Kenya, 12,000 kilometres away. And some of these growers actually went under. As much as Rob said, what are you doing? Can you not find something a little bit easier? But I just had this burning desire to make a difference, because I knew I was actually in a position to be able to do that. Flowerdale is known for its productive volcanic soil. Growing up, there were plenty of farm jobs for the four Sadler kids, as their parents added flowers to milking 700 cows and growing potatoes. Jan and John's diversification into carnations in 1982 surprised many. There was no ag department that could tell us how to grow flowers, because nobody grew flowers. The dairy cows went, new flower varieties were added, and more polytunnels went up. At their peak, there were 86 growing tunnels, and the couple were shipping to most capital cities. Did you ever think that you would have a business this big that could employ three of your children? No, no. And about 30 other people. In 2014, the next generation consolidated the business by importing a greenhouse from the Netherlands. It covers two hectares. Everything is climate controlled, all the fans, the air exchange, everything is done by an algorithm. It'll predict what the weather's going to do. It's very clever. It's been a big investment. For us, it's an insurance policy. It's allowed us to go all year round and to grow really good product that's really consistent, because the consistency is the key. The 800,000 lily bulbs in here will produce about 4 million stems a year. Bulbs are planted every week. The saddlers used to grow in their own productive soil, but problems controlling nematodes forced a move to hydroponics. Rob and Pip have seen the impact imports are having in Australia. As they've grown, others have got out. In the past, there might have been 30 growers. Now there's maybe five to eight major growers that have all invested in technology. They've all got fairly sophisticated setups. I guess that's the future of agriculture as well, to continue to invest, to get the efficiencies. Rob and Pip are proud of Sister Bec and her advocacy for the industry, while Bec's proud of the business her siblings have developed. Jan and John Sadler are proud of all three. And while they know many have tried, they hope Bec's message gets through and people start asking, grown or flown? I make Korean-style bulgogi. Yes, it's like Gangnam-style. Yeah, you know Gangnam-style. Boom, boom, boom, boom, boom. A global experience in Western Australia's Great Southern region. Aussie lamb. It's awesome lamb. Recently, 16 chefs, known as Lambassadors, travelled from around the world to the small town of Borden, 380 kilometres south-east of Perth, to cook for local farmers, all bringing their unique flavours and showcasing locally grown lamb. What I'm preparing is we grilled, barbecued lamb neck, beautiful lamb neck from Australia. Then we served the onion soup. Wow. Yeah, something because our team from the Vietnam, USA, Japan. So we tried to put something together on the dish. So what you mean by that is you're trying to bring your own little flair to Australian lamb. Yes, yes, of course, you know, because every country using Australian lamb in a different way. Japanese, they have the Japanese way. Chinese have Chinese way. That was why I tried to align all the flavours and, you know, together on the one dish. Clinton Zhu owns his own cooking school in Shanghai, China, and was one of the many culinary professionals who volunteered their time to come to our country with Meat and Livestock Australia to learn about the red meat supply chain. So I have the culinary school in Shanghai. So we was educated, you know, for 100 and 100 young chefs every year. So I think it's very important to let young chefs and people to know about the quality of the Australian lamb. It's not only about the lamb, it's about this country, the people. So I think this is important why I'm here. Hi. Is this your music? Yeah. Where are you from? I'm from Saudi Arabia. Chefs travelled to Western Australia from 11 different countries and you could really hear it in all the different music and the languages that were being used. Lindsay Noto travelled all the way from America to join this year's delegation, which was the largest group the Lambassador Program has ever seen. It's 27 flight hours and five different airplanes that it took me to get here. I lost an entire day to get here and it was worth every minute. There's a huge opportunity where I'm from in the South in Alabama. You know, barbecue, meat is such a prevalent thing in our cuisines, but lamb is very, there's not a lot of knowledge around it and experience. And so my hope was that I could come here, learn more and then bring that knowledge and information and new techniques from these other chefs back to the States. Obviously there's a lot going on in the geopolitical world at the moment. How do you think that's impacting, you know, what you're able to cook with over there? episodes.description: Birds and fish flock to farm, as wetland is restored; Indigenous rangers on the frontline of fight against invasive weed on remote Tasmanian island; farming region's community spirit staying strong in the face of shrinking population; couple…
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. I'm David Clawton and this is A Big Country. Thanks for tuning in for a trip around regional Australia. This week we're visiting a wetland on a windy sheep farm in southern Tasmania. The farm's owners are working with conservationists to bring the Ramsar-listed wetland on the farm back to life. It's proving a boon for coastal bird life and local fish stocks. We'll get along to a local footy game in a farming region in western Victoria and hear how sport is helping the community spirit stay strong in the face of a stark population decline. And we'll meet a couple who've made a career change to horticulture. A former science teacher and accountant are growing a tiny variety of citrus that was popular generations ago. We'll learn more about kumquats and how the fruit is being used in everything from marmalade to beverages. That's coming up. First today we're heading to Truwana, Cape Barron Island, off the coast of Tasmania. Indigenous rangers on the island are on the front line of a fight against a weed that's threatening coastal ecosystems right across the southern half of Australia. To battle this weed they're using a fungus. And it's proving so successful that the method is now being rolled out across the rest of the country. Louise Moylan has the story. The beaches of Truwana, Cape Barron Island, off the coast of Tasmania, are pristine. But there's something in the sand that shouldn't be here.
