episodes.title: Cycling around Australia and little farm breeding big cattle
episodes.description: Pedalling hard to raise funds and awareness for dementia; cattle breeders raising Italian variety that can weigh as much as a car; field days celebrate centenary of Caterpillar tractors and scientist awarded peace prize for work in international…
episodes.transcript: This is an ABC podcast. We'll talk about the biggest production tractor in the world. Also from a Merino sheep farm to cycling all the way across Australia, you'll meet a remarkable man who's putting the foot to the pedal to raise awareness and a million dollars for Dementia Australia. And a Victorian agronomist has been celebrated with an international peace prize for his groundbreaking work, helping farmers in West Africa regenerate the land. And there's an incredible figure for every 10% increase in what's called the green index, the vegetation index. So how green we have this landscape. For every 10% increase, deaths of women and children in conflict situations reduces 25%. First today, let's head to Western Australia's southwest region of Carradale, where Anne and Noel Cochran breed the biggest cows in the world. Some of these cattle can weigh more than 1.7 tonnes, and stand about two metres tall. The ancient breed is called Chianina, and their genetics come all the way from Italy. Georgia Hargraves went to the farm to find out more. We initially had Chianus cattle and an Angus bull, and then we thought, well, our property's really quite small, it's only 50 acres. So to do what we kind of dreamed of doing, we thought, well, we'll fulfil that, we'll fulfil that dream. And as Noel said before, not go for profit, but for passion. I like that phrase, yeah. For people who are listening and can't see them, can you just describe what they look like? Well, I guess the signature thing about them is that they are big, white cattle. They're an Italian breed that's got a very long history. They have black eyeliner eyes. They have a little black switch on their tail and black hooves. And the thing about them is that although they're a very big animal, they're elegant. So to my eyes, they're actually very beautiful. Maybe not to everybody else, but to my eyes, they are very beautiful. And they are very elegant to look at, aren't they? But they're also enormous. They're known as being the biggest breed of cattle in the world. Is it difficult to manage cattle that get that big? In all honesty, I don't manage them. My husband does. And he has a really lovely, gentle way of doing it. They're very respectful of their nature. We try very hard to be calm with them, to not sort of push them around or yell at them or, you know, force them to do things, but to find ways that they'll do it by their nature. And so can you take me back to when you first saw them? What happened? The first time I ever saw Ken in a cattle was at the Royal Show, the Perth Royal Show, during the Grand Parade. And it was in about 1984, I think. And I was there at the show with my two young daughters at the time. And so there's horses and cows and goat sheep and then the cattle. And at the time, I'm a social worker, working in Perth, married to somebody else, with two little girls. And when these cattle came around, the Keanina cattle came around, I was absolutely amazed by them, by their size, by their elegance, by their, just their physical presence. They have quite a magical, physical presence. And I thought to myself, if ever I have cattle, then I'm having Keaninas. So, oh, it's really crazy. But it does make me really emotional, actually. They were majestic. They were majestic to see and to watch them walk. And it was a bull, a cow and a calf. And ironically, when we did buy our farm and did decide to go into Keanina, it was exactly that same breeder that we went to, to buy our cattle. And that was 17 years ago, that we actually went to Doug Corker, who'd been breeding them since the 70s. Yeah, that was the start of it. They're over 2,000 year history. They believe that it's before Roman times, just with the cave paintings and the paintings and that in Italy. And what were they used for in Italy hundreds of years ago? Mainly draft animals. And that's why they're so big, because I think Italians over years have selected the biggest animals for the draft. And then lately they've gone into more of a beef animal, mainly because the beef is, you know, you've got some of the richest beef or the healthiest beef in the world, you know, like with protein levels, cholesterol levels. And in Italy they call it Bistecca alla Florentina, is that right? And it's a delicacy? Yeah, that Bistecca is a big T-bone steak, about 1.5 kilograms. But that Bistecca goes back, you know, back to the 1360s with English knights entering Tuscany. So that history started for that steak way back then when those English knights would go into town and ask for a beef steak. That Bistecca came into the Tianling language. But that history alone is, it's surrounded just one part of Tuscany. So in a 50 kilometer area you had the English knights, all the counts, all those sort of herds, like the Medici family and all that. So the history is just all linked together throughout Tuscany and the Italian history. It's quite incredible when you look back and read it. There was something big at the Henty Field Days this year, and I had all of the farmers talking. It's pretty big and fancy. It's quite good. Yeah, if I had the money I would. It should be a big price tag for a big tractor. But yeah, I'd get one if I could. Big, that's your first thought. But yeah, it's very impressive. Dubbed the biggest production tractor in the world, the John Deere 9RX830 was on full display. To put it into perspective, the average tractor has a horsepower of around 150 to 200. This tractor has a horsepower of 830. Oh, it's amazing. It's amazing to see how big it is up close. 830 horsepower, that's just insane from where we've come over the last 50 years. It's revolutionary, really. Are you going to climb into the cab and have a look? Oh, I'm in a tractor more than enough. I'm the same. I said enough time in there, so on a day off we'd like to stay away from it. There were plenty of people circling this beast of a tractor. Kids climbing into the cab, farmers looking under the bonnet. There was plenty of intrigue. But Thomas Dewhurst, a group sales manager at Hutchin and Pierce, said not many people were pulling out the checkbooks at Henty this year. Significantly bigger than previous models. I know if you're standing next to it, kind of well over six feet every track. Huge footprint, and that's required because the tractor, fully ballasted, is 38 tonnes. So what would you use a tractor like this for in farming? A lot of seeding application mostly, and maybe wider tillage application from efficiency and scale point of view. The wider you go, the more efficient. So we've seen seeding rigs pushing out past 80 feet recently, and the current horsepower that we have is not necessarily always doing the job. So, yeah, really great to have another option for farmers that can kind of potentially take them from two machines back to one. And kind of increase their efficiencies. Is bigger better in this case? In this case, bigger is definitely better. And a lot of people are probably thinking listening to this, and I'm sure you've been asked this already a million times, but what's the price tag on a tractor like this? We're fortunate. Everything from John Deere we're ordering straight from factory, so we can change lots and lots of options depending on exactly what the customer needs. Probably looking somewhere in the $1.5 million range. But again, completely dependent on options. But when you look at it from a dollars per horsepower point of view, it compares really favorably to all current machines in the market. Have you sold any at Henty this weekend? None at Henty, but we've plenty of interest, which has been great. And we do have units in the market already. I heard someone say before, the bonnet's so big you could almost roll your swag out on the front of it if you needed. That's true, but it's funny. The bonnet opens with one hand. Really well designed. In terms of, I guess, machinery sales in general, I mean, this is one of the biggest machinery field days in the country, so people coming to have a look. But what's happening in that space? Are people spending? Are people buying? It's been an incredibly tough year, especially around here in Henty. Yeah, it's been a really interesting season, especially in our part of the world here. I'd say it's probably a bit quieter year, but there's still a lot of interest. The recent rain has kind of made people interested again, but we just have to see what harvest does. It's really hard to make any decisions without knowing exactly how the crops are going to come off, and that's probably what we're seeing at the moment. Are sales down? Not necessarily down. They're probably a little bit quieter right now, but that's not uncommon at this time of year. Do you find a lot of farmers buy at a field days, or are they coming to have a look and more of a feel of what's on offer? No, yeah, it's definitely more to come and see what's available, have a look at the new technology. We're really lucky with the tech site set up here. We've got the full technology set up that customers can come and look at. It's the biggest tractor in the world here at Henty Field Days. It's really cool to come and have a look at it. Can tractors get bigger than this, or do you expect them to get bigger? Everything can always get bigger, but I think this might be the ceiling for a little bit. Thomas Dewhurst from farm equipment supplier Hutchin and Pearce, speaking to Annie Brown at the recent Henty machinery field days in southern New South Wales. You can read more about those amazing Chianina cattle online and have a look at just how big they really are. You'll find it on the ABC homepage at abc.net.au. Just look for the Big Country program page. I'm David Corden with you for A Big Country. Still to come, you'll meet a cyclist on a gruelling journey to fight for a better future for people with dementia. But first, the verdant hills of Druin in West Gippsland may feel a world away from the barren desert landscape of West Africa. But it's where agronomist Tony Renato has settled down after decades working with primary producers in Nigeria, regenerating the landscape. Tony has recently been celebrated with an International Peace Prize. The ABC's Madeleine Stutchbury went to find out more about his work. So I studied and we moved to Niger Republic in West Africa in 1980. And the landscape that confronted us when we arrived there, even though in my lifetime, I was 24 years old, in my lifetime, this had been a biodiverse forest with fertile farms in the clearings, permanent springs and even wildlife. In my lifetime, that forest had been cleared and it created barren windswept plains. And there are consequences for that kind of degradation. The land was at the point of ecological collapse and barely able to support life. Can you explain to me what is your regenerative principle and how did you deploy that? So I figured if deforestation was one of the major root causes of all those problems that I listed, then surely replanting trees would go a long way towards solving those problems. And the solution actually came as an answer to prayer. One day I was delivering a ute load of seedlings to the villagers, knowing full well most would die. And the people thought this was ridiculous anyway. And I stopped to reduce the air pressure to get through the sandy soil. And this, what appeared as a useless bush, caught my attention. And I walked over to take a closer look. And if you look at the leaf of most species of plants, it's like having a signature that tells you exactly what that plant is. Immediately, I realised that it's not a bush, it's not a weed, that's a tree. And if you bend down and brush away the sand, sure enough, there was a stump under those shoots. That changed everything. Once you were outside of that acute learning period, what was the impact of your work long term in the African context? If we take the Niger case alone, over the following 20 years, from 1984, when we really had a strong promotion, from that time on, this method spread at the rate of a quarter of a million hectares per year for those 20 years. Coming to 5 million hectares, 200 million hectares, 200 million hectares regenerated across that agricultural landscape. Economic and social benefits were very, very significant. Farmers in Niger, to give context, it's one of the poorest countries in the world, in an extremely harsh environment on the edge of the Sahara Desert. Farmers in Niger, by virtue of now working with the direction of nature instead of fighting against it, earn an additional gross income in the order of $900 million US dollars every year without subsidies or incentives to do this. Farmers in Niger are growing an additional 500,000 tonnes of grain every year, enough to feed 2.5 million people because their crop yields have increased and that's not including the benefits to their livestock. The award was the Luxembourg Peace Prize and it was recognition that when we restore environmental conditions it's actually a great precursor to creating conditions for peace. There's an incredible figure for every 10% increase in what's called the green index, the vegetation index. So how green we have this landscape. For every 10% increase deaths of women and children in conflict situations reduces 25%. So what's happening when you degrade landscapes and there's a shortage of food, fuel, fodder, water, there's more competition for those scarce resources and more likelihood that conflict will arise. As you restore the environment there's an abundance of greater abundance of those elements and less reason for people to fight over resources. So it was a recognition for that. And for me, yes of course I'm honoured, but it highlights the incredible work of millions of smallholder farmers who took this risk with this crazy white guy and restored their land. It's a tribute to them and I would say also to World Vision which has now taken this relatively obscure technique and it's spreading it globally. When you first started your career in agronomy, did you ever imagine that this would be the impact of your work and your passion? I certainly hoped to have an impact, but I could never have imagined the scale that it's taken off and today, largely through World Vision, it's spread to some 40 countries around the world and counting. Cycling more than 40,000 kilometers across the country isn't for the faint-hearted. And as Nicholas Tremain settles up for another day on the roads, he explains why he decided to take on this gruelling year-long journey. Dementia has obviously hit our family quite hard with the diagnosis of my mother and also my uncle. I just wanted to do something that might drive more awareness for the disease here in Australia and hopefully raise some money. I thought, what's the craziest thing I can come up with? And yeah, I thought riding around Australia wasn't just enough. I thought I'd add a few kilometers to it. Cycling a distance equivalent to the circumference of the earth isn't just a physical test for Nick, but an emotional too. Nick, I've got a lot of time out on the bike to think things over and how I feel about certain things and what I should be doing and spending the time I can with my mom while she's still here. And sometimes trying to remember the times before she had dementia. Growing up on a Merino sheep farm near Pandana on Kangaroo Island, his mother Marilyn was heavily involved in farm life and the town's tight-knit neighborhood. Mom was a very active member of the community. There's probably not a job that she wouldn't put her hand up to do. So she was on the local show committee. She was an umpire for netball. She always tried to get to my football games as a supporter. She was on the local Lions club as well, so cooking barbecues at events and doing catering. She helped in the canteen at the local sports club. So many different aspects of the community. His mother first got diagnosed with dementia in 2019. But her rapidly declining health meant she had to move into a full-time healthcare facility, as Nick's father, Mervyn Tremain, explains. She had had a seizure during the night and we had to get the ambulance. And next morning after the doctors have to, oh well, she's not going home. She's staying. Coming to terms with Marilyn having to leave the home has been painful for the family. Leaving a big gap and heartbreak Mervyn is battling to accept. When one disappears, the other one is lost. And I feel that I'm partly lost with not having Marilyn around. In Australia, dementia has become the leading cause of death. Dementia Australia's chief executive officer, Tanya Buchanan, explains why the number of people living with dementia is increasing. There are around 433,000 Australians currently living with dementia. And of that, 29,000 are living with younger onset dementia. And of course, around 1,500 children are living with conditions that also cause dementia. There's a number of reasons that dementia rates are expected to rise. As we get older, our risk of developing dementia increases. But it's really important to know that age, getting older, doesn't mean that you will invariably develop dementia. Dementia is not a normal part of aging. And there are a number of modifiable risk factors that we can all tackle to reduce our risk of developing dementia. And there are things about keeping healthy, stopping smoking, having a healthy diet, staying physically active, socially connective, and of course, doing things that are cognitively challenging on a regular basis. The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare's latest data projects the number of people living with dementia will more than double to over 1 million Australians by 2065. Dementia Australia's CEO, Tanya Buchanan, is calling for more discussions on brain health. There's a lot of stigma attached to the diagnosis of dementia. And so people don't tend to talk about it. And it's really important that we start this conversation about reducing our risks of developing dementia and looking after our brain health right across our life. It's a conversation Nick's been eager to share on his ride, passing through Australian communities during the past 268 days on the road. I get a great response from people because they share their story of how they're connected with dementia as well. And whether it's a loved one, a close friend or a family member, it affects so many people in Australia and you don't realise how big this issue is. As an active member of SA Country Shows, he makes sure to call in on the town's big annual agricultural event to share his message. It's a pleasure and an honour to be here today to open the Mount Barker Show. 2025, I'm on a new mission to raise awareness and money for Dementia Australia. I'm currently riding my bike around Australia unsupported for the next year. While the journey has come with highlights like these, it's also thrown him plenty of challenges, testing his willpower. I probably shouldn't be stopping today. It's way too cold for that. It isn't easy to have to say this, but after 133 days and over 17,000 kilometres, it might be possible that this coming week might be my last on the bike. Despite the challenges, he's committed to his goal to create more awareness about dementia and some of the additional hurdles it comes with for people living with it in remote and rural areas. The biggest fear is mum wandering off, which did happen on occasions, and having such a large farm, it's just like, well, which direction did she go into? Where do we start looking? And then what hazard we have out on the farm that could potentially cause harm to her if she had an accident? While people who live in regional Australia experience a higher prevalence of dementia compared to those living in major cities, researchers say there's limited scientific understanding about how dementia risk factors cluster differently in these communities. Associate Professor of Healthy Ageing Dr. Ashley Smith and her academic team from the University of South Australia are working on a study with regional communities to find out. Our research project involves three phases. The first phase is to look at the clustering of risk factors for dementia in rural compared to urban participants. And then in phase two and three, we're going to work with the rural communities to start to identify where the pain points are for dementia in their communities. And in phase three, we're interested in working with rural communities to develop a toolkit. Dr. Smith says they'll focus on the 14 modifiable risk factors of dementia. Dementia is really a lifelong condition. In early life, factors such as lower levels of education increases people's risk of dementia. In midlife, there's factors like physical inactivity and vascular health, which contribute to people's risk of dementia. So what we're really trying to do is work with these rural communities about how can we tackle these different modifiable risk factors. With more than 33,000 kilometers already clocked up, Nick's sheer determination to get back on the bicycle is driven by his biggest motivator. It's mum. Sorry. It's just, I can see her if she was able to. I know she would be at the finish line to see me finish. And with less than 7,000 kilometers to cross the finish line in Sydney on December 31st, he wants others to know that you're not alone. And there's others that are going through the same situation. So there's always someone to talk to. Nicholas Tremaine, ending that story by Jessica Schremer. You can watch the full story on ABC Landline anytime on ABC iview. You'll find it at the ABC homepage at abc.net.au. Just look for the Big Country program page. And that's the show for today. I'm David Claughton. I'll be back with you again next week with more great stories from regional Australia. I'll chat to you then. You've been listening to an ABC podcast. And in Italy they call it Bistecca alla Florentina, is that right?
And it's a delicacy?
Yeah, that Bistecca is a big T-bone steak, about 1.5 kilograms.
But that Bistecca goes back, you know, back to the 1360s with English knights entering Tuscany.
So that history started for that steak way back then when those English knights would go into town and ask for a beef steak.
That Bistecca came into the Tianling language.
But that history alone is, it's surrounded just one part of Tuscany.
So in a 50 kilometer area you had the English knights, all the counts, all those sort of herds, like the Medici family and all that.
So the history is just all linked together throughout Tuscany and the Italian history.
It's quite incredible when you look back and read it.
There was something big at the Henty Field Days this year, and I had all of the farmers talking.
It's pretty big and fancy.
It's quite good.
Yeah, if I had the money I would.
It should be a big price tag for a big tractor.
But yeah, I'd get one if I could.
Big, that's your first thought.
But yeah, it's very impressive.
Dubbed the biggest production tractor in the world, the John Deere 9RX830 was on full display.
To put it into perspective, the average tractor has a horsepower of around 150 to 200.
This tractor has a horsepower of 830.
Oh, it's amazing.
It's amazing to see how big it is up close.
830 horsepower, that's just insane from where we've come over the last 50 years.
It's revolutionary, really.
Are you going to climb into the cab and have a look?
Oh, I'm in a tractor more than enough.
I'm the same.
I said enough time in there, so on a day off we'd like to stay away from it.
There were plenty of people circling this beast of a tractor.
Kids climbing into the cab, farmers looking under the bonnet.
There was plenty of intrigue.
But Thomas Dewhurst, a group sales manager at Hutchin and Pierce, said not many people were pulling out the checkbooks at Henty this year.
Significantly bigger than previous models.
I know if you're standing next to it, kind of well over six feet every track.
Huge footprint, and that's required because the tractor, fully ballasted, is 38 tonnes.
So what would you use a tractor like this for in farming?
A lot of seeding application mostly, and maybe wider tillage application from efficiency and scale point of view.
The wider you go, the more efficient.
So we've seen seeding rigs pushing out past 80 feet recently, and the current horsepower that we have is not necessarily always doing the job.
So, yeah, really great to have another option for farmers that can kind of potentially take them from two machines back to one.
And kind of increase their efficiencies.
Is bigger better in this case?
In this case, bigger is definitely better.
And a lot of people are probably thinking listening to this, and I'm sure you've been asked this already a million times, but what's the price tag on a tractor like this?
We're fortunate.
Everything from John Deere we're ordering straight from factory, so we can change lots and lots of options depending on exactly what the customer needs.
Probably looking somewhere in the $1.5 million range.
But again, completely dependent on options.
But when you look at it from a dollars per horsepower point of view, it compares really favorably to all current machines in the market.
Have you sold any at Henty this weekend?
None at Henty, but we've plenty of interest, which has been great.
And we do have units in the market already.
I heard someone say before, the bonnet's so big you could almost roll your swag out on the front of it if you needed.
That's true, but it's funny.
The bonnet opens with one hand.
Really well designed.
In terms of, I guess, machinery sales in general, I mean, this is one of the biggest machinery field days in the country, so people coming to have a look.
But what's happening in that space?
Are people spending?
Are people buying?
It's been an incredibly tough year, especially around here in Henty.
Yeah, it's been a really interesting season, especially in our part of the world here.
I'd say it's probably a bit quieter year, but there's still a lot of interest.
The recent rain has kind of made people interested again, but we just have to see what harvest does.
It's really hard to make any decisions without knowing exactly how the crops are going to come off, and that's probably what we're seeing at the moment.
Are sales down?
Not necessarily down.
They're probably a little bit quieter right now, but that's not uncommon at this time of year.
Do you find a lot of farmers buy at a field days, or are they coming to have a look and more of a feel of what's on offer?
No, yeah, it's definitely more to come and see what's available, have a look at the new technology.
We're really lucky with the tech site set up here.
We've got the full technology set up that customers can come and look at.
It's the biggest tractor in the world here at Henty Field Days.
It's really cool to come and have a look at it.
Can tractors get bigger than this, or do you expect them to get bigger?
Everything can always get bigger, but I think this might be the ceiling for a little bit.
Thomas Dewhurst from farm equipment supplier Hutchin and Pearce, speaking to Annie Brown at the recent Henty machinery field days in southern New South Wales.
You can read more about those amazing Chianina cattle online and have a look at just how big they really are.
You'll find it on the ABC homepage at abc.net.au.
Just look for the Big Country program page.
I'm David Corden with you for A Big Country.
Still to come, you'll meet a cyclist on a gruelling journey to fight for a better future for people with dementia.
But first, the verdant hills of Druin in West Gippsland may feel a world away from the barren desert landscape of West Africa.
But it's where agronomist Tony Renato has settled down after decades working with primary producers in Nigeria, regenerating the landscape.
Tony has recently been celebrated with an International Peace Prize.
The ABC's Madeleine Stutchbury went to find out more about his work.
So I studied and we moved to Niger Republic in West Africa in 1980.

And the landscape that confronted us when we arrived there, even though in my lifetime, I was 24 years old, in my lifetime, this had been a biodiverse forest with fertile farms in the clearings, permanent springs and even wildlife.
In my lifetime, that forest had been cleared and it created barren windswept plains.
And there are consequences for that kind of degradation.
The land was at the point of ecological collapse and barely able to support life.
Can you explain to me what is your regenerative principle and how did you deploy that?
So I figured if deforestation was one of the major root causes of all those problems that I listed,
then surely replanting trees would go a long way towards solving those problems.
And the solution actually came as an answer to prayer.
One day I was delivering a ute load of seedlings to the villagers, knowing full well most would die.
And the people thought this was ridiculous anyway.
And I stopped to reduce the air pressure to get through the sandy soil.
And this, what appeared as a useless bush, caught my attention.
And I walked over to take a closer look.
And if you look at the leaf of most species of plants, it's like having a signature that tells you exactly what that plant is.
Immediately, I realised that it's not a bush, it's not a weed, that's a tree.
And if you bend down and brush away the sand, sure enough, there was a stump under those shoots.
That changed everything.
Once you were outside of that acute learning period, what was the impact of your work long term in the African context?
If we take the Niger case alone, over the following 20 years, from 1984, when we really had a strong promotion,
from that time on, this method spread at the rate of a quarter of a million hectares per year for those 20 years.
Coming to 5 million hectares, 200 million hectares, 200 million hectares regenerated across that agricultural landscape.
Economic and social benefits were very, very significant.
Farmers in Niger, to give context, it's one of the poorest countries in the world, in
an extremely harsh environment on the edge of the Sahara Desert.
Farmers in Niger, by virtue of now working with the direction of nature instead of fighting
against it, earn an additional gross income in the order of $900 million US dollars every
year without subsidies or incentives to do this.
Farmers in Niger are growing an additional 500,000 tonnes of grain every year, enough
to feed 2.5 million people because their crop yields have increased and that's not including
the benefits to their livestock.
The award was the Luxembourg Peace Prize and it was recognition that when we restore environmental
conditions it's actually a great precursor to creating conditions for peace.
There's an incredible figure for every 10% increase in what's called the green index,
the vegetation index.
So how green we have this landscape.
For every 10% increase deaths of women and children in conflict situations reduces 25%.
So what's happening when you degrade landscapes and there's a shortage of food, fuel, fodder,
water, there's more competition for those scarce resources and more likelihood that conflict
will arise.
As you restore the environment there's an abundance of greater abundance of those elements and less
reason for people to fight over resources.
So it was a recognition for that.
And for me, yes of course I'm honoured, but it highlights the incredible work of millions
of smallholder farmers who took this risk with this crazy white guy and restored their land.
It's a tribute to them and I would say also to World Vision which has now taken this relatively
obscure technique and it's spreading it globally.
When you first started your career in agronomy, did you ever imagine that this would be the
impact of your work and your passion?
I certainly hoped to have an impact, but I could never have imagined the scale that it's taken
off and today, largely through World Vision, it's spread to some 40 countries around the
world and counting.
Cycling more than 40,000 kilometers across the country isn't for the faint-hearted.
And as Nicholas Tremain settles up for another day on the roads, he explains why he decided
to take on this gruelling year-long journey.
Dementia has obviously hit our family quite hard with the diagnosis of my mother and also
my uncle.
I just wanted to do something that might drive more awareness for the disease here in Australia
and hopefully raise some money.
I thought, what's the craziest thing I can come up with?
And yeah, I thought riding around Australia wasn't just enough.
I thought I'd add a few kilometers to it.
Cycling a distance equivalent to the circumference of the earth isn't just a physical test for
Nick, but an emotional too.
Nick, I've got a lot of time out on the bike to think things over and how I feel about certain
things and what I should be doing and spending the time I can with my mom while she's still
here.
And sometimes trying to remember the times before she had dementia.
Growing up on a Merino sheep farm near Pandana on Kangaroo Island, his mother Marilyn was heavily
involved in farm life and the town's tight-knit neighborhood.
Mom was a very active member of the community.
There's probably not a job that she wouldn't put her hand up to do.
So she was on the local show committee.
She was an umpire for netball.
She always tried to get to my football games as a supporter.
She was on the local Lions club as well, so cooking barbecues at events and doing catering.
She helped in the canteen at the local sports club.
So many different aspects of the community.
His mother first got diagnosed with dementia in 2019.
But her rapidly declining health meant she had to move into a full-time healthcare facility,
as Nick's father, Mervyn Tremain, explains.
She had had a seizure during the night and we had to get the ambulance.
And next morning after the doctors have to, oh well, she's not going home.
She's staying.
Coming to terms with Marilyn having to leave the home has been painful for the family.
Leaving a big gap and heartbreak Mervyn is battling to accept.
When one disappears, the other one is lost.
And I feel that I'm partly lost with not having Marilyn around.
In Australia, dementia has become the leading cause of death.
Dementia Australia's chief executive officer, Tanya Buchanan, explains why the number of people living with dementia is increasing.
There are around 433,000 Australians currently living with dementia.
And of that, 29,000 are living with younger onset dementia.
And of course, around 1,500 children are living with conditions that also cause dementia.
There's a number of reasons that dementia rates are expected to rise.
As we get older, our risk of developing dementia increases.
But it's really important to know that age, getting older, doesn't mean that you will invariably develop dementia.
Dementia is not a normal part of aging.
And there are a number of modifiable risk factors that we can all tackle to reduce our risk of developing dementia.
And there are things about keeping healthy, stopping smoking, having a healthy diet, staying physically active, socially connective,
and of course, doing things that are cognitively challenging on a regular basis.
The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare's latest data projects the number of people living with dementia
will more than double to over 1 million Australians by 2065.
Dementia Australia's CEO, Tanya Buchanan, is calling for more discussions on brain health.
There's a lot of stigma attached to the diagnosis of dementia.
And so people don't tend to talk about it.
And it's really important that we start this conversation about reducing our risks of developing dementia
and looking after our brain health right across our life.
It's a conversation Nick's been eager to share on his ride,
passing through Australian communities during the past 268 days on the road.
I get a great response from people because they share their story of how they're connected with dementia as well.
And whether it's a loved one, a close friend or a family member,
it affects so many people in Australia and you don't realise how big this issue is.
As an active member of SA Country Shows, he makes sure to call in on the town's big annual agricultural event to share his message.
It's a pleasure and an honour to be here today to open the Mount Barker Show.
2025, I'm on a new mission to raise awareness and money for Dementia Australia.
I'm currently riding my bike around Australia unsupported for the next year.
While the journey has come with highlights like these,
it's also thrown him plenty of challenges, testing his willpower.
I probably shouldn't be stopping today.
It's way too cold for that.
It isn't easy to have to say this, but after 133 days and over 17,000 kilometres,
it might be possible that this coming week might be my last on the bike.
Despite the challenges, he's committed to his goal to create more awareness about dementia
and some of the additional hurdles it comes with for people living with it in remote and rural areas.
The biggest fear is mum wandering off, which did happen on occasions,
and having such a large farm, it's just like, well, which direction did she go into?
Where do we start looking?
And then what hazard we have out on the farm that could potentially cause harm to her if she had an accident?
While people who live in regional Australia experience a higher prevalence of dementia
compared to those living in major cities,
researchers say there's limited scientific understanding about how dementia risk factors
cluster differently in these communities.
Associate Professor of Healthy Ageing Dr. Ashley Smith and her academic team
from the University of South Australia are working on a study with regional communities to find out.
Our research project involves three phases.
The first phase is to look at the clustering of risk factors for dementia in rural compared to urban participants.
And then in phase two and three, we're going to work with the rural communities
to start to identify where the pain points are for dementia in their communities.
And in phase three, we're interested in working with rural communities to develop a toolkit.
Dr. Smith says they'll focus on the 14 modifiable risk factors of dementia.
Dementia is really a lifelong condition.
In early life, factors such as lower levels of education increases people's risk of dementia.
In midlife, there's factors like physical inactivity and vascular health,
which contribute to people's risk of dementia.
So what we're really trying to do is work with these rural communities
about how can we tackle these different modifiable risk factors.
With more than 33,000 kilometers already clocked up,
Nick's sheer determination to get back on the bicycle is driven by his biggest motivator.
It's mum. Sorry.
It's just, I can see her if she was able to.
I know she would be at the finish line to see me finish.
And with less than 7,000 kilometers to cross the finish line in Sydney on December 31st,
he wants others to know that you're not alone.
And there's others that are going through the same situation.
So there's always someone to talk to.
Nicholas Tremaine, ending that story by Jessica Schremer.
You can watch the full story on ABC Landline anytime on ABC iview.
If this story raises any concerns for you or anyone you know,
you can contact Lifeline on 13 11 14.
You can read more about Nicholas's incredible journey and Tony's work in Africa online.
You'll find it at the ABC homepage at abc.net.au.
Just look for the Big Country program page.
And that's the show for today.
I'm David Claughton.
I'll be back with you again next week with more great stories from regional Australia.
I'll chat to you then.

episodes.title: Gather Round banner ban leads Adelaide man on unexpected AFL adventure
episodes.description: When local footy fan Clint Rule headed to the Melbourne V Essendon clash at Adelaide Oval, with tongue-in-cheek banner in tow, he couldn't have predicted the colourful night ahead.
episodes.transcript: Now I was a little bit ticked off, a little bit bemused, and I said, actually I'm going to leave on principles because I should be allowed to have the banner. A banner that was controversial. Clint from Cumberland Park, I got the spirit of the banner. I'd love you to share the story and tell me why you took it to the Bombers-Demons game. I love footy, I love gather round. I'm a power guy, but I wanted to go to a true gather round game that's a non-power and I guess a non-Adelaide game. So I got some tickets to the Essendon Melbourne game and I thought I'm going to be a little bit funny, a little bit cryptic, and I haven't done a banner for a long time, so I'm doing a banner today. And that banner had the words, I don't particularly like either side. I thought it might project a bit of humour and a bit of warmth to say that I'm at the game, even though I don't particularly like either side. That's the beauty of gather round. Okay, so you've put it up. Were there people around you that got the joke? Yes, there was. And I spoke to an Essendon supporter who'd driven over and he liked it. And I was hanging out with my mates there and within five minutes the security came over and started to have an elongated conversation with me and about the banner, which I told them that it was tongue-in-cheek and showed in the Facebook post. The guy was very good, number 235, but he had his boss in his ear and he said, just hang on a minute. I turned to my mates and said, decision pending. And then the boss said, sorry, you can't have the banner. You have to go and check it in the cloakroom. Now, I was a little bit ticked off, a little bit bemused, and I said, actually, I'm going to leave on principles because I should be allowed to have the banner. So you decided to leave. Where did you go? So I went outside and started scratching my head and then I saw the Shane Maughan health checks booth and I thought, I'm turning this negative into a positive. And I went and did a health check. It actually told me that my health age was 68 and I'm only 55, so that was a bit of a scare. I had something to do in the evening and I had to kill some time. So I went and had a nap at uni grandstand at my beautiful university oval where I played some footy. Fortunately, my banner also used to be a blanket and it was a tad cold. So I wrapped up a nap and settled in for a nap. I love a nap. Meanwhile, the Premier had heard about it and he gave me a call. He played at our footy club and he played in a premiership with me back in 2013. And he's a great bloke and a great mate. And he never forgets the pass and he takes everyone with him. And he said, what's going on? Do you want to ride to the Nord game? Because he was driving past and I said, OK. So I went to the Sydney and Gold Coast game. I don't particularly like either side, but I loved being there at that gather round game. Did you wave that around at Norwood Oval? He took me to the footsteps of Andrew Dillon, the head honcho of the AFL. So I had some scones and cream and a chat with him and he loved it. So that's an official OK for me. So I whipped out into the crowd at the hill end. Got a bit of banner work in the crowd with some mates. And then I got another offer for tickets back at Adelaide Oval for the night game. Hawks versus Bulldogs. I did get it up to the president's room at Adelaide Oval. And while I had a lovely lamb dinner, the marvellous catering staff went and found one for me. Sat down with a nice swanky end to a curious day for this footy fan.

and started to have an elongated conversation with me and about the banner,
which I told them that it was tongue-in-cheek and showed in the Facebook post.
The guy was very good, number 235, but he had his boss in his ear and he said,
just hang on a minute.
I turned to my mates and said, decision pending.
And then the boss said, sorry, you can't have the banner.
You have to go and check it in the cloakroom.
Now, I was a little bit ticked off, a little bit bemused,
and I said, actually, I'm going to leave on principles because I should be allowed to have the banner.
So you decided to leave.
Where did you go?
So I went outside and started scratching my head and then I saw the Shane Maughan health checks booth
and I thought, I'm turning this negative into a positive.
And I went and did a health check.
It actually told me that my health age was 68 and I'm only 55, so that was a bit of a scare.
I had something to do in the evening and I had to kill some time.
So I went and had a nap at uni grandstand at my beautiful university oval where I played some footy.
Fortunately, my banner also used to be a blanket and it was a tad cold.
So I wrapped up a nap and settled in for a nap.
I love a nap.
Meanwhile, the Premier had heard about it and he gave me a call.
He played at our footy club and he played in a premiership with me back in 2013.
And he's a great bloke and a great mate.
And he never forgets the pass and he takes everyone with him.
And he said, what's going on?
Do you want to ride to the Nord game?
Because he was driving past and I said, OK.
So I went to the Sydney and Gold Coast game.
I don't particularly like either side, but I loved being there at that gather round game.
Did you wave that around at Norwood Oval?
He took me to the footsteps of Andrew Dillon, the head honcho of the AFL.
So I had some scones and cream and a chat with him and he loved it.
So that's an official OK for me.
So I whipped out into the crowd at the hill end.
Got a bit of banner work in the crowd with some mates.
And then I got another offer for tickets back at Adelaide Oval for the night game.
Hawks versus Bulldogs.
I did get it up to the president's room at Adelaide Oval.
And while I had a lovely lamb dinner, the marvellous catering staff went and found one for me.
Sat down with a nice swanky end to a curious day for this footy fan.

episodes.title: Government set to announce NDIS reforms
episodes.description: It costs 50 billion dollars a year and it's plagued by rorts, so how can the Government reform the NDIS to protect its budget while maintaining services to those who need it?
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Good morning. Welcome to AM. It's Wednesday the 22nd of April. I'm Melissa Clark in Canberra, coming to you from Ngunnawal country and acknowledging other custodians. US President Donald Trump says he will extend the ceasefire with Iran, just hours from its scheduled end, despite no progress on negotiations for peace talks. In a social media post, Mr Trump says he will hold off attacking Iran until Tehran's negotiating teams come up with a unified proposal for a peace agreement. Correspondent Rachel Clayton is in Washington, D.C. Rachel, President Trump says the ceasefire is being extended. What are the details? That's right. So there'd been significant uncertainty for the past few hours about whether these peace talks were going to go ahead to extend this ceasefire. We've now heard from the president on social media who says the US is going to hold off its attacks on Iran and that this ceasefire will continue to give Iran more time to come up with a proposal for a peace plan. So he said on Truth Social that based on the fact the government of Iran is what he calls seriously fractured. And because he'd been requested by Pakistani officials, including the prime minister, who asked the US to hold off its attack on the country of Iran until, as he says, until such time as their leaders and representatives can come up with a unified proposal. He goes on and says that he's directed the military to continue the blockade of Iranian ports, but to also extend the ceasefire until the proposal is submitted. So it's interesting that he's extending the ceasefire because days ago he told Bloomberg that he was definitely not going to extend the ceasefire, that if the talks failed, he was ready to bomb Iran. He said as early as this morning to CNBC that the military was gearing up to continue the fight. This is now a complete 180 where he said that the ceasefire will continue and he won't attack Iran. And it really, I think, shows not just how fluid the situation is and how quickly things can change. But the pressure that these Pakistani leaders and officials are under to make sure that the fighting does not continue. They've been under significant pressure to ask Washington to make some concessions to get Iran to the table. That hasn't worked. One of the main things was that blockade. Iran wanted that blockade of its ports lifted. Washington was unwilling to do that. And in this post, we've heard from the president saying that that blockade will continue, but that the ceasefire will also continue. So it seems to have worked. The pressure the Pakistani leaders have been putting on Washington has worked and the talks will go ahead, it seems, just a little later than when we were expecting. But as you say, the blockade continuing and we still have action from the US Navy that boarded another ship as part of this blockade. So what do we know about that? That's right. So this happened overnight in the US. It was a tanker that was allegedly carrying sanctioned Iranian oil towards Singapore, flying the flag of Botswana, allegedly part of Iran's shadow fleet that we've heard quite a bit about from General Dan Kane. He calls it a dog fleet. And it was boarded. It's been taken over by the United States. What happens to it now is a bit unknown. It will be handed over to the Coast Guard. And I've been told that there'll be discussions with various countries around the Bay of Bengal in South Asia, where the tanker was seized to decide what to do with the oil on board. The other development that's happened today is that the Treasury Department has announced new sanctions on 14 people and aircraft from Iran, the UAE and Turkey that the US says are helping Iran obtain weapons or parts of weapons. So the pressure from the United States on Iran has continued all day. And now it's culminated in this extension of the ceasefire, which is giving everyone a bit more breathing room. Rachel Clayton in Washington, D.C. And Iran has responded to the latest announcement by President Trump. A spokesman has said the ceasefire extension is a ploy to buy time for a surprise attack by the US. Back home, the federal government is set to announce major reforms to the $50 billion National Disability Insurance Scheme today, when the minister in charge of the program, Mark Butler, gives a speech at the National Press Club. Changes such as mandatory registration of providers, altering pricing rules and tightening of certain types of support have all been under consideration. For more, I was joined earlier by our National Disability Affairs reporter, Naz Campanella. Naz, why is today's speech so important? Well, today is a really hotly anticipated speech, purely because a lot of the talk in the recent years about the NDIS has been about its cost. So in its original projections, the Productivity Commission said that in its maturity, the NDIS would support about 400,000 participants, and that has now swelled to 760,000 participants, and it's now costing $50 billion, so more than Medicare, and edging pretty close to defence spending as well. Now, the government has had a target of 10%, and it has said in recent time that it is on track to meet that target, but it is now going to be talking about plans to reach a 5% target, and how they will achieve that is what will be unveiled today. So can you talk me through some of the things that are likely to be the key areas of focus if the government is looking to try and further constrain the growth of the NDIS? Well, I have to say the government has been really tight-lipped about what this is, so it's all predictions from me and from conversations with many people, but I think the really key things is firstly, mandatory registration. So it is voluntary for many organisations and providers to be registered. It is not illegal to operate as an NDIS provider unregistered, but some providers, particularly in accommodation and sort of platform providers which connect participants with support workers, will have to be registered by July 1st. That was recently announced, and my feeling is that that will go even further today. Another big thing is what to do with groups outside of the NDIS, and one in particular is people with psychosocial disability. There are about 65,000 of them on the NDIS, but hundreds of thousands still outside the scheme who require support. So what will be done across the states and territories really to support those people? And finally, it's pricing, Mel. There's a quite a, I guess it's described as a flat pricing structure at the moment. So you could be a support worker going in and providing, for example, you know, showering, feeding, or you could be a nurse that goes in and supports someone to have medication or a feeding tube, and the prices are very similar. So people talking about looking at prices of therapies, who can get them, how frequently they can get them. And also looking at, I guess, the price of services according to quality. So maybe perhaps a tiered approach. So that'll be really interesting to see what happens there. So depending on what the government announces today, there could be some big changes coming. What's the feeling in the community? Yeah, it's safe to say the changes will be big. And the feeling in the community, to put it in a word, is anxiety. I know of one particular group that ran an online town hall last night for people to try and quell concerns, have a bit of a sit down with everyone and have a chat and just kind of say, you know, we're all in this together. But, you know, I've heard weekly for years now about people having cuts to plans, being very concerned that they have significant permanent disability, and feeling like a lot of their services are being cut. Everyone has consensus that something needs to change. The trajectory of the scheme cannot continue this way because the community wants this scheme to last into the future for generations. So there's consensus on that. It's how the reforms are done that the community is concerned about. They want it done with transparency and proper communication. Naz Campanella there. Hundreds of parents are already dealing with the impact of earlier changes to the NDIS aimed at reining in its growing costs. A key provider of specialised childcare centres for autistic children, the AEIOU Foundation, went into liquidation last month. The abrupt closure of its 11 sites followed cuts to plans for NDIS recipients. Emma Pollard reports. Hands on the steering wheel. In the garden of a brick home north of Brisbane, five-year-old Dimitri plays with a toy car alongside his father. When he was two, Dimitri was diagnosed with the most severe level of autism. He didn't speak or interact with people. Single dad, Eric Moore, who's a teacher, says Dimitri had to leave three mainstream childcare centres. They asked me to find somewhere else for him because they couldn't manage him. Then early last year, he started at an AEIOU centre, which provided autistic children with high support needs with daycare and therapies under one safe roof. Dimitri was making steady progress. He started being more expressive of his needs and what he wanted. We started learning some basic ways to communicate back and forth. His understanding vastly improved. But last month, their lives were turned upside down when the AEIOU Foundation went into liquidation. All 11 centres in Queensland, Adelaide and Canberra telling hundreds of parents like Eric not to return. We're closed. We no longer have jobs. We're shut down. Don't bring him back tomorrow. So I initially had to take time off work to care for him during the day while we start trying to piece everything back together. For 20 years, AEIOU provided thousands of autistic children with early intervention services. Devastated parents and staff blame NDIS cuts for its demise. Cancer doctor, James Morton started the foundation after his own son's autism diagnosis and was on the board. And in 2024, suddenly packages got dramatically cut. So from six hours of therapy, which they were funded at the time, down to two hours of therapy. And parents were told that they had to have their children in mainstream or look after them at home. Canberra-based Dr Martin Laverty helped design and implement the NDIS and now heads a disability service. He says the AEIOU Foundation likely won't be the last to fold. Right around the country, we are seeing therapy providers who have faced a seven-year freeze in the therapy price, fighting viability challenges to survive. In a statement, a spokesperson for the NDIS Minister Jenny McAllister says the scheme funds individual supports in line with the child's assessed needs, not entire programs designed by providers. Griffith University autism researcher Jessica Painter previously worked for AEIOU. The associate professor says benchmarking shows the centres had positive outcomes and their closure is unacceptable. By cutting funds from one place, such as NDIS, we're only going to increase costs in other places, such as mental health, emergency wards or education settings. The agency running the NDIS says it has worked closely with families affected by the closures to assist children to transition to alternative services. Dimitri's dad says his son's behaviour deteriorated after his centre shut. He's since enrolled the five-year-old in a special school, an option not open to parents with younger children. It is grossly unfair because it is the children, ultimately, who suffer. Queensland father Eric Moore, ending that report by Emma Pollard. The leadership of UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer is under pressure as the fallout over the appointment and subsequent sacking of Peter Mandelson as ambassador to Washington, widens. A senior civil servant was blamed and fired for not informing the Prime Minister Mandelson had failed to pass security vetting. But the controversy has emboldened critics of Keir Starmer, who was already under political pressure. Stephanie Smale reports. The probe into how Labor power broker Peter Mandelson was appointed the British ambassador to the US, despite concerns about his past, continues. And the now former Foreign Office boss says there was pressure to make it happen, coming from the top. I'm afraid I walked into a situation in which there was already a very, very strong expectation coming from number 10 that he needed to be in post and in America as quickly as humanly possible. Sir Ollie Robbins was sacked last week after it emerged his department had granted Lord Mandelson security clearance in January 2025. Lord Mandelson formally took up the role the following month, but was sacked seven months later over his ties to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. episodes.title: Iran won't commit to peace talks
episodes.description: JD Vance heading to Pakistan for peace talks - it's unclear if Iran is attending but Donald Trump's warning he won't extend the ceasefire if there's no deal.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Good morning. Welcome to AM. It's Tuesday the 21st of April. I'm Melissa Clark in Canberra, coming to you from Ngunnawal country and acknowledging other custodians. The Middle East ceasefire hangs in the balance this morning, with Iran refusing to commit to a second round of peace talks with the United States. Iran's foreign ministry is citing what it describes as repeated US violations of the fragile truce as the reason. As the end of the ceasefire nears, the Strait of Hormuz remains closed with no clear pathway to peace. Nonetheless, Donald Trump has told the US media he's willing to meet with Iranian leaders if a breakthrough is reached during talks. Middle East correspondent Matthew Doran is in Jerusalem for us this morning. Mel, good morning. It does appear that Iran is delaying showing its hand here. It doesn't want to necessarily say that it is going to take part in these talks, even though there does appear to be some willingness and at least some back-channeling happening, wrangling happening behind the scenes to ensure that an Iranian delegation does travel to Pakistan in the next 24 hours or so. The official word which is being put out by people like the spokesperson for the Iranian foreign ministry, Esmail Begehi, is that the US continues to show aggression. It continues to violate the ceasefire by doing things such as blockading the Strait of Hormuz and Iranian ports and vessels there. And as a result, there isn't a lot of goodwill or a lot of intention from Iran to take what the US is saying in these negotiations and move forward. Masoud Perzeshkian, who is the Iranian president, has gone so far as to say that there is deep historical distrust between the two sides and that continues even through this process. So there really is this confusion as to whether or not these talks are going to go ahead. And that position was best summed up by Esmail Begehi, the Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson, when he made an address to the media a couple of hours ago. We're still in a state of war. It's true a ceasefire has been announced, but unfortunately, it's been met from the very beginning with repeated violations by the United States. And the announcement that Iran's ports and vessels would be targeted by the US has further complicated the situation. So Esmail Begehi from the Iranian foreign ministry there. So Matt, what could this mean for the region? Well, Mel, it means that the entire region is really in a state of anxiety at the moment as to what could come next. And again, the big C word that is lingering here, confusion, certainly abounds. We know that if we are to look at the ceasefire as a purely a fortnight of this pause in hostilities, that means that the ceasefire would be lapsing in the very early hours of Wednesday morning local time. So before 9am Australian Eastern time on Wednesday morning. However, we have also just heard from the US President Donald Trump in an interview with Bloomberg suggesting that the truce will not lapse until Wednesday night, Washington time, which takes it into Thursday Australia time. Again, this confusion as to exactly how long it's going to last, what will happen then? Will it be a return to fighting that we saw over the course of six weeks? Donald Trump seeming to suggest, yes, that is the case. There's also mixed messaging as to whether or not the US is going to send its delegation to Pakistan if this top level Iranian delegation doesn't go. And that means the US Vice President, J.D. Vance, he is having to effectively keep his diary open before jumping on Air Force Two and making that journey as well. This shows just how tight these negotiations are going to come down to the wire. Even if we don't get a deal in the next short while, the next couple of days, on a lasting peace in this war, there was a hope that at least this ceasefire could be extended. And at the moment, both of them are looking very, very unlikely as we speak this morning. Matthew Doran in Jerusalem there. Back home, supermarket giant Woolworths will face the courts today for a major trial. It's being sued in the federal court by the consumer watchdog over allegations it misled shoppers with fake discounts on hundreds of items. Woolworths is defending the case. National Consumer Affairs reporter Michael Atkin has more. Stella Kelly has noticed her regular shop in a Woolworths store in Melbourne's northeast is costing more. I look at what I'm spending between my partner and I in our shops that we do. And you're shopping for two people and a dog. But it looks significantly, when you buy a full week's worth of groceries, it's minimum $200, which is a lot. The 26-year-old is keen to see if the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission can prove its case against the supermarket giant, which alleges it misled shoppers with fake discounts on 266 items. 100%. Everybody's feeling the pinch, I think, at the moment. It's good to know that someone else is looking out for the everyday person. Former ACCC boss Alan Fels believes the economic shock caused by the Iran conflict means the public will be paying close attention. Consumers have never been more aware in the last 20 years of prices, price rises as they are now, and that will affect the atmospherics of the Woolworths case. It's the second major legal case against the two big supermarket chains over very similar allegations of misleading discounts, with a judgement involving Coles eagerly weighted. The Woolworths case is the sequel to the Coles case of the century. The ACCC is doubling down, down, down on Woolworths. This is episode two of the series Bogus Business Discounts. There's probably quite a few more episodes to come with non-supermarket businesses. The Consumer Watchdogs lawsuit claims Woolworths spiked the prices of products, making them at least 15% more expensive for 45 days or less, before selling them at a reduced price on a prices drop promotion. However, the ACCC alleges while customers were told they were saving money, they were really being charged more or the same as the original price, making the discount illusory. Consumer law expert Jeannie Patterson says Woolworths has rejected those claims, arguing customers were given a legitimate discount. Woolworths defence is that prices change. The price rise in question occurred over a time of inflation. The price rise was initiated by its suppliers. The price went up, time of inflation, it then went down. The discount is genuine, it's off a previous price. She believes the stakes are significant. If Woolworths loses, it faces a massive fine, a class action payout and huge reputational damage. But if it defeats the case, there could be blowback for the consumer watchdog. I think many people would say the pricing games that supermarkets have been playing with their campaigns may not pass the pub test. But whether it's against the law is not so clear. So it's a really litmus test of how far the law goes and how far the regulator goes. Woolworths told AM that after the COVID pandemic, there was rampant inflation that put pressure on suppliers and it maintains the prices drop program tried to reduce the impact on customers and wasn't misleading. The federal court case is expected to run eight days. Michael Atkin reporting there with Lucy Kent. Labor MP Ed Husic says it'll be a missed opportunity if the federal government doesn't use the upcoming budget to put a new tax on gas exports. A parliamentary inquiry will look into the topic today as the proposal gains momentum in the community. But the industry is warning higher taxes could end up impacting the nation's security. Evelyn Manfield reports from Parliament House. The debate about whether or not Australia should impose a new gas tax is about to heat up. A parliamentary inquiry is beginning today due to report ahead of the budget in three weeks' time. If it doesn't happen in this budget, it's not a lost opportunity, it's a missed one. That's Labor MP Ed Husic who, from the backbench, wants the government to impose a new 25% tax on gas exports. People think that a lot of these multinational gas companies have had an obscenely sweet deal for way too long and the country has been the poorer for it. According to him, there's growing support from both Labor MPs and rank and file party members, as well as the community more broadly. It's something that we should be standing up and fighting for and particularly the Labor Party. I think this is something that for average Australians, it speaks to them and that we should be the champions of this change. He wants the tax applied to uncontracted gas, which is gas that's not locked into long-term sales agreements, to help boost the amount of gas for Australians. episodes.description: With negotiators heading back to Islamabad for peace talks, Donald Trump again threatens Iran to make a deal or face devastating consequences.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Good morning. Welcome to AM. It's Monday the 20th of April. I'm Melissa Clark in Canberra, coming to you from Ngunnawal country and acknowledging other custodians. The United States is preparing for another round of talks about a possible end to the war in Iran. Vice President J.D. Vance will be in Pakistan later today for more negotiations, though Iranian state media has cast doubt on the regime's participation. But before talks can even begin, tensions have escalated, with President Donald Trump posting on social media that the US Navy has taken custody of an Iranian cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman. The ABC's America's editor, John Lyons, is in Washington. John, realistically, could we be looking at moves towards the end of the war with another round of peace talks apparently about to get underway? Well, Melissa, I think it is possible that there could be a peace deal this week, although obviously nobody can be sure. This situation is very fluid. It's fast moving. There's now the reports that the US Navy has intercepted and seized an Iranian-flared cargo ship coming through. President Trump has talked about that, which is obviously a deterioration in that sense. However, this will be the second face-to-face meeting that Vice President Vance has in Pakistan with Iranian officials. I don't think that Vice President would accept to go unless there's a serious possibility of a breakthrough. It would be humiliating to twice have to return to the United States, having been seen to have failed to come up with any agreement. What's been happening behind the scenes is the Pakistanis, Egypt, Syria, Saudi Arabia have all been trying to broker a deal. In fact, the Pakistani military senior officials have been shuttling between Islamabad, Tehran and Washington DC to come up with this to lay the groundwork for it. So yes, it's a possibility, but of course, we can't assume it's going to happen until it's done. So how much does President Trump want to see the end of the war? What's the level of motivation there on the US side? He very much wants to see an end to the war, but I think the real story of what's happening at the moment is there's a monumental power struggle, an extraordinary military and diplomatic arm wrestle going on between the United States and Iran. Donald Trump had assumed clearly, because he's commander in chief of the most powerful military in human history, that what he said would happen. For example, he said that after Iran and the US agreed that they would reopen the Strait of Hormuz for a period, Donald Trump later, almost as an afterthought, said, but your ships can't come through. Everybody else's ships can. The Iranians had the view, we brokered this deal, therefore we're not going to allow our ships not to come through, and they reclosed it. Donald Trump's not used to not getting his way, and I think he's realising that Iran is a tougher negotiator than he had assumed. What is the latest status of the Strait of Hormuz and the passage of vessels through that strait that is what the rest of the world is keeping an eye on? Well, at the moment, the Strait of Hormuz, which of course 20% of the world's energy goes through is in chaos. Now, the Iranians see this as their single best and perhaps only real negotiating leverage, and so they're guarding that like anything. But the bottom line is that at the moment, nothing of any significance is moving through. So the world's energy crisis deteriorates by the day, and the Iranians know that puts huge pressure on Donald Trump. His polling is going down, for example, with non-college educated whites in the United States. That's one of his strongholds. His approval rating is tanking. They did a joint Fox, CNN and CBS. They put all of those polls together. He's in deep political trouble, and he knows that, and he wants an end to this war quickly. John Lyons in Washington there. Patrick Clausen is the Director of the Iran Program at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. He joined me earlier. Patrick Clausen, thanks very much for speaking to me this morning. Happy to do it. What's at stake for the US with this second round of talks with Iran? Well, the big question is whether or not Iran can be counted on to follow through on commitments that the United States thinks Iran has made. And this whole episode of a foreign minister saying, oh, the Straits of Hormuz is open, and then other parts of the government saying, well, not so fast, suggests that decision-making in Iran is not so clear and not so efficient. And the US has to worry about whether or not Iran would follow through on other parts of any accord that might be agreed to. So what outcome would be acceptable to the Iranian regime, do you think, given that they've now seen the power that they can wield by controlling the Strait of Hormuz? Well, I think the Iranian government's hardliners certainly want to see the US blockade on Iranian ships lifted. And they will also insist that Iran has a considerable say over what happens in the Strait. Maybe not tolls, maybe not permission, but a considerable Iranian influence over what happens in the Strait. And then, of course, there's other issues like the nuclear program, where, again, Iran will want to have things going a considerable way towards what it's demanded. Much has been made of the gulf between what Iran wants out of these talks and what America wants. Do you think there is enough motivation from both parties to be able to bridge that gap? Certainly, there are important voices in the United States and in Iran who want to see that gap bridged. But there are also important voices in Iran who think that the military confrontation was working to Iran's advantage and would like to see it resumed. How that's going to play out in a situation where decision-making in Iran is no longer centralized in the hands of the supreme leader the way it used to be, it's not clear what's going to happen.
