episodes.title: Israel and Lebanon agree to temporary ceasefire
episodes.description: US President Donald Trump says the leaders of Israel and Lebanon have agreed to a 10-day ceasefire.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Good morning. Welcome to AM. It's Friday the 17th of April. I'm Melissa Clark in Canberra, coming to you from Ngunnawal country and acknowledging other custodians. US President Donald Trump says the leaders of Israel and Lebanon have agreed to a 10-day ceasefire, starting from this morning, Australian time. It would bring a temporary end to hostilities in Lebanon, with Israel's campaign against Iranian-backed militant group Hezbollah killing more than 2,000 people. It also now removes a major hurdle for possible peace talks between the US and Iran, which President Trump says could happen soon. ABC correspondent Tim Swanston is in Dubai. Tim, talk us through what President Trump said when announcing this ceasefire. Well, Mel, there's been a lot of speculation that some kind of ceasefire could be announced. There's reports that Israel's been pressured by Washington to declare a ceasefire in Lebanon. That's particularly after the historic meeting in Washington earlier this week between representatives from Israel and Lebanon. I guess it's important to note, though, at this stage that Israel has been fighting with Hezbollah, not with Lebanon. At any rate, though, this post on social media by President Trump said that he'd just had excellent conversations with the highly respected Lebanese President Joseph Oun, as well as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel, said that these two leaders have agreed that in order to achieve peace between their countries, they'll formally begin a 10-day ceasefire. He also added that he's going to be inviting the pair to the White House for meaningful talks. He says the first meaningful talks between Israel and Lebanon since 1983. But ultimately, this could bring a temporary end to hostilities. Israel launched its attacks on Lebanon after Hezbollah fired on Israel in solidarity with Iran and the start of the war on Iran. But that's led to an extensive ground campaign in Lebanon, which, according to its health ministry, has killed more than 2,100 people. So where does this leave things with the wider war? Because, of course, this flashpoint has been critical in the talks between the US and Iran. Yeah, it really does sort of leave a little bit of clearer air, I guess, between the United States and Iran. You know, Pakistan, the mediator between the US and Iran, had said that this was a crucial sticking point, really, for the US and Iran to come together to achieve a peace agreement to end the war. We have, though, recently heard from United States President Donald Trump that he appears he's quite optimistic, you know, that a deal could be reached in the coming days. He said that the Iran war may be nearing an end. He was speaking just outside the White House and he said that Iran had offered not to have nuclear weapons for more than two decades. He also said that he didn't think that a ceasefire necessarily needed to be extended because he believed that Iran wanted to make a deal. So certainly he's really leaving the door wide open there for there to be a return to Islamabad, Pakistan, for there to be further talks between the United States and Iran. But meanwhile, that blockade continues of Iran's coastlines and ports. We've also heard earlier from US Secretary of Defence that the United States remained locked and loaded if Iran didn't make a deal. So while they're really leaving the door open to an agreement there, they've stepped up the rhetoric that if Iran doesn't make an agreement, that the US is ready to return to war. Tim Swanston in Dubai there. Australia's newly unveiled defence strategy has been heralded by the federal government as a commitment to preparedness and self-reliance in the face of a dangerous decade ahead. But a former chief of the Defence Force is calling for elements of the plan to be overhauled, saying it does not recognise Australia's closest ally could pose the greatest risk. Here's political reporter Lexi Juniwik. Australia's national defence strategy set out to equip the Defence Force of today for the challenges of the future. But a former chief of the ADF believes it's missed the mark. Well, I'm not saying the whole plan goes down the gurgle of it, but I am saying that strategic assumptions which underpin this plan need to be redone to take account of what a changing world is delivering for our security. Retired Admiral Chris Barry, who was also founder of the Australian Security Leaders Climate Group, suspects the government largely constructed the latest national defence strategy prior to the US-Israeli strikes on Iran. The government's plan as delivered talks about risks, but it doesn't talk about the United States potentially being the largest risk. And it then goes on to talk about the foundations of our alliance relationship and how valuable it is and so on. I think that is all now under question and it needs to be redone. Peter Dean is a professor of strategic studies at the Australian National University and worked on the 2023 Defence Strategic Review. I'm Rachel Mealy coming to you from the lands of the Turbul and Yaghera people in Brisbane. A major fire is burning at one of Australia's only operating oil refineries. The blaze broke out last night at Viva Energy's Geelong facility, 75 kilometres south-west of Melbourne and is still burning out of control. The facility supplies more than 50% of Victoria's fuel and 10% of Australia's. Our reporter Kathleen O'Connor is covering the story. Rachel, the fire is large and it's been burning since around 11 o'clock last night, producing flames of up to 50 metres in height. There's also been several explosions, according to Fire Rescue Victorian authorities. Around 50 firefighters have been on scene all night putting water on the fire, but with it being an oil plant, it's been difficult for them to bring it under control. Now, the Viva Energy refinery is Victoria's only oil refinery, supplying approximately 50% of the state's fuel. It's one of just two refineries remaining in Australia, employing over 1,100 people. Authorities from Fire Rescue Victoria say the blaze started in the MOGAS plant. Now, MOGAS stands for motor gasoline. So it's the section of the refinery that produces petrol or unleaded premium gasoline, things that motorists can get at the Bowser. I spoke to Fire Rescue Victoria's Chief Assistant Fire Officer Michael McGinnis a short time ago. This is what he had to say. There's been some sort of leak of hydrocarbon, some of the liquids, which had very readily caught fire. And it has now been quite a major fire. It's been burning all night and still is burning. We're likely to be here for several more hours. It depends on how we can continue our combat and firefighting strategies, and that's by slowly isolating pipe work and some of the plant area that's feeding hydrocarbons into this fire. It's also not the first fire at the plant. It had a significant fire last year due to failing pumps. Fire Rescue Victoria's Chief Assistant Fire Officer Michael McGinnis says it's still quite unclear how much fuel is still in there, but it could burn for hours. But the intensity has decreased, which is a good sign. And Kathleen, obviously fuel supply is on everyone's minds right now. Is this likely to impact the country's fuel supply? Yeah, Rachel, look, people are obviously very worried about this, and it could very well put further pressure on the current fuel crisis. We just don't know yet. The company was ordered to boost output by the state government due to supply pressures about a month ago. It's unclear just how much fuel has been lost as a result of the fire, but authorities say they've been told by the company Viva that there's no immediate impact on fuel supply at this point. In terms of the damage caused, it will take some time for fire crews to bring the fire under control before an investigation is launched. Victoria Police will also be involved in that investigation, looking into how this could have happened and what overall impact this will have on the country's fuel supply. And before I let you go, because of those heightened tensions in the world right now, I have to ask, is sabotage something that police will look into? Yeah, Rachel, authorities say that they're not treating it as suspicious at this stage, but investigators will be looking at everything. Kathleen O'Connor. As that fire threatens to worsen the situation, the Prime Minister, Anthony Albanese, continues his tour of Southeast Asia to shore up fuel supplies. Here's political reporter Lexi Juniwick. Ben Bennett's dairy farm in southwest Victoria is a world away from the war in the Middle East, but the impact of the conflict is hitting home for the farmer. You know, we're not sitting here swimming in cash, like it's particularly this time of year, coming out of summer, going into autumn, and we're sort of all hanging out for the autumn break. And on that basis, we need fertiliser, particularly in the form of urea, which is quite common for the far majority of dairy farmers. That's gone from $800 a tonne to $1,800 a tonne. In a bid to better equip Aussie exporters and importers with the ongoing shipping and cargo disruptions stemming from the war, the federal government has activated a new service providing real-time logistics advice to businesses. Trade Minister Don Farrell says the initiative will offer up advanced systems used by the government. What this system will do is, in real time, look at alternative ways of getting your products into that market or bringing the products to Australia. Farmer Ben Bennett, who also heads up Australian dairy farmers, isn't convinced the measure will make a difference. Well, I suppose the analogy is, we've got a freight train that's going to run us over, and now he's just giving us a better view of the freight train that's coming at us. But the Export Council of Australia, which represents thousands of exporters and international trade professionals, can see the value. Its CEO is Arnold Jorge. Exporters, what they want right now is straight, timely information about what's happening in terms of the shipping, air routes, sanctions, the market risk. They also want government agencies working off the same page, so the advice is consistent. The National Farmers' Federation's president, Hamish McIntyre, is also welcoming the initiative. We also need the federal government to keep looking laterally and looking for new opportunities that we can obviously enter into and markets that we may be able to start providing for due to what's going on around the world. The Australian government is set to join more than 40 other countries at an upcoming international summit led by the United Kingdom and France, focused on safeguarding shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. As the world grapples with the current uncertainty, the CEO of the Export Council of Australia is urging the Treasurer to provide exporters with targeted support in the upcoming budget. The messaging that's being received at the moment is that the government is focused on budget repair, for example. And unfortunately what that means is that they're now fearful that whatever support that might still exist there is going to be shut or reprioritised or put to something else. And that will actually literally pull the rug from under them. Arnold Jorge from the Export Council of Australia ending that report from Lexi Juniwik. Another interest rate rise is looking more likely for Australians next month. The International Monetary Fund has painted a grim picture, warning of a rise in inflation and a global recession, depending on how long the Middle East war continues. Isabel Massali reports. Asha Golding's life is a little different ever since fuel prices and interest rates started to climb this year. Her partner has a fly-in-fly-out job and used to work the occasional week away. Now he's away two or three weeks at a time. And we work as a team, but the reality is that our family feels that absence and that's the hardest part. The mother of three is juggling her own work as a nurse in regional New South Wales. I've always believed life should be about thriving and not just surviving. This impending interest rate is one expected bill away from everything becoming overwhelming. The public may also be overwhelmed by the International Monetary Fund's latest economic outlook, which considers the impact of the Middle East crisis under different scenarios. National Australia Bank Chief Economist Sally Auld explains. Yeah, so it makes a pretty sobering reading. And, you know, they have done to their forecasts what most economists are doing to their own forecasts. And that in very simple terms is they have cut their growth forecasts for the global economy, but also increase their inflation forecasts. Dr Auld says the Reserve Bank of Australia will also be looking at its own forecasts. They'll be revising up forecasts for inflation here in Australia and inflation globally, and they'll be also revising down growth forecasts domestically and globally. But the IMF is pretty clear on saying that, you know, central banks have got to be vigilant. They've got to be prepared to act clearly and decisively, you know, in line with their mandates. That could mean lifting interest rates. So we're still forecasting an interest rate rise from the Reserve Bank in May. And I think it's fair to say with everything going on in the world, you know, it's hard to have a huge amount of conviction in that view. But I think we anchor back to this idea that for Australia, the starting point for inflation was already a bit unfavourable before the war happened. Paul Bloxham agrees. He's HSBC's Chief Economist for Australia and New Zealand. So what this does is it makes it clear that the challenge is even more difficult to deal with, because inflation is likely to be even higher than was expected. And growth is going to be weaker. And so the RBA has some difficult, tricky choices on their hands. And we think, at least in the first instance, the RBA is going to have to focus on the high inflation challenge. And so we think they'll end up lifting interest rates. And he warns that challenge remains even if the war ends soon. There's a long tail from the effects of already what's been, what's happened. So a part of that stems from the fact that you've already blocked supply of all the things that come out of the Middle East for a little over six weeks already. The RBA's next board meeting will be in early May. Isabel Massali reporting. Australia's defence spending is set to climb by $53 billion over the next decade as the federal government responds to intensifying global risks. But is it enough to keep Australia safe? Defence correspondent Tom Lowry joined me earlier. Tom, is this spending increase likely to satisfy those who've been calling for significant hikes? Look, Rachel, it is a significant lift in spending, both $14 billion over the next four years. So that's one spending that's going to land on the budget papers when that's handed down next month. And $53 billion over the decade proper. And in the context of a budget where the government's looking to constrain spending, not hike it, those are certainly big numbers. But the short answer is probably not. The US, for example, has been asking allies like Australia to lift spending to 3.5% of GDP. That's the message Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth gave to Australia's Defence Minister, Richard Miles, when they met in Singapore last year in person. So it does fall short there, I suppose, of that benchmark still. The government says this spending hike will get it to 3% of GDP. And that's calculated using what it's calling the NATO methodology. And look, this gets a bit technical, but traditionally when we've measured Defence spending in Australia, we've measured direct Defence spending. And on that score, we're currently at around 2% of GDP. When NATO measures Defence spending, they include other things like Defence pensions and housing subsidies. And the government says when you use those figures, you can get to 3% of GDP by 2033 with this new funding the government has announced. But look, that is still unlikely to satisfy those critics, both in the US but also domestically. The Coalition, for example, and some Defence analysts have said Australia needs to get to 3% of GDP on Defence spending, but they're arguing for direct spending, not for these other sorts of bits of funding from around the budget to be added in. So what's on the shopping list, Tom? What's this new funding going to buy? Oh, look, Rachel, as I said, there is a lot of new money coming into Defence through this announcement. You know, $14 billion over four years, 53 billion over 10 years. That is a fair bit of cash. And there is still a bit of detail to come today when the Defence strategy is handed down around lunchtime that'll outline all of that. But we do know a few things. For example, money going into AUKUS-related projects, $12 billion to upgrade the Henderson shipyards in WA. That was announced late last year, and that's included in these new figures. There's a few billion in funding for drone technology that was announced earlier this week. The government says it's looking at a few different things too. Alternative financing is one thing it's mentioned. That's taking equity in companies. You know, for example, just as a bit of speculation, perhaps small drone companies in Australia to help get them off the ground. Another big question we're still waiting to see answered is reprioritisations. This is something the government has flagged as hard decisions that need to be made to perhaps axe or scale back or delay some Defence projects too. We're going to see a bit of that today. So that's something to look out for too. Defence correspondent Tom Lowry. Palestinians in Gaza fear they've been forgotten as the broader Middle East deals with the war between the US, Israel and Iran. It's now more than six months since the ceasefire between Israel and Hamas was agreed to, but Israeli strikes continue to be launched in the war-ravaged strip. And even Donald Trump's hand-picked envoy for Gaza is warning the humanitarian crisis remains dire. Middle East correspondent Matthew Doran reports. In a tent community south of Deir al-Bala, another deadly Israeli strike hits an already devastated community. Palestinians running to safety, carrying the dead and the injured. This is the biggest proof that the war is not over. 46-year-old Rana Khedera and her family have been living in the tent camp that was hit. Her fragile shelter all but destroyed, forcing her to seek refuge with neighbours also living in tents. Wherever we go, there are strikes. In the streets, at home, also the place we rented was struck. You don't know where you can go to. Since the ceasefire began last October, Palestinian health authorities say around 760 people have been killed in Israeli strikes and many more injured. Israel claiming it's targeting Hamas militants, not civilians, even though many women, children and the elderly are listed among the dead. But it's not only missiles that pose a threat. 55-year-old Fatima Hamdonna is trying to keep her tent dry. Heavy winter rains lasting later into the year than usual have flooded these camps. As you can see, we have been soaked in water and our mattresses are soaked, our clothes are soaked, our tent is soaked. I need a proper tent like the ones from Wood. I need food, I need water. I want to live. I want my life to be clean. It's a simple plea which many fear is going unheard with the world's attention elsewhere. Nikolai Mladenov, the man appointed as high representative for Gaza by the US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace, making this call to the United Nations late last month. As tensions in the region escalate, we should not lose sight of the situation in Gaza. Mohammed Abu Jiyab is an economist and newspaper editor in Gaza. He says at the height of the Iran war, Israel imposed more restrictions on the flow of aid into the strip. The rise in prices is noticeable in the local markets in Gaza. Mohammed argues it's putting extra strain on the local economy, with most industries, including agriculture, decimated over years of war. For part of the Iranian war, the Rafa border crossing to Egypt was also shut down, with Palestinians wanting to leave unable to pass. Dr Khalil Dedran is a spokesperson for Gaza's Ministry of Health. We have in the Gaza Strip more than 20,000 sick and wounded that are in need of medical treatment outside Gaza. Israel has repeatedly rejected accusations it's failing to let enough aid into the strip, insisting sufficient supplies are crossing the border. It's also continued to argue it's facilitating medical evacuations. But in Gaza's tent camps, Fatima Hamdona worries it's only going to get worse. We have been forgotten. No one is caring about us. No one is looking for us. Who is looking after us? This is Matthew Doran in Jerusalem, reporting for AM. Insurance premiums are skyrocketing across the country, but some Australians are facing up to 500% spikes in their premiums. It's led a handful of Queensland councils to become insurers themselves to try to drive down the prices. Grace Nakamura reports. In southern Queensland, the Belon River is vital for farmers and treasured by the St George Township. It's bloody second to none living out somewhere like this. Adam Osborne has lived by the river for a decade. All these residents all use this body of water. I think down here on the weekend there was five or six boats plus kayaks the locals all fishing. You know, it's just all getting along. But the Belon River can flood dramatically. Levy banks have been built to try to protect the town, but insurance premiums are surging regardless. When we went to renew our policy, the figure that we were paying somehow went through the roof to thousands of dollars compared to what we were paying. Adam Osborne's annual home insurance premium has been $7,000. This year, he was quoted about $60,000. No one in their right mind can afford that sort of thing. It's a wage, effectively, isn't it, for one of us in the household. So that makes it very difficult to live, especially with the cost of living these days. He's just one of many residents hit by skyrocketing premiums since 2020. Belon Shire Mayor Samantha O'Toole chairs Queensland's Southwest Regional Organization of Councils. I often get told that now people's insurance payments are greater than their mortgage, so it's really staggering. In 2024, the council submitted dozens of examples of rising premiums to the Senate inquiry into the impact of climate risk on insurance. She's doubtful that insurers are taking expensive measures like flood levies into consideration. An insurance council spokesperson said individual insurers determine prices and risk reduction is taken into account. They said insurers are working with the Queensland Reconstruction Authority on strengthening flood resilience to put downward pressure on premiums. And the insurance council says the industry is facing higher payouts to cover the 40% rise in construction costs since 2020. But Councillor O'Toole is sceptical. Obviously there's inflation and other things, but we firmly believe there's a bit of proud scourging in the market. So the six southern regional Queensland councils are taking matters into their own hands and becoming insurers themselves. So we started to think creatively, you know, what are the other solutions that are out in the market, things that have been done elsewhere that we could look at, hence the idea of a community protection mutual and how we could progress that. The councils have engaged international insurance broker JLT to draw up a proposal with a feasibility study expected within weeks. Grace Nakamura. And that's AM for today. Thanks for your company. I'm Rachel Mealy. Hi, I'm Sam Hawley, host of the ABC News Daily podcast. Debate over the US leaders' mental health has reignited since he began verbally attacking the Pope and posted an AI image depicting himself as Jesus. Today, David A. Graham from The Atlantic magazine on what Trump's behaviour says about his ability to govern. Look for the ABC News Daily podcast on ABC Listen. of the ABC News

episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Good morning. Welcome to AM. It's Wednesday the 15th of April. I'm Rachel Mealy coming to you from the lands of the Turbul and Yagora people in Brisbane. A dire scenario predicting long-term scarring of the world's economy. In its latest World Economic Outlook report, the IMF has produced three scenarios that get progressively worse depending on how long Middle East energy supplies are disrupted. Shane Oliver is Chief Economist at AMP. He joined me a short time ago. Shane Oliver, the IMF has warned the war in Iran has turned the global economy upside down and the resulting inflation pressures could take years to overcome. Is Australia headed for recession? Look, it's not my base case, but it's certainly a risk. And I think the IMF is simply reflecting that risk. The reality is that the clock is ticking. There's talk of more talks between the US and Iran. But the key is that the flow of oil out of the Middle East needs to start up again pretty soon to avoid the recession scenario because the reality is it's now starting to bite. Over the last six weeks, countries, including Australia, have still been getting oil because of the ships that had been coming out of the Middle East and got a refinery process and they arrive in Australia. But eventually that will stop. There will be less oil going into refineries in Asia and therefore less refined product available to come to Australia. So that's a serious risk. And the longer the crisis continues, the blockage continues, the greater the risk that we do slide into recession as we have to eventually cut back on fuel usage. The IMF paints a picture of stagflation. What is that and what does it mean for Australians? Well, stagflation is a phenomenon that was quite common in the 1970s. And of course, that was partly related to oil shocks at the time. That's a situation where you have a supply side shock to an economy that pushes up prices and constrains economic activity at the same time. So you end up with both higher inflation and lower economic growth, possibly recession and higher unemployment occurring simultaneously. We have experienced little bits of that over the years, but it hasn't been a common phenomenon like it was in the 1970s. And the reality is that we are heading for some, at least a mild form of stagflation. Economists have already been revising up their inflation forecast. General talkers of inflation going up to around 5% could be higher if the situation in the Middle East isn't resolved quickly. And then, of course, at the same time, as Australians have to fork out more for fuel, they will cut back their spending. And if we get to a point where we're actually restricted in our fuel use, then that could actually cut back economic activity even further. And then you get a combination of higher inflation and weaker growth. With a federal budget now just weeks away, how would Treasury officials be factoring this into their budget this year? Look, I think this is a really difficult time for policymakers like the government and the Treasury, just as it is for the Reserve Bank, because you've got this double-edged sword hitting the economy. On the one hand, higher inflation pressures, and on the other hand, a hit to economic activity at the same time. So, I think the – and, of course, federal government needs to be careful because – as does the Reserve Bank, because you don't know how long the crisis is going to go for. If we overreact and do the wrong thing in the short term, you could damage things in the longer term. I suspect that the budget probably will, and the government seems to be heading in this direction, announce more cost-of-living support. The key is that that support be timely, impacts fairly quickly, temporary, and targeted. In other words, that it doesn't blow budget spending out indefinitely, and that it's also targeted to those who actually need it, particularly low- and middle-income earners and those businesses that are most affected potentially by fuel shortages, along with high fuel costs. So, we probably will see an element of that in the budget, but longer term, I think the government has to continue to focus on ways to boost productivity in the economy because the reality is that the global economy has become more fraught. You can't align at being stable, as we found out over the last few years, and therefore we have to improve our own game, and that means make it easier for Australian businesses to employ people and make things. AMP Chief Economist Shane Oliver. U.S. President Donald Trump has foreshadowed a possible return to peace talks with Iran. His latest comments have come as Israel and Lebanon met for historic talks in Washington, D.C. But even the U.S. mediators have acknowledged it's only the beginning of a long process. The Iran-backed militia Hezbollah was not party to the talks and says it will not abide by any resulting agreement. Shantel Al-Khoury is in our Washington Bureau. She joined me earlier. Well, these direct talks between Lebanon and Israel are highly unusual. They concluded around two hours, but any sort of big breakthrough at this meeting was always going to be highly unlikely. Now, after the meeting, the U.S. put out a statement saying that the talks covered the prospect of future direct negotiations. They said the participants held productive discussions on steps towards launching direct negotiations between Israel and Lebanon. Now, Lebanon went into this discussion wanting a ceasefire for Israel's attacks on the country to stop. Those attacks have killed more than 2,000 people and displaced more than 1.1 million since March. And Israel has been ramping up those strikes and its invasion since the war in Iran began. Israel, on the other hand, says it wants to disarm Hezbollah and says there will be no ceasefire with the group. Hezbollah is not party to these talks that have happened today. In a practical sense, Lebanon wouldn't be able to disarm Hezbollah. It does not have control over the group. I've been speaking to the International Crisis Group, who says that Israel and the U.S. have been aggressively pushing for that disarmament of Hezbollah and for the Lebanese government to take steps that would essentially, potentially trigger a civil war. It also says that these talks today are a useful vehicle for the U.S. to be able to manage the progress between Israel and Lebanon, given Israel's attacks are for them standing in the way of its already fragile ceasefire arrangement with Iran. Now, Hezbollah has responded to these talks. Before they happened, they said that they wouldn't abide to any agreements that came out of the talks. It had been urging the Lebanese government to pull out of the talks as well, and we know that both Hezbollah and Israel have since continued their attacks. So how are people on the ground in both Lebanon and Israel feeling about the prospects of these talks? Well, for many Lebanese people, it's hugely controversial and divisive for Lebanon to be meeting with Israel at all. There was a lot of scepticism because they see little guarantee that a diplomatic agreement would stop Israel's strikes on the country. For people in Israel that the ABC has spoken to, they've said that they're exhausted by the fighting. They want a resolution. We've heard from some of those people in both Lebanon and Israel, from our colleagues who've spoken with them. Here's Michelle Keren, who lives in northern Israel. I hope it will be useful for Israel and for Lebanon. But in my opinion, I can't think that it will help because Hezbollah is more bigger than the government in Lebanon. They are not strong to bring a peace. But I hope they will bring something. We have to finish this. We also heard from many in Lebanon who our colleagues from the ABC have spoken to. This is Loretta Jajour in southern Lebanon. I hope that these negotiations in the end bring us to peace and safety, for us to finish with this war, not to reach negotiations or a ceasefire just for a few days like they did before. We had started to get our lives back, and now we're back to a war that's much harder than before. That's Loretta Jajour in southern Lebanon. And Chantel, Donald Trump is saying negotiations between the US and Iran could resume within days. Yeah, that's right. The US president says that talks with Iran could resume after both parties failed to come to any sort of agreement in Islamabad on the weekend. He told the New York Post that something could be happening over the next two days, and he says we're more inclined to go there. Now, Gulf, Pakistani and Iranian officials also said negotiating teams from the US and Iran could return to Pakistan later this week. We know the US has meanwhile continued its blockade on Iranian ports, and that most ships already weren't moving through the straits since Iran's closure over a month ago. We also know that the US Central Command says no ships have made it past its naval blockade of Iran's ports, and six merchant ships have followed orders to turn back. Shantel Alkoury in Washington. Australia's tourism sector is cautiously waiting to see the impact from a Qantas decision to cut back its flights and raise prices. Airlines across the world are struggling with the rising cost of jet fuel and a drop in demand from travellers. Qantas will temporarily suspend four regional routes from next month, while a fifth route has no return date. Isabel Massali reports. Sydney travel agent Helen George has been helping clients book flight routes that avoid the Middle East, but some no longer feel it's the right time for a holiday. I've had about 30% of my customers cancel their future travel, even though it's outside of the, what we call the disruption period, which was February, March and April. We're just finding that people now are just holding off making decisions in travelling to Europe. She hopes consumer confidence will bounce back soon, but that depends on the wall. We spend a lot of time just looking at the existing bookings, you know, talking through to our clients, reassuring them, maybe readjusting their itineraries. For me, it's uncharted waters. Australian Travel Industry Association CEO, Dean Long, has seen mixed consumer sentiment. Now there's a new challenge to navigate, with Qantas announcing it's made changes to its international network, increased fares and adjusted capacity, to mitigate the impact of the conflict and highly volatile jet fuel prices. Look, I think the reduction in the overall, the 5% reduction in the overall network size, is a response to the global impact on increased aviation fuel. It's good that it's 5%. The changes include a temporary suspension of four regional routes, but flights between Adelaide and Mount Gambier will stop next month until further notice. Affected customers are being offered alternative flights or refunds. The longer this conflict goes on, the higher the aviation fuel prices are maintained. There will be increased pressure on airlines to reduce their schedules to those profitable routes, and that will unfortunately have an inflationary impact on the price that people are paying for their airfares. The National Rural Health Alliance is less forgiving. Chief Executive Susie Teagan used to rely on flights out of Mount Gambier to access specialist health services for her child. Those communities like Mount Gambier are already challenged in terms of service provision, being able to access care, and access services that, you know, many people in the city take for granted. Shadow Transport Minister Bridget McKenzie has the same concerns. She says at a recent Senate inquiry, Qantas gave no indication that it was considering flight cancellations. Local travellers are going to be the ones that pay the price to keep Qantas international flights in the air, and that's a real kick in the guts for particularly rural and regional passengers who pay a higher price to access aviation services and a lower service provision. In a statement, a spokesperson for Transport Minister Catherine King said the government is focused on securing fuel supply and is engaging strongly across the aviation sector. That includes weekly fuel security meetings with key representatives from airlines. Isabel Massali reporting. The Coalition's new migration policy promises to lift Australia's immigration standards through measures including cutting migrant numbers and more intensive screening. But as Angus Taylor's first big test as opposition leader looms in next month's FARA by-election, a former Liberal Party strategist has warned the key to winning back voters shed to One Nation isn't necessarily through the issue of migration. Here's political reporter Lexi Juniwick. Coalition leader Angus Taylor has pledged to put Australian values at the heart of the opposition's new immigration policy, but that pitch does nothing to change the heart of 77-year-old Brisbane local Garth, who's currently considering supporting One Nation. Past governments and present governments will not even talk to each other in reference to our immigration policy. Have we got one? 61-year-old South Australian Vince, whose family migrated to Australia in the 1960s, now backs the minor party after voting for a major party his entire life. When you see the government throwing money away to things that don't involve us, that just, I don't know, like we've got so much mess in our own backyard, we need to clean that up first. The first instalment of the opposition's immigration policy was unveiled in a speech by Mr Taylor yesterday. The Coalition will make learning English an obligation for permanent visa holders, not an option. The plan also promises to reduce immigration, increase screening of visa applicants via a legally binding Australian values test, and boot out those who don't abide by Australian values with a deportation task force. But Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke describes it as a diatribe entirely about sending a vibe to One Nation. Independent MP Zali Stegall agrees. The Coalition is desperate for relevance. They are losing votes to One Nation. So rather than coming up with a sensible policy around areas like housing, like good tax reform, like good support for small businesses that are struggling, they've presented this dog whistle to try and attract back One Nation voters. Tony Barry from the Redbridge Group ending that report by Lexi Juniwik. Since Australia closed its refugee processing centres on Manus Island, the federal government has continued to give undisclosed sums of money to PNG to manage refugees there. the higher the aviation fuel prices are maintained.
There will be increased pressure on airlines to reduce their schedules to those profitable routes,
and that will unfortunately have an inflationary impact on the price that people are paying for their airfares.
The National Rural Health Alliance is less forgiving.
Chief Executive Susie Teagan used to rely on flights out of Mount Gambier
to access specialist health services for her child.
Those communities like Mount Gambier are already challenged
in terms of service provision, being able to access care,
and access services that, you know, many people in the city take for granted.
Shadow Transport Minister Bridget McKenzie has the same concerns.
She says at a recent Senate inquiry,
Qantas gave no indication that it was considering flight cancellations.
Local travellers are going to be the ones that pay the price
to keep Qantas international flights in the air,
and that's a real kick in the guts for particularly rural and regional passengers
who pay a higher price to access aviation services and a lower service provision.
In a statement, a spokesperson for Transport Minister Catherine King
said the government is focused on securing fuel supply
and is engaging strongly across the aviation sector.
That includes weekly fuel security meetings with key representatives from airlines.
Isabel Massali reporting.
The Coalition's new migration policy promises to lift Australia's immigration standards
through measures including cutting migrant numbers and more intensive screening.
But as Angus Taylor's first big test as opposition leader looms in next month's FARA by-election,
a former Liberal Party strategist has warned the key to winning back voters shed to One Nation
isn't necessarily through the issue of migration.
Here's political reporter Lexi Juniwick.
Coalition leader Angus Taylor has pledged to put Australian values
at the heart of the opposition's new immigration policy,
but that pitch does nothing to change the heart of 77-year-old Brisbane local Garth,
who's currently considering supporting One Nation.
Past governments and present governments will not even talk to each other in reference to our immigration policy.
Have we got one?
61-year-old South Australian Vince, whose family migrated to Australia in the 1960s,
now backs the minor party after voting for a major party his entire life.
When you see the government throwing money away to things that don't involve us,
that just, I don't know, like we've got so much mess in our own backyard,
we need to clean that up first.
The first instalment of the opposition's immigration policy was unveiled in a speech by Mr Taylor yesterday.
The Coalition will make learning English an obligation for permanent visa holders, not an option.
The plan also promises to reduce immigration, increase screening of visa applicants
via a legally binding Australian values test,
and boot out those who don't abide by Australian values with a deportation task force.
But Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke describes it as a diatribe entirely about sending a vibe to One Nation.
Independent MP Zali Stegall agrees.
The Coalition is desperate for relevance.
They are losing votes to One Nation.
So rather than coming up with a sensible policy around areas like housing,
like good tax reform, like good support for small businesses that are struggling,
they've presented this dog whistle to try and attract back One Nation voters.
Tony Barry is a former Liberal Party strategist and is now a director at Redbridge Group.
He says the Coalition's stance on migration
isn't necessarily the way to win back votes from One Nation,
which has seen the fastest polling rise in modern Australian politics.
I think there's certainly some political reward for having a strong policy on that issue,
but they're going to get more reward by having a stronger policy on cost of living, housing,
and probably tax reform is what underpins that.
A crucial test of Angus Taylor's leadership will materialise in the Farrer by-election in New South Wales next month.
Tony Barry predicts Independent Michelle Milthorpe and One Nation candidate David Farley
will be the main contenders for the seat,
most recently held by deposed Liberal leader Susan Lee for 25 years.
I think it will be a contest between the Teal Independent and the One Nation candidate,
which means that preferences will be incredibly important.
Tony Barry from the Redbridge Group ending that report by Lexi Juniwik.
Since Australia closed its refugee processing centres on Manus Island,
the federal government has continued to give undisclosed sums of money to PNG to manage refugees there.
But a hotel owner in the capital, Port Moresby, says he's owed over $11 million for housing the refugees,
claiming he hasn't been paid since 2021.
PNG correspondent Marion Farr reports.
When Australia began winding up its offshore processing centres on Manus Island in 2017,
hotel owner Mose Copioto struck a deal to accommodate some of them in Port Moresby.
We came into an understanding that they will pay me on a weekly basis.
He says the verbal agreement was reached with Australian Border Force officials,
and for a few years, Australia paid the bills directly to his hotel.
We have no problem. Business is smooth, normal. We're all happy.
But in 2021, things changed.
Australia announced it was ending its refugee program in Papua New Guinea,
and transferring responsibility for all remaining refugees to the PNG government.
That's when, according to Mose Copioto, the payments dried up.
He claims he's now owed over $11 million, and the debt continues to grow.
And it's really painful. It's really unfair.
This can't operate like that. We can't operate.
Mr Copioto has taken the PNG Immigration Department to court to claim the outstanding costs,
but the PNG government has denied responsibility.
Ralph Salip is the lawyer representing the hotel.
The refugees are still here. They're still being looked after.
But unfortunately, PNG Immigration Services has shifted the blame to Australia and said,
no, it's not us. We're not responsible. But Australia is responsible.
Today, the National Court of PNG will hear an application to make the Commonwealth of Australia
and the Department of Home Affairs defendants in the case.
But the matter has raised bigger questions about the funding Australia has given to PNG
to manage refugees.
So I would suggest to the Australian taxpayers that they ought to be asking themselves what Papua New Guinea
has done with the money that Australia has given to it.
While the exact amount has never been disclosed, the Australian government says it made a substantial
payment to PNG in 2021 and another in 2024.
Green Senator David Shoebridge predicts an eye-watering figure.
What we do know from history is that the so-called Pacific solution costs hundreds of millions here,
billions of dollars there.
In 2023, the PNG government announced an audit after allegations the refugee funds had been misused,
but the results have never been publicised.
Senator Shoebridge says the public deserves answers.
How much money has Australia given to the Papua New Guinea government for this cohort of men and their
families? And what is it that we're meant to be seen in return?
The Australian Department of Home Affairs told the ABC it doesn't have any role in the ongoing
management of individuals remaining in PNG.
Marion Farr, and that's AM for today.
Thanks for your company.
I'm Rachel Mealy.
Hi, it's Sam Hawley here, host of the ABC News Daily podcast.
What does Trump's blockade in the Strait of Hormuz mean for our fuel supply?
Well, it's not great.
Today, Sol Kavanick, energy expert at MST Financial,
on why we're facing a doomsday scenario that's been wargamed for decades.
Look for the ABC News Daily podcast on ABC Listen.
And I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like.
Thank you.

episodes.title: Trump's blockade begins
episodes.description: Donald Trump warns Iranian ships challenging his naval blockade will be taken out as he insists Tehran wants a deal 'very badly'.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Good morning. Welcome to AM. It's Tuesday the 14th of April. I'm Melissa Clark in Canberra, coming to you from Ngunnawal country and acknowledging other custodians. A United States blockade of Iranian ports and coastlines is now in effect after US President Donald Trump ordered the operation in response to Iran's control over the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has stepped up its threats in response, saying if its ports aren't safe, no ports in the region will be safe. Correspondent Tim Swanston filed this report. Mr President, are another round of talks planned with Iran? Just hours after what the US President described as a blockade of the Strait of Hormuz began, Donald Trump was quite vague about what he wanted it to achieve. Mr President, what's the endgame? Is it to force Iran back to the negotiating table? Is it to open up the Strait so the gas prices ultimately come down? Maybe everything. I mean, both of those things, certainly, and more. We can't let a country blackmail or extort the world. The US military announced in a note to seafarers that the US was enforcing a blockade of the Iranian coastline, including ports and oil terminals, and any vessel entering or departing the blockaded area without authorisation would be subject to interception, diversion and capture. The note said the blockade would not impede ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz to or from non-Iranian destinations. On Iranian state media, a TV anchor read a fiery statement by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps threatening Gulf countries if the US pressed ahead with the blockade. If the security of the ports of the Islamic Republic of Iran in the waters of the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman is threatened, no port in the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman will remain safe. It set up a dramatic escalation around the Strait of Hormuz, which is threatening an already very fragile ceasefire. President Trump also claimed that other countries would support the blockade. We don't need other countries, frankly, but they've offered the services. We'll let it be known probably tomorrow. But US allies in NATO, including Britain and France, said they wouldn't be drawn in, instead saying the waterway needed to be reopened. French President Emmanuel Macron has said France, along with the UK, are working on bringing together a range of countries on a mission to restore freedom of navigation in the Strait. In a statement on social media, he said this strictly defensive mission, separate from the warring parties to the conflict, is intended to be deployed as soon as circumstances permit. In UK's Parliament, British Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer elaborated on a proposed summit involving dozens of countries to be held this week. The summit will be focused on two things. First, diplomatic efforts to bring pressure to bear for a negotiated end to the conflict and for the strait to be opened. Second, military planning to provide assurance to shipping as soon as a stable environment can be established. This is Tim Swanston in Dubai reporting for AM. The federal government has reassessed Australia's defence strategy and has decided to spend billions of dollars more on drones and other autonomous technology. A new national defence strategy will be unveiled on Thursday, taking into account lessons learnt from recent conflicts around the world. The Defence Minister joins me. Richard Miles, thanks for speaking with AM this morning. Good morning, Melissa. How are you? Good, thank you. Can you take me through how much extra money there is for drones and other autonomous capabilities and what exactly will it fund? So this, we're spending $12 to $15 billion over the next decade on autonomous capabilities, which is a significant increase, $2 to $5 billion extra relative to what we had in NDS 24. So it is a very big step up in terms of the spending that we're doing on this. And really, it's driven by the way in which modern warfare has changed. I think everyone has been really amazed at how the war in Ukraine has unfolded but evolved over the period in which it's been contested. And clearly, autonomous systems now are really central to how contest happens, how war happens. We can see that also playing out in the Middle East. So it's very important that we are maintaining pace with that and we're very much increasing our focus on autonomous systems as a result. So an extra $2 to $5 billion on top of what had already been planned to be spent in this area. So what's being deprioritised to spare up funding to shift towards drones and other autonomous vehicles? Well, we'll go through all of that on Thursday. But I guess the point I would simply say in terms of the broader picture around the funding of defence, what you'll see on Thursday is a continuation of our track record, which is to increase our investment in defence. And we'll talk about that on Thursday. But clearly, a focus on autonomous systems has to be a part of how we are thinking about the defence force that we are building today. And so be it Ghost Shark, which we announced in the course of the last year, $1.7 billion over the next five years, which is the largest underwater autonomous system in the world today, or Ghostbat, which is really the leading collaborative combat aircraft, which is being developed in Australia. And again, we spent $1.4 billion just recently in terms of the next phase of Ghostbat. These are really critical, cutting edge, world leading technologies that are autonomous, obviously, but which also fit the Australian circumstance. They're at the larger end of that spectrum, given where we are and the distances that we need to deal with. And it's now a very central part of the defence force we're building. Do we need to look more at counter-drone capabilities as well? Or does our geographic situation mean that's less of a priority than the sorts of initiatives you just outlined? No, we definitely are looking at counter-drone technology as well. So it is very much across the spectrum. I mean, I think what would be fair to say is that given our geography, we are becoming specialists in terms of the development of technology here in Australia at the larger end. But in terms of the capabilities that we will need for our defence force, it is across the full spectrum. What you get at the smaller end is mass, lots of units, and that's what we are seeing play out in Ukraine. But if we look at what's happening in the Middle East right now, you need counter-drone technology as well. And that's a critical part of the whole equation of what we're putting together here. Well, we also see that US and Gulf countries have really burnt through years of missiles and interceptors to deal with the threats from drones and missiles. We've even seen missiles meant for Ukraine being diverted to the Middle East. Does that leave Australia a little bit exposed, given we're still in the process of developing our own domestic manufacturing of missiles? Is Australia at the back of the queue now for new missile systems? Well, in terms of missile systems, it has been really clear for some time that for Australia to have the war stocks that we need, we've got to be building missiles in Australia. And that's why we've greatly brought forward the development of a missile manufacturing capability in Australia, which has now actually seen us for the first time manufacture missiles in Australia. And we began that process last year. And that, relative to what we inherited, we've brought that forward years and years in order to be developing that now. And that will be a really critical capability because, to use your language, it will ensure that Australia is at the front of the queue when we have our own capability. I think so. Just. Sorry, you go. I just wanted to, just with time pressing, wanted to ask you about the Strait of Hormuz before we run out of time. The US is now blockading Iranian ports and its coastline. Does the government support this kind of action by the US? Well, what we support is to see, ultimately, the Strait of Hormuz open. And that's what the US wants as well. Another blockade doesn't really help that, though, does it? Well, we need to see freedom of navigation, obviously, through the Strait of Hormuz. Obviously, we're deeply invested in having an open Strait of Hormuz and the global fuel supply chain return to normality. We're working with all of our partners, and that includes the US. But we are very much working with countries like the UK and France. And you reported on the summit that's coming up later this week. We are working with all of our partners around efforts that are being taken forward in respect of the Strait of Hormuz and how Australia can best contribute. But what I'd say about that is that, you know, all of those are predicated on when conditions allow that to occur. And right now, you know, that is very uncertain. And we really need to see what plays out throughout the remainder of the ceasefire and as to what the circumstances are in the Straits of Hormuz, which would allow some effort to begin. Richard Miles, thanks very much for speaking to AM this morning. Thanks, Melissa. The coalition is promising a hardline approach to immigration with opposition leader Angus Taylor to outline his concerns that some migrants aren't adhering to Australian values and are what he's called a net drain on Australia. He'll propose screening the social media activity of visa applicants and reassessing visas already given to Palestinians who've arrived in Gaza in a speech he'll give this morning. The opposition leader joined me earlier. Angus Taylor, thanks very much for speaking with AM this morning. Great to be with you, Mel. So in this speech, you're describing some migrants as a net drain on the community. Can you explain for me what you mean by that? Well, what we're announcing today is that we need to put Australian values first. And that hasn't been the case in our immigration system in the past. And it needs to change. We know people have come to our country in recent times who don't share our core values, our belief in democracy, our belief in the rule of law, our belief in basic freedoms. And what we're proposing here is that we would put our values first. They must accept our core values. And that would mean establishing a legally binding and enforceable values test in the Migration Act as a visa condition. Breach of that would mean refusal or cancellation. I'll get into that more in a moment. But can I just get a sense from you of how much of Australia's migrant community you think falls into this category of not adhering to Australian values? The vast majority of migrants who come to this country do the right thing. They're patriotic. They love Australia. They realise we are what I believe is the greatest country in the world. And the problem is the system loses integrity. And worst of all, we see erosion of our values and what we believe in if we don't screen for those people, if we don't put up a red light to radicals and if we don't shut the door to people who are abusing the system. So when it comes to this Australian values statement, there is currently one that visa applicants already have to sign to. The difference you're proposing is that you could revoke a visa if action is taken that doesn't adhere with that. Is that right? Yeah, there's two parts to this. One is it would be legally binding and enforceable. And the second, which follows from it, is that that would enable refusal or cancellation where those values have clearly been breached. Would that be to minister's discretion? Because things around values aren't necessarily as clear cut as whether or not someone's broken the law, for example. Well, it can be clear cut. It'll depend on the circumstances. I mean, if someone has clearly demonstrated that they don't believe in our legal system, then they shouldn't be here on a visa. I think that's pretty straightforward. If they clearly don't believe in our parliamentary democracy and the importance of it, and they've shown a very clear behaviour that is at odds with that, then again, they shouldn't have a visa. So, look, there will always be, as always with these things, grey cases, but every system has to deal with those. But I think the most important thing here is putting Australian values first, shutting the door to abusers of the system and putting up red lights to radicals. And we have seen radicals come to this country on visas, and that's not appropriate. You're also suggesting that you would like a strengthened national security screening process, including standard checking of social media activity of people applying for a visa. How would that practically work? Well, we're establishing the proposal here is to establish a cross-agency task force, including the border force, the federal police and ASIO. So, and they would screen people coming to this country with a focus, obviously, on... Well, it would be risk-weighted, as these things always are. You have to look at where someone's coming from and any signs that there's some risk. Doesn't that already happen? Can't ASIO already check people's social media if they have concerns? Well, what we don't have is a legally binding and enforceable values test in the Migration Act, and we don't have a cross-agency task force set up in this way, which would receive extra funding. So, that is a big step forward. It's, I think, desperately needed because we have seen people come to this country... Sorry, can I just go back to the social media checking? Because I'm not entirely clear what is different. If it's dependent on the risk and the risk is being assessed, doesn't that already happen? Well, we don't have this cross-agency task force that I'm proposing, and we don't have the resources allocated, the additional resources that we're proposing here. So, it's different people doing the assessment of the social media? Well, it's bolstering it and giving it extra resources and putting this team together in a way where they can ensure that extremists, that radicals who do not believe in our way of life, don't come into the country. And look, Mel, you know, the fact that we have seen what we saw at Bondi last year is an indication that we aren't seeing enough of this. We do need to do more of this. It does need to be bolstered. It does need extra resourcing. And it does need that very strong cross-agency coordination that's necessary. Angus Taylor, thanks very much for speaking with me this morning. Great to be with you. And Angus Taylor is the opposition leader. Fiji police have revealed they want to put an Australian man on trial for allegedly orchestrating the importation of more than four tonnes of methamphetamine, the largest drug seizure in the island nation's history. It comes as the volume of illicit drugs seized in the South Pacific hits record levels, as it's becoming a pit stop on the drug smuggling route from the Americas to Australia. Foreign correspondent Stephanie March reports. For more than 20 years, barge skipper Tui has been navigating the waters surrounding his native Fiji. In late 2023, when a man hired the barge to collect rubbish off a superyacht, he thought it was a good deal. When I heard of superyacht, I thought, oh, that's good. Good money on the superyacht. But actually, he was duped into picking up more than four tonnes of meth sent by the ruthless Sinaloa cartel in Mexico. When I saw the first box that landed on the floor, I know this is different. This is not the stuff that we were supposed to do. What comes into my mind, it's drugs. And how did you feel when you... Scared. I was frightened. I was scared. Weeks later, police discovered more than a thousand containers of meth stockpiled in Fiji's tourist gateway of Nandi. Police believed the drugs were destined for Australia. Very likely, they would have made landfall in New South Wales. Assistant Commissioner Scott Cook is the head of the New South Wales Police State Crime Command. The Pacific is a waypoint for a lot of the importations that come to Australia via sea. Almost all organised crime groups in New South Wales of serious and organised crime use the Pacific. Barge skipper Tui was lucky and wasn't charged. Nine Fijians were convicted over that haul. But now Fiji Police Assistant Commissioner, Maseki Wanga, says they have their sights on an Australian, Sydney businessman, Sam Armeen. As I said, Sam Armeen is always the person of interest when it comes to drugs in Fiji. Late last year, a Fiji High Court judge labelled Armeen a drug kingpin who orchestrated the importation. He has a gym and property in the premier island resort of Denarao, including crucially, a warehouse where the drugs were stored for several days. Fiji's top prosecutor, John Rambuku, believes Armeen knew about the drugs. I would think that with such a large amount of methamphetamines, Sam Armeen would have had to have a say in the drugs being moved to his warehouse. Using the encrypted app Threema, Armeen helped arrange and pay to get the drugs into the country, according to evidence accepted by a Fiji High Court judge. Why has Sam Armeen not been charged here in Fiji over that importation? Investigations are still underway. We will only rest once we charge those responsible, those international crime syndicates. It's all my wish that Sam Armeen to face trial here in Fiji. Months after the Fiji seizure, New South Wales Police caught Armeen supplying drugs and a gun to an undercover cop via the encrypted app Threema. He's pleaded guilty. At a bail hearing, the court heard Armeen has links to organised crime in Australia, including the KVT, a gang of mostly Fijian Australians based out of Western Sydney. Assistant Commissioner Scott Cook again. We've hit KVT particularly hard recently because of what they've been involved in. They're importing drugs. They're selling drugs, distributing drugs. It's pretty serious. Armeen is due to be sentenced in a New South Wales court in July. He's declined to comment on his alleged involvement in the Fiji importation and in organised crime. Stephanie March. And that's AM for today. Thanks for your company. I'm Melissa Clark. Hi, it's Sam Hawley here, host of the ABC News Daily podcast. The peace talks failed. So now Donald Trump wants to disrupt the vital oil shipping route, the Strait of Hormuz, even further. A US blockade will stop ships entering or departing Iranian ports. Today, Husayna Bish from the Arab Gulf States Institute on what to expect. Look for the ABC News Daily podcast on ABC Listen.
