And we really need to see what plays out throughout the remainder of the ceasefire and as to what the circumstances are in the Straits of Hormuz, which would allow some effort to begin.
Richard Miles, thanks very much for speaking to AM this morning.
Thanks, Melissa.

The coalition is promising a hardline approach to immigration with opposition leader Angus Taylor to outline his concerns that some migrants aren't adhering to Australian values and are what he's called a net drain on Australia.
He'll propose screening the social media activity of visa applicants and reassessing visas already given to Palestinians who've arrived in Gaza in a speech he'll give this morning.
The opposition leader joined me earlier.
Angus Taylor, thanks very much for speaking with AM this morning.
Great to be with you, Mel.
So in this speech, you're describing some migrants as a net drain on the community.
Can you explain for me what you mean by that?
Well, what we're announcing today is that we need to put Australian values first.
And that hasn't been the case in our immigration system in the past.
And it needs to change.
We know people have come to our country in recent times who don't share our core values, our belief in democracy, our belief in the rule of law, our belief in basic freedoms.
And what we're proposing here is that we would put our values first.
They must accept our core values.
And that would mean establishing a legally binding and enforceable values test in the Migration Act as a visa condition.
Breach of that would mean refusal or cancellation.
I'll get into that more in a moment.
But can I just get a sense from you of how much of Australia's migrant community you think falls into this category of not adhering to Australian values?
The vast majority of migrants who come to this country do the right thing.
They're patriotic. They love Australia. They realise we are what I believe is the greatest country in the world.
And the problem is the system loses integrity.

And worst of all, we see erosion of our values and what we believe in if we don't screen for those people, if we don't put up a red light to radicals and if we don't shut the door to people who are abusing the system.
So when it comes to this Australian values statement, there is currently one that visa applicants already have to sign to.
The difference you're proposing is that you could revoke a visa if action is taken that doesn't adhere with that.
Is that right?
Yeah, there's two parts to this.
One is it would be legally binding and enforceable.
And the second, which follows from it, is that that would enable refusal or cancellation where those values have clearly been breached.
Would that be to minister's discretion?
Because things around values aren't necessarily as clear cut as whether or not someone's broken the law, for example.
Well, it can be clear cut.
It'll depend on the circumstances.
I mean, if someone has clearly demonstrated that they don't believe in our legal system, then they shouldn't be here on a visa.
I think that's pretty straightforward.
If they clearly don't believe in our parliamentary democracy and the importance of it, and they've shown a very clear behaviour that is at odds with that, then again, they shouldn't have a visa.
So, look, there will always be, as always with these things, grey cases, but every system has to deal with those.
But I think the most important thing here is putting Australian values first, shutting the door to abusers of the system and putting up red lights to radicals.
And we have seen radicals come to this country on visas, and that's not appropriate.
You're also suggesting that you would like a strengthened national security screening process, including standard checking of social media activity of people applying for a visa.
How would that practically work?
Well, we're establishing the proposal here is to establish a cross-agency task force, including the border force, the federal police and ASIO.
So, and they would screen people coming to this country with a focus, obviously, on...
Well, it would be risk-weighted, as these things always are.
You have to look at where someone's coming from and any signs that there's some risk.
Doesn't that already happen?
Can't ASIO already check people's social media if they have concerns?
Well, what we don't have is a legally binding and enforceable values test in the Migration Act,
and we don't have a cross-agency task force set up in this way, which would receive extra funding.
So, that is a big step forward.
It's, I think, desperately needed because we have seen people come to this country...
Sorry, can I just go back to the social media checking?
Because I'm not entirely clear what is different.
If it's dependent on the risk and the risk is being assessed, doesn't that already happen?
Well, we don't have this cross-agency task force that I'm proposing,
and we don't have the resources allocated, the additional resources that we're proposing here.
So, it's different people doing the assessment of the social media?
Well, it's bolstering it and giving it extra resources and putting this team together
in a way where they can ensure that extremists, that radicals who do not believe in our way of life,
don't come into the country.
And look, Mel, you know, the fact that we have seen what we saw at Bondi last year
is an indication that we aren't seeing enough of this.
We do need to do more of this.
It does need to be bolstered.
It does need extra resourcing.
And it does need that very strong cross-agency coordination that's necessary.
Angus Taylor, thanks very much for speaking with me this morning.
Great to be with you.
And Angus Taylor is the opposition leader.
Fiji police have revealed they want to put an Australian man on trial for allegedly orchestrating
the importation of more than four tonnes of methamphetamine,
the largest drug seizure in the island nation's history.
It comes as the volume of illicit drugs seized in the South Pacific hits record levels,
as it's becoming a pit stop on the drug smuggling route from the Americas to Australia.
Foreign correspondent Stephanie March reports.
For more than 20 years, barge skipper Tui has been navigating the waters surrounding his native Fiji.
In late 2023, when a man hired the barge to collect rubbish off a superyacht,
he thought it was a good deal.
When I heard of superyacht, I thought, oh, that's good.
Good money on the superyacht.
But actually, he was duped into picking up more than four tonnes of meth sent by the ruthless
Sinaloa cartel in Mexico.
When I saw the first box that landed on the floor, I know this is different.
This is not the stuff that we were supposed to do.
What comes into my mind, it's drugs.
And how did you feel when you...
Scared.
I was frightened.
I was scared.
Weeks later, police discovered more than a thousand containers of meth stockpiled in Fiji's
tourist gateway of Nandi.
Police believed the drugs were destined for Australia.
Very likely, they would have made landfall in New South Wales.
Assistant Commissioner Scott Cook is the head of the New South Wales Police State Crime Command.
The Pacific is a waypoint for a lot of the importations that come to Australia via sea.
Almost all organised crime groups in New South Wales of serious and organised crime use the Pacific.
Barge skipper Tui was lucky and wasn't charged.
Nine Fijians were convicted over that haul.
But now Fiji Police Assistant Commissioner, Maseki Wanga, says they have their sights on an Australian,
Sydney businessman, Sam Armeen.
As I said, Sam Armeen is always the person of interest when it comes to drugs in Fiji.
Late last year, a Fiji High Court judge labelled Armeen a drug kingpin who orchestrated the importation.
He has a gym and property in the premier island resort of Denarao, including crucially,
a warehouse where the drugs were stored for several days.
Fiji's top prosecutor, John Rambuku, believes Armeen knew about the drugs.
I would think that with such a large amount of methamphetamines, Sam Armeen would have had
to have a say in the drugs being moved to his warehouse.
Using the encrypted app Threema, Armeen helped arrange and pay to get the drugs into the country,
according to evidence accepted by a Fiji High Court judge.
Why has Sam Armeen not been charged here in Fiji over that importation?
Investigations are still underway.
We will only rest once we charge those responsible, those international crime syndicates.
It's all my wish that Sam Armeen to face trial here in Fiji.
Months after the Fiji seizure, New South Wales Police caught Armeen supplying drugs and a gun
to an undercover cop via the encrypted app Threema.
He's pleaded guilty.
At a bail hearing, the court heard Armeen has links to organised crime in Australia,
including the KVT, a gang of mostly Fijian Australians based out of Western Sydney.
Assistant Commissioner Scott Cook again.
We've hit KVT particularly hard recently because of what they've been involved in.
They're importing drugs.
They're selling drugs, distributing drugs.
It's pretty serious.
Armeen is due to be sentenced in a New South Wales court in July.
He's declined to comment on his alleged involvement in the Fiji importation and in organised crime.
Stephanie March.
And that's AM for today.
Thanks for your company.
I'm Melissa Clark.
Hi, it's Sam Hawley here, host of the ABC News Daily podcast.
The peace talks failed.
So now Donald Trump wants to disrupt the vital oil shipping route, the Strait of Hormuz, even further.
A US blockade will stop ships entering or departing Iranian ports.
Today, Husayna Bish from the Arab Gulf States Institute on what to expect.
Look for the ABC News Daily podcast on ABC Listen.

episodes.title: US to blockade Strait of Hormuz
episodes.description: Oil prices could soar even higher as Donald Trump announces a blockade of the Strait of Hormuz following the failure of peace talks over the weekend.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Good morning. Welcome to AM. It's Monday the 13th of April. I'm Melissa Clark in Canberra, coming to you from Ngunnawal country and acknowledging other custodians. United States President Donald Trump says the US Navy will begin a blockade of the Strait of Hormuz after negotiations between the US and Iran failed to land an agreement to end hostilities. It comes as the fragile two-week ceasefire holds for now, with other leaders in the region urging both parties to continue talking. Correspondent Tim Swanston filed this report. Boarding Air Force Two with a wave to Pakistani mediators. US Vice President J.D. Vance left Islamabad empty-handed. Earlier in a short press conference, after what he said were 21 hours of negotiations, the Vice President said a deal to end the war hadn't been reached. We've had a number of substantive discussions with the Iranians. That's the good news. The bad news is that we have not reached an agreement. And I think that's bad news for Iran much more than it's bad news for the United States of America. In the wash-up of the meeting, both sides were blaming one another for not reaching an agreement. Vice President Vance said Iran had chosen not to accept US terms, saying the US needed a commitment that Iran would not seek a nuclear weapon. For Iran's part, an Iranian semi-official news outlet said the demands were excessive, and Parliamentary Speaker Mohamed Bakay Ghalibaf, who led the Iranian delegation, said the US had not won his team's trust. Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Esmail Bagay, said it shouldn't have been expected that a result would be achieved from one day of talks. We reached understandings on a number of issues. That's the reality. However, regarding two or three important issues, the views were distant and ultimately did not lead to an agreement. But if the ceasefire was already looking perilous leading into talks, it became even more fragile hours after. Joining me now live on the telephone with the very latest is the nation's 45th and 47th President of the United States, President Donald J. Trump. Phoning in to Fox News, US President Donald Trump elaborated on a social media post he'd just made, saying he'd directed the US Navy to blockade the Strait of Hormuz. We've got a lot of ships, so we're bringing them up. We think that numerous countries are going to be helping us with this also, but we're putting on a complete blockade. Iran has maintained a stranglehold over the Strait of Hormuz since the beginning of the war, threatening and attacking commercial ships and causing chaos in global energy markets. President Trump said Iran promised to reopen the Strait with the ceasefire and knowingly failed. Taking aim at reports Iran was charging a toll for ships to pass through the Strait and that sea mines had been placed by Iran. Mr Trump described Iran's actions as world extortion and a US blockade of the Strait would begin shortly. Speaking to Fox News, he also said work would begin on destroying sea mines. So we have minesweepers there now. We have highly sophisticated underwater minesweepers, which are the latest and the greatest, but we're also bringing in more traditional minesweepers. And so I understand is the UK and a couple of other countries are sending minesweepers. A lot of countries don't have minesweepers. The US president weighed in on negotiations and said while points that were agreed to were better than continuing military operations, those points didn't matter compared to the single most important issue of Iranian nuclear ambitions. The other issue complicating the ceasefire is Israel's continuing assault on Lebanon and the Iranian-backed militant group Hezbollah. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu crossed into southern Lebanon on Sunday, visiting Israeli soldiers and saying there is more to do. Talks are scheduled between Israeli and Lebanese officials on Tuesday, although crucially, those aren't talks between Israel and Hezbollah. This is Tim Swanston in Dubai reporting for AM. Professor Usha Haley is an international business expert from Wichita State University in the United States. Professor Haley, what's the most likely short-term impact on oil prices if the US Navy continues to blockade the Strait of Hormuz? Well, oil prices are expected to rise when they open on Monday. And so that's what's going to happen right away because, well, there's going to be reduced supply. They're already talking about, I think, maybe a one and a half to two. They've already gotten about 10 billion barrels a day stopped and this is going to be another one and a half billion or so more. And what happens in the longer term if the straits aren't reopened? The International Monetary Fund is expected to meet this coming week and the prognostication is reduced global growth. The global growth projections have varied from half a percent to one percent down. And so that's what we're expecting. It really depends on how long this conflict goes on, how long the blockade of the strait goes on and whether critical infrastructure is damaged. And what's this doing to certainty and the planning prospects for businesses worldwide at the moment as they try and figure out what's happening and how long it might last? Oh, it's just heightened economic uncertainty all around. Can't make projections. People are expecting prices to rise. It's not just oil, but also everything associated with oil. So certain plastics, certain pharmaceuticals and, of course, fertilizer. It's going to hit farmers really hard. And how does this current crisis differ from some of the past oil shocks, particularly in terms of that long-term impact? There's a lot of uncertainty and then one keeps wondering what we're doing in the Strait of Hormuz. This is not unexpected. It's the only card that Iran has, the Strait of Hormuz. And it's always been factored into any response that Iran would take to aggressive action. So this shouldn't have come as a surprise. The long-term effects really depend on how long this war continues. In my opinion, it's something that could have been avoided, self-inflicted, and it's creating a lot of consternation around the world. Do you think it will have a broader impact in terms of prompting many governments to consider more sovereign capability? Or is this something that doesn't necessarily disrupt the globalized economic supply chains that have been developed over the last few decades? Is it more of a bump that needs to be negotiated? No. I mean, it has already affected the global supply of oil. But it's not just that. It's affected fertilizer. It's affected certain other chemicals that flow through. And there is a lot of uncertainty. It has affected the supply chain. It just depends on how long. If it keeps prolonging, it's going to lead to stagflation. I think that's what the IMF is going to come out with in about a week or so. It's a crucial point. I mean, you can't really turn the Strait of Hormuz into a toll booth. And that is what President Trump seems to be wanting to do. It should be a free pathway for ships to go in and out. But I do think, perhaps, although he hasn't really elaborated on it, that this is a hit at China. Because Chinese ships were allowed to go through. No one else, really. And mostly Chinese ships. And it will affect China. But minimally, because China doesn't depend as much on this oil from the Middle East. Professor Hayley, thank you very much for speaking to me this morning. Thank you. And Professor Hayley is an international business expert from Wichita State University. Back home, the federal government is focused on shoring up relations with Southeast Asian nations that supply Australia with petrol, diesel and jet fuel. Madeleine King is the Federal Resources Minister. Madeleine King, thanks very much for speaking to AM this morning. It's a delight to be here. Thanks, Mel. We've seen overnight President Donald Trump say that the US will blockade the Strait of Hormuz. This development can't be helpful to getting fuel supply back to normal. Australia, as you can imagine, supports freedom of navigation. It's really very important for all of global trade. But as a nation that depends on trading maritime lanes, it's even more important. So on the negotiations themselves, we hope that the parties can resume talks. De-escalation is what we've consistently called for as a government. I think it's what the Australian people would like to see as well. As for the blockade, that poses a very difficult position for global trade. And having any suggestion there might be some kind of permanent tolling on an important trade route by a regime that's listed as a terrorist organisation is just not a sustainable position. So will the government be pressing the US government to not blockade the Strait? Will there be direct discussions with counterparts to try and dissuade the US from taking that course of action? We always talk with all of our partners. That's really important to remember. Obviously, America's our most important strategic partner in global affairs. So we continue to maintain our position about de-escalation. What the United States chooses to do around the blockade that they've suggested is a matter for them. And we'll wait to see how that eventuates. It's really the best thing Australia can do is encourage that both parties go back to the negotiating table and respect the work that all negotiators are doing, in particular Pakistan. Hosting these talks have been very important over the weekend. But having a blockaded – well, having a tolling system around the Strait of Humoz would be a very, very difficult position for not only Australia but for other countries in the region. When it comes to securing fuel supply for Australia, we've seen the Prime Minister visit. Singapore is heading off to Brunei and Malaysia this week. Is this a goodwill tour with those nations or are there concrete outcomes that are expected from these visits? Well, we've got great relationships with these countries already. The Singaporean trip to Singapore that the Prime Minister has just come back from was really important. And that's a depth of relationship with Singapore in this country. But this is more about reinforcing that relationship rather than a new agreement? Well, that's right. And the Foreign Minister is travelling as well. And I think it's really important that our Prime Minister and our Foreign Minister go there and be there and meet with their counterparts. It sends a very strong signal about where Australia sits in the geostrategic positioning in the world, but also a will to engage with our partners. They rely on us for lots of energy as well as we rely on them. So we want to remind everyone of that. And it's not just energy. It's food security as well. I mean, Australia does export a great deal of protein into the region. And to get that protein, we need our agriculture industry to thrive. And that does rely on diesel. So it's a very important chain here. As we get closer to the budget being announced, can you give us any clarity about what changes to taxation for gas exports? What's on the table? What's off the table? Because I'm not sure the message is clear from the government at this point. Well, it's going to be a difficult budget. We all know that. The budget's constrained by the disruption to global trade. We can't avoid that disruption. We can just manage it as best we can as a country. And the Treasurer's already said we'll be working on this until the very last minute to try and get the best position that we can for the nation. And when it comes to gas exports specifically? Well, there's been a lot of talk about different taxes and different systems, including on gas. So the thing I think it's important to remember is PRRT, the petroleum resource rent tax, doesn't apply to all gas exports. So I think that's what generates some of this discussion. For mine, I think it's worth people remembering that to have created this gas industry, which provides most of the domestic gas in this country, you know, those companies had to invest tens of billions of dollars. If I think of Chevron as an $80 billion project, IMPEX as another $80 billion project. And that's before we even talk about the Queensland project. So you wouldn't want to see a change there? You think the settings are right? Oh, no, no. I am. You know, it's a matter for the Treasurer and the whole Cabinet to decide. I'm not going to preempt any decision ahead of the budget. I just think it's worth thinking about what goes into these projects. They're not something that anyone can switch on and off. You know, they're multi-decadal investment projects. In a country where, you know, the government doesn't own the infrastructure, you know, this is something we depend on private capital to build out these industries, which is different to what other countries are referred to in this debate sometimes. Madeleine King, thanks very much for speaking to AM this morning. Thanks so much, Mel. And Madeleine King is the Federal Resources Minister. One of Donald Trump's biggest supporters in Europe has conceded defeat in the Hungarian election. Right-wing populist Viktor Orban has suffered a massive electoral loss, with Hungary's opposition set to record a landslide victory. Europe correspondent Elias Kluwer is in Budapest. He joined me a short time ago. Elias, it seems like it's a crushing defeat for Viktor Orban. Absolutely, Mel. Also, most polls had Viktor Orban losing by up to 10, 15 percentage points. And the early results are indicating that Viktor Orban will likely lose by that amount. His challenger, Peter Magyar, is looking like he'll finish on about 55% of the vote. And I've been speaking to political insiders that say this is really a catastrophe, a political catastrophe for Viktor Orban in terms of just how much support he has lost. And the fact he has been gerrymandering constituencies, engineering the electoral system to make it almost impossible for anyone to defeat him. This really is such a momentous victory for Peter Magyar, who has led a very slick, flawless grassroots campaign here in Hungary. So tell me a bit more about Peter Magyar. He used to be an ally of Viktor Orban, but he's become quite the critic and he's promising to bring Hungary back closer to Europe. So how much do we know about how he will act as prime minister? Well, we know that, as you say, he was a former Orban ally, but he claims that he left because he became disillusioned with how Fidesz was running the country. He's 45 years old, a former lawyer. He has grown in popularity and, as I say, really run a slick campaign here. But he is treated with some suspicion. People were just desperate for change, which is a big part of why he has been elected. But people are also concerned that perhaps Peter Magyar might be just more of the same. We'll wait and see. As you said, he's promising to bring Hungary back into the European foe, which would prevent or allow the EU to put more money into Hungarian coffers. It's been withheld due to the way in which Orban has been running the country. So that's what he's promising, promising more support for Ukraine as well. But in terms of some of the other things that Viktor Orban has introduced in terms of restricting the judiciary, restricting LGBTQ rights, muzzling the free press, well, he hasn't really been that open about how he'll change or wind back some of the very draconian laws that Viktor Orban has introduced over his 16 years in power. Elias Kluwer in Budapest there. Australia's democracy, like many around the world, is under sustained pressure. A citizens report increasing disillusionment with the major political parties, according to a new national report. Catherine Gregory has the details. Father and son, Jared and Rob Zamet, are fairly confident Australia's political system and its institutions work. I think our system serves as well with preferential voting and compulsory voting. I think the AEC does a good job of remaining independent compared to a lot of other democracies. I think globally we're doing all right, but I think there's democracy fraying at the edges in some cases. They're not so certain everyone shares their faith. You know, the system's not working as well as it should for a lot of Australians, and I think there's frustration in that. We're seeing an increase in the rise of popularity of minor parties, particularly One Nation. Do you think that's a reflection on that sort of disillusionment that we've been talking about? Yeah, I'd say I'd agree with that disillusionment is pushing support for those minor parties, and I think it probably goes back to people perhaps frustrated with the status quo, and there not being really a lot of alternatives. These views on the fragile state of Australia's democracy are encapsulated in a Grattan Institute report. It found democracy around the world is in decline, and while Australia is still upholding some democratic values and some belief in our government's public service, education and legal systems, and even the media, there's a significant risk it may not last. We see growing economic pessimism, worry about the prospects for future generations, concerns about unfairness, and a declining sense of belonging. Kate Griffiths is the Deputy Director of the Grattan Institute's Democracy Program. So satisfaction with democracy is typically lower among groups who are less well served by the status quo. The report suggests building better community, protecting sources of information such as the media, ensuring governments are well prepared to withstand global shocks like the current fuel crisis, and building stronger policymaking processes. So in terms of Parliament, what we see is an opportunity for an independent review, and the review could look at quite a few questions. The size of Parliament has been a question out there at the moment. Ian McAllister is a Professor of Politics at ANU. He says the report confirms what recent elections have shown, that people are moving away from the major political parties. What drives the vote is generation, education and gender, and that's a really fundamental change in terms of how people vote. The two major political parties have not really come to terms with this change, and that's one of the things that's leading people to de-align from the two major political parties. So there's a whole variety of things which are used overseas. A lot of these things could be evaluated here in terms of trying to restore faith and democracy. Professor Ian McAllister from ANU, ending that report by Catherine Gregory. And that's AM for today. Thanks for your company. I'm Melissa Clark. Hi, I'm Sydney Pead from the ABC News Daily podcast. The ABC's Alan Kohler thinks the Treasurer should nationalise the childcare system. As concerns remain about the quality, safety and affordability of some centres, is now the time for a radical shake-up. Today, Alan on If His Idea Could Work, and a childcare policy expert on The Case for Change. Look for the ABC News Daily podcast on ABC Listen. And of course, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like. I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like. Thank you.

I am.

I'm not going to preempt any decision ahead of the budget.
I just think it's worth thinking about what goes into these projects.

Madeleine King, thanks very much for speaking to AM this morning.
Thanks so much, Mel.
And Madeleine King is the Federal Resources Minister.

Elias Kluwer in Budapest there.

I think globally we're doing all right, but I think there's democracy fraying at the edges in some cases.
They're not so certain everyone shares their faith.
You know, the system's not working as well as it should for a lot of Australians, and I think there's frustration in that.
We're seeing an increase in the rise of popularity of minor parties, particularly One Nation.
Do you think that's a reflection on that sort of disillusionment that we've been talking about?
Yeah, I'd say I'd agree with that disillusionment is pushing support for those minor parties,

Professor Ian McAllister from ANU, ending that report by Catherine Gregory.

episodes.title: What is lost when buildings become casualties of war?
episodes.description: One of the greatest tragedies of war is the loss of innocent life, and it’s rightly at the forefront of how we measure the cost of conflict. Against that reality, the protection of buildings and monuments can seem frivolous — even misplaced.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. I want you to think about where you live. The places that shape your everyday life. The corner shop where you buy milk. The cafe you pass each morning. The street you always walk up to catch the bus. How much of that material world is part of who you are? And how would you feel if it were all suddenly gone? Erased by the chaos of war. The emotional loss and the trauma connected with losing the landmarks. You know, when you walk around your beloved city, you have these landmarks. They're part of your sort of internal navigational axis. And when they're gone, you feel that every day when you walk the streets. This is a destruction that aims at uprooting people from their land and their history. And it's done in a very scientific and methodological way. Where you go to these villages, the level of destruction is so high that you can't find the road. Today, on By Design, we're exploring what it means to protect buildings during times of conflict. Not just the famous monuments or World Heritage Sites, but the ordinary streets, homes and neighbourhoods that hold local memory and lived history. What does it mean to destroy a building during times of war? Beirut has been split. It's a split city by now, where some areas are being extremely targeted by the bombing. And the bombing is expanding. So before, it was limited to the southern suburb. But on every day, there are what is called targeted bombing or targeted killing, which you never know what part of the city that will take. That's Joanne Bajali, former journalist, now heritage activist, living and working in Beirut, a city under attack. And her work, it's extraordinary. As bombs are falling on her city, Joanne is trying to protect important buildings and homes. I mean, forget your Nimbis and your Yimbis. This is a battle for the built environment unlike anything you've ever seen. No stranger to war, Joanne was reporting during the 2003 Iraq War when she witnessed the looting of the Baghdad Museum. That moment changed everything, leading her to found Biladi, an NGO dedicated to protecting heritage sites like museums and cultural artefacts. In recent years, her focus has expanded to include the streetscapes of southern Lebanon. So after the 2024 war, we started working on documenting the destruction that was taking place in south Lebanon on the villages that were either located on the border or far away from the border. We are talking about villages located within Lebanon. So this is Lebanese territory, these are Lebanese villages. And when we went there, it was the deliberate act of destruction, not regular destruction. This is not my first war. I have been from Iraq to Lebanon to many wars. This is a destruction that aims at uprooting people from their land and their history. And it's done in a very, very scientific and methodological way. Where you go to these villages, the level of destruction is so high that you can't find the road. So you don't know where the road is. You just walk on any road that is there. And the landmarks that were there have all disappeared. Even the graveyards, you know, tanks were driven on graveyards. So people didn't just lose their houses. They lost their landmarks. They lost everything that is related to their villages. You can walk from one destruction to the other, not knowing where is the historical element, because the modern element have been thrown the rubbles of the modern element over the historical element. And both have been moved away. So that even the roads are no longer clear. So this is a technique that is being used so that people cannot find any link to their history, to their previous history or their previous memory as a person. Forget the passing on of the memory from one space, from one person to the other and one generation to the other. Plus you add to all this, that there was a deliberate action of destruction of the natural heritage by using phosphorus, for instance, or different kinds of pesticides that are killing the crops. And the trees. So there's a complete kind of reset through this absolute destruction that's going on there. Yeah? Yes. Anthony, it's something that we have witnessed that is extremely new, which is void. So you feel that there is no more energy there. There's no more life there. Beyond emptiness, it's void. These kinds of villages, I mean, they've evolved over generations, haven't they? They've been people's houses, they've been in the family through a number of generations. So these aren't sort of new suburbs. No, no, no. There's absolutely no new suburbs there. We're talking about villages that are old between, some of them will have monuments that are 500 years old. Others will have monuments that sometimes they go back to 700 years old. The ancestral family villages go back to at least 200 years old. So we're talking about historical villages that have organically grown with time, with the family expansion, and the children adding houses to the ancestral family house. We're not talking about anything modern here. We're talking about traditional houses and traditional villages that have been passed on from one generation to the other for the last 500, 600, 700 years. And we're talking about also the historical monuments, such as the mosques, such as the churches, or even the shrines. Everything have been destroyed in southern Lebanon, up next to the border. And the area that is a little bit located, a little bit more further to the border, that's where the destruction is taking place. And it's an uprooting of the population. But because people were able to go back in 2024, before they were able to rebuild some of it. When, you know, they have worked this house, where in one area they have made it impossible to return, and in other areas people were able to return. So amongst all of this, like, systematic destruction that's going on, what is the work you're trying to do here? What's the value that you're trying to bring to this diabolical situation? We work on two different levels. Either we work on antiquities and archaeological sites and storages, which is done with private collections, or with the government institutions, where we try to secure the collections outside of the bombing areas. Or we work on the villages and the communities where we try to document what they had and what they have lost. Because once you know, you cannot unknow. And we want them to know what they have lost, as it being part of the history. So adding the scientific element of architectural history, or the value of the historical houses, it adds another layer of pain that is true, where you even know even more that the house that you have lost is not just your family house, it's also a historical building. But at the same time, it adds also an element of pride that now we know what we have lost. In terms of not just me and my memories, but as a general loss for the nation. So we document what have been lost in order to assess the level of damage assessment or destruction assessment. And we provide this information back to the communities. And we give this to the policy level at the government level for any reconstruction plan that will be worked upon for the South in order for it to include the historical buildings as part of the reconstruction plan and remunerate people accordingly in order to push for the preservation of the history. So there's a kind of an archaeology of resistance going on here. And the uses of this archive that you're, or the work that you're doing, the surveying work and the archaeology that you're doing, is about maintaining that memory, maintaining its access to that memory. Is that right? Yes, absolutely. We see it also as an act of resistance to a war that aims at also eradicating the history of the place. Of course, it's a Pacific resistance, but it's still resistance. And it's a cultural resistance to any act of cutting the link between people and their history or a population and their history and keeping the knowledge and the membranes alive. Our streetscapes are a core part of our identity, especially when those streets and homes carry generations of family and cultural history. But they're not the only parts of the built environment that matter. From places of worship to fountains and statues, these spaces shape who we are and how we belong. In 1954, the Hague Convention became the first international treaty to protect cultural heritage during war, requiring armies to safeguard significant sites and avoid targeting them in conflict. But getting combatants to follow the convention isn't always straightforward. Professor Peter Stone understands that challenge. As president of Blue Shield International, which works to protect cultural heritage during armed conflict, he realised that if heritage was going to be protected, the military first had to see it through their own lens. I actually had to learn a new language. And the language I had to learn was military speak. So I stopped talking about World Heritage Sites and national institutions and started talking about potential force multipliers. What that means to you and me is that it is something that they can do with very little extra staffing or thought. But it is something that can make their job significantly more easy. And this is where you get into the real issues about why protecting cultural property can be so important. So in 2003-04, the Iraqi population were beginning to say, why are coalition troops still here? By 2006, they were saying, we really want the coalition troops to go home. And there was still no protection of heritage or religious sites. So it was dead easy for a group of Sunni extremists to walk into the Al-Aqshiri mosque in Samara, the third holiest place in Shia Islam, and blow it up. And that is seen by many of the political commentators on that conflict and the situation as one of the key tipping points into the full-scale sectarian civil war. And that led to a civil war of five years just over. And in political coalition minds, that led to the coalition troops having to stay in Iraq for that further five years. If it's not bad enough, taking five years worth of casualties and fatalities, spending five years losing the propaganda war. And that war was won by the so-called insurgents and provided the environment for the re-emergence of Al-Qaeda in Iraq and allowed for the oxygen for the emergence of the so-called Islamic State. Now, neither of those are going to disappear in my lifetime. And I'm not saying there was a simple, direct, and one only link between the destruction of the mosque and the emergence and re-emergence of those two organisations. But there was a very firm, heavily dotted line between the two. That's a strong argument for protecting places of cultural significance during war. But I can't imagine that when the bombs are falling, it's an easy point to get across. This is why Peter Stone says that the work of protection should be happening before the conflict erupts. We have to work in peacetime with all of those different groups. So we work, as an example at the moment, closely with NATO on their exercises and training work. And what we try to do is embed ideas about cultural property protection into that training and those exercises so that they begin to slowly realise that actually the protection of heritage could be as important as the logistics for keeping the ammunition going to the frontline troop. They are beginning to understand. That was my next question. Are they starting to listen? They are starting to listen. So there is a thing that most people generically call a no-strike list that the military pull together if they're going into a conflict. And that is always headed by medical facilities, educational facilities, and quite often sort of community facilities. But they now add to that heritage sites. And we work fairly closely with them to provide information for those heritage sites. So as one example of that, troops loyal to President Gaddafi in Libya. And NATO targeteer, sitting on an airfield in the Netherlands, identified six vehicles of a mobile radar and communications unit loyal to Gaddafi, parked up inside and immediately outside a large derelict building. And they identified a weapon to take all of those out in one go. So one large weapon that would hit this derelict building, destroy all six of the vehicles. And that would be delivered from literally miles away so that no NATO Air Force troops or whoever would be under any particular danger. I don't know the detail of what happened next, but it was the equivalent of a red light flashed on his or her computer because the coordinates for their derelict building were the same coordinates for a Roman monument that we had asked not to be damaged, if at all possible. And so the decision went further up the military food chain and a decision was taken to, in military speak, modify the ordinance. So instead of using one big bomb to destroy everything, they used six precision weapons which targeted each of the individual vehicles. And we have photographic evidence from a team that went in soon afterwards from Blue Shield. And there were all six of those essentially tangled mebs of metal. And there's a tiny bit of shrapnel damage on one wall of the Roman monument. Okay. So the precision from the big, you know, the big attack became a very precise attack to save the monument, effectively, because of the vice coming from the Blue Shield. NATO got something that they were very unused to at the time, which was a lot of good international publicity. And they got so much of that publicity that they actually decided to set up a report as to what they had done. So with something like the Hague Convention, has anyone actually been prosecuted under that convention and found guilty for destroying major heritage sites? Have there been any successful prosecutions? Yeah, unfortunately, under Hague, no. But Hague is seen as the primary piece of international legislation that links to other elements. So the key one is the 1998 Rome statute, the statute that created the International Criminal Court. And lawyers, as you'll no doubt be aware, are very conservative individuals, and they like to prosecute under something that there is a history of prosecution. So because nobody has prosecuted anybody under Hague, they don't want to be the first to try because that may be more difficult. There are examples under the Rome statute and under the International Tribunal for former Yugoslavia where people have been prosecuted and convicted for crimes against cultural property. Wow. And the most sort of famous of those are the gentlemen who first fired on the World Heritage site of the city of Dubrovnik back in the 1990s and Mr. Almadi who was in charge of an Ansandine team in Timbuktu in Mali where he and his team destroyed a mosque and nine mausoleah because they were in his words idolatrous because they had a building above ground. And so it can be done, it has been done, it's a good process that we should be pushing it as well. When it comes to protecting an existing structure, a strike list can save it from destruction. But what happens when that fails? For heritage activists, the pen really can be mightier than the sword with documentation becoming one of their most powerful tools. Dr. Anya Kottaba is the president of Blue Shield Australia, an associate professor at the University of Adelaide and an archaeologist trained across the Middle East, even teaching first aid for cultural heritage in conflict zones. I had to start by asking what that actually entails. The concept really stems from first aid in medicine, right? So it's providing this very first response which may not necessarily be perfect, but it's there to stabilise, it's there to document and it's there to preserve as much as possible. So there are numerous sort of frameworks in which we work and an algorithm for protection of these sites that are in some form of distress as the patient would be. So in many cases the only thing that we can do in a first instance is to check for safety, is to document as much as possible with the advancement of 3D modelling and documentation techniques. It is actually possible to now turn a photograph, a simple one photograph taken on your mobile phone and build a 3D model of the site out of that. So the documentation is absolutely the key part of the first aid and everything is obviously recorded. Often there is obviously stabilisation of the site and all of the architectural elements and materials that have been for example shattered or destroyed so that they can be then catalogued and labelled and sort of set aside and put in a safe place if that is possible obviously for future reconstruction. So now you work in documenting and modelling heritage spaces. Maybe just for our listeners how can you describe the ways in which the technology that you're using has changed over the last let's say decade or so? Oh the advancements were absolutely huge. episodes.title: Extraordinary Everyday : Gravestones
episodes.description: Gravestones may be stark reminders of our mortality, but they’re also powerful records of history, identity and belief. What can the design of these enduring markers tell us about the people they commemorate — and the eras they lived through?

But on Extraordinary Every Day, we turn the spotlight elsewhere, focusing on the ingenious designs that have been with us far longer and that many of us use every day. Today, we're exploring the surprisingly fascinating world of gravestones. It's an epitaph meant to endure across generations, your final footprint on the world. Gravestones may be stark reminders of our mortality, but they're also rich repositories of history and memory. So what can the design of these markers tell us about the people they commemorate and, the errors they lived through? And how have these designs changed over time? Satch Killam is a stonemason and heritage specialist who works at Rookwood Cemetery in Sydney. Hi, Satch. Hello. Let's get into headstones and gravestones then. And I suppose the first really obvious question is, what's the difference between a headstone and a gravestone? And why is that a good thing to know about? I think in this space and in stonemasonry, there's often people will say something very definitive, but really, it's all right to have a little bit of difference on this. A gravestone is the wider term, and a headstone is actually quite literally started off being as a headstone. You'd have a headstone and a footstone, or perhaps a headstone, a body stone and a footstone. So you're indicating where the person is. But I think the idea of a headstone is actually quite evocative because we want to know where the person's buried and which is the head of the grave. So we orientate ourselves. We know where the dead person is, which is kind of culturally significant if you think about it, that that's important to us. It's not just a space. It's an exact space. What's the earliest recorded gravestones that we know of then? That's a very difficult question because that's how you define gravestones. So very early peoples often had grave goods. There's different markings. Often shells were associated with burials. Shells are a very good object, and they'll come up into our conversation, I'm sure, later because shells are calcium carbonate. So they have a double diffraction, and they're very bright. They're bright in dusk. They're bright at night. You can see them by the moon. So they're a fantastic way to mark a grave and to be able to find a spot. And really, that's one of the key elements of a headstone, a gravestone, is that you want it to be seen. You want it to be a place that someone knows to come to and a place of remembrance. But it all starts with somewhere that you have to be able to find it. I would have thought that sandstone was too soft a stone to use for a gravestone or a headstone because it does weather, sandstone, more than something like granite. I mean, these must be choices that are being made all the time, I suppose, about the longevity of these markers. Yeah. Yeah. People choose their gravestones based on what's available. So the cemeteries that look the best to us now that are the most accessible are where the stone was actually a good stone for cemeteries. However, masons have known this, architects have known this for a long time, what is a good stone. And Sydney sandstone, there are Sydney sandstones that are fantastic and will last hundreds and hundreds of years, if not thousands of years. So what are the oldest cemeteries in Australia then? I just came from the oldest extant cemetery in mainland Australia, which is St. John's Parramatta, right across from the ABC Studios. And a fantastic place to look at if one is interested in the history and the evolution of gravestones because it's all written there in the landscape. The oldest cemetery that's kind of still active is actually in Norfolk Island and is a fantastic cemetery to go to if you ever have the opportunity. Coral gravestones that have lasted hundreds of years. So a coral limestone. And you work at Rookwood Cemetery, is that correct? Yes. So I work for Metropolitan Memorial Parks, which actually is eight cemeteries in Sydney and Sandgate in Newcastle. Right. And that, I mean, I'm thinking of Rookwood and that was a mid-Victorian period in my architectural mind. So what was it about that Victorian period and the gravestones from then that was so specific, do you think? Well, the Victorian period and especially the kind of later Victorian is just a remarkable time for cemeteries because they were so culturally popular. They were a place to come and visit, have a picnic, spend your day in a way that would, you know, increase your morals and be good for the soul. And cemeteries were a picnic places and places to visit. But they were also, as you've said, architecturally interesting. And the Victorians and their kind of love of death and the symbols of death mean that Rookwood is just full of extravagant mishmashes of different times of what would be potentially somber gravestones in the past put together flamboyantly in the late Victorian period. So talk to me about the technology of gravestones for a second. And I'm thinking at this point of things like engravings and the fonts and the motifs and those sorts of things that are all embellished upon the stone. How has that changed over time? Well, it has changed a lot less than one might expect. So at St. John's Parramatta, where I just was, the earliest gravestones, so, you know, 1790s through to the 1840s, those monuments, which you see in the earliest cemeteries in Australia for the first 50 years, are all ones that you would see and you can see at the back of the Parthenon. If you go down past the Agora in ancient Athens to the Kerimikos, a cemetery that was rediscovered and set up again in the 1860s. And the gravestones here, many of them would not be out of place at all in the Kerimikos. So the design is very much the same design with some new flourishes. So the Greeks used, we call them stabbed letters. So the letters were scratched and then stabbed in with a chisel. So they had rounded chisels and it makes for a lettering that does stand up. And there's ancient Greek lettering that's great. But the Romans really came up with a new technology, which was to cut a long letter. And we call it V-cut lettering and perfected it, you know, in a monumental scale. And that is something that survived really until sandblasting in the 1920s. Wow. So that idea of technology, it hasn't changed. I'm really fascinated by that because I would have thought there'd be a very clear reflection of the sign of the times, if you like, in the stones themselves. But what you're saying is actually, though, there's this much longer enduring legacy that is a slow time there, which seems totally appropriate to a cemetery. It is. It is appropriate. Changes come slowly. Changes do come. So the Egyptians used granite. And for essentially 2,500 years, granite was too hard a stone to use for cemetery monuments because it was just so expensive and hard to work. And so in the middle of the 1800s, Scottish engineers developed a steam-powered bush hammer, which essentially allowed them to recreate. And it was a conscious attempt to recreate Egyptian technology. And I mean, it took us 2,500 years to redevelop the ability to work granite as gravestones. But you see that creep through the cemeteries. And so one of my co-workers has this great expression that at Rookwood, you can start in one era. And as you walk down a road, because Rookwood is such a large cemetery and such an outside of human scale, as you walk down the road, you can actually watch as the architectural patterns change. We revisit Egyptian-style iconography. We revisit Greek. We revisit Roman. And then with the Victorians, we put them all together and make wonderful melanges. And then things become simpler, as a lot of stonemasons were killed in World War I and World War II. And the trade really, well, dived. Lots of skills were reduced and also with mechanization and mechanical cutting. Skills were never lost, but they were, you know, they were no longer front and center. Yeah, yeah. So what's that then done to the actual design of gravestones, you know, since that moment? With that sort of dearth of traditional skills, how has that changed the design of contemporary gravestones? After World War II, labor became expensive. So a simpler gravestone and ones that could be mechanically cut. So we moved to desks and maybe a marble inscription plaque, but simplified versions, mechanical parts that can get cut by machine. And then the lettering eventually also becomes machine laid out. And now we have computer graphic lettering, which doesn't have the soul of the earlier lettering and certainly doesn't have the interest of perhaps the rustic lettering that we see in the very earliest of inscriptions. Before there were professional kind of monumental masons in Australia. So I could definitely understand how you'd have a simplification of the headstones based on that idea of technology starting to get applied. But I would have thought maybe today with CNC milling and these kinds of computer controlled processes, are we seeing a rebirth of more decorative and more elaborate headstones? Yes, we're definitely seeing a rebirth. And some of them involve a lot of hand finishing as well. So it's a combination. And you could imagine that there is a future for that. The vast majority of gravestones now are granite, pre-shaped, done with machine, often finished in places where labor costs are much lower than here. So very little is done in Australia. However, there is that kind of higher end. And there's also natural burials, people having very simple gravestones again. So we're sometimes coming back to the head markers and the 1840s style, maybe just a person's name in some sandstone. Tell me about the future then. Of the gravestone. And I'm thinking because, as you said, a gravestone or a headstone is a necessary mark left on the planet of someone who has passed. But I'm thinking those marks are being replaced by digital photographs and even avatars and all sorts of wild ideas about how to live on into the future. What do you think that means for the gravestone? At some point, it may be time to retire the physical gravestone. I'm still hoping that I'll be around taking care of them and the next generations will be taking care of the old ones. I'm interested in this and certainly virtual cemeteries and reconstructing them so that you can go to a place that you're not at. I mean, yes, we can imagine that in 20 years we may all be visiting places and not actually physically being in them. Yeah. Virtual picnics. Virtual picnics. And yet there's some quite confronting replications of people. I mean, the simple version right now is you have solar powered little motion censored devices that as you come on a grave, someone will talk to you. Oh my goodness. Certainly more common than that, but already around in some cemeteries are ones where a song will play or something prayer will sound as you walk close to it. But yeah, we can imagine. Someone speaking from beyond the grave as you trip the motion sensor is so Victorian and so creepy. Yes, yes. Well, I mean, there are lots of creepy Victorian ideas. It's such a beautiful history you've just given us there. And I particularly love the way you described walking through Rookwood as a kind of a physical archive or like flicking through the pages of history as you stroll amongst the headstones and the gravestones there. Thank you so much for sharing all that with us. Not at all. My pleasure. Satch Killam, stonemason and heritage expert at Rookwood Cemetery. Just search Anthony Burks by Design. Thank you. Thank you.

episodes.title: Is adaptive reuse worth the investment?
episodes.description: Heritage buildings can be pretty … but are they worth the money? Adaptive reuse advocates argue that reworking existing structures isn’t about nostalgia — it’s about unlocking potential.
episodes.transcript: We're often told heritage buildings should be preserved, carefully protected and left untouched. Don't get me wrong, I love an old building that's been thoughtfully brought back to life. But there's something else that can happen in these spaces, something beyond restoration. Speaking of country towns, let's head back to Carlton in Tasmania, where Hannah Chapman is staring down a long list of renovations, each with a hefty price tag attached.
I asked whether the cost of bringing this little piece of Riverside history back to life ever gave her pause.
Yeah, look, absolutely.
There were several kind of evolutions of what it might be that we would do once we finally could do anything.
And then simultaneously, I think interest rates had been going through the roof and we didn't know how long this period of uncertainty would last.

So we actually decided to sort of free up the equity in our family home and sell that and rent so that we could actually, when we finally could do something, first just to relieve the pressure, but then also so that we had options.
Restoring the post office and turning it into a genuinely livable home meant Hannah had to stretch herself financially.
In the end, a heritage grant helped ease some of that pressure.
But beyond the cost of the build, one of the biggest hurdles was something less tangible.
Before a single dollar could be spent on renovations, Hannah had to navigate an extraordinary amount of bureaucratic red tape, a process that proved just as challenging as the construction itself.

They were considering that it was a commercial building and we would need to do a change of use in order to make it something residential, which would have been an impossible disaster because it would have invoked the modern building code.
And as you know, there is basically not a straight line in that cottage, which again is part of the charm, but completely kind of unapproachable if you're going to try to attempt modern standards.
So that was a really long protracted battle and a really big barrier.
But really in those early colonial days, these very humble, almost huts really with this split slab construction were just put up and they were serving really as a dwelling for the postmaster.
So there would be a humble kitchen, there would be, you know, a humble bedroom.
Emphasis on the word humble.
I'm saying that a lot, aren't I?
No, but I'm agreeing with you.
Yeah, so and actually eventually we did convince council, the relevant council involved, that that was the case, but it did take two years.
And red tape isn't just an issue for small residential projects like the post office in Tasmania.
Hannah Louie again.
We interviewed a whole raft of design architects in our project and they all talked about that.
So that's real.
But we also interviewed Australian state government architects and they were really on board to thinking differently about that regulatory framework.
But I think also Australia needs to look here.
You know, I'm not always saying we need to look over our shoulder at other places that are doing it better.
But there are examples in Europe, in the UK and in specific cities that have put forward ways of getting through this regulation burdens.
And, you know, that's a balance between fostering good design, about heritage protections, value for money.
So it's complex.
But I think there are ways in which you might be able to incentivise adaptive reuse and make that pathway quicker and more efficient.
And that's partly by, yeah, getting policymakers on board to say, you know, maybe rather than no, I guess.
Okay, I'll take a maybe for now over a no.
So does that, in your mind, does that red tape sort of land mostly in the planning and zoning kind of area or more in, let's say, the standards of contemporary building versus older buildings?
Like, I think it's all of those things.
And ironically, also, a lot of the architects are saying that it's actually the sustainability regulation, which is not kind of calibrated right yet here.
So that to make a building perform to standard, it's really difficult.
And that needs to be rethought so that there's some offsets for say, okay, you get sort of some stars in your rating system for retaining fabric, for retaining materials.
And then we'll work to see how we can make it perform.
But at the moment, yeah, there's some big barriers in making them to code.
I'm hearing also, I guess, that adaptive reuse is becoming more popular.
It's certainly becoming more prolific.
Do you sort of see it becoming more popular?
And how can we help that along?
Well, I think it's just by necessity and by desire.
You need both of those things.
You need the regulation, but you also need the want to, you know, yeah.
And so I hope it's becoming more popular.
And that's partly, I think, we use the word old in our title of our book of rather than existing.
And someone said that we had a book launch the other day and someone said, why didn't you use the word existing buildings instead of old buildings?
And I was sort of saying, well, I kind of want to be a bit provocative that Australians need to love old things a bit more.
You know, we're quite good at getting rid of old things.
And then we mourn them when they're gone.
And so we need to rethink obsolescence and make it popular, make it desirable, make it the places to be.
And it's already happening in hospitality and in, you know, all sorts of venues that are capitalizing on that.
So, yeah, it needs to become more widespread.
I was also thinking about it with a stupid analogy because I'm going to the dentist tomorrow.
Oh, I can't wait for this.
It might be.
You know, it's a bit like what dentistry used to be, which is basically too difficult to deal with your old teeth.
So they used to take them all out and put in a set of false teeth, which we now know was really bad for the health of the whole body, for all sorts of things.
And now we nurse each tooth, or they do in my old mouth, you know, we nurse each tooth along and tinker with it and keep it there.
And so I sort of feel like that's our cities as well.
Where do you think the major opportunities are for future adaptive reuse projects?
The opportunities, like the things that will really make a difference for us?
Well, I think we're not bad at valuing 19th century buildings.
And when we did this work and seeing a lot of examples, you tend to get the same kind of aesthetic of, yeah, we want to keep old red brick, timber, buildings of that era.
We're less good about thinking about 20th century, mid-20th century, late 20th century buildings.
But they are so substantial.
And again, that's what things like these heritage surveys have happened in the Hoddle Street grid survey in Melbourne as one, but they're happening everywhere.
There's all this sort of, yeah, 1950s, 60s building stock.
And that embodies so much calm and so much materials.
I mean, I happen to really like modern architecture.
I know a lot of people don't.
But I think there is such opportunities in imaginatively reusing that building stock.
Back in Tasmania, Hannah Chapman's post office was finished and is now an Airbnb.
For her, tinkering with the old post office in Carlton was definitely worth the time and money.
We sort of have this idea that one day we'll retire there and perhaps, you know, build a modern extension.
And so long as I can drag my husband away from the city.
But it's just, you know, it does bring us a lot of joy.
And as much as sharing it with other people might have seemed like, you know, something that we felt hesitant to do,
it's actually been incredibly rewarding to see other people also fall in love with it.
And to see people really relax there and appreciate the history of the building, the significance of it and the way that it's been conserved.
Falling for a sweet little riverside cottage can come with its fair share of headaches.
Red tape, rising costs and plenty of uncertainty.
But stories like Hannah's make it clear that there are real rewards in investing in our past in this way.
For me, it's a space where I think some of our best architectural design is happening.
Because you need to think in detail.
There is no off-the-shelf solution for taking non-standard circumstances and making them new ones.
And after all, you're breathing new life into the stories that give a building meaning and depth,
which we know is so important to our sense of belonging and place.
If we take the opportunity, as Hannah Louie suggests, to rethink what we've labelled as obsolete and instead see possibility,
we're not only making a more environmentally responsible choice,
we're opening the door to a whole lot of creative ones too.
Do you have a favourite building or home that has been adapted?

He says,
I enjoyed your program featuring your engagement with the exceptionally vivacious Indonesian artist, Josephine.
And I was thinking a nice follow-up might be a show featuring or drawing connection with Australia's northern Aboriginal batik weavers.
Great idea, Ian.

Thanks for being a part of By Design.
Follow the podcast to catch future episodes and listen out for our bonus series,
Extraordinary Every Day, released every Thursday.

This is a technique that is clear, that is being used so that people cannot find any link to their history,
to their previous history or their previous memory as a person.
Forget the passing on of the memory from one space, from one person to the other and one generation to the other.
Join me for that next time on By Design, because in a rapidly changing world, design matters.

And the executive producer is Rhiannon Brown.
