episodes.title: Extraordinary Everyday: Pockets
episodes.description: Men expect them in every pair of pants, every jacket, every coat. And yet, for women, pockets have been mysteriously withheld, removed, resized, or declared “unnecessary” for centuries. Why?
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. We spend most of our days using ordinary objects that make our life easier, but each one of those objects holds a delightful design story. Welcome to Extraordinary Every Day, where we bring that history back to life. Podcasts, could anything in clothing seem more ordinary? Probably not. I expect every pair of pants or jacket I buy to come with them, but that hasn't always been true for women's fashion. Throughout history, the need for pockets never disappeared, even when designers inexplicably removed them from women's clothing. Even now, the rare dress or skirt with pockets sparks a little thrill of surprise. So, I want to know more. Let's dive into the unexpected and quietly revolutionary story of pockets. And to talk all things pockets, I'm joined by Nicole Jenkins, who's a fashion historian. Hi, Nicole. Hi, Anthony. Thanks for joining me today. Pockets, who knew? So exciting. This is one of those things I guess I've never really given much thought to, but there's a huge history here, isn't there? There is, there is. And you're in a very fortunate position being a man because your clothes will automatically give you pockets, so you don't need to worry about it. I see. So, this has been gendered from the very beginning, yes? Pretty much, pretty much. So, when were the first pockets included in women's clothing then? Well, it's very hard to sort of differentiate because they are a kind of purse, a kind of handbag, a kind of bag that women originally would hang around their waist. And so, it started during about the 15th century, they think. But my feeling, I'm a sewer, and sewers know that when you're a sewer, when you make clothes, you just make clothes that fit your purpose. And so, I'm pretty confident that women would have been sewing pockets into garments or on top of them or, you know, they would have been customising their garments to suit their purposes for a long, long time. So, much earlier than the 15th century. Absolutely. We don't have evidence for it, but I know what people who sew do. So, what did those early pockets look like then? The early ones are called hanging pockets, and they're like little sort of bags that would hang on a cord around your waist. So, I guess in a way, a bit like a sort of waist version of a cross-body bag. Okay. So, they're quite big then, yeah? They're like a little, more like a satchel. Yeah. A small satchel. Well, they're as big as they needed to be. And back in the day, back in the Middle Ages or in the 15th century, 16th century, women didn't need to carry very much most of the time. And so, they didn't, it all depends on what your function is, you know, what you need and use. So, they were probably fairly small. The ones that I've seen are kind of little flat things, pretty much like a pocket with an opening at the top, and you just put in the things that you have. So, I should say men also had bags at this time as well, and also similar pockets. So, in the beginning, they weren't really gendered at all, but people would put them on around their waist and carry them, fill them with what they needed and go about the day. You're describing a very functional address to a real issue, which is where on earth do I put my coins, for example? But was there a fashion side to this? Was there any kind of, I guess, statement being made by having a pocket or not having a pocket? Well, exactly. It's very much a fashion thing because generally, in the history of fashion, menswear tends towards functionality and womenswear tends to fashionability. And womenswear, at any given time, reflects the fashionable silhouette of the time. And depending on your social status, where you are in the class system, the more fashionable you'll dress. And pockets can get in the way of that. You know, they can sort of spoil a nice, beautiful line of a dress. And this is probably why they've fallen foul of the world and why they fell out of favour and why they're only starting to come back again in about the last 50 or so years. Yeah. Wouldn't want any sort of utilitarian kind of, you know, accoutrement to spoil the silhouette of a beautiful dress, for example. Well, that's right. And also by making the pockets a separate external thing, i.e. a handbag, you have a whole new industry that you can support. And the handbag industry is a very important industry. Makes a lot of money for people. We like our handbags. So it has been a part of men's clothing all along and it has been a part of women's clothing only more recently is what I'm sort of hearing. Well, I think that the concealed pockets were always there because women, especially working class women or middle class women who had functions to do, would find ways to carry the things they needed. For example, in the Victorian era, housekeepers would need a number of tools like scissors or thimbles, a lot of sewing materials. And so they would carry them around their waist in the form of chatelaine. And a chatelaine isn't a pocket, but it does sort of hang these things from your waist so that you can easily get at them and use them in your day-to-day life. Sorry, what's a chatelaine? A chatelaine. It's like a strange little sort of metal. It sort of clasps on with a bit like a brooch and it has chains. And at the end of each chain is a device. So a tiny pair of scissors or a thimble or a little clock or whatever it is that you need for your day. Oh, that sounds so useful. Bring back the chatelaine, I say. Oh, they're wonderful things. They're wonderful things. And they make you look so efficient. Yes, of course. You look like you're ready for anything. Exactly. It's a bit like a very genteel lady-like version of the modern tradie who has a belt with all of his tools hanging from it, except that they're delicate, beautifully designed tools, suitable for delicate ladies. So, all right, then we've heard about chatelaines now. So now talk to me about tie-on pockets. Tie-on pockets. Well, you do see them in museum collections and you do see them around the place and you just tie it around. It's a very simple device that you just tie around your waist, a bit like a belt that happens to have little pockets hanging down. But I secretly think that most women probably went for the hidden pocket because through most of history, women are wearing voluminous skirts and petticoats. And it's very easy just to insert a little pocket between your skirt and your petticoat that you can access through one of your seams. So there's always been that useful side to it, snuck in there somehow. That's right. And it's invisible. It doesn't spoil the line of your dress. And you can hide all manner of things like love letters or handkerchiefs or trinkets. Yes. Who knows what a lady might have in her skirts? Indeed. And one doesn't ask. One definitely doesn't ask. It is a very private and intimate business. What comes between a lady and her skirt is no one's business but her own. I love that. So then it's sounding to me a lot like we've had pockets. They've been disguised. They've been snuck in between the layers of voluminous dresses and all the rest. But then they become fashionable again. They kind of get expressed in the garments and so on. So is it a sort of a bit of a merry-go-round of style they come into and out of fashion? Well, increasingly over the years, women start to want a lot more functionality from their clothes. And we can thank the suffragettes and their ilk for this in part because women are agitating. You know, in the early part of the 20th century, we want the vote. We want to have rights. We want to be able to do all the things that men can do. And part of that is we want to be able to have things in our pockets. So one of the big changes that happens around this time is World War I. And of course, women are fighting behind the scenes, you know, in the factories and in the offices, stepping into all the roles that the men are doing because while the men are off fighting. And so the women are wearing nurses' uniforms and versions of militarised uniforms. And so these come with pockets, of course. So the Red Cross nurses will, they need to carry things. So they need to have pockets. So you start to see the pockets come back a bit just for usefulness because a lady who's working on the factory floor or whatever can't have a reticule by her side. She needs to be able to access whatever she needs quickly and easily. So this happens also again in World War II. And after the war, women don't want to give up those freedoms. They don't want to give up what they've benefited from, what they've got used to using. So you do see a few pockets in the first half of the 20th century before World War II. But they're usually smallish ones, decorative things that really don't hold very much at all. Maybe a tiny key or a very carefully folded up lace handkerchief. But it's really only after World War II that women start pushing those boundaries and start wanting proper pockets. And it starts to get much bigger in the 60s and the 70s when there's a lot more masculine influence coming in and women are sort of saying they want it. But it's still, you know, small, delicate little pockets that don't affect the line of the clothing, who don't change the silhouette. More of a feature than anything practical. Okay. So it's an interesting kind of dance that's going on here, isn't it? Again, ebbing and flowing between very practical and utilitarian ideas to a decorative patch that becomes a bit more leaning towards the fashion side of the equation, I guess. But all of it symbolizing, you know, women's rights. And like women should be able to carry whatever they want in their pockets. And so there's a sort of a form of resistance that's being symbolized in all of this. Absolutely. And through a lot of these times, most of the clothing is custom made by women. And so, as I mentioned earlier, I'm sure that they're putting in pockets if they want to. They've never been fully replaced, have they, by the handbag? I think we're getting to the point now, actually. Really? Yeah. Handbags are another thing that go in and out of fashion as far as size. At the moment, we're very big on crossbody bags. Walking down here just now, I was checking out all the bags that people were carrying. There were some ladies who were off to see the Vivian Westwood exhibition at the NGV, and they were wearing very lovely designer, quite big handbags. But most of the women were just walking casually with very small crossbody bags. Like me. I was one of them as well. I was just saying that. I'm thinking, yeah, I suppose. But we are carrying a lot more stuff around with us, it seems. Like our phones, for example. That's one thing we didn't have in our pockets, you know, like 20 years ago, but they're with us all the time now. Um, and yes, the car keys, the additions of the wallets and all the rest of it. So we're not kind of trimming down, at least it seems to me, we're not trimming down the stuff that we're taking with us. So I don't know if pockets, I think they've got a pretty good future. Would you say? Well, I disagree, actually. I think we are carrying a lot less. Women didn't used to carry very much until about the 1960s. So the handbags were small and delicate, usually, unless you've got a big bag, like a carpet bag or something like that, where it's more of a purpose thing. But over the 60s, 70s, 80s, 90s, we've started to get used to big bags. But especially since the pandemic, a lot of us have, well, I mean, I just did without my handbag for a couple of years and just started using pockets. I deliberately prefer to buy clothes that have pockets. Or if I don't have pockets in something, I'll sew them in. I'll add them in. So I think a lot of us are carrying a lot less now than we used to. Almost like a modern day version of the pocket is the bag that just carries your mobile phone. It's just a little slip of leather that you put your mobile phone in and has a thin strap to go around your neck or around your body. And it might carry your bus pass or your bank card. And that's all a lot of us need these days. Yeah. Yeah. Well, I stand corrected. Absolutely. But it does sound like the future of the pocket is bright. I think so. And I think that it's become such a thing that I think that we're only going to want and demand cheer for more and more pockets. Because it's such an exciting thing for women to be able to walk through the streets. Handbags do have their downsides. One of them is it makes you feel vulnerable because you're always worried that someone's going to come and grab your handbag. And if you talk to women about handbag thefts, we've all had this experience or fear. You know, you go in, where do you put your handbag when you sit in a bar or a cafe? You know, is it vulnerable to someone helping themselves to it? Much easier to just have a pocket. Bring back the pocket. Bring back the pocket. I love it. I love it. For all the right reasons, for all the safety, the utilitarian side to it all. And of course, all the possibilities of fashion that come with that. That sounds like we've got actually a very bright future for pockets after all. So that's great to hear. And don't forget the equality. We just want the same freedoms that men have. Wonderful. Well, yes. Here's to the pocket. Hurrah. Hurrah for the pocket. Nicole, thank you so much for talking to me today and introducing me. And as I said, schooling me a little on the history of the pocket and its future. Oh, you're welcome. I hope you're converted now to the course. Absolutely. One hundred percent. Nicole Jenkins, fashion historian from Circa Vintage. Got an everyday object you think is hiding an unexpected backstory? If something comes to mind and you'd like us to dig into it, send us an email at bydesign at abc.net.au. As always, if you enjoyed the episode, make sure you follow the show on ABC Listen. Just search Anthony Burks by design. You've been listening to an ABC podcast. Discover more great ABC podcasts, live radio and exclusives on the ABC Listen app. You've been listening to an ABC Listen app.

More of a feature than anything practical.
Okay.

but they're with us all the time now.

we're not trimming down the stuff that we're taking with us.
So I don't know if pockets, I think they've got a pretty good future.

unless you've got a big bag, like a carpet bag or something like that,
where it's more of a purpose thing.

But especially since the pandemic, a lot of us have, well, I mean,
I just did without my handbag for a couple of years and just started using pockets.
I deliberately prefer to buy clothes that have pockets.
Or if I don't have pockets in something, I'll sew them in.
I'll add them in.
So I think a lot of us are carrying a lot less now than we used to.
Almost like a modern day version of the pocket is the bag that just carries your mobile phone.
It's just a little slip of leather that you put your mobile phone in and has a thin strap to go around your neck or around your body.
And it might carry your bus pass or your bank card.
And that's all a lot of us need these days.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Well, I stand corrected.
Absolutely.
But it does sound like the future of the pocket is bright.
I think so.
And I think that it's become such a thing that I think that we're only going to want and demand cheer for more and more pockets.
Because it's such an exciting thing for women to be able to walk through the streets.
Handbags do have their downsides.
One of them is it makes you feel vulnerable because you're always worried that someone's going to come and grab your handbag.
And if you talk to women about handbag thefts, we've all had this experience or fear.
You know, you go in, where do you put your handbag when you sit in a bar or a cafe?
You know, is it vulnerable to someone helping themselves to it?
Much easier to just have a pocket.
Bring back the pocket.
Bring back the pocket.
I love it.
I love it.
For all the right reasons, for all the safety, the utilitarian side to it all.
And of course, all the possibilities of fashion that come with that.
That sounds like we've got actually a very bright future for pockets after all.
So that's great to hear.
And don't forget the equality.
We just want the same freedoms that men have.
Wonderful.
Well, yes.
Here's to the pocket.
Hurrah.
Hurrah for the pocket.
Nicole, thank you so much for talking to me today and introducing me.
And as I said, schooling me a little on the history of the pocket and its future.

Nicole Jenkins, fashion historian from Circa Vintage.

episodes.title: How AI is reshaping architecture
episodes.description: Algorithms are sketching, rendering, optimising, and quietly reshaping who holds creative power. In this episode, we ask the uncomfortable questions: Is AI a tool, a collaborator, or a threat?
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. When I look at a building, I don't just see the finished structure. I see the many steps that brought it to life. The creative conversations, the sketches and drawings, the site meeting where ideas are tested, challenged and refined. It's this human collaboration between architects and builders that shapes the world we live in. But what happens to that process and to the buildings it produces when artificial intelligence enters the picture? I'm Professor of Architecture Anthony Burke and this is By Design on ABC Radio National. It's the new kid on the block when it comes to technology and it's changing everything from how we analyse data to the way we communicate. But just how much is artificial intelligence reshaping the way we build? Can anyone now design their own home? James Loder is a partner at Wardle, an award-winning architectural firm based in Sydney and Melbourne. Wardle is known for the texture, tone and handmade materials that bring their work to life. They pay extraordinary attention to detail. Not exactly what you might associate with the output of AI. But James says AI is simply a tool and what matters is how you use it. When we first started using the more image-based tools like Mid Journey, this was probably a couple of years ago, we were having a bit of fun just sort of experimenting with what we could produce. And I think some of the more sort of beautiful conceptual imagery that was pretty unrealistic to ever build was certainly something interesting for us to kind of draw inspiration from or even build into an overarching concept that we would then develop into a model. So sort of inspiring yourselves, sort of, you know, tricking yourself in a way and like opening the box of design a little broader than you ever imagined. Yeah, I think both being expansive in the way we're able to experiment, but then I think as a means of particularly communicating a really early concept, say to a client, you could use some evocative imagery with, say, a diagram that pairs with the potential without having to go the full distance. We found that quite effective. Yeah, right. So there's a sort of a shorthand to some visualisation. It's a kind of a promise, but not an actual design. That's right. And I think the trap is users or architects are trying to create the kind of full final image. For us, it's trying to create something more abstract and evocative that communicates an idea rather than a final potential outcome. So that's one way to use AI. That's the kind of image generation side of things. Do you use it in other ways? Yeah, look, I mean, chat GPT is interesting. It's obviously probably the most broadly used tool sort of as far as AI goes in most industries. I think the challenges around it are its reliability. And I think what we've looked at doing, and I know a lot of other firms are investing in, is kind of creating their own chat GPT chatbot where it harvests all the information and data of a practice. And you can use it to interact with, to pull up old projects or information very, very quickly. The challenge there really is in data management. It's all very dry, but it relies on a really robust back end that I think it's kind of out of reach for most architectural practices. Right. It's a bigger enterprise than you'd imagine. Yeah, very much so. So, I mean, I have heard of that. Like that is practices training their own AIs so that they avoid the trap of firstly intellectual property that's been brought into large models. They can control that content. But then also give it a language, I suppose, cultivate a language that is appropriate to the office itself. Do you see that as something that's going to continue, do you think? Or do you think that's the way forward? I think from a language of a tone of voice perspective or the way in which a practice communicates is certainly also something we've looked to use it for. And the way in which we write for reports and bids and the way we would outwardly communicate inward, though, is a little more complex to pull off. And again, the reliability of the data is one of the biggest hurdles, I think. So can you give me a specific example in your practice where you've used AI? So on a regular basis, we would use it to almost copyright and proofread large bodies of text, whether it's for a design report. It can edit down, reduce content and I think overall review the overall pitch, perhaps. So it's a really kind of useful kind of copywriting tool. What about in the design space, the visualization and so on? Pretty broad. And I'd say from the spectrum of a kind of high level exploration of ideas in a very early phase to the most common tool that everyone's using for is highly polished renderings, which, you know, used to be quite expensive to output and time consuming. Now it is at the click of a button. You can knock it out in 10 seconds and endlessly iterate. I think that's where we're using it kind of on a day to day basis the most. So that super quick response. Super quick response and really high quality renderings that you could just about, you type any prompt in, changing an image, you can change materials, the entourage. It's, yeah, it's sort of really limitless. Are the architects in the office getting a bit nervous about design being, you know, like taken over by the new kid on the block, which happens to be living in the hard drive just under my desk? It's interesting because like at the end of the day, I've always felt that AI really is just a tool for greater efficiency. It's just speeding up a process that used to take us longer to undertake. And with regards to it being a design tool to iterate ideas, I'd liken to, you know, giving a task to a room full of graduates to say, here's my prompt, here's my instruction. Come up with 10 different scenarios, bring it back to me, I'll pick one and we'll go from there. That's effectively how we see the kind of engagement with the tool. And whilst you might worry that it's removing it from the graduate, the notion there is it's the grads, it's the younger generation who are actually most attuned to using the software. So it's actually them really come on board with the kind of processes and workflows of that iterative process. We're still in the early days of AI, but it's already making a noticeable impact on architectural studios like Wardle. James says it's giving designers the freedom to push their imaginations further than ever before, expanding what's possible in the conceptual stage. And it's streamlining data in ways that might sound dull at first, but as James points out, those efficiencies matter. For architect Philip Alsop, AI and access to vast troves of research data represents one of the biggest potential breakthroughs in how we design and build for human health and well-being. Bet you didn't see that coming. Philip is the co-chair of the Royal Institute of British Architects expert advisory panel on AI, and he has a deep interest in how the built environment affects our physical and mental health. If you ask any wildlife biologist, what makes a species thrive? They'll invariably give you a short answer as habitat. But our species has decided to turn its habitat into a kind of a real estate commodity, a line item, a market, a transaction. And yet it is habitat. It is the places that we inhabit that play such a profound role in who we are as people, how we get on in life, how kids learn to explore the world around them and become adults. That being able to analyze all of the information pertaining to the design of environments and the full integration of biodiversity within that, which is so vitally important, becomes something where AI can play a massively important role in helping architects to grapple with the very things they've always wanted to do, which is to know more about how design works and why it works better in certain circumstances than in others. And at the same time, that ability to grapple with complex and very disparate data gives architects a significant leg up in being able to say, well, look, if you come to us and use us for this design work, we can operate almost as if we are conducting gene therapy on the DNA of where you live. And we can do it very well. And we have access to information. And we can manipulate that information to optimize the design solution that is likely to work. And it also gives great agency for clients to become much more engaged with architects in that process. So I think it suggests to me, at least, that there is an opportunity for greater transparency in what it is that architects do and the process of actually creating a design from the very idea of a need of a building all the ways through to the making of it as well. So that's that releasing that positive value that's currently under-realized for architects back into the process, not just the process, I suppose, but the conversation with clients and stakeholders for any project. It is. It is. And the way you talk about AI, it's analytic. It's, I mean, again, most people would think, oh, it's creating images. It's kind of, you know, fictioning up master plans of all kinds. But what you're talking about here is actually really scientific and looking at the analytical side of architecture to formulate the situation with much more depth. In my career, I spent quite a bit of time in the public health field because that's the sort of left or right term, whichever way you want to do it, that I took after becoming an architect. It was just my love of biology and science, actually, that got me into that direction. But what I found was in my work in healthcare analytics, conducting analysis of lots and lots of data, paid health insurance claims, you name it, was the unmistakable fingerprint of built environments in a whole range of chronic disease conditions and mental health conditions. And that's not just me saying it. It's also public health professionals and professionals in the environmental neuroscience field where they're looking at how environmental circumstances shape behavior, shape cognitive abilities, shape educational attainment, shape how kids learn to understand the world around them in a way that gives them some sense of agency and control, as opposed to being put into a very poorly thought through environments where it's dangerous. They never get a chance to really explore much of the world around them. And then suddenly they're an adult. These kinds of dynamics are very, very important and can be built into the spectrum of work that architects are able to do. As you're just saying that, I'm imagining this whole field of scientific research and other kinds of research that needs to be collated into some usable form so that architects can bring that to the design task in front of them. And if that's housing or whatever it is, that's really what you're saying. It's that ability that AI brings that makes it possible. It absolutely does. And if you look at the way in which clinicians record why somebody shows up at a doctor's office or an emergency room, there is a huge compendium of diagnoses categories called the International Classification of Disease, ICD. And there is actually a category in there for diagnoses that fall under poor or inadequate housing. And children born into inadequate and poor housing, where very little design work has been done, it's just throw up the house, make sure the parking spaces are there, give them a bit of a backyard, call it quits and leave and go. Children born into those circumstances have between a seven and nine year lower life expectancy than other kids. The data is there. It's kind of yelling in a very silent way at us. And I think that with more data, more scientific approaches, we can get to the very practical things that mean something for people. You know, instead of a flat wall in an affordable housing scheme where somebody sits near a window, the ability to quite easily make that a little reading alcove that kids love to be in, that makes all the difference in the world to how people inhabit their environments. And we see such little attention being paid to that today, where built environments are often seen as just a real estate commodity. And I guess, you know, people put up with it and try to do their best with it. But we can do better than that. This is the part of AI that really grabs me. I believe that architects have a responsibility to design buildings that work for people and the environment. And what Philip's talking about is essentially drawing on all these new streams of real world data, actual health outcomes, and using that to guide how we build. So we can integrate evidence with the design process, and we can create environments that genuinely support us. And if we can do that for human health, imagine what's possible when it comes to designing buildings that work better with the environment too. But of course, as everyone keeps reminding us, AI is just a tool. And it's how people choose to use that tool that will end up shaping the future of architecture. Philip again. I think the downsides exist at the other end of the building spectrum, which is where you can use AI-enhanced robotic code to convert a building information modeling design, a BIM design, into production line code. And the tendency to sort of supercharge cookie cutter solutions to design needs. Not everybody necessarily does very well inside of, you know, a former sneaker container from some country. Not everybody does well in that. But there is, I think, a danger in assuming that because we've got robotic production and we can componentize buildings for rapid assembly on site with very little waste, if any, little to no waste, that we can kind of claim success. I think there is a danger in making that assumption. And in the same way that we need to be diligent at the, shall we say, policy end that we've just been talking about relative to the healthcare impacts, long-term healthcare impacts. We also need diligence at that end to see what is happening when we start to make production line buildings the norm. And are we doing ourselves a disservice by doing that? Because we've seen plenty of examples of so-called modular buildings, which might sort of go up quickly and they might be okay for a few months. But some of the places don't shape up too well over time. And so there's a lot of diligence needs to be placed at that end of the spectrum where AI is going to be used and is already being used to inform robotic production line code for a patronized building. So with thinking about AI then again in that context, I mean, the genie is kind of out of the bottle at this point. The last I read about the most recent releases of ChatGPT and Claude were that they were basically designing themselves now. I mean, that's the kind of the rumor. I don't know if it's true or not. So, I mean, in that context, how do you manage an industry and the way that it would use AI? When we've got Claude and ChatGPT literally designing themselves and beginning to become more sentient, the question then becomes, when we design environments for people, we're actually engaged in making a large number of judgment calls about whether we should do this, whether that window should be that, whether the door should be this big, whether the house or the office or the factory should be in this particular location or another one. It's not clear to me that at the moment, that even with the meteoric rise of large language models like Claude and others, that they're going to be necessarily great at making those judgment calls. They're great at doing analytics and rapid pattern recognition. There's no question about that. And that's very valuable. But are they any good at mathematics? I'm not so sure about that. Are they any good at making judgment calls? Because, I mean, if something happened to a building and it fell apart because of it just didn't work, but there was a complete reliance on AI to actually do all the detailing, it's going to be pretty difficult to stand up in front of a judge in a court and say, well, it wasn't me that did it, it was the AI, that there's a level in our society, at least we hope that it's the case eventually everywhere, that there is a certain level of accountability for the actions you make and the judgment calls you make. And at the moment, it doesn't seem to me that there is much in the way of accountability being placed on the development of these AI environments. Even though Philip Alsop sees huge potential for AI in shaping healthier built environments, he's clear about one thing. Nothing replaces human ethical judgment. For James Loder, AI works best when it's paired with a creative human mind, a collaborator, not a replacement. So while AI is already making a significant impact, humans are still in the driver's seat, at least for now. I think the difference between creating your own image to print out and put it on a wall to having something built is a very long stretch. And I think that's where the industry is relatively safe for now, that the complexity of taking an image and having it built is a massive gap and process that occurs. One of the critiques I've heard is that there's a much higher propensity towards the kind of cookie cutter outcomes by using these kinds of systems in the background, because they tend to drive towards a certain sort of solution that is, let's say, less creative, if I could put it that way. More efficient, less creative. So it sort of tends to the middle. And I wonder if there's any validity, you think, in that idea of the cookie cutter outcome. But also, how do you kind of get around the idea that less ethical or more profit-hungry studios could use AI badly? Look, it's yes. And to the cookie cutter notion, I think there'd be firms doing the cookie cutter notion without using AI. I think there is, it already exists, and it exists for a more commercial and efficient approach to what that output needs to be in a certain part of the industry. And that's fine. There's got to be a balance. And I think the introduction of AI may generally make things more efficient for most practices. But I think there will always be a want for a level of design excellence that really comes from beyond just the use of AI. And it's really engaging with the practice and the culture of that practice. And the future of AI in architecture? Still uncertain. But James and Philip are optimistic about where it could lead. James Loder again. What I see coming is a more general AI tool, because at the moment it's all segregated into text, image. There's many different tools. You know, Microsoft have their co-pilot, which is probably where I'm going with this. You can have a conversation with a tool and it can work across a number of different facets. And I think there's always going to be a line of how far to engage with it, apply trust, and where to bring it back to a kind of a human level conversation, particularly in the creative end. You're really curating the content. And to do so, you have to know in the first instance, what is the right approach? What is the right solution? And you're bringing your own personality to that. And that's what people are interested in. I think we're going to see through the efforts of more architects who are becoming much more engaged in scientific inquiry, that we will begin to see new collaborations of players coming together around the built environment. One of the victims of the economic system we have, which is basically rewarding anybody who can strip mine people's lives and the planet for money, for short-term money, is that it's created huge risk. And it is the property casualty insurers and their reinsurers who are really hurting badly. And I think we may see that more and more architects in collaboration with folks in the public health field and folks in the property casualty insurance will start to collaborate on ways of de-risking the way we inhabit this planet. And by de-risking it, I mean making environments that work for people and enable people to actually feel as if they belong somewhere and they belong in the home that they try to make. And so I think it's those new collaborations that we'll see, certainly in the field of architecture, most of the collaborations occur with closely allied professionals, structural engineer, mechanical engineer, civil engineering, MEP, and so on. But just in a fairly closely related orbit, just outside of that, are these other players from the finance industry, from the healthcare industry, who are right now dealing with the problems that result from basically treating human habitat as if it was a throwaway real estate commodity? And that hurts everybody. Philip Alsop, co-chair, RIBA Expert Advisory Group on AI. Next time on By Design, are we prepared to pay for history? We actually decided to free up the equity in our family home and sell that and rent. It's been incredibly rewarding to see other people also fall in love with it and to see people really relax there and appreciate the history of the building, the significance of it and the way that it's been conserved. Join me for that next time on By Design. Because in a rapidly changing world, design matters. The producer of By Design is Siobhan Hunt and the executive producer is Rhiannon Brown. This program was produced on Gadigal Land and the lands of the Rundjeri. The producer of By Design is Siobhan Hunt and the executive producer is Rhiannon Brown. The producer of By Design is Siobhan Hunt and the executive producer is Rhiannon Brown. You've been listening to an ABC podcast. James says it's giving designers the freedom to push their imaginations further than ever before, expanding what's possible in the conceptual stage.
And it's streamlining data in ways that might sound dull at first, but as James points out, those efficiencies matter.
For architect Philip Alsop, AI and access to vast troves of research data represents one of the biggest potential breakthroughs in how we design and build for human health and well-being.
Bet you didn't see that coming.
Philip is the co-chair of the Royal Institute of British Architects expert advisory panel on AI, and he has a deep interest in how the built environment affects our physical and mental health.
If you ask any wildlife biologist, what makes a species thrive?
They'll invariably give you a short answer as habitat.
But our species has decided to turn its habitat into a kind of a real estate commodity, a line item, a market, a transaction.
And yet it is habitat.
It is the places that we inhabit that play such a profound role in who we are as people, how we get on in life, how kids learn to explore the world around them and become adults.
That being able to analyze all of the information pertaining to the design of environments and the full integration of biodiversity within that, which is so vitally important,
becomes something where AI can play a massively important role in helping architects to grapple with the very things they've always wanted to do,
which is to know more about how design works and why it works better in certain circumstances than in others.
And at the same time, that ability to grapple with complex and very disparate data gives architects a significant leg up in being able to say,
well, look, if you come to us and use us for this design work, we can operate almost as if we are conducting gene therapy on the DNA of where you live.
And we can do it very well.
And we have access to information.
And we can manipulate that information to optimize the design solution that is likely to work.
And it also gives great agency for clients to become much more engaged with architects in that process.
So I think it suggests to me, at least, that there is an opportunity for greater transparency in what it is that architects do
and the process of actually creating a design from the very idea of a need of a building all the ways through to the making of it as well.
So that's that releasing that positive value that's currently under-realized for architects back into the process,
not just the process, I suppose, but the conversation with clients and stakeholders for any project.
It is. It is.
And the way you talk about AI, it's analytic.
It's, I mean, again, most people would think, oh, it's creating images.
It's kind of, you know, fictioning up master plans of all kinds.
But what you're talking about here is actually really scientific and looking at the analytical side of architecture to formulate the situation with much more depth.
In my career, I spent quite a bit of time in the public health field because that's the sort of left or right term,
whichever way you want to do it, that I took after becoming an architect.
It was just my love of biology and science, actually, that got me into that direction.
But what I found was in my work in healthcare analytics, conducting analysis of lots and lots of data, paid health insurance claims, you name it,
was the unmistakable fingerprint of built environments in a whole range of chronic disease conditions and mental health conditions.
And that's not just me saying it.
It's also public health professionals and professionals in the environmental neuroscience field where they're looking at how environmental circumstances shape behavior,
shape cognitive abilities, shape educational attainment,
shape how kids learn to understand the world around them in a way that gives them some sense of agency and control,
as opposed to being put into a very poorly thought through environments where it's dangerous.
They never get a chance to really explore much of the world around them.
And then suddenly they're an adult.
These kinds of dynamics are very,
very important and can be built into the spectrum of work that architects are able to do.
As you're just saying that, I'm imagining this whole field of scientific research and other kinds of research
that needs to be collated into some usable form so that architects can bring that to the design task in front of them.
And if that's housing or whatever it is, that's really what you're saying.
It's that ability that AI brings that makes it possible.
It absolutely does.
And if you look at the way in which clinicians record why somebody shows up at a doctor's office or an emergency room,
there is a huge compendium of diagnoses categories called the International Classification of Disease, ICD.
And there is actually a category in there for diagnoses that fall under poor or inadequate housing.
And children born into inadequate and poor housing, where very little design work has been done,
it's just throw up the house, make sure the parking spaces are there,
give them a bit of a backyard, call it quits and leave and go.
Children born into those circumstances have between a seven and nine year lower life expectancy than other kids.
The data is there.
It's kind of yelling in a very silent way at us.
And I think that with more data, more scientific approaches,
we can get to the very practical things that mean something for people.
You know, instead of a flat wall in an affordable housing scheme where somebody sits near a window,
the ability to quite easily make that a little reading alcove that kids love to be in,
that makes all the difference in the world to how people inhabit their environments.
And we see such little attention being paid to that today,
where built environments are often seen as just a real estate commodity.
And I guess, you know, people put up with it and try to do their best with it.
But we can do better than that.
This is the part of AI that really grabs me.
I believe that architects have a responsibility to design buildings that work for people and the environment.
And what Philip's talking about is essentially drawing on all these new streams of real world data,
actual health outcomes, and using that to guide how we build.
So we can integrate evidence with the design process,
and we can create environments that genuinely support us.
And if we can do that for human health,
imagine what's possible when it comes to designing buildings that work better with the environment too.
But of course, as everyone keeps reminding us, AI is just a tool.
And it's how people choose to use that tool that will end up shaping the future of architecture.
Philip again.
I think the downsides exist at the other end of the building spectrum,
which is where you can use AI-enhanced robotic code
to convert a building information modeling design, a BIM design,
into production line code.
And the tendency to sort of supercharge cookie cutter solutions to design needs.
Not everybody necessarily does very well inside of, you know,
a former sneaker container from some country.
Not everybody does well in that.
But there is, I think, a danger in assuming that because we've got robotic production
and we can componentize buildings for rapid assembly on site with very little waste,
if any, little to no waste, that we can kind of claim success.
I think there is a danger in making that assumption.
And in the same way that we need to be diligent at the, shall we say, policy end that we've just been talking about
relative to the healthcare impacts, long-term healthcare impacts.
We also need diligence at that end to see what is happening when we start to make production line buildings the norm.
And are we doing ourselves a disservice by doing that?
Because we've seen plenty of examples of so-called modular buildings,
which might sort of go up quickly and they might be okay for a few months.
But some of the places don't shape up too well over time.
And so there's a lot of diligence needs to be placed at that end of the spectrum where AI is going to be used
and is already being used to inform robotic production line code for a patronized building.
So with thinking about AI then again in that context, I mean, the genie is kind of out of the bottle at this point.
The last I read about the most recent releases of ChatGPT and Claude
were that they were basically designing themselves now.
I mean, that's the kind of the rumor.
I don't know if it's true or not.
So, I mean, in that context, how do you manage an industry and the way that it would use AI?
When we've got Claude and ChatGPT literally designing themselves and beginning to become more sentient,
the question then becomes, when we design environments for people,
we're actually engaged in making a large number of judgment calls
about whether we should do this, whether that window should be that,
whether the door should be this big, whether the house or the office or the factory
should be in this particular location or another one.
It's not clear to me that at the moment,
that even with the meteoric rise of large language models like Claude and others,
that they're going to be necessarily great at making those judgment calls.
They're great at doing analytics and rapid pattern recognition.
There's no question about that.
And that's very valuable.
But are they any good at mathematics?
I'm not so sure about that.
Are they any good at making judgment calls?
Because, I mean, if something happened to a building and it fell apart because of it just didn't work,
but there was a complete reliance on AI to actually do all the detailing,
it's going to be pretty difficult to stand up in front of a judge in a court and say,
well, it wasn't me that did it, it was the AI, that there's a level in our society,
at least we hope that it's the case eventually everywhere,
that there is a certain level of accountability for the actions you make and the judgment calls you make.
And at the moment, it doesn't seem to me that there is much in the way of accountability
being placed on the development of these AI environments.
Even though Philip Alsop sees huge potential for AI in shaping healthier built environments,
he's clear about one thing.
Nothing replaces human ethical judgment.
For James Loder, AI works best when it's paired with a creative human mind,
a collaborator, not a replacement.
So while AI is already making a significant impact, humans are still in the driver's seat,
at least for now.
I think the difference between creating your own image to print out and put it on a wall
to having something built is a very long stretch.
And I think that's where the industry is relatively safe for now,
that the complexity of taking an image and having it built is a massive gap and process that occurs.
One of the critiques I've heard is that there's a much higher propensity towards the kind of
cookie cutter outcomes by using these kinds of systems in the background,
because they tend to drive towards a certain sort of solution that is, let's say, less creative,
if I could put it that way.
More efficient, less creative.
So it sort of tends to the middle.
And I wonder if there's any validity, you think, in that idea of the cookie cutter outcome.
But also, how do you kind of get around the idea that less ethical or more profit-hungry studios
could use AI badly?
Look, it's yes.
And to the cookie cutter notion, I think there'd be firms doing the cookie cutter notion without
using AI.
I think there is, it already exists, and it exists for a more commercial and efficient
approach to what that output needs to be in a certain part of the industry.
And that's fine.
There's got to be a balance.
And I think the introduction of AI may generally make things more efficient for most practices.
But I think there will always be a want for a level of design excellence that really comes
from beyond just the use of AI.
And it's really engaging with the practice and the culture of that practice.
And the future of AI in architecture?
Still uncertain.
But James and Philip are optimistic about where it could lead.
James Loder again.
What I see coming is a more general AI tool, because at the moment it's all segregated into
text, image.
There's many different tools.
You know, Microsoft have their co-pilot, which is probably where I'm going with this.
You can have a conversation with a tool and it can work across a number of different facets.
And I think there's always going to be a line of how far to engage with it, apply trust, and
where to bring it back to a kind of a human level conversation, particularly in the creative
end.
You're really curating the content.
And to do so, you have to know in the first instance, what is the right approach?
What is the right solution?
And you're bringing your own personality to that.
And that's what people are interested in.
I think we're going to see through the efforts of more architects who are becoming much more
engaged in scientific inquiry, that we will begin to see new collaborations of players coming
together around the built environment.
One of the victims of the economic system we have, which is basically rewarding anybody
who can strip mine people's lives and the planet for money, for short-term money, is that it's
created huge risk.
And it is the property casualty insurers and their reinsurers who are really hurting badly.
And I think we may see that more and more architects in collaboration with folks in the public health
field and folks in the property casualty insurance will start to collaborate on ways of de-risking
the way we inhabit this planet.
And by de-risking it, I mean making environments that work for people and enable people to actually
feel as if they belong somewhere and they belong in the home that they try to make.
And so I think it's those new collaborations that we'll see, certainly in the field of architecture,
most of the collaborations occur with closely allied professionals, structural engineer,
mechanical engineer, civil engineering, MEP, and so on.
But just in a fairly closely related orbit, just outside of that, are these other players
from the finance industry, from the healthcare industry, who are right now dealing with the
problems that result from basically treating human habitat as if it was a throwaway real
estate commodity?
And that hurts everybody.
Philip Alsop, co-chair, RIBA Expert Advisory Group on AI.
Next time on By Design, are we prepared to pay for history?
We actually decided to free up the equity in our family home and sell that and rent.
It's been incredibly rewarding to see other people also fall in love with it and to see
people really relax there and appreciate the history of the building, the significance of
it and the way that it's been conserved.

episodes.title: Extraordinary Everyday: Surfboards
episodes.description: Australia’s surfing story has been influenced from far beyond our shores, from ancient Peruvian reed boards to Hawaiian royalty and the design revolutions that shaped the modern surfboard.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. As humanity keeps chasing the next big leap forward, it's worth remembering that innovation also thrives in the quiet, ordinary things woven into daily life. I'm Anthony Burke and this is Extraordinary Every Day, a weekly segment on ABC Radio Nationals by Design. And today, we're going surfing. Australia's surfing story has been influenced from far beyond our shores, from ancient Peruvian reed boards to Hawaiian royalty and the design revolutions that shaped the modern surfboard. So, how did we get from the earliest surfboards of heavy wooden planks to the sleek high-performance boards written today? Andrew McKinnon is a surf reporter, historian and a surfer for over 60 years. Let's talk about the history of surfing because we all think of it as sort of a fun sport, but it's got this pretty interesting and really long history that I didn't really know about. As I understand it, and correct me if I'm wrong here, surfing actually originated in Peru and not in Hawaii, like I thought, but in Peru. Is that true? Well, the Caballito de Toro, the Peruvian Reed Board, de Toro means reeds, board of reeds. This goes back 3,000 to 5,000 years as part of the Moche civilization, Chumu, pre-Inca. I mean, it's sort of well known now that the Peruvians were the early seafarers. They were getting across the Pacific before anybody else. They had been explorers and they were expert seafarers and they designed this special fishing boat, like a canoe, called the Caballito de Toro. So, we call it the Peruvian Reed Board. And they designed it in such a way because the home of the Caballito is in Huanchaco, northern Peru, and they designed it so that it could go through waves. And when the Spanish came, they watched them going up and down the waves and it looked like they were riding horses, hence the term seahorses. But what they would do is go out, catch the fish and then ride the waves back in. And then that became a recreational pursuit for others in the village that just wanted to go out there and catch waves. So, the Peruvians lay claim that this is the first wave-catching craft. Wow. And it was made literally out of reeds? Is that right? You said reed board, right? We're talking about long grasses. Yeah, board of reeds. So, they've got these ponds of reeds that are just behind the town there at Huanchaco. They grow the reeds and then they pull them out, dry them out. They're big, long reeds. And then they basically wrap them up with string and create this Caballito de Toro, Peruvian reed board. So, we had a 500th descendant come out, Huabito, and he was actually able to construct a Peruvian reed board in front of everybody at the World Serving Conservation Conference as a live activation. And he was so quick. He basically put it together the night before with a couple of bundles and then he brought that into the university auditorium and then he had it all wrapped up within about an hour and a half. Well, there's a 12-foot stand-up Caballito de Toro, Peruvian reed board, and he uses a big, long bamboo paddle, like a big rudder, like a big anchor, like a sweep and a surf boat in a way, to steer out in the water and steer onto the waves. Because there's no fin, right? So, he's got to have this big anchor bamboo paddle. So, this is a long, long board. Yeah, it's a long, long board. So, back to Hawaii for a second. One thing about the Hawaiian history that I didn't quite realise was, you correct me if I'm wrong here, but it was a royal sport. Is that correct? Yeah, it was the sport of the ali, the royals, the kings, but then it became really popular amongst the community. So, like the Peruvian reed board, it was essentially for the fishermen. And then the local community also thought, oh, we would like to get out on those as well, and it became like a community sport. And that's basically what happened in Hawaii as well, and especially the women. The women were really good surfers. So, you know, when Captain Cook sailed in, he called it the sport of kings because he was told that it was only the kings could surf. But in actual fact, everyone was surfing. And it was so popular until the Christian monasteries turned up and they banned it. They banned the culture, they banned the language, and they banned surfing. No. So, by the end… I'm outraged. On behalf of every surfer out there, I'm outraged. Yeah. Well, of course, and the Hawaiians weren't going to give it all up. They were just waiting for the appropriate time to bring it back. And it was three young Hawaiian princes from Waikiki on the island of Oahu that went over to San Francisco, and they were able to get some wooden surfboards. And they demonstrated over there in 1890 how to surf, which started surfing in California. So, you know, it was only a matter of time for the Hawaiians to lead the charge. So, they really get credited for being the first surfboard riders. But as far as wave catching is concerned, the Peruvians go way back, 3,000 to 5,000 years. There's ruins in Triilo behind Wanchaco, pottery artifacts that show the Mocha, the Chumu, surfing on these reed boards. And that's evidence to show how far back it goes. You've been surfing since 1962, if I understand that correctly. And can you take us back to what the surf scene and surfboards were like when you first started surfing? I was only nine years of age and the family next door, they were all surfing on nine to 10 foot boards. The foam and feral glass boards had just started. But there was still some balsa wood boards because before the foam and feral glass, there was balsa wood. And then before the balsa wood, there were the hollow skis, the hollow plywood skis. They're called toothpicks because they had really narrow noses, didn't they? And they basically went straight into the beach, the Iron Cross style. Well, when the balsa boards came out in the 50s, they were able to maneuver those boards a little bit easier. And they had a back fin with so-called a skeg. And then it went from that balsa skeg to the foam fiberglass. And they sculptured the fin a little bit more like a dorsal fin, like a dolphin's fin. So they could maneuver even more. But the boards were still really big when I learned to surf. And so I was only a little guy. So I was on an eight foot board, which was considered small then. But then the boards went down in length. When the shortboard revolution started in 67, by 1970, the boards were underneath six feet. And I was really stoked because I was a little guy and I preferred a smaller board. Plus, it was easy to surf. So there's a great transition that you've just described there, going from balsa and foam, fiberglass and shortboards and longboards. And then, of course, there's the thruster sort of arrives at some point in time. Do you think that was the biggest transformation that we saw in recent history, if you know what I mean? Yeah, unquestionably. When Simon Edison came up with the three-fin board, the thruster, as you said, it was to try and outmaneuver Mark Richards, who'd gone to a twin fin. And Mark Richards won four world titles on that flyer-swallowtail twin fin. And everybody was sort of getting a bit irritated by that and really wanted to try and beat Mark. But it was almost impossible on a single fin because Mark could outmaneuver them on the twin fins. A lot easier to turn. So Simon thought, why don't I have a twin fin but put a back fin on it and allow you had the thruster in 1981. And that just became the standard equipment. And even to this day, the majority of surfers, especially those on tour, 99.9% on tour will ride three-fin boards. You know, the quad fin becomes sort of popular. Kelly Slater really liked the quad fin. I like the quad fin too. But these days, there's all types of surfboards, all types of craft. So looking ahead, do you think surfboard design still has changes that are being discussed and are being talked about now? Or do you think we're kind of just refining the classics? And I imagine sustainability might be something that's on the agenda there. Absolutely. Sustainability is a real thing. But the basic materials are still the same in terms of foam and fiberglass. These are oil products. And so, you know, they're trying to find alternatives for this. It would just be amazing if you could make a surfboard out of waste. But you can create a mold. But the thing about a surfboard, it's a particular type of shape. And everybody has their own idea of what's best for them. And, you know, just having subtle edges, having channels, the shape of the nose, the shape of the tail, the rocker, the curve. Everything is so specific. So that's why people like hand-shaped surfboards. And, you know, unfortunately, foam is the easiest one to shape. But you would hope that one day that we would come up with some material that's not an oil-based product that would be lighter and harder and easier to surf as far as and easier on the environment. But that still seems to be a way off. You know, it's the same materials that go back to the 60s. So there's the design challenge. I'll throw that gauntlet down now for anyone listening. Design challenge, surfboard made from recycled materials or waste. That's what we're looking for. That's right. And like I said, it's easy to make a mould. You just come up with a plug. But, you know, surfers like to hand-shape their boards. So you've got to come up with a product that you can do in individual shape. So that's the challenge. You're totally on it. Thank you so much, Andrew. Thanks so much. See you soon. Aloha and mahalo. Andrew McKinnon, surf reporter, historian and a surfer for over 60 years. While I suspect at least half the work of the surfboard is done on the beach as an accessory, for those aficionados out there, the technical development of the surfboard is as interesting as the cultural one, from reeds in Peru to royalty in Hawaii. But, as Andrew explains, it sounds like that material evolution is actually due for its next iteration, with a new generation of sustainably made boards now being called for. So, designers, it's time to hit the waves. After all, it's hard to think of a better ambassador for ocean health and sustainability than someone who loves the water as much as a surfer. As always, if you enjoyed the episode, make sure you follow the show on ABC Listen, just search Anthony Burks by Design. You've been listening to an ABC podcast. Discover more great ABC podcasts, live radio and exclusives on the ABC Listen app.
