episodes.description: Batik is a material that is both ancient and modern.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Some materials hold stories on their surface. Some keep them buried in their threads. Batik is one of those fabrics. Wax, dye, cloth and of course so much more. A language of pattern and patience. A textile that's made and then often lived in, passed on and protected. This is By Design on ABC Radio National and I'm Professor Anthony Burke. Today we arrive at our final stop in our Material Cultures series. Meeting designers and artisans who think deeply about their materials. And who let those materials speak in ways that feel utterly right for their time and place. Over the last few years, I've spent a fair bit of time in Asia filming for ABC International. Including a TV series called Culture By Design. You can find it on ABC iview. And along the way, I had conversations that stayed with me long after we stopped recording. And I'm so happy to share them here with you. Today we're talking about a fabric with a whole lot of history. Batik. For centuries, it has carried deep meaning. Worn by royals. Used in ceremonies. Even wrapped around newborns for luck. But rising costs and fading demand nearly pushed it to the margins. Now, Batik is stepping back into the spotlight. Welcome to By Design, the ABC Radio National Show exploring the ideas, objects and people shaping the way we live. This is hand spun, hand woven. This is batik. And then embroidered. If you touch the textures here. The lines are embroidered. This is the paddy fields. The paddy fields. And then you have the rivers running. And then you have the current down with your death. This is Indonesia. And this is what it's all about. Josephine, affectionately known as Oban Kamara, uses long-established processes to both champion traditional Indonesian batik and create contemporary stories in cloth. Made into sophisticated cocktail dresses, bespoke tailored shirts or gently draping shawls, batik has become as much a fashion choice as a Chanel or Hermes for many in Southeast Asia and internationally. Walking into Josephine Oban Kamara's workshop, which is also her home and office in central Java, there's an immediate sense of energy and colour and smell. Hey! How do you do? Welcome. Thank you so much. You must be Anthony. I'm Anthony. I'm Bin. Pleasure to meet you. Pleasure to meet you too. This is your showroom, studio? This is where I work and this is where I live. Aha. Come. Yeah. Pick me again. I can see, I can see it's all happening. It's happening. This is all prepared for you. They're batik-ing, they're waxing. This is the skill that I've heard so much about. And the beauty of the fabrics that you produce sort of starts here, yeah? Can you smell the wax? Yeah. Come, sit down. Josephine Obin Kamara didn't have a traditional pathway into weaving cloth and dyeing batik. It's a fascinating story of absorbing the diversity of Indonesian culture. Oh, Bin, this is a remarkable space you brought me into. But tell me, where did all of this come from? Where does your story start? So I was gallivanting around Indonesia when all the children my age were in school. But I saw a lot. I saw a lot. I traveled a lot. I stayed in Java for a while. I was exposed to the culture there. One of my mentors was the late Mr. Harjo Nagoro. He was sort of like the chancellor and the lord of, and the keeper of the treasures of the palace of Solo, Surakarta. He has just passed away. He's a beautiful dancer. Watching him and listening to him talk, I learned so much. I absorbed so much. I could smell the Java solo and its surrounding regions. I could feel the pace and the pulse. The colors, the motifs, the people, the sounds. It's all there. And in Indonesia, it's so diverse. You drive the car for one hour to another city and they're speaking a different dialect. The food is different. You call dialect. It's language. The language different. Sometimes similar. West Java, Central Java. But West Java and East Java, like Surabaya, are very different. And it gets more distinct as you go further on and further on until you go to the outer islands like Flores and Medan. You go to Sumatra. You go to Sulawesi celibacy. What you're describing there is you're opening up to an empathy for beauty and color and texture and senses. The people, the color, the music. The differences. The differences. And for me, they're all rolled into one. So why was cloth or weaving, why was that a natural medium for you to express these things? In 1979. Yeah. Around 1979. How old was I? I was born in 1955. So how old am I? 1979. Not a day over 45. Well, anyway, around that time. By that time, I've been collecting. I love beautiful things. And it just so happens that the antiques are beautiful. They're well made. Indonesia's a treasure trove of culture, for antiques from 9th, 11th, 10th, 13th, 14th century. Weather, whatever it is. Fabrics. Unfortunately for the antiques, the fabrics don't last much. I mean, that long because of the weather. But I collected a lot of things. Beautiful. Because they're beautiful and they're meaningful and they just, my mind goes crazy. I can imagine what it was before. But of all the things that I collected, the jewelry, the ceramics, the furniture, the bronzers, the terracottas, the cloth. It was the cloth that really, I was dealing too because I couldn't pay for everything without selling. But then I started to weave raw silk. Plain. Plain. And then checks. And then stripes. And then ikat. Raw silk is very thick. So it was used usually for interior, like upholstery, curtains and stuff. Maybe I was doing the right thing at the right time in 1979. But the Hilton Hotel was being built. Mandarin Hotel. Arya Dutta Hotel. And the designers, the architects and the designers, they couldn't find any interior fabric. You had to import. So they used, I was making bed covers, curtains, lampshades. So I had a little industry going. You took off. I guess I went crazy. Yeah. I collected all the lampshade makers from Jalan Kebon Siri. There's a little street there. And where all the lampshade makers used to be. And I brought them over to the garage at home. And we made lampshades. And we made this. And we made that. And then I went on weaving and weaving and weaving. And the fabric from very thick got to be very thin. You know, weaving course of yarns are easy. But weaving very thin yarns are very difficult. Because it's so thin. And when you weave, it's white. It's so thin that sometimes when the yarn breaks, you can't see. That's why. The people, the weavers, had to wear very dark. To see the cloth. To see the yarns. Yeah, yeah. So from very thick, we were able to do very fine yarns. And then I got bored. Something happened in around 1985. And I got bored. And I just shut down. I didn't want to do anything. I was divorced. I had Elang, my son. And I'm going to share with you all something that happened. It was called the Big Bang. I call it the Big Bang. It was like 3 o'clock in the morning. And I was having a cigarette and having a glass of wine. And by that time, I had two big chests. Two chests. Two antique chests. One was full of weavings from the outer islands. From Sulawesi. From Batak. From, you know, from everywhere. And one chest was full of antique batiks. Mind you, batiks are only made in Java. Especially throughout the coastal, the Java coastal area. So one day, I spread them out. And I looked at all the weavings. Which I was trying to redo the techniques. And I saw all the batiks. Mind you, by that time, I could already weave very, very fine, thin silk. See-through. Transparent, but very thin. So in my mind's eye, I saw a very thin piece of cloth. Hand spun. Hand woven. With a batik motif on top. So this is the moment where batik... This was the moment. ...walked into your life. Yeah. This was the moment when batik entered my life. I've always loved it, but I've never done it. Yeah. And for me, this is something new. Let me explain. All the vintage batiks that you see. All the old antique batiks that you see are on cotton. Indonesia does not produce cotton. The cottons were a result of bartering with China, India, and England. England, because of Industrial Revolution, they were overproducing. So the companies, the Dutch company and the British company said that we have overproduction of cotton. And the Dutch say, oh, there is a tradition in Indonesia that's called batik. So... And they get their cloths, their cottons from China and India. So from the antique batiks, I could learn. The ones with this width are the ones from China. The ones with this width, that one's from England. The one, the wide ones, are from India. Because in India, it's the men who weave. So they're taller and so it's wider. That's right. I learned so much. I learned so much just by looking at it. Anyway. Every piece of fabric has a story. Exactly. And you have that ability to see all of the stories. Oh, I was just nosy. I was curious. You were nosy. But for me, being able to do the hand weaving, Indonesian, and then doing the batik on it, putting it together. For me, it was like putting Indonesia together by doing this one thing. I'm Anthony Burke, and this is By Design on Radio National, exploring how a material with an ancient heritage is making a comeback. Creating batik with its extraordinary range of distinct patterns that have evolved over time is an incredibly complex and skillful process, as we've been hearing. Josephine Obin-Kamara and her team are a one-stop shop. They spin the thread. They weave the cloth. Each step with its own intricacies. When you look around her studio, the bolts of raw fabric are already full of texture and shape and pattern. And that's even before they've ever touched wax or dye. The final cloth is fine, but rich, layered, deep with meaning and craft. I call myself Tukangkain, cloth maker, because I start from scratch. I spin, I weave, and I do batik, or whatever cloth manipulation that can be done to it. So where did you learn all of those skills? It's not one thing. Watching. My mother used to sew. She used to make her patterns using newspapers. Okay. And she'd roll them. This was her blouse. This was her thing. This was her house coat. I mean, all mothers used to do that. Yeah. I think all the mothers, I don't know. But that's one. And then you see her sew, and you have the sewing machine, the singer sewing machine, you know. I see her darning. And then when the colors are dirty, she likes to change the colors. And I see how she does it. Yeah. So you're just that capacity to see those sorts of things and to take them on for yourself. If I'm a camera, I go in it. You're like a highly tuned design radar. I like to look at things small, you know, microscopic. And then where does design fit into all of this? When you then go into a creative mode. When you talk about design. Yeah. It's actually not so much the visual, but more the technique. Because design is making. You know the antique textiles, the one I told you, the woven ones? Many of them are ripped and torn. And that makes me so happy. One is cheaper. And the other one is also because if it's torn, I can take a loop and I can go in. I can see the steps from the tear. Yeah. This is your magic. You can see it into that process. That's the magic of the cloth. But you can see that, the tradition of making the particular cloth, the issue of the material itself. And then you bring your design sort of approach to things, which this turns it into something new again. But can you imagine the tear in the cloth? Where there is the warp? And then there is the weft and all the funny foot dancing there. You know, the supplementary weaving going up and down. But then you can see all that. And then you do something even more sinful. You take the weft and you pull it. You tear it even more to see where it goes and where it goes up and then it goes down. You're scaring me at this point. It was in the making. It happened. And the batik-ing, I just went to the batik workshops all over Jawa. Like I told you, I lived in Jawa. And I used to sit there for hours watching them with the gamelan music at the back, you know, and listening to them talking between each other and then smelling the wax. And I see the way they were. Then I went to Pekalongan and I saw the famous batik house. I saw that their batiks were different. They were all European colors. They were pinks and blues and more. The patterns were of flowers that were not Indonesian, of peonies and chrysanthemums and everything. Then I realized this was the residential area of the Dutch, the Dutch-Chinese. So the colors were European. And then I asked, why is it the batiks from Pekalongan, they were all in bouquets. One, two, three. And they're all the same and the same format for many of the batiks. I was informed that the Dutch ladies who were residing in Pekalongan region, they would order their embroidery pattern from Holland. And the embroidery patterns were of bouquets and flowers. And they would take those patterns and also give it to the batikers and use them as patterns for the batiks. So did this give you a sort of a license then to think, well, I can take traditional batik and I can... I didn't. I can take it places. I didn't just make the sum of it. I didn't come to a conclusion. All this information just came in. Yeah. Then I saw the batik from Jambi, which is Sumatra. They don't make batiks. Then I realized, and I studied from the books. We have books from all over the world by dealers long before me who were writing and scholars who were writing about it. And the kingdom, the king of Jambi made a pact with the king of Chirbon to make motifs for them. It was blue and red. And the Chirbon did it for them and did not make it for anybody else. The designs and everything were specific. So specific. There were traders from India, Gujarat, Islam, India. And they would bring their stamps with them. They would go to Chirbon and go to the people and have them stamped. And then this. And then they would take back their stamps and finish the batiks. And then they'd sell them to Sumatra. So when you see a piece of fabric, that is what you're looking at. That's what I... That entire story. The whole story. That's in one piece. And you know it. Yeah. Oh, this is this. This was done by this. And mind you, batik. Batik. Batik is penmanship. But you don't use pen. You use chanting, yeah? The copper funnel with the bamboo handle. You dip it in the wax. Hot. So it's melted. And you drag. The part which is covered by the wax. That when you dye, the dye doesn't enter. Very often people look at batikers and they think that batikers are drawing the patterns. No. Batik is a wax resist dye technique. The part that you'd wax is the part that the dye doesn't enter. Yeah. And if you have eight colors, what you do is you wax, you dye, you boil, de-waxing, and then you dry it. And then you say, what is the next color I want to dye now? Red. You cover every part which is, you don't want the red to enter. Yeah. And you do it and you do it and you do it until it's eight times. So when people tell me, can I wash this? Batik has gone through death in the boiling. I mean, you know, like... To get to this point. It's been boiled to death because you have to de-wax everything. Nice, pleasant, balanced, feeling good. And sometimes there's music. For me, design is like music. It's a whole orchestra. The this, the dots, the lines, the dashes, the this, the... It's a whole symphony. It has to feel good. You know, I said 15 years ago, I was talking to my late husband. He's always, he's an academic. And I said, you know, Ronnie, I said, I like the word architecture. Because cloth for me is like architecture. Because you know, you know, weaving, you have to warp. You set the foundations. You set the foundations. And then you weave in the weft. And that's the walls. You know what I mean? The cornice, the stuff, and everything. So you see the structure in the cloth. Yes. And you build it out in those layers. Yeah. Like it's a three-dimensional, four-dimensional emotional space. Everything starts from two singular things. And I don't know what you do to it. And then it becomes one entity. I will never see a piece of cloth as 2D ever again. There's so much in this. Thank you so much for sharing your story with us. Josephine Obankamara, who's reviving interest in wearing batik creation. What we've heard today is that batik isn't just a fabric. It's a living record. History, landscape, and daily life are all carried in its threads. The environment, the paddy fields, the flora and fauna, are woven into the cloth that's meant to be worn, moved in, lived in. It's also a reminder that tradition evolves. It's not static. And I hope you enjoyed our three-part journey into Asia to meet some of the great artisans and designers at work. If you missed the other two episodes of Material Cultures, follow the show on ABC Listen. Just search for Anthony Burks by Design. Not everybody necessarily does very well inside of a former sneaker container from something. I think there is a danger in making that assumption. How exactly will AI in architecture impact you? Join me for that next time on By Design. Because in a rapidly changing world, design matters. Hot.

It's versatile.
The way they wear it.

episodes.title: Extraordinary Everyday: Kites
episodes.description: Kites aren’t just toys—they’re one of the most influential inventions in the history of science. Sure, they look playful drifting across a windy sky, but the humble kite has quietly powered some of humanity’s biggest breakthroughs.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. What secret histories hide in the objects we use every day? Each object carries a hidden story, a design journey shaped by culture, innovation and necessity. I'm Anthony Burke and this is Extraordinary Every Day. Today, thanks to a story suggestion from listener Louisa, we're off to fly some kites. If you saw our next item whipping through the sky on a windy day, you might shrug and think, oh, pretty, fun. But don't be fooled. This isn't just colourful airborne decoration. The kite has been a secret agent of world-shaping science, sparking experiments, discoveries and breakthroughs that shifted the course of history. Not bad for something held together with string. John Murray is the president of the Australian Kite Flyer Society. Thanks for having me, Anthony. Let's talk about the history for a second. Now, as I understand it, traditionally, it's thought that kites came from China. Yeah. Yeah? But you've got a slightly different thesis here. Well, that is the oldest written records about kites are from China. 5th century BC. So, you know, a long, long time ago. But more recently, they've discovered some petroglyphs, rock carvings in Indonesia. And they're about 12,500 years old. And initially, when they were discovered, it was a matter of people just saying, oh, yeah, it's just a rock carving. And I guess what I would be saying is that in Sulawesi in Indonesia and Lampung, they actually use kites to catch fish. Oh, get out of here. Really? Yeah. How does that work? Well, you've got like a leaf off a local plant. I guess the Australian equivalent would be a staghorn, something like that. So you shape the leaf. You then tie a line to the leaf. From the leaf, you then let it drop down into the water. But you've got like a little circular noose of fishing line into which you feed a bait. And that skips across the water. And the fish you're trying to catch is quite, well, it's like a garfish, but it's quite a big garfish with quite big teeth. So the fish says, oh, a live piece of bait, a flying fish, something like that. I'll go and get that. The jaw goes through. It's a noose. And they catch the fish. Hooks, line and sinker, all done from above. All done from above. And I guess personally, I think, you know what? People would look to feed their family before they would look to knock off and go down the beach and fly kite for fun. So amazing. So back to China for a second, though. How were kites used in China? Well, initially for military purposes, because that is this first recorded history is a general putting a kite up in the air, theoretically with someone attached to it. So they could look. Yeah. Like an elevator? Well. Like a lift to get a perspective on the approaching enemy? Yeah. Either a basket or whether they tied them to it. I guess the jury's out on that as well. And that was then used to gauge how far, because they were, the city was, that they were trying to attack was under siege. And they want to know how long and how straight a tunnel they had to build to go under the wall's defences. Wow. That's amazing. I thought you were going to say maybe signalling or something like this, but it's actually far more elaborate than that. Yeah. And well, there was another of the same general who did the signalling, but he tied someone to the kite and he flew it over the enemy's camps and their job was to make scary noises to pretend there was a demon. So that would unsettle the... I know. Crazy stuff. Crazy stuff. This is getting far more interesting than I ever imagined, actually. This is great. So, all right, let's talk about, let's talk about other ideas then around kites. We've had fishing, we've had flying demons, and we've had surveillance. What other uses have kites been put to? Well, warfare as barrage, you know, to keep wires up in the sky, to try and stop bombers coming through. There was also the Americans in the Second World War used kites as target practice. Oh. And so they could have the equivalent of a Japanese plane on it and they would zoom that around the sky and they would try and shoot that down. And if you were an American that was shot down, in your life raft was a kite called the Gibson Girl, which was a aluminium and cloth kite, which you hoisted up into the sky and came with a little radio transmitter. So people could, you would crank the radio transmitter and send out a signal and hopefully people would find you. And that to me sounds like a great idea, except I guess if you've just been shot down and you're in the middle of a stormy sea and you're going, okay, right now, first of all, I've got to get the kite up. Get the kite up. And now I've got to attach it all. And now I've got to wind. And now I've got to... I suppose any search and rescue in a situation you'll go for though, right? Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. So, okay, that's great. But what about Benjamin Franklin? I've got to mention the famous lightning kite story. Oh, okay. You're going, oh, geez, that's just a myth. It's immortalised. All I would say is theoretically the next number of people who tried it, guess what? Were electrocuted. So if you're going to try and convince me that, okay, I'm going to go fishing for electricity. It's going to come down the line and I'm magically not going to get injured. Okay. Yeah. You know, once again, I don't want to upset historians and I don't want to upset, you know, the stamp that the US have put out, which shows all of that happening. But I guess the more scientific things that I would look at is Marconi lifting a piece of wire up in the sky to be the aerial. So the first transatlantic radio signal came to Signal Hill in Newfoundland, in Canada. So across the Atlantic. So very useful scientific apparatus here. Can I just get you to rewind for a second though and just tell in a brief way the story of Benjamin Franklin? Because it is sort of mythologised so much. Like what's the real story as you understand it? The story is meant to be he's flying a kite in a storm looking to indicate that lightning was electricity. And he had a key attached to that for the purpose of attracting the lightning. And the mythology says he attracted the lightning. When I think of a kite from a design perspective, I'm really just thinking of a lightweight rod and fabric assembly. Yes. Very basic kind of, you know, typological design in my mind. Explain for me like how varied the types of kites can get. Kites come into basic style. So you've got kites with sticks. If we just broke it down into kites with sticks, kites without sticks. And if you go with kites with sticks, then you've got, I guess, the kite that you would maybe go down to the beach with. Now, whether that's a diamond kite, because everybody knows a diamond kite or a delta. That's the first kite I ever made was a diamond kite with newspaper made of paddle pop sticks glued together by flour and water from the kitchen on holiday with my grandfather-in-law. I was probably about six. So you've got the diamond kite, easy to make. The next, probably most popular would be the delta kite. So a bit of a, you know, looks like a triangle and like a stealth bomber sort of triangle. Is that the one? Yeah. Yeah. So let's talk about the Australian history of kites then. What is our particular version of this story? Australia pretty much punches above its weight. First of all, let's go back to probably about 120, 125 years ago. The man on the $20 note, the old $20 note, Lawrence Hargrave. The rest of the world was working on the basis of heavier than manned flight and, you know, people with flapping wings and that sort of thing. Lawrence, quietly sitting in Stanwell Park, came up with the curved box kite, which was the world changer, literally. He didn't necessarily believe in painting things. So he just said to the world, hey, look what I've done. And the Wright brothers in America then go, oh, look at that. Wow, really? So this, we've got a direct line of kite flying in Australia to the Wright brothers. Well, yes, yes. Well, let's talk about those kite festivals because when I think of kite festivals, it's a sea of colour, very beautiful, you know, like a really romantic kind of idea, really. So do you think kites have this artistic side to them? I would say yes, because if you went along to a big kite festival now, what you would find is some people who've made their beautiful artistic kites with sticks and then you would have these huge inflatable ram air inflated kites. What is that? Okay, if you can imagine, well, if you take a shopping bag and hold it open and you turn it so the wind comes into it, it'll fill the bag. Sure. So the idea is that the kite shape has an opening, the air goes in there, it fills the kite in the shape of what you want. You then have the kite having taken a shape and the air then lifts it to the sky. Sort of like a step towards a parachute. Yeah, yeah, yeah. So tell me about the world's largest kite. Let's get to the beginning. We've talked about the homemade sort of sticks and newspaper version. What's the other end of the spectrum? That really big kite. Okay. How big do you imagine the world's biggest kite is? This is it. At this point, if you'd asked me this question five minutes ago, I'd have a good answer for you. But at this point, all bets are off. Okay. What about five tennis courts in size? Really? Yeah. It's a little over 1,200 square metres of lifting space. So where is it and what does it look like? Okay. The world's largest kite has had a number of different styles, but all of them primarily built by Peter Lynn Kite Factory in New Zealand. That is, it's called The Hope and it's about world peace and water and sustainability, that sort of thing. It's 1,800 linear metres of fabric. Oh my goodness. Two and a half kilometres of line inside it. Not the line you're holding onto, just supporting it. And so, yes, it's a team and you can only really fly detached to dump trucks and bulldozers and there's a whole process. John, that's amazing. Thank you so much for coming in and giving me that great history of kite flying and particularly the dimensions of kites that are not just the physical dimensions. I mean, the uses and so on that you've just described there. Sounds amazing. Appreciate it. Thank you. It's amazing, isn't it? Something as light as a kite can leave such a heavy mark on history, shaping science, survival, even whole cultures. Proof that the extraordinary often hides in the objects we barely think about. What other everyday object might have a story hiding in plain sight? If you have ideas, drop us a line at bydesign at abc.net.au. As always, if you enjoy the episode, make sure you follow the show on ABC Listen. Just search Anthony Burks by Design. You've been listening to an ABC podcast. Discover more great ABC podcasts, live radio and exclusives on the ABC Listen app.

episodes.title: Material Cultures: Bamboo in Bali
episodes.description: Bamboo is nothing short of extraordinary - growing fast, bending without breaking, and carrying the strength of steel. In Bali, it’s more than a material; it’s a philosophy of design grounded in flexibility, resilience, and imagination.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. There's something almost uncanny about bamboo. A material that grows like a weed, bends without breaking and somehow carries the strength of steel. In Bali, it isn't just a plant. It's a way of thinking. A design philosophy rooted in flexibility, resilience and imagination. This is By Design on ABC Radio National and I'm Professor Anthony Burke. Today, we're continuing our three-part journey into material cultures, where designers we meet aren't just shaping their materials, they're listening to them. Over the last few years, I've spent a fair bit of time in Asia filming for ABC International, including a TV series I'm really proud of called Culture By Design. You'll find it on ABC iview. And on those trips, I met makers who completely changed the way I think about materials. Today, we're in Bali, Indonesia, where bamboo becomes architecture. Light, strong, fluid. And where craft meets engineering in the most astonishing ways. Bamboo is dynamic, fast-growing, flexible and tough. A material that can bend towards almost any purpose. It's been with us for millennia and it's still proving just how timeless it really is. We, as designers, are more interested in what bamboo's taught us than what we're building out of bamboo. So, the lessons we've learned from working with this natural, sustainable material has really brought us into a design philosophy that informs how we think about space and what, like, a sense of place makes possible in the relationships between people and the natural world and culture. You see their work everywhere in Bali. Astonishing architecture made almost entirely from bamboo. Ibuku's buildings don't look built. They look grown, alive, fluid, as if nature had been coaxed, not forced into shape. You can feel it in the towering bamboo arcs of the Lumi Shala, a yoga pavilion that rises like a woven cathedral in the jungle. Or in the gently sloping roofline of the Mali Beach Club, curling down towards the sand like a breaking wave. All realised with bundles of bamboo bent and stitched together with extraordinary grace. Ibuku's founder, Elora Hardy, wants to push the material even further. Born in Canada but raised in Bali, she returned after years overseas, inspired by her parents, who created Bali's famous Green School, that wall-less campus of bamboo structures where children learn inside the landscape itself. It's a place that taught her, from the beginning, that nature could be a collaborator in design, not a constraint. Bamboo is a very particular material to work with. It has so much of its own personality, especially when you're working with it in the round, that you need to design with it. So when we're working with bamboo, there's so many different ways to interpret it and to play with it. We have honestly just touched the tip of the iceberg. So much of what you see in Asia, especially today, looks so much like what we've been doing for the past decade. But that's not how it should be. There should, there can be, there will be, just a plethora of different visual expressions of this material and technical expressions of the material. So we are really just getting to know it at like a molecular level in a way that relates to engineering. So when we're engineering with bamboo, what's been happening for the past decade is honestly just a lot tied to like the craftsman's experience. And now with engineering processes, with Atelier One who designs our most sophisticated engineered bamboo projects, we are looking deeply into the fibers of the material to understand how it's so strong. Because it's really unbelievably strong. And when we do that, we really get to play with it more on the edge of what's possible. Like bring it into, bring it into shapes and forms that we haven't imagined before. So it's continuing to show you. It's, you know, opening up more and more, not less and less. Yeah. Yeah. We'll look back decades from now and see this like, like charming little flowering of what was possible. There's just a little, little bit and it will look like a million different shapes. Yeah. The bamboo has a sort of a geometry and a bend to it that you seem to have this, it's like playing a musical instrument. Like expertly playing the bend in that, that material to get the kinds of effects that you get, which is so, so lyrical. Well, the interesting thing is that bamboo is so flexible and that's what makes it great for earthquakes. Yeah. It can bend before it breaks under pressure. As a pole though, it isn't flexible in the way that it appears to be in some of our structures. When we bend it, we aren't always bending it. We're often cutting it to, to bring it into the alignment of what we want it to be in the building. There's also possibilities of bending it. That's a new technique we're working with. Right. And when you split it up, take it away from its original round form and you split it up, you really unleash its flexibility. Yeah. So then you're creating what they call glulam. This is very advanced in wood. There's a lot of technical innovation. There's big factories set up with how to turn wood into glulam parts of buildings, including curves. Yeah. And so when we tap into that and we bring bamboo into that equation, we're sort of substituting the bamboo in a way because it just grows faster and has really great properties that lend itself to that technique. But that's probably where we'll see the most advancement and the most scale of bamboo building in the world. When we talk about glulam, that's really where we'll see bamboo show up in cities and show up in places that don't have craftsmen available or even in rural settings that need a broader scale and can be preassembled and brought to the site without so much care. But our world has really been in the artistry of it because each of our projects, our whole trajectory has been guided by each of our clients, each of our projects and what they aspired to. And very often that was from a dreaming of what's possible place, not filling a practical need place. So you're moving bamboo into the engineered lumber space, glulam and those sorts of things. What other innovations are you working on? Where else is it taking you? A lot of the innovation that's exciting in the design and bamboo world is the software, including augmented reality where we can use goggles and see where things will be in space and how the different stages and how that can connect the design process with the construction process. Typically in the design and construction world, and we are the same, we have a whole ream of paper attached to a whole lot of computer files that represents what should be done on site. And very often the people on site don't even relate to how to read all those papers. And it's counterintuitive for humans to go from three dimensions into one dimension and then into three dimensions again. So in technology, I'm most interested in how we can stay in three dimensions. We design at desks. Even in this office, we spend a lot of time at the desks. We have flat screens, we have flat paper. But we're making something three-dimensional. It's ironic. You used to, correct me if I'm wrong here, but didn't you used to make the beautiful models that we see around us? But that was what you would take to site and what people would build from to create your earlier work. Do you still, is that true and do you still do that? Yeah. From the early days of working with bamboo, it was really only possible because we de-emphasized the drawing stage. We might have a sketch or two along the way, but there are many buildings in the first years of our work where we really, like we made a bamboo structural model and the craftsmen built that. They replicated it at a bigger scale, which is a very direct, visceral, clear communication that skips over a lot of the issues with language barriers or technical knowledge and engineering degrees and things like this. Just replicate this and we can talk a bit about some of the details. So we still do that, including of the other materials, not just of the bamboo. And that is really why it's all possible. But to complement it, and especially because of the engineering, we also need to have a lot of 3D computer models. And that, in turn, lets us do things that you wouldn't think possible from just an intuitive understanding of the material. Yeah. It lets us stretch outside of that. Yeah. Push a little bit further, a little bit harder. Yeah. Yeah. I mean, it's very exciting to think of augmented reality and those sorts of texts coming into a very traditional material and then the way that you're going to take both of those things together. I suppose part of that's necessary because the scale of your work is continuing to grow. I mean, you're doing bigger and bigger and more and more fantastic things with your practice. How is that step into this bigger space going? I mean, there's a finite amount of craftsmanship and a really big need for buildings in the world and a really, really big need for buildings to be created with a sustainable approach, with fundamentally good materials that won't harm our future. I think it's really important to bring the past with us into the future. And one expression of that is the artisanal, the traditional techniques and knowledge, also stylistically. We don't want to look completely different. We want to look like we connect as we evolve our style. But also we want to create a world that we wish to live in. We want to create what we most imagine is the best future. As we design buildings that will last for decades and centuries and will be sheltering us in a world that we don't really grasp and understand yet. We have to figure out how to make them dynamic and protective in a way that lets us live in the best possible future. So when we're imagining a building, we've got to think, what will it be like decades from now? And what will the world be like? And that's kind of a scary question, actually. So the best that I can do is say, what do we imagine is that best possible scenario and what do we want that to look at? How does what we're building and creating, in terms of its style and its sense of place and its practicalities, but also in terms of what it means for that society and how we can speak about what we want for humanity and for nature in a building in the next hundred years. And there is, there are fundamental threads of culture that humans have been weaving for millennia. And some of those carry through, but we're not trying to recreate the past. We're trying to create the future. So we need to, we need to ask ourselves what we want that to look like. That leads me to sort of think about where you are, which is here in Bali, in Indonesia. And you've been obviously working here. Your practice began here. What have you learned and what do you continue to learn from the Indonesian cultures that you're drawing on and taking into the future? I mean, so much of what I do with my life just comes out of a love of Bali, where I got the privilege of growing up. And what's underlying everything is like, how can I bring out into the world, like, what I got out of growing up here? And Bali is a place that everyone knows as being, like, creative and dynamic and beautiful and natural. And I think that that holds so much for the future. Laura Hardy, founder of Ibuku, has her eye firmly on the future, pioneering new ways to use bamboo as a strong, sustainable building material in environments far beyond Bali. I'm Anthony Burke, and this is ABC Radio Nationals by Design. And we're continuing our series, Material Cultures, exploring how materials can shape and sometimes even renew design culture. At Ibuku, Elora and her team blend traditional craft with emerging technologies to push bamboo into entirely new territory. But at the heart of their philosophy is a beautifully simple idea. Creating shelter with nature, not against it. A return to building in dialogue with the world around us, rather than in defiance of it. Because we want to also get back to, like, why are we creating buildings? It's to create shelter. And that's, like, an age-old human need is to protect ourselves. We don't have scales. We don't have fur. We need shelter. We need a layer of protection and closure. But what we've done in the world is we have taken that way too far. We take conclusions that we've come to about how humans need to be protected from nature in cold climates and deserts. And created this bland average of box culture that has imbued all of architecture. So much of architecture is based on an assumption that we need a layer of protection that is not contextual. And in Bali and in much of Asia, we need to shelter ourselves from maybe heat more than cold in some cases. We need to shelter ourselves from bugs or from smog. There are many things we still need to account for. But we have the privilege of the possibility of some days of the year when we can open things up. And so what if we weren't designing from a defensive mentality? What if we were designing for all the best days? And also could shelter ourselves as we needed to on the worst day. And that's fair enough. There's like such an anxiety in the world about what will our worst days look like in the coming decades. Yeah. We have good cause to be very nervous about that. Yeah, indeed. But I can't let it pervade the design thinking. There's a definite optimism in the work. You feel the sense of, I was going to say playfulness. There's a joy when you walk into a space like this one that we're sitting in. I can imagine the work, the team you have out there working your way are happy to come to work in a beautiful context like this every day. I mean, that's a gift. Yeah. So that's what you sort of want for everyone. Yeah. Yeah. We get to work barefoot. That is genius. With that in mind, I mean, do you miss the old days? You're bigger. You've got a lot more responsibilities. The mission has grown. You know, those early days of the innovation curve when everything is new, then it kind of flattens out and you kind of start to sort of get into a routine. Do you find you miss that cutting edge moment when it was all coming to life? I really strive to keep some spontaneity structured in to our design work because I remember the early days in the houses that we made at Green Village where we would come up with the best possible solution on site in the moment as the craftsmen where they're talking about it with us. And when you've got to get it all on paper and in a 3D and in a bamboo model and all those things have to match and you've got to do that a year before they're going to be building it in some cases, it can definitely constrain the reality of what would be the best thing there. And so sometimes we even plan in our designs. We're like, okay, we've got most of it figured out. We're going to leave this area bubbled and we know that we're going to need to come on site and dedicate some time to figuring it out there and we're going to allocate a budget to that. Because we can't pretend as designers that we're going to get it right on paper in advance. And 3D helps, but not as much as being there on site. When you actually have the privilege of standing on site and saying like, how far away should the wall be from here and wouldn't it be nicer if it were this shape and let's weave that. Like that, that's something that we can exercise to do more and more in our creativity and anticipate it. But we can't pretend we can anticipate everything. So wherever we can, we like to do that. It seems to me you're already changing people's perceptions of what architecture can be. It seems the next challenge for you is to change that same idea in the construction industry. How do we build? How do we go about those processes? How do we make things like this come to life in a way which, as you say, maybe even leave space for that on-site conversation as the most important part. Otherwise, a contract would button everything up well before you got to turning any soil anywhere. Yeah. Yeah. So with that in mind, is that a target for you, the construction industry itself, trying to skill up a workforce that you can then sort of, I guess, use to teach the construction industry as it is happening in the world in a way? That would be amazing, but we haven't articulated that. We haven't tackled that. Yeah. I imagine, though, you've got the design equation well under control. There's a lot of innovation there already, but your next sort of target must be the construction industry because it's such a behemoth to move. It needs innovation. It needs your innovation, Elora. Are you thinking about that space? If we had had to design things and get them all documented on paper and quantity surveyed and fully detailed in order to then build the buildings that we had created so far, it would have been almost impossible. Yeah, right. And there's such a grind in the construction world of having to have things all set up that way. There's so much pressure on construction teams to be competitive at tender and to guarantee things, even when they're innovative, that really limits innovation, that really limits creativity, that really limits flexibility. So, in my ideal world, there would be a way in all of our projects around the world to just have much more room to develop things together on site. So much of the world in general is so compartmentalized, and I think we're seeing more and more across various industries and across education that when you bring experts in different fields together to tackle an issue, that that's very often where the new insights come. That we're so divided up into design, construction, engineering, interior design, lighting design. On one hand, I really value expertise, and being able to deep dive into a field really makes you more likely to be excellent at it. What we're missing is more of the glue, more of the bridgers. In the early days of our projects, like with Green School, it was possible because it had one founding couple who was really able to dedicate their resources a little bit in the unknown. To say, we've got to make this happen, we're going to build it, and we're not going to figure out exactly how much it's going to cost in advance, and we don't even know all the technical solutions in advance. But just to be able to kickstart it that way. So much of what was innovated at Green School was also just built on the seeds of innovations that had already happened in other parts of the world. And those people bringing that into this melting pot. Then more recently, we've had a whole new layer of innovation that has to do with engineering and technologies. But to translate that into buildings that really get built, which is really all that matters. But you need the balance of the resources, the intention, the dedication, and that's also what we need to make sure that the world survives in a way that's healthy for humans for coming decades or centuries. We don't know how to tackle all the obstacles that we're going to have to tackle. We're going to have to come up with it along the way and figure out skylights and trap doors to open to be able to succeed. With that in mind, such a progressive agenda that the practice has, you must have had some pushback from industry at some point. Have you ever had any pushback that you've gone, wow, that came from somewhere I didn't expect, or that's a challenge that I never anticipated? Or maybe that surprised you? I mean, I'm constantly being surprised. There's constantly pushback in different ways that you don't realize. Just having everything communicated and aligned in a way that gets a project to keep going forward is an amazing orchestration or just alignment of things. My last question for you. Tell me, I'm interested to know, with someone with your expertise, experience, and philosophy of design, what do you think good design is? I think that if we're talking about our fundamental approach to design, I think what I need to keep reminding myself, I think that what's often missing is seeing ourselves as a layer in a hole. It's like a piece in a puzzle. We're very often just addressing little bits of the world and little bits of reality. But what if we could plug everything back into seeing ourselves as part of nature? Like humans talking about anything is actually part of the conversation that I think the natural world is having with itself. Because we are part of the natural world. We talk about it. Our language separates it. Technically, English anyway, separates it to be humans versus nature. I think that's just an idea that came up a few hundred years ago that we need to totally take apart. Because it's led us to make things that will never go away and get in our way and make us sick. And so if we could just remember and recognize and realize that everything that we made sort of connected up with everything else, then we wouldn't do stupid things like making plastic at all. It wouldn't happen. But when we think about how do we make money this year at the expense of everything else, then it's a disaster. It's a diabolical equation, isn't it? And yet we're always in the business of making sure we all get our next meal. So that's the puzzle, I guess. Yeah. So where does design fit into that scenario? Well, everything that's ever made is designed. And it's to do with, like, what's the intention? What's the fundamental intention? What are the rules, the parameters of how to make that thing? And right now it's like whatever you can get away with and whatever can fit in to the box that's been planned. The budget box, the regulation box, the expectation based on culture norms box. There's only boxes. Part of the beauty of our process is that pretty soon after the bamboo is harvested, it shows up in the workshop right next door. And then it's carried by all these hands throughout that process of getting dried and treated, in some cases processed into different size splits and into furniture and into building components. And so we stay really connected to the physicality of that. Design can get very ethereal, intellectual, and technical in ways that can really pull you away from what it really is. This is a material with a personality. Each piece of bamboo is different. I mean, we're making castles out of grass, right? Like, that shouldn't be possible. We're taking a wild weed that grows on the steep cliffs at the edge of river valleys that's been growing there for hundreds of years and people have been doing cool things with it. But now that we can make it last, now that we have treatment solutions and technical understandings that allow us to build permanent structures, long-lasting structures that'll last as long as wooden buildings that are properly designed and treated and cared for wood, we can make something new possible. Do you ever wake up and just pinch yourself and say, I can't believe I'm doing this? Yeah, sometimes I think about what my childhood self would think if they got, because I love seeing kids experience the world. So a kid running through the project that I made, and sometimes, actually what's amazing about that is a kid, I took my kids to see a yoga shala that I made at Alchemy, and they kind of ignored it. They didn't comment on it, but they just ran in circles around the room, delighted, and started playing. So they weren't even like, wow, they weren't articulating what they think about a space or how it makes them feel. My kids go into the ARC at Green School, and they're like, oh yeah, the gym, whatever. But when you see how they are in the space, and if that could happen to adults too, if they could catch that sense of childlike awe and contagion, that's when something's possible. All that I need is for what I do, what we do, to make something possible in the world that leads us toward a world that I'm proud to be part of. Just to be a little piece of the tipping point of that, the percolation of that, that's the honour. Elora Hardy, creative force and CEO of Ibuku. What I love about Elora's work is that it reminds us that the future doesn't have to be made of steel and concrete alone. Sometimes the most radical ideas begin with a simple, natural material and a willingness to listen to what it wants to be. Bamboo bends, adapts, and holds the memory of place. And through Ibuku, it's reshaping how we imagine shelter. I spoke to Elora Hardy while making my ABC International TV series, Culture by Design. Check it out on iview. A second season is coming soon. I'd love to know if you've visited any incredible bamboo structures. Send me a line at bydesign at abc.net.au. Thanks for spending time with us on By Design. If you enjoyed today's episode, follow the podcast to be first in line for new shows. And be sure to look out for our bonus series, Extraordinary Every Day, released every Thursday. In our next episode, the final stop in our material cultures series, we're staying in Indonesia and travelling to Jakarta, where we'll meet one of the people responsible for reviving interest in the beautiful tradition of batik cloth making. Join me for that next time on By Design, because in a rapidly changing world, design matters. The producer of By Design is Siobhan Hunt, with extra production by Anita Barrow. You can feel it in the towering bamboo arcs of the Lumi Shala, a yoga pavilion that rises
like a woven cathedral in the jungle.
Or in the gently sloping roofline of the Mali Beach Club, curling down towards the sand
like a breaking wave.
All realised with bundles of bamboo bent and stitched together with extraordinary grace.
Ibuku's founder, Elora Hardy, wants to push the material even further.
Born in Canada but raised in Bali, she returned after years overseas, inspired by her parents,
who created Bali's famous Green School, that wall-less campus of bamboo structures
where children learn inside the landscape itself.
It's a place that taught her, from the beginning, that nature could be a collaborator in design,
not a constraint.
Bamboo is a very particular material to work with.
It has so much of its own personality, especially when you're working with it in the round,
that you need to design with it.
So when we're working with bamboo, there's so many different ways to interpret it and
to play with it.
We have honestly just touched the tip of the iceberg.
So much of what you see in Asia, especially today, looks so much like what we've been doing for the past decade.
But that's not how it should be.
There should, there can be, there will be, just a plethora of different visual expressions of this material
and technical expressions of the material.
So we are really just getting to know it at like a molecular level in a way that relates to engineering.
So when we're engineering with bamboo, what's been happening for the past decade is honestly just a lot tied to like the craftsman's experience.
And now with engineering processes, with Atelier One who designs our most sophisticated engineered bamboo projects,
we are looking deeply into the fibers of the material to understand how it's so strong.
Because it's really unbelievably strong.
And when we do that, we really get to play with it more on the edge of what's possible.
Like bring it into, bring it into shapes and forms that we haven't imagined before.
So it's continuing to show you.
It's, you know, opening up more and more, not less and less.
Yeah.
Yeah.
We'll look back decades from now and see this like, like charming little flowering of what was possible.
There's just a little, little bit and it will look like a million different shapes.
Yeah.
The bamboo has a sort of a geometry and a bend to it that you seem to have this, it's like playing a musical instrument.
Like expertly playing the bend in that, that material to get the kinds of effects that you get, which is so, so lyrical.
Well, the interesting thing is that bamboo is so flexible and that's what makes it great for earthquakes.
Yeah.
It can bend before it breaks under pressure.
As a pole though, it isn't flexible in the way that it appears to be in some of our structures.
When we bend it, we aren't always bending it.
We're often cutting it to, to bring it into the alignment of what we want it to be in the building.
There's also possibilities of bending it.
That's a new technique we're working with.
Right.
And when you split it up, take it away from its original round form and you split it up, you really unleash its flexibility.
Yeah.
So then you're creating what they call glulam.
This is very advanced in wood.
There's a lot of technical innovation.
There's big factories set up with how to turn wood into glulam parts of buildings, including curves.
Yeah.

And so when we tap into that and we bring bamboo into that equation, we're sort of substituting the bamboo in a way because it just grows faster and has really great properties that lend itself to that technique.
But that's probably where we'll see the most advancement and the most scale of bamboo building in the world.

When we talk about glulam, that's really where we'll see bamboo show up in cities and show up in places that don't have craftsmen available or even in rural settings that need a broader scale and can be preassembled and brought to the site without so much care.
But our world has really been in the artistry of it because each of our projects, our whole trajectory has been guided by each of our clients, each of our projects and what they aspired to.
And very often that was from a dreaming of what's possible place, not filling a practical need place.
So you're moving bamboo into the engineered lumber space, glulam and those sorts of things.
What other innovations are you working on?
Where else is it taking you?

A lot of the innovation that's exciting in the design and bamboo world is the software, including augmented reality where we can use goggles and see where things will be in space and how the different stages and how that can connect the design process with the construction process.
Typically in the design and construction world, and we are the same, we have a whole ream of paper attached to a whole lot of computer files that represents what should be done on site.
And very often the people on site don't even relate to how to read all those papers.
And it's counterintuitive for humans to go from three dimensions into one dimension and then into three dimensions again.
So in technology, I'm most interested in how we can stay in three dimensions.
We design at desks.
Even in this office, we spend a lot of time at the desks.
We have flat screens, we have flat paper.
But we're making something three-dimensional.
It's ironic.
You used to, correct me if I'm wrong here, but didn't you used to make the beautiful models that we see around us?
But that was what you would take to site and what people would build from to create your earlier work.
Do you still, is that true and do you still do that?
Yeah.
From the early days of working with bamboo, it was really only possible because we de-emphasized the drawing stage.
We might have a sketch or two along the way, but there are many buildings in the first years of our work where we really, like we made a bamboo structural model and the craftsmen built that.
They replicated it at a bigger scale, which is a very direct, visceral, clear communication that skips over a lot of the issues with language barriers or technical knowledge
and engineering degrees and things like this.
Just replicate this and we can talk a bit about some of the details.
So we still do that, including of the other materials, not just of the bamboo.
And that is really why it's all possible.
But to complement it, and especially because of the engineering, we also need to have a lot of 3D computer models.
And that, in turn, lets us do things that you wouldn't think possible from just an intuitive understanding of the material.
Yeah.
It lets us stretch outside of that.
Yeah.
Push a little bit further, a little bit harder.
Yeah.
Yeah.
I mean, it's very exciting to think of augmented reality and those sorts of texts coming into a very traditional material and then the way that you're going to take both of those things together.
I suppose part of that's necessary because the scale of your work is continuing to grow.
I mean, you're doing bigger and bigger and more and more fantastic things with your practice.
How is that step into this bigger space going?

I mean, there's a finite amount of craftsmanship and a really big need for buildings in the world and a really, really big need for buildings to be created with a sustainable approach, with fundamentally good materials that won't harm our future.
I think it's really important to bring the past with us into the future.
And one expression of that is the artisanal, the traditional techniques and knowledge, also stylistically.
We don't want to look completely different.
We want to look like we connect as we evolve our style.
But also we want to create a world that we wish to live in.
We want to create what we most imagine is the best future.
As we design buildings that will last for decades and centuries and will be sheltering us in a world that we don't really grasp and understand yet.
We have to figure out how to make them dynamic and protective in a way that lets us live in the best possible future.
So when we're imagining a building, we've got to think, what will it be like decades from now?
And what will the world be like?
And that's kind of a scary question, actually.
So the best that I can do is say, what do we imagine is that best possible scenario and what do we want that to look at?
How does what we're building and creating, in terms of its style and its sense of place and its practicalities,
but also in terms of what it means for that society and how we can speak about what we want for humanity and for nature in a building in the next hundred years.
And there is, there are fundamental threads of culture that humans have been weaving for millennia.
And some of those carry through, but we're not trying to recreate the past.
We're trying to create the future.
So we need to, we need to ask ourselves what we want that to look like.
That leads me to sort of think about where you are, which is here in Bali, in Indonesia.
And you've been obviously working here.
Your practice began here.
What have you learned and what do you continue to learn from the Indonesian cultures that you're drawing on and taking into the future?
I mean, so much of what I do with my life just comes out of a love of Bali, where I got the privilege of growing up.
And what's underlying everything is like, how can I bring out into the world, like, what I got out of growing up here?
And Bali is a place that everyone knows as being, like, creative and dynamic and beautiful and natural.
And I think that that holds so much for the future.
Laura Hardy, founder of Ibuku, has her eye firmly on the future, pioneering new ways to use bamboo as a strong, sustainable building material in environments far beyond Bali.
I'm Anthony Burke, and this is ABC Radio Nationals by Design.
And we're continuing our series, Material Cultures, exploring how materials can shape and sometimes even renew design culture.
At Ibuku, Elora and her team blend traditional craft with emerging technologies to push bamboo into entirely new territory.
But at the heart of their philosophy is a beautifully simple idea.
Creating shelter with nature, not against it.
A return to building in dialogue with the world around us, rather than in defiance of it.
Because we want to also get back to, like, why are we creating buildings?
It's to create shelter.
And that's, like, an age-old human need is to protect ourselves.
We don't have scales.
We don't have fur.
We need shelter.
We need a layer of protection and closure.
But what we've done in the world is we have taken that way too far.
We take conclusions that we've come to about how humans need to be protected from nature in cold climates and deserts.
And created this bland average of box culture that has imbued all of architecture.
So much of architecture is based on an assumption that we need a layer of protection that is not contextual.
And in Bali and in much of Asia, we need to shelter ourselves from maybe heat more than cold in some cases.
We need to shelter ourselves from bugs or from smog.
There are many things we still need to account for.
But we have the privilege of the possibility of some days of the year when we can open things up.
And so what if we weren't designing from a defensive mentality?
What if we were designing for all the best days?
And also could shelter ourselves as we needed to on the worst day.
And that's fair enough.
There's like such an anxiety in the world about what will our worst days look like in the coming decades.
Yeah.
We have good cause to be very nervous about that.
Yeah, indeed.
But I can't let it pervade the design thinking.
There's a definite optimism in the work.
You feel the sense of, I was going to say playfulness.
There's a joy when you walk into a space like this one that we're sitting in.
I can imagine the work, the team you have out there working your way are happy to come to work in a beautiful context like this every day.
I mean, that's a gift.
Yeah.
So that's what you sort of want for everyone.
Yeah.
Yeah.
We get to work barefoot.
That is genius.
With that in mind, I mean, do you miss the old days?
You're bigger.
You've got a lot more responsibilities.
The mission has grown.
You know, those early days of the innovation curve when everything is new, then it kind of flattens out and you kind of start to sort of get into a routine.
Do you find you miss that cutting edge moment when it was all coming to life?

I really strive to keep some spontaneity structured in to our design work because I remember the early days in the houses that we made at Green Village where we would come up with the best possible solution on site in the moment as the craftsmen where they're talking about it with us.

And when you've got to get it all on paper and in a 3D and in a bamboo model and all those things have to match and you've got to do that a year before they're going to be building it in some cases, it can definitely constrain the reality of what would be the best thing there.
And so sometimes we even plan in our designs.
We're like, okay, we've got most of it figured out.
We're going to leave this area bubbled and we know that we're going to need to come on site and dedicate some time to figuring it out there and we're going to allocate a budget to that.
Because we can't pretend as designers that we're going to get it right on paper in advance.
And 3D helps, but not as much as being there on site.
When you actually have the privilege of standing on site and saying like, how far away should the wall be from here and wouldn't it be nicer if it were this shape and let's weave that.
Like that, that's something that we can exercise to do more and more in our creativity and anticipate it.
But we can't pretend we can anticipate everything.
So wherever we can, we like to do that.
It seems to me you're already changing people's perceptions of what architecture can be.
It seems the next challenge for you is to change that same idea in the construction industry.
How do we build?
How do we go about those processes?
How do we make things like this come to life in a way which, as you say, maybe even leave space for that on-site conversation as the most important part.
Otherwise, a contract would button everything up well before you got to turning any soil anywhere.
Yeah.
Yeah.

So with that in mind, is that a target for you, the construction industry itself, trying to skill up a workforce that you can then sort of, I guess, use to teach the construction industry as it is happening in the world in a way?
That would be amazing, but we haven't articulated that.
We haven't tackled that.
Yeah.
I imagine, though, you've got the design equation well under control.
There's a lot of innovation there already, but your next sort of target must be the construction industry because it's such a behemoth to move.
It needs innovation.
It needs your innovation, Elora.
Are you thinking about that space?

If we had had to design things and get them all documented on paper and quantity surveyed and fully detailed in order to then build the buildings that we had created so far, it would have been almost impossible.
Yeah, right.
And there's such a grind in the construction world of having to have things all set up that way.

There's so much pressure on construction teams to be competitive at tender and to guarantee things, even when they're innovative, that really limits innovation, that really limits creativity, that really limits flexibility.
So, in my ideal world, there would be a way in all of our projects around the world to just have much more room to develop things together on site.

So much of the world in general is so compartmentalized, and I think we're seeing more and more across various industries and across education that when you bring experts in different fields together to tackle an issue, that that's very often where the new insights come.
That we're so divided up into design, construction, engineering, interior design, lighting design.
On one hand, I really value expertise, and being able to deep dive into a field really makes you more likely to be excellent at it.
What we're missing is more of the glue, more of the bridgers.
In the early days of our projects, like with Green School, it was possible because it had one founding couple who was really able to dedicate their resources a little bit in the unknown.

To say, we've got to make this happen, we're going to build it, and we're not going to figure out exactly how much it's going to cost in advance, and we don't even know all the technical solutions in advance.
But just to be able to kickstart it that way.
So much of what was innovated at Green School was also just built on the seeds of innovations that had already happened in other parts of the world.
And those people bringing that into this melting pot.
Then more recently, we've had a whole new layer of innovation that has to do with engineering and technologies.
But to translate that into buildings that really get built, which is really all that matters.

But you need the balance of the resources, the intention, the dedication, and that's also what we need to make sure that the world survives in a way that's healthy for humans for coming decades or centuries.
We don't know how to tackle all the obstacles that we're going to have to tackle.
We're going to have to come up with it along the way and figure out skylights and trap doors to open to be able to succeed.
With that in mind, such a progressive agenda that the practice has, you must have had some pushback from industry at some point.
Have you ever had any pushback that you've gone, wow, that came from somewhere I didn't expect, or that's a challenge that I never anticipated?
Or maybe that surprised you?
I mean, I'm constantly being surprised.
There's constantly pushback in different ways that you don't realize.
Just having everything communicated and aligned in a way that gets a project to keep going forward is an amazing orchestration or just alignment of things.
My last question for you.
Tell me, I'm interested to know, with someone with your expertise, experience, and philosophy of design, what do you think good design is?
I think that if we're talking about our fundamental approach to design, I think what I need to keep reminding myself, I think that what's often missing is seeing ourselves as a layer in a hole.
It's like a piece in a puzzle.
We're very often just addressing little bits of the world and little bits of reality.
But what if we could plug everything back into seeing ourselves as part of nature?
Like humans talking about anything is actually part of the conversation that I think the natural world is having with itself.
Because we are part of the natural world.
We talk about it.
Our language separates it.
Technically, English anyway, separates it to be humans versus nature.
I think that's just an idea that came up a few hundred years ago that we need to totally take apart.
Because it's led us to make things that will never go away and get in our way and make us sick.
And so if we could just remember and recognize and realize that everything that we made sort of connected up with everything else, then we wouldn't do stupid things like making plastic at all.
It wouldn't happen.
But when we think about how do we make money this year at the expense of everything else, then it's a disaster.
It's a diabolical equation, isn't it?
And yet we're always in the business of making sure we all get our next meal.
So that's the puzzle, I guess.
Yeah.
So where does design fit into that scenario?
Well, everything that's ever made is designed.
And it's to do with, like, what's the intention?
What's the fundamental intention?
What are the rules, the parameters of how to make that thing?
And right now it's like whatever you can get away with and whatever can fit in to the box that's been planned.
The budget box, the regulation box, the expectation based on culture norms box.
There's only boxes.
Part of the beauty of our process is that pretty soon after the bamboo is harvested, it shows up in the workshop right next door.
And then it's carried by all these hands throughout that process of getting dried and treated, in some cases processed into different size splits and into furniture and into building components.
And so we stay really connected to the physicality of that.
Design can get very ethereal, intellectual, and technical in ways that can really pull you away from what it really is.
This is a material with a personality.
Each piece of bamboo is different.
I mean, we're making castles out of grass, right?
Like, that shouldn't be possible.
We're taking a wild weed that grows on the steep cliffs at the edge of river valleys that's been growing there for hundreds of years and people have been doing cool things with it.

But now that we can make it last, now that we have treatment solutions and technical understandings that allow us to build permanent structures, long-lasting structures that'll last as long as wooden buildings that are properly designed and treated and cared for wood, we can make something new possible.
Do you ever wake up and just pinch yourself and say, I can't believe I'm doing this?
Yeah, sometimes I think about what my childhood self would think if they got, because I love seeing kids experience the world.
So a kid running through the project that I made, and sometimes, actually what's amazing about that is a kid, I took my kids to see a yoga shala that I made at Alchemy, and they kind of ignored it.
They didn't comment on it, but they just ran in circles around the room, delighted, and started playing.
So they weren't even like, wow, they weren't articulating what they think about a space or how it makes them feel.
My kids go into the ARC at Green School, and they're like, oh yeah, the gym, whatever.
But when you see how they are in the space, and if that could happen to adults too, if they could catch that sense of childlike awe and contagion, that's when something's possible.
All that I need is for what I do, what we do, to make something possible in the world that leads us toward a world that I'm proud to be part of.
Just to be a little piece of the tipping point of that, the percolation of that, that's the honour.
Elora Hardy, creative force and CEO of Ibuku.
What I love about Elora's work is that it reminds us that the future doesn't have to be made of steel and concrete alone.
Sometimes the most radical ideas begin with a simple, natural material and a willingness to listen to what it wants to be.
Bamboo bends, adapts, and holds the memory of place.
And through Ibuku, it's reshaping how we imagine shelter.
I spoke to Elora Hardy while making my ABC International TV series, Culture by Design.
Check it out on iview.
A second season is coming soon.
I'd love to know if you've visited any incredible bamboo structures.
Send me a line at bydesign at abc.net.au.
Thanks for spending time with us on By Design.
If you enjoyed today's episode, follow the podcast to be first in line for new shows.
And be sure to look out for our bonus series, Extraordinary Every Day, released every Thursday.
In our next episode, the final stop in our material cultures series, we're staying in Indonesia and travelling to Jakarta,
where we'll meet one of the people responsible for reviving interest in the beautiful tradition of batik cloth making.
Join me for that next time on By Design, because in a rapidly changing world, design matters.
The producer of By Design is Siobhan Hunt, with extra production by Anita Barrow.
The sound engineer is Ross Richardson, and the executive producer is Rhiannon Brown.
This program was produced on Gadigal Land and the lands of the Wurundjeri.

episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Hello and welcome to the final in ABC Radio National's Boyer Lecture Series for 2025. I'm Julia Baird and thus far our previous four speakers have offered compelling insights into the theme of Australia's unique, radical experiment in democracy, both its strengths and vulnerabilities in a world where democracy is in decline. In this lecture, author and professor of modern history from Sydney University, James Curran, in a pointed and powerful address entitled Trump's Gift, identifies the opportunities the presidency of Donald Trump now presents. episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Welcome to ABC Radio National and to the 2025 Boyer Lectures. I'm Julia Baird and I was asked by the ABC Chair, Kim Williams, to curate a series of lecturers who would outline to our well-informed audience not only the strengths behind Australia's democracy and its institutions, but also the current threats we are facing. For years now, we've watched our world, our lives, our behaviour being shaped by a group of billionaires in America, often called tech bros, the most prominent of which have been earning the favour of President Donald Trump in recent months. These men hold immense power without much accountability and are holding the reins to a world which is changing at lightning speed in unpredictable and dizzying ways. Which is exactly why we are joined now by acclaimed journalist, Amelia.
