Here's neoclassical composer Boyd. Hi, my name is James Boyd-Haw. I release and perform music under the title Boyd. I sit down at the piano and I play the piano with no intention of what's coming out. It's more so I play the piano to allow me to understand what's going on. And it isn't until I understand where I start to look down and really look at what I've created and try and form some kind of structure and piece to it. And for me, that's how it comes about. This is the first piece from my album titled A Gone. It's a solo piano work about a difficult time in my life. It reminded me that sometimes we need to let go of what we hope.

title: Come By Chance - ABC listen
description: If you've ever been to Newfoundland, you know it's a place where fog can envelop you so deeply, you don't know where you're going or where you came from. When two men, born in the same rural Newfoundland hospital on the same day, discover an unbelievable 52-year-old secret, it changes the way they see themselves forever. But this isn't the end of the story. Because it turns out these men are not alone. A series of other close calls and near misses have begun to emerge, and not only at Come by Chance hospital. Come By Chance is a story about what it means to belong in a family — and how a twist of fate can upend the life you thought you knew. New episodes every Friday

I'm Luke Quinton from CBC. This is Come By Chance. Available now.

episodes.title: 01 | The Birthday Party
episodes.description: At a worksite on Newfoundland's coast, the staff take a break for birthday cake in honour of Craig Avery's 52nd birthday.
episodes.transcript: We're at the edge of the Atlantic Ocean, at the edge of the North American continent, in a little town on the neck of a peninsula that connects two parts of the island of Newfoundland. And at this moment, in this place, a little baby is about to be born into the world. On this December evening in 1962, Rita Hines has two choices. She can go to the hospital in Marystown, further down the Beerm Peninsula. Or she can go to another hospital, to the east. But tonight, there's a snowstorm. So she gets in the taxi and heads east, on a narrow gravel road, to the town of Come By Chance. With the car's yellow headlights shining on snowflakes and asphalt, Rita makes it to the hospital.

episodes.title: How to build a dragon
episodes.description: When Anita realises Bendigo's golden dragon will soon be too old to parade, she’s catapulted into the project of a lifetime: build a new dragon, the longest in the world, and make sure the over-a-century-long streak won’t be broken.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. As a child in 1970s Bendigo, Anita lives a double life. Growing up, being an Australian-born Chinese was often special and difficult. For the majority of the year, there's social discord, racism, no one there looking the same as you, no one there eating the same food that you ate. And in the months leading up to Easter, the rumours start swirling. Anita's family, Anita's dad, they've got a dragon. Be scared of her, you know. It was, you know, this sort of myth. But by the time Easter Sunday rolls around, the switch flips. Our culture was front and centre and I could be the person I was at home in a public space. That's because thousands of people are lining the streets for the biggest event of the year.

episodes.title: Aussie udon — From wheatbelt to noodle bowl
episodes.description: Udon noodle making in Japan goes back 1,200 years, so when did Western Australia become one of its top suppliers of noodle wheat?
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Among the everyday foods of Japan, one of the most common and popular are udon noodles. In Japan, noodles are an everyday staple and a cultural symbol. They are loved by all ages, from children to seniors. They are an essential part of daily life in Japan. They have a long and layered history in the country. Wheat-based noodles were introduced to Japan around 1,200 years ago, possibly by Buddhist monks travelling to and from China. And as the nation urbanised during the Edo era from the 17th century, noodle stalls flourished with the promise of a quick, cheap, hearty meal at any time of the year.

An audit by the Fair Work Ombudsman of 45 businesses found 35...

episodes.title: Faithful fasting — What we gain when we refrain
episodes.description: For Waleed Aly, refraining from food and drink from sunrise to sunset during Ramadan brings about not only a physical transformation but a spiritual one as well.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. The Islamic holy month of Ramadan is a time for fasting. Every day, from the first hint of light on the horizon right through until sunset, no food, no drink. But come the night, the light fades and at the streets of Lakemba in Sydney or Dandenong in Melbourne, they come alive with hungry people ready to break fast. And it isn't just for Muslims. These days, more than a million people flock to the night markets for a kebab right off the grill, a famous camel burger, a rare find.

episodes.title: Cooking community — A recipe for connection
episodes.description: Who doesn't love a passionfruit sponge, jam roly-poly or nice fluffy scone? Many of these classic recipes have been shared via community cookbooks, compiled by community groups and sold to raise funds for different causes and organisations.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Imagine small-town Australia in the early 20th century. A simpler time. Maybe a tougher time. But a time of sponge cakes, of oat and golden syrup biscuits, of steamed puddings and Sunday roasts. Food is a common social vocabulary. Food is a thread of unity and connection. Set that down in black and white. Gather all those loose slips of butter-stained paper, the recipes that make a house a home. Put it all together and what do you get? 20 recipes for passion fruit sponge. And a community cookbook. A unique snapshot of a particular community at a particular moment in time. Some of the really fascinating key attributes of the recipes when you start looking and flicking through these old cookbooks.

title: Forged with Adrian Stimson - ABC listen
description: Known as the 'Picasso of the North', Norval Morriseau is one of the most celebrated Indigenous artists in the world. But when a rock star gets a tip about the authenticity of his Morrisseau painting, he finds a sinister underworld with thousands of forged paintings, millions of dollars in profits, multiple fraud rings, and even a suspected murder. In this six-part series, from CBC in Canada and ABC Australia, host Adrian Stimson, an artist from the Siksika Nation, travels from Thunder Bay to the Northern Territory of Australia, to reveal the largest art crime fraud in the world. Adrian questions what this story tells us about how Indigenous art, and lives, matter.

episodes.title: Game Show Interview: Christopher Young & Gil Young (Deadpool VR)

episodes.transcript: If you've seen a scary movie any time between the 1980s and today, there is a good chance Christopher Young is the composer sending shivers down your spine. Among many others, he scored the films Hellraiser, The Grudge, Pet Sematary, and The Exorcism of Emily Rose. His expansive career includes the action of swordfish, the thrills of entrapment, the drama of the shipping news, and the comedy of Miss Congeniality 2. After tackling superheroes on screen, such as Spider-Man and Ghost Rider, Christopher Young returns to this world through a new medium, virtual reality video games. Scoring the 2025 title Deadpool VR, an immersive experience starring Marvel Comics' fourth wall-breaking Merc with the Mouth.

episodes.transcript: Rock, curiosity, and sounds from around the world. These are a few of the many elements that makes Stuart Chatwood the unique composer he is in the world of video games. He began his professional journey in the 1990s as a member and co-founder of The Tea Party, a power trio with a love of blending rock and multicultural instruments. Chatwood began to carve his parallel path as a game composer with the Prince of Persia reboot trilogy in the mid-2000s. His scores bring together the ancient and the contemporary and feature contributions from his fellow Tea Party bandmates. Chatwood's exploration into interactive entertainment continues with the Darkest Dungeon series diving deeper into the realms of gothic horror. episodes.title: Game Show Interview: Stuart Chatwood (Prince of Persia, Darkest Dungeon)
episodes.description: Meena Shamaly chats to composer Stuart Chatwood about his rock band origins, his musical curiosity, and how a love of music from around the world led him to scoring video games.
episodes.transcript: Rock, curiosity, and sounds from around the world. These are a few of the many elements that makes Stuart Chatwood the unique composer he is in the world of video games. He began his professional journey in the 1990s as a member and co-founder of The Tea Party, a power trio with a love of blending rock and multicultural instruments. Chatwood began to carve his parallel path as a game composer with the Prince of Persia reboot trilogy in the mid-2000s. His scores bring together the ancient and the contemporary and feature contributions from his fellow Tea Party bandmates. Chatwood's exploration into interactive entertainment continues with the Darkest Dungeon series diving deeper into the realms of gothic horror. episodes.transcript: If forgiveness is the gift you give yourself when someone does you wrong, what can you give when the harm done to you is unforgivable? Hi, I'm James Carlton. Welcome to God Forbid on ABC Radio National and across the Pacific on ABC Radio Australia, the panel show about the things we believe. And it's hard to believe, but some families endure unspeakable harm and somehow remain intact, while others fracture over what seems like nothing at all. How do we hold space for the reality of suffering, even trauma, but also the possibility of redemption? Our culture justifies righteous anger. The victim must be vindicated, not blamed. But the question remains challenging for all of us.

episodes.title: I found a hair in my library
episodes.description: Plagued by the question "Am I a hoarder?" journalist Annabel Crabb visits Australia's oldest library and learns that her own issues with 'collecting' historical items are MINOR.
episodes.transcript: Hey there, Mark Fennell here, and I have a brand new podcast, No One Saw It Coming. Each week we hunt for seemingly insignificant moments that change the course of history, and La McDellia, we've found some wild ones. Like the murder that caused Absinthe to be banned pretty much everywhere for around a century, and the wrong turn that started a world war. It's the podcast that will completely change the way you look at history. No One Saw It Coming. Find it now on the ABC Listen app. ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Hello, I'm Annabelle Crabb. Welcome to History or Hoarding, a podcast about the stuff we hang on to and why. Now I wouldn't say I'm a hoarder exactly, but I do hang on to things that, while being utterly without value, are simultaneously irreplaceable to me.

episodes.title: INTRODUCING History Or Hoarding? With Annabel Crabb
episodes.description: Annabel Crabb — who personally struggles to declutter, just ask Annabel's husband — visits Australia's oldest library and immediately feels better about her own habits. Above ground, this place is all books. But below?
episodes.transcript: I've always felt a bit self-conscious about the random junk that I have knocking around in my house. I mean, I can't bear to throw out Granny's old colander or the cookbooks I haven't opened in years or the baby teeth in the dresser drawer. Do I know exactly whose teeth they are? Ladies and gentlemen of the jury, I do not. I am without question retaining items that are beyond my practical remit. God, sorry, where are my manners? My name is Annabelle Crabb. I'm an ABC journalist, writer and host of a new podcast called History or Hoarding. It's about the stuff that we hang on to and why. Making this podcast is definitely not an excuse for me to avoid tidying up. Because in the last few months, I've been hanging out somewhere fascinating, at Australia's oldest library. A venerable collector... ...

episodes.description: A Tasmanian Devil has been spotted trapped in an illegal steel-jaw leg hold trap, Paula Wriedt steps away from politics and agriculture Ministers across the country met to discuss the impact of the Middle East conflict on farmers.

episodes.title: Drive
episodes.description: On Monday we heard from the Environment Protection Authority that over 9,000 tonnes of farmed salmon died in the first three months of this year, the CEO of Salmon Tasmania responds to those numbers.

episodes.title: Drive

episodes.title: Drive
episodes.description: The removal of the two giant sequoia trees in St Davids Park is now underway, Greens call for a permanent ban on the antibiotic 'florfenicol' in salmon pens and paramedics walk off the job at all public hospitals.

episodes.title: Drive
episodes.description: Get the latest on negotiations at the Bell Bay manganese smelter, find out how the state's fuel supply is tracking, and what's an infamous footy umpire up to in regional Tassie?

episodes.title: Drive

title: Tasmania Saturdays with Mel Bush - ABC listen
description: Join Mel Bush and ABC Hobart to explore what's happening in your community, garden and lifestyle.

episodes.title: Saturdays
episodes.description: On the 20th anniversary of the Beaconsfield mine collapse, Mel speaks with Professor Bill Shorten, former national secretary of the Australian Workers Union

episodes.title: Saturdays
episodes.description: What are those blobby critters in the alpine freshwater tarn at Mt Field National Park? Mel talks to biologist, author and jellyfish expert, Lisa-Ann Gershwin to solve the mystery.

episodes.title: Saturdays
episodes.description: Is it a bird? Is it a plane? No, it’s just Mel Bush taking you to outer space, as she chats with Dr. Sharolyn Anderson about Dark Sky Week, before speaking with Dr Martin George after the Artemis II splashdown.

episodes.title: Saturdays
episodes.description: Mel chats to visual art coordinator at Devonport Regional Gallery, Brigitta Magnussen-Reid, for a celebration of the life of Tasmanian arts luminary, Greg Leong.

episodes.title: Saturdays
episodes.description: Get an update on the local boat builder, Matt Morris, who is building a 40-foot pilot cutter inspired wooden boat. When is he going to launch his beautiful vessel, Tarkine? Mel finds out.

episodes.title: Saturdays
episodes.description: Young guitar virtuoso, Tommaso Girotto stops by to talk about his national tour and plays us a relaxing classical piece.

episodes.title: Saturdays
episodes.description: Lindsay Millar OAM, executive Board Member with the Tasmanian Aviation Historical Society tells Mel the tale of the DC-3 aircraft that crashed into Seven Mile Beach on the 80th anniversary of this tragic accident.

episodes.title: Saturdays
episodes.description: John O’Hara finds out how Bridgewater local and Burnie Water Clock inventor, Chris King, transported an entire church all the way from Somerset to Bridgewater.

episodes.title: Saturdays
episodes.description: Matt Heyward has just been named assistant director of Opera Australia’s upcoming production Phantom of the Opera on Sydney Harbour. John chats to the Tassie boy about his journey.

episodes.title: Saturdays
episodes.description: Take a stroll around the streets of Hobart on the Taverns of Rebellion tour, delving into the history of Hobart’s working-class pubs and taverns. John O’Hara speaks with historian, Professor Hamish Maxwell-Stewart and organiser Liz Clark.

episodes.title: Afternoons
episodes.description: Today we are learning what it takes to run a wildlife refuge, to drive a pilot boat, and to kill monsters!

title: Insiders Podcast with David Speers - ABC listen
description: David Speers unpacks important stories shaping Australia's future on ABC TV's Insiders. The show includes an interview with an Australian politician and a discussion with top journalists. The aim is to help you understand the factors driving national conversations.

episodes.title: Government's NDIS shakeup and Coalition leaves door ajar on property tax breaks
episodes.description: The government is spending some political capital. They've announced plans to rein in the NDIS and are inching closer to revealing changes to property tax breaks. But will the opposition get on board?

episodes.title: Analysis: Are NDIS cuts the exception or the template?
episodes.description: As far as tough budget decisions go, we haven't seen anything on this scale since Joe Hockey's ill-fated 2014 effort.
episodes.transcript: Hi, this is David Spears, the ABC's national political lead and the host of Insiders, and this is some analysis I've written on the major NDIS changes announced by Mark Butler. As far as tough budget decisions go, we haven't seen anything on this scale since Joe Hockey's ill-fated 2014 effort. After yet another forecast cost blowout, the changes laid out by Mark Butler to salvage the NDIS would save a whopping $35 billion over four years. Butler, affectionately dubbed the smiling assassin by one of his cabinet colleagues, has taken a far more unsparing approach than expected to deliver what he called a complete reset of the scheme. Nor is the minister squeamish about apportioning blame for what's caused the problem. He's not reaching for the usual crutch of blaming the other side. He's dropped the pretense, this is simply about shonks and fraudsters. Butler is conceding.

episodes.title: Analysis: Albanese government's frustration rises alongside fuel prices
episodes.description: Fuel prices and inflation aren't the only metrics climbing as the Strait of Hormuz remains shut. The Albanese government's level of frustration is rising just as fast.
episodes.transcript: Hi, this is David Spears, the ABC's national political lead and the host of Insiders, and this is some analysis I've written on the growing levels of frustration within the Australian government over the ongoing US-Iran war. Fuel prices and inflation aren't the only metrics climbing as the Strait of Hormuz remains shut. The Albanese government's level of frustration is rising just as fast. Whether it's Donald Trump threatening to wipe out an entire civilisation, posting a Jesus-like image of himself, or taking potshots at the Pope, there's daily disbelief at what's coming out of the White House. This general sense of dismay wasn't helped by Trump's Treasury Secretary, Scott Besant's tone-deaf response yesterday to the International Monetary Fund's warnings of economic doom. A small bit of economic pain is worth it, Besant insisted, to deprive Iran of a nuclear weapon.

episodes.title: breith eun by Eartha Davis
episodes.description: Eartha Davis is a woman of Ngāpuhi and Celtic heritage living on unceded Wurundjeri land. Her work has appeared in the Australian Poetry Anthology, Express Media, & Cordite, among others.
episodes.transcript: I was trained to feather, forge tenderness from wounded forevers, loosen impaled voices. I was trained to deny the breaker, become the braider, whittle wilting into aching blossoms. And we are told, yes, to undo the animal, feed flesh like hungered hands, private valleys guzzling light, which is to say guzzling themselves. Listen, we must remember river, river whirs like a soundtrack of kissing, gulps lungfuls of forest. It was we who did the breaking, and then it is we who must do the whittling. Breathe loud, breathe like loud living. Remember, we are earth's little darlings, the limbs over the eucalyptus trees always arch towards ours.

episodes.title: The Octopus by Judith Beveridge
episodes.description: New Australian Judith Beveridge lives on Wallumedegal land. She has published eight collections of poetry and has edited several anthologies. Her book Sun Music: New and Selected Poems was awarded the 2019 Prime Minister’s Award for poetry.
episodes.transcript: At the jetty's end, one rod palping like an alert antenna. Suddenly an octopus flailing, whirling its arms like a small Hindu goddess, switching colour as rapidly as a firework, stretching taut the gussets between its arms, desperate to free itself from the hook, and suck a kiss, a shell or rock. I hurry along the pier to tell the fishermen the octopus has three hearts, nine brains, that it solves problems, uses tools, that its skin can copy the texture of sand, shell and rock, that it can taste what its tentacles touch. Too late, he skewers it, then tosses it to his mate, who props it on his head, prancing around like a court jester, both laughing, jeering, piling on the irreverence.

episodes.title: Keeping the Minotaur by Debbie Lim
episodes.description: Keeping the Minotaur is a poem about the difficult parts of ourselves we might compartmentalise. It was written during the lockdown of 2020.
episodes.transcript: For years I have kept a tiny minotaur in the drawer of my bedside. Most nights I hear him pacing the walls of his locked and wooden box. He snorts moist puffs of air so minute, wet matches rasped. Smells richly of beast and burnt fur. Doesn't ask for much. I slip in morsels of my voice, cold remnants of dreams, the day's watery disappointments. Gradually he has learnt over the years to love me. But it is a stunted form of love and born purely from captivity. I think he simply longs to be whole, like us all. Still I do not let him out. I know how he's lonely.

episodes.transcript: It's not about the thing, but the this and that of it. It's not about the codex, but the pot of dal, earthy, inviting, endless. It's not about the word, but the grammar of incompletion. It's not about the house, but the copied key. It's not about the note, but the vibration, the blur of union. It's not about the pattern, but the wonk of our warp and weft. It's not about the object, but the sweepings, coal, fur, timber, silk, sugar, pins, needles, tobacco, calico, coffee, indigo, cochineal, tea. It's not about the hold, but the release. engagement.takeaway: Filming Hornblower at sea caused severe seasickness. Production moved to a land-based ship, where actors simulated ocean movement, revealing cinema's hidden practical challenges.
bestQuotes: Paul Verhoeven: "He said that you shot the first series of Hornblower at sea, but then they realised that was too much of a nightmare because people kept throwing up. episodes.title: Restore resilience with Hildegard

episodes.title: Love it or leave it: Mussorgsky's Pictures at an Exhibition

episodes.transcript: Listen closely. This is Nocturnal Worlds. Journeys through nature for sleep and relaxation. Shhh. Do you hear that? It's the sound of the gentle movements of the night. Join us as we take you on three magical nighttime journeys. We'll meet some of Australia's amazing nocturnal animals. The red-crowned toadlet. The powerful owl. The majestic long-finned eel.

Here, the whispers of the powerful owl and the secrets of the long-finned eel aren't just sounds; they're the keys to unlocking a primal calm, a deep sleep beyond the reach of the city's neon glare. This isn't just nature; it's an escape, a necessary descent into the wild heart of the night for the weary soul.

title: Someone Knows Something - ABC listen
description: In 1964, the partial remains of two black teenagers — Charles Moore and Henry Dee — were pulled from a backwater of the Mississippi River. Brutally murdered by the Ku Klux Klan, no one was ever convicted. In one of his first-ever cold case investigations, Someone Knows Something host David Ridgen joins the victim's brother Thomas Moore, as he returns to Mississippi 40 years later to discover the truth, confront the Klansmen involved, and find justice. Season 2: New case. New leads. New hope. Documentarian David Ridgen is back, investigating another cold case. This time, he heads to Hamilton, Ontario to investigate the disappearance of Sheryl Sheppard. On December 31, 1997, at a New Year's Eve party broadcast on live TV, Sheppard accepted a marriage proposal from her boyfriend, Michael Lavoie. Two days later, she disappeared. In Season 2 of SKS, David Ridgen joins Sheppard's mother Odette on her search for answers. Season 1: David Ridgen investigates the case of Adrien McNaughton, a five-year-old who vanished during a family fishing trip in 1972. He explores the mysterious circumstances of Adrien's disappearance, providing insights into the investigation and the impact on the family. This is a CBC podcast.

episodes.title: Reforming mainstream perceptions of the education system
episodes.description: Dr Chris Sarra shares his widely celebrated work on reforming the education system and making it more culturally appropriate for Indigenous students.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Welcome to Speaking Out. We're mainly discussing land rights and economic empowerment. Aboriginal enterprises in mining, exploration and energy. I just need to talk a little bit about Indigenous constitutional recognition. With Larissa Berendt. It's a fresh view coming. On ABC Radio. Having very explicit conversations with kids and with parents and saying, yeah, look, this is a school. It's a white institution, essentially. But I'm not here to make your kids. I'm not here to turn black kids into being like white kids. I want to make them stronger as young black boys and girls so that they can go on and survive in high school. So I want them to be strong in their sense of culture and identity. And I also want them to be smart enough to be able to mix it so that year three kids in Cherbourg should be doing the same work.

episodes.title: Remembering Aunty Rhoda Roberts AO: A defining voice of a generation
episodes.description: Aunty Rhoda Roberts, was a trailblazer in the arts and media scene. We reflect on her legacy and the impact she has made on Indigenous communities across the country and the world.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Welcome to Speaking Out. Mainly discussing land rights and economic empowerment. Aboriginal enterprises in mining, exploration and energy. I just want to talk a little bit about indigenous constitutional recognition. With Larissa Berendt. It's a fresh view coming. On ABC Radio. I think what occurred back in the 80s, particularly when we were looking at creatives, we were developing our own theatre companies. We were looking at, you know, Bermali, Bangdara. All these companies were forming that were Aboriginal-led. And so there was a shift in the control and the power of product that the authorship and control was from a First Nations lens. And we went on to see some great developments. I think the film industry, that has been a great catalyst to look at the model they used.

episodes.title: Tributes to James Valentine, beloved ABC Radio legend
episodes.description: Beloved 702 ABC Sydney radio host James Valentine has died aged 64, two years after a cancer diagnosis. He was remembered on 702 ABC Sydney Mornings by listeners and special guests.
episodes.transcript: Good morning. This is ABC Radio. I'm Hamish Macdonald. It is Thursday the 23rd of April. A very warm welcome to listeners across Sydney and across New South Wales. We're setting aside our regular programming for this morning because we have some very sad news to share with you. James Valentine has died. He was 64. James is survived by his wife Joanne and their two children, Ruby and Roy. Our beloved friend and colleague presented the afternoon show here on 702 for more than 20 years. James retired from 702 back in February. He wanted to focus on his cancer treatment. He died yesterday at home using voluntary assisted dying, a detail that he wanted shared with you. It was two years after his cancer diagnosis. It was back in March of 2024 that James first announced his initial diagnosis, esophageal cancer.

episodes.title: What's it like being a bugler on ANZAC Day?
episodes.description: Every Anzac Day, the last post rings out at ceremonies across the country, followed by the words "lest we forget".
episodes.transcript: At the foot of the snowy mountains on a cool drizzly day, the stillness at Tumut Cemetery is cut by the sound of a familiar but stirring tune. Adam Farquharson is here most days, but even the days he's away from his southern New South Wales home, the ritual is the same. Once I get to the grave, I stand there at a tension play of the last post, recite the old Plara Valley, then I just wander off. A lot of them, it says less we forget on the bottom of the headstone, and at least I'm not going to forget. If they've had relatives, if they're maybe the last of their line, there's nobody left to come and see them, and I don't want them to be forgotten. Without a lie, you don't really know how it's going to go until you finish. It's big pressure, and to get it right, I take it very, very seriously. Certainly better at it than I used to be, and I do this mainly to try and contain the nerves, and it kind of works. Adam's dad was a cook at Nui Da. Thank you very much. Thank you very much.

episodes.title: The ridiculous outfits that beat Jarvis' anxiety
episodes.description: Law student Jarvis Leith felt social anxiety in his first year of study, always worrying about what people thought of him.
episodes.transcript: Heading to uni for the first time in Wollongong, New South Wales, Jarvis Leith felt anxious. I think everyone has social anxiety, even just a little bit, some more than others, but I definitely was quite a shy person, particularly at the start of uni, a bit scared of what other people thought of me, and always felt that everything I did was kind of watched in a way, even though 9 out of 10 it's not. Overanalyzing everything from the point of view of someone else, wondering what other people thought of me, how my hair was, or what shoes I was wearing. It's quite a difficult thing to have. So the law student did something, well, a bit terrifying. Yeah, so I decided to just wear some crazy outfits and really try to stand out in class instead of hiding and putting my hood on, being bold and being out there.

episodes.description: The name of World War I soldier C Gordon is etched on a memorial in the NSW town of Araluen, but local historians are still searching to find out who he his.
episodes.transcript: Every Anzac Day, the names etched into the Araluan War Memorial are read aloud, along with one or two of those soldiers' stories. What it's been great to be able to do through the history group is to put a little bit more of the human stories in, and I say this a lot, in my view, the history comes alive through the stories of the people. But there is one name on the memorial, C. Gordon, whose story for the Araluan History Group remains a mystery. Judy Angelai is a member of the group, which has been searching for information about the World War I digger for more than two years. On the memorial, which was unveiled in March 1931, there are eight names of those who fell in World War I, as well as, I think, about 18 names of those who served. The history group, through the research and through looking at a whole heap of information that's available online and family stories, which have been wonderful, have managed to uncover a lot of information about most of those people.

episodes.title: Tributes to James Valentine, beloved ABC Radio legend
episodes.description: Beloved 702 ABC Sydney radio host James Valentine has died aged 64, two years after a cancer diagnosis. He was remembered on 702 ABC Sydney Mornings by listeners and special guests.
episodes.transcript: Good morning. This is ABC Radio. I'm Hamish Macdonald. It is Thursday the 23rd of April. A very warm welcome to listeners across Sydney and across New South Wales. We're setting aside our regular programming for this morning because we have some very sad news to share with you. James Valentine has died. He was 64. James is survived by his wife Joanne and their two children, Ruby and Roy. Our beloved friend and colleague presented the afternoon show here on 702 for more than 20 years. James retired from 702 back in February. He wanted to focus on his cancer treatment. He died yesterday at home using voluntary assisted dying, a detail that he wanted shared with you. It was two years after his cancer diagnosis. It was back in March of 2024 that James first announced his initial diagnosis, esophageal cancer.

title: The ABC Jazz Sessions - ABC listen
description: Explore the vibrant and the evolving sounds of Australian jazz captured in the ABC's studios around the country.

episodes.title: 'Quartet' Tessie Overmyer
episodes.description: Saxophonist Tessie Overmyer has been hard at work studying over in New York of late, but she cut this session with her Aussie compatriots in Sydney.

episodes.title: 'Women Of Jazz '26'
episodes.description: ABC Jazz is marking International Women's Day with a new compilation release celebrating contemporary women from across the Australian jazz scene.

episodes.title: 'Bye For Now' Lauren Tsamouras + Tom Avgenicos
episodes.description: Following on from their tribute album to Judy Bailey, pianist Lauren Tsamouras and trumpeter Tom Avgenicos bring their expansive duet sound to a series of original compositions on the new EP 'Bye For Now'.

episodes.title: '50 Years Of Jazztrack: The Studio Sessions'
episodes.description: Listen back to 50 years worth of highlight recordings captured for Jazztrack.

episodes.title: 'Time Passes' David Jones, Ben Robertson & Tony Gould
episodes.description: Exploration and interplay are at the heart of a new project fronted by Australian jazz stalwarts David Jones on drums and percussion, Ben Robertson on bass and Tony Gould on piano.

episodes.title: 'For Judy' Lauren Tsamouras + Tom Avgenicos
episodes.description: Judy Bailey was a pioneering force in Australian jazz, a brilliant composer and pianist, and a passionate educator whose influence shaped generations of musicians.

episodes.title: The Best Of ABC Jazz '25
episodes.description: To mark Ausmusic Month 2025, ABC Jazz is proud to release this compilation of studio recordings from Australian artists.

episodes.title: Somesh Putcha - Ever Playful
episodes.description: Discover the debut album from Canberra drummer and composer Somesh Putcha and his quartet of young-gun players.

episodes.title: The ABC Jazz Sessions: Michelle Nicolle
episodes.description: Singer Michelle Nicolle celebrates her tenth album with a series of original tunes captured live with her quartet at The Jazzlab in Melbourne.

episodes.title: The ABC Jazz Sessions: Eucalyptus Treeo
episodes.description: Eucalyptus Treeo is Rafael Karlen on saxophone, Steve Barry on piano and Hannah James on bass.

title: The Dinner Set with Kate Wadey - ABC listen
description: Kate Wadey joins us to share some of her favourite tunes from across the history of jazz.

episodes.title: All Aboard The Night Train
episodes.description: Join Kate Wadey as she revisits a classic cut from the legendary Canadian pianist Oscar Peterson.

episodes.title: Revisiting Beverly Kenney
episodes.description: Kate Wadey revisits an unsung heroine of the 1950s - vocalist Beverly Kenney. Enjoy her work alongside members of the Count Basie Orchestra who went by the name 'The Basie-ites' as well as alongside the guitar player Johnny Smith.

episodes.title: Diggin' Bill Evans
episodes.description: Join Kate Wadey as she delves into the sophomore LP from pianist and composer Bill Evans. Cut right before he joined Miles Davis, this record featured Bill alongside the trumpeter's sideman - drummer Philly Joe Jones and bassist Sam Jones.

episodes.title: Billie Meets Lester
episodes.description: One of jazz's great friendships is on full display across this first episode from Kate Wadey! Singer Billie Holiday and saxophonist Lester Young were fast friends, and they worked together on a series of recordings back in the swing era.

episodes.title: Kate Wadey fills in for Monica Trapaga on The Dinner Set
episodes.description: Over the next little while, Monica Trapaga will be taking a sabbatical to trace her family roots in Spain. Fellow vocalist Kate Wadey will be keeping Monica's seat warm, and two caught up on the show to share some music.

episodes.title: Monica's Spanish Heart
episodes.description: Join Monica Trapaga as she celebrates music from Spain! This will be her last Dinner Set for a little while, but Monica will also share some news about who will be keeping her seat warm over the next few months.

episodes.title: Getting to know Björn Ingelstam
episodes.description: Dig some fresh tunes from Swedish trumpeter and singer Björn Ingelstam on the show!

episodes.title: Catching Up With Kurt
episodes.description: Monica's catching up with the brilliant vocalist and band leader Kurt Elling, who joins the WDR Big Band on his latest release.

episodes.title: Ron Carter talks 'Sweet, Sweet Spirit' with Eric Ajaye
episodes.description: Jazz Legends presenter Eric Ajaye recently caught up with master bassist Ron Carter to talk about his life and music, as well as his latest album - 'Sweet, Sweet Spirit' - a record dedicated to his mother.

episodes.title: Stompin' In New Orleans
episodes.description: Monica Trapaga celebrates International Women's Day 2026 with a concert by clarinettist Aurora Nealand, paying tribute to the pioneering Sidney Bechet.

episodes.title: Have drones and distance dulled our sense of war’s brutality?
episodes.description: Does the gamified footage we see of missile strikes and drone attacks lead to a detached view of what war is really like?
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Hello, I'm Frank Kelly and this is the Radio National Hour, coming to you from the land of the Gadigal people of the Eora Nation in Sydney. There's a growing gap between the sanitised, pixelated war imagery we consume online of drones and helmet cams and missile strikes and the lived reality of the soldiers in battle. So as we commemorate Anzac Day, how does this detachment affect the way we think about war? Also ahead, as reports of AI chatbots encouraging people to harm themselves or others continue to grow, are we heading into a world where the AI companies simply can't control what their bots are doing? By design.

title: The Screen Show with Jason Di Rosso - ABC listen
description: The Screen Show, hosted by renowned Sydney-based film critic Jason Di Rosso, is your ultimate guide to the world of film, television, and streaming. Each episode explores the latest films, TV shows and streaming originals through reviews, analysis and exclusive conversations with directors, actors, screenwriters, cinematographers, producers, showrunners and production designers, from A-list Hollywood talent to Australian creatives and emerging and established talent from around the world, providing you with VIP access to the minds shaping today's entertainment landscape. From blockbusters to award season predictions (including the Oscars, Golden Globes, Emmys, BAFTAs and AACTAs) and film festival coverage (including Cannes, Venice, Berlinale, and all the Australian film festivals), The Screen Show keeps you on top of cinematic trends, award nominees and winners, international favourites, indie darlings, Australian gems, cult classics, retrospectives, and box office hits. Whether your interest lies in cinema or TV streaming, The Screen Show covers it all, celebrating cinematic storytelling in all its forms.

episodes.transcript: ABC Radio National is asking Australians to vote for their top books of the 21st century. What a big ask. But don't panic, we bring you inspiration. episodes.description: Folk forward-thinker The Weather Station roams into the Tower for a chat
episodes.transcript: My process tends to be, you know, when I'm writing songs, I like to write in the morning. I like to do it first thing before doing anything else and, you know, just sit with whatever instrument I'm writing on. And there's always that element of the first words that come out of your mouth and you don't quite know why or what they mean. And I tend to write them down and think about it and let more flow and then edit and be thoughtful about what I'm keeping and what I'm leaving out, which is the hardest part. But I think the muse for me is always things I don't fully understand. You know, aspects of my experience that are undigested are always the things that come to the fore in a song. I've realized too recently that I think sometimes I'm not even writing songs about my feelings. I think the feelings of others. And then when I say it's okay with others.

episodes.transcript: This is a CBC Podcast. I've been thinking about what it means to be 15 years old. When you're 15, you don't have the responsibility yet of a driver's license, and you don't need to have clear answers about who you want to be. You're still more kid than adult. But you can feel that starting to change. You can sense that you're at the beginning of having real agency. Where you're like, what am I good at? Where do I want to go? What do I want all of this to look like? To be 15 is to still be a child, but a child first grasping the raw, undiluted potential of life. It's the age Sheena Walker was in 1990, when she first disappeared from her mother, her siblings, her friends. Her mother got the call that they'd found her six years later.

episodes.title: Western Australia Country Hour

episodes.title: Western Australia Country Hour

engagement.takeaway: The immense scale of WA's agricultural and mining sectors, exemplified by Rawlina's shearing and critical fuel supply deals, drives significant regional economic activity.
bestQuotes: Narrator: 'Today the new owner of Australia's biggest sheep station, Rawlina, has completed its first shearing with 27,000 sheep through the shed, producing close to 700 bales of wool.'
Narrator: 'And Kimberley fuel supplier Cambridge Golf Limited, or CGL, has signed a long-term diesel supply deal with Boab Metals for its Sorby Hills silver and lead project.'
engagement.whyListen: In the vast, untamed heart of Western Australia, where fortunes are shorn from the land and deals are forged in the dust, this broadcast unearths the raw economic power fueling the region. This is the pulse of industry, stark and unyielding.

engagement.takeaway: Even after decades of isolation, human connection remains a powerful, overwhelming force, especially for those who've witnessed history's most intense moments.

This is the pulse of a world in flux, stripped bare.
